parole.significato: forms nouns denoting a rank or office

parole.significato: A cavity.

parole.significato: horn(s)

parole.significato: Forming abstract nouns denoting conditions, qualities, or states.

parole.significato: Forming nouns denoting patients or recipients of actions.

parole.significato: A process of becoming (growing or increasing in the trait specified by the prefixed stem).

parole.significato: Used to form nouns denoting condition, action, or process.

parole.significato: Used to indicate qualities or states.

parole.significato: Forms nouns related to flowers.

parole.significato: Having the shape or form of; looking like.

parole.testo: From Latin abāctiō.

parole.significato: A small tile of glass, marble, or other substance, of various colors, used in making ornamental patterns in mosaic pave…
parole.testo: From Latin abaculus, diminutive of abacus.

parole.significato: A table or tray scattered with sand which was used for calculating or drawing.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English abacus, abagus, agabus (“abacus; art of counting with an abacus”), from Latin abacus, abax (“sideboard or table with a slab at the top; slab at the top of a column; counting board, sand table; board for playing games”) (compare Late Latin abacus (“art of arithmetic”)), from

parole.significato: To make another's that which was once yours; to transfer the title of from one to another; to alienate.
parole.testo: From Latin abaliēnātus, perfect passive participle of abaliēnō (“alienate; remove”); from ab- (“by, from; away”) + aliēnō (“alienate, estrange”); from aliēnus (“foreign, alien”), from alius (“other, another”). Equivalent to ab- + alienate.

parole.significato: The act of abalienating; alienation; estrangement; transferring a legal title.
parole.testo: From Latin abalienatio. Equivalent to abalienate + -ion.

parole.significato: Away from the joints; not articular.
parole.testo: From ab- + articular, from Latin ab- (“away from”) + articulus (“joint”).

parole.significato: Father, an honorific title given to God in the New Testament, especially used in prayers.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Latin abba, from Ancient Greek ἀββα (abba), from Aramaic אבא/ܐܒܐ (ʼabbāʼ, “father”).

parole.significato: Father; religious superior; in the Syriac, Coptic, and Ethiopic churches, a title given to the bishops, and by the bish…
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Latin, from Ancient Greek, from Aramaic אבא/ܐܒܐ (ʼaḇā, “father”); see abbot, Abraham for more.

parole.significato: The superior or head of an abbey or monastery.
parole.testo: From Middle English abbot, abbod, abbed, from Old English abbat, abbad, abbod, from Latin abbās (“father”), from Ancient Greek ἀββᾶς (abbâs), from Aramaic אבא (’abbā, “father”). Doublet of abba, abbé, and bwana.

parole.significato: An inhabitant or native of Abdera, in Thrace.
parole.testo: From Latin Abderita, Abderites, from Ancient Greek Ἀβδηρίτης (Abdērítēs).

parole.significato: To disclaim and expel from the family, as a father his child; to disown; to disinherit.
parole.testo: First attested in 1532; borrowed from Latin abdicātus (“renounced”), perfect passive participle of abdicō (“to renounce, reject, disclaim”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), formed from ab (“away”) + dicō (“proclaim, dedicate, declare”), akin to dīcō (“to say”). Compare Middle English abdicat (“fors

parole.significato: The act of disowning or disinheriting a child.
parole.testo: First attested in 1552. From Latin abdicātiō (“renunciation”), from abdicō. By surface analysis, abdicate + -ion.

parole.significato: A reasoning from the negative
parole.testo: From Latin abdicativus.

parole.significato: Having the quality of hiding
parole.testo: From Latin abditīvus (“removed or separated from”), from abdō (“hide, conceal”).

parole.significato: A group of cirriped crustaceans having abdominal appendages.
parole.testo: From Latin.

parole.significato: Removal of the uterus via an incision made in the abdominal wall rather than via the vagina.
parole.testo: From Latin abdomino- + hysterectomy.

parole.significato: the cremaster muscle.
parole.testo: From Latin abdomen (“abdomen”) + New Latin scrotalis, from Latin scrotum; abdomino- + -scrotal.

parole.significato: Relating to the abdomen and the vagina
parole.testo: * From Latin abdomen (“abdomen”) + New Latin vaginalis, from Latin vagina (“scabbard, sheath”) * abdomino- + -vaginal

parole.significato: To draw; to conduct away; to take away; to withdraw; to draw to a different part; to move a limb out away from the cent…
parole.testo: (1530's) From Latin abdūcō (“lead away”), formed from ab (“from, away from”) + dūcō (“lead”). * See duke, and compare abduct.

parole.significato: Rectus lateralis muscle of the eye; muscle that moves the eye away from the center of the face.
parole.testo: Shortening of "abducens nerve", in turn from Latin nervus abducens, from abducent, abducens

parole.significato: Musculus rectus lateralis bulbi.
parole.testo: From Latin abducō (“drawing away”) + Latin oculus (“eye”).

parole.significato: Drawing away from the median axis of the body, as a muscle; see etymology abducting.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin abducō (“to lead away”).

parole.significato: To take away by force; to carry away (a human being) wrongfully and usually with violence or deception; to kidnap.
parole.testo: From Latin abductus, perfect passive participle of abduco (“to lead away”), from ab (“away”) + duco (“to lead”). * (physiology): Back-formation from abduction.

parole.significato: A leading away; a carrying away.
parole.testo: From Latin abductiō(n) (“a robbing; an abduction”), from abdūcō (“to take or lead away”), from ab (“away”) + dūcō (“to lead”). By surface analysis, abduct + -ion or abduce + -tion. * (physiology): From French, from Latin abductus. * Compare French abduction.

parole.significato: One who abducts; a kidnapper.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin abductor, By surface analysis, abduct + -or.

parole.significato: A muscle that draws the eye outwards
parole.testo: From Latin.

parole.significato: A book used to teach the alphabet; alphabet book; primer.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin abecedārium. Doublet of abecedary.

parole.significato: An acrostic poem in which the lines begin with the letters of the alphabet in sequence.
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin abecedārius, from Late Latin. Doublet of abecedary.

parole.significato: Relating to organs outside of the intestine.
parole.testo: From Latin ab- (“away from”) + Ancient Greek ἔντερον (énteron, “intestine”) + -ic.

parole.significato: To go astray; to err.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aberrō, from ab- (“from, away from”) + errō (“wander, stray”).

parole.significato: State of being aberrant; a wandering from the right way; deviation from truth, rectitude.
parole.testo: From aberr (“to stray”), from Latin aberrō (“to wander from the way”) + -ance.

parole.significato: Differing from the norm.
parole.testo: From Latin aberrāns, present active participle of aberrō (“go astray; err”), from ab (“from”) + errō (“to wander”). See aberr.

parole.significato: To go astray; to diverge; to deviate (from); deviate from.
parole.testo: From Latin aberrātus, perfect passive participle of aberrō (“wander, stray or deviate from”), formed from ab (“from, away from”) + errō (“stray”).

parole.significato: The secretion of milk from an abnormal location, not from the mammary glands.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aberratio (“aberration”) + lactis (“milk”).

parole.significato: A testis that is descending to a wrong position after born, or not descending at all (cryptorchidism).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aberratio (“aberration”) + testis (“of a testis”), genitive of testis.

parole.significato: The act of wandering; deviation from truth, moral rectitude; abnormal; divergence from the straight, correct, proper, n…
parole.testo: A learned borrowing from Latin aberrātiō(n) (“relief, diversion”), first attested in 1594, from aberrō (“wander away, go astray”), from ab (“away”) + errō (“wander”). Compare French aberration. By surface analysis, aberrat(e) + -ion.

parole.significato: Of, or relating to the grammatical case used in some languages to indicate absence.
parole.testo: From Latin abesse (“to be absent”), infinitive of absum, from ab- (“away”) + sum (“be”, verb). Compare English absent.

parole.significato: An abnormal evacuation.
parole.testo: From Latin ab (“from”) + evacuare (“evacuation”).

parole.significato: Inhuman; obsolete form of abominable.
parole.testo: From Latin abhominalis, from ab (“away from”) + hominis (“man”), but in practice from English abominable, which was erroneously folk-etymologized as this word, leading to this spelling and abhominable, which see for more.

parole.significato: Inconsistent with, or far removed from, something; strongly opposed.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin abhorrēns, abhorrēntis, present active participle of abhorreō (“abhor”). Equivalent to abhor + -ent.

parole.significato: Characterized by avoidance or withdrawal.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin abiens present participle of abeō (“to go away”), from ab (“from, away”) + eō (“to go”).

parole.significato: A volatile oil distilled from the resin or balsam of the nut pine (Pinus sabiniana).
parole.testo: From Abies, from Latin abiet- + -ene, oblique stem of abiēs (“silver fir”).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or derived from fir trees
parole.testo: From Abies, from Latin abiet- + -ic, oblique stem of abiēs (“silver fir”).

parole.significato: A yellowish resin acid isolated from rosin and used in varnishes and esters for plasticizers; C₁₉H₂₉COOH.
parole.testo: From Latin abiet, abies (“silver fir”) + English -ic (“having the character of”), + acid.

parole.significato: A substance resembling mannite, found in the needles of the common silver fir of Europe (Abies alba).
parole.testo: From Abies, from Latin abiet- + -ite, oblique stem of abiēs (“silver fir”).

parole.significato: Theft of cattle by driving it away with the intention of feloniously appropriating it.
parole.testo: From Latin abigeatus, from the verb ab agō (“to drive”).

parole.significato: A thief who steals livestock in large quantities.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin abigeus.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Abila
parole.testo: From Latin Abilēnus, from Ancient Greek Ἀβιληνός (Abilēnós). By surface analysis, Abila + -ene.

parole.significato: Tending to make abject.
parole.testo: From abject + -ive. From Middle English abjecten, from the adjective abject, of Latin origin.

parole.significato: abjection; forlornness
parole.testo: From Latin abiectura.

parole.significato: To confiscate by judicial decision.
parole.testo: * ab- + judge, from Latin abiudicare. Doublet of abjudicate.

parole.significato: To reject by judicial sentence.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin abiūdicātus, perfect passive participle of abiūdicō (“deprive or take away by judicial sentence”), from ab (“from, away from”) + iūdicō (“pass judgement; determine, conclude”). Doublet of abjudge. See judge.

parole.significato: Rejection or confiscation by judicial sentence.
parole.testo: From abjudicate + -ion or from Latin abiūdicātiō. First attested in 1623.

parole.significato: To unyoke; set free; uncouple.
parole.testo: From Latin abiugātus, perfect passive participle of abiugō (“remove, separate from”); from ab- (“away from”) + iugō (“bind, connect”).

parole.significato: Exceptional, isolated, disconnected, separate,
parole.testo: From Latin abiūnctus, past participle of abiungō (“remove, separate”); from ab (“of, from, by”) + iungō (“join, connect, attach”).

parole.significato: A solemn recantation or renunciation on oath; as, an abjuration of heresy.
parole.testo: First attested around 1439. From Middle English abjuracioun, from Latin abiūrātiō (“forswearing, abjuration”), from ab (“from, away from”) + iūrō (“swear or take an oath”), from iūs (“law, right, duty”). Compare French abjuration.

parole.significato: To wean.
parole.testo: From Latin ablactātus, perfect passive participle of ablactō (“wean”), from ab + lactō (“suckle”), from lac (“milk”).

parole.significato: To lay bare, as the roots of a tree, by loosening or removing soil.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ablaqueātus (“loosened, dug up”), past participle of ablaqueō (“to disentangle”), formed from ab- + laqueō (“noose”).

parole.significato: The act or process of laying bare the roots of trees to expose them to the air and water.
parole.testo: From Latin ablaqueātiō (“the process or act of digging or loosening the soil around the roots of a tree”), from ablaqueō (“disentangle”), from ab (“from, away from”) + laqueō (“entangle, ensnare”).

parole.significato: To remove or decrease something by cutting, erosion, melting, evaporation, or vaporization.
parole.testo: From Middle English ablat (“taken away”), from Latin ablātus, past participle of auferō (“to remove”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). First attested in the 1500s, it became obsolete by the early 1600s. Returned into use as a back-formation from ablation.

parole.significato: Synonym of ablation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ablātiō (“carrying away”). Doublet of ablation.

parole.significato: Synonym of placental abruption.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ablatio (“carrying away”) + placentae (“flat cake”).

parole.significato: Detachment of the retina.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ablatio (“carrying away”) + Middle English rethina, from Medieval Latin retina, from Latin rete (“net”).

parole.significato: A construction in Latin and other sister languages in which an independent phrase with a noun in the ablative case has…
parole.testo: Calque of Latin ablativus absolutus.

parole.significato: Expulsion; banishment.
parole.testo: From Latin ablēgātio (“a sending away, banishment”).

parole.significato: To tie up, especially a body part.
parole.testo: From Latin ab- + ligātus, perfect passive participle of ligāre (“to tie”).

parole.significato: To be unlike; to differ.
parole.testo: From Latin ablūdō (“differ from”), from ab (“from”) + lūdō (“play; trick”).

parole.significato: Washing away; carrying off impurities; detergent.
parole.testo: From Latin abluēns, present active participle of abluō (“to wash off or away; cleanse, purify”), from ab (“from, away from”) + lavō (“to wash, cleanse”). See lave.

parole.significato: A person who fears bathing.
parole.testo: From Latin ablutio (“a washing”) + Ancient Greek φόβος (phóbos, “fear”).

parole.significato: A pathological fear of washing or bathing.
parole.testo: From Latin ablutio (“a washing”) + Ancient Greek φόβος (phóbos, “fear”) (equivalent to -phobia).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to or suffering from ablutophobia.
parole.testo: From Latin ablutio (“a washing”) + Ancient Greek φόβος (phóbos, “fear”).

parole.significato: To deny (oneself something); to renounce or give up (a right, a power, a claim, a privilege, a convenience).
parole.testo: First attested in 1657. * Perhaps from Latin abnegō (“to refuse, reject”) from ab (“away from”) + negō (“to deny”), * Alternatively, perhaps a back-formation from abnegation.

parole.significato: A denial; a renunciation; denial of desire or self-interest.
parole.testo: First attested before 1398. From Middle English abnegacioun, borrowed from Latin abnegātiō, from abnegō (“refuse, deny”), from ab (“off”) + negō (“deny; refuse, say no”). Compare French abnégation.

parole.significato: Denying; renouncing; negative
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin abnegativus.

parole.significato: Abnormal; irregular; misshapen.
parole.testo: From Latin abnormis, from ab- + norma (“rule”), + -ous. For more, see normal.

parole.significato: A cloak made of a piece of cloth folded double, worn by Ancient Greeks and Romans draped over one shoulder and fastened…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin abolla.

parole.significato: Bdelygmia.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin abōminātiō. Doublet of abomination.

parole.significato: One who abominates.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin abōminātor. By surface analysis, abominate + -or.

parole.significato: Abominable, detestable, execrable.
parole.testo: From Latin abominosus.

parole.significato: Away from the oral opening or mouth (compare with ventral)
parole.testo: From ab- (“away from”) + orad (“toward the mouth”), from Latin ōris (“mouth”).

parole.significato: The original people of a location; originally used of ancient Greek and Roman peoples.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin aborīginēs.

parole.significato: An early termination of a mission, action, or procedure in relation to missiles or spacecraft; the craft making such a…
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Latin abortus, perfect active participle of aborior (“miscarry”), formed from ab + orior (“to come into being”). Doublet of abortus.

parole.significato: To miscarry; to bring forth (non-living) offspring prematurely.
parole.testo: From Latin abortare, from abortus, from aboriri (“miscarry”), from ab- (“not”) + oriri (“come into being, arise, appear”).

parole.significato: Producing miscarriage.
parole.testo: First attested in 1875. abort + -facient (“causing an”), from Latin facere (“to make”).

parole.significato: The expulsion from the womb of a foetus or embryo before it is fully developed, with loss of the foetus.
parole.testo: From Latin abortiōnem (“miscarriage, abortion”), from aborior (“to miscarry”). Equivalent to abort + -ion. Displaced native Old English ǣwyrp (literally “throwing out, rejection”).

parole.significato: To rub or wear off; erode.
parole.testo: From Latin abrādō (“scrape off”), from ab (“from, away from”) + rādō (“scrape”). First attested in 1677.

parole.significato: A shop selling cheap and low-quality clothes, especially in the East End of London.
parole.testo: From Middle English Abraham, from Old English Abraham, from Late Latin Ābrahām, from Ancient Greek Ἀβρᾱᾱ́μ (Abrāā́m), from Hebrew אַבְרָהָם ('aḇrāhām, “Abraham”). Thomas L. Thompson suggests that the meaning of the name in Genesis was forgotten due to its age and that its original meaning was "Fathe

parole.significato: Synonym of Abraham man
parole.testo: From Latin Abram, from Koine Greek Ἀβράμ (Abrám), from Hebrew אַבְרָם (ʾaḇrām), from אָב (áb, “father”) + רָם (rám, “high, exalted”). Doublet of Abramo and Avram. As an American placename, particularly named for local resident Abram Dillard, a Texas ranger.

parole.significato: abradable
parole.testo: From Latin abrāsibilis, from abrādō.

parole.significato: Rubbed smooth or blank.
parole.testo: From Latin abrāsus, perfect passive participle of abrādō (“abrade”), from ab (“from, away from”) + rādō (“scrape”).

parole.significato: A snatching away.
parole.testo: From Latin abreptus, perfect passive participle of abripiō (“snatch away”); from ab (“away”) + rapiō (“snatch”).

parole.significato: capable of being abrogated.
parole.testo: From Latin abrogō. Equivalent to abrogate + -able.

parole.significato: To annul (as a law, decree, ordinance, etc.) by an authoritative act; to abolish by the authority of the maker or their…
parole.testo: First attested in 1526, from Middle English abrogat (“abolished”), from Latin abrogātus, perfect passive participle of abrogō (“repeal”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), formed from ab (“away”) + rogō (“ask, inquire, propose”). See rogation.

parole.significato: Broken away (from restraint).
parole.testo: First attested in 1583. Borrowed from Latin abruptus (“broken off”), perfect passive participle of abrumpō (“break off”), formed from ab (“from, away from”) + rumpō (“to break”).

parole.significato: An abrupt pause or stop; an abruption.
parole.testo: From Latin abruptiō.

parole.significato: A sudden termination or interruption.
parole.testo: From abrupt + -ion. From Latin abruptio, from abrumpo (“to break off”).

parole.significato: A cavity caused by tissue destruction, usually because of infection, filled with pus and surrounded by inflamed tissue.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin abscessus (“a going away; gathering of humors, abscess”), from abscēdō (“go away, depart”), from abs (“away from”) + cēdō (“go”). See cede.

parole.significato: A separating; a removal; a going away.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin abscessio (“a separation”); from abscedere. See abscess.

parole.significato: To cut off.
parole.testo: From Latin abscindere (“cut off”), from ab (“from, away from”) + scindō (“cut, rend”).

parole.significato: To cut off.
parole.testo: From Latin abscīsus, perfect passive participle of abscīdō (“cut off”); formed from abs- + caedō (“cut”).

parole.significato: A cutting away.
parole.testo: From Latin abscisiō.

parole.significato: The first of the two terms by which a point is referred to, in a system of fixed rectilinear coordinate (Cartesian coor…
parole.testo: By ellipsis from Latin [linea] abscissa, feminine of abscissus, perfect passive participle of abscindō (“cut off”). See abscind.

parole.significato: A logical process of elimination by eliminating successively all of the inapplicable cases.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin abscissio infiniti (“abscission of that which is infinite”).

parole.significato: The act or process of cutting off.
parole.testo: From Latin abscissiō, from abscindō (“to cut, to tear”).

parole.significato: Cavity; fossa.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin absconsiō (“shelter”).

parole.significato: Denoting the effect that irradiation of a tissue has on remote nonirradiated tissue.
parole.testo: From Latin ab (“away from”) and Ancient Greek σκοπός (skopós, “target, aim”). Term first described by Dr. R. J. Mole in 1953 in the British Journal of Radiology, "Whole body irradiation- radiobiology or medicine?" . Br. J. Radiol., 26: 234-241, 1953.

parole.significato: absence
parole.testo: From Latin absentia (“being away, absence”), from absēns (“absent”), present active participle of absum (“to be away or absent”); compare absent.

parole.significato: A momentary lapse of consciousness; a minor epileptic seizure.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin absentia (“absence”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to absence or to that which is absent.
parole.testo: In form apparently from rare Latin absentiālis; as if from absence + -ial with the ending changed as in other pairs like essence, essential.

parole.significato: To impregnate with wormwood.
parole.testo: Latin absinthium: compare absinthiatus.

parole.significato: The principal compound found in wormwood (Artemisia absinthium), having a bitter taste: C₁₅H₂₀O₄
parole.testo: From Latin absinthium + -in.

parole.significato: Common wormwood (Artemisia absinthium), an intensely bitter herb used in the production of absinthe and vermouth, and a…
parole.testo: From Middle English absinthium, from Latin absinthium, from Ancient Greek ἀψίνθιον (apsínthion). Doublet of absinthe.

parole.significato: To stand apart from; to leave off; to desist.
parole.testo: Latin absistere (“desist”); from ab (“from, away from”) + sistō (“stand”).

parole.significato: Formal permission to be away from a college for the greater part of the day or more.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin absit (“let (him or her) be absent”), the third-person singular present active subjunctive of absum (“be absent”).

parole.significato: Literally, "may envy be lacking (from my words)".
parole.testo: From Latin. As found, for example, in Livy, Ab Urbe Condita Book IX, Chapter 19, line 15.

parole.significato: May what is said not come true.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin absit omen (“may what is said not come true”, literally “may omen be absent”).

parole.significato: In Semitic languages, the condition of a noun not being grammatically linked to another noun – where it would use the c…
parole.testo: Calque of Latin status absolūtus.

parole.significato: Serving to absolve; absolving; giving absolution.
parole.testo: From Latin absolūtōrius, from absolvō (“absolve”).

parole.significato: To set free, release or discharge (from obligations, debts, responsibility etc.).
parole.testo: First attested in the early 15th century. From Middle English absolven, from Latin absolvere (“set free, acquit”), from ab (“away from”) + solvō (“loosen, free, release”). Doublet of assoil.

parole.significato: Absolving.
parole.testo: An adaptation of the Latin absolvēns (“absolving”, stem: absolvent-), from absolvō (“to absolve”).

parole.significato: A decision or decree made by a court in favour of the defendant in a given action; dismissal.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin absolvitor (literally “let him be acquitted”), the third-person singular future passive imperative form of absolvō (“to absolve, acquit, or declare innocent”). Compare absolutory.

parole.significato: Discordant; harsh; contrary; unreasonable.
parole.testo: From ab- + sonant, from Latin sonans (“sound”).

parole.significato: Discordant; inharmonious; incongruous.
parole.testo: From Latin absonus, from ab- (“away”) + sonus (“sound”).

parole.significato: Having the ability or tendency to absorb; able to soak up liquid easily; absorptive.
parole.testo: From Latin absorbēns, present active participle of absorbeō (“absorb”). By surface analysis, absorb + -ent.

parole.significato: absorbed
parole.testo: From Latin absorptus, perfect passive participle of absorbeō (“absorb”).

parole.significato: The act or process of absorbing or of being absorbed as,
parole.testo: First attested in 1597. From Latin absorptiō (“a sucking in”), from absorbeō (“absorb”). Morphologically absorb + -tion.

parole.significato: Without doubt; used in pleadings where a statement needs no proof.
parole.testo: From Latin absque (“without”) + dubiō (“doubt”).

parole.significato: The technical words of denial used in denying what has been alleged.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin absque hoc (literally “without this”).

parole.significato: Refraining from freely consuming food or strong drink; sparing in diet; abstinent, temperate.
parole.testo: From Latin abstēmius (“abstaining from wine”); from ab, abs (“from”) + tēmus, a root of tēmētum (“intoxicating drink, especially strong mead or wine”) (possibly from Proto-Indo-European *temH- (“dark (referring to the colour of wine)”)) + -ous.

parole.significato: To absterge; to cleanse; to purge away.
parole.testo: From Middle English absterse, from Latin abstersus, perfect passive participle of abstergeō (“wipe off, wipe away”); formed from abs- + tergeō (“wipe”).

parole.significato: To wrest by force or persuasion.
parole.testo: From Latin abs- + tortus, past participle of torqueō (“I twist”).

parole.significato: An abridgement or summary of a longer publication.

parole.significato: Something which is abstract or exists abstractly.

parole.significato: To unbind; to loosen.

parole.significato: An illogical conclusion or state.

parole.significato: Caution used to justify preemptive measures that are likely not strictly necessary.

parole.significato: Used to introduce the statement of the real cause of action, in those cases where it was necessary to allege a fictitio…

parole.significato: A shrub or tree of the tribe Acacieae.

parole.significato: A member of the former Acalephae group, now a part of the Cnidaria phylum.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin acalephe, from Ancient Greek ἀκαλήφη (akalḗphē, “stinging nettle”).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or resembling, the plant acanthus, or its leaves.
parole.testo: From Latin acanthinus, from acanthus + English -ine (“relating to”).

parole.testo: From Latin acanthopodius. This is the only English word in -podious in the English Wiktionary, as of December 2024.

parole.testo: From Latin acanthus, from Ancient Greek ἄκανθος (ákanthos, “thorn”), from ἀκή (akḗ, “point”) + ἄνθος (ánthos, “flower”).

parole.significato: Incapable of being comprehended; incomprehensible; inconceivable.

parole.significato: To agree or assent [with to ‘a proposal, a request’]; to give way.

parole.significato: Acedia.

parole.significato: A nerve that speeds up the heartbeat by emitting noradrenaline.
parole.testo: From Latin accelerāns (“quickening”).

parole.significato: To cause to move faster; to quicken the motion of; to add to the speed of.

parole.significato: The act of accelerating, or the state of being accelerated; increase of motion or action; as opposed to retardation or…

parole.significato: acceleration

parole.significato: To set on fire; to kindle.

parole.significato: Any bird of the Eurasian genus Prunella, such as the dunnock.

parole.significato: The quality of being acceptable; acceptableness.

parole.significato: One who accepts.

parole.significato: A coming to; the act of acceding and becoming joined.

parole.significato: An honorable mention in an academic contest.

parole.significato: Something that belongs to part of another main thing; something additional and subordinate, an attachment.
parole.testo: From Middle English accessorie, from Medieval Latin accessōrius, from Latin accessor (“helper, subordinate”), from accessus. Compare access, from same root.

parole.significato: In electing a pope, a method by which cardinals could change their most recent vote to accede to another candidate in a…

parole.significato: The inflection of words.

parole.significato: Someone who, or something which, accepts (willingly receives).

parole.significato: Any hawk of the genus Accipiter.

parole.significato: The feigning of disinterest in something while actually desiring it.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin accismus, from Ancient Greek ακκισμός (akkismós, “prudery”).

parole.significato: To shout; to call out.
parole.testo: * First attested in the early 14th century. * (to applaud): First attested in the 1630s. * Borrowed from Latin acclāmō (“raise a cry at; applaud”), formed from ad- + clāmō (“cry out, shout”).

parole.significato: A shout of approbation, favor, or assent; eager expression of approval; loud applause.

parole.significato: Synonym of acclivous (“sloping upwards”).

parole.significato: sloping upward; rising like a hillside.

parole.significato: A combining together.

parole.significato: To accrue.

parole.significato: Growing; increasing.

parole.significato: The act or posture of reclining on a couch, as practiced by the ancients at meals.

parole.significato: One who, or that which, accumulates.

parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin accūrātus, perfect passive participle of accūrō (“to take care of”), from ad- (“to, towards, at”) + cūrō (“care for”). First attested in 1610. Compare English cure.

parole.significato: Liable to be accused or censured; chargeable with a crime or breach; blamable
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin accūsābilis (“accusable”), corresponding to accuse + -able; compare French accusable.

parole.significato: Categoria.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the accusative case.

parole.significato: A fetus affected by acephaly.

parole.significato: Sourness and harshness; acerbity.

parole.significato: In Ancient Rome, a small box for holding incense.

parole.significato: A person who does not cut their hair.
parole.testo: From Latin acersecomes.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a heap.
parole.testo: From Latin acervalis, from acervus (“heap”).

parole.significato: Heaped, or growing in heaps, or closely compacted clusters.
parole.testo: From Latin acervātus, perfect passive participle of acervō (“heap or pile up”), from acervus (“heap”).

parole.significato: Departing from the normal syntax of a series to increase its effect.
parole.testo: From Latin acervātiō (“heaping up”), from acervō (“heap up”) + -ātiō. Doublet of acervation.

parole.significato: A heaping up; accumulation

parole.significato: A small cluster, as of fungi appearing on bark or leaves.

parole.significato: Turning sour; readily becoming tart or acid; slightly sour.

parole.significato: An ancient Roman measure, equivalent to about one eighth of a pint.

parole.significato: Furnished with fleshy cups for adhering to bodies, as cuttlefish, etc.

parole.significato: The bony cup of the hip bone which receives the head of the femur.

parole.significato: Used in salads or as salad
parole.testo: From Latin acētāria (“salad”, plural noun) + -ous, the former from acētum (“vinegar”), from aceō (“to be sour”).

parole.significato: To convert into acid or vinegar.

parole.significato: An instrument for estimating the amount of acetic acid in vinegar
parole.testo: From Latin acetum (“vinegar”) + -meter.

parole.significato: Containing a methyl group bonded to a carbonyl group (CH₃CO-); e.g., acetophenone
parole.testo: From Latin acētum (“vinegar”), because acetic acid is a constituent of vinegar.

parole.significato: Having a sour taste; sour; acid.

parole.significato: In botanical medicine, a vinegar extract of herbs.
parole.testo: Blend of Latin acētum (“vinegar”) and extract.

parole.significato: Vinegar, sometimes medicated.

parole.significato: The univalent radical CH₃CO- derived from acetic acid.
parole.testo: aceto- + -yl. From Latin acētum (“vinegar”) + Ancient Greek ὕλη (húlē, “substance”).

parole.significato: An inhabitant or resident of Achaea, especially a member of an ancient Hellenic tribe that inhabited the region of Acha…

parole.significato: Any dry indehiscent fruit.

parole.significato: A sulfide of bismuth, lead, and copper.

parole.significato: A needlelike spine or bristle, specially the seta of an annelid
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?]. Compare English acicula.

parole.significato: To make something (more) acidic or sour; to convert into an acid.
parole.testo: From acid + -ify, from Latin acidus (“sour, acid”); compare French acidifier.

parole.significato: An instrument for ascertaining the strength of acids.
parole.testo: From acid + -i- + -meter, from Latin acidus (“sour, acid”).

parole.significato: Both sour and sweet.

parole.significato: (of bacteria) growing in acidic medium, but preferring an alkaline medium
parole.testo: From Latin acidum (“acid”) + dūrō (“endure”).

parole.significato: The full attention of one's sight, hearing or other senses, as directed towards a particular object.

parole.significato: Meaningless activity engaged in just for show; deceptive nonsense.

parole.significato: The poisonous herb aconite; also, an extract from it.

parole.significato: An oral discourse.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Ceraunian Mountains.

parole.significato: Relating to the Adriatic Sea.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Adrianople (modern-day Edirne).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Hadriānopolītānus.

parole.significato: A kind of adoption in Ancient Rome.
parole.testo: From Latin adrogatio, arrogatio, from adrogare. See arrogate.

parole.significato: Frustration with the amount of time required to become truly familiar with someone.
parole.testo: Coined by American author and neologist John Koenig in 2013, creator of The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows, with reference to Latin andronitis, described by him as a "hallway connecting the front part of the house with a complex inner atrium" in Ancient Roman architecture. parole.significato: Derived or acquired from something extrinsic; not part of the real, inherent, or essential nature of a thing.
parole.testo: From Latin adscitus, from past participle of adscisco (“admit”).

parole.significato: A feudal serf or labourer who is attached to an estate and sold or transferred with it.
parole.testo: From Latin adscriptus, past participle of adscribere (“to enroll”). See ascribe.

parole.significato: Attached or annexed to the glebe or estate and transferable with it.
parole.testo: From Latin adscriptivus. See adscript.

parole.significato: To denote additionally.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin adsignificare (“to show”). By surface analysis, ad- + signify.

parole.significato: To improve something by augmentation or supplementation:
parole.testo: From Latin past participle stem astruct- (“erected”), from verb astruo, from ad (“towards”) + struo (“pile up, build”).

parole.significato: To flatter effusively.
parole.testo: A learned borrowing from Latin adūlor.

parole.significato: One who lavishes excessive praises or flattery; one who adulates.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin adūlātor.

parole.significato: Adulatory, flattering.
parole.testo: From Latin adūlātōrius.

parole.significato: Exhibiting adulation; overly flattering.
parole.testo: From Latin adulatorius.

parole.significato: An adulterer, especially a male one.
parole.testo: From Latin adulter.

parole.significato: To commit adultery.
parole.testo: From Latin adulterō.

parole.significato: Corrupted or made impure by being mixed with something else; adulterated.
parole.testo: From Latin adulterātus (“adulterate, adulterated, defiled, polluted, counterfeited”), perfect passive participle of adulterō (“to adulterate, defile, commit adultery (with), counterfeit”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from ad- (“to, in the direction of”) + alter (“other”) + -ō (verb-forming

parole.significato: To corrupt, to debase (someone or something).
parole.testo: From Latin adulterātus, see Etymology 1 and -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Spurious; due to adulteration.
parole.testo: From Latin adulterīnus.

parole.significato: Giving a faint shadow, slight resemblance, or foreboding. By extension, faint or slight.
parole.testo: An adaptation of adumbrant-, the oblique stem of the Latin adumbrāns, the present active participle of adumbrō (“to cast a shadow upon”).

parole.significato: To foreshadow vaguely.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin adumbrātus (“represented in outline”), from adumbrāre (“cast a shadow on”), from umbra (“shadow”).

parole.significato: The state of being in shadow or shade; (countable) a shadow.
parole.testo: From Latin adumbrātiō (“sketch; outline, silhouette; pretence, semblance”) + -ion (suffix indicating a condition or state). Adumbrātiō is derived from adumbrāre (present active infinitive of adumbrō (“to represent an object with light and shade, to shade; to represent in outline, to outline, silhoue

parole.significato: The act of uniting; union.
parole.testo: From Latin adūnātiō, from ad + ūnus (“one”).

parole.significato: Curved inward, hooked.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aduncus.

parole.significato: Crookedness, curvaceousness, hookedness.
parole.testo: From Latin aduncitās (“hookedness”), from aduncus + -itās. By surface analysis, adunc + -ity.

parole.significato: To burn, completely or slightly.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin adūrere.

parole.significato: The act of burning, or heating to dryness; the state of being thus heated or dried.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin adustiō.

parole.significato: The horizontal movement of a body of atmosphere (or other fluid) along with a concurrent transport of its temperature,…
parole.testo: From Latin advectio (“act of bringing”), from advectus (past participle of advehere (“to carry to”), from ad- + vehere (“to convey”)) + -io.

parole.significato: Brought to a place from somewhere else; imported, foreign.
parole.testo: From Latin advectīcius + -ous.

parole.significato: To accede or to come to; to be superadded to, to be added to something or become a part of it, though inessential.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin advenire (“to come to, arrive at”), from ad (“to”) + venire (“to come”). Compare convene, intervene, supervene.

parole.significato: Caused by outside forces; coming from without; external, additional.
parole.testo: From the present participle of Latin advenīre.

parole.significato: Arrival; onset; a time when something first comes or appears; the time when it is approaching.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin adventus (“arrival, approach”).

parole.significato: The outermost layer of epithelial tissue encasing a visceral organ.
parole.testo: From the Latin adventitius (“extraneous”).

parole.significato: Accidental.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin adventīvus, from adveniō (“to come (to)”) + -īvus (verbal-adjective suffix).

parole.significato: Of or relating to an adverb.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin adverbiālis. By surface analysis, adverb + -ial.

parole.significato: The evolution of a mimic to resemble its model more closely.
parole.testo: Coined by evolutionary biologists L. P. Brower and J. van Z. Brower in 1972 for the paper "Parallelism, convergence, divergence, and the new concept of advergence in the evolution of mimicry" on the pattern of convergence, substituting ad- for con- to emphasize the one-sidedness of the approach.
