parole.significato: Opposed; adverse.
parole.testo: From Latin adversus + -ant.

parole.significato: (treated as plural) A collection of miscellaneous notes, remarks, or fragments of writing, typically preserved in a not…
parole.testo: From Latin adversāri.

parole.significato: Expressing opposition or difference.
parole.testo: From Latin adversativus (“of conjunctions, expressing opposition”).

parole.significato: A tendency or wish to avoid someone or something.
parole.testo: From Latin adversiōnem, from adversiō.

parole.significato: Attentive.
parole.testo: Apparently a back-formation from inadvertent, or a learned borrowing from Latin advertent-, advertens, present participle of advertere, from the verb adverto (“to give or draw attention to”)

parole.significato: To draw towards evening.
parole.testo: From Latin ad- + vesper.

parole.significato: The approach of evening.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin advesperātiō. See advesperate.

parole.significato: Advocacy; the act of advocating or pleading.
parole.testo: From Latin advocātiō. Doublet of advowson

parole.significato: A female advocate, especially as a title of Mary, mother of Jesus.
parole.testo: From Latin advocātrīx, from advocāre (“advocate”) + -trīx (“-ess”, forming feminine agent nouns), from ad- (“to, toward, on behalf of”) + vocāre (“speak”). By surface analysis, advocate + -trix.

parole.significato: A medieval officeholder, particularly important in the Holy Roman Empire, who was delegated some of the powers and func…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin advocatus. Doublet of advocate and avocat.

parole.significato: To summon or call (to a higher tribunal).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin advocare, formed from ad + vocare (“to call”). Doublet of advocate, avouch, and avow.

parole.significato: A rolling toward something; goal orientation.
parole.testo: From Latin advolutum, past participle of advolvere (“to roll to”).

parole.significato: The innermost sanctum of a temple, in which oracles are announced.
parole.testo: From Latin adytum.

parole.significato: The innermost sanctuary or shrine in a temple, from where oracles were given.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin adytum, from Ancient Greek ἄδυτον (áduton, “innermost sanctuary; shrine”), inflected form of ἄδυτος (ádutos, “not to be entered”).

parole.significato: A painted framed niche giving the appearance of depth.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aedicula.

parole.significato: A small house or room.
parole.testo: From Latin aedicula (“small house”), diminutive of aedēs (“a house”) + -culus.

parole.significato: An elected official who was responsible for the maintenance of public buildings, regulation of festivals, supervision o…
parole.testo: From Latin aedīlis (“commissioner or magistrate”), from aedēs + -īlis.

parole.significato: The office of an elected official responsible for festivals and the maintenance of public buildings.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin aedīlitās, from Latin aedīlis (“commissioner or magistrate”), from aedēs + -īlis. By surface analysis, aedile + -ity.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Aegean Sea or the regions bordering it.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin aegaeus (from Ancient Greek Αἰγαῖος (Aigaîos, “Aegean”)) + English -an. The name might be connected to αἶγες (aîges, “waves”).

parole.significato: Absent and excused from one’s classes due to illness
parole.testo: From Latin aeger (“sick”).

parole.significato: An ulcer or fistula in the inner angle of the eye.
parole.testo: From Latin aegilōps, from Ancient Greek αἰγίλωψ (aigílōps, “haver-grass (Aegilops neglecta)”).

parole.significato: A goat-like creature resembling a satyr, sometimes portrayed as having a fish's tail.
parole.testo: From Latin Aegipān, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek Αἰγίπαν (Aigípan), from αἴξ (aíx, “goat”) + Πάν (Pán, “Pan”).

parole.significato: A mythological shield associated with the Greek deities Zeus and Athena (and their Roman counterparts Jupiter and Miner…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aegis, from Ancient Greek αἰγίς (aigís, “goatskin; shield of Athena”), probably from αἴξ (aíx, “goat”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eyǵ- (“goat”). The plural form aegides (/ˈiːd͡ʒɪdiːz/) is borrowed from Latin aegides, from Ancient Greek αἰγῐ́δες (aigĭ́des).

parole.significato: A certificate indicating that a student is ill, excusing attendance at lectures and examinations and allowing courses t…
parole.testo: UK 19th century. Latin aegrotat, literally “he/she is ill”, third-person singular present active indicative form of aegrōtō.

parole.significato: Bronze-colored.
parole.testo: From Latin aēneus (“made of copper or bronze”).

parole.significato: Of the Anatolian region Aeolis, Aeolia.
parole.testo: From Latin aeolicus, from Ancient Greek Αἰολικός (Aiolikós, “like the Aeolians”).

parole.significato: Commonwealth standard spelling of eon.
parole.testo: From Latin aeon, from Ancient Greek αἰών (aiṓn, “age, era”).

parole.significato: The case conveying an equality with another noun, equivalent to “like” or “as” in English. This case is used in some la…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin aequālis (“equal”). Doublet of equal and egal.

parole.significato: Of or relating to that ancient people who resided in Italy.
parole.testo: From Latin Aequi + -ian.

parole.significato: marine; oceanic
parole.testo: From Latin aequoreus + -al.

parole.significato: The state treasury of Ancient Rome.
parole.testo: From Latin aerārium.

parole.significato: A spongy, airy tissue found especially in the roots of aquatic plants.
parole.testo: From Latin āēr (“air”) + -enchyma.

parole.significato: Resembling or consisting of air.
parole.testo: From Latin aer + -ous.

parole.significato: Of, or like copper or brass; brassy.
parole.testo: From Latin aerōsus (“full of copper”), from aes (“copper, brass”) + -ōsus.

parole.significato: Metallic rust, particularly of brass or copper; verdigris; patina.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aerūgō, from aes (“copper, bronze, brass”).

parole.significato: Aerial; ethereal; incorporeal; visionary.
parole.testo: From Middle English aery, from Latin āerius.

parole.significato: Related to or concerning the Greek fabulist Aesop.
parole.testo: From Latin Aesopius (“Aesopian”), from Ancient Greek Αἴσωπος (Aísōpos, “the famous Greek fabulist Aesop”).

parole.significato: As the tide, turbulent; ebbing and flowing.
parole.testo: From Latin aestus (“heat, tide”) + -ferous (“bearing, bringing”).

parole.significato: A state of inactivity and metabolic depression during summer: the summer version of hibernation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aestīvātiō, from Latin aestīvō, aestīvāre (“to spend or pass the summer in a place”), from aestīvus (“of or pertaining to summer”), from aestās (“summer”) + -īvus.

parole.significato: Of or relating to summer.
parole.testo: From Latin aestīvus (“related to summer”), from aestas (“summer”).

parole.significato: Relating to or happening in summer and autumn.
parole.testo: From Latin aestīvus (“summer”) + autumnus (“autumn, fall”) + -al.

parole.significato: Full of passion; agitated.
parole.testo: From Latin aestuōsus (“excessively hot, having a high body temperature, tumult, rage, passion”).

parole.significato: Aged; at the age of.
parole.testo: Shortened from Latin aetatis, genitive of aetas (“age”).

parole.significato: Attributing a cause for a statement or claim made, often as a simple relative clause of explanation.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin aetiologia, from Ancient Greek αἰτιολογία (aitiología). Doublet of aetiology.

parole.significato: The establishment of a cause, origin, or reason for something.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aetiologia. By surface analysis, aetio- + -logy. Doublet of aetiologia.

parole.significato: Any assumption of an age-based norm and particularly the assumption that adults and adult experiences are normative whi…
parole.testo: Coined in 2009 by Maria Nikolajeva, from Latin aetas (“age”) + normativity.

parole.significato: Synonym of eternity (“existence without end”).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin aeviternus (“eternal, perpetual”) + English -ity (suffix forming nouns, especially abstract nouns), probably modelled after eternity. Aeviternus is derived from aevum (“infinite time; eternity, timelessness; undefined long period of time, age, era; generation, lifespan,

parole.significato: The temporal mode of existence between time and eternity, said to be experienced by angels, saints, and celestial bodie…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin aevum (“temporal mode of existence between time and eternity”). Doublet of aeviternity and aye.

parole.significato: Executed in a workmanlike manner; ingeniously made.
parole.testo: From Latin affaber (“workmanlike”), from ad + faber.

parole.significato: To influence or alter.
parole.testo: From Middle English affecten, from Latin affectāre, from Latin affectus, the participle stem of Latin afficere (“to act upon, influence, affect, attack with disease”), from ad- + facere (“to make, do”). By surface analysis, af- + Latin -fect.

parole.significato: A subjective feeling experienced in response to a thought or other stimulus; mood, emotion, especially as demonstrated…
parole.testo: From Middle English affect, from Latin affectus, adfectus (“a state of mind or body produced by some (external) influence, especially sympathy or love”), from afficere (“to act upon, influence”).

parole.significato: affected
parole.testo: From Latin affectātus, perfect passive participle of affectō (“strive after”).

parole.significato: Having affection or warm regard; loving; fond.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin affectiōnātus. By surface analysis, affection + -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Doublet of aficionado.

parole.significato: Pertaining to or consisting in disposition or desire.
parole.testo: From Latin affectus (“mental disposition, desire”).

parole.significato: passionate or affectionate.
parole.testo: From Latin affectuosus, from affectus. Compare affectueux. Doublet of affettuoso.

parole.significato: Carrying towards.
parole.testo: From Latin adferens (“bringing to”), present participle of adferre (“to bring to”), from ad (“to, toward”) + ferre (“to carry, bear”). By surface analysis, af- + -fer + -ent.

parole.significato: Any afferent vessels, whether blood or lymph vessels; specifically, the afferent arteries of the kidneys.
parole.testo: From Latin afferentia. Doublet of afference.

parole.significato: Assigning finite values to finite quantities.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin affinis, from ad + fīnis (“boundary”).

parole.significato: Someone who affirms or asserts.
parole.testo: From Latin affirmans, present participle of affirmo.

parole.significato: Making a statement as if it were in response to a question or were in dispute, especially when it is not.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin affirmātiō (“affirmation; confirmation”). Doublet of affirmation.

parole.significato: Something that is affirmed.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin affirmatum.

parole.significato: A bound morpheme added to a word’s stem, such as a prefix or suffix.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin affixus, perfect passive participle of affigere (from ad- + figere). By surface analysis, af- + fix.

parole.significato: To fill, especially with divine inspiration.
parole.testo: From Latin afflātus, perfect passive participle of afflō (“to blow or breathe on or towards”).

parole.significato: A blowing or breathing on.
parole.testo: From Latin afflatus, past participle of afflare (“to blow or breathe on”), from ad + flare (“to blow”).

parole.significato: A sudden rush of creative impulse or inspiration, often attributed to divine influence.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin afflātus (“breath, blowing or breathing on, spiritual inspiration”), from afflō (“to blow, breathe on or towards”) + -tus (forming action nouns), from ad- (“to, towards”) + flō (“breathe, blow”). See also af-.

parole.significato: To cause (someone) pain, suffering or distress.
parole.testo: From Middle English afflicten (attested in past participle afflicte), from Latin afflīctō (“to damage, harass, torment”), from ad- + flīctus, past participle of afflīgō (“strike, beat”), from ad- + flīgō (“strike”) (whence af-).

parole.significato: An upward rush of fluid.
parole.testo: From Latin affluĕre, affluxum. See affluent.

parole.significato: A single speech sound produced combining a plosive and a fricative.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin affricātus.

parole.significato: The act of rubbing against.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin affricare (“to rub on”). See friction.

parole.significato: To pour out or upon.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin affundō (“I pour, sprinkle, or scatter onto”, perfect passive participial stem: affūs-).

parole.significato: The pouring of liquid, especially as a hydrotherapy.
parole.testo: From Latin affusio, from Latin affundō (“to pour or sprinkle onto”), from Latin fundō (“to pour”), from Proto-Italic *hundō (“to pour out”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰewd- (“to pour”).

parole.significato: African.
parole.testo: Circa 1425; from Middle English Affrike, Affrique, Affryke, from Latin Āfricus. Compare early Old English Africe (attested only in one translation).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Africa.
parole.testo: Attested as a noun in early New English Aphricane, Africans (plural), Middle English as Affrican, Aufrican and Old English as Africanas (“Africans”) (only plural). From Latin āfricānae, from āfricānus, from Āfricus. The adjective appears in the 16th century, as Affricane, Africane, African. Latin Āf

parole.significato: Collectible objects, such as maps, documents and artifacts, peculiar to Africa, especially Southern Africa.
parole.testo: From Latin āfricāna, the neuter plural of āfricānus (“African”). By surface analysis, Africa + -ana (“things (plural)”), analogous to Americana. First attested in 1908.

parole.significato: African
parole.testo: Derived from Latin Āfrī, Āfer + -o-. Abstracted from Afro-American (attested 1902) and becoming generally popular from the 1960s.

parole.significato: Synonym of agalloch.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin agallochum, from Ancient Greek ἀγάλοχον (agálokhon).

parole.significato: Any of various fungi, principally of the order Agaricales, having fruiting bodies consisting of umbrella-like caps, on…
parole.testo: From Latin agaricum, from Ancient Greek ἀγαρικόν (agarikón, “a tree fungus (Phellinus pomaceus”)), from the country of Agaria, in Sarmatia.

parole.significato: A tribe of Sarmatia
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Agathyrsī, from Ancient Greek Ἀγάθυρσοι (Agáthursoi).

parole.significato: A temporally organized plan for matters to be attended to.
parole.testo: From Latin agenda (“things that ought to be done”), future passive participle (gerundive) of agō (“to do, act, make”).

parole.significato: A task which ought to be done; an item on an agenda.
parole.testo: From Latin agendum, substantive use of the neuter singular of agendus (“which ought to be done”), future passive participle (gerundive) of agō (“to do, act, make”).

parole.significato: One who exerts power, or has the power to act.
parole.testo: From Latin agēns, present active participle of agere (“to drive, lead, conduct, manage, perform, do”).

parole.significato: The public land of Ancient Rome, usually acquired by expropriation from enemies of Rome.
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: Thomist metaphysical and moral principle that indicates the connection of ontology, obligation, and ethics.
parole.testo: From Latin agere sequitur esse (“doing follows being”).

parole.significato: Positioned near, or on both sides of, the genital area.
parole.testo: From Latin aggenitalis.

parole.significato: A double tide, particularly a high tide in which the water rises to a given level, recedes, and then rises again (or on…
parole.testo: From Middle English agger (“heap, pile”), from Latin agger (“earthwork, rubble, rampart”), from ad- (“toward, towards”) + gerere (“to carry”).

parole.significato: A small ridge on the lateral side of the nasal cavity.
parole.testo: From Latin agger nāsī (“rampart of the nose”).

parole.significato: A piling up; accumulation.
parole.testo: From Latin aggeratio.

parole.significato: To heap up.
parole.testo: From Latin aggestus, past participle of aggerere. See agger.

parole.significato: collected into a ball, heap, or mass
parole.testo: From Latin agglomerātus, past participle of agglomerō (“to wind into a ball”), from ad- (“to”) + glomerō (“to wind into a ball”), from glomus (“a ball”), akin to globus (“a ball”).

parole.significato: The act or process of collecting in a mass; a heaping together.
parole.testo: From Latin agglomerātiō. By surface analysis, agglomerate + -ion.

parole.significato: United with glue or as with glue; cemented together.
parole.testo: From Latin agglūtinātus, past participle of agglūtināre, adglūtināre (“to glue or cement to a thing”), from ad (“to”) + glūtināre (“to glue”), from glūten (“paste, glue”).

parole.significato: To favour; to grace.
parole.testo: From Latin aggratiare, from ad (“to”) and gratia (“grace”).

parole.significato: aggravating
parole.testo: From Latin aggravātus, perfect passive participle of aggravō (“weigh down”) + -able.

parole.significato: To make (an offence) worse or more severe; to increase in offensiveness or heinousness.
parole.testo: The adjective is first attested in 1471 in Middle English, the verb in 1530; from Latin aggravātus, perfect passive participle of aggravō (“to add to the weight of, make worse, oppress, annoy”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from ad- (“to”) + gravō (“to make he

parole.significato: To bring together; to collect into a mass or sum.
parole.testo: From Middle English aggregaten (“to aggregate”), from its earlier borrowed past participle aggregat(e) + -en (verb-forming suffix), from Latin aggregātus, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more.

parole.significato: The act of collecting together, of aggregating.
parole.testo: From Latin aggregātiō, from aggregō (“aggregate”).

parole.significato: Aggression.
parole.testo: From Latin aggressum, past participle of aggredi (“to attack, assail, approach, go to”), from ad (“to”) + gradi (“to walk, go”), from gradus (“step”); see grade.

parole.significato: The person or country that first attacks or makes an aggression; that begins hostility or a quarrel; an assailant.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin aggressor (“attacker, assailant, aggressor”).

parole.significato: Possible to be done; practicable.
parole.testo: Compare Latin agibilis, from Latin agere to move, do. See agent.

parole.significato: Having the faculty of quick motion in the limbs; apt or ready to move; loose-jointed.
parole.testo: From earlier agil, borrowed from Latin agilis (“agile, nimble”), from agō (“do, act; move”). See agent.

parole.significato: A shop owner.
parole.testo: From Latin agina (“opening of the upper part of a balance”) + -tor.

parole.significato: To disturb or excite; to perturb or stir up (a person).
parole.testo: From Middle English agitat(e) (“set in motion”), borrowed from Latin agitātus, perfect passive participle of agitō (“to put in motion”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), frequentative of agō (“to drive, move, push”), see -tō. Cognate with French agiter. See also act and agent.

parole.significato: A woman who agitates; a female agitator.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin agitātrīx, feminine of agitātor. By surface analysis, agitate + -trix.

parole.significato: An asymmetric crescent that is a symbol of the Paralympic movement.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin agitō (“to chase”).

parole.significato: Very fast writing, normally with unintentional omission of words
parole.testo: From Latin agitō (“to put something in motion, drive, impel”) + -graphia.

parole.significato: agitophasia
parole.testo: From Latin agitō (“to put something in motion, drive, impel”) + -lalia.

parole.significato: A condition characterized by abnormally rapid speech in which words, sounds, or syllables are unconsciously omitted, sl…
parole.testo: From Latin agitō (“to put something in motion, drive, impel”) + -phasia.

parole.significato: Inability to swallow.
parole.testo: From a- (“not”) + Latin glutire (“to swallow”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to an army or a troop.
parole.testo: From oblique stem of Latin agmen, agminis + -al, ultimately from Latin agminālis, from agmen (“march, train”).

parole.significato: agminate
parole.testo: From agminate + -ed, from oblique stem of Latin agmen, agminis + -ate.

parole.significato: An appellation over and above the given name and surname.
parole.testo: From Latin agnōmen, with the second element replaced with name. By surface analysis, ag- + name.

parole.significato: A relative whose relation is traced only through male members of the family.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin agnātus (“paternal kinsman”).

parole.significato: consanguinity by a line of males only, as distinguished from cognation
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin agnatio. Compare French agnation.

parole.significato: Acknowledgement.
parole.testo: From Latin agnitio, from agnoscere. See notion.

parole.significato: To recognise; to acknowledge.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin agnōscō.

parole.significato: Of unknown etiology.
parole.testo: From a- + Latin gnōscō (“know”) + -genic.

parole.significato: An additional cognomen given, as an honour, to a Roman citizen.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin agnōmen. By surface analysis, ag- + nomen.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to an agnomen.
parole.testo: From Latin agnomen + -al.

parole.significato: A paronomasia, or allusion of one word to another
parole.testo: From Latin agnominatio.

parole.significato: Any of a family of viral proteins that play indirect roles in the biological processes and activities of viruses
parole.testo: From a- + Latin gnōscō (“know”) + protein, in reference to agnogene, the gene from which polyomavirus family of agnoprotein emerges.

parole.significato: A liturgical chant recited as part of the Mass, beginning with those words, or the music to which it is set.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Agnus Deī (“Lamb of God”).

parole.significato: A struggle or contest; conflict; especially between the protagonist and antagonist in a literary work.
parole.testo: From Latin agōn, from Ancient Greek ἀγών (agṓn, “contest”).

parole.significato: A halting of the growth of a colony of cells.
parole.testo: Coined by Thea D. Tlsty et al. in a 2001 paper. Explained as Latin agōn (“contest”) + -escence.

parole.significato: Of a cell: Undergoing agonescence.
parole.testo: From Latin agōn (“contest”) + -escent. See agonescence.

parole.significato: Competitive struggle (especially political).
parole.testo: From agon + -ism, from Latin agōn, from Ancient Greek ἀγών (agṓn, “contest”).

parole.significato: Someone involved in a contest or battle (as in an agon), protagonist.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin agōnista, from Ancient Greek ἀγωνιστής (agōnistḗs, “combatant, champion”). By surface analysis, agon or agony + -ist.

parole.significato: One who trained persons to compete in public games and contests.
parole.testo: From Latin agonistarcha, from Ancient Greek *ἀγωνιστάρχης (*agōnistárkhēs), from ἀγωνιστής (agōnistḗs, “contestant”) + ἀρχός (arkhós, “leader”).

parole.significato: The fear of wide open spaces, crowds, or uncontrolled social conditions.
parole.testo: From Latin agoraphobia, from Ancient Greek ἀγορά (agorá, “assembly”) + φοβία (phobía, “fear”). By surface analysis, agora + -phobia. Coined by Karl Friedrich Otto Westphal in 1871.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the fields; rural; rustic, unpolished
parole.testo: From Latin agrestis (“rustic, boorish, wild”) (from ager (“a field, a farm”)) + -ic

parole.significato: Agriculture.
parole.testo: Originally from Latin ager, agrī (“field”), reinforced by English agriculture, of the same etymology. Doublet of acre.

parole.significato: agriculture
parole.testo: From Latin agricolatio.

parole.significato: agriculturist, farmer
parole.testo: From Middle English agricultor, from Latin agricultor.

parole.significato: A land surveyor in Ancient Rome.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin agrimensor.

parole.significato: agriculture
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin ager.

parole.significato: To act for another (as a law agent or solicitor).
parole.testo: Probably from Latin age, imperative of Latin agere.

parole.significato: A wing or winglike anatomic process or part, especially of bone.
parole.testo: Originated 1730–40, borrowed from Latin āla (“wing”). Doublet of aisle.

parole.significato: bastard wing
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: The title of the governor or chief magistrate of the Jews in Alexandria under the Ptolemies and Roman emperors.
parole.testo: From Latin alabarches, more correctly arabarches, from Ancient Greek Ἀλαβάρχης (Alabárkhēs), more correctly Ἀραβάρχης (Arabárkhēs, “the prefect of the Arabian nome in Egypt, in Josephus appar. as in def.”), from Ἄραψ (Áraps) pl. Ἄρᾰβες (Árăbes, “Arabs”) + ἀρχός (arkhós, “leader”).

parole.significato: Lively and joyfully involved.
parole.testo: From Latin alacer.

parole.significato: Eagerness; liveliness; enthusiasm.
parole.testo: Mid-15th century; from Middle English alacrite, from Latin alacritās, from alacer (“brisk”) + -itās (“-ity”).

parole.significato: A member of a group of Sarmatian tribes, nomadic pastoralists of the 1st millennium AD who spoke an Eastern Iranian lan…
parole.testo: From Latin Alānī, from Ancient Greek Ἀλανοί (Alanoí), from Proto-Sarmatian *Āllān.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the armpit; axillary.
parole.testo: From Latin ala (“wing”) + -ar (adjectival suffix).

parole.significato: Pertaining to wings.
parole.testo: From Latin alarius, from ala (“wing”).

parole.significato: Having wings or winglike extensions or parts; winged.
parole.testo: From Latin ālātus, from āla (“wing”).

parole.significato: An ornamental evergreen shrub (Rhamnus alaternus; Italian buckthorn).
parole.testo: From Latin alaternus (“the shrub Rhamnus alaternus”), of unknown origin.

parole.significato: A white-flowered shrub rose of the hybrid Rosa × alba.
parole.testo: First attested in 1848; borrowed from Latin alba (the feminine form of albus (“white”)) in the now-disused species name of binomial nomenclature Rosa alba (it is now considered a hybrid and is accordingly called Rosa × alba).

parole.significato: Pertaining to the ancient Latin city of Alba Longa.
parole.testo: From Latin Albānus (“resident of Alba”) (a mountain region and an ancient city of Latium).

parole.significato: A form of lime, made by heating marble, used for stucco.
parole.testo: From Latin albārium (“white stucco”).

parole.significato: The hawthorn.
parole.testo: From Latin albus (“white”) + spine. Cognate with French aubépine.

parole.significato: A white alloy of copper, nickel and zinc, once used to make cheap cutlery etc
parole.testo: From Latin albata (“whitened”), the past participle of albāre (“to whiten”), from albus (“white”) + -āre (suffix forming verbs).

parole.significato: The fraction of incident light or radiation reflected by a surface or body, commonly expressed as a percentage.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin albēdō (“whiteness”).

parole.significato: The act of becoming white; whitening.
parole.testo: Mid 18th century. From Latin albescens, present participle of albescō. By surface analysis, Latin alb(us) + -escence.

parole.significato: Becoming white or whitish; moderately white.
parole.testo: 18th century. From Latin albescens, present participle of albescere (“to grow white”), from albus (“white”). By surface analysis, Latin alb(us) + -escent.

parole.significato: light in colour due to the absence of iron oxides
parole.testo: Latin albus (“white”) + -ic.

parole.significato: Growing or becoming white.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin albicāns (“whitening, becoming white”, oblique stem: albicant-), present participle of albicō (“to be white”).

parole.significato: The act or process of making white.
parole.testo: From Latin albus (“white”) + -fication.

parole.significato: A plagioclase feldspar, the first member of the Albite-Anorthite solid solution series.
parole.testo: From Latin albus (“white”), the common color of the mineral, + -ite.

parole.significato: white
parole.testo: From Latin albus (“white”).

parole.significato: Governance by white people, especially Europeans.
parole.testo: From Latin albus (“white”) + -cracy, equivalent to albo- + -cracy.

parole.significato: A kind of cement consisting mostly of magnesia and silica.
parole.testo: From Latin albus (“white”) + -lith.

parole.significato: White.
parole.testo: From Latin albus, + -ous.

parole.significato: A leucoma.
parole.testo: From Latin albūgō, from albus (“white”).

parole.significato: In Ancient Rome, a white tablet or register on which the praetor's edicts and other public notices were recorded.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin album (“blank white writing tablet”), from albus (“white”).

parole.significato: The dung of dogs or hyenas, turned white by exposure to air, formerly used in dressing leather and in medicine.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin, literally, “Greek white”.

parole.significato: An instrument, usually made of wood, for determining the quantity of albumen in a liquid, generally urine.
parole.testo: From Latin albumen, albuminis + -meter. Compare French albuminimètre.

parole.significato: Producing albumin.
parole.testo: From Latin albumen + parere (“to bear, bring forth”).

parole.significato: of albumin
parole.testo: From albumin (from Latin albumen (“egg white”) via French albumine) + -oid. Ultimately from Latin albus (“white”).

parole.significato: Relating to, containing, or having the properties of albumen or albumin.
parole.testo: From Latin albūminōsus, from albūmen + -ōsus. By surface analysis, albumin + -ous.

parole.significato: sapwood; the soft, newer wood in the trunk of a tree found between the bark and the hardened heartwood.
parole.testo: From Latin alburnum, from albus (“white”), since it is often paler in color than the heartwood.

parole.significato: Pertaining to Alcaeus, a Greek lyric poet of around 600 BC; especially, of a verse meter in a four-line stanza which he…
parole.testo: From Latin Alcaicus, from Ancient Greek Ἀλκαϊκός (Alkaïkós), from Ἀλκαῖος (Alkaîos, “Alcaeus”) + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic”). By surface analysis, Alcaeus + -ic.

parole.significato: An elk.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin alcē. Doublet of Alcis, Algiz, and elk.

parole.significato: Of or relating to a kingfisher or kingfishers.
parole.testo: From Latin alcedo + -ine.

parole.significato: Aleatoricism.
parole.testo: From Latin ālea + -ation.

parole.significato: Having an element of chance.
parole.testo: From Latin āleātōrius (see aleatory) + -ic.

parole.significato: Depending on the throw of a die; random, arising by chance.
parole.testo: From Latin āleātōrius, from āleātor (“dice-player”), from ālea (“a die”).

parole.significato: An anchovy or herring, especially pickled or dried.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin alec (“herring”).

parole.significato: The plant costmary (Tanacetum balsamita), formerly much used for flavoring ale.
parole.testo: From ale + Latin costus (“an aromatic plant”). Compare costmary.

parole.significato: A magical stone said to be found in the gizzard of cocks.
parole.testo: From Latin alectoria, formed from Ancient Greek ἀλέκτωρ (aléktōr, “cock”).

parole.significato: A form of divination in which the diviner observes a bird or birds (preferably a white rooster or cockerel) pecking at…
parole.testo: From Latin alectryomantia, from Ancient Greek ἀλεκτρυών (alektruṓn, “rooster”) + Latin -mantia.

parole.significato: A group of Germanic peoples living between the Rhine, Main, and Danube Rivers from the third to the sixth century.
parole.testo: From Latin Alemannī (“the confederation of German tribes related to Suebi who lived near the upper reaches of Danube”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Alemannic language or dialect group.
parole.testo: From Latin Alemannicus, from Latin Alemannī (“the confederation of German tribes related to Suebi who lived near the upper reaches of the Danube”), from Proto-Germanic *Alamanniz, corresponding to *allaz + *mann-.

parole.significato: The act of making something more refined or pure; distillation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin alembicatio, from Latin alembīcum.

parole.significato: The "salt of wisdom" of the alchemists, a double salt composed of the chlorides of ammonium and mercury, formerly used…
parole.testo: From post-classical Latin alembrottus, likely derived from an Arabic term; further etymology uncertain.

parole.significato: Something which protects against, or cures, a poison; an antidote.
parole.testo: From Latin alexipharmacum, from Ancient Greek ἀλεξιφάρμακον (alexiphármakon).

parole.significato: Of or relating to Alfonso X of Castile (1221–1284) or the Alfonsine tables, astronomical tables prepared under his patr…
parole.testo: Equivalent to Alfonso + -ine, by way of earlier Alphonsine from Latin Alphōnsīnus.

parole.significato: Any of many aquatic photosynthetic organisms, including the seaweeds, whose size ranges from a single cell to giant kel…
parole.testo: From Latin alga.

parole.significato: Making cool; cooling.
parole.testo: From Latin algeō (“become cold”) + faciēns (“making”), present active participle of faciō (“make”).

parole.significato: Cold, chilly; used of low body temperature, especially in connection with certain diseases such as malaria and cholera.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin algidus (“cold”).

parole.significato: Very cold; covered in ice or cold air.
parole.testo: From Latin algificus, from algus (“cold”) + facere (“to make”).

parole.significato: alga
parole.testo: Combining form of Latin alga.

parole.significato: The branch of botany dealing with algae.
parole.testo: From Latin alga + -logy.

parole.significato: Cold, chilliness.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin algor.

parole.significato: The reduction in body temperature following death.
parole.testo: From Latin algor (“cold, coldness”) + mortis (“of death”, genitive singular of mors), literally, “the cold of death”.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the algae, or seaweeds; algal.
parole.testo: From Latin algosus, from alga (“seaweed”).

parole.significato: lateral expansion
parole.testo: Representing the Latin āla (“wing”).

parole.significato: Otherwise; at another time; in other circumstances; otherwise called; also known as; formerly known as.
parole.testo: From Latin alias (“at another time; at another place, elsewhere, under other circumstances, otherwise”). See else and alien.

parole.significato: The plea or mode of defense under which a person on trial for a crime proves or attempts to prove being in another plac…
parole.testo: From the 18th century, from Latin alibī (“elsewhere, at another place”, adverb). Probably after French alibi, which has this use since the late 14th century.

parole.significato: Nourishing.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin alibilis, from alō (“feed, nourish”) + -ibilis (“-ible”). First attested in c. 1650.

parole.significato: Negating, denying, modifying, or casting doubt on the applicability of its modificand.
parole.testo: From Latin aliēnāns, present active participle of aliēnō (“make something another's”), from aliēnus (“another's, foreign”).

parole.significato: Estranged; withdrawn in affection; foreign
parole.testo: From Middle English alienat(e) (“deranged; uncertain; sequestred, secluded”), from Latin aliēnātus, perfect passive participle of aliēnō (“to estrange, alienate”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from aliēnus. By surface analysis, alien + -ate. See alien, and compare aliene.

parole.significato: To convey or transfer to another, as title, property, or right; to part voluntarily with ownership of.
parole.testo: Either from the above adjective or directly borrowed from Latin alienātus, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more. Cognate with French aliéner.

parole.significato: foreign-born
parole.testo: From Latin aliēnigenus (“foreign-born”).

parole.significato: The fact or condition of being alien; alienation, separation; strangeness, foreignness.
parole.testo: From alien + -ity, after Latin alienitas.

parole.significato: Shaped like a wing.
parole.testo: From Latin ala (“wing”) + -form.

parole.significato: winged
parole.testo: From Latin aliger (from ala (“wing”) + gerere (“to carry”)) + -ous.

parole.significato: A court-mandated allowance made to a former spouse by a divorced or legally separated person.
parole.testo: Known since the 17th century, from Latin alimōnia (“food, support, nourishment, sustenance”) (English aliment, as in alimentary), itself from alō (“to nourish”) + -mōnia (“action, state, condition”).

parole.significato: A wing-footed animal; a chiropter or a bat.
parole.testo: From Latin ala (“wing”) and pes (“foot”) (ali- + -ped).

parole.significato: An official responsible for training and anointing athletes for the games.
parole.testo: From Latin alipta (“trainer of wrestlers or gymnasts”), from Ancient Greek ἀλείπτης (aleíptēs).

parole.significato: An integer that is less than another, but that does not divide the other integer into integral parts.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aliquantus.

parole.significato: otherwise
parole.testo: From Latin aliter (“otherwise”), from alius (“other”).

parole.significato: The segment of an insect's body to which the wings are attached; the thorax or mesosoma.
parole.testo: From Latin ala (“wing”) + truncus (“trunk”).

parole.significato: From another source; from elsewhere.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aliunde, from alius (“other”) + unde (“whence”).

parole.significato: Alkaline.
parole.testo: From post-classical Latin alcalizatus, past participle of alcalizo.

parole.significato: Different paths can take one to the same goal.
parole.testo: Modern wording of medieval sentiment; apparently originally a reference to Roman roads generally and the Milliarium Aureum (Golden Milestone) specifically. Appears in the Latin form mīlle viae dūcunt hominēs per saecula Rōmam (“a thousand roads lead men forever to Rome”) in Liber Parabolarum, 591 (1

parole.parola: all that glitters is not gold
parole.significato: Things that appear valuable or worthwhile might not actually be so; things that appear nice might not be as good as the…
parole.termine_origine: nōn omne quod nitet aurum est

catena.termine: nōn omne quod nitet aurum est

parole.testo: Calque of Latin nōn omne quod nitet aurum est (“not all that shines is gold”). Popularized by William Shakespeare in The Merchant of Venice, see quotations.

parole.significato: Knowing everything: all facts, all actions taken by everyone, and so on.
parole.testo: From all- + knowing. Partially a calque of Latin omnisciens (literally “all-knowing”)

parole.significato: The surgical removal of the corpus allatum from an insect.
parole.testo: From Latin allatum + + -ectomy.

parole.significato: To bark.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin allātrō.

parole.significato: To praise, laud.
parole.testo: From Latin allaudāre. Doublet of allow.

parole.significato: To allure; to entice; to sway.
parole.testo: From Latin allectare, frequentative of allicere, allectum.

parole.significato: enticement; allurement
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin allectatio, allectationis.

parole.significato: A liturgical or variant form of hallelujah.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin allēlūia, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀλληλούϊα (allēloúïa), borrowed from Biblical Hebrew הַלְּלוּיָהּ (halləlūyɔh, “praise the Lord”), from הַלְּלוּ (halləlū, “praise!”) + יָהּ (yɔh, “Lord, Jah”).

parole.significato: Alleviation.
parole.testo: From Latin allevātiō.

parole.significato: Smelling or tasting of garlic or onion.
parole.testo: From Latin allium (“garlic”) + -aceous.

parole.significato: That attracts; attractive.
parole.testo: From Latin alliciens, present participle of allicere (“to allure”); ad + lacere (“to entice”).

parole.significato: To impact a stationary object.
parole.testo: From Latin allīdō (“to dash or crush against”), from ad- (“to, toward, against”) + laedō (“to strike, collide, hurt”) (whence al- (“assimilated form of ad-”)).

parole.significato: To bind or tie; to unite.
parole.testo: From Latin alligatus (“tied, bound”), past participle of alligo (“to bind”), from ad + ligo (“to bind”). Doublet of alloy.

parole.significato: The act of tying together or attaching by some bond.
parole.testo: From Latin alligatio (“tying, binding, bond”), noun formation (from alligō + -tiō) of past participle of alligo (“to bind”), from ad + ligo (“to bind”).

parole.significato: A sulfoxide derived from cysteine, primarily responsible for the aroma of freshly chopped garlic.
parole.testo: From Latin allium (“garlic”) + -in.

parole.significato: The striking of a vessel against a fixed object; the act of alliding or an instance thereof.
parole.testo: From Latin allisiō (“striking or dashing against”) (whence -ion (“noun suffix denoting action, result, process, state, condition”)), from allīsus (“dashed or crushed against”), past participle of allīdō (“to dash or crush against”) (whence allide), from ad- (“to, toward, against”) + laedō (“to strik

parole.significato: Able to be allocated.
parole.testo: By surface analysis, allocate + -able, on model of Latin allocare, rather than from allocate.

parole.significato: To set aside for a purpose.
parole.testo: From Latin allocātus, perfect passive participle of Latin allocō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ad- (“to”) + locō. Doublet of allow. By surface analysis, al- + locate.

parole.significato: allocated
parole.testo: From Middle English allocat(e) (“allocated”), originally used as the past participle of allocate, from Latin allocātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more.

parole.significato: The allowance of a proceeding, writ, order, etc., by a court, judge, or judicial officer.
parole.testo: From Latin allocātur (“it is allocated”), from allocāre (“to allocate”).

parole.significato: A formal speech, especially one which is regarded as authoritative and forceful.
parole.testo: From Latin allocūtiō (“address”).

parole.significato: Allodial.
parole.testo: From Latin allōdium + -an.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a speech or address made to someone, particularly in a formal or public setting.
parole.testo: From alloquy, from Latin alloquium, from alloqui, + -al.

parole.significato: Act of speaking to another; an address to another person.
parole.testo: From Latin alloquium, from alloqui.

parole.significato: An indirect reference; a hint; a reference to something supposed to be known, but not explicitly mentioned.
parole.testo: From Latin allūsiōnem, accusative singular of allūsiō (“the act of playing with”), from allūdō (“play with; allude”), from al-, combining form of ad (“to”), + lūdō (“play”): compare French allusion.

parole.significato: that contains or makes use of allusions (indirect references or hints)
parole.testo: From Latin allūs-, past participle stem of allūdere (“to joke, jest”; see allude) + -ive. See also al-.

parole.significato: Pertaining to the soil deposited by a stream.
parole.testo: From Latin alluvius (“alluvial”), from alluviō (“an overflowing, inundation”), from alluō (“wash against”). By surface analysis, alluvium + -ial.

parole.significato: The increase in the area of land due to the deposition of sediment (alluvium) by a river.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin alluviō.

parole.significato: alluvial
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin alluvius.

parole.significato: A school, college, or university which a person has graduated from or attended.
parole.testo: From Latin alma māter (literally “nourishing mother”). Derives from the full name ("Alma Mater Studiorum Università di Bologna") of the oldest European university, the University of Bologna, founded in 1088.

parole.significato: A type of garnet having a deep red color, inclining to purple, with the chemical formula Fe₃Al₂(SiO₄)₃.
parole.testo: An alteration of the earlier alabandine, from Latin alabandina, from Alabanda, a town in Caria, a province of Asia Minor, where the mineral was found.

parole.significato: The resins of the tree Aquilaria malaccensis (syn. Aquilaria agallocha), known for their fragrant aroma, produced after…
parole.testo: From Old English alwe (“fragrant resin of an East Indian tree”), from Latin aloē, from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓λόη (ălóē), from Hebrew אָהָל (ʾāhāl) or related Aramaic forms, ultimately from Tamil அகில் (akil); reinforced in Middle English by Old French aloes.

parole.significato: unreasonableness, absurdity
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin alogia, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: Baldness.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin alōpecia, from the Ancient Greek ἀλωπεκία (alōpekía, “fox-mange”), from ἀλώπηξ (alṓpēx, “fox”) + -ία (-ía, a formative ending used in Ancient Greek, especially used in naming diseases).

parole.significato: Synonym of male pattern baldness.
parole.testo: From alopecia (“loss of hair”) + andro- (“men”) + Latin genetica (“genetic”).

parole.significato: shad
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin alausa, from Gaulish *alausa. Doublet of alose.

parole.significato: Pertaining to the Alps, or other high mountains; Alpine.
parole.testo: Latin Alpestris.

parole.significato: The prefix a- (or an- when prefixing a root which begins with a vowel) found in some English words of Greek derivation.…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin alpha prīvātīvum, from Ancient Greek ἄλφα στερητικόν (álpha sterētikón).

parole.significato: Any disease causing dull white or silvery spots on the skin, including non-contagious forms of leprosy and psoriasis.
parole.testo: From Latin alphos, from Ancient Greek ἀλφός (alphós, “dull white, used for some leprosy, psoriasis, etc.”).

parole.significato: Alpine.
parole.testo: From Latin Alpēs (“Alps”) + -ian.

parole.significato: Any of several plants, native to mountain habitats, often grown in rock gardens.
parole.testo: From Latin Alpīnus, from Alpēs (“the Alps”). Cognates include French alpin.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Alsinaceae (Caryophyllaceae) family, especially chickweed.
parole.testo: From Alsinaceae, from Alsine + -aceae, from Latin alsine (“chickweed”), + -ous.

parole.significato: Of a voice or instrument, high pitch; especially, the octave above the top line of the treble stave.
parole.testo: From Latin altus (“high”). Doublet of old and alto.

parole.significato: An individual's alternate personality or persona; another self.
parole.testo: From Latin alter ego (literally “other me”).

parole.significato: A medicine or treatment which works by changing processes within the body, rather than by evacuating something etc.
parole.testo: From Latin alterativum, noun use of alterativus.

parole.significato: To argue, quarrel or wrangle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin altercor.

parole.significato: An angry or heated dispute.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin altercātiō. Cognates * Catalan altercació * Italian altercazione * Occitan altercatio, altercassion * Portuguese altercação * Spanish altercación

parole.significato: Acting by turns; alternate.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin alternus (“every other, alternate”).

parole.significato: Happening by turns; one following the other in succession of time or place; first one and then the other (repeatedly).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin alternātus, the perfect passive participle of Latin alternō (“to take turns”) (see -ate (1,2 and 3)), from alternus (“one after another, by turns”), from alter (“other”) + -nus. Doublet of altern; see also alter.

parole.significato: The reciprocal succession of (normally two) things in time or place; the act of following and being followed by turns;…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin alternatio; compare French alternation. By surface analysis, alternate + -ion.

parole.significato: Any of several plants of the genus Althaea; the hollyhocks and mallows, native to Eurasia.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin althaea.

parole.significato: Pompous language; lofty speech.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin altiloquentia.

parole.significato: An apparatus for measuring altitude.
parole.testo: Coined based on Latin altus (“high”) + -meter.

parole.significato: High-sounding; lofty or pompous.
parole.testo: From Latin altus (“high”) + sonans, present participle of sonare (“to sound”).

parole.significato: The absolute height of a location, usually measured from sea level.
parole.testo: From Middle English, borrowed from Latin altitūdō (“height”), from altus (“high”).

parole.significato: Of or in relation to altitude
parole.testo: From Latin altitūdin- + -al, from oblique stem of Latin altitūdō, from altus + -tūdō. By surface analysis, altitude + -al.

parole.significato: Lofty in doctrine, aims, etc.
parole.testo: From Latin altitūdin- + -arian, from oblique stem of Latin altitūdō, from altus + -tūdō. By surface analysis, altitude + -arian.

parole.significato: Lofty; very high.
parole.testo: From Latin altitūdin- + -ous, from oblique stem of Latin altitūdō, from altus + -tūdō. By surface analysis, altitude + -ous.

parole.significato: Flying high; soaring.
parole.testo: From Latin altivolans. See volant.

parole.significato: A theodolite.
parole.testo: From Latin altus (“high”) + -meter. By surface analysis, alto- + meter.

parole.significato: altricial birds.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin altrīcēs, plural of altrīx (“nourisher”).

parole.significato: Aluminum oxide, especially when used in mining, material sciences or ceramics, a refractory solid compound.
parole.testo: From the combining form of Latin alumen + -a.

parole.significato: A female pupil or student (especially of a university or college).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin alumna.

parole.significato: An individual alumnus or alumna.
parole.testo: From Latin alumni.

parole.significato: A male pupil or student.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin alumnus (“foster child, nourished one”).

parole.significato: leathery in color or texture.
parole.testo: Latin alutacius, from aluta (“soft leather”).

parole.significato: A beehive, or anything resembling a beehive.
parole.testo: From Latin alvearium (“beehive”). In the sense of the hollow of the ear, because it is where the wax accumulates. In the sense of a repository: originally the name of a dictionary encompassing several languages, because of the many contributors being like "busy bees".

parole.significato: The lowest point on the septum between the central incisors of the upper jaw.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin alveolus, a diminutive of alveus (“a tray, trough, basin”), from alvus (“the belly, the stomach, bowels, womb, etc.”).

parole.significato: Having a structure containing honeycomb-like cavities.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin alveolatus, from alveolus (“cavity”). For the protists, a borrowing of taxonomic name Alveolata.

parole.significato: Having the form of alveoli, or little sockets, cells, or cavities.
parole.testo: From Latin alveolus (“cavity”) + -iform.

parole.significato: A small cavity or pit.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin alveolus (“a small hollow or cavity”), diminutive of alveus (“a hollow, cavity”).

parole.significato: The bed or channel of a river, especially when the river is flowing in its natural or ordinary course; (also) the troug…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin alveus (“hollow trough-shaped vessel, trough, bath tub, hull, hold, ship, boat, channel or bed (of a river or trench), beehive”). First attested in the late 17th century in an earlier sense.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the belly or intestines.
parole.testo: From Latin alvus (“belly”) + -ine (compare French alvin).

parole.significato: sexual attraction to or paraphilia involving the stomach or belly
parole.testo: From Latin alvus (“belly”) + -ine + -o- + -lagnia.

parole.significato: Synonym of alvinolagnia.
parole.testo: From Latin alvus (“belly”) + -ine + o + -philia (See also alvine)

parole.significato: lovableness
parole.testo: From Latin amabilitas.

parole.significato: To send away; dismiss.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin amando, from ab (“from, away from”) + mando (“to order”).

parole.significato: The act of sending someone away.
parole.testo: Either from amand + -ation, or from Latin amandatio.

parole.significato: One employed to take dictation, or copy manuscripts.
parole.testo: From Latin āmanuēnsis (“secretary”), from ab- (“from, off (of)”) + manus (“hand”) + -ensis (“of or from (a place)”), early 17th c.

parole.significato: Marjoram.
parole.testo: From Latin amāracus.

parole.significato: amaranth (rare, formal)
parole.testo: From Latin amarantus.

parole.significato: A belladonna lily (Amaryllis belladonna), native to South Africa.
parole.testo: From Latin Amaryllis.

parole.significato: A male paramour, typically in extramarital or illicit contexts
parole.testo: From the Latin amāsius (“a male lover”).

parole.significato: The assumption that all human beings pursue love or romance, especially by means of a monogamous long-term relationship.
parole.testo: A compound of Latin amātō or amātus and normativity, modeled on heteronormativity and coined by philosophy professor Elizabeth Brake in 2011.

parole.significato: amatory
parole.testo: From Latin amatorius, from amare (“to love”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to love, especially sexual love.
parole.testo: From Latin amātōrius (“pertaining to love or a lover”, adjective), from amātor (“a lover”), from amō (“to love”).

parole.significato: The absence of one or both of the mammary glands, with the nipple and areola present.
parole.testo: From Modern Latin [Term?]. If so, from the hypothetical Ancient Greek *ἀμαζία (*amazía), ultimately from ἀ- (a-) + μαζός (mazós) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā).

parole.significato: A member of a mythical race of female warriors inhabiting the Black Sea area.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Latin, from Ancient Greek Ἀμαζών (Amazṓn); perhaps Ionian Greek pronunciation of Old Persian *hamazan- (“warrior”), as the Amazon women were known warriors. A popular folk etymology, of Ancient Greek provenance, claims that the word derives from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + μαζός (mazó

parole.significato: The outline of a spore or pollen grain, as seen in a polar view.
parole.testo: From ambit, from Latin.

parole.significato: Roundabout, circuitous, vague.
parole.testo: From Latin ambāgiōsus, from ambāgēs (“roundabout path”).

parole.significato: Either or both.
parole.testo: From Latin ambo (“both”). Doublet of amphi-.

parole.significato: Encompassing on all sides; surrounding; encircling; enveloping.
parole.testo: From Latin ambiēns (“going around”), from ambiō (“go around”).

parole.significato: Of two kinds or natures.
parole.testo: From Latin ambō (“both”) + genus (“kind”).

parole.significato: act of ambiguating
parole.testo: Stem of ambiguous (from Latin ambiguus) with suffix -ation.

parole.significato: Open to multiple interpretations.
parole.testo: From Latin ambiguus (“moving from side to side, of doubtful nature”), from ambigere (“to go about, wander, doubt”), from ambi- (“around, about, on both sides”) + agere (“to drive, move”).

parole.significato: Having equally bad ability in both hands; clumsy; butterfingered.
parole.testo: First attested in English in 1646: from Latin ambilaevus (ambi- (“both”) + laevus (“left”)), a calque of Ancient Greek ἀμφαρίστερος (ampharísteros, “with two left hands, awkward, clumsy”) from ἀμφί (amphí, “on both sides”) + ἀριστερός (aristerós, “left”).

parole.significato: The extent of actions, thoughts, or the meaning of words, etc.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English ambyte, borrowed from Latin ambitus (“circuit; circumference, perimeter; area within a perimeter; ground around a building; cycle, orbit, revolution”) (compare Late Latin ambitus (“neighbourhood; wall of a castle, monastery, or town; cloister; parish boundary”)), from ambīre

parole.significato: The range of a melody, especially those of ecclesiastical chants.
parole.testo: From Latin ambitus (“circuit, ostentation”). Doublet of ambit.

parole.significato: abortion (termination of pregnancy)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin amblosis, from Ancient Greek ἄμβλωσις (ámblōsis).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the city of Ambracia; Ambracian.
parole.testo: An adaptation of the Latin Ambraciōtēs and the Ancient Greek Ἀμβρᾰκῐώτης (Ambrăkĭṓtēs).

parole.significato: The food of the gods, thought to confer immortality.
parole.testo: From Latin ambrosia (“food of the gods”), from Ancient Greek ἀμβροσία (ambrosía, “immortality”), from ἄμβροτος (ámbrotos, “immortal”), from ἀ- (a-, “not”) + βροτός (brotós, “mortal”).

parole.significato: Having the qualities of ambrosia; delicious.
parole.testo: Either from ambrosia + -ac or Latin ambrosiacus; compare French ambrosiaque.

parole.significato: Pertaining to or worthy of the gods.
parole.testo: Partly from ambrosia and partly from Latin ambrosius, + -al.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Saint Ambrose.
parole.testo: From Middle English ambrosien, from Latin ambrosiānus; equivalent to Ambrose + -ian.

parole.significato: An early coin struck by the dukes of Milan, and bearing the effigy of St. Ambrose on its horseback.
parole.testo: From Latin ambrosīnus (nummus), from Ambrosius (“Ambrose”), the patron saint of Milan.

parole.significato: A row of pores in an echinoderm, for the protrusion of appendages such as tube feet.
parole.testo: From Latin ambulacrum, from ambulō (“walk; travel”).

parole.significato: Able to walk; ambulatory.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ambulans, present participle of ambulare (“to walk”).

parole.significato: To walk; to relocate oneself under the power of one's own legs.
parole.testo: From Latin ambulātus, past participle of ambulō (“to walk, go about”). Doublet of amble.

parole.significato: Walking.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin ambulātiō.

parole.significato: A walker; one who walks.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ambulātor.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or adapted to walking.
parole.testo: From Latin ambulatorius. By surface analysis, ambulate + -ory, or, by surface analysis, ambulator + -y.

parole.significato: A disorder involving walking.
parole.testo: From Latin ambulō (“to walk”) + -ism.

parole.significato: Any of various forms of divination that involve walking, often in circles.
parole.testo: From Latin ambulō (“walk”) + -mancy.

parole.significato: Fear of walking or standing.
parole.testo: From Latin ambulō (“to walk”) + -phobia.

parole.significato: An ancient expiatory procession round the city of Rome at which sacrifices were offered.
parole.testo: From Latin amburbium.

parole.significato: A burn or scald.
parole.testo: From Latin ambustio.

parole.significato: Relating to amensalism.
parole.testo: From a- + mensal, from Latin mensa (“table, food”).

parole.significato: A catkin or similar inflorescence.
parole.testo: From Latin āmentum (“thong, string”).

parole.significato: Mental impairment; state of being mentally handicapped.
parole.testo: From Latin āmentia (“madness; senselessness”), from āmēns (“mad, insane; foolish”), from ab (“from, away from”) + mēns (“mind”).

parole.significato: A catkin.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin amentum (“thong”).

parole.significato: killing of a friend
parole.testo: From Latin amicus + -cide.

parole.significato: A person or entity who has been allowed by the court to plead or make submissions but who is not directly involved in t…
parole.testo: From Latin, amīcus (“friend”) + cūriae (“of the court”), genitive singular of cūria (“court”).

parole.significato: Liable or likely to be lost.
parole.testo: From Latin āmissibilis. Compare French amissible.

parole.significato: deprivation; loss
parole.testo: From Latin amissio. Compare French amission.

parole.significato: To lose.
parole.testo: From Latin āmittō (“to lose, to send away”).

parole.significato: One of the genus Ammodytes of fishes; the sand eel.
parole.testo: From Latin ammodytes, from Ancient Greek "sand burrower, a kind of serpent".

parole.significato: hippocampus
parole.testo: Calque of Latin cornū Ammōnis.

parole.significato: A gaseous, toxic compound of hydrogen and nitrogen, NH₃, with a pungent smell and taste.
parole.testo: From Latin sal ammoniacus (“salt of Amun, ammonium chloride”), named so because it was found near the temple of (Jupiter) Ammon in Egypt. Ammon derives from Ancient Greek Ἄμμων (Ámmōn), from Egyptian jmn (i-mn:n-A4).

parole.significato: A gum-resin exuded from the several perennial herbs in the genus Ferula of the umbel family (Apiaceae).
parole.testo: From Middle English armoniacum, from Latin ammōniacum, armōniacum.

parole.significato: Loss of memory; forgetfulness.
parole.testo: From modified Latin amnesia, from Ancient Greek ἀμνησία (amnēsía, “forgetfulness”), a noun derivation from μιμνήσκω (mimnḗskō, “to remind, to remember”) prefixed with the alpha privative.

parole.significato: The innermost membrane of the fetal membranes of reptiles, birds, and mammals; the sac in which the embryo is suspended.
parole.testo: From Latin amnion (“membrane around a fetus”), from Ancient Greek ἀμνίον (amníon).

parole.significato: Any of the Amniota group of vertebrates having an amnion during the development of the embryo; mammals, birds and repti…
parole.testo: From scientific Latin Amniota. Thus, by surface analysis, amnio- + -ote.

parole.significato: A poem in which people are represented speaking alternately.
parole.testo: From the neuter of Latin amoebaeus, from Ancient Greek ἀμοιβαῖος (amoibaîos, “alternate”).

parole.significato: Describing a form of prosody (amoebaeum) featuring alternating responses.
parole.testo: From Latin amoebaeus, from Ancient Greek ἀμοιβαῖος (amoibaîos, “reciprocal”), from ἀμοιβή (amoibḗ, “change; alternation”).

parole.significato: A putting away; a forcible removal; the act of amolishing.
parole.testo: From Latin āmōlītiō, from āmōlior + -tiō.

parole.significato: Any of several spices of genus Amomum, family Zingiberaceae, including cardamom.
parole.testo: From Latin amomum.

parole.significato: An asteroid that orbits between the orbits of Earth and Mars.
parole.testo: From the type object, 1221 Amor, itself from Latin Amor, the god of love.

parole.significato: An attitude in which one sees everything that happens in one's life, including suffering and loss, as good or at least…
parole.testo: A learned borrowing from Latin amor fātī (literally “love of fate”).

parole.significato: removal; ousting
parole.testo: From Latin amotio. See amove.

parole.significato: To remove.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin amoveō (“to remove”).

parole.significato: An earth abounding in pyrites, used by the Ancients Greeks as a pesticide on vines.
parole.testo: From Latin ampelitis, from Ancient Greek ἀμπελῖτις (ampelîtis, “of or for vines”), from ἄμπελος (ámpelos, “vine”).

parole.significato: The amphibians.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin amphibia.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the class Amphibia.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin amphibius [from Ancient Greek ἀμφίβιος (amphíbios), from ἀμφίς (amphís, “of both kinds”) + βίος (bíos, “life”)] + -an.

parole.significato: Ambiguity of grammatical structure.
parole.testo: From Latin amphibologia, alternative form of amphibolia (“ambiguity”).

parole.significato: Ambiguous; doubtful or unclear.
parole.testo: From Latin amphibolus, Ancient Greek ἀμφίβολος (amphíbolos, “thrown about, doubtful”). See amphibole.

parole.significato: A metrical foot in ancient Greek or Latin consisting of two short syllables surrounding one long one (e.g. amāta).
parole.testo: From Latin amphibrachys, from Ancient Greek ἀμφίβραχυς (amphíbrakhus, “short at both ends”), from ἀμφί (amphí) + βραχύς (brakhús, “short”).

parole.significato: Consisting of amphibrachs, metrical feet consisting of either a long syllable between two that are short, or an accente…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin amphibrachicus. By surface analysis, amphibrach + -ic.

parole.significato: One of the deputies from the confederated states of Ancient Greece to a congress or council. They considered both polit…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Amphictyones, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek Ἀμφικτύονες (Amphiktúones), both of which are only attested in the plural. Probably the word originally meant "dwellers around, neighbours".

parole.significato: A metrical foot consisting of an unaccented or light syllable between two accented or heavy syllables; a cretic.
parole.testo: From Latin amphimacrus, from Ancient Greek ἀμφίμακρος (amphímakros, “long at both ends”); see amphi-, macro-.

parole.significato: Having columns at either end but not along the sides.
parole.testo: From Latin amphiprostȳlos, from Ancient Greek ἀμφι- (amphi-) + πρόστῡλος (próstūlos, “having pillars”).

parole.significato: A mythical serpent having a head at each end of its body, able to move in either direction.
parole.testo: From Latin amphisbaena, from Ancient Greek ἀμφίσβαινα (amphísbaina, from ἀμφίς (amphís, “both ways”) + βαίνω (baínō, “to go”)).

parole.significato: An open, outdoor theatre (which may be a theatre in the round, or have a stage with seating on only one side), especial…
parole.testo: From Latin amphitheatrum, from Ancient Greek ἀμφιθέατρον (amphithéatron) from ἀμφί (amphí, “on both sides”) + θέᾱτρον (théātron, “theatre”).

parole.significato: A large, two-handled vessel, especially a thin-necked clay vat used in ancient Greece and Rome for storing and transpor…
parole.testo: From Latin amphora (“large wine vessel, Roman unit of liquid measure”), from Ancient Greek ἀμφορεύς (amphoreús, “two-handled pitcher, Greek units of liquid measure”), ultimately from Mycenaean Greek 𐀀𐀠𐀡𐀩𐀸 (a-pi-po-re-we, “carried on both sides”).

parole.significato: Of or related to an amphora, either as a large vessel or a Roman unit of liquid measure.
parole.testo: From Latin amphoricus (“of or related to an amphora”), from amphora + -icus (“-ic: forming adj.”). Equivalent to amphora + -ic.

parole.significato: To embrace.
parole.testo: From Latin amplector.

parole.significato: An embrace.
parole.testo: From Middle English amplection, amplexion, from Latin amplexiō (“act of embracing”), from amplex-, past participial stem of amplector (“surround; embrace”), + -iō. In this form, with remodelling after Latin amplector. By surface analysis, amplect + -ion.

parole.significato: To engage in amplexus.
parole.testo: Either from Latin amplexor or amplex-, past participial stem of amplector.

parole.significato: An embrace.
parole.testo: From Latin amplexāt-, past participial stem of amplexor (“to embrace”), + -ion.

parole.significato: A form of pseudocopulation, found chiefly in amphibians and horseshoe crabs, in which a male grasps a female with his f…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin amplexus (“embrace”).

parole.significato: Synonym of coitus reservatus.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin amplexus reservātus.

parole.significato: Having the outer edge prominent; said of the wings of insects.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ampliātus, past participle of ampliō (“to make wider”). By surface analysis, ample + -i- + -ate.

parole.significato: The use of an epithet for effect, when that epithet is not truly applicable to the referent.
parole.testo: From Latin ampliātiō (“extending; a deferring of the decision of a judge”). Doublet of ampliation.

parole.significato: Enlargement; amplification.
parole.testo: From Latin ampliatio. Compare French ampliation. Doublet of ampliatio.

parole.significato: To amplify.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin amplificātus, passive perfect participle of amplificō (“I enlarge, amplify”). Also an independent back-formation from amplification. For its use by non-native speakers, compare Catalan, Portuguese, and Spanish amplificar and Italian amplificare.

parole.significato: The act, or result of amplifying, enlarging, extending or adding.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin amplificātiō.

parole.significato: Relating to amplitude.
parole.testo: From Latin amplitūdin- + -al, from oblique stem of Latin amplitūdō, from amplus + -tūdō. By surface analysis, amplitude + -al.

parole.significato: An Ancient Roman two-handled vessel.
parole.testo: From Latin ampulla. Doublet of ampoule.

parole.significato: Having an ampulla; flask-shaped; bellied.
parole.testo: From Latin ampullatus. Equivalent to ampulla + -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Having the shape of a flask.
parole.testo: From Latin ampulla (“vessel with a swollen middle”) + -form.

parole.significato: To cut off, to prune.
parole.testo: From Latin amputō (“prune, cut away”). The original sense of pruning (a tree, etc.) became obsolete. The OED considers uses related to anything other than an animal limb to be figurative uses of the modern sense.

parole.significato: The sediment in olive oil.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin amurca.

parole.significato: Akin to, or derived from, the almond.
parole.testo: From Latin amygdala (“almond tree”) + -aceous.

parole.significato: Tonsil.
parole.testo: From Latin amygdala, from Ancient Greek ἀμυγδάλη (amugdálē, “almond”), named for the almond shape.

parole.significato: tonsillitis
parole.testo: From amygdala, amygdale (“tonsils”) + -itis, from Latin amygdala, from Ancient Greek ἀμυγδάλη (amugdálē, “almond”), named for the almond-shape.

parole.significato: Synonym of gentiobiose.
parole.testo: From Latin amygdala (“almond”) + -ose.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to starch
parole.testo: From Latin amylum (“starch”), from Ancient Greek ἄμυλον (ámulon, “starch”) from ἀ- (a-, “privative”) + μύλη (múlē, “mill”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to, or of the nature of, starch; starchy.
parole.testo: From Latin amylum (“starch”) + -aceous.

parole.significato: Bearing or producing starch.
parole.testo: From Latin amylum (“starch”) + -iferous.

parole.significato: A bacillus (Clostridium butyricum) which develops in vegetable tissue during putrefaction. It has medicinal uses
parole.testo: From Latin amylum (“starch”) + bacterium.

parole.significato: Relating to the measurement of the amount of starch in a substance.
parole.testo: From Latin amylum + -metric.

parole.significato: starch
parole.testo: From Latin amylum, from Ancient Greek ἄμυλον (ámulon), from ἀ- (a-, “privative”) + μύλη (múlē, “mill”).

parole.significato: A collection of things associated with a person or place, especially a personal collection of anecdotes or conversation…

parole.significato: A raised seat, chair or platform; a pulpit.

parole.significato: A headband, especially a garland of flowers.

parole.significato: Someone who reads aloud, especially who reads lessons, passages etc. during a church service.

parole.significato: Being or relating to an anagram.

parole.significato: Of, related to, intended for or involving the anus.

parole.significato: Something to be analyzed.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or composed of, anapests.

parole.significato: A syllable that can be either short or long.

parole.significato: Resembling or having the character of an anchor.

parole.significato: A slave girl; a servant-girl.

parole.significato: Two-edged instead of round; said of certain flattened stems, such as those of bluegrass, and rarely also of leaves.
parole.testo: From Latin anceps.

parole.significato: The corner of a wall or rafter.

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to the city of Ancona and associated province, Marche region, Italy.

parole.significato: A hermaphrodite.

parole.significato: Soothing; helping to relieve a malady.

parole.significato: A winding channel or crevice, such as occur in the depths of the sea or in mountains.

parole.significato: Belonging to, or proceeding from, angels; resembling, characteristic of, or partaking of the nature of, an angel.

parole.significato: A narrow road passing between two houses or a row of houses, or an alley leading to a single house.

parole.significato: To make English, as to customs, culture, pronunciation, spelling, or style.

parole.significato: The quality or state of being anonymous (nameless or unidentified).

parole.testo: From Latin antenna (“pole”) + -form.

parole.significato: Describing the period before childbirth; antenatal
