parole.testo: First attested in 1860; from the Latin antepaenultima (“antepenult”), a feminine substantive of antepaenultimus (“antepenultimate”).

parole.significato: The placing of something in front of something else, especially of words in a sentence.
parole.testo: From Latin anteponere.

parole.significato: Nearer the forward end, especially in the front of the body; nearer the head or forepart of an animal.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin anterior (“that is before, foremost”).

parole.significato: The largest of the muscles of each of the front shoulder.
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: Coming before; preceding.
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: To prevent, to avert.
parole.testo: From Latin antevertere, from ante + vertere (“to turn”).

parole.significato: To fly before or in front of.
parole.testo: From antevolāt-, the perfect passive participial stem of the Latin antevolō (“to fly before”), from ante (“before”, “in front of”) + volō (“to fly”).

parole.significato: A form of carbonized ancient plants; the hardest and cleanest-burning of all the coals.
parole.testo: Via Latin from Ancient Greek ἀνθρακῖτις (anthrakîtis, “a kind of coal”), from ἄνθραξ (ánthrax, “charcoal”). By surface analysis, anthrac- + -ite.

parole.significato: A man-eater; a cannibal.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin anthrōpophagus.

parole.significato: The frontal points.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin antiae (“forelock”).

parole.significato: Expectant.
parole.testo: From Latin anticipans, present participle of anticipo (“anticipate”).

parole.significato: To act before (someone), especially to prevent an action.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin anticipātus, perfect passive participle of anticipō (“to anticipate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ante- (“before”), + capiō (“to take”, cip- when prefixed) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). See capable.

parole.significato: A dangerous inflammatory swelling of a horse's breast, just opposite the heart, caused by the friction of a harness.
parole.testo: From anti- + Latin cor (“heart”); compare French anticœur.

parole.significato: Facing toward the axis, or central part, of the flower
parole.testo: From Latin anticus (“in front, foremost”), from ante (“before”).

parole.significato: A remedy to counteract the effects of poison.
parole.testo: From Latin antidotum, from Ancient Greek ἀντίδοτον (antídoton, “antidote, remedy”), Clipping of ἀντίδοτον φάρμακον (antídoton phármakon, “drug given against”), from ἀντιδίδωμι (antidídōmi, “to give in return, repay”), from ἀντί (antí, “against”) + δίδωμι (dídōmi, “to give”). Compare French antidote.

parole.significato: A manuscript from which a copy (apograph) is made.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin antigraphum, from Ancient Greek ἀντίγραφον (antígraphon, “a transcribing”); compare French antigraphe.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Antinous.
parole.testo: From the Latin Antinoānus.

parole.significato: A contradiction within a law, or between different laws; also, a contradiction between authorities.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin antinomia, from Ancient Greek ἀντινομία (antinomía), from ἀντι- (anti-, prefix meaning ‘against’) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ent- (“face; forehead; front”)) + νόμος (nómos, “custom, usage; law, ordinance”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā, suffix forming feminine abstract nouns

parole.significato: A handsome young man.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Antinous, from Ancient Greek Ἀντίνοος (Antínoos).

parole.significato: Synonym of Antiochian (of or pertaining to ancient Antioch)
parole.testo: From Latin Antiochēnus.

parole.significato: Having or showing a strong aversion or repugnance.
parole.testo: From Latin antipatheticus.

parole.significato: Counteracting, or preserving from, putrefaction; antiseptic.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin antiputrēscēns. By surface analysis, anti- + putrescent.

parole.significato: A style of typeface used to mimic styles of handwriting or calligraphy common during the 15th and 16th centuries.
parole.testo: From Latin antīqua, feminine of antīquus.

parole.significato: A person who is knowledgeable of, or who collects antiques (especially one holding an official position); an antiquaria…
parole.testo: From Latin antīquārius (“pertaining to antiquity, one fond of or employed in antiquities”), from antīquus (“ancient”) + -ārius; equivalent to antique + -ary.

parole.significato: To cause to become old or obsolete.
parole.testo: From Latin antiquātus, perfect passive participle of antiquō (“to make old, restore to a pristine state”). Also see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Antirrhinum of snapdragons.
parole.testo: From Latin antirrhīnum, variant form of antirrhīnon, anti- + rhino- + -um.

parole.significato: The chief minister of the Swiss Reformed Church in a given canton, from the sixteenth to the nineteeth centuries.
parole.testo: From Latin antistes (“bishop”).

parole.significato: In Greek choruses and dances, the returning of the chorus, exactly answering to a previous strophe or movement from rig…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin antistrophe, from Ancient Greek ἀντιστροφή (antistrophḗ, “turning about”).

parole.significato: A proposition that is the diametric opposite of some other proposition.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin antithesis, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἀντίθεσις (antíthesis). By surface analysis, anti- + thesis.

parole.significato: An antithetical or contrasted statement; a statement containing antithesis
parole.testo: From Latin antithetum, antitheton, from Ancient Greek ἀντίθετον (antítheton), substantivization of the neuter form of ἀντίθετος (antíthetos, “opposing, contrasting”).

parole.significato: Diametrically opposed.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin antitheticus.

parole.significato: Synonym of antivenom.
parole.testo: From anti- + venene (“venom”), from Latin venēnum (“juice; venom”). Doublet of antivenom and antivenin.

parole.significato: The spiral tubular proboscis of butterflies.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin antlia (“pump”), from Ancient Greek ἀντλία (antlía).

parole.significato: The inhabitants at two points on the globe that share a longitude and for which the sum of their degrees of latitude eq…
parole.testo: From the Latin antoecī, from the Ancient Greek ἄντοικοι (ántoikoi, “dwellers opposite”), from ἀντί (antí, “opposite”) + οἶκος (oîkos, “dwelling”).

parole.significato: The substitution of an epithet or title in place of a proper noun.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin antonomasia, Ancient Greek ἀντονομασία (antonomasía, “antonomasia”).

parole.significato: Relating to, or characterized by, antonomasia.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin antonomasticus, Ancient Greek ἀντονομασία (antonomasía, “antonomasia”).

parole.significato: Curved or pointed forward or upward.
parole.testo: From Latin antrorsum, contracted form of *anteroversum, from anterior (“before”) + versum (“turned”), corresponding to English antero- + -verse.

parole.significato: A bodily cavity, especially one having bony walls, especially one in the sinuses.
parole.testo: From Latin antrum, from Ancient Greek ἄντρον (ántron, “cave”). Doublet of antre.

parole.significato: The state or condition of being troubled, worried, or anxious; anxiety.
parole.testo: From Latin anxietudo. By surface analysis, anxie(ty) + -tude.

parole.significato: An unpleasant state of mental uneasiness, nervousness, apprehension and obsession or concern about some uncertain event.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ānxietās, from ānxius (“anxious, solicitous, distressed, troubled”), from angō (“to distress, trouble”), akin to Ancient Greek ἄγχω (ánkhō, “to choke”). Equivalent to anxious + -ety. See anger; angst.

parole.significato: Nervous and worried.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin anxius, from angō (“to cause pain, choke”); akin to Ancient Greek ἄγχω (ánkhō, “to choke”). See anger; angst.

parole.significato: Synonym of Apamean.
parole.testo: From Latin Apamēnus, from Ancient Greek Ἀπαμηνός (Apamēnós).

parole.significato: A master artist.
parole.testo: From the Latin Apellēs, from the Ancient Greek Ἀπελλῆς (Apellês) (Apellēs, Apelles of Kos, a renowned painter in the time of Alexander the Great).

parole.significato: Having a gentle laxative effect.
parole.testo: Attested since the early 17th century, from Latin aperiens, present participle of aperire (“to open”).

parole.significato: Causing the body to open; dissolving blockages or having a purgative or diuretic effect.
parole.testo: From Latin apertūra (“opening”) + -ive.

parole.significato: The dehiscence of anthers.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin apertūra. Doublet of aperture and overture.

parole.significato: A small or narrow opening, gap, slit, or hole.
parole.testo: From late Middle English, from Latin apertūra (“an opening”), from aperiō (“to uncover, make or lay bare”) + -tūra (“-ure”, action noun suffix). Doublet of overture and apertura.

parole.significato: The highest or the greatest part of something, especially forming a point.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin apex (“point, tip, summit”).

parole.significato: Synonym of aphelion.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin aphelium.

parole.significato: Elision, suppression, or complete loss of a letter or sound (syllable) from the beginning of a word, such as the develo…
parole.testo: From Latin aphaeresis, from Ancient Greek ἀφαίρεσις (aphaíresis, “a taking away”), from ἀφαιρέω (aphairéō) (from ἀφ- (aph-), variant of ἀπό (apó, “off, away from”) before an aspirated vowel) + αἱρέω (hairéō, “to take; to snatch”)) + -σις (-sis, suffix forming nouns of action); the grammatical sense

parole.significato: Feeding on aphids.
parole.testo: From aphis + Latin vorare (“to devour”).

parole.significato: A figure of speech that questions whether a word is properly used, as in "How can you call yourself a man?".
parole.testo: From Latin aphorismus, though the meaning is closer to Ancient Greek ᾰ̓φορῐσμός (ăphorĭsmós).

parole.significato: Forming terms related to bees or honeybees.
parole.testo: From Latin apis (“bee”).

parole.significato: Relating to bees.
parole.testo: 19th century, from Latin apiānus, from apis (“bee”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to bees or beekeeping.
parole.testo: First attested as an adjective in 1801 and as a noun in 1858; formed by suffixing either English apiary or its etymon, Latin apiārium, with English -an.

parole.significato: A place where bees and their hives are kept.
parole.testo: 17th century, from Latin apiārium, from apis (“bee”).

parole.significato: Only used in apic acid
parole.testo: Latin apis (“bee”) + -ic

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Marcus Gavius Apicius, a notorious Roman epicure.
parole.testo: From Latin Apīciānus, from Apīcius + -ānus, equivalent to Apicius + -an.

parole.significato: The killing of bees.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin apis (“bee”) + -cide.

parole.significato: Inflammation of the apex of an anatomical part.
parole.testo: From apic- + -itis, from Latin apicis.

parole.significato: Situated at, or near, the apex; apical.
parole.testo: From Latin apiculus, diminutive of Latin apex, apicis.

parole.significato: Having a short, sharply pointed tip.
parole.testo: Latin apiculatus

parole.significato: A short, slender, flexible point
parole.testo: From Latin apic- + Latin -ulum, ultimately from Latin apex.

parole.significato: The part of a spore which attaches to the sterigmata at the end of a basidium.
parole.testo: From Latin apic- + Latin -ulus, ultimately from Latin apex.

parole.significato: An excessive interest in bees.
parole.testo: From Latin apis (“bee”) + -mania.

parole.significato: A glucoside of apiose
parole.testo: From apiose + glucoside. The combining form of apiose comes from Latin apiō, a declensive form of Latin apium (“parsley, celery”).

parole.significato: The scientific study of bees and honey-making.
parole.testo: From Latin apis + -logy.

parole.significato: A branched-chain sugar, 3-C-(hydroxymethyl)-D-glycerotetrose, that occurs in parsley and many other plants
parole.testo: From Latin apium (“parsley”) + -ose.

parole.significato: An apiphobic person.
parole.testo: From Latin apis (“bee”) + -phobe.

parole.significato: An inordinate fear of bees.
parole.testo: From Latin apis (“bee”) + -phobia.

parole.significato: Pertaining to or afflicted with apiphobia, the fear of bees.
parole.testo: From Latin apis (“bee”) + -phobic.

parole.significato: The venom found in a honey bee's sting.
parole.testo: From Latin apis (“bee”) + toxin.

parole.significato: An organism that eats or consumes bees.
parole.testo: From Latin apis (“bee”) + -vore.

parole.significato: That feeds on bees
parole.testo: From Latin apis (“bee”) + -vorous.

parole.significato: An ornamental appendage of wood at the stern of a Roman ship, usually spreading like a fan and curved like a bird's fea…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aplustre.

parole.significato: A revealing, especially a prophecy of, or the unfolding of, supernatural events.
parole.testo: From Middle English apocalips, from Latin apocalypsis, from Ancient Greek ἀποκάλυψις (apokálupsis, “revelation”, literally “uncovering”), from ἀποκαλύπτω (apokalúptō, “to reveal”), from ἀπό (apó, “back, away from”) + καλύπτω (kalúptō, “to cover”), + -σις (-sis, suffix forming nouns). The sense evolu

parole.significato: Of or relating to an apocalypse:
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin apocalypticus, from Ancient Greek ἀποκαλυπτικός (apokaluptikós, “revelatory”), from ἀποκάλυψις (apokálupsis, “revelation”), from ἀποκαλύπτω (apokalúptō, “to reveal, uncover”).

parole.significato: Writings which are apocalyptic or which are about an apocalypse.
parole.testo: Either from Latin, or apocalyptic + -ica.

parole.significato: Restoration, renovation, reestablishment
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin apocatastasis, itself from Ancient Greek ἀποκατάστασις (apokatástasis, “restoration, reëstablishment”), from ἀποκαθίστημι (apokathístēmi, “to stand up again”), from ἀπό- (apó-, “back again”) + καθίστημι (kathístēmi, “to set, place, constitute, appoint”), from κατά- (katá

parole.significato: Shortened by apocope; lacking a final sound or syllable
parole.testo: From Latin apocopātus (“cut off”), from Ancient Greek ἀποκόπτω (apokóptō, “cut off”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to apocope; lacking a final sound or syllable.
parole.testo: From apocope, from Latin, from Ancient Greek ἀποκοπή (apokopḗ, “a cutting off, termination, apocope”).

parole.significato: A high diplomatic representative, approximately equivalent to a papal nuncio.
parole.testo: From Latin apocrisiarius, apocrisarius, from Ancient Greek ἀπόκρισις (apókrisis, “separation, answer, embassy or commission”).

parole.significato: Incontrovertible; demonstrably true or certain.
parole.testo: From the Latin apodīcticus (“proving clearly”, “demonstrative”), from the Ancient Greek ἀποδεικτικός (apodeiktikós, “affording proof”, “demonstrative”), from ἀποδείκνυμι (apodeíknumi, “to demonstrate”). In turn, from ἀπο- (apo-, “separate, without”), and δεικτικός (deiktikós, “capable of proof”).

parole.significato: Emphatic rejection or dismissal of an opponent or an opposing proposition.
parole.testo: From Latin, from ἀποδίωξις (apodíōxis), from Ancient Greek ἀποδιώκειν (apodiṓkein, “to drive away”).

parole.significato: The apartment at the entrance of the baths, or in the palestra, for getting undressed.
parole.testo: From Latin, from Ancient Greek ἀποδυτήριον (apodutḗrion), from ἀποδύω (apodúō, “strip oneself”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the god Apollo.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Apollineus. By surface analysis, Apollo + -ine.

parole.significato: Any of several papilionid butterflies of the genus Parnassius, especially Parnassius apollo of Eurasia (also known as t…
parole.testo: From Latin Apollō, from Ancient Greek Ἀπόλλων (Apóllōn).

parole.significato: The point of an elliptical lunar orbit where the distance between the satellite and the Moon is at its maximum.
parole.testo: From apo- (“far”) + Latin lūna (“moon”).

parole.significato: An expression of deliberation with oneself regarding uncertainty or doubt as to how to proceed.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aporia, from Ancient Greek ἀπορία (aporía), from ἄπορος (áporos, “impassable”), from ἀ- (a-, “a-”) + πόρος (póros, “passage”). By surface analysis, a- + pore + -ia.

parole.significato: An abrupt breaking-off in speech, often indicated in print using an ellipsis (…) or an em dash (—).
parole.testo: From Latin aposiopesis, from Ancient Greek ἀποσιώπησις (aposiṓpēsis), from ἀποσιωπάω (aposiōpáō, “be silent”), from ἀπό (apó, “off, from”) + σιωπάω (siōpáō, “to be silent”).

parole.significato: The renunciation of a belief or set of beliefs.
parole.testo: From Latin apostasia, from Ancient Greek ἀποστασία (apostasía, “defection, revolt”), from ἀφίστημι (aphístēmi, “to withdraw, revolt”), from ἀπό (apó, “from”) + ἵστημι (hístēmi, “to stand”).

parole.significato: Apostate.
parole.testo: Latin apostaticus, Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: The formation of an aposteme; the process of suppuration.
parole.testo: Latin apostematio: compare French apostémation.

parole.significato: Pertaining to apostles or their practice or teaching; pertaining to the apostles (of early Christianity) or their teach…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin apostolicus (“apostolic”), from Ancient Greek ἀποστολικός (apostolikós, “apostolic”).

parole.significato: A sudden exclamatory piece of dialogue addressed to someone or something, especially absent.
parole.testo: From Latin apostrophe, from Ancient Greek ἀποστροφή (apostrophḗ), from ἀποστρέφω (apostréphō, “to turn away”), from ἀπό (apó) + στρέφω (stréphō, “to turn”).

parole.significato: The omission of a vowel or syllable from a word, usually indicated by the apostrophe symbol ( ' ). examples: 'til, can't
parole.testo: From Latin apostrophus.

parole.significato: One of an ancient sect of Christians in Asia Minor, originating in the third century AD, who renounced all their posses…
parole.testo: From Latin plural Apotactitae.

parole.significato: The fact or action of becoming or making into a god; deification.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin apotheōsis, from Ancient Greek ἀποθέωσις (apothéōsis), from verb ἀποθεόω (apotheóō, “deify”) (factitive verb formed from θεός (theós, “God”) with intensive prefix ἀπο- (apo-)) + -σις (-sis, “forms noun of action”). By surface analysis, apo- + theo- + -sis.

parole.significato: A decoction or infusion.
parole.testo: From Latin apozema, from Ancient Greek ἀπόζεμα (apózema, “to extract by boiling”), from the root ζέω (zéō, “to boil, seethe”), q. v.

parole.significato: apparatus
parole.testo: From Latin apparātus.

parole.significato: A preparation.
parole.testo: From Latin apparō (“to make ready”).

parole.significato: The entirety of means whereby a specific production is made existent or task accomplished.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin apparātus. Doublet of apparat.

parole.significato: Synonym of critical apparatus.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: The quality of being apparent; apparentness.
parole.testo: From Middle English apparancie, from Latin appārentia. Doublet of apparence and appearance.

parole.significato: An officer who attended magistrates and judges to execute their orders.
parole.testo: Latin appāritor (“public servant”), from appareo (“to wait upon”).

parole.significato: That can be (legally) appealed to, especially of a court that hears appeals of decisions by a lower court.
parole.testo: From Latin appellātus.

parole.significato: Containing or pertaining to a legal appeal.
parole.testo: From Latin appellātōrius, from appellō.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or of the nature of an appendix or appendices (chiefly of books).
parole.testo: From Latin appendic- (stem of appendix) + English -al.

parole.significato: The epiploic appendices.
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: A small appendage.
parole.testo: From Latin appendicula, diminutive of appendix.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a limb or appendage.
parole.testo: From appendix + -ule + -ar, from Latin appendicis, genitive of appendix.

parole.significato: Having the nature of an appendage, such as the leg or antenna of an insect.
parole.testo: From appendix + -ule + -ate, from Latin appendicis, genitive of appendix.

parole.significato: Something attached to something else; an attachment or accompaniment.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin appendix.

parole.significato: peril
parole.testo: From Latin ad + peril.

parole.significato: Eagerly desirous; greedy.
parole.testo: From Latin appetēns, present participle of appetō.

parole.significato: Desirable; capable or worthy of being the object of desire.
parole.testo: From Latin appetibilis, from appetere: compare French appétible.

parole.significato: A desire, longing for, or seeking after of something.
parole.testo: From Latin appetītiō (“a longing or desire”).

parole.significato: Applause; applauding.
parole.testo: From Middle English applauden, from Latin applaudere (“to clap the hands together, applaud”), from ad (“to”) + plaudere (“to strike, clap”).

parole.significato: The act of applauding; approbation and praise publicly expressed by the clapping of hands, stamping or tapping of the f…
parole.testo: From Latin applausus, from applaudō (“to strike against, to applaud”) (whence applaud).

parole.significato: Conveying applause.
parole.testo: Formed as *applaus- (the perfect passive participial stem of the Latin applaudō) + -ive, thus resembling a regular Anglicisation of a hypothetical Latin etymon of the form *applausīvus. By surface analysis, applause + -ive.

parole.significato: One who applies for something; one who makes a request; a petitioner.
parole.testo: From Latin applicans, present participle of applicare. See apply.

parole.significato: An applied material; an application
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin applicātus.

parole.significato: Synonym of apply.
parole.testo: From Middle English applicaten, a learned borrowing from Latin applicāt-, the past participial stem of applicō. In later use perhaps an independent back-formation from application. For its use by non-native speakers, compare Catalan, Galician, Portuguese, and Spanish aplicar and Italian applicare.

parole.significato: The supposed paranormal transference of an object from one place to another, or the appearance of an object from an unk…
parole.testo: From Latin apportō (“to bring, to carry”).

parole.significato: A bringer in; an importer.
parole.testo: From Latin apportō (“to carry in”) + -er.

parole.significato: To place next or to or near to; to juxtapose.
parole.testo: Coined based on Latin appōnō, by analogy with compose, suppose etc.

parole.significato: Strikingly appropriate or relevant; well suited to the circumstance or in relation to something.
parole.testo: From Latin appositus, past participle of adponere, from ad- + ponere (“to put, place”). See apposition.

parole.significato: Addition of an element not syntactically required for purpose of description or explanation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin appositiō.

parole.significato: Earnest prayer; devout wish.
parole.testo: From Latin apprecari (“to pray to”), from ad + precari (“to pray”), from prex, precis (“prayer”).

parole.significato: Someone who appreciates a given thing, especially:
parole.testo: From appreciate + -or and Latin appreciātor.

parole.significato: The taking of something.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin apprehensio, apprehensionis, compare with French appréhension. See apprehend.

parole.significato: Anticipating something with anxiety, fear, or doubt; reluctant.
parole.testo: From Latin apprehensīvus, from apprehensus, perfect passive participle of apprehendō (“to apprehend, understand, learn”) + -īvus (“-ive”).

parole.significato: To press close to.
parole.testo: An adaptation of appress-, the perfect passive participial stem of the Latin apprimō (“to press close to”).

parole.significato: Approved.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin approbatus. Doublet of approve.

parole.significato: A person who gives formal approval.
parole.testo: From Latin approbātor.

parole.significato: To approach; to near.
parole.testo: From Latin appropinquāre (“to approach”), from ad- ("towards") + propinquō (“draw near”), verbalization of propinquus (“near”); compare prope ("near").

parole.significato: The act of drawing near; an approach.
parole.testo: Latin appropinquatio.

parole.significato: To take to oneself; to claim or use, especially as by an exclusive right.
parole.testo: From Middle English appropriaten, from appropriat (“appropriated”) + -en, borrowed from Latin appropriātus, perfect passive participle of appropriō (“to make one's own”), from ad (“to”) + propriō (“to make one's own”), from proprius (“one's own, private”) + -ō (first conjugation verb-forming suffix)

parole.significato: A consonant sound made by slightly narrowing the vocal tract, while still allowing a smooth flow of air. Liquids and gl…

parole.significato: Someone with an Aries star sign.
parole.testo: From Latin Aries, from aries (“ram”), calque of Ancient Greek Κριός (Kriós), calque of Akkadian 𒅈𒌺𒊑𒈨 (immeru, “sheep”).

parole.significato: The use of a battering ram, or similar.
parole.testo: From Latin arietātiō, from arietāre, from ariēs.

parole.significato: Synonym of Arian, of or related to Aries, its nature, or its influence.
parole.testo: From Latin Arietianus, from Aries + -ianus (“-ian”), from aries (“ram”).

parole.significato: Having the shape of a ram's head or of the astrological symbol of Aries, ⟨♈︎⟩.
parole.testo: From Latin arietis (the genitive singular of ariēs (“a ram”)) + English -form (suffix meaning ‘having the shape or form of’). Ariēs is derived from Proto-Indo-European *h₁r-i-(e)t- (“a certain domestic animal”).

parole.significato: Of, like, or pertaining to rams.
parole.testo: From Latin arietīnus, from ariet(is) (“ram”) + -īnus, from oblique form of ariēs.

parole.significato: one who practices the art of divination and uses interpretation to produce omens.
parole.testo: From Latin ariolor, hariolor, hariolus.

parole.significato: Soothsaying; prophecy.
parole.testo: From (the stem of) Latin ariolari, hariolari, from hariolus (“soothsayer”) + -ation.

parole.significato: A severe critic.
parole.testo: From the Latin Aristarchus, from the Ancient Greek Ἀρίσταρχος (Arístarkhos) (Aristarkhos; “Aristarchus of Samothrace”, a severe critic of Homeric poetry).

parole.significato: Having a long bristle at its apex.
parole.testo: From Latin aristatus, from arista. See arista.

parole.significato: Having the bristlelike shape or fibrillar structure of aristae.
parole.testo: Latin arista (“awn”) + -form

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Aristophanes, his plays or his poetry.
parole.testo: Latin Aristophanēus + -an

parole.significato: Aristophanean
parole.testo: From the Latin Aristophanicus.

parole.significato: A proponent of the philosophical or logical theories of Aristotle.
parole.testo: From Latin Aristotelī(us) or Aristotelē(us) + -an. By surface analysis, Aristotle + -ian.

parole.significato: A large box with a flat lid.
parole.testo: From Middle English arke, from Old English earc, ærc, from Latin arca (“chest, box, coffer”), from arceō (“to enclose”).

parole.significato: A body of forces equipped for war.
parole.testo: From Latin armāmentum, from armō (“to arm”).

parole.significato: All of the equipment available for carrying out a task, especially all the equipment used by a physician in the practic…
parole.testo: From Latin armāmentārium (“arsenal”), from armāmenta (“tools, equipment, rigging”) + -ārium. By surface analysis, armament + -arium.

parole.significato: An armory or arsenal (place to store weapons)
parole.testo: From Latin armamentarium, from armamentum. Compare French armamentaire.

parole.significato: Synonym of ambry (“cupboard or storage area”).
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin armārium. Doublet of ambry, armoire, and almirah.

parole.significato: The librarian in a medieval monastery, who kept, repaired and catalogued its manuscripts and books.
parole.testo: From Latin armarius.

parole.significato: Bearing arms (weapons).
parole.testo: From Latin armifer, from arma (“arms”) + ferre (“to bear”).

parole.significato: An esquire, originally carrying the armour of a knight; (hence, later) a man of the gentry ranking below a knight.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin armiger (“carrying weapons or armour or having coat of arms”).

parole.significato: Resembling a bracelet or armilla; consisting of rings or circles.
parole.testo: Early 1700s, from Latin armilla (“bracelet; armlet; arm ring”), from Latin armus (“shoulder; upper arm”).

parole.significato: Power in arms; military might.
parole.testo: From Latin armipotentia, from armipotents.

parole.significato: Powerful in battle.
parole.testo: From Latin armipotēns.

parole.significato: Resounding with arms, or weapons.
parole.testo: From Latin armisonus + -ant.

parole.significato: Divination using the shoulder blade of an animal. It was taken from a dead animal and thrown into a fire, and the crack…
parole.testo: From Latin armus (“shoulder blade”) + -mancy.

parole.significato: Any of various medical remedies.
parole.testo: Contraction of aroma philosophorum, from Latin.

parole.significato: To direct.
parole.testo: From Latin arrēctus, perfect participle of arrigō.

parole.significato: Synonym of erector.
parole.testo: From Latin arrigō (“to raise, erect”).

parole.significato: Any of the small muscles attached to hair follicles in mammals, the contraction of which causes the hairs to stand on e…
parole.testo: Latin.

parole.significato: The act of taking away; removal
parole.testo: From Latin arripere, arreptum (“to seize, snatch”), from ad + rapere (“to snatch”). See rapacious.

parole.significato: Possessed; raving; isolated from reality.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin arreptīcius.

parole.significato: Of, from or pertaining to Arezzo, Italy.
parole.testo: From Latin ārrētīnus, from Ārrētium (“Arezzo”) + -īnus (relation suffix).

parole.significato: Money or some other valuable item given to evidence a contract; a pledge or earnest.
parole.testo: From Latin arrha (“deposit, pledge”).

parole.significato: To please; to gratify.
parole.testo: From Latin arrīdēre, from ad + rīdēre (“to laugh”).

parole.significato: Arrogance.
parole.testo: From Latin arrogāntia.

parole.significato: To appropriate or lay claim to something for oneself without right.
parole.testo: From Latin arrogātus, perfect passive participle of adrogō, arrogō (“ask of, adopt, appropriate, assume”), from ad (“to”) + rogō (“ask”).

parole.significato: The wasting away of a vessel wall under pressure.
parole.testo: From Latin arrodere, arrosum (“to gnaw”). Compare French arrosion.

parole.significato: The medieval music of Europe during the High Middle Ages, between approximately 1170 and 1310.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin ars antīqua (literally “old art”).

parole.significato: Synonym of art for art's sake.
parole.testo: Latin translation of French l'art pour l'art. See the main entry for more.

parole.significato: A musical style that flourished in the Kingdom of France and its surroundings during the Late Middle Ages, particularly…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin ars nova (literally “new art”). Compare art nouveau.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Parthian dynasty established by Arsaces I which ruled the Parthian Empire during 247 BC – 224 A…
parole.testo: From Latin Arsacidēs, from Ancient Greek Ἀρσακίδης (Arsakídēs), from Ancient Greek Ἀρσάκης (Arsákēs, “Arsaces”) [from Old Persian 𐎠𐎼𐏁𐎣 (a-r-š-k /⁠aršaka-⁠/); see there for more] + -ίδης (-ídēs, patronymic suffix). By surface analysis, Arsaces + -id.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to, or containing, arsenic.
parole.testo: From Latin arsenicum + -al.

parole.significato: Raising of the voice in prosody, accented part of a metrical foot
parole.testo: From Latin Arsis, from Ancient Greek ἄρσις (ársis, “elevation”).

parole.parola: art is long, life is short
parole.significato: Art is more enduring than an individual's lifetime.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin ars longa, vīta brevis

parole.significato: A square foresail on a Roman oared ship.
parole.testo: From Latin artemōn (“foresail”).

parole.significato: Synonym of artery.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin artēria (“a windpipe; an artery”), from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓ρτηρῐ́ᾱ (ărtērĭ́ā). Doublet of artery.

parole.significato: The innominate artery or brachiocephalic artery.
parole.testo: From Latin artēria (“artery”) and innōmināta (“unnamed”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the arteries; arterial.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin arteriacus, from Ancient Greek ἀρτηριακός (artēriakós). By surface analysis, artery + -ac.

parole.significato: The opening of an artery, especially for bloodletting.
parole.testo: Latin arteriotomia.

parole.significato: Synonym of liberal arts
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin artēs līberālēs (literally “dignified arts”).

parole.significato: Synonym of servile arts
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin artēs servīlēs (literally “slave arts”).

parole.significato: Of, or affected by arthritis.
parole.testo: From Latin arthriticus (“gouty, arthritic”), from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: Inflammation of a joint or joints causing pain and/or disability, swelling and stiffness, and due to various causes suc…
parole.testo: From Latin arthrītis, from Ancient Greek ἀρθρῖτις (arthrîtis, “joint-disease, gout”), from ἄρθρον (árthron, “a joint”). By surface analysis, arthr- + -itis.

parole.significato: Of, at, or relating to the joints of the body.
parole.testo: From Latin articularis. By surface analysis, article + -ar.

parole.significato: To make clear or effective.
parole.testo: The adjective is first attested in 1531, the verb in 1551; borrowed from Latin articulātus (“distinct, articulated, jointed”), perfect passive participle of articulō, see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3). Regular participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English.

parole.significato: A joint of the cirri of the Crinoidea.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin articulus. Doublet of article.

parole.significato: Using, exhibiting, performed with or characterized by artfulness or skill
parole.testo: Latin artificiosus.

parole.significato: The Artotyrites.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: A flower or plant in the genus Arum
parole.testo: From the botanical name Arum, from Latin arum, from Ancient Greek ἄρον (áron).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or resembling a reed or cane
parole.testo: From Latin arundinaceus, from arundo (“reed”).

parole.significato: Abounding in reeds; reedy.
parole.testo: From Latin arundineus, from arundo (“reed”).

parole.significato: A member of the Arverns or Arverni, the ancient Gaulish (Celtic) tribe which inhabited what is now the Auvergne region…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Arvernus, borrowed from Gaulish.

parole.significato: An ancient, powerful Gallic tribe living in what is now the Auvergne region of France, who opposed the Romans on severa…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin Arvernī m pl.

parole.significato: field mouse (US, Canada), vole
parole.testo: From Latin arvum (“field”) + colo (“to inhabit”); compare Italian arvicola.

parole.significato: That inhabits meadows; rural
parole.testo: From Latin arvum (“field”) + colo (“to inhabit”) + -īnus.

parole.significato: arable farming
parole.testo: From Latin arvum (“field”) + cultura (“cultivation”).

parole.significato: A libra, a Roman pound.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin as. Doublet of ace.

parole.significato: Away from.
parole.testo: Assimilated form of ab- + before -s-, from Latin ab (“of, off, from, away”).

parole.significato: An acrid herbaceous plant, Asarum europaeum, the leaves and roots of which were used for emetic and cathartic purposes.
parole.testo: From Latin asarum + baccar.

parole.significato: Synonym of ascendable (“Capable of being ascended; climbable”).
parole.testo: Latin ascendibilis.

parole.significato: ascians
parole.testo: From Latin asciī, plural of ascius, from Ancient Greek ἄσκῐος (áskĭos, “shadowless”).

parole.significato: An accumulation of fluid in the peritoneal cavity, frequently symptomatic of liver disease.
parole.testo: From Latin ascītēs, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀσκίτης (askítēs), from ἀσκός (askós, “wineskin”).

parole.significato: Any one of the children of Asclepius and Epione (or Aristodama).
parole.testo: From Latin Asclēpiadēs, from Ancient Greek Ἀσκληπιάδης (Asklēpiádēs).

parole.significato: A choriambic verse consisting of four metrical feet: a spondee, two choriambi, and an iambus. First used by the ancient…
parole.testo: From Latin Asclēpiadēus, from Ancient Greek Ἀσκληπιάδειος (Asklēpiádeios), from Ἀσκληπιάδης (Asklēpiádēs) + -ειος (-eios).

parole.significato: ascus
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting a New Latin combining form, from Latin ascus via back-formation from Ascomycetes, which see.

parole.significato: Ascribed to.
parole.testo: Short for Latin āscrīptus (“ascribed to”).

parole.significato: ascribed
parole.testo: From Latin ascriptitius, from ascribere.

parole.significato: A person from the continent of Asia, or a descendant thereof - especially:
parole.testo: From Latin āsiānus. By surface analysis, Asia + -an. The modern North American and Australasian usage, referring to East and Southeast Asians collectively, seems to be a shortened form of "Asian American", a term whose origins activists and academics trace back to 1968 and University of California,

parole.significato: One of the chiefs or pontiffs of the Roman province of Asia, who had the superintendence of the public games and religi…
parole.testo: From Latin Asiarcha, from Ancient Greek Ἀσιάρχης (Asiárkhēs).

parole.significato: Asian, specifically, relating to the parts of Asia east of Egypt, i.e the Middle East or West Asia.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin āsiāticus; equivalent to Asia + -atic.

parole.significato: Synonym of asinine (“ass-like, donkey-like, in sutbbornness, foolishness, or other ways”).
parole.testo: From Latin asinārius.

parole.significato: The killing of an idiot.
parole.testo: From Latin asinus (“donkey, ass; idiot”) + -icide. In Laura Cereta (1997; see quotation), via nonce Latin asinicīda.

parole.significato: Very foolish; failing to exercise intelligence or judgement or rationality.
parole.testo: From Latin asinīnus (“of a donkey or ass”).

parole.significato: Without a material body; incorporeal.
parole.testo: Latin asomatus, Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: Any member of the genus Aspalathus of flowering plants.
parole.testo: From Latin aspalathus, from Ancient Greek ἀσπάλαθος (aspálathos).

parole.significato: Any specific feature, part, or element of something.
parole.testo: From Middle English aspect, from Latin aspectus (“look, sight; appearance”), from aspiciō (“see; catch sight of; inspect”), from ad- (“to, towards, at”) + speciō (“look, look at, behold; observe”).

parole.significato: Capable of being seen; visible.
parole.testo: From Latin aspectabilis.

parole.significato: The act of viewing; a look.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin aspectiōnem, from aspicere (“to look at”), whence aspect. First attested in 1646.

parole.significato: To make rough or harsh.
parole.testo: From Latin asperatus, from asperare (“to make rough”), from asper (“rough”).

parole.significato: Harshness; unpleasantness.
parole.testo: From Middle English asperacione, from Latin asperationem.

parole.significato: To sprinkle.
parole.testo: From Latin aspergō (compare aspersion from the same verb).

parole.significato: An aspergillum.
parole.testo: From the verb asperge, ultimately a learned borrowing from Latin aspergō.

parole.significato: A Christian rite in which the congregation is sprinkled with water.
parole.testo: From Latin aspergō (“to sprinkle”); the rite is so called from the words "Asperges me, Domine, hyssopo et mundabor" (Psalm 51).

parole.significato: Having rough leaves.
parole.testo: Latin asper (“rough”) + folium (“leaf”).

parole.significato: A cloud formation characterized by wavy undulations in the cloud base.
parole.testo: From Latin asperitās, replacing the older undulatus asperatus. Doublet of asperity.

parole.significato: Rough, rugged, uneven.
parole.testo: From Latin asper (“rough, coarse”) + -ous.

parole.significato: To sprinkle or scatter (liquid or dust).
parole.testo: From Latin aspersus, past participle of aspergere.

parole.significato: An attack on someone's or something's reputation or good name; often in the phrase to cast aspersions upon….
parole.testo: From Latin aspersiōnem, from aspersiō (“sprinkling”).

parole.significato: A basin that holds holy water with which worshippers sprinkle themselves.
parole.testo: From Latin aspersōrium (“sprinkling-place”).

parole.significato: Synonym of aspersorium.
parole.testo: From Latin aspersōrium. By surface analysis, asperse + -ory.

parole.significato: aspersive
parole.testo: From Latin aspersōrius. By surface analysis, asperse + -ory.

parole.significato: Having a surface which is roughened by many small points or warts.
parole.testo: From Latin asperum (“harsh place”) + -ulus, diminutive + -ate.

parole.significato: Any of the flowering plants of the family Asphodelaceae, especially Asphodelus ramosus and Asphodelus albus; the flower…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin asphodelus, from Ancient Greek ἀσφόδελος (asphódelos). Doublet of daffodil.

parole.significato: The puff of air accompanying the release of a plosive or fricative consonant.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin aspīrātus.

parole.significato: The action of aspirating.
parole.testo: From aspirate + -ion or borrowed from Latin aspīrātiō.

parole.significato: To take and move to a certain other place, to carry away.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin asportō.

parole.significato: The illegal movement of goods or carrying away of a person.
parole.testo: From Latin asportatio.

parole.significato: melanoidin.
parole.testo: From Latin assare (“to roast”) + amarus (“bitter”).

parole.significato: A female assassin.
parole.testo: From Latin assassinatrix. By surface analysis, assassinate + -trix.

parole.significato: Assurance; certainty.
parole.testo: From Latin assecuratio, from assecurare.

parole.significato: To make safe or sure; to assure.
parole.testo: Latin assecurare. Doublet of assure.

parole.significato: Insincere or obsequious assent; hypocritical or pretended concurrence.
parole.testo: From Latin assentatio. See assent.

parole.significato: An obsequious flatterer; a yes man.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin assentātor, from assentari (“to assent constantly”).

parole.significato: To declare with assurance or plainly and strongly; to state positively.
parole.testo: From Latin assertus, perfect passive participle of asserō (“declare someone free or a slave by laying hands upon him; hence free from, protect, defend; lay claim to, assert, declare”), from ad (“to”) + serō (“join, range in a row”).

parole.significato: The act of asserting; positive declaration or averment.
parole.testo: From Middle English assercioun, from Latin assertiō. By surface analysis, assert + -ion.

parole.significato: assertoric
parole.testo: From Latin assertōrius, from asserō (“assert”).

parole.significato: To assert earnestly, seriously, and confidently
parole.testo: From Latin assevērāre, from assevērō (“to assert”).

parole.significato: An earnest affirmation; a declaration of support.
parole.testo: From Latin assevērātiō, from assevērō.

parole.significato: To change into or pronounce with the accompaniment of a sibilant sound or sounds.
parole.testo: From Latin assībilātus (“murmured, whispered at, hissed”), past participle of assībilō (“hiss at”, verb), from ad (“at”) + sībilō (“hiss”, verb), from sībilus (“a hissing, whistling”), of imitative origin.

parole.significato: Of a symptom, generally, but not always, accompanying a disease; indicative of the presence of a disease but not a nece…
parole.testo: From Latin assideō (“to be beside”).

parole.significato: unremitting, requiring a lot of effort
parole.testo: From Latin assiduātus, past participle of assiduō (“to apply constantly”).

parole.significato: Great and persistent toil or effort.
parole.testo: From Latin assiduitas, from Latin assiduus. Equivalent to assiduous + -ity.

parole.significato: Hard-working, diligent or regular (in attendance or work); industrious.
parole.testo: A learned borrowing from Latin assiduus, from assidere (“to sit down to”), from ad- (“to”) + sedere (“to sit”). Compare sedulous. Cognate (via assidere) to assess.

parole.significato: Capable of being assimilated; susceptible to assimilation.
parole.testo: From Latin assimilabilis.

parole.significato: Synonym of assimilation.
parole.testo: From as- + similitude, from Latin similitūdō, from similis + -tūdō. By surface analysis, Latin simil(is) + -itude.

parole.significato: To assimilate.
parole.testo: From Latin assimulatus, past participle of assimulare, equivalent to assimilare. See assimilate.

parole.significato: Joined with another or others and having lower status.
parole.testo: From Middle English associat(e) (used participially as well as adjectively up to Early Modern English), from Latin associātus, the perfect passive participle of associō (“to join, unite”), from ad- + sociō, from socius (“shared, common, kindred”) + -ō (first conjugation verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The act of associating.
parole.testo: From Latin associātiō, from associō (perhaps via French association). Morphologically associate + -ion. The Philippine sense is a calque of Spanish gremio.

parole.significato: Characterized by assonance; having successive similar vowel sounds.
parole.testo: From Latin assonāns, present participle of assonō.

parole.significato: To correspond or exhibit agreement in (particularly vowel) sounds.
parole.testo: From Latin assonō, from ad (“to, towards”) + sonō (“to sound, resound”).

parole.significato: Accustomedness; habit.
parole.testo: From Latin assuetudo, from assuetus (“accustomed”).

parole.significato: To authenticate by means of belief; to surmise; to suppose to be true, especially without proof.
parole.testo: From Latin assūmō (“accept, take”), from ad- (“to, towards, at”) + sūmō (“take up, assume”).

parole.significato: A patch; an addition; a piece put on.
parole.testo: From Latin assūmentum.

parole.significato: A promise or undertaking, either express or implied, founded on a consideration.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin assūmpsit (“he undertook”), preterite of assūmere. Doublet of assume.

parole.significato: That which is assumed; an assumption.
parole.testo: From Latin assumptum, past participle neuter of assumō.

parole.significato: The introduction of a proposition into a speech, especially an extraneous one.
parole.testo: From Latin assūmptiō. Doublet of assumption.

parole.significato: The act of assuming, or taking to or upon oneself; the act of taking up or adopting.
parole.testo: From Middle English assumpcioun, from Medieval Latin assūmptiō (“a taking up (into heaven)”) and Latin assūmptiō (“a taking up, adoption, the minor proposition of a syllogism”) (whence -ion), from Latin assūmō (whence as- (“assimilated form of ad-”). See also assume. Doublet of assumptio.

parole.significato: Held as true or valid without evidence.
parole.testo: From as- + Latin sūmptus + -ive, from past participle of sūmō (“to take”).

parole.significato: Rising or tending to rise.
parole.testo: From Latin assurgens, present participle of assurgo (“rise up”).

parole.significato: Synonym of Assyrian
parole.testo: From Latin Assyriacus, from Ancient Greek Ἀσσυριακός (Assuriakós).

parole.significato: Witty dialog or response.
parole.testo: From Latin astĕïsmŏs (“the more refined style of speaking”), from Ancient Greek ἀστείσμός (asteísmós).

parole.significato: Any of several plants of the genus Aster; one of its flowers.
parole.testo: From Latin astēr, from Ancient Greek ἀστήρ (astḗr). Doublet of star; related to estoile, étoile, stella, and stelo.

parole.significato: Relating to stars.
parole.testo: From Latin aster, from Ancient Greek ἀστήρ (astḗr).

parole.significato: One of the otoliths found in the lagena of many nonmammalian vertebrates.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin asteriscus. Doublet of asterisk.

parole.significato: Having the characteristics of asthma.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin āsthmaticus. By surface analysis, asthma + -ic.

parole.significato: To assent.
parole.testo: From Latin astipulari, from ad- + stipulari (“to stipulate”).

parole.significato: stipulation; agreement
parole.testo: Latin astipulatio.

parole.significato: Pertaining to the astragalus, the anklebone
parole.testo: By surface analysis, astragal(us) + -o-, ultimately from Latin astragalus, from Ancient Greek ἀστράγαλος (astrágalos).

parole.significato: Synonym of anklebone.
parole.testo: From Latin astragalus, from Ancient Greek ἀστράγαλος (astrágalos). Doublet of astragal.

parole.significato: To bind, constrain, or restrict.
parole.testo: From Latin astrictus, past participle of astringere. See astringe.

parole.significato: The act of binding; restriction; obligation.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin astrictio.

parole.significato: Bearing stars.
parole.testo: From Latin astrifer, from astrum (“star”) + ferre (“to bear”).

parole.significato: A substance which draws tissue together, thus restricting the flow of blood.
parole.testo: From Latin adstringere (“to bind fast”), from ad (“toward”) + stringere (“bind, pull tight”). Compare stringent.

parole.significato: Synonym of astroite.
parole.testo: Latin astroites: compare French astroite.

parole.significato: That rules the stars.
parole.testo: From Latin astripotens, likely through Middle French astripotent.

parole.significato: Synonym of astroite.
parole.testo: Latin astroites: compare French astroite.

parole.significato: A radiated fossil or stone; a starstone.
parole.testo: Latin astroites: compare French astroite.

parole.significato: One who studies or practices astrology.
parole.testo: From Middle English astrologer, astrologier, astrologere, formed from Middle English astrologie or Latin astrologus + Middle English -ere, equivalent to astrology + -er. Ousted imported Middle English astrologien (“astrologer”), borrowed from Old French astrologien. Displaced Old English tungolwītga

parole.significato: An astrologer.
parole.testo: From Middle English astrolog, from Latin astrologus. Equivalent to astro- + -logue.

parole.significato: Divination by the stars; astrology in its modern prophetic aspect.
parole.testo: From astro- + -mancy. From Latin astromantīa, from Ancient Greek ἀστρομαντεία (astromanteía), from ἄστρον (ástron, “star”) + μαντεία (manteía, “divination”).

parole.significato: constructive.
parole.testo: From Latin astructus, past participle of astruere (“to build up”), from ad + struere (“to build”).

parole.significato: Quickly and critically discerning.
parole.testo: From Latin astūtus, from astus (“craft”).

parole.significato: A place of safety or refuge.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin asȳlum, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἄσυλον (ásulon).

parole.significato: A pattern of spoken or written discourse demonstrating inability or diminished capacity to connect ideas.
parole.testo: From Latin asyndesis, from Ancient Greek ἀσύνδεσις (asúndesis), from ἀ- (a-, “a-, un-: without”) + σύνδεσις (súndesis, “binding, joining”), from συνδεῖν (sundeîn, “to join, to bind”) + -σῐς (-sĭs, “-sis: forming nouns”), from σῠν- (sŭn-, “together”) + δεῖν (deîn, “to bind, to tie”). Equivalent to a-

parole.significato: Omission of conjunctions, especially for rhetorical effect.
parole.testo: From Latin asyndeton, from Ancient Greek ἀσύνδετον (asúndeton), from ἀ- (a-, “a-, un-, non-”) and the neuter substantive of σῠ́νδετος (sŭ́ndetos, “bound, joined”), from συνδεῖν (sundeîn, “to join, to bind”), from σῠν- (sŭn-, “together”) + δεῖν (deîn, “to bind, to tie”). Equivalent to a- + syndeton.

parole.significato: Prefix meaning at, close to, to, away, off.
parole.testo: Assimilated form of ad- before t. From Latin ad-.

parole.significato: Of, from, or pertaining to Atella in ancient Italy.
parole.testo: From Latin Atellanus, from Atella (“an ancient town of the Osci, in Campania”).

parole.significato: imperturbability, ataraxia
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin athambia, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀθαμβία (athambía), from θάμβος (thámbos).

parole.significato: A woman who colludes with the patriarchy rather than actively opposing it.
parole.testo: From Middle English Athena, from Latin Athēna, from Ancient Greek Ἀθηνᾶ (Athēnâ). Doublet of Athina.

parole.significato: An inhabitant, resident, or citizen of Athens, Greece.
parole.testo: From Latin athēniēnsis; compare Middle English Athenyensis pl and Old English Athēniense pl. By surface analysis, Athens + -ian.

parole.significato: An abnormal fatty deposit which develops within the walls of arteries.
parole.testo: From Latin athērōma (“tumor/mass full of gruel-like matter”), from Ancient Greek ἀθήρωμα (athḗrōma). By surface analysis, ather- + -oma.

parole.significato: A participant in any of a group of sporting activities including track and field, road running, cross country running a…
parole.testo: From Middle English athlete, from Latin āthlēta (and probably also partly from Middle French athlete), from Ancient Greek ἀθλητής (athlētḗs), from ἀθλέω (athléō, “compete for a prize”), from ἆθλον (âthlon, “prize”) or ἆθλος (âthlos, “competition”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to the Atlantic Ocean.
parole.testo: From Middle English Atlantyke, from Latin Ā̆tlanticus, from Ancient Greek Ἀτλαντικός (Atlantikós, “Atlantean, of Atlas”), from Ancient Greek Ἄτλᾱς (Átlās), either from ἁ- (ha-, copulative prefix) + Proto-Indo-European *telh₂- (“bear, undergo, endure”) or of Pre-Greek origin.

parole.significato: A bound collection of maps often including tables, illustrations or other text.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Atlas, from the name of the Ancient Greek mythological figure Ἄτλας (Átlas, “Bearer (of the Heavens)”), from τλῆναι (tlênai, “to suffer”, “to endure”, “to bear”). The sense referring to books of maps comes from the Atlas of Mercator, which he named thus in honor of Atlas, who was

parole.significato: Synonym of atom.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin atomus, from Ancient Greek ἄτομος (átomos). Doublet of atom.

parole.significato: A tiny particle; an atom, a mote, a speck.
parole.testo: A variant of atomi, the plural of atomus (“hypothetical particle posited as an ultimate and indivisible component of matter; mote of dust in a sunbeam”) treated as a singular form. Atomus is derived from Latin atomus, from Ancient Greek ἄτομος (átomos, “indivisible”, adjective), from ᾰ̓- (ă-, prefix

parole.significato: Characterized by melancholy or glum; atrabilarious; atrabilious.
parole.testo: From Latin ātra bīlis (“black bile”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to black bile.
parole.testo: From Latin ātrabīlārius.

parole.significato: Of or relating to black bile.
parole.testo: From Latin ātra bīlis (“black bile”) (āter (“dark, black”) + bīlis (“bile”)) + -ary.

parole.significato: Having an excess of black bile.
parole.testo: From Latin ātra bīlis (“black bile”) (āter (“dark, black”) + bīlis (“bile”)) + -ous (“full of”), referring to the humour which ancient Hippocratic and later Galenic medicine associated with sadness and despondency.

parole.significato: Ink or an inklike substance.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English atrament, from Latin ātrāmentum, from ātrāre (“to blacken”), from āter (“black”). First attested in the 14th century.

parole.significato: Like ink; suitable for making ink.
parole.testo: From Latin ātrāmentārius (“pertaining to ink”), from ātrāmentārium (“inkstand”) + -ius. Compare French atramentaire.

parole.significato: Synonym of inky, black, inklike.
parole.testo: From Latin ātrāmentōsus, from ātrāmentum (“black liquid, ink”). Equivalent to atrament + -ous.

parole.significato: A condition in which a body orifice or passage in the body is abnormally closed or absent.
parole.testo: From Latin atresia, from Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “not, without”) and τρῆσις (trêsis, “perforation”).

parole.significato: A central room or space in ancient Roman homes, open to the sky in the middle; a similar space in other buildings.
parole.testo: From Latin ātrium (“entry hall”), from Etruscan.

parole.significato: Frightful, evil, cruel, or monstrous.
parole.testo: From Latin atrōx (“cruel, fierce, frightful”) + -ious.

parole.significato: Synonym of Atropatian
parole.testo: From Latin Atropatēnus, from Ancient Greek Ἀτροπατηνός (Atropatēnós), from Ἀτροπάτης (Atropátēs, “Atropates”) + -ηνός (-ēnós). By surface analysis, Atropates + -ene.

parole.significato: Jet-black in color.
parole.testo: From Latin āter (“dark, black”) + -ous.

parole.significato: An endopeptidase enzyme, found in the venom of the diamondback rattlesnake Crotalus atrox, that catalyzes the cleavage…
parole.testo: From Latin atrox + -ase.

parole.significato: An ancient privilege granted to forest officers to take for their own any thorns, brushwood, and windfalls within their…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin attachiamenta de spinis et boscis.

parole.significato: A grey partridge (Perdix perdix) of Eurasia.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin attagēn.

parole.significato: tempered; proportioned; properly adapted.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin attemperatus. Doublet of attemper.

parole.significato: Attentive, heedful; intent.
parole.testo: From Latin attentus.

parole.significato: Anything whatsoever, as a ruling, by the judge of a lower court in a matter pending an appeal.
parole.testo: A variant of attemptate assimilated to Latin attentātus and French attentat.

parole.significato: Mental focus.
parole.testo: From Middle English attencioun, borrowed from Latin attentio, attentionis, from attendere, past participle attentus (“to attend, give heed to”); see attend. Equivalent to attend + -tion.

parole.significato: archaic Making thin; diluting or thinning; rendering less dense and viscid.
parole.testo: From Latin attenuans, present participle of attenuare: compare French atténuant. See attenuate.

parole.significato: To reduce in size, force, value, amount, or degree.
parole.testo: The verb is first attested in 1530, the adjective in 1626; borrowed from Latin attenuātus, the perfect passive participle of attenuō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from ad- (“to, towards, at”) + tenuo (“to make thin”), itself from tenuis (“thin”) + -ō (verb-for

parole.significato: A gradual diminishing of strength.
parole.testo: From Middle English attenuacioun, a borrowing from Latin attenuātiō (“a diminishing”). Equivalent to attenuate + -ion.

parole.significato: Of or related to Attica, ancient Athens and its hinterland
parole.testo: From Latin Atticus, from Ancient Greek Ἀττικός (Attikós), from some Pre-Greek demonym or toponym for Athens and its hinterland of Attica + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic: forming adjectives”). Equivalent to a modified and clipped Athens + -ic. Doublet of Atticus.

parole.significato: Pointed and delicate wit.
parole.testo: Attic + salt; a calque of Latin sāl Atticus or sāl Atticum. In classical times “salt” was a frequent metaphor for “wit”.

parole.significato: Epitympanic recess or the uppermost part of the middle ear cavity located above the tympanic membrane and containing th…
parole.testo: From Latin atticus, from Ancient Greek Ἀττικός (Attikós) + -o-. By surface analysis, attic + -o-.

parole.significato: To touch lightly.
parole.testo: From Latin attingō (“to touch”). Doublet of attain and attainder.

parole.significato: The property of being attingent; adjacency.
parole.testo: From atting(ent) + -ence, ultimately from Latin attingēns (“touching”, passive participle), from Latin attingō (“to touch; to come into contact with”, verb).

parole.significato: touching; adjacent
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin attingēns (“touching”, passive participle), from Latin attingō (“to touch; to come into contact with”, verb). Further from Latin tangō (“to touch, to grasp”, verb), from Proto-Italic *tangō and Proto-Indo-European *teh₂g-, both verbs of the same meaning.

parole.significato: Expressive of or pertaining to attitude.
parole.testo: From Italian attitudine + -al, from Latin aptitūdin- + -al, from oblique stem of Latin aptitūdō, from aptus + -tūdō. By surface analysis, attitude + -al.

parole.significato: One who attitudinizes; one who postures or behaves in a stilted and pretentious manner.
parole.testo: From Italian attitudine + -arian, from Latin aptitūdin- + -arian, from oblique stem of Latin aptitūdō, from aptus + -tūdō. By surface analysis, attitude + -arian.

parole.significato: To cause (someone or something) to assume an attitude or pose; to pose, to posture.
parole.testo: From Italian attitudine + -ize, from Latin aptitūdin- + -ize, from oblique stem of Latin aptitūdō, from aptus + -tūdō. By surface analysis, attitude + -ize.

parole.significato: Having a bold and possibly unfriendly attitude; sassy.
parole.testo: From Italian attitudine + -ous, from Latin aptitūdin- + -ous, from oblique stem of Latin aptitūdō, from aptus + -tūdō. By surface analysis, attitude + -ous.

parole.significato: Lifting up, raising (said of muscles, especially the levator palpebrae superioris ).
parole.testo: From Latin attollens, present participle of attollo; ad + tollo (“to lift”).

parole.significato: To pull toward without touching.
parole.testo: From Latin attractus, past participle of attrahere (“to draw to, attract”), from ad (“to”) + trahere (“to draw”).

parole.significato: That attracts; drawing, attracting.
parole.testo: From attrahent-, the stem of the Latin attrahēns (“drawing, pulling, or dragging to or toward with force”; “drawing”, “alluring”, “leading”, “bringing”, “moving”, “attracting”), the present active participle of attrahō (“to draw, pull, or drag to or toward with force”; “to draw, allure, lead, bring,

parole.significato: Frequent handling or touching; fingering.
parole.testo: From Latin attrectatio, from ad + tractare (“to handle”).

parole.significato: A characteristic or quality of a thing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin attributus.

parole.significato: One who attributes; an imputer.
parole.testo: From the Latin attribūtor.

parole.significato: To wear down through attrition, especially mechanical attrition.
parole.testo: From Latin attrītus, past participle of atterō. Said by multiple dictionaries to be a back-formation from attrition, but it is not a recent one, being centuries old.

parole.significato: Regretful of one's wrongdoing merely due to fear of punishment.
parole.testo: From Latin attrītus (“ground”).

parole.significato: material pulverized by attrition
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: According to the Roman era, which reckons the number of years passed from the foundation of the city of Rome by Romulus…
parole.testo: From Latin AUC, (anno) ab urbe condita (“from the founding of the city”) or anno urbis conditae (“in the year of the city's having been founded”), both in reference to Rome's legendary establishment by Romulus. The era was not in common use by the Romans, who preferred dating by the years' consuls,

parole.significato: A public event where goods or property are sold to the highest bidder.
parole.testo: From Latin auctiō (“an increase, auction”), from augere (“to increase”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to an auction.
parole.testo: Latin auctionarius.

parole.significato: A class of natural faculty.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin auctrīx.

parole.significato: To hunt, to seek with vigilance.
parole.testo: From Latin aucupātus.

parole.significato: Showing willingness to take bold risks; recklessly daring.
parole.testo: From Latin audacia (“boldness”) + -ious, from audax (“bold”), from audeō (“to be bold, to dare”).

parole.significato: A non-competitive long-distance (often over 200 km) cycling event.
parole.testo: From Latin audāx, via Italian.

parole.significato: "Hear both sides." A legal principle of fairness given to ensure that the accused has the chance to refute an accusatio…
parole.testo: From Latin audī (second-person singular present active imperative of audiō (“hear”)) + alteram (feminine accusative singular of alter (“the other”)) + partem (accusative singular of pars (“part, side”)).

parole.significato: Listening, paying attention.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin audientem, accusative singular of audiēns (“hearing, listening; attending, paying attention to”) (or directly from audiēns), the present active participle of audiō (“to hear, listen to; to attend, pay attention to”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewis (“clearly, manifestly”) (from

parole.significato: Audibly.
parole.testo: From Latin audient- + -ly. Compare later audient.

parole.significato: A person whose mental imagery consists of sounds.
parole.testo: Irregular formation from Latin audire + -ilis. By surface analysis, audio + -ile.

parole.significato: Sound.
parole.testo: From the root audi of Latin audiō (“to hear; to listen”) + -o-. Cognates include Proto-Germanic *awiz (“obvious”), Sanskrit आविस् (āvís, “manifestly, evidently”) and Ancient Greek αἰσθάνομαι (aisthánomai, “perceive, notice”) whence English aesthetic.

parole.significato: An early electronic amplifying tube consisting of a partially evacuated glass tube with three electrodes, a heated fila…
parole.testo: Neologism based on Latin audio (“to hear”).

parole.significato: A judicial examination.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin audītus, from audiō (“to hear”). The sense of examine is because examinations were originally presented orally, and the examiner listened.

parole.significato: A writ which lies for a party against whom judgment is recovered, but to whom good matter of discharge has subsequently…
parole.testo: Latin audita querela (“the complaint having been heard”).

parole.significato: A large room for public meetings or performances.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin audītōrium, from audītōrius (“pertaining to hearing”). Equivalent to auditory + -ium.

parole.significato: Of, or relating to hearing, or to the sense or organs of hearing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin audītōrius (“pertaining to a hearer or hearing”), from audiō (“to hear”) + -tōrius (“-tory”, adjectival suffix).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or characteristic of Augeas.
parole.testo: From Latin Augeas + -an. Augeas is a figure in Greek mythology whose stables were never cleaned until Hercules was given the task of cleaning them.

parole.significato: A quantity to which another is added.
parole.testo: From Latin augendum.

parole.significato: A variety of pyroxene, usually of a black or dark green color, occurring in igneous rocks, such as basalt.
parole.testo: From Latin augītēs.

parole.significato: A diviner who foretells events by the behaviour of birds or other animals, or by signs derived from celestial phenomena…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin augur, of uncertain origin; akin to augurō (“interpret omens”).

parole.significato: prophetic
parole.testo: From Latin augurālis. By surface analysis, augur + -al.

parole.significato: The position or office of an augur.
parole.testo: From Latin augurātus (“augurate”). By surface analysis, augur + -ate (forms nouns denoting rank or office).

parole.significato: To make or take auguries; to augur; to predict.
parole.testo: From Latin augurātus, perfect passive participle of augurō (“to predict, foretell”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). By surface analysis, augur + -ate.

parole.significato: augury; divination
parole.testo: From Latin auguratio.

parole.significato: Relating to augurs or to augury.
parole.testo: Latin augurialis.

parole.significato: Pertaining to the times of the Roman emperor Augustus (63 B.C.E. - 14 C.E.).
parole.testo: From the Latin Augustānus, from Augustus, a Roman emperor who ruled a period of peace and prosperity known as the Pax Romana or Pax Augusta.

parole.significato: An Augustinian.
parole.testo: From Latin Augustīnus, derivative of Augustus. Doublet of Austin.

parole.significato: Of, or relating to St Augustine of Hippo or his doctrines, especially on predestination and grace.
parole.testo: From Middle English Augustinen, from Latin Augustīniānus, from Augustīnus + -iānus, after Augustine of Hippo. By surface analysis, Augustine + -ian.

parole.significato: A member of a supposed radical group of the early Reformation, who allegedly believed that humans would not enter Heave…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Augustīniānī pl, from Augustīnus + -iānus, after an unidentified person so named. By surface analysis, Augustine + -ian.

parole.significato: A court or hall.
parole.testo: From Latin aula (“forecourt”), from Ancient Greek αὐλά (aulá), the form of αὐλή (aulḗ, “forecourt”) in dialects other than Ionic and Attic.

parole.significato: A great hall or large classroom used for special occasions at a university.
parole.testo: From Latin aula (“hall”) magna (“great”).

parole.significato: A tail-like longitudinally differentiated appendage found in mitrates and cornutes, originally believed to be used for…
parole.testo: From Latin aulax (“furrow”) or its etymon Ancient Greek αὖλαξ (aûlax, “furrow”) + -phore (“bearer, carrier”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to a musical pipe or piper.
parole.testo: Latin auleticus, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a royal court; courtly.
parole.testo: From Latin aulicus (“of a prince's court”), from aula (“royal court”), from Ancient Greek αὐλή (aulḗ, “courtyard”).

parole.significato: gold
parole.testo: First productive in the 1575 coinage auripotent: representing aur-, the stem of the Latin aurum (“gold”).

parole.significato: ear
parole.testo: First productive in the 1678 coinage aurist: representing aur-, the stem of the Latin auris (“ear”).

parole.significato: A subtle emanation or exhalation of any substance, such as an aroma or odour.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin aura (“a breeze, a breath of air, the air”), from Ancient Greek αὔρα (aúra, “breeze, soft wind”), from ἀήρ (aḗr, “air”). Doublet of east, auster, air, and aria. Sense 4 originated in the early 2020s and was popularized on TikTok around May 2024.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the ear.
parole.testo: From Latin auralis, from auris (“ear”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to an aura.
parole.testo: From Latin aura (“moving air, breeze, vital air”) + -al.

parole.significato: Having or resembling ears.
parole.testo: Coined based on Latin auris (“ear”).

parole.significato: Golden in color or shine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aureatus (“adorned or decorated with gold”). Equivalent to Latin aureus (“golden, gilded”) + -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The enhancement of the seriousness of a topic by the use of elaborate circumlocutions or polysyllabic or Latinate words…
parole.testo: From aureate + -ion, from Latin aureatus (“decorated with gold”).

parole.significato: The particular property peculiar to gold; goldenness.
parole.testo: From Latin aureitās, with the suffix adapted to -ity.

parole.significato: Characteristic of the Roman emperor Aurelius
parole.testo: From Latin Aurelianus, derivative of the gens name Aurelius (“golden”).

parole.significato: Radiance of luminous cloud that surrounds the figure in a painting of a sacred personage.
parole.testo: From Latin aurea (“golden”) + -ola.

parole.significato: A yellow pigment used in painting, composed of potassium cobaltinitrite.
parole.testo: From Latin aureolus + suffix -in.

parole.significato: A gold coin, minted in the Roman Empire from approximately 100 B.C.E. to 309 C.E., equal to 25 denarii.
parole.testo: From Latin aureus (“golden; gold coin equivalent to 25 denarii”), noun use of adjective, from aurum (“gold”). Doublet of eyrir, öre, øre, and oyra.

parole.significato: Any appendage in the shape of an ear or earlobe.
parole.testo: From Latin auricula (“the external ear”), diminutive of auris (“the ear”). Doublet of auricula.

parole.significato: Having golden hair; yellow-haired.
parole.testo: From Latin auricomus (“golden-haired”), from aurum (“gold”) + coma (“hair of the head”). Compare English floricomous.

parole.significato: The external part of the ear.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin auricula (“external ear; ear”). Doublet of auricle.

parole.significato: The larvae of the sea cucumber.
parole.testo: From Latin auriculāria (“ear-shaped things”).

parole.significato: Containing or producing gold; gold-bearing.
parole.testo: From Latin aurifer (“gold-bearing”) + the English suffix -ous. The Latin term in turn derived from aurum (“gold”) + ferō (“to carry”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a chariot.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aurīgālis, from aurīga (“charioteer”).

parole.significato: The act of driving a chariot or a carriage.
parole.testo: From Latin aurigatio, from aurigare "to be a charioteer", from auriga.

parole.significato: The art of writing with or in gold.
parole.testo: From Latin aurum (“gold”) + -graphy.

parole.significato: A red colouring matter derived from phenol. Used as an indicator.
parole.testo: From Latin aurum (“gold”) + -in.

parole.significato: An earpick.
parole.testo: From Latin auris (“ear”) + scalpere (“to scrape”).

parole.significato: Auriscalpium, a genus of mushrooms.
parole.testo: The word is compounded of the Latin auris (“ear”) and scalpo (“to scratch”).

parole.significato: Gold-devouring.
parole.testo: From Latin aurum + -vorous.

parole.significato: An atmospheric phenomenon created by charged particles from the sun striking the upper atmosphere, creating coloured li…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin aurōra (“dawn”). Doublet of Eos.

parole.significato: Belonging to the dawn, or resembling it in brilliant hue.
parole.testo: Either the Latin aurōre(us) + the English -an or formed from the two English elements auror(a) + -ean.

parole.significato: Gold in color.
parole.testo: From Latin aurulentus (“golden”).

parole.significato: Gold (used in the names of various substances, see "Derived terms").
parole.testo: From Latin aurum (“gold”). Doublet of or.

parole.significato: Diagnosis of disorders by listening to the sounds of the internal organs, usually using a stethoscope.
parole.testo: From Latin auscultātio (“act of listening”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to auscultation
parole.testo: Probably from Latin auscultātor (“listener, heeder”) + -y

parole.significato: Of ancient Ausonia or the Ausonians.
parole.testo: From Latin Ausonia (“Lower Italy”), extended poetically to “Italy”, from Ancient Greek Αὐσονία (Ausonía), from Αὔσων (Aúsōn), a son of Ulysses, who is said to have settled there.

parole.significato: To foreshow; to foretoken.
parole.testo: From Latin auspicatus, past participle of auspicari "to take auspices", from auspex "bird seer", "augur", a contraction of avispex; avis "bird" + specere, spicere, "to view".

parole.significato: Of good omen; indicating future success.
parole.testo: From auspice + -ious, from Latin auspicium (“augury”), from auspex (“augur”), possibly via French.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or coming from the south.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin australis (“southern”).

parole.significato: Southern.
parole.testo: From Latin australis (“southern”), from Latin auster (“south wind”).

parole.significato: A particular polyhydroxylated pyrrolizidine alkaloid.
parole.testo: From Latin australis + -ine. By surface analysis, austral- + -ine.

parole.significato: A prenylflavonoid found in Morus australis.
parole.testo: From Latin australis + -one.

parole.significato: Southern; southerly; austral.
parole.testo: From Latin austrinus, from auster (“south”).

parole.significato: Soothsaying or divination from observing the winds or clouds.
parole.testo: From Latin auster (“south wind”); austro- + -mancy.

parole.significato: A person’s own handwriting, especially the signature of a famous or admired person.
parole.testo: From Latin autographum, in turn from Ancient Greek αὐτόγραφον (autógraphon, “a writing in one’s own hand”). Equivalent to auto- + -graph.

parole.significato: Birds that are able to run about and obtain their own food as soon as they are hatched.
parole.testo: From auto- (“by oneself”) + Latin -phagus (“eater”, plural -phagī). The attested Ancient Greek αὐτοφάγος (autophágos) would have meant "self-devouring, autophagous".

parole.significato: Of or relating to autumn.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin autumnāl(is). By surface analysis, autumn + -al.

parole.significato: auxiliary
parole.testo: From Latin auxiliaris.

parole.significato: Helping; giving assistance or support.
parole.testo: From Latin auxiliārius (“assistant, ally”), equiv. to auxiliāris (“helping, aiding”), from auxilium (“help, aid”), from augēre (“to increase”).

parole.significato: Growth or increase.
parole.testo: From Latin auxi, perfect stem of augeo (“enlarge”).

parole.significato: Avaricious.
parole.testo: Latin avarus

parole.significato: A salutation.
parole.testo: From Latin ave.

parole.significato: Hail Mary (Catholic prayer, part of the rosary)
parole.testo: From Middle English Ave Maria, Ave Marie, Ave Mary(e), from Latin Avē Marīa.

parole.significato: To pull away.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin āvellō.

parole.significato: Belonging to, or resembling, oats or the oat grasses.
parole.testo: Latin avena + -aceous

parole.significato: Having the appearance of oats.
parole.testo: From Latin avena (“oats”) + -iform.

parole.significato: Pertaining to the Aventine Hill, one of the seven hills on which Rome stood.
parole.testo: From Latin Aventinus.

parole.significato: To avert; to ward off.
parole.testo: From Latin āverruncāre (“to avert”), from āb (“off”) + verruncāre (“to turn”), but interpreted as being āb + ēruncāre (“to weed out”), and spelled accordingly.

parole.significato: Turned to show the back: said of a hand (or gauntlet).
parole.testo: From Latin āversantem, from āversāns.

parole.significato: Having a repugnance or opposition of mind.
parole.testo: From Latin aversus, past participle of avertere (“to avert”).

parole.significato: Apostrophe.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin āversiō. Doublet of aversion.

parole.significato: Opposition or repugnance of mind; fixed dislike often without any conscious reasoning.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin āversiō, āversiōnem. Doublet of aversio.

parole.significato: bird
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin avis (“bird”).

parole.significato: Characteristic of or pertaining to birds, or to bird-like or flying creatures.
parole.testo: From Latin avis (“bird”) + -ian.

parole.significato: A house, enclosure, large cage, or other place for keeping birds confined; a birdhouse.
parole.testo: From Latin aviārium, from avis (“bird”).

parole.significato: That is parasitic on birds
parole.testo: From Latin avis (“bird”) + -colous.

parole.significato: A tetrameric protein produced in the oviducts of birds, reptiles and amphibians and deposited in the whites of their eg…
