parole.testo: From Latin avidus (“hungry”) + -in, based on its "hunger" for biotin.

parole.significato: Having the shape of a bird
parole.testo: From Latin avis (“bird”) + -form.

parole.significato: Characteristic of or pertaining to birds, or to bird-like or flying creatures.
parole.testo: From Latin avis (“bird”) + -ine.

parole.significato: Relating to a grandfather or ancestor.
parole.testo: From Latin avus (“grandfather”).

parole.significato: To call off or away; to withdraw; to transfer to another tribunal.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin avoco, avocatus. Doublet of avoke.

parole.significato: A calling away; a diversion.
parole.testo: From Latin āvocātiō (“a distraction”), from āvocō (“to call off, distract”).

parole.significato: To call back again or revoke
parole.testo: Compare avocate. Ultimately from Latin āvōcō, āvōcāre.

parole.significato: To escape; to dissipate into the air.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin āvolō (“to fly away”).

parole.significato: Evaporation; dissipation into the air.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin āvolātiō (“flying away”), or formed directly from avolate + -ation.

parole.significato: To tear off forcibly.
parole.testo: From Latin avulsus, past participle of avello: ab- + vellō.

parole.significato: The loss or separation of a body part, either by surgery or due to trauma.
parole.testo: From Latin avulsio from a- + vellō.

parole.significato: The killing of one's uncle.
parole.testo: From Latin avunculus (“maternal uncle”) + -icide.

parole.significato: Characterized by couples living with the husband's maternal uncle.
parole.testo: Latin avuncul(us) (“maternal uncle”) + -o- + local.

parole.significato: Relating to the axis
parole.testo: Clipping of axis, from Latin axis.

parole.significato: The angle or point of divergence between the upper side of a branch, leaf, or petiole, and the stem or branch from whic…
parole.testo: From Latin axilla. Doublet of axilla.

parole.significato: Divination by saws or axes.
parole.testo: Latin axinomantia, from Ancient Greek ἀξινομαντεία (axinomanteía), from ἀξίνη (axínē, “axe”) and μαντεία (manteía, “prophecy”)

parole.significato: An axiom.
parole.testo: From the Latin axiōma, from the Ancient Greek ἀξίωμα (axíōma): see axiom.

parole.significato: An imaginary line around which an object spins (an axis of rotation) or is symmetrically arranged (an axis of symmetry).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin axis (“axle, axis”) in the 16th century. Via Latin cognate with ala, aisle, atelier. Via Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱs- cognate with inherited English axle and borrowed axo-, axon.

parole.significato: A deer native to Asia, of species Axis axis.
parole.testo: From Latin, name of an Indian animal mentioned by the Roman senator Pliny.

parole.significato: The axis of Earth between the celestial poles, important in ancient geocentric coordinate systems.
parole.testo: From Latin axis mundi.

parole.significato: A tribe of Pannonia
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Azalī.

parole.significato: One who administers the Eucharist with unleavened bread, in particular a member of the Latin Church or Roman Catholic C…
parole.testo: From Latin azȳmita, from Ancient Greek ἀζῡμίτης (azūmítēs), from ἄζῡμος (ázūmos) + -ῑ́της (-ī́tēs, suffix forming masculine nouns meaning being connected to or a member of something, or coming from a particular place). ἄζῡμος is derived from ᾰ̓- (ă-, the alpha privativum, a prefix forming words havi

parole.significato: unleavened, unfermented.
parole.testo: From Latin azymus (“unleavened, uncorrupted”).

parole.significato: A confused mixture of sounds and voices, especially in different languages.
parole.testo: From Latin Babel, from Biblical Hebrew בָּבֶל (bāḇel, “Babylon”), from Akkadian 𒆍𒀭𒊏𒆠 (Bābilim); in Genesis associated with the idea of confusion. Doublet of Babylon.

parole.significato: Any mammal in the genus Babyrousa in the pig family Suidae, in which the upper tusk grows upward.
parole.testo: From scientific Latin babyroussa (later as specific name), and its source, Malay babi rusa, from babi (“pig”) + rusa (“deer”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to the city of Babylon, or the Babylonian Empire.
parole.testo: From Latin Babylōnius (“of Babylon, Babylonian”) (from Ancient Greek Βαβυλώνιος (Babulṓnios)) + -an. By surface analysis, Babylon + -ian. Piecewise doublet of Babelian.

parole.significato: Pertaining to Babylon, or made there.
parole.testo: From Latin Babylōnicus.

parole.significato: Stand back! give place!
parole.testo: back and Latin -āre. A cant word of the Elizabethan writers, probably in ridicule of some person who pretended to a knowledge of Latin which he did not possess.

parole.significato: Pulpy throughout, like a berry; said of fruits.
parole.testo: From Latin baccātus (“set or adorned with berries or pearls”), from bacca (“berry; pearl”) + -ātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Relating to Bacchus or his festival.
parole.testo: From Latin Bacchānālis (“of or pertaining to Bacchus”). See Bacchanalia.

parole.significato: A priest of Bacchus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bacchantem, present active participle of bacchor (“to celebrate rites of Bacchus; to revel”), from Bacchus (“the god of wine”), from Ancient Greek Βάκχος (Bákkhos).

parole.significato: Of or relating to Bacchus.
parole.testo: From Latin Bacchicus.

parole.significato: Producing berries.
parole.testo: From Latin baccifer (“bearing berries”), bacca (“berry”) + -ferous.

parole.significato: Having the form of a berry.
parole.testo: From Latin baca (“berry”) + -iform.

parole.significato: Eating, or having a diet based on, berries
parole.testo: Latin bāca (“berry”) + -vorous

parole.significato: Shaped like a rod or staff.
parole.testo: From Latin bacillum (“little staff”).

parole.significato: Any of various rod-shaped, spore-forming aerobic bacteria in the genus Bacillus, some of which cause disease.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin bacillus (“little staff, wand”), diminutive of baculum (“stick, staff, walking stick”).

parole.significato: A rod-like element on the surface of some pollen.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin baculum.

parole.significato: Shaped like a bacillus; rod-shaped.
parole.testo: Latin baculum (“staff”) + -iform

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a rod or cane, or punishment with either of them.
parole.testo: Latin baculum (“staff”).

parole.significato: Any member of the genus †Baculites of extinct cephalopod heteromorph ammonites.
parole.testo: From Latin baculum (“stick”) + -ite.

parole.significato: Any large rod-shaped virus of the family Baculoviridae, including the granuloviruses and nucleopolyhedroviruses.
parole.testo: From baculo- + virus, from Latin baculum (“rod”).

parole.significato: A bone found in the penis of some placental mammals.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin baculum (“stick, staff, sceptre, cudgel”).

parole.significato: Chestnut-coloured.
parole.testo: From Latin badius (“reddish brown, chestnut colored”), with the suffix adapted to -ous.

parole.significato: Of or relating to a region of southern Spain, the mountain range that dominates it, and the language spoken there.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin baeticus.

parole.significato: A meteorite or similar-looking rough stone thought to be of divine origin and worshipped as sacred.
parole.testo: From Latin baetulus, from Ancient Greek βαίτυλος (baítulos, “a meteoric stone”).

parole.significato: Bearing or producing acorns.
parole.testo: From Latin balanus (“acorn”) + -ferous. By surface analysis, balan(us) + -i- + -fer + -ous.

parole.significato: Relating to the glans.
parole.testo: From Latin balanus, from Ancient Greek βάλανος (bálanos). By surface analysis, balan(us) + -o-.

parole.significato: The glans
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin balanus, from Ancient Greek βάλανος (bálanos, “acorn”).

parole.significato: A buffoon; one who speaks a lot of nonsense and is characterized by self-indulgence.
parole.testo: From Latin balatrō (“jester, buffoon”). Cognate with Galician baladrón, Spanish baladrón, both meaning "braggart".

parole.significato: The red roselike flower of the pomegranate, having a bitter taste and sometimes used as an astringent in folk medicine.
parole.testo: Latin balaustinus

parole.significato: To stammer.
parole.testo: Latin balbutire, from balbus (“stammering”): compare French balbutier.

parole.significato: stammering
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin balbūtiēs.

parole.significato: Meum athamanticum, an ornamental plant in the Apiaceae family.
parole.testo: Apparently a corruption of Latin valdē bona (“very good”) (a plant mentioned in Leonhart Fuchs's Great Herbal). Earliest forms seem to come from an intermediate, unattested French form baudemoine (modern French baudremoine) and by analogy to the plant name agrimony.

parole.significato: nonsensical
parole.testo: From Latin balducta (“the curds of milk”).

parole.significato: An ancient military engine, in the form of a crossbow, used for hurling large missiles.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ballista, from Ancient Greek βαλλίστρα (ballístra), from βάλλω (bállō, “to throw”).

parole.significato: A crossbowman.
parole.testo: From Latin ballistārius.

parole.significato: Of or relating to ballistics.
parole.testo: From Latin ballista (“a military siege engine for throwing stones”) + -ic.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to baths or to bathing
parole.testo: From Latin balneum (“bath, bathing place”) + -al.

parole.significato: A room for bathing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin balnearium, from balneum (“bath”), from Ancient Greek βαλανεῖον (balaneîon).

parole.significato: The act of bathing.
parole.testo: From Latin balneum (“bath”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to a bath
parole.testo: Latin balneatorius.

parole.significato: bath
parole.testo: From Latin balneum (“bath”).

parole.significato: A description or study of therapeutic baths.
parole.testo: From Latin balneum (“bath”) + -graphy.

parole.significato: The treatment of disease by bathing.
parole.testo: From Latin balneum (“bath”) + therapy.

parole.significato: A sweet-smelling oil or resin derived from various plants.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin balsamum, from Ancient Greek βάλσαμον (bálsamon, “balsam”), of Semitic origin (Hebrew בושם (“spice, perfume”)); compare Old English balsam, balsamum (“balsam, balm”), Doublet of balm and desman. Not related to balsa.

parole.significato: A plant, the Impatiens balsamina, or garden balsam.
parole.testo: From Latin balsamina (“balsam plant”) (perhaps via French balsamine), from Ancient Greek βαλσαμίνη (balsamínē). The Latin name of the unrelated balsam plant must have been applied to Impatiens balsamina soon after it arrived in Europe- Leonhart Fuchs referred to it as balsamina as early as 1542.

parole.significato: The girdle of a biblical Jewish priest.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin balteus (“belt, girdle”).

parole.significato: A very large wine bottle with the capacity of about 12 liters, equivalent to 16 standard bottles.
parole.testo: From Middle English Balthasar, from Latin Baltassar, from Ancient Greek Βαλτάσαρ (Baltásar), from Hebrew בֵּלְשַׁאצַּר (bēlšaṣṣar), attested in the Tanakh and the Old Testament (Daniel 5:1), from Akkadian 𒁹𒀭𒂗𒈗𒋀 (Bēl-šarra-uṣṣur, literally “May Bel protect the king”). Doublet of Belshazzar.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Baltic region or the Baltic Sea.
parole.testo: From Latin Balticus, from Latin Balthae (“dwellers near the Baltic sea”); equivalent to Balt + -ic. The ultimate origin of the ethnonym is unknown, but possibilities include: * Related to Lithuanian baltas (“white”) and Proto-Slavic *bolto (“swamp, bog, mud”), which are likely from Proto-Indo-Europe

parole.significato: Being or relating to a type of court involving a bench of judges, often an appeals court.
parole.testo: From in banco, from Latin in banco.

parole.significato: The act of expulsion.
parole.testo: From Latin bannitio. See banish.

parole.significato: Synonym of ban (“gathering for war; mulct or penalty”).
parole.testo: From Latin bannum.

parole.significato: Baptism.
parole.testo: From Middle English baptizacion, from Latin baptizātiō. By surface analysis, baptize + -ation.

parole.significato: A pit, especially one at Athens into which criminals were thrown.
parole.testo: From Latin barathrum, from Ancient Greek βάραθρον (bárathron).

parole.significato: Relating to beards.
parole.testo: From Latin barba (“beard”) + -al.

parole.significato: Rule by barbarians.
parole.testo: From Latin barbarus (“foreigner, savage”), from Ancient Greek βάρβαρος (bárbaros, “foreign, strange”) + -cracy.

parole.significato: Not classical or pure.
parole.testo: Late Middle English, from Latin barbarus (“foreigner, savage”), from Ancient Greek βάρβαρος (bárbaros, “foreign, strange”).

parole.significato: bearded; having long thin hairs
parole.testo: PIE word  *bʰardʰéh₂ Borrowed from Latin barbātus, from barba (“beard”) + -ātus (“-ate”). By surface analysis, barb + -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Having a beard; bearded; hairy.
parole.testo: From Latin barbiger from barba (“beard”) + gerō (“carry, wear”).

parole.significato: an ancient stringed musical instrument, apparently a type of lute or lyre
parole.testo: From Latin barbiton, from Ancient Greek βάρβιτον (bárbiton).

parole.significato: An ancient stringed musical instrument from Greece, apparently a type of lute or lyre.
parole.testo: From Latin barbitos, from Ancient Greek βάρβιτος (bárbitos).

parole.significato: A small barb or beard.
parole.testo: PIE word  *bʰardʰéh₂ Borrowed from Latin barbula (“little beard”).

parole.significato: Kiss.
parole.testo: From Latin bāsium (“kiss”).

parole.significato: A basaltic extrusive rock, similar to chert.
parole.testo: From Latin basanites; more at basalt.

parole.significato: Positioned at the base; forming a base
parole.testo: From Latin basis.

parole.significato: Kissing.
parole.testo: From Latin bāsiātiō.

parole.significato: A Christian church building having a nave with a semicircular apse, side aisles, a narthex and a clerestory.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin basilica, from Ancient Greek βᾰσῐλῐκή (băsĭlĭkḗ), from βᾰσῐλῐκὴ στοά (băsĭlĭkḕ stoá, “royal hall”), ultimately from βασιλικός (basilikós, “royal”), from βασιλεύς (basileús, “king, chief”). Doublet of basoche.

parole.significato: A physical base or foundation.
parole.testo: From Latin basis, from Ancient Greek βάσις (básis), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷémtis, derived from Proto-Indo-European *gʷem- (whence also come). Doublet of base.

parole.significato: An overwhelming urge to be kissed.
parole.testo: From Latin bāsium (“kiss”) + -orexia. The term is not recorded in other major dictionaries and is likely a neologism. By surface analysis, bas- + -orexia.

parole.significato: An ancient Germanic tribe living in the region of Batavia around Nijmegen.
parole.testo: From Latin Batavi.

parole.significato: A variety of lettuce with broad flat leaves.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin Batavia, from Proto-Germanic *Batawjō. Doublet of Betawi and Passau.

parole.significato: A gelatinous substance found in mud dredged from the Atlantic and once supposed to be a free living protoplasm, later f…
parole.testo: Latin, from Ancient Greek. See bathy-. Coined by Thomas Henry Huxley.

parole.significato: A pale greenish-grey variety of montmorillonite.
parole.testo: From Latin batrachītēs, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: A wild plant related to chives; ramsons, Allium ursinum.
parole.testo: Calque from Latin Allium ursinum.

parole.significato: Blessed, blissful, heavenly.
parole.testo: From Latin beātificus (“making happy or blessed”), from beātus (“blessed”) + -ficus (“making”).

parole.significato: To beatify.
parole.testo: From Latin beātificāt-, the perfect passive participial stem of beātificō (“to bless, to make happy”). Equivalent to beatific + -ate.

parole.significato: A person who has been beatified.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin beātus.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a beak or bill.
parole.testo: From Latin beccus (“beak”).

parole.significato: The name of the Latin script letter B/b.
parole.testo: From Middle English [Term?], from Old English be, from Latin be (the name of the letter B).

parole.significato: To engage in the logical fallacy of begging the question (petitio principii).
parole.testo: Translating Latin petītiō prīncipiī, itself translating Ancient Greek τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ αἰτεῖσθαι (tò en arkhēî aiteîsthai, “to assume from the beginning”).

parole.significato: A group of tribes living in northern Gaul, between the English Channel and the west bank of the Rhine, from at least th…
parole.testo: From Latin Belgae, an Iron-Age European group of tribes located between the rivers Seine and Rhine.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Belgae, a Germanic tribe.
parole.testo: From Latin Belgicus, from Belgae (“the Belgians”).

parole.significato: A female warrior.
parole.testo: From Latin bellatrix, assumably through French.

parole.significato: An inclination to war; warlike policy or behaviour.
parole.testo: From Latin bellic(us) + -ism.

parole.significato: An adherent of bellicism; one who advocates war.
parole.testo: From Latin bellicus (“of or pertaining to war; warlike”), + -ist; possibly adapted from the French neologism belliciste (about Bismarck, 1871; in Émile Faguet, 1908).

parole.significato: Warlike or combative in nature; aggressively hostile.
parole.testo: From Middle English bellicose, from Latin bellicosus.

parole.significato: Engaged in warfare, warring.
parole.testo: From Latin belligerans (“waging war”), present active participle of belligerō (“to wage war”), from belliger (“waging war, warlike”), from bellum (“war”) + -ger (from gerō (“to lead, wage, carry on”)).

parole.significato: Mighty in war.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bellipotēns.

parole.significato: A woman of great spirit and vigour.
parole.testo: From Latin Bellōna, related to bellum.

parole.significato: Of, characteristic of, or pertaining to beasts; animal, bestial; brutal.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin belluīnus, an alternative spelling of bēluīnus (“animal, bestial; brutal”) (whence the English beluine) + -ine (“suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’”). Bēluīnus is derived from bēlua (“(wild) beast; monster; brute”) + -īnus (“suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’”) (from Proto-In

parole.significato: To swear fealty or allegiance to another person.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin genūflectō. Popularized by its use on the television series Game of Thrones (2011-2019).

parole.significato: Good.
parole.testo: UK C16. Probably from Latin bene or Italian bene.

parole.significato: A canticle, the Latin version of which begins with the word benedīcite (“praise ye!”), which may be used in the order f…
parole.testo: From Latin benedīcite, a plural imperative of benedīcō (“to bless; to praise”, literally “to say well (of)”).

parole.significato: Having mild and salubrious qualities.
parole.testo: From Latin benedictus, past participle of benedicere (“to bless”). See benison. Doublet of bennet.

parole.significato: Blessed; benedict.
parole.testo: From Middle English benedyght, benedight, from Latin benedictus. More at benedict, benediction.

parole.significato: An act of doing good; a benefit, a blessing.
parole.testo: From Latin benefactiōnem, from benefacere (“to benefit”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the linguistic form or case or the semantic role of the beneficiary of an action. Expressed in Engl…
parole.testo: From Latin benefactus (“benefited”) plus -ive. Attested since the twentieth century.

parole.significato: A female benefactor.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin benefactrīx. By surface analysis, benefactor + -trix.

parole.significato: An act of doing good; benefaction, beneficence.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin benefactūrus, future active participle of benefaciō (“to do good, to benefit”) + -ure (noun-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Favorable; beneficent.
parole.testo: From Latin beneficus. See benefice.

parole.significato: The practice of doing good, such as acts of philanthropy, kind deeds; or other acts which benefit someone else.
parole.testo: From Middle English beneficence, from Latin beneficentia.

parole.significato: Given to acts that are kind, charitable, philanthropic or beneficial.
parole.testo: From Latin *beneficens, *beneficent-, from bene (“well, good”) + -ficens, combining form from faciens, present participle of facere (“to make or do”). Compare English beneficence.

parole.significato: One who benefits or receives an advantage.
parole.testo: From Latin beneficiarius (“enjoying a favor, granted a privilege”) from beneficium (“benefit”), perhaps via or influenced by French bénéficiaire (“beneficiary”). Indirectly, by way of the etymology of the Latin word beneficium, the English word beneficiary ultimately has the same origin as the Engli

parole.significato: Synonym of benefice.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin beneficium.

parole.significato: kind; benevolent
parole.testo: Latin benevolus.

parole.significato: Normal occlusion (alignment) of the teeth when the jaws are closed.
parole.testo: Probably coined by Simeon Hayden Guilford ante 1905: Latin ben(e) (“well, properly”) + occlusion (“alignment of the teeth in closed jaws”), after malocclusion (“misalignment of the upper and lower sets of teeth”).

parole.significato: A medieval English sheep farm.
parole.testo: From Latin bercaria (“sheepcote”).

parole.significato: A small, oval, transparent jellyfish, of genus Beroe (phylum Ctenophora).
parole.testo: Latin Beroe (“one of the Oceanidae”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Berytus (“the ancient city of Beirut”).
parole.testo: From Berytus + -ian (suffix meaning ‘from, related to, or like’; or ‘one from, belonging to, relating to, or like’). Berytus is derived from Latin Bērȳtus, from Ancient Greek Βηρῡτός (Bērūtós), from a Semitic source.

parole.significato: A bronze coin of the Roman Republic, worth two thirds of an as.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bes.

parole.significato: A class of red and yellow indole-derived water-soluble pigments found in beets and other plants of the Caryophyllales a…
parole.testo: Coined to describe the pigments as derivatives from betalamic acid, from Latin bēta (“beet”), + -in.

parole.parola: better an egg today than a hen tomorrow
parole.significato: It is better to have a sure thing now than a possibility of more later.
parole.termine_origine: ad praesens ova cras pullis sunt meliora

catena.termine: ad praesens ova cras pullis sunt meliora

parole.testo: Calque of Latin ad praesens ova cras pullis sunt meliora, from Gargantua and Pantagruel by Rabelais.

parole.significato: A person's spouse or lover, most commonly a man's wife.
parole.testo: Ultimately from such Latin poetic phrases as animae dīmidium meae (“half of my soul”) (Horace writing about Virgil), when it instead referred to a close friend (compare soulmate). First written instance of it meaning “spouse” was in 1580 by Sir Philip Sidney.

parole.significato: It is better to do something late, than to never do it at all.
parole.testo: Perhaps a calque of Latin potius sero quam numquam from the 4th book of Ab Urbe condita (History of Rome) by Titus Livius, around 27 BC.

parole.significato: An enzyme that hydrolyzes the glucoside of methyl salicylate.
parole.testo: From Latin betula (“birch tree”) + -ase.

parole.significato: An organic compound with chemical formula C₃₆H₅₂O₁₆, obtained by adding betulin to nitric acid.
parole.testo: From betulin and Latin amārus (“bitter”).

parole.significato: One should not trust one's enemies.
parole.testo: Alludes to the ancient story of the Trojan horse, a gift for the Trojans which secretly contained Greeks. The prototype of the phrase is found in a Latin phrase in the Aeneid, book 2, lines 48–49: equō nē crēdite, Teucrī. / Quidquid id est, timeō Danaōs et dōna ferentēs. (“Do not trust the horse, Tr

parole.significato: Two in number.
parole.testo: PIE word  *dwóh₁ Borrowed from Latin bi-, from Proto-Italic *dwi-, from Proto-Indo-European *dwi-. Doublet of twi- and di-.

parole.significato: Addicted to drinking alcohol; alcoholic
parole.testo: From Latin bibāx, bibācis, ultimately from bibō + -acious. See bib.

parole.significato: The practice or habit of drinking too much alcohol.
parole.testo: From Latin bibāx, bibācis, ultimately from bibō + -acity.

parole.significato: Drinking, act of drinking (especially alcohol), imbibing.
parole.testo: From Latin bibō (“I drink”) + -ation (“act of”).

parole.significato: penchant for drinking, love of liquids (not necessarily alcoholic), thirst.
parole.testo: Coined circa 1843, by Orson Squire Fowler, as variant of earlier aquativeness (1843), by analogy with earlier alimentiveness (1828). From Latin bibō (“I drink”) + -ative (“related to”) + -ness (“the quality of”); compare Latin bibāx (“tending to drink”).

parole.significato: A medieval Bible consisting of mainly pictures rather than text.
parole.testo: Latin [Term?] (literally “paupers' Bible”)

parole.significato: A bookseller.
parole.testo: From Latin bibliopōla, from Ancient Greek βιβλίον (biblíon, “paper, document, tablet”) + πωλέω (pōléō, “to barter, sell”) — (compare with the etymology of monopoly).

parole.significato: Bookselling.
parole.testo: From bibliopole (“bookseller”) + -poly (suffix denoting sellers in a market). Bibliopole is derived from Latin bibliopōla (“bookseller”), from Ancient Greek βῐβλῐοπώλης (bĭblĭopṓlēs, “bookseller”), from βῐβλῐ́ον (bĭblĭ́on), βυβλίον (bublíon, “book; letter; tablet; strip of papyrus; writing”) (from β

parole.significato: A library.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin bibliothēca, borrowed from Ancient Greek βιβλιοθήκη (bibliothḗkē, “library”). Equivalent to biblio- + -theca. Doublet of bibliotheque.

parole.significato: Belonging or pertaining to a library.
parole.testo: From Latin bibliothēcālis. See bibliotheque.

parole.significato: A librarian.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin bibliothēcārius (“librarian”), from bibliothēca (“library”) + -ārius, from Ancient Greek βῐβλῐοθήκη (bĭblĭothḗkē, “library”), from βῐβλῐ́ον (bĭblĭ́on) + θήκη (thḗkē). Compare French bibliothécaire and Italian and Spanish bibliotecario. By surface analysis, bibliotheca +

parole.significato: Very absorbent.
parole.testo: From Latin bibulus from bibō (“drink”) + -ulus from Proto-Italic *pibō, from Proto-Indo-European *píph₃eti, from root *peh₃- (“drink”); whence also imbibe and beverage via Old French beivre.

parole.significato: Having two tails
parole.testo: From bi- + caudal, from Latin cauda (“tail”).

parole.significato: Any muscle having two heads.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin biceps (“double-headed, two-peaked”), from bis (“twice”) + -ceps (“headed”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a biceps.
parole.testo: From Latin biceps (“double-headed”).

parole.significato: Having two colours
parole.testo: From Latin bicolor; also analyzable as bi- + colour.

parole.significato: A two-cornered hat, worn by European and American military and naval officers from the 1790s.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bicornis (“two-horned; two-pronged”). Compare French bicorne (“two-cornered hat; two-horned monster”) and Middle English bicorne (“two-horned anvil; two-pronged fork; fabulous (two-horned) beast”). Doublet of bicorne.

parole.significato: twice a day, two times per day
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bis in diē.

parole.significato: A form of spear having two prongs.
parole.testo: PIE word  *dwóh₁ From Latin bidentis (“two-toothed”).

parole.significato: In Ancient Rome, a place that had been struck by lightning and consecrated and enclosed.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bidental.

parole.significato: Continuing for two days.
parole.testo: From Latin biduus.

parole.significato: Synonym of biennial: of or concerning a two-year period; lasting or occurring every two years.
parole.testo: From Latin biennium (“a two-year period”) + -ary (“forming adjectives”).

parole.significato: Happening every two years.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bienni(um) (“two-year period”) [from bis, bi- (“twice”) + annus (“year”)] + -al (suffix forming adjectives). By surface analysis, bi- + -ennial.

parole.significato: A period of two years, particularly for purposes involving intercalation or fiscal calculations.
parole.testo: From Latin biennium, from biennis (“2-year”) + -ium (suffix forming abstract nouns), from bi- (“two”) + annus (“year”), q.v.

parole.significato: twofold, double
parole.testo: From Latin bifārius (“twofold, double”), back-formed from the adverb bifāriam.

parole.significato: Cleft; divided into two principal or main parts, such as two lobes.
parole.testo: From Latin bifidus (“divided in two”), from bi- (“two”) + -fidus, combining form of findere (“to split”).

parole.significato: Bifid, divided into two main parts.
parole.testo: First attested in 1847; borrowed from Latin bifidātus, from bifidus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix). By surface analysis, bifid + -ate.

parole.significato: Bearing two flowers or blooms.
parole.testo: Latin bis twice + flos, floris (“flower”) + English -ous. By surface analysis, bi- + Latin flor- + -ous.

parole.significato: An oval sac or cell, found in the idioblasts of the leaves of certain araceous plants, with an opening at each end thro…
parole.testo: From Latin biforis, biforus (“having two doors”), from bis (“twice”) + foris (“door”).

parole.significato: Biforate.
parole.testo: From Latin biforis (“having two doors”), from bis (“twice, two”) + foris (“door”).

parole.significato: bifurcate
parole.testo: From Latin bifurcus, from bis (“twice”) + furca (“fork”).

parole.significato: A Roman racing chariot drawn by two horses abreast.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bīga.

parole.significato: A bigamist, or one who has married a widow.
parole.testo: From Latin bigamus (“twice married”): compare French bigame. See bigamy.

parole.significato: Bearing the figure of a bigae (pair of horses).
parole.testo: From Latin bīgātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Occurring in pairs; doubled or twinned
parole.testo: Latin bigeminus (“doubled”), from bi- (“two”) + geminus (“double”).

parole.significato: bijugate
parole.testo: From Latin bijugus (“yoked two together”), from bis (“twice”) + jugum (“yoke, pair”).

parole.significato: Bile.
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting a New Latin combining form, from Latin bīlis (“bile”).

parole.significato: A brownish-green pigment, derived from bilirubin, found in human gallstones and in old bile.
parole.testo: From Latin bilis (“bile”) + fuscus (“dark”) + -in.

parole.significato: Any of various biological pigments formed in many organisms as a metabolic product of certain porphyrins.
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, and clearly reflecting New Latin, from Latin bīlis (“bile”). By surface analysis, bili- + -in, although according to American Heritage Dictionary, bilin was back-formed from phycobilin (as opposed to phycobilin being derived from bilin as surface analysis su

parole.significato: Having the ability to speak two languages fluently.
parole.testo: From Latin bilinguis + -al; equivalent to bi- + lingual.

parole.significato: Double-tongued, deceiving.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin bilinguis (“double-tongued”).

parole.significato: bilingual.
parole.testo: Latin bilinguis.

parole.significato: A dark green pigment found in small quantities in human gallstones.
parole.testo: From Latin bilis (“bile”) + prasinus (“green”).

parole.significato: Signifying that a presenter has furnished probable evidence, and is worthy of further consideration, presented to a par…
parole.testo: From the Latin, literally "the bill is true".

parole.significato: An alkylresorcinol and strong skin irritant found in Gingko biloba fruits.
parole.testo: From Latin biloba + -ol.

parole.significato: The ability to speak in two different voices, especially as a ventriloquist.
parole.testo: Probably coined by American novelist Charles Brockden Brown (1771-1810), from the Latin bi- (“two”) + loquor (“to speak”) + -ium.

parole.significato: Having two hands (rather than any other distal part of a forelimb).
parole.testo: From Latin bi (“two”) + manus (“hand”) + -ous.

parole.significato: Having two members.
parole.testo: From Latin bis (“twice”) + membrum (“member”).

parole.significato: The 2,000th anniversary of an event or happening.
parole.testo: From Latin bimillennialis, from bi- (“two”) mill- (“thousand”) + enni(us) (“yearly”). By surface analysis, bi- + millennial. Compare bicentennial.

parole.significato: To perform bination; to hold Mass twice on the same day.
parole.testo: From Latin bīnātus, past participle of bīnō (“to binate”), from bīnus (“two each, in pairs”). Equivalent to Latin bīnō + -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A name having two parts.
parole.testo: Latin bis (“double, twice”) + nōmen (“name”).

parole.significato: Consisting of two names.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin binōminis (“having two names”).

parole.significato: A horizontally bedded stratum of fossilized remains of sedentary organisms
parole.testo: bio- (“life”) + Latin stroma (“coverlet”), from Ancient Greek στρῶμα (strôma, “bed, mattress”).

parole.significato: Dividing into two parts.
parole.testo: From Latin bis (“twice”) + partiens, present participle of partire (“to divide”).

parole.significato: Having two parts (two principal or main parts).
parole.testo: From Latin bipartītus (“bisected”), perfect passive participle of bipartiō (“to divide into two parts, bisect”). By surface analysis, bi- + part + -ite.

parole.significato: An animal, being, or construction that goes about on two feet (or two legs).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bipēs, bipedis. Alternatively analyzable as bi- + -ped.

parole.significato: An axe with an edge or blade on each side of the handle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bipennis (“two-winged”).

parole.significato: The larva of certain starfishes as developed in the free-swimming stage.
parole.testo: From Latin bis (“twice”) + pinna (“feather”).

parole.significato: The state of being twice folded; reduplication.
parole.testo: From Latin bi- (“twice”). Bailey (1736) suggests borrowing from Latin biplicitas, but this is not well attested. Compare duplicity, from Latin duplicare (“double”).

parole.significato: Relating to books printed at Zweibrücken in Bavaria.
parole.testo: See bi- and Latin pōns (“bridge”). Zweibrücken means "two bridges".

parole.significato: a neume denoting either a single tone, either elongated or rearticulated.
parole.testo: From Latin bipunctum (“double point”).

parole.significato: An ancient galley having two banks of oars, one above the other.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin birēmis.

parole.significato: Two-wheeled.
parole.testo: From bi + rotate (“wheel-shaped”), ultimately from Latin rota (“wheel”).

parole.significato: A microsclere that has a straight shaft and umbrella-shaped ends
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin birota, feminine of birotus, from bi- (“two, double”) + rota (“wheel”) + -us.

parole.significato: Twice; showing that something is, or is to be, repeated, such as a passage of music, or an item in accounts.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin bis (“twice”).

parole.significato: Something (e.g., payment, assistance, etc.) given promptly is much more valuable than if given after considerable delay.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bis dat qui cito dat.

parole.significato: Bisexual, hermaphroditic (having both male and female parts or functions).
parole.testo: From Latin bis (“twice”) + sexus (“sex”). Compare French bissexe.

parole.significato: The bissextile intercalary day.
parole.testo: From Middle English bisext, from Latin bisextus, bissextus.

parole.significato: Being or having an intercalary day, particularly the quadrennial leap day of the Julian and Gregorian calendars traditi…
parole.testo: From Latin bisextilis/bissextilis (annus) (“bissextile year”), from bisextus + -ilis, from bis- (“two; twice; doubled”) + sextus (“sixth”) + dies (“day”), from the Julian calendar's original reckoning of its quadrennial intercalary day as a 48-hour February 24, subsequently distinguished as the two

parole.significato: A member of the Bistons or Bistones
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Bistōn, from Ancient Greek Βίστων (Bístōn).

parole.significato: Any of several perennial herbs, classified in genera Bistorta, Persicaria, or Polygonum, having spikes of pink flowers.
parole.testo: From Latin bistorta, from bis (“twice”) and torta (“twisted”), in reference to its twisting roots.

parole.significato: bisulcate
parole.testo: From Latin bisulcus, from bis (“twice”) + sulcus (“furrow”).

parole.significato: A sticky, black, highly viscous liquid or semi-solid form of petroleum, burning with a bright flame. It occurs as an ab…
parole.testo: From Middle English bithumen, bitumen, from Latin bitūmen. Doublet of bitume.

parole.significato: Both two and one at the same time (for example, Jesus Christ as God the Son and the Son of Man).
parole.testo: From bi- + Latin unus (“one”).

parole.significato: Having, or leading, two ways.
parole.testo: From Latin bivius (“two-way, having two approaches”) + English -ous.

parole.significato: One side of an echinoderm, including a pair of ambulacra, in distinction from the opposite side (trivium), which includ…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bivium (“a place with two ways”).

parole.significato: One of the four humours of ancient and mediaeval physiology, that was believed to be secreted by the kidneys and spleen…
parole.testo: Calque of Latin ātra bīlis, itself a calque of Ancient Greek μελαγχολία (melankholía).

parole.significato: The metal lead.
parole.testo: In the sense of lead, calque of Latin plumbum nigrum (“lead”, literally “black lead”).

parole.significato: Cygnus atratus, a swan with black plumage and a red bill which is endemic to Australia.
parole.testo: From Middle English blak swan, calqued from a Latin quotation from Satire VI (written late 1st century – early 2nd century B.C.E.) of the Roman poet Juvenal: “Rara avis in terris, nigroque simillima cygno [a bird as rare upon the earth as a black swan]!”. Equivalent to black + swan. Sense 2.1 (“some

parole.significato: A small Old World warbler, Eurasian blackcap (Sylvia atricapilla), which is mainly grey with a black crown.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin ātricapillus (“blackcap; black-haired”), itself a calque of Ancient Greek μελαγκόρυφος (melankóruphos). By surface analysis, black + cap.

parole.significato: The extortion of money or favors by threats of public accusation, critique, or exposure.
parole.testo: From black + mail (“a piece of money”). Compare Middle English blak rente (“a type of blackmail levied by Irish chieftains”). The word is variously derived from the tribute paid by English and Scottish border dwellers to border reivers in return for immunity from raids and other harassment. This tri

parole.significato: Having a soothing effect; not irritating or stimulating.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin blandus (“pleasant”).

parole.significato: flattery
parole.testo: Compare Latin blanditia, blandities, from blandus. See bland, blandishment.

parole.significato: Flattery.
parole.testo: From Latin blandus (“flattering”) + loquor (“speak”).

parole.significato: Speaking, or spoken, in a mild, flattering manner.
parole.testo: From Latin blandus (“flattering”) + loquēns (“speaking”).

parole.significato: Blandishment; flattery.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin blandīmentum (“blandishment, pleasure, remedy”).

parole.significato: Lacking piety or respect for the sacred; resembling blasphemy.
parole.testo: From Latin blasphēmus (“blaspheming”), from Ancient Greek βλάσφημος (blásphēmos, “uttering ill-omened words”), equivalent to blaspheme + -ous.

parole.significato: Blather; foolish talk.
parole.testo: From Latin blaterāre. Influenced by other expressive verbs ending in -er.

parole.significato: blather; foolish talk
parole.testo: Latin blateratio (“a babbling”).

parole.significato: A senseless babbler or boaster.
parole.testo: From Latin blatero + -onis.

parole.significato: A true blenny, any of various marine fishes from the suborder Blennioidei or order Blenniiformes that are generally sma…
parole.testo: From Latin blennius, blendius, from Ancient Greek βλέννα (blénna, “mucus, slime”) (whence Modern Greek βλέννα (vlénna)), because of its slimy coating. From Proto-Indo-European *mel- (“soft”).

parole.significato: The plant Amaranthus blitum, purple amaranth.
parole.testo: From Latin blitum.

parole.significato: Any of a group of large American snakes, of the genus Boa, subfamily Boinae, or family Boidae, including the boa constr…
parole.testo: From Middle English boa, from Latin boa (“large snake”), a species of serpent mentioned in Pliny's Naturalis Historia (Natural History). The scarf was named attributively, for its resemblance to the snake when worn.

parole.significato: Bellowing.
parole.testo: From Latin boātiō (“roaring”, “bellowing”), noun of action of boō (“to roar”, “to bellow”).

parole.significato: The collective body of a nation or state as politically organized.
parole.testo: From body + politic (postpositive adjective), calque of Latin corpus polīticum.

parole.significato: Any of a group of rotenoids present in spiderlings of the genus Boerhavia.
parole.testo: From Latin Boerhavia + -one.

parole.significato: A Gallic tribe of the later Iron Age.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Boiī.

parole.significato: A type of hornblendic gabbro.
parole.testo: From Latin Boiī + -ite, coined in 1898 by E. Weinschenk.

parole.significato: A boys' game where two or three children form a base, and others jump on them to make the base collapse.
parole.testo: From Afrikaans. Possibly Latin bucca bucca quot sunt hic. See Talk page.

parole.significato: A type of fruiting body produced by certain fungus species in the order Boletales, especially those of genus Boletus, m…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bōlētus (“edible mushroom”), from Ancient Greek βωλίτης (bōlítēs).

parole.significato: An edible mushroom of genus Boletus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bōlētus.

parole.significato: A bolide or fireball (type of meteor)
parole.testo: From Latin bolis, from Ancient Greek βολίς (bolís, “missile, arrow, javelin”). Doublet of bolide.

parole.significato: Any member of the genus Bombax of tropical trees in the mallow family.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: An acid obtained from the silkworm, now found to be acetic acid.
parole.testo: Latin bombyx (“silk, silkworm”): compare French bombique.

parole.significato: To hum or buzz.
parole.testo: From Latin bombizātum, supine form of bombizō (“buzz, fart”).

parole.significato: A buzzing or humming.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bombus.

parole.significato: silken; made of silk
parole.testo: From Latin bombycinus. See bombazine.

parole.significato: Buzzing like a bumblebee.
parole.testo: From Latin bombyx (“bumblebee”) + English -ious.

parole.significato: In good faith; genuinely, sincerely.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin bonā fidē (“in good faith”).

parole.significato: Sincerity, good faith.
parole.testo: From Latin bona (nominative feminine singular of bonus (“good”)) + fidēs (“faith”).

parole.significato: perishable goods
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: The principle that there is no unowned property, and that if there is no other owner then property vests in the Crown.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: A bonnacon.
parole.testo: From Latin bonāsus, from Ancient Greek βόνᾱσος (bónāsos).

parole.significato: Naturally good-moraled.
parole.testo: From Latin bonus (“good”) + -form.

parole.significato: Something extra that is good; an added benefit.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bonus (“good”). Doublet of bona.

parole.significato: A small wooden doll that is covered with a cape and made to vanish as part of a magic trick.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin bonus genius (literally “good spirit”).

parole.significato: A member of the Borani
parole.testo: From Latin Boranus.

parole.significato: The low-level tenure by which a bordar held his cottage.
parole.testo: Latin bordagium.

parole.significato: A person ranking below villeins and above serfs in the social hierarchy of a manor, holding just enough land to feed a…
parole.testo: From Latin bordarius, of Teutonic origin. See board.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or coming from the north.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin boreālis (“northern”), from Boreās, from Ancient Greek Βορέᾱς (Boréās, “personification of the north wind”).

parole.significato: A strait or narrow sea between two seas, or a lake and a sea.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: Having the shape of a sausage
parole.testo: Latin botulus (“sausage”), + -iform.

parole.significato: An anaerobic soil bacterium, Clostridium botulinum, that secretes the toxin botulin
parole.testo: From Latin botulus (“sausage”) + -īnum.

parole.significato: botulinum toxin
parole.testo: Latin botulus (“sausage”) + toxin, because botulism was linked to sausage poisoning.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to cattle.
parole.testo: From Latin bovīnus, from bōs (“ox”). Cognate to beef.

parole.significato: The rearing and care of cattle.
parole.testo: From Latin bos (“cattle”) + cultura (“cultivation”); stem ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷṓws which also gave Ancient Greek βοῦς (boûs), and English cow.

parole.significato: Shaped like an ox.
parole.testo: From Latin bos, bovis (“ox”) + -form.

parole.significato: A Mediterranean food fish of the genus Boops, which is a variety of sea bream; a bogue or oxeye.
parole.testo: From Latin bōx, from Ancient Greek βῶξ (bôx, “box (marine fish)”), from βοῦς (boûs, “ox”) + ὤψ (ṓps, “eye, view”), a reference to the large size of the fish's eyes relative to its body.

parole.significato: The box tree, Buxus sempervirens.
parole.testo: From box + wood; box from Latin buxus (“box-tree, object made of boxwood”), of uncertain origin; compare Ancient Greek πύξος (púxos).

parole.significato: Shapeless trousers of wool or skin tied at the waist and ankles by cords, worn chiefly by the ancient Gauls.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bracae, plural of braca, from Gaulish *brāca, of Celtic origin, cognate with Proto-Germanic *brōks; akin to Old High German bruoh (“a pair of breeches”) and to Dutch broek (“a pair of trousers”).

parole.significato: Pertaining or belonging to the arm.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bracchialis, from bracchium (“arm”). Doublet of brachialis.

parole.significato: A muscle in the upper arm that flexes the elbow joint, in conjunction with the biceps brachii.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bracchialis, brachialis. Doublet of brachial.

parole.significato: Having decussate branches.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin brachiātus, from brachium (“arm, branch”) + -ātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Arm.
parole.testo: From Latin bracchium.

parole.significato: The second stage of larval development in many sea stars, following the bipinnaria
parole.testo: From Latin brachiolum, diminutive of brachium (“arm”).

parole.significato: The upper arm.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bracchium (“arm”). Doublet of braccio.

parole.significato: brachyural
parole.testo: From Latin brachyūrus, from Ancient Greek βραχύουρος (brakhúouros, “short-tailed”), from βραχύς (brakhús, “short”) + οὐρά (ourá, “tail”).

parole.significato: A leaf or leaf-like structure from the axil out of which a stalk of a flower or an inflorescence arises.
parole.testo: From Latin bractea (“a thin plate of metal; gold leaf”).

parole.significato: Having bracts.
parole.testo: From Latin bracteātus (“gold-plated, golden”), from bractea (“gold leaf, veneer, glitter”) + -ātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-forming suffix). By surface analysis, bract + -eate (second element from -ea + -ate).

parole.significato: A gill or other organ having the same function.
parole.testo: From Latin branchia, from Ancient Greek βράγχια (bránkhia, “gills”).

parole.significato: Gill-shaped.
parole.testo: From Latin branchia, branchiae (“gills”) + -form.

parole.significato: Any of many plants of the genus Brassica, including cabbage, mustard and rapes
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin brassica.

parole.significato: The triazole β-[(4-chlorophenyl)methyl]-α-methyl-α-phenyl-1H-1,2,4-triazole-1-ethanol that inhibits brassinosteroid bio…
parole.testo: From brassine + -azole, from Latin brassica.

parole.significato: The indole phytoalexin methyl (1H-indol-3-ylmethyl)carbamodithioate present in Chinese cabbage (Brassica campestris)
parole.testo: From brassin + -in, from Latin brassica.

parole.significato: A brassinosteroid that promotes cell elongation and division.
parole.testo: From brassin + -ol + -ide, from Latin brassica.

parole.significato: Any of a family of steroidal plant hormones produced by members of the genus Brassica; the brassins
parole.testo: By surface analysis, brassine + -o- + steroid, from Latin brassica.

parole.significato: Food and entertainment provided by the state, particularly if intended to placate the people.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin panem et circenses, a reference to Satire 10 of the Roman poet Juvenal’s Satires (early 2nd century C.E.). The relevant passage states: “… nam qui dabat olim imperium, fasces, legiones, omnia, nunc se continet atque duas tantum res anxius optat, panem et circenses” (“[F]or that sover

parole.significato: Short.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin brevis (“short”). Doublet of brie- (bri-).

parole.significato: A book containing prayers, hymns, and so on for everyday use at the canonical hours.
parole.testo: From Latin breviārium (“summary”) (compare abbreviation), ultimately from brevis (“short”). Doublet of brevier and brimborion.

parole.significato: A short account, brief statement; a summary, abridgement or precis
parole.testo: First attested in 1581; borrowed from Latin breviātum, from the perfect passive participle of breviō (“shorten, abridge”), see -ate (noun-forming suffix).

parole.significato: To abbreviate, shorten.
parole.testo: First attested in the beginning of the 16ᵗʰ century; either borrowed from Latin breviātus, the perfect passive participle of breviō (“shorten, abridge”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)) or apheretic form of abbreviate.

parole.significato: A pertinent and terse style of speech; a style of speech exhibiting brevity.
parole.testo: Latin breviloquentia.

parole.significato: A brevipennate (short-winged) bird, in a former proposed classification, Brevipennes
parole.testo: From Latin brevis (“short”) + penna (“wing”). Compare French brévipenne.

parole.significato: short-winged; having short wings.
parole.testo: From Latin brevis (“short”) + pennate.

parole.significato: Having a short beak or bill
parole.testo: Latin brevis (“short”) + English rostral.

parole.significato: The situation where a short syllable at the end of a line can be counted as long.
parole.testo: From Latin brevis in longō (brevis (“short (syllable)”) + in (“in”) + longus (“long”)).

parole.significato: 23491Pa, a short-lived isotope of protactinium.
parole.testo: Latin brevis (“brief”) + -ium

parole.significato: Relating to, or resembling, Briareus, a giant fabled to have a hundred hands; many-handed.
parole.testo: From Latin Briareius, from Briareus (“a mythological hundred-handed giant”).

parole.significato: A scouring pad used for cleaning dishes, made from steel wool containing soap.
parole.testo: From a trademark, probably related to brilliant. The company has claimed that the name derives from a Latin word for bright, but there is no such fitting word in attested Latin; the ancestor of such verbs as Italian brillare (“to shine”) would be a hypothetical Vulgar Latin *b(e)rillāre.

parole.significato: An ancient Briton.
parole.testo: From Middle English brytayn, from Latin Britannus (adjective and noun, plural Britannī), apparently from Brythonic (compare Old Welsh Priten).

parole.significato: of or pertaining to Britain, Great Britain or the United Kingdom; British
parole.testo: From Latin britannicus.

parole.significato: bronchus, relating to the trachea, or airways to the lungs.
parole.testo: From Latin bronchus.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the bronchia, bronchi or bronchioles.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bronchiālis. By surface analysis, bronchium + -al.

parole.significato: Any of various plants, of the genus Orobanche, that are parasitic on the roots of other plants.
parole.testo: From broom + rape, a partial calque of translingual Orobanche rapum-genistae, where Latin rapum means turnip and genista means broom. Orobanche rapum-genistae is parasitic on broom plants. Compare rapeseed. Cognates include Dutch bremraap.

parole.significato: Belonging to winter; winterlike; wintry.
parole.testo: From Latin brūmālis (“of or pertaining to the winter solstice; wintry”), from brūma (“the winter solstice; winter”), which is a contraction of *brevima (“the shortest (day)”).

parole.significato: A lethargic state that some ectothermic animals, such as many reptiles, assume during cold conditions. Partly analogous…
parole.testo: From Latin brūma (“winter solstice”) + -tiō, by analogy with hibernation.

parole.significato: Of or relating to John Brown (physician, born 1735), Scottish physician who taught that disease was caused by either ex…
parole.testo: From Bruno + -n- + -ian. From Latin Bruno (“Brown”), from Medieval Latin brunus (“brown”), from Old High German brun (“brown”).

parole.significato: A judgement without effect.
parole.testo: From Latin brutum (“stupid”) + fulmen (“lightning”), derived from a 1680 pamphlet by Thomas Barlow of that title, originally from a passage of Pliny's Natural History: "hinc bruta fulmina et vana" ("these senseless and ineffectual thunder-claps", intended as a literal description of lightning).

parole.significato: A kind of wig.
parole.testo: From Latin Brutus.

parole.significato: A perennial herb of the genus Bryonia, especially the common wild subspecies Bryonia cretica dioica (syn. Bryonia dioic…
parole.testo: From Middle English brionie, from Latin bryōnia (“bryony”), from Ancient Greek βρυωνία (bruōnía, “bryony”), from βρύω (brúō).

parole.significato: Any of several North African antelopes of the genus Alcelaphus.
parole.testo: PIE word  *gʷṓws From Latin būbalus, from Ancient Greek βούβαλος (boúbalos). Doublet of buffalo and buffle.

parole.significato: Synonym of cheek.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin bucca (“the cheek”). Doublet of bocca and bouche.

parole.significato: A curved brass instrument used by the Ancient Roman army.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin būcina, buccina. Doublet of buisine and posaune.

parole.significato: Shaped or sounding like a trumpet.
parole.testo: Latin bucina (“a crooked horn or trumpet”).

parole.significato: A thin broad muscle forming the wall of the cheek.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin buccinātor (“trumpeter”), from buccinō (“blow the trumpet”) + -tor (“-ator, -er”).

parole.significato: buccal; related to the cheek.
parole.testo: From buccal, from Latin bucca (“mouth; cheek”). By surface analysis, bucc- + -o-.

parole.significato: A fold of fat beneath the chin.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin buccula. By surface analysis, bucc(a) + -ula.

parole.significato: Possessing a wide mouth.
parole.testo: From Latin bucculentus.

parole.significato: A formation of escort troops used in the Roman Empire in Late Antiquity.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Bucellarius (“biscuit-eater”), from buccellātum (“hardtack”) + -arius.

parole.significato: Any horse used for riding.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Būcephalus, from Ancient Greek Βουκέφαλος, Βουκεφάλας (Bouképhalos, Boukephálas), from βοῦς (boûs, “ox”) + κεφᾰλή (kephălḗ, “head”) + -ᾱς (-ās).

parole.significato: Any of several, often thorny shrubs or small trees, especially
parole.testo: Calque of Latin cervī spīna (“deer's thorny shrub”), cervi (“deer's”) being the genitive singular of cervus (“deer”), from Proto-Italic *kerwos, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱr̥h₂wós, from *ḱerh₂- (“horn”) + *-wós, spīna (“thorny shrub”) from Proto-Italic *speinā, from Proto-Indo-European *spey- (“shar

parole.significato: Rustic, pastoral, country-styled.
parole.testo: PIE word  *gʷṓws Borrowed from Latin būcolicus, from Ancient Greek βουκολικός (boukolikós, “rustic, pastoral; meter used by pastoral poets”, literally “pertaining to cowherds”).

parole.significato: A pastoral poem.
parole.testo: From Latin būcolicum, neuter substantive of būcolicus.

parole.significato: The depiction of the head of an ox, as ornamental flourishes in architectural works.
parole.testo: From Latin būcrānium, from Ancient Greek βουκράνιον (boukránion).

parole.significato: A particular enzyme inhibitor derived from a toad toxin.
parole.testo: See Latin būfo (“toad”) and -genic, -in.

parole.significato: Resembling a toad.
parole.testo: From Latin būfō (“toad”).

parole.significato: A fossil consisting of the petrified teeth and palatal bones of fishes belonging to the family of pycnodonts, whose rem…
parole.testo: From Latin bufo (“toad”) + -ite. It was once believed to be formed in the head of a toad.

parole.significato: The bulb-shaped underground portion of a plant such as a tulip, consisting of a shortened stem and many fleshy scale le…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English bulb, bolbe, from Latin bulbus (“bulb, onion”), from Ancient Greek βολβός (bolbós, “plant with round swelling on underground stem”).

parole.significato: bulbous
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bulbāceus. See bulb.

parole.significato: Shaped like a bulb.
parole.testo: From Latin bulbus (“bulb”) + -form.

parole.significato: Having the shape of or resembling a bulb, bloated.
parole.testo: From bulb + -ous or alteration of Latin bulbosus.

parole.significato: A small bulb; a bulblet.
parole.testo: From Latin bulbulus, diminutive of bulbus. See bulb.

parole.significato: An erectile tissue structure on the penis of canid mammals and some pinnipeds, which swells up and locks inside the fem…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin bulbus glandis, from bulbus (“bulb”) + glandis (“acorn”).

parole.significato: An eating disorder characterized by a binge-and-purge cycle: extreme overeating followed by self-induced vomiting.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin būlīmia, from Ancient Greek βουλῑμῐ́ᾱ (boulīmĭ́ā, “ravenous hunger”), from βοῦς (boûs, “ox”) + λῑμός (līmós, “hunger, famine”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā, “-ia”), and Latin nervōsa (“nervous”).

parole.significato: A blister, vesicle, or other thin-walled cavity or lesion, as
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bulla (“bubble”). Doublet of bill and bull (“papal bull; bubble”).

parole.significato: Having a blistered appearance; bullate.
parole.testo: Latin bulla (“any swollen round object”), + -iform

parole.significato: The action of boiling.
parole.testo: From Latin bullire, bullitum (“to boil”). See boil (verb) and ebullition.

parole.significato: Any of a number of jewel beetles of the family Buprestidae, usually with shiny metallic colours.
parole.testo: Latin buprestis, Ancient Greek a poisonous beetle, which, being eaten by cattle in the grass, caused them to swell up and die; ox, cow + to blow up, swell out.

parole.significato: The duty of a party in a legal proceeding to prove an assertion of fact; it includes both the burden of production and…
parole.testo: Calque of Latin onus probandi.

parole.significato: A pilgrim's staff.
parole.testo: From Latin burdonem.

parole.significato: A city or town.
parole.testo: The historical sense is from Late Latin burgus, from Frankish *burg, from Proto-Germanic *burgz (“borough, fortification”). Doublet of borough, Brough, burgh, burh, and bury. Also compare burgess. The modern sense may have been formed in part by analogy with the many North American city names that a

parole.significato: The governing body of a burgh or borough; burgage.
parole.testo: Probably from Latin burgāria. By surface analysis, burg + -ery.

parole.significato: A Germanic tribe dwelling near the territory of the Marcomanni
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Būrī.

parole.significato: Any of a class of isoflav-3-enes found in the flowering plant Erythrina burttii.
parole.testo: From Latin burttii + -ol.

parole.significato: Any of the broad-winged soaring raptors of the genus Buteo.
parole.testo: From the genus name Buteo, from Latin būteō.

parole.significato: butyric substance.
parole.testo: Combining form of Latin būtȳrum (“butter”).

parole.significato: Invocation of the Roman god Jupiter.
parole.testo: From Latin pro Iovem. Ellipsis of a full oath of the form "I swear by Jove that…" Originally a literal oath; later a minced oath.

parole.significato: Invocation of the Roman god Jupiter.
parole.testo: From Latin pro Iuppiter. Ellipsis of a full oath of the form "I swear by Jupiter that…". Originally a literal oath; later a minced oath.

parole.significato: By divine will and benevolence.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin Deī grātiā. Doublet of Dei gratia.

parole.significato: A wallet.
parole.testo: PIE word  *dwóh₁ From Old English bīsæc, from Latin bisaccium.

parole.significato: Relating to, or possessing a byssus
parole.testo: From Latin byssus + -ate.

parole.significato: Made of, or resembling, silk; silken.
parole.testo: From Latin byssinus (“made of byssus”), from Ancient Greek βύσσινος (bússinos, “made of byssus”). See byssus.

parole.significato: The long fine silky filaments excreted by several mollusks (particularly Pinna nobilis) by which they attach themselves…
parole.testo: From Latin byssus, from Ancient Greek βύσσος (bússos, “flax; flax cotton”), from a Semitic source cognate to Hebrew בּוּץ (būṣ, “byssus”) and Aramaic בּוּצָא (būṣā, “byssus”)

parole.significato: A dark shade of purple, close to Tyrian purple and palatinate purple.
parole.testo: From Latin Bȳzantium, from Ancient Greek Βῡζᾰ́ντῐον (Būzắntĭon), named after its legendary founder, Byzas.

parole.significato: Of, or pertaining to, a horse.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin caballīnus (“horse-related”).

parole.significato: Having cachexia; wasting away from a disease or chronic illness.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cachecticus.

parole.significato: To laugh immoderately, loudly, or too often.
parole.testo: From Latin cachinnō (“laugh aloud”), of onomatopoeic origin.

parole.significato: To defecate.
parole.testo: From Middle English cakken, from Old English *cacian, from Old English cac (“dung; excrement”), from Latin cacāre (“excrete feces”). Cognate with English caca. Compare Dutch kakken (“to defecate”), German kacken (“to relieve oneself; defecate”), Latin cacō (“defecate”) (see there for more); compare

parole.significato: Compulsion; mania.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cacoēthes, from Ancient Greek κακοήθης (kakoḗthēs, “ill-disposed”) from κακός (kakós, “bad”) + ἦθος (êthos, “disposition, nature”).

parole.significato: Ill-conditioned, malignant; cacoethical.
parole.testo: Latin, from Ancient Greek κακοήθης (kakoḗthēs, “ill-disposed”) (κακός (kakós, “bad”) + ἦθος (êthos, “disposition, nature”)) + -ic

parole.significato: dysphemism
parole.testo: From Latin cacophemia + -ism.

parole.significato: A stylistic affectation of diction, such as throwing in foreign words to appear learned.
parole.testo: From Latin cacozēlia (“a bad, faulty, awkward imitation”), from Ancient Greek κᾰκοζηλία (kăkozēlía, “unhappy imitation, affectation”).

parole.significato: The smallest possible piece of matter, making up part of an atom.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cacūmen.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a point, top, or crown.
parole.testo: From oblique stem of Latin cacūmen, cacūminis (“extremity, point, peak”) + -al.

parole.significato: To make sharp or pointed.
parole.testo: From oblique stem of Latin cacūmen, cacūminis (“extremity, point, peak”) + -al, ultimately from Latin cacūminātus, past participle of cacūminō, from cacūmen.

parole.significato: Having a pyramidal top.
parole.testo: From oblique stem of Latin cacūmen, cacūminis (“extremity, point, peak”) + -ous.

parole.significato: A dead body; especially the corpse of a human to be dissected.
parole.testo: From Middle English cadaver, from Latin cadāver.

parole.significato: Corpselike; hinting of death; imitating a cadaver.
parole.testo: From Latin cadāverōsus; compare Middle English cadaverous (“gangrenous, mortified”).

parole.significato: An ornate capital letter used in calligraphy, consisting of interlaced pen strokes. See :Commons:Cadel letters.
parole.testo: From Latin capitellum, diminuitive of Latin caput (“head”), from Proto-Indo-European *kauput- (English head), itself from Proto-Indo-European *kap-. Doublet of captain. Cognate with French cadeau. Doublet of caddie, cadet, capital, capitellum, and caudillo.

parole.significato: Falling.
parole.testo: From the Latin cadens (“falling”), present active participle of cado (“to fall”).

parole.significato: Synonym of calamine, a pink form of zinc oxide.
parole.testo: From Latin cadmia, ultimately from Ancient Greek Καδμεία (Kadmeía), from Κάδμος (Kádmos, “Cadmus”) + -εια (-eia, “-ia: forming related substances”). Doublet of calamine, calaminaris, and lapis calaminaris.

parole.significato: caduceus.
parole.testo: From Latin cādūceus, cādūceum.

parole.significato: The official wand carried by a herald in ancient Greece and Rome, specifically the one carried in mythology by Hermes,…
parole.testo: Via Latin cādūceus, cādūceum, adaptation of Doric Ancient Greek καρύκειον (karúkeion, “herald’s wand or staff”). This and Attic Greek κηρύκειον (kērúkeion) are derived from κῆρυξ (kêrux, “herald, public messenger”). Related to κηρύσσω (kērússō, “to announce”).

parole.significato: With temporary gills; applied to those amphibians (most amphibians do this) in which the gills do not remain in adult l…
parole.testo: From Latin caducus (“falling”) (from cadere (“to fall”)) + English branchiate.

parole.significato: Having deciduous horns or antlers.
parole.testo: From Latin caducus (“falling”) + -corn.

parole.significato: Having deciduous leaves
parole.testo: From Latin caducus (“that easily falls”) + folium (“leaf”).

parole.significato: Of a part of an organism, disappearing in the normal course of development.
parole.testo: Latin cadūcus (“falling; transitory”).

parole.significato: Any of a group of burrowing amphibians of the order Gymnophiona that resemble earthworms or snakes.
parole.testo: From Latin caecilia + -an, feminine form of Caecilius, from Caeculus + -ius, from caecus + -ulus.

parole.significato: A cavity open at one end (such as the blind end of a duct), especially a blind pouch connected to the large intestine b…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin caecum (“invisible, hidden”), clipping of intestīnum caecum (“blind gut”), translation of Ancient Greek τῠφλὸν ἔντερον (tŭphlòn énteron).

parole.significato: An official in charge of religious ceremonies.
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: A follower of Julius Caesar.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Caesariānus, from Caesar + -iānus. By surface analysis, Caesar + -ian. Piecewise doublet of tsarian. For the sense “Caesarean section”, see also "Caesarean section § Etymology" on Wikipedia.

parole.significato: Having a blue color very low in chroma.
parole.testo: Latin caesius (“bluish-grey”); probably akin to Latin caelum (“sky”); see celestial.

parole.significato: The chemical element (symbol Cs) with an atomic number of 55. It is a soft, gold-colored, highly reactive alkali metal.
parole.testo: From Latin caesius (“sky-blue”), in reference to the radiation spectra, + -ium.

parole.significato: A pause or interruption in a poem, music, building, or other work of art.
parole.testo: Latin caesūra (“cutting, hewing”), from caesus, perfect passive participle of caedō (“to cut down, hew”).

parole.significato: A short Spanish shield.
parole.testo: From Latin caetra.

parole.significato: Synonym of star apple.
parole.testo: From Latin cainito, from Spanish caimito, from Lokono.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Cairo, the capital of Egypt.
parole.testo: From Latin Cairenus, from Cairo + -nus (“-ene: forming related nouns”). Equivalent to Cairo + -ene.

parole.significato: A squid.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin calamārius, from calamus (“a reed pen”), because of the ink emitted by squids.

parole.significato: Having or producing reeds.
parole.testo: From Latin calamus (“reed”) + -iferous. Compare New Latin calamifer, used in Botanical Latin and taxonomic names.

parole.significato: To curl (the hair).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin calamistrātus, perfect passive participle of calamistrō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: curled or frizzed
parole.testo: Latin calamistratus (“curled with a curling iron”), from calamistrum (“curling iron”).

parole.significato: A comb-like structure on the metatarsus of the hind legs of cribellate spiders (Ciniflonidae), used to comb out fine ba…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin calamistrum (“a curling-iron”).

parole.significato: Rod-shaped; long and thin.
parole.testo: From Latin calamus (“a reed”).

parole.significato: Sweet flag (Acorus calamus).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin calamus (“reed, cane”). Doublet of culm, haulm, helm (Etymology 4, stalk), qalam, and shawm.

parole.significato: Basket-shaped.
parole.testo: From Latin calathus (“wicker basket”) + -iform.

parole.significato: A vase-shaped basket made from reeds or twigs, used in Ancient Greece.
parole.testo: From Latin calathus, from Ancient Greek κάλαθος (kálathos).

parole.significato: The calcaneus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin calcāneum, from Latin calx, calcis (“heel”).

parole.significato: The large bone making up the heel of the human foot, the heel bone.
parole.testo: From Latin calcāneus (“heel”), rare form of calx (“heel”).

parole.significato: A spur-like projection.
parole.testo: From the Latin calcar (“spur”).

parole.significato: Having a spur; spurred.
parole.testo: From Latin calcarātus (“spurred”).

parole.significato: Resembling, containing, or composed of calcium carbonate or limestone; chalky.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin calcārius (“of or pertaining to lime”), derived from calx (“lime”). Similar to calcium.

parole.significato: Synonym of trample: to crush or stomp underfoot.
parole.testo: From Latin calcātus, the past participle of calcāre (“to trample”), parsed via English -ate (verb-forming suffix), from calx (“heel”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of calque.

parole.significato: Synonym of trampling, the act of trampling someone or something, an instance of trampling.
parole.testo: From calcate (“to trample”) + -ion (“forming abstract nouns”), from Latin calcatus (“trampled”), the past participle of calcāre (“to trample”) parsed via English -ate (“forming verbs”), from calx (“heel”) + -āre (“forming verbs”). Doublet of calque.

parole.significato: Synonym of winepress, particularly a location where grapes are crushed underfoot to produce juice or wine.
parole.testo: From Latin calcātōrium, from calcāre (“to trample”) + -tōrium (“-ory: forming locations”), from calx (“heel”) + -āre (“forming verbs”). Equivalent to calcate + -ory.

parole.significato: A red silk embroidered sandal forming part of the insignia of the Holy Roman Empire.
parole.testo: From Latin calceamentum.

parole.significato: Synonym of shod: wearing shoes, particularly (Christianity) as opposed to the barefoot mendicant orders.
parole.testo: From Latin calceātus, participle of calceāre (“to shoe, to provide with shoes”), from calceus (“calceus, shoe”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix), from calx (“heel”) + -eus (“-y”, adjective-forming suffix). Equivalent to Latin calceus + -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Synonym of shod: wearing shoes, particularly (Christianity) as distinguished from the barefoot mendicant orders.
parole.testo: From Latin calceātus + English -ed under influence from English -ate (verb-forming suffix), past participle of calceāre (“to shoe, to provide with shoes”), from calceus (“calceus, shoe”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix), from calx (“heel”) + -eus (“-y”, adjective-forming suffix). Doublet of calcated.

parole.significato: Synonym of shod, wearing shoes, particularly (Christianity) religious orders that do not eschew normal footwear.
parole.testo: A back-formation from discalced, with reference to Latin calceus (“calceus, footwear”).

parole.significato: Shoe-shaped, shaped like a shoe.
parole.testo: From Latin calceus (“calceus, footwear”) + English -form (“-shaped”) after the model of French calcéiforme.

parole.significato: A kind of low leather Roman boot or hightop shoe.
parole.testo: From Latin calceus, substantive use of calx (“heel”) + -eus (“-y: forming adjectives”).

parole.significato: Containing lime.
parole.testo: From Latin calcis (“genitive singular of calx (chalk, limestone)”) + -gerous (“bearing”); compare calciferous.

parole.significato: A form of whitewash (inexpensive white paint) made from calcium carbonate, glue and water, used to coat wooden or plast…
parole.testo: Alteration of kalsomine, after Latin calcis, genitive of calx (“lime”).

parole.significato: A very widely distributed crystalline form of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃, found as limestone, chalk and marble.
parole.testo: From Latin calx + -ite.

parole.significato: stubborn; refractory
parole.testo: From Latin calcitrans, present participle of calcitrare (“to kick”), from calx (“heel”), calcis (“heel”).

parole.significato: To kick.
parole.testo: From Latin calcitratus, past participle of calcitrare.

parole.significato: The chemical element (symbol Ca) with atomic number 20: a soft, silvery-white alkaline earth metal which occurs natural…
parole.testo: Coined by British chemist Humphry Davy in 1808, from Latin calx (“lime, limestone”) because it occurs in limestone. By surface analysis, calc- + -ium.

parole.significato: drawing with chalk
parole.testo: From Latin calx (“chalk”) + English -graphy (“written”).

parole.significato: An equation, ratio, or other quantitative problem designated for calculation; “that which is to be calculated”.
parole.testo: A substantivisation in English of the Latin calculandum (the nominative neuter singular form of calculandus, “which is to be calculated”, “which is to be computed”, the future passive participle (gerundive) of calculō, “I calculate”, “I compute”), on the pattern of analysandum, cogitandum, explicand

parole.significato: To determine the value of something or the solution to something by a mathematical process.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin calculātus, perfect passive participle of calculō (“to reckon, compute, calculate”, originally by means of pebbles) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from calculus (“a pebble”), further from calx (“limestone”, calc- in compounds) + -ulus (forms diminutives).

parole.significato: The act or process of calculating.
parole.testo: From Middle English calculation, borrowed from Latin calculatio, calculationis. Morphologically calculate + -ion.

parole.significato: A mechanical or electronic device that performs mathematical calculations; (now usually) an electronic one specifically.
parole.testo: In the sense of a person, from Middle English calkelatour (“a mathematician, an astrologer”), borrowed from Latin calculātor, equivalent to calculate + -or. The other meanings arose in Modern English.

parole.significato: Having the shape of a pebble
parole.testo: Latin calculus (“little stone”) + -iform

parole.significato: Calculation; computation.
parole.testo: * Borrowed from Latin calculus (“a pebble or stone used as reckoning counters in abacus”), diminutive of calx (“limestone”) + -ulus. * Mathematical topic is from differential calculus.

parole.significato: In Roman baths, the hottest room, with a plunge-pool. It preceded the tepidarium and frigidarium.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin caldārium (“room containing warm water for bathing”), substantive of caldārius (“of, pertaining to or suitable for bathing”), from caldus (“warm, hot”) + -ārius, alternative form of calidus, from caleō (“to be warm or hot; glow”).

parole.significato: The act of warming or heating.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin calefactiō, calefactiōnem.

parole.significato: warming
parole.testo: * Borrowed from Latin calefactorius.

parole.significato: A calendar or timeline or events.
parole.testo: From Latin calendārium. Doublet of calendar.

parole.significato: Often with initial capital: the first day of a month.
parole.testo: From Middle English calendes, calendas, calendis, kalandes, kalendas, kalendes, kalendez, kalendis, kalendus (also in the singular forms calende, kalend, kalende), from Latin kalendās, accusative plural of kalendae (“first day of a Roman month”), an archaic variant of calandae, from calandus (“which

parole.significato: To undergo calescence; to become or grow warm; to heat up; to warm; to glow with heat.
parole.testo: From Latin calescere.

parole.significato: Cup, cup-like.
parole.testo: From Latin calicis, genitive of calix. See also calyx.

parole.significato: Having the shape of a cup or calyx.
parole.testo: Latin calyx (“calyx”) + -iform. By surface analysis, calic- + -i- + -form.

parole.significato: Any cup-shaped depression.
parole.testo: From Latin caliculus, diminutive of calix. By surface analysis, calic- + -le.

parole.significato: Warm, hot.
parole.testo: From Latin calidus (“hot”), from caleō (“to be warm or hot; glow”) + -idus, from Proto-Italic *kalēō, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱelh₁-. Cognate with Italian calido (“hot”), French chaud (“warm, hot”), Portuguese cálido (“warm”), and Spanish cálido (“warm”).

parole.significato: Synonym of caldarium.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin calidārium.

parole.significato: Heat.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin caliditās, whence the Italian calidità. Compare calid.

parole.significato: A pipe or duct used, especially in ancient times, to convey hot air or steam for heating purposes.
parole.testo: Coined in 1624. From Latin calidus (“warm”) + -duct.

parole.significato: a type of water heater
parole.testo: Genericized trademark from Latin cali(dus) (“warm”) + font.

parole.significato: A heavy ancient Roman military sandal.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin caliga.

parole.significato: Wearing caligae or military boots.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin caligātus (“wearing soldiers’ boots, booted”), from caliga (“a Roman military leathern boot”) + -ātus (“-ed, -ate”, suffix forming adjectives), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: dimness; cloudiness
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin caligatio, from caligare (“to emit vapour, to be dark”), from caligo (“mist, darkness”).

parole.significato: darkness; obscurity.
parole.testo: From Latin cālīginōsus (“misty, dark”), from cālīgō (“fog; darkness”).

parole.significato: dimness or obscurity of sight, caused by a speck on the cornea
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cālīgō (“darkness”). Doublet of garua.

parole.significato: A Utraquist.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin calix (“chalice”); so called from their demanding the cup as well as the bread for the laity.

parole.significato: cunning or shrewd; crafty.
