parole.testo: From Latin callidus, from callere (“to be thick-skinned, to be hardened”), from callum, callus (“callous skin, callosity, callousness”).

parole.significato: craftiness, cunning
parole.testo: Latin calliditas.

parole.significato: painless vivisection
parole.testo: From Latin callere (“to be insensible”) + English section.

parole.significato: An African primate.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin callithrix. First attested in 1572.

parole.significato: A green monkey.
parole.testo: From Latin callithrix.

parole.significato: Emotionally hardened; unfeeling and indifferent to the suffering/feelings of others.
parole.testo: From Latin callōsus (“hard-skinned”), from callum (“hardened skin”) + -ōsus.

parole.significato: A hardened area of the skin (especially on the foot or hand) caused by repeated friction, wear or use.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin callum (“hard skin”). Displaced Old English wearr.

parole.significato: The study of heat flow and heat transfer.
parole.testo: From calorie + -ics. From Latin calor (“heat”).

parole.significato: An apparatus for measuring the heat generated or absorbed by either a chemical reaction, change of phase or some other…
parole.testo: From Latin calor (“warmth, heat”) + -meter.

parole.significato: The science of measuring the heat absorbed or evolved during the course of a chemical reaction or change of state.
parole.testo: From Latin calor (“warmth, heat”) + -metry.

parole.significato: A voltaic battery, from the 19th century, with a large surface of plate, producing (by the then standards) powerful hea…
parole.testo: Latin calor (“heat”) + English motor.

parole.significato: To form a protective surface on (a ferrous metal) by coating with aluminum powder and then heating.
parole.testo: From Latin calor (“heat”) + -ize.

parole.significato: In mathematical physics, a finite temperature instanton.
parole.testo: From Latin calor (“heat”) + -on.

parole.significato: A plant of the genus Caltha; a marsh marigold.
parole.testo: From the genus name (Latin caltha).

parole.significato: Any secondary calcareous deposit, created by the action of water outside the natural cave environment. They are typical…
parole.testo: From Latin calx (“lime”) + Latin < Ancient Greek θέμα (théma, “what is laid down”), (also Mediaeval Latin thema, "deposit") and the Latin -īta < Ancient Greek -ίτης (-ítēs) – used as a suffix indicating a rock or mineral.

parole.significato: To make hurtful untrue comments about.
parole.testo: First attested in 1554; borrowed from Latin calumniātus, perfect passive participle of calumnior (“to blame, cavil at; to accuse falsely”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A person who calumniates (slanders, or makes personal attacks upon, others).
parole.testo: From Latin calumniātor.

parole.significato: The calvaria; the dome or roof of the skull.
parole.testo: From Latin calva (“the scalp”).

parole.significato: The dome or roof of the skull, the skullcap.
parole.testo: From Latin calvāria (“skull”). Doublet of calvarium, calavera, and calvary.

parole.significato: The upper, domelike portion of the skull (without the lower jaw).
parole.testo: From Latin calvāria (“skull”), from calva, from calvus (“bald”).

parole.significato: Baldness, the condition of being bald.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin calvitiēs (“baldness”).

parole.significato: Baldness.
parole.testo: From Latin calvitium (“baldness”), from calvus (“bald”).

parole.significato: Lacking most or all of one's hair; bald, hairless.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin calvus (“bald, hairless”) (of unclear origin, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *kl̥h₂wós or *kalw- (“bald; naked”), from a root *kl̥H- + *-wós (suffix forming adjectives from verb stems)) + -ous (suffix forming adjectives from nouns, denoting possession or presence of a quality).

parole.significato: The substance which remains after a metal or mineral has been thoroughly burnt, once seen as being the essential substa…
parole.testo: From Latin calx (“lime”). Doublet of cauk and chalk.

parole.significato: Calyx, bud, or cup of a flower or nut.
parole.testo: From Latin calycis, genitive of calyx, from Ancient Greek κάλυξ (kálux, “case of a bud, husk”). By surface analysis, calyc- + -i-.

parole.significato: Having the petals and stamens adnate to the calyx.
parole.testo: Latin calyx (“calyx”), calycis (“calyx”) + flos (“flower”), floris (“flower”). By surface analysis, calyc- + -i- + flor + -al.

parole.significato: calyculus
parole.testo: From Latin calyculus (“small flower bud, calyx”), diminutive of calyx. See calyx and compare calicle. By surface analysis, calyc- + -le.

parole.significato: Any cup-shaped structure.
parole.testo: From Latin calyculus (“small flower bud, calyx”), diminutive of calyx. By surface analysis, calyc- + -ulus.

parole.significato: A bulbous bog orchid of the genus Calypso, Calypso bulbosa
parole.testo: From Latin, itself from Ancient Greek Καλυψώ (Kalupsṓ, “name of a sea nymph”)

parole.significato: The outermost whorl of flower parts, comprising the sepals, which covers and protects the petals as they develop.
parole.testo: From Latin calyx, from Ancient Greek κάλυξ (kálux, “case of a bud, husk”). Doublet of chalice and kelch.

parole.significato: That contains either of two or more different metal atoms
parole.testo: From Latin cambialis.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to camels.
parole.testo: From Latin camelinus.

parole.significato: Synonym of giraffe.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin camēlopardus, variant of camēlopardalis, from Ancient Greek καμηλοπάρδαλις (kamēlopárdalis, “giraffe”).

parole.significato: A group of prophetic goddesses associated with childbirth, wells, and fountains.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Camēnae.

parole.significato: A device for taking still or moving pictures or photographs.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin camera (“chamber or bedchamber”), from Ancient Greek καμάρα (kamára, “anything with an arched cover, a covered carriage or boat, a vaulted chamber, a vault”), of Old Iranian origin, from Proto-Iranian *kamarā- (“something curved”), from *kamárati, from Proto-Indo-Iranian

parole.significato: An instrument that uses a shaped prism or mirrors to cause an apparent image of external objects to appear as if projec…
parole.testo: Latin camera lucida

parole.significato: Relating to a chamber, especially to a judicial or legislative one
parole.testo: Formed from the root of Latin camera (“room; chamber”), with the suffix -al, perhaps corresponding to a Late Latin, Medieval Latin cameralis.

parole.significato: To build in the form of a vault; to arch over.
parole.testo: From Latin camerātus, perfect passive participle of camerō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A vaulting or arching over.
parole.testo: Latin cameratio.

parole.significato: Dressed with a shirt over the other garments.
parole.testo: From Latin camisia.

parole.significato: An ancient kind of shirt or nightgown.
parole.testo: From Latin camisia.

parole.significato: A Roman military boot.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin campagus.

parole.significato: A smallish suspended bell used in medieval monastic cloisters.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin campānella, from campāna (“steeple bell”) + -ella (diminutive suffix).

parole.significato: In the shape of a bell.
parole.testo: Latin campana (“bell”) + -form

parole.significato: A phytosterol, found in many vegetable oils, related to sitosterol
parole.testo: From Latin campester + -ol, campestris, from campus + -estris.

parole.significato: Relating to open fields or uncultivated land.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin campester (“of a field”), from campus (“field”), with the suffix -al.

parole.significato: A device used to measure a person's field of vision
parole.testo: From Latin campus (“field, scope”) + -meter.

parole.significato: The grounds or property of a school, college, university, business, church, or hospital, often understood to include bu…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin campus (“field”). Doublet of camp and champ. First used in its current sense in reference to Princeton University in the 1770s.

parole.significato: Channeled lengthwise; grooved.
parole.testo: From Latin canāliculātus (“channelled”).

parole.significato: canaliculus.
parole.testo: From Latin canaliculus.

parole.significato: Any of many small canals or ducts in the body, such as in the bone, or in some plants.
parole.testo: From Latin canāliculus (“small channel, pipe or gutter”), diminutive of canālis (“channel; pipe, gutter”), from canna (“cane, reed”), from Ancient Greek κάννα (kánna, “reed”).

parole.significato: Consisting of a network of veins, without intermediate parenchyma; lattice-like.
parole.testo: From Latin cancellatus, past participle of cancellare.

parole.significato: The act, process, or result of cancelling; as, the cancellation of certain words in a contract, or of the contract itse…
parole.testo: From Latin cancellātiō, from cancellō + -tiō.

parole.significato: Having low density and strength but high surface area, of the kind that fills the inner cavity of long bones.
parole.testo: From Latin cancellus (“lattice”).

parole.significato: A barrier, balustrade or railing, or screen, dividing the main body of a church from the chancel.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin cancellus (“little crab”). Doublet of chancel.

parole.significato: Someone with a Cancer star sign.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin cancer (“crab”), calque of Ancient Greek Καρκίνος (Karkínos, “crab”), calque of Akkadian 𒀀𒇻𒌅 (allutu, “crab”), from Sumerian 𒀯𒀠𒈜 (ᵐᵘˡAL.LUL, “crab; name of constellation”).

parole.significato: A disease in which the cells of a tissue undergo uncontrolled (often rapid) proliferation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cancer (“crab”), a calque of Ancient Greek καρκίνος (karkínos, “crab; ulcer; cancer”), possibly cognate, applied to cancerous tumors because of a supposed resemblence between their enlarged veins and the legs of a crab. Doublet of canker and chancre.

parole.significato: To grow into a cancer; to become cancerous.
parole.testo: From Latin cancerātus (“eaten by a cancer”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the astrological sign of Cancer.
parole.testo: From Cancer + -ian; from Latin Cancriana, from Cancer + -iana.

parole.significato: Relating to or affected with cancer.
parole.testo: From Middle English cancerous, from Latin cancerōsus, from cancer (“crab; tumor, cancer”) + -ōsus (adjective-forming suffix). By surface analysis, cancer + -ous.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to crabs.
parole.testo: From Latin cancer (“crab”) + -īnus, as if from *cancrīnus. The poetry sense comes from the fact that most species of crab can walk sideways, either left or right.

parole.significato: That feeds on crabs and other crustaceans
parole.testo: From Latin cancer (“crab”) + -vorous.

parole.significato: noma, a gangrenous disease of the face
parole.testo: From Latin cancrum ōris, from cancrum (“canker”) and ōris (“of the mouth, face”), genitive singular of ōs (“mouth, face”). The Latin phrase itself is first attested in a source that gives it as a translation of an English common name "mouth canker" or "canker of the mouth".

parole.significato: In the International System of Units, the base unit of luminous intensity; the luminous intensity, in a given direction…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin candēla (“candle”). Doublet of candle and chandelle.

parole.significato: A candle holder with branches to hold more than one candle.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin candēlābrum (“candlestick”), from candēla. Doublet of chandelier. Displaced native Old English candeltrēow (literally “candle tree”).

parole.significato: Glowing as a result of its high temperature; incandescent, glowing with heat.
parole.testo: From Latin candentem, from candere.

parole.significato: Glowing with heat; white-hot, incandescent.
parole.testo: From Latin candēscēns, present participle of candēscō (“to brighten, radiate, become red hot”).

parole.significato: Somewhat white, or turning white.
parole.testo: From Latin candicans, present participle of candicare (“to be whitish”).

parole.significato: Impartial and free from prejudice.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin candidus (“white”).

parole.significato: A person who seeks to be elected or appointed to a position or privilege.
parole.testo: From Latin candidātus (“a person who is standing for public office”, noun), from candidus (“dazzling white, shining, clear”) + -ātus, -āta, -ātum (participial adjective-forming suffix), in reference to Roman candidates wearing bleached white togas as a symbol of purity at a public forum. By surface

parole.significato: To make white; to whitewash.
parole.testo: From Latin candidātus (“dressed in white”, adjective); see Etymology 1 for further derivations. By surface analysis, candid + -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A light source consisting of a wick embedded in a solid, flammable substance such as wax, tallow, or paraffin.
parole.testo: From Middle English candel, from Old English candel (“candle”), borrowed from Latin candēla (“candle”), from Latin candeō (“be white, bright, shining”, verb); see candid. Doublet of candela and chandelle.

parole.significato: The state of being sincere and open in speech; honesty in expression.
parole.testo: From Latin candor (“brightness, whiteness”), from candeō (“to shine”).

parole.significato: Turning white or gray.
parole.testo: From Latin canescens, present participle of canescere (“to become gray or white”).

parole.significato: The killing of a dog.
parole.testo: From Latin canis (“dog”) + -cide.

parole.significato: Synonym of Sothic: of or related to the star Sirius.
parole.testo: From Latin canīculāris (“of or related to a puppy; Sothic”), from Canīcula (“puppy; Sirius”) + -aris (“forming adjectives”).

parole.significato: Synonym of dog days.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin diēs caniculārēs (literally “puppy days”), from Canīcula (“the Puppy”), a semantic loan of Ancient Greek Κῠ́ων (Kŭ́ōn, “the Dog”) in reference to Sirius, which appears in Epic Greek as κῠ́ων Ὠρίωνος (kŭ́ōn Ōríōnos, literally “Orion’s dog”) in its elided accusative form κύν’ Ὠρίωνος (

parole.significato: Characteristic of, or relating to the Caniformia.
parole.testo: From Latin canis (“dog”) + -form.

parole.significato: Of, or pertaining to, a dog or dogs.
parole.testo: From Latin canīnus (“of dogs, doglike, dogtooth”), from canis (“dog”). Compare French canin.

parole.significato: Synonym of cuspid, one of the pointed teeth behind the incisors and in front of the premolars.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin dens canīnus (“doglike tooth”), from canis (“dog”), from their prominence in dogs and wolves. Compare dogtooth.

parole.significato: The caninus muscle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin caninus, from canis + -inus.

parole.significato: A cylindrical or rectangular container usually of lightweight metal, plastic, or laminated pasteboard used for holding…
parole.testo: From Middle English canustyr (“basket”), a borrowing from Latin canistrum. Doublet of canaster and knaster. * (metal receptacle): Through influence of unrelated can. * (projectile): Short for canister shot, so called for its casing.

parole.significato: The condition of having gray hair.
parole.testo: From Latin cānitiēs (“gray hair, old age”).

parole.significato: A plant disease marked by gradual decay.
parole.testo: From Middle English canker, cancre, from Old English cancer (“cancer; crab”), akin to Dutch kanker, Old High German chanchar. Ultimately from Latin cancer (“a cancer”). Doublet of cancer, a later borrowing from Latin, and chancre, which came through French.

parole.significato: Relating to hemp; hempen.
parole.testo: Latin cannabinus.

parole.significato: A tall annual dioecious plant (Cannabis, especially Cannabis sativa), native to central Asia and having alternate, palm…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin cannabis (“hemp”), borrowed from Ancient Greek κάνναβις (kánnabis). See there for more. Further reading at Etymology of cannabis on Wikipedia. Doublet of canvas and hemp.

parole.significato: A woman who holds a canonry in a conventual chapter.
parole.testo: From canon + -ess. Compare Latin canonissa.

parole.significato: The office of a canon; a canonry.
parole.testo: From Latin canonucatus canonical: compare French canonicat.

parole.significato: From or relating to the ancient city of Canopus in northern Egypt.
parole.testo: From Latin Canōpicus.

parole.significato: An Egyptian pottery container in which the entrails of a mummy have been placed.
parole.testo: From Latin Canōpicus, from Canopus + -icus.

parole.significato: A canopic jar.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Canōpus.

parole.significato: melodious
parole.testo: From Latin canōrus.

parole.significato: An argot, the jargon of a particular class or subgroup.
parole.testo: From Latin cantō, probably via Old Northern French canter (“sing, tell”). Doublet of chant.

parole.significato: A graduate of the University of Cambridge.
parole.testo: Clipping of Cantabrigian, from Latin Cantabrigia (“Cambridge”).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to or characteristic of Cambridge or its university
parole.testo: From Latin Cantabrigia (“Cambridge”) + -n.

parole.significato: A singing.
parole.testo: Latin cantatio.

parole.significato: Spanish fly, Lytta vesicatoria (syn. Cantharis vesicatoria).
parole.testo: Late Middle English, from Latin cantharides, plural of cantharis.

parole.significato: A large drinking cup with two handles.
parole.testo: From Latin cantharus, from Ancient Greek κάνθαρος (kántharos).

parole.significato: Canthus, corner of the eye where the upper and lower lids meet.

parole.significato: Either corner of the eye, where the eyelids meet.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin canthus (“corner of the eye”), from Ancient Greek κανθός (kanthós, “corner of the eye”).

parole.significato: A chant, hymn or song, especially a nonmetrical one, with words from a biblical text.
parole.testo: From Latin canticulum, diminutive of cantus (“song”).

parole.significato: A canticle.
parole.testo: From Latin canticum (“chant, song”).

parole.significato: To chant, or to recite musically (especially in a synagogue).

parole.significato: A song, poem or incantation.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin cantiō, from canere (“to sing”). Doublet of chanson and canzone. By surface analysis, Latin cant- + -ion.

parole.significato: A singer, especially someone who takes a special role of singing or song leading at a ceremony.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cantor, agent noun from canere (“to sing”) + -tor (agent suffix). Doublet of chanter.

parole.significato: Of the side of the chancel, apse, altar or choir on which the cantor's (later precentor's) stall is placed (the left ha…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cantōris (“of the cantor”).

parole.significato: A female singer.
parole.testo: From Latin cantrīx.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Canterbury, England.
parole.testo: From Latin Cantuaria.

parole.significato: Synonym of superius.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin cantus (literally “song, chant”).

parole.significato: A preexisting melody forming the basis of a polyphonic composition.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin cantus firmus (literally “fixed chant”).

parole.significato: To qualify, to allow.
parole.testo: From Latin capax, capacis (“capacious”) + -fy.

parole.significato: grandorder.
parole.testo: From Latin capax (“large, spacious”) + order.

parole.significato: The pungent grayish green flower bud of the European and Oriental caper (Capparis spinosa), which is pickled and eaten.
parole.testo: From Latin capparis, from Ancient Greek κάππαρις (kápparis).

parole.significato: An arrest warrant; a writ commanding officers to take a specified person or persons into custody.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin capiās (“you should seize, you are to seize”), from capiō (“to seize”).

parole.significato: An instrument for removing foreign bodies from a cavity, such as placental remnants from the uterus.
parole.testo: From Latin capiat (“let it take”).

parole.significato: A filament.
parole.testo: From Latin capillamentum, from capillus (“hair”). Compare French capillament.

parole.significato: Resembling or pertaining to hair, especially in slenderness or fineness.
parole.testo: From Latin capillāris (“pertaining to the hair”), from capillus (“the hair, properly of the head”), from caput (“head”).

parole.significato: A capillary (blood vessel).
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?] (“hair”).

parole.significato: A bush of hair; frizzing of the hair.
parole.testo: Latin capillatura.

parole.significato: Having the form of a hair
parole.testo: From Latin capillus (“hair”) + -iform.

parole.significato: Hooded, cowled.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin capistrātus, participial adjective from capistrō (“to halter”), from capistrum (“halter”) + -ō, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Synonym of phorbeia.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin capistrum. Doublet of capstan.

parole.significato: person
parole.testo: From the Latin capita, plural of caput.

parole.significato: Having a distinct globular tip.
parole.testo: From Latin capitātus (“having a head”), from caput (“head”) + -ātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-forming suffix). The noun comes from the clipping of capitate bone.

parole.significato: per head
parole.testo: From Latin capitatim, from caput + -atim.

parole.significato: Performing a headcount; the counting of people.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin capitātiōnem, from caput (“head”).

parole.significato: An ancient English tenure, abolished in 1660, by which either person or land was held immediately of the king, or of hi…
parole.testo: From Latin caput (“head”).

parole.significato: Synonym of capitulum.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin capitellum, diminuitive of Latin caput (“head”), from Proto-Indo-European *kauput- (English head), itself from Proto-Indo-European *kap-. Doublet of caddie, cadel, cadet, capital, and caudillo.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Capitoline Hill in Rome or (historical) the various temples there in antiquity.
parole.testo: From Latin Capitolīnus (adj. & n.), from Capitolium (“Capitoline Hill”) + -inus (“-ine: forming adjectives”), from the oblique stem of caput (“head”) + -ō (“forming nouns”) or -ōlus (“-ole: forming diminutives”) + -ium (“forming location names”).

parole.significato: Synonym of capitol, similar citadels in ancient Italian and Roman towns.
parole.testo: From Latin Capitōlium (“Capitoline Hill, its temples; similar citadels”), from the oblique stem of caput (“head”) + -ō (noun-forming suffix) or -ōlus (“-ole”, diminutive suffix) + -ium (suffix forming place names). Doublet of capitol and capitoul.

parole.significato: A densely clustered inflorescence composed of a large number of individual florets arising from a platform-like base.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin capitulum. Doublet of chapiter and chapter.

parole.significato: A voluminous mantle worn by clergymen: in the Roman Catholic church, bishops wear violet, cardinals wear red.
parole.testo: From Latin cappa (“cape”) + magna (“great”).

parole.significato: Having a tendril or tendrils.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin capreolātus, from capreolus (“wild goat, tendril”) + -ātus, from caper (“goat”); see -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Compare French capréolé.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the subfamily Capreolinae.
parole.testo: From Latin capreolus (“wild goat”), from caper (“goat”).

parole.significato: Goat.
parole.testo: From Latin caper (“male goat”) (genitive caprī). By surface analysis, capr- + -i-.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or derived from capric acid
parole.testo: From Latin caper (“goat”), after its smell + -ic. By surface analysis, capr- + -ic.

parole.significato: Someone with a Capricorn star sign.
parole.testo: From Latin Capricornus. By surface analysis, capri- + corn (“horn”).

parole.significato: A process for ripening, or pollinating, figs by means of their being punctured artificially, in a manner designed to re…
parole.testo: From Latin caprifīcātiōnem, ultimately from Latin caprifīcus (“wild fig tree”).

parole.significato: A hermaphrodite fruit, inedible to humans, of certain usually uncultivated species of Ficus, which is the source of the…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin caprifīcus.

parole.significato: The woodbine or honeysuckle.
parole.testo: From Latin caper (“goat”) + folium (“leaf”).

parole.significato: Having the form of a goat
parole.testo: From Latin capra (“she-goat”) + -form.

parole.significato: To pollinate (figs) by caprification.
parole.testo: From Latin caprifīcus + -ify. By surface analysis, capri- + -fy.

parole.significato: Resembling or originating from goats.
parole.testo: From Latin capra or caper (“goat”), + -genous.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Caprinae (goats, sheep, and certain wild relatives).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin caprīnus. The taxonomic sense is a semantic loan from translingual Caprinae.

parole.significato: Having or relating to feet like those of a goat.
parole.testo: From Latin capriped-, capripēs.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or derived from caproic acid
parole.testo: From Latin caper (“goat”), after its smell + -oic. By surface analysis, capr- + -oic.

parole.significato: A liquid fatty acid, CH₃(CH₂)₄COOH, obtained from animal fats, and used in the manufacture of pharmaceuticals and flavo…
parole.testo: From Latin caper (“goat”) because of its smell. From capr- + -oic and acid.

parole.significato: A form of mead made with chili peppers.
parole.testo: capsicum + Latin mel (“honey”).

parole.significato: A courting of favor or applause, by flattery or address; a captivating quality; an attraction
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin captatio, captationis, from capto. Compare French captation.

parole.significato: The descriptive heading or title, of a document or part thereof.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin captiō (“deception, fraud”), from the past participle of capiō (“to take, to seize”) (English capture). Compare Middle English capcioun (“seizure, capture”).

parole.significato: A female captivator.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin captīvātrīx. By surface analysis, captivate + -trix.

parole.significato: One who has been captured or is otherwise confined.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English captif; derived from Latin captīvus, probably through a borrowing from a Middle French intermediate. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“seize, hold”). Doublet of caitiff.

parole.significato: The state of being captive.
parole.testo: From Middle English captivite, from Latin captīvitās. By surface analysis, captive + -ity. Entered into the English lexicon around the 14th century.

parole.significato: Worthless residue of sublimation or distillation.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin caput mortuum (literally “dead head”).

parole.significato: A neonatal condition involving a serosanguinous, subcutaneous, extraperiosteal fluid collection with poorly defined mar…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin caput succēdāneum.

parole.significato: An ancient small boat made of wickerwork covered with a hide or leather.
parole.testo: From Latin carabus. The entomological sense is borrowed from translingual Carabus, from the same Latin source.

parole.significato: A mark or sign.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin character.

parole.significato: Accumulation of wasteful elements of carbon or mere carbon inside blood.
parole.testo: From carbo- + -hæmia, conjunction: Latin carbo (“charcol”) and Ancient Greek αἷμα (haîma, “blood”).

parole.significato: An excessive amount of carbon, particularity carbon dioxide, in the blood.
parole.testo: From carbon + -aemia, conjunction: Latin carbo (“charcol”) and Ancient Greek αἷμα (haîma, “blood”).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or resembling a carbuncle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin carbunculāris. By surface analysis, carbuncle + -ar.

parole.significato: The blasting of something, by excessive heat or cold.
parole.testo: Latin carbunculatio.

parole.significato: An invasive malignant tumour derived from epithelial tissue that tends to metastasize to other areas of the body.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin carcinōma (“tumour; ulcer; carcinoma”), from Ancient Greek κᾰρκῐ́νωμᾰ (kărkĭ́nōmă, “sore, ulcer; cancer”), from καρκινόω (karkinóō, “to make (something) resemble a crab”, in the mediopassive "to become cancerous; to suffer from cancer") + -μᾰ (-mă, action noun suffix). parole.testo: From Latin cardinālis (“pertaining to a hinge (hence applied to that on which something turns or depends), important, principal, chief”).

parole.significato: A piece of body armour—originally a metal breastplate or pair of plates—worn in classical antiquity to protect the regi…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cardiophylax, derived from Ancient Greek καρδία (kardía) + φύλαξ (phúlax).

parole.significato: inflammation of the heart (any or all parts of it).
parole.testo: From Latin cardītis. By surface analysis, cardi- + -itis.

parole.significato: The basal joint of the maxilla in insects
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cardō (“hinge”). Doublet of kern.

parole.significato: An oily yellow phenolic compound C₂₁H₃₀O₃ extracted from the shell of the cashew nut and one of the primary components…
parole.testo: From Anacardium (“generic name of the cashew”) + Latin oleum (“oil”).

parole.significato: Synonym of carenum (“reduction of must or sweet wine in ancient European cuisine”).
parole.testo: From Latin carēnum or caroenum, from Ancient Greek κάροινον (károinon), q.v.

parole.significato: A reduction of must or sweet wine produced by boiling it in large kettles until it was reduced by half or two-thirds in…
parole.testo: From Latin carēnum or caroenum, from Ancient Greek κάροινον (károinon), q.v.

parole.significato: A mark ⟨ ‸ ⟩ used by writers and proofreaders to indicate that something is to be inserted at that point.
parole.testo: From the Latin caret (“it lacks”), the third-person singular present active indicative form of careō (“to lack”).

parole.significato: Any member of the genus Carex of sedges.
parole.testo: From Latin carex.

parole.significato: A junction of four roads.
parole.testo: From Middle English carfukes, an Anglicisation of Latin quadrifurcus (“four-pronged, four-forked”). Doublet of carfour.

parole.significato: Shaped like a fig.

parole.significato: figs, especially those from Caria

parole.significato: A longitudinal ridge or projection like the keel of a boat.

parole.significato: Shaped like a boat's keel.

parole.significato: Synonym of scaphoid abdomen.
parole.testo: From Latin carinatus, from carina (“keel”), + Middle French abdomen, from Latin abdomen, possibly from abdō (“conceal”), from ab (“away”) + dere (“to put, place”).

parole.significato: charitable
parole.testo: From Latin cāritās.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the caritive case.

parole.significato: Either of two amino acid toxins produced by the sea anemone species, Actinia cari.

parole.significato: A visual poem in the shape of an object.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin carmen figuratum.

parole.significato: Relieving the discomfort of gas in the digestive tract, either by reducing its production (by the gut microbiota) or by…
parole.testo: From Latin carminātus (“carded”), past participle of Latin carminō (“to card, produce by carding; hence to cleanse”), from carmen (“a card for freeing wool or flax from the coarser parts, and from extraneous matter”).

parole.significato: The state of being carnal.
parole.testo: From Middle English carnalitee, carnalyte, carnalite, from Latin carnālitās, equivalent to carnal + -ity. Compare Old French charnalité.

parole.significato: A crypt, a charnel house.
parole.testo: From Latin carnarium, from caro, carnis (“flesh”).

parole.significato: A pale pink or beige color; peach or flesh-tone.
parole.testo: Latin carneus.

parole.significato: An executioner.
parole.testo: From Latin carnifex (“butcher”).

parole.significato: To form flesh; to become like flesh.
parole.testo: From Latin carnificare, from Latin carnis (“flesh”) + facere (“to make”). Compare French carnifier.

parole.significato: Carnivorans.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin carnivora.

parole.significato: greedy appetite for meat
parole.testo: From oblique stem of Latin caro, carnis (“flesh, meat”) + -i- + voracity.

parole.significato: Of, or relating to carnivores, or the taxonomic order Carnivora.
parole.testo: From Latin carnivorus (“flesh-eating”).

parole.significato: Any writing, films, images, or other material that contains gratuitous amounts of bloodshed or violence.
parole.testo: From Latin carnis (“meat”) and Ancient Greek γραφή (graphḗ, “writing”), by analogy to pornography. Although it is often taken to be a blend carnage and pornography, this is not the case.

parole.significato: A strong fear or dislike of meat.
parole.testo: From Latin carnis (“meat”) + -phobia.

parole.significato: Fleshy.
parole.testo: From Latin carnosus.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a person named Charles or its variants and cognates; or places, things, or eras so named.
parole.testo: From Latin Carolus (“Charles”) + -ean. May be decomposed as Carol (“Charles”) + -ean.

parole.significato: A former gold coin of Germany
parole.testo: Latin Carolus (“Charles”).

parole.significato: Synonym of Carolean (“relating to the time of Kings Charles I and II of England or Charles III of the United Kingdom, o…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin carolīnus.

parole.significato: An old English gold coin, worth 20 (or later 23) shillings.
parole.testo: From Carolus, Latin for Charles. Doublet of Charles.

parole.significato: A Spanish-American peso or piece of eight issued by Charles III (1759–88) and Charles IV (1788–1808) of Spain.

parole.significato: Any of the eight bones of the wrist (carpus).

parole.significato: Enjoy the present, make the most of today, (common mistranslation) seize the day.

parole.significato: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see carry, over.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Carthage.
parole.testo: Latin carthāginiānus, from Carthāgō + -iānus.

parole.significato: The formation of cartilage.

parole.significato: Comprising soft cartilage rather than bone.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cartilāginōsus (“full of cartilage, very gristly”), from cartilāgō (“cartilage, gristle”) + -ōsus (“-ous, -ose”); compare French cartilagineux. Equivalent to cartilage + -ous, with modifications made to its morphology.

parole.significato: Synonym of caruncle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin caruncula (“a little piece of flesh”). Doublet of caruncle.

parole.significato: An exoenzyme that hydrolyzes casein.
parole.testo: From Latin cāseus (“cheese”) + -ase.

parole.significato: To make or become cheeselike.
parole.testo: From Latin cāseus (“cheese”), + -fy.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or resembling cheese.
parole.testo: Compare French caséique, from Latin caseus (“cheese”). Doublet of cheesy. By surface analysis, Latin case(us) + -ic

parole.significato: Casein.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin caseum (“cheese”).

parole.significato: The spice made from the bark of members of the genus Cinnamomum other than true cinnamon (C. verum), when they are dist…
parole.testo: From Latin cassia (“cinnamon”), from Ancient Greek κασσία, κασία, κάσια (kassía, kasía, kásia), from Hebrew קְצִיעָה (qəṣīʿā), from Aramaic קְצִיעֲתָא (qəṣīʿătā), from קְצַע (qṣaʿ, “to cut off”). Compare Kezia.

parole.significato: An American bird (Psarocolius decumanus, syn. Cassicus cristatus), allied to the starlings and orioles, remarkable for…
parole.testo: From Latin cassis (“helmet”).

parole.significato: Shaped like a helmet; applied to a corolla with a broad, helmet-shaped upper petal, as in aconite.
parole.testo: Latin cassis meaning "helmet".

parole.significato: An ellagitannin found in oak and chestnut wood.
parole.testo: From Latin castanea (“chestnut”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to Castalia, a mythical fountain of inspiration on Mount Parnassus, sacred to the Muses.
parole.testo: Latin Castalius

parole.significato: Having the colour of a chestnut; chestnut-coloured.
parole.testo: From the Latin castanea (“a chestnut, a chestnut tree”) + -ous (“full, full of”).

parole.significato: The study of castles.
parole.testo: Based on Latin castellum (“castle, fortress”) and Ancient Greek λόγος (lógos, “word”)

parole.significato: A small Roman detached fort or fortlet used as a watch tower or signal station.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin castellum. Doublet of cashel, castell, castle, and château.

parole.significato: One who is castigated.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin castīgāns, present active participle of castīgō (“to castigate”). By surface analysis, castigate + -ant.

parole.significato: To punish or reprimand someone severely.
parole.testo: First attested in the beginning of the 17ᵗʰ century; borrowed from Latin castīgātus, perfect passive participle of castīgō (“to reprove”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from castus (“pure, chaste”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱes- (“to cut”). Doublet of chastise

parole.significato: The bitter exudate of the castor sacs of mature beavers, used as a scent mark, and as a tincture in some perfumes.
parole.testo: From Latin castoreum, from Ancient Greek καστόριον (kastórion).

parole.significato: An extract from the glands of a beaver, reputed to have medicinal value.
parole.testo: From Latin castor (“beaver”).

parole.significato: Planning and construction of a military camp.
parole.testo: From Latin castra (“a camp”) and metāri (“to measure off”).

parole.significato: A castrated man; a eunuch.
parole.testo: Likely from an unattested sense of Middle English castrat (“(adjective) castrated; (noun) a castrated animal”), substantivized borrowing of Latin castrātus, perfect passive participle of castrō (“to prune, amputate, castrate”), see -ate (noun-forming suffix)).

parole.significato: To remove the testicles of a person or animal.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin castrātus, perfect passive participle of Latin castrō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Displaced native geld in its broader sense.

parole.significato: A female who castrates (either literally or metaphorically).
parole.testo: From Latin castratrix or castrate + -trix with feminine agent-nounal suffix; compare castrator.

parole.significato: Belonging to a (military) camp.
parole.testo: From Latin castrēnsis + -ial, from castra (“camp”).

parole.significato: castrensial
parole.testo: From Latin castrēnsis + -i- + -an, from castra (“camp”).

parole.significato: Among the Ancient Romans, a building or plot of land used as a military defensive position.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin castrum. Doublet of Caister, Chester, ksar, and qasr.

parole.significato: Synonym of casuistry, particularly in its neutral sense.
parole.testo: From casuistic + -s, equivalent to Latin casus + -istics, in the medical sense under the influence of English case. Also by surface analysis, casu(al) + -istics or by surface analysis, casu(al) + -ist + -ics or by surface analysis, casuist + -ics.

parole.significato: A chasuble.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin casula.

parole.significato: An act seen as justifying or causing a war; an act of war.
parole.testo: From Latin cāsus (“occasion”) + bellī (“for war”, literally “of war”).

parole.significato: A situation covered by the terms of an international treaty (or similar understanding), and which consequently requires…
parole.testo: From Latin casus (“case”) + foederis, genitive of foedus (“treaty”).

parole.significato: A force majeure
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: A case not provided for by the statute.
parole.testo: Latin [Term?]. Compare Spanish hacer caso omiso

parole.significato: The nominative case, sometimes grouped with the vocative case, as a single morphological case contrasted with the obliq…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin cāsus rēctus (literally “straight case”).

parole.significato: Either of two types of misuse of a word or misapplication of a concept.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin catachrēsis, borrowed from Ancient Greek κατάχρησις (katákhrēsis, “misuse (of a word)”).

parole.significato: A rhetorical device in which a series is arranged in "proper order", particularly
parole.testo: From the Latin form of the Ancient Greek κατακόσμησις (katakósmēsis, “arrangement”).

parole.significato: (said of a line with incomplete meter) lacking a syllable at the end or ending with an incomplete foot.
parole.testo: From Latin catalecticus, from Ancient Greek καταληκτικός (katalēktikós, “leaving off, incomplete”) from κατάληξις (katálēxis).

parole.significato: A boy or younger man in a homoerotic relationship with an older man.
parole.testo: From Latin catamītus (“boy kept as a sexual partner”), from Catamītus, from Etruscan 𐌂𐌀𐌕𐌌𐌉𐌕𐌄 (catmite), from Ancient Greek Γανυμήδης (Ganumḗdēs, “Ganymede”), an attractive Trojan boy supposedly abducted to Mount Olympus by the god Zeus to become his cupbearer and lover. Doublet of Ganymede.

parole.testo: From Latin cēreus, from cēra (“wax”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Roman goddess Ceres

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Roman goddess Ceres.
parole.testo: From Latin Ceresius (as in Ceresius lacus, Lake Lugano), from Cerēs. Often a nonce coinage for Cererian (vd. 1866).

parole.significato: Inclining or nodding downward; pendulous; drooping.
parole.testo: Latin cernuus (“with the face turned toward the earth”).

parole.significato: wax
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cēra.

parole.significato: A waxy substance obtained from the bark of sugar cane. Probably the same as sugarcane wax

parole.significato: A white waxy solid obtained from Chinese wax, and by the distillation of cerotin.
parole.testo: From Latin cerotum (“a pomade”). See cerate.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Turkey oak.
parole.testo: From Latin cerreus, from cerrus (“a kind of oak”).

parole.significato: A team competition in which contestants answer questions about classical history, culture, and mythology, and the Latin…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin certāmen (“contest”). Ultimately from Latin certus (“certain, fixed, settled, firm”).

parole.significato: A grant of the right of an appeal to be heard by an appellate court where that court has discretion to choose which app…
parole.testo: From the present passive infinitive of Latin certiōrō (“to make certain”), from the words used at the beginning of these writs when they were written in Latin: certiorārī volumus (“[we] wish to be made certain”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to certitude.
parole.testo: From Latin certitūdin- + -al, from oblique stem of Latin certitūdō, from certus + -tūdō. By surface analysis, certitude + -al.

parole.significato: Characterised by certitude.
parole.testo: From Latin certitūdin- + -ous, from oblique stem of Latin certitūdō, from certus + -tūdō. By surface analysis, certitude + -ous.

parole.significato: Cerulean.
parole.testo: From Latin caerulus.

parole.significato: The act of becoming blue; bluing
parole.testo: From Latin caerulescens, from caeruleus (“cerulean”), from caelum + -uleus, equivalent to cerulean + -escence. By surface analysis, cerule + -escence.

parole.significato: A greenish-blue pigment consisting essentially of cobalt stannate.
parole.testo: From Latin ceruleum (“dark blue, dark green”).

parole.significato: A blue metalloprotein that contains copper; it acts as a ferroxidase in association with transferrin.
parole.testo: cerulo (derived from Latin caeruleus (“colored blue”)) + plasmin

parole.significato: A mineral form of lead carbonate, PbCO₃, that is an ore of lead.
parole.testo: From Latin cērussa (“white lead”) + -ite.

parole.significato: neck pain
parole.testo: From Latin cervīcis (genitive of cervīx) + -algia. By surface analysis, cervic- + -algia.

parole.significato: The killing of deer.
parole.testo: Latin cervus (“deer”) + -cide, from the combining form of the Latin verb caedō (“to kill”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the cervix.
parole.testo: From Latin cervīcis, genitive of cervīx. By surface analysis, cervic- + -o-.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or characteristic of deer (in the broad sense).
parole.testo: By anglicisation from Latin cervīnus; by surface analysis, Latin cerv(us) (“deer”) + -ine.

parole.significato: The neck.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cervīx (“neck”), see below.

parole.significato: A radical, C₂₇H₅₅, supposed to exist in several compounds obtained from waxes.
parole.testo: From Latin cera (“wax”) + -yl.

parole.significato: An oil obtained by distillation of peat, containing various members of the pyridine series.
parole.testo: From Latin caespes, caespitis (“a turf”).

parole.significato: tufty; growing in tufts.
parole.testo: Latin caespes (“turf”).

parole.significato: Dormant, inactive.
parole.testo: From Latin cessans, present participle of cessare. See cease.

parole.significato: A writ given by statute to recover lands when the tenant has for two years failed to perform the conditions of his tenu…
parole.testo: Latin [Term?], meaning "he has ceased".

parole.significato: Of the air, yielding.
parole.testo: From Latin cess-, past participle stem of cedere (“cede”).

parole.significato: Before 1880, a debtor's surrender of his estate to his creditors in return for a judicial protection from imprisonment…
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: The person who receives transfer or cession of a personal obligation from the cedent.
parole.testo: From Latin cedere (“to yield”).

parole.significato: Of, or pertaining to a boxer's gloves
parole.testo: Latin cestus (“boxing glove”)

parole.significato: A leather fighting glove, frequently weighted with metal.
parole.testo: From Latin caestus.

parole.significato: A girdle, especially that of Aphrodite (or Venus) which gave the wearer the power to excite love.
parole.testo: From Latin cestus.

parole.significato: The aliphatic hydrocarbon C₁₆H₃₄ (hexadecane) used as a standard for diesel fuel.
parole.testo: From Latin cetus (“whale”) + -ane.

parole.significato: All things being equal; with all other things or factors remaining the same; other things held constant; all else uncha…
parole.testo: From Latin cēterīs, the ablative plural of cēterus (“the other, the rest”), + paribus, the ablative case plural of pār (“equal”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to cetoleic acid or its derivatives
parole.testo: From Latin cetus + oleic.

parole.significato: Compare; compare to; compare with.
parole.testo: From Latin cf., abbreviation of cōnfer (“compare”), imperative of cōnferō (“to compare”).

parole.significato: A form of fine-grained quartz that is nearly transparent or has a milky translucence; it fractures conchoidally.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin chalcēdōnius, from Ancient Greek χαλκηδόνιος (khalkēdónios), from Ancient Greek χαλκηδών (khalkēdṓn), cognate to Arabic كَرْكَنْد (karkand).

parole.significato: Synonym of Chalcidian
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Chalcidicus, from Ancient Greek Χαλκιδικός (Khalkidikós).

parole.significato: In ancient Roman architecture, the vestibule or portico of a public building opening on to the forum.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin chalcidicum, from Chalcidicum, neuter singular of Chalcidicus (“Chalcidian”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Chaldea.
parole.testo: From Latin chaldaicus. By surface analysis, Chalda- + -ic.

parole.significato: An idiom or peculiarity in Biblical Aramaic.
parole.testo: From Latin Chaldaismus. By surface analysis, Chalda- + -ism.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Chaldea specifically, or ancient Babylonia in general.
parole.testo: From Latin chaldaeus [from Ancient Greek Χαλδαῖος (Khaldaîos)] + -an.

parole.significato: Synonym of Chaldean.
parole.testo: From Latin chaldaeus via Middle French Chaldee.

parole.significato: A chapel within the jurisdiction of a church; a subordinate ecclesiastical foundation.
parole.testo: Compare English chapellenie, Latin capellania. See chaplain.

parole.significato: Any ferryman.
parole.testo: From Latin Charōn, from Ancient Greek Χάρων (Khárōn). The name of the moon was coined by American astronomer James W. Christy in 1978, in reference to a fictional moon of Pluto in a novel by Edmond Hamilton but also influenced by its similarity to Char, a pet name for Charlene, his wife's name — hen

parole.significato: Resembling paper or parchment; papery.
parole.testo: From Latin chartaceus. See charta.

parole.significato: A small piece of paper for the storage of one dose of a medicinal powder.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin chartula (“little paper”). Doublet of charter.

parole.significato: A deep, steep-sided rift, gap or fissure; a gorge or abyss.
parole.testo: From Latin chasma, from Ancient Greek χάσμα (khásma, “abyss, cleft”). Doublet of chasma. Compare schism. Displaced native Old English swelh and Old English elh.

parole.significato: A pincer-like claw of a crustacean or arachnid.
parole.testo: From Latin chele, from Ancient Greek χηλή (khēlḗ).

parole.significato: pseudoscorpion
parole.testo: From Latin chēlē (“claw”) (from Ancient Greek χηλή (khēlḗ, “claw”)) + -fer.

parole.significato: The branch of natural science that deals with the composition and constitution of substances and the changes that they…
parole.testo: First coined 1605, from chemist + -ry. From chemist, chymist, from Latin alchimista, from Arabic اَلْكِيمِيَاء (al-kīmiyāʔ), from article اَل (al-) + Ancient Greek χυμεία (khumeía, “art of alloying metals”), from χύμα (khúma, “fluid”), from χυμός (khumós, “juice”), from χέω (khéō, “to pour”).

parole.significato: to chemisorb
parole.testo: Blend of chemo- (“chemical”) + adsorb, from Latin sorbere (“to suck”)

parole.significato: alchemy, chemistry (prior to their being properly distinguished)
parole.testo: From the post-Classical Latin chemia, chymia, chimia. Doublet of Kimiya.

parole.significato: A hyrax.
parole.testo: From Latin choerogryllus, from Ancient Greek χοιρογρύλλιος (khoirogrúllios), a compound of χοῖρος (khoîros) and γρῦλος (grûlos), both meaning “pig”. The Greek word was used in the Septuagint to render Hebrew שפן (“hyrax”).

parole.significato: A peninsula.
parole.testo: From Latin Chersonēsus, from Ancient Greek χερσόνησος (khersónēsos, “originally, the Gallipoli peninsula; later, any peninsula”), from χέρσος (khérsos, “dry land”) + νῆσος (nêsos, “island”).

parole.testo: From Middle English cherub, cherube, cherubin, cherubine, cherubym, cherubyn, cherybin, gerubin, jerubin (“angel of the second highest order; depiction of such an angel”), from Old English cerubin, cerubim, ceruphin, cherubin, from Latin cherūbīm, cherūbīn, from Ancient Greek χερουβῑ́μ (kheroubī́m),

parole.significato: A cherub.

parole.significato: The twenty-second letter of the Classical and Modern Greek alphabets.
parole.testo: From Latin chī, from Ancient Greek χεῖ (kheî).

parole.significato: An inversion of the relationship between the elements of phrases.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin chiasmus, borrowed from Ancient Greek χιασμός (khiasmós), from χῑᾰ́ζω (khīắzō, “to mark with an X”) + -μός (-mós).

parole.significato: thousand; thousandfold.
parole.testo: From Latin chilias, itself from Ancient Greek χίλιοι (khílioi, “thousand”). Doublet of kilo-.

parole.significato: A group of 1000 things, particularly
parole.testo: From Latin chilias (“the number 1000, a group of 1000 things”), possibly via French chiliade, from Ancient Greek χιλιάς (khiliás, “the number 1000, any large amount, a millennium”), from χῑ́λιοι (khī́lioi, “1000”) + -ᾰ́ς (-ắs, “-ad: forming collective nouns”). Equivalent to chilia- + -ad.

parole.significato: A regiment of 1000 soldiers, typically commanded by a chiliarch.
parole.testo: From Latin chiliarchia, from Ancient Greek χιλιαρχία (khiliarkhía), from χῑ́λιοι (khī́lioi, “1000”) + -αρχία (-arkhía, “-archy: rule by”). Equivalent to chilia- + -archy.

parole.significato: Synonym of millenarian: a person who believes the Second Coming of Jesus Christ will involve his physical rule on Earth…
parole.testo: From Latin chiliasta, possibly via French chiliaste, from Ancient Greek χιλιαστής (khiliastḗs), from χῑ́λιοι (khī́lioi, “thousand”) + -αστής (-astḗs, “-ast, -ist: forming agent nouns”). Equivalent to chilia- + -ast.

parole.significato: Producing chyle.
parole.testo: From Latin chilus, chylus (“chyle”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a chimera.
parole.testo: From chimera, from Latin chimaera, from Ancient Greek χίμαιρα (khímaira, “she-goat”). This term entered English in or around 1638.

parole.significato: Gout in the hand.
parole.testo: From Latin chīragra, from Ancient Greek χειράγρα (kheirágra).

parole.significato: Chironomy.
parole.testo: From Latin chīronomia, from Ancient Greek χειρονομία (kheironomía, “gesticulation”).

parole.significato: A form of oriental ruby, carbuncle or possibly jasper
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin chodchod, a transliteration of Hebrew כַּדְכֹּד. parole.significato: An ancient dry measure of two pints or greater.
parole.testo: From Latin choenix, from Ancient Greek χοῖνῐξ (khoînĭx).

parole.significato: Any of several acute infectious diseases of humans and domestic animals, caused by certain strains of the Vibrio choler…
parole.testo: From Latin cholera (“bilious disease”), from Ancient Greek χολέρα (kholéra, “cholera”). Doublet of choler.

parole.significato: A limping iamb.
parole.testo: From Latin choliambus, from Ancient Greek χωλίαμβος (khōlíambos).

parole.significato: A chorus leader, especially one who provided at his own expense and under his own supervision one of the choruses for t…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin chorāgus, from Doric Greek χορᾱγός (khorāgós), from χορός (khorós, “chorus”) + -ᾱγός (-āgós, Doric form of -ηγός (-ēgós, “-leader”)), literally “chorus-leader”. Compare Attic Greek χορηγός (khorēgós).

parole.significato: notochord
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: A country or suffragan bishop, appointed in the ancient church by a diocesan bishop to exercise episcopal jurisdiction…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin chōrepiscopus, from Ancient Greek χωρεπίσκοπος (khōrepískopos); χώρα (khṓra, “place, country”) + ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos, “overseer, bishop”) (from ἐπί (epí, “on, upon, over”) + σκοπός (skopós, “watcher”)). Compare bishop.

parole.significato: A trochee.
parole.testo: From Latin choreus, from Ancient Greek χορεῖος (khoreîos), related to χορός (khorós, “choir, chorus”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to a choriamb.
parole.testo: Latin choriambicus, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: A metrical foot consisting of four syllables, of which the first and last are long, and the others short; a choreus, or…
parole.testo: From Latin choriambus, from Ancient Greek. Equivalent to choreus + iambus.

parole.significato: Including or involving a Greek chorus
parole.testo: From Latin choricus.

parole.significato: Someone who describes a particular region or country.
parole.testo: From Latin chōrographus, from Ancient Greek χωρογράφος (khōrográphos, “describing countries”), from χώρα (khṓra), χῶρος (khôros, “region, country”).

parole.significato: The study of provinces, regions, cities, etc., as opposed to larger-scale geography.
parole.testo: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin chōrographia, from Ancient Greek χωρογραφία (khōrographía), from χωρογρᾰ́φος (khōrogrắphos) [itself from χώρα (khṓra) + -γρᾰ́φος (-grắphos)] + -ία (-ía). By surface analysis, choro- + -graphy.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to chrism.
parole.testo: Latin chrismalis.

parole.significato: A figure or other artistic depiction of Jesus Christ.

parole.significato: The Christian religion.
parole.testo: From Latin chrīstiānismus; compare French christianisme, equivalent to Christian + -ism.

parole.significato: A vitreous mineral, often pale green, a mixed oxide of aluminium and beryllium with the chemical formula BeAl₂O₄, used…
parole.testo: From Latin chrysoberyllus, from Ancient Greek χρῡσοβήρυλλος (khrūsobḗrullos, “gold beryl”), from χρυσός (khrusós, “gold”) after its color, and βήρυλλος (bḗrullos, “beryl”), equivalent to chryso- + beryl.

parole.significato: One of a number of male Christian writers from Antiquity whose doctrinal work is considered authoritative by the later…
parole.testo: Calque of Latin Pater Ecclēsiae.

parole.significato: chylification (The formation of chyle).
parole.testo: chyle + Latin facere (“to make”)

parole.significato: Relating to food.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cibarius, from cibus (“food”).

parole.significato: The act of consuming food.
parole.testo: From Latin cibatio, from cibare (“to feed”).

parole.significato: Any of several insects in the superfamily Cicadoidea, with small eyes wide apart on the head and transparent well-veine…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cicāda, ultimately onomatopoeic. Doublet of cicala.

parole.significato: cicatricula
parole.testo: Compare French cicatricule, from Latin cicatricula (“a small scar”), from cicatrix (“a scar”).

parole.significato: The point, in the yolk of an egg, from which the embryo is formed.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cicātrīcula, diminutive of cicātrīx (“scar”).

parole.significato: A scar that remains after the development of new tissue over a recovering wound or sore (also used figuratively).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cicatrix.

parole.significato: Myrrhis odorata, a plant in the genus Myrrhis, in the family Apiaceae.
parole.testo: From Latin seselis, from Ancient Greek σέσελις (séselis).

parole.significato: Of or relating to Marcus Tullius Cicero, or the ideas in his philosophical treatises.
parole.testo: From the Latin Cicerōniānus.

parole.significato: Pertaining to storks.
parole.testo: From Latin ciconia (“stork”).

parole.significato: To tame, domesticate.
parole.testo: From Latin cicurare (“to tame”), from cicur (“tame”).

parole.significato: Hemlock.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cicūta. Apparently related to kex/kix.

parole.significato: Made, or consisting, of hair.
parole.testo: From Latin cilicium (“a covering, originally made of Cilician goat hair”), from Cilicious (“Cilician”), from Cilicia (“a province of Asia Minor”).

parole.significato: A short microscopic hairlike organelle projecting from a eukaryotic cell (such as a unicellular organism or one cell of…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cilium (“eyelid”).

parole.significato: A superintendent or keeper of a church's valuables; a churchwarden.
parole.testo: Latin cimeliarcha, from Ancient Greek treasurer.

parole.significato: Any member of the genus Cimex, especially the bedbug.
parole.testo: From the genus name Cimex, from Latin cīmex (“bug”). Doublet of chinch.

parole.significato: Any of the mythical people supposed to inhabit a land of perpetual darkness.
parole.testo: From the Latin Cimmerius, from Ancient Greek Κιμμέριος (Kimmérios, “pertaining to the Cimmerii”) + -an.

parole.significato: A soft clayey mineral of whitish or greyish colour.
parole.testo: First attested in 1801; formed as Latin Cimōlia (from the Ancient Greek Κιμωλία γῆ (Kimōlía gê, “earth of Kimolos”) — Cimōlus being the former name of Argentiera) + English -ite.

parole.significato: A 7–9 or 8–10 split (result of a first throw).
parole.testo: Named after the Society of the Cincinnati, which is named after Lucius Quinctius Cincinnatus; see Latin Cincinnāti and Cincinnātus.

parole.significato: A type of monochasium on which the successive axes arise alternately in respect to the preceding one; a scorpioid cyme.
parole.testo: From Latin cincinnus (“a lock of hair”).

parole.significato: An enclosure, or the act of enclosing, encircling or encompassing
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin cinctūra. Cognate with Spanish cintura (“waist”). Doublet of ceinture.

parole.significato: incineration; reduction to ashes
parole.testo: From Latin cinefactio, from cinis (“ashes”) + facere (“to make”). Compare French cinéfaction.

parole.significato: Like ashes; ash-coloured; cinerous.
parole.testo: From Latin cineraceus, from cinis (“ashes”).

parole.significato: A place or receptacle for depositing the ashes of cremated people.
parole.testo: Latin cinerarium.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or containing ashes, especially those of a cremated person.
parole.testo: From Latin cinerārius.

parole.significato: The reducing of anything to ashes by combustion; incineration.
parole.testo: Latin cinis (“ashes”): compare French cinération.

parole.significato: The grey matter of the brain
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cinereus (“ashy”).

parole.significato: Of an ash-gray colour.
parole.testo: Latin cinereus, from cinis, cineris (“ashes”).

parole.significato: A sedimentary rock composed mostly of volcanic ash
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin cinis (“ash”) and -ite.

parole.significato: Cinereous.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cinericius.

parole.significato: Full of ashes; resembling ashes.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cinerulentus, from cinis (“ashes”) (oblique stem ciner-) + -ulentus.

parole.significato: A dimeric protein found in tight junctions

parole.significato: cingulum
