parole.significato: The girdle of an alb.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cingulum (“girdle”), from cingō (“to gird”).

parole.significato: cinnamic
parole.testo: From Latin cinnamomum (“cinnamon”) + -ic.

parole.significato: A small, low pillar, square or round, commonly having an inscription, used by the ancients for various purposes, as for…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cippus (“stake, post”). Doublet of cep.

parole.significato: Synonym of around, about, approximately, particularly used with historical dating.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin circā.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or held in, the Circus Maximus of Ancient Rome
parole.testo: From Latin circēnsis (“circus”) + -i- + -an, from circus.

parole.significato: Of a leaf or similar part: coiled on itself from the apex toward the base.
parole.testo: From Latin circinatus, past participle of circinō (“to make round”).

parole.significato: A circling motion; a rotation.
parole.testo: From Latin circinationem, from circinare, from circinus.

parole.significato: The act of going round; a circuit, an encircling.
parole.testo: From Latin circuitiōnem, from circuīre. Compare circuit.

parole.significato: Not direct or to the point.
parole.testo: First attested in 1664. From Latin circuitōsus, from circuitus, from circumeō (“to go around”), from circum (“around”) + eō (“to go”). By surface analysis, circuit + -ous.

parole.significato: The act of moving in a circle, or in a course which brings the moving body to the place where its motion began.
parole.testo: From Middle English circulacioun, from Latin circulatio. Morphologically circulate + -ion.

parole.significato: A small circle, used in printed matter as a reference mark to refer the reader to a note.
parole.testo: Either borrowed from Latin circulus, or from circle + -ule.

parole.significato: Synonym of encircle.
parole.testo: From Latin circulus + -ize.

parole.significato: A social group of reptiles where there is interaction and personal exchange between individuals.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin circulus.

parole.significato: around, surrounding
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin circum-, from circum, from circus. See also circle and circus.

parole.significato: Including all aspects of; encompassing.
parole.testo: From Latin circum (“around”) + ambiō, from amb- (“both side”) + eō (“go”), literally "go on both sides of". Synchronically circum- + ambient.

parole.significato: To walk around something in a circle, especially for a ritual purpose.
parole.testo: Latin circumambulātus, past participle of circumambulāre (“to walk around”). Equivalent to circum- + ambulate.

parole.significato: The act of walking around something in a circle, especially for a ritual purpose.
parole.testo: From circum- + ambulation, borrowed from Latin circumambulātiō.

parole.significato: Someone who walks around something.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: indirect or roundabout
parole.testo: * From Latin circum (“round about”) (compare English circum-) + English bend + Latin -ibus

parole.significato: One who carries out circumcision.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin circumcīsor. By surface analysis, circumcise + -or.

parole.significato: The act of enclosing on all sides.
parole.testo: From Latin circumcludere, circumclusum (“to enclose”).

parole.significato: The act of running or rambling around.
parole.testo: From Latin circumcursare, circumcursatum (“to run round about”).

parole.significato: The circular (or, more precisely, conical) movement of a body part, such as a ball-and-socket joint or the eye. It cons…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin circumductiō (“a leading or conducting around”), from circumdūcō (“to lead or draw around”) + -tiō (nominal suffix). Equivalent to circumduct + -ion.

parole.significato: To bear or carry around.
parole.testo: From Latin circumferre.

parole.significato: The line that bounds a circle or other two-dimensional figure.
parole.testo: From Latin circumferentia, from circum (“around”) + ferō (“to carry”). Displaced native Old English ymbgang.

parole.significato: A diacritical mark (ˆ) placed over a vowel in the orthography or transliteration of many languages to change its pronun…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin circumflexus (“bent about”), calqued from Ancient Greek περισπώμενος (perispṓmenos, “drawn around”).

parole.significato: Synonym of circumflex.
parole.testo: From circumflex + accent or calque of Latin accentus circumflexus.

parole.significato: Flowing round; surrounding in the manner of a fluid.
parole.testo: From Latin circumfluere, from circum- (“around”) + fluere (“flow”).

parole.significato: Wandering from market to market; vagabond, itinerant.
parole.testo: From Latin circumforaneus + -an.

parole.significato: Wandering from place to place or market to market.
parole.testo: From Latin circumforāneus (“itinerant”), from circum- (“around”) + forum (“marketplace”) + -aneus (“-aneous”).

parole.significato: The act or process of carrying about.
parole.testo: From Latin circumgestare (“to carry around”), from circum + gestare (“to carry”).

parole.significato: The reciprocal existence in each other of the three persons of the Trinity.
parole.testo: From circum- + Latin incedere, incessum (“to walk”).

parole.significato: Lying or located in the area around something.
parole.testo: From Latin circa (“around”) + jacēre (“to lie down”).

parole.significato: A cycle, circulation, or rotation; the movement of something in a circular course.
parole.testo: From Latin circumlātiō (“a carrying around, circulation”), from circumferō (“to carry around”), from circum (“around”) + ferō (“to carry”).

parole.significato: A roundabout or indirect way of speaking; thus
parole.testo: From Latin circumlocūtiō (“the act of speaking around; circumlocution, periphrasis”). By surface analysis, circum- (“around”) + locution (“talk”), thus "getting around (a problem) in speaking or writing". Probably a calque of Ancient Greek περίφρασις (períphrasis, “periphrasis”).

parole.significato: To surround with, or as if with, a wall.
parole.testo: From circum- + Latin murus; compare immure.

parole.significato: To travel completely around somewhere or something (especially the Globe), especially by sail.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin circumnāvigātus, perfect passive participle of circumnāvigō (“sail round something, circumnavigate”), from circum (“about, around”) + nāvigō (“sail, navigate”), from nāvis (“ship”) + agō (“do”). By surface analysis, circum- + navigate.

parole.significato: To put round; to place around; to place or arrange circularly.
parole.testo: From Latin circumpōno (“to put round”).

parole.significato: The act of positioning something around something else; or the state of being so positioned
parole.testo: From circum- + position. From Latin circumpositio, from circumpōno (“to put round”).

parole.significato: A symbol consisting of a point or dot surrounded by a circle (ʘ).
parole.testo: From Latin circum (“around”) + Latin pūnctum (“point”).

parole.significato: To draw a line around; to encircle.
parole.testo: From Latin circumscrībō, from circum (“around”) + scrībō (“write”). By surface analysis, circum- + scribe.

parole.significato: Limited, circumscribed.
parole.testo: From Latin circumscrīptus, past participle of circumscrībere (“to circumscribe”).

parole.significato: The act of circumscribing or the quality of being circumscribed.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin circumscrīptiō.

parole.significato: To cut around the circumference (of some part of an organ or structure).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin circumsectus perfect passive participle of circumsecō (“to cut around”), from circum- (“around”) + secare (“to cut”).

parole.significato: Carefully aware of all circumstances; considerate of all that is pertinent.
parole.testo: From Latin circumspectō (“look around”). Compare periscope.

parole.significato: Looking around in all directions; cautious or watchful of danger.
parole.testo: From Latin circumspicere.

parole.significato: Standing or placed around; surrounding.
parole.testo: From Latin circumstāns, present participle of circumstō.

parole.significato: Pertaining to or dependent on circumstances, especially as opposed to essentials; incidental, not essential.
parole.testo: From Latin circumstantia + English -al, equivalent to circumstance + -ial.

parole.significato: To surround with, or as if with, a rampart.
parole.testo: From Latin circumvallare, from circum- + vallum (“rampart”).

parole.significato: A rampart or other defensive entrenchment that entirely encircles the position being defended.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin circumvāllātiō. By surface analysis, circumvallate + -ation.

parole.significato: The act of movinging around, such as in orbit, or the state of being so carried.
parole.testo: From Latin circumvectio, from circum + vehere (“to carry”).

parole.significato: to avoid or get around something; to bypass
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin circumveniō.

parole.significato: The act of evading or going around (bypassing).
parole.testo: From Latin circumventio, equivalent to circumvent + -ion.

parole.significato: To cover round, as with a garment; to invest.
parole.testo: From Latin circumvestire, from circum (“around”) + vestire (“to clothe”).

parole.significato: The act of flying round.
parole.testo: From Latin circumvolate, circumvolatum (“to fly around”), from circum + volare (“to fly”).

parole.significato: To cause (something) to revolve or roll around; to put (something) into a circular motion.
parole.testo: From Latin circumvolvere.

parole.significato: A traveling company of performers that may include acrobats, clowns, trained animals, and other novelty acts, that give…
parole.testo: From Middle English circus, circo, from Latin circus (“ring, circle”), from Ancient Greek κρίκος (kríkos), κίρκος (kírkos, “ring”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to bend, turn”). Doublet of cirque. Cognate with Old English hring (whence English ring) and Old English hringsetl (“circus”, litera

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or fringed with cirri.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cirrātus (“having ringlets”), from cirrus (“a curl”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-forming suffix). By surface analysis, cirr- + -ate.

parole.significato: Resembling a fringe
parole.testo: From cirrus (“cloud-type”) and Latin cirrus (“fringe”). By surface analysis, cirr- + -o-.

parole.significato: Synonym of tendril (“a thin, spirally coiling stem that attaches a plant to its support”).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin cirrus (“curl; fringe of clothes; mane (especially forelock) of a horse; etc”); further etymology unknown. Sense 2 (“type of cloud”) was coined by the British chemist and amateur meteorologist Luke Howard (1772–1864): see the 1803 quotation. The plural form cirri is also

parole.significato: Having two mutations on two genes on the same chromosome of a homologous pair.
parole.testo: From Latin cis (“on this side (of), on the near or same side”). Doublet of he, it, here, hither, and hence.

parole.significato: On this side of.
parole.testo: From the Latin preposition cis (“on this side of”). The earliest known use of the prefix relating to sexuality in any language was in a German-language book on sexology published in 1914. According to the Oxford English Dictionary, the earliest use of the prefix in the context of gender in English d

parole.significato: A small receptacle for sacred utensils carried in festivals in Ancient Greece.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cista, from Ancient Greek κίστη (kístē). Doublet of chest.

parole.significato: The capsular shield of some lichens.
parole.testo: From Latin cistella, from cista (“a box”).

parole.significato: Any of the various membranes sections comprising some organelles like the Golgi apparatus and the endoplasmic reticulum.
parole.testo: From Latin cisterna. Doublet of cistern.

parole.significato: A dilated sac at the lower end of the thoracic duct into which lymph from the intestinal trunk and two lumbar lymphatic…
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: A region in the brain posterior to the medulla oblongata, below the cerebellum; cerebrospinal fluid enters from the fou…
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: A little box or chest.
parole.testo: From Latin cistula.

parole.significato: An index of citations of legal cases and other sources
parole.testo: From Latin citator, agent noun of citare (“to cite”).

parole.significato: Chiefly in place names: situated on the nearer side.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin citerior (“(particularly in province names) nearer”), comparative of citer (“on this side; near”) (from cis (“on or to this or the near side of; short of; before”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱe (“here”)) + -ior (suffix forming comparatives). The English word is cognate with Frenc

parole.significato: An ancient Greek stringed instrument, which could be considered a forerunner of the guitar.
parole.testo: From Latin cithara, from Ancient Greek κιθάρα (kithára). Doublet of cither, guitar, kithara, kissar, and zither.

parole.significato: Relating to a cithara or a citharist.
parole.testo: From Latin citharoedicus, from Ancient Greek κιθαρῳδικός (kitharōidikós), from κιθάρα (kithára, “cithara”) + ἀοιδός (aoidós, “singer”).

parole.significato: An archaic musical instrument whose exact form is uncertain, generally shown with four strings
parole.testo: Probably a French diminutive form of Latin cithara, and not from Latin cista (“a box”).

parole.significato: Of the colour of citron or a citrus fruit; yellowish.
parole.testo: From Latin citreus.

parole.significato: A "yellowing" process, one of the four major stages of the alchemical magnum opus.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin citrīnitās (“yellowness”).

parole.significato: Reacted with, or converted to, citrulline.
parole.testo: From Latin citrullus (“watermelon”) + -ine + -ate + -ed.

parole.significato: Any of several shrubs or trees of the genus Citrus in the family Rutaceae.
parole.testo: From Latin citrus (“a citron tree, thuja”), probably via Etruscan from Ancient Greek κέδρος (kédros); compare Middle English citurtre, cytyr tre. Thus a possible doublet of cedar.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or belonging to a city, a citizen, or citizenship; municipal or civil.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cīvicus (“pertaining to a city or citizens”).

parole.significato: A crown or garland of oak leaves and acorns, bestowed on a soldier who had saved the life of a citizen in battle.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin corōna cīvica, the adjective being from cīves (“citizen”).

parole.significato: The study of good citizenship and proper membership in a community.
parole.testo: From Latin civicus (“having to do with citizens or a town or city”).

parole.significato: A war fought between factions of the inhabitants of a single country, or a similar political entity.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin bellum cīvīle, in English from 1651 in reference to the English Civil War, with possible early use in the 15th and 16th centuries as wer cyuile or ciuill warre. Displaced native Old English inġewinn.

parole.significato: Speech or behaviour that is fit for civil interactions; politeness, courtesy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin civilitas: compare French civilité. English equivalent civil + -ity.

parole.significato: the social body of the citizens united by law
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin cīvitās. Doublet of city.

parole.significato: Urgent.
parole.testo: Latin clāmāns, present participle of clāmō (“yell”). Doublet of claimant.

parole.significato: An exclamation; a crying-out or call.
parole.testo: From Latin clamationem.

parole.significato: UK and Canada standard spelling of clamor.
parole.testo: From Latin clāmor (“a shout, cry”), from clāmō (“cry out, complain”).

parole.significato: Conducted with secrecy; clandestine; concealed.
parole.testo: From Latin clanculārius, from clanculum (“secretly”), adverbial diminutive of clam (“secretly”).

parole.significato: Done or kept in secret, sometimes to conceal an illicit or improper purpose.
parole.testo: From Latin clandestīnus (“secret, concealed”); compare French clandestin.

parole.significato: The quality or state of being clandestine.
parole.testo: From clandestine + -ity, borrowed from Latin clandestinitas (“illegality, clandestiness, underground life”).

parole.significato: A loud, repeating clanging sound; a loud racket; a din.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin clangor.

parole.significato: Synonym of Poor Clare: a nun of the Order of Saint Clare.
parole.testo: Medieval English vernacular form of Clara, from the Latin clara, feminine of clarus (“bright, shining, clear”), a post-classical name made famous by the 13th century Saint Clara of Assisi. In Oxfordshire, from Clarora, a clay slope.

parole.significato: An organ stop with a soft, fluty sound.
parole.testo: From Latin clarus (“clear”) + bellus (“fine”).

parole.significato: An old musical instrument similar to a spinet, manichord or clavichord.
parole.testo: From Latin clarus (“clear”) + chorda (“string”). See chord.

parole.significato: Clarity or splendour.
parole.testo: From Latin claritudo, from clarus (“clear”).

parole.significato: Salvia sclarea, a biennial or short-lived herbaceous perennial.
parole.testo: See Latin sclarea.

parole.significato: A class or order; sort; type; kind.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin classis. Doublet of class.

parole.significato: Having a lattice-like structure.
parole.testo: From Latin clāthrātus, from clāthrī (“lattice”) + -ātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix). The noun is from the clipping of clathrate compound, see -ate.

parole.significato: limping
parole.testo: From Latin claudicans, present participle of claudico (“to limp”), from claudus (“crippled”).

parole.significato: Limping.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin claudicātiō (“limping”, noun), from claudicō (“to limp, halt, be lame”) + -ātiō (“-ation”, nominal suffix).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a cloister.
parole.testo: Based on Latin claustrum (“cloister”). Doublet of cloistral.

parole.significato: Shutting up or enclosing, usually in a religious cloister.
parole.testo: From Latin clōstra (“lock, enclosure”).

parole.significato: The love of, or arousal from, enclosed, tight places.
parole.testo: Based on the Latin claustrum (“a shut in place”), from claudere (“to close”) + -philia ("love").

parole.significato: One who has claustrophilia.
parole.testo: Latin claustrum (“a shut in place”) + -philiac

parole.significato: Of or relating to claustrophilia.
parole.testo: Latin claustrum (“a shut in place”) + -philic

parole.significato: One who suffers from claustrophobia.
parole.testo: From Latin claustrum (“a shut-in place”), from claudō (“to shut, close; to imprison, confine”) + -phobe.

parole.significato: The abnormal fear of closed, tight places.
parole.testo: From Latin claustrum (“a shut-in place”), from Latin claudō (“to shut, close; to imprison, confine”) + -phobia. First attested in the British Medical Journal.

parole.significato: A thin, irregular sheet of grey matter underneath the inner part of the neocortex on both sides of the brains of mammal…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin claustrum (“a bolt, bar”). Doublet of cloister.

parole.significato: The conclusion of a passage; cadence.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin clausula.

parole.significato: Consisting of, or having, clauses.
parole.testo: From Latin clausula. See clause. By surface analysis, clause + -ule + -ar.

parole.significato: Synonym of gracile tubercle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin clāva (“club, staff, knotty branch”).

parole.significato: Having antennas shaped like clubs; used especially of the Clavicornes group of beetles
parole.testo: From Latin clavus (“key”) + cornu (“horn”).

parole.significato: Larger at the tip than at the base; club-shaped.
parole.testo: The adjective is derived from Latin clāvifōrmis (“club-shaped, claviform”), from Latin clāva (“a club”) (from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₂- (“to beat; to break”)) + -fōrmis (suffix meaning ‘having the form of’) (equivalent to -form, -iform). The English word is cognate with French claviforme. By surfa

parole.significato: Shaped like a nail (“a metallic spike-shaped fastener”).
parole.testo: From Latin clāvifōrmis (“nail-shaped, claviform”) (attested since 1677), from Latin clāvus (“a nail (metal spike)”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kleh₂w- (“a crook, hook; a peg”), + -fōrmis (suffix meaning ‘having the form of’), equivalent to -form, -iform.

parole.significato: One who carries a club; a club bearer.
parole.testo: From Latin claviger, from clava (“club”) + gerere (“to carry”).

parole.significato: One who carries the keys to a place; a keyholder.
parole.testo: From Latin clāviger, from clāvis (“key”) + gerere (“to carry”).

parole.significato: A mechanical device for projecting lumia (an art form consisting of light patterns).
parole.testo: Coined by the musician and inventor Thomas Wilfred (1889-1968), from Latin clavis (“key”) and lux (“light”).

parole.significato: A Roman key.
parole.testo: From Latin clāvis (“a key”). Doublet of clave and clef.

parole.significato: A ciliated bristle of some sea urchins
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin clāvula (“scion, graft”). By surface analysis, clav(a) + -ula.

parole.significato: A club-shaped part of the receptacle of some fungi
parole.testo: From Latin clāvula, diminutive of clāva (“club”).

parole.significato: A callous growth, especially on the foot; a corn.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin clāvus (“a nail”). Doublet of clove.

parole.significato: The gentle or kind exercise of power; leniency, mercy; compassion in judging or punishing.
parole.testo: From Middle English clemency, clemencie, from Latin clēmentia. Gradually eclipsed Middle English clemence, from Old French clemence, from the same Latin origin.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Clement, especially to Pope Clement I and the spurious homilies attributed to him, or to Pope Clement…
parole.testo: From Latin clēmentīnus, from Late Latin Clēmens (“Clement”) (genitive Clēmentis) + -īnus (“of or pertaining to”), from clēmens (“merciful”). By surface analysis, Clement + -ine (adjectival suffix).

parole.significato: A woman of great seductive beauty.
parole.testo: From Middle English Cleopatra, from Latin Cleopatra, from Ancient Greek Κλεοπάτρα (Kleopátra), meaning "glory of her father", from κλέος (kléos, “glory”) + πατήρ (patḗr, “father”).

parole.significato: Synonym of water clock, especially (historical) ancient Greek and Roman forms.
parole.testo: From Latin clepsydra, from Ancient Greek κλεψύδρα (klepsúdra), from κλέπτειν (kléptein, “to steal”) + ὕδωρ (húdōr, “water”).

parole.significato: stealing, theft
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin clepto-, a combining form of Ancient Greek κλέπτης (kléptēs, “thief”), κλέπτω (kléptō, “to steal”), from Proto-Indo-European *klep- (“to steal”). Doublet of klepto-.

parole.significato: government by clerics
parole.testo: From Latin clerus [Term?] + -cracy.

parole.significato: Pertaining to any of several supposedly critical years of a person's life.
parole.testo: From Latin clīmactēricus, from Koine Greek κλιμακτηρικός (klimaktērikós), from κλιμακτήρ (klimaktḗr, “scale, progression, gradation”).

parole.significato: A neume denoting a descending set of three tones.
parole.testo: From Latin clīmax, from Ancient Greek κλῖμαξ (klîmax, “ladder, staircase”), from κλίνω (klínō, “to lean, slant”).

parole.significato: A rhetorical device in which a series is arranged in ascending order.
parole.testo: From Latin clīmax, from Ancient Greek κλῖμαξ (klîmax, “ladder, staircase, [rhetorical] climax”), from κλίνω (klínō, “to lean, slant”).

parole.significato: A particular region defined by its weather or climate.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin clima, from Ancient Greek κλίμα (klíma, “(zone of) latitude”, literally “inclination”), from κλίνω (klínō, “to slope, incline”). See also climate.

parole.significato: The unpredictable swerve of atoms, introduced as a concept by Lucretius to defend the atomistic doctrine of Epicurus.
parole.testo: Related to Latin clīnō.

parole.significato: A shield worn by soldiers of ancient Greece and Rome.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin clipeus.

parole.significato: A neume representing two notes descending.
parole.testo: From Latin clivis (“by means of slopes”), ablative plural of clivus.

parole.significato: inclination, slope; ascent or descent; gradient
parole.testo: Latin clivus (“hill”).

parole.significato: Part of the cranium at the skull base, a shallow depression behind the dorsum sellae that slopes obliquely backward.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin clīvus (“slope, hill”).

parole.significato: A sewer.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cloāca (“sewer”), related to cluō (“cleanse; purge”), but the derivation is uncertain.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, resembling or living in a cloister.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin claustrālis (“of the cloister”), probably via Middle French cloistral. Doublet of claustral.

parole.significato: A muscular spasm with regular contractions.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin clonus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek κλόνος (klónos), meaning a "violent, confused motion."

parole.significato: of or relating to a group of cutaneous nerves of the buttocks
parole.testo: From Latin clunis (“rump, buttock”).

parole.significato: Shaped like a round buckler or shield; scutate.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin clipeātus, perfect passive participle of clipeō (“to arm with a shield”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from clupeus, clipeus (“shield”).

parole.significato: shaped like a round shield; clypeate
parole.testo: From Latin clypeus (“shield”) + -form.

parole.significato: The shield-shaped front part of an insect's head or a spider's cephalothorax.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin clypeus, clipeus (“round shield”).

parole.significato: Together: the root word is done co-incidently.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin co-, from con-, from Proto-Italic *kom-, from *kom, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱóm, possibly from *ḱe.

parole.significato: A person in the relationship of a godfather to the other god-parents, and the legal parents, of a child.
parole.testo: From co- + father, in sense 1 as a calque of Latin compater, French compère.

parole.significato: The relationship of a godmother to the other god-parents, and the legal parents, of a child.
parole.testo: * com- + mother, as calque of Latin commater, French commère.

parole.significato: To elect as a fellow member of a group, such as a committee.
parole.testo: From Latin cooptō (“to choose, elect”), from co(m)- + optō (“to opt”).

parole.significato: Clumped together, clustered.
parole.testo: From Latin coacervātus.

parole.significato: To compel, constrain, force.
parole.testo: From the participle stem of Latin cōgō.

parole.significato: Force; compulsion, either in restraining or impelling
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English coaccioun, from Latin coāctiō.

parole.significato: Serving to compel or constrain; compulsory; restrictive.
parole.testo: See Latin coactum.

parole.significato: To cooperate (with).
parole.testo: From co- + adjute, on the type of an assumed Latin *coadjūtō.

parole.significato: A female coadjutor
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin coadiūtrīx. By surface analysis, coadjutor + -trix.

parole.significato: Closely joined (by growing together).
parole.testo: The verb is first attested in 1607, the adjective in 1839; borrowed from Latin coadūnātus, perfect passive participle of coadūnō (“to unite, collect or join into one”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Union into a single body or mass; unity.
parole.testo: Latin coadūnātiō, from coadūnō.

parole.significato: To join together; to fuse.
parole.testo: From Latin coagmentare, from coagmentum (“a joining together”), from cogere. See cogent.

parole.significato: The act of joining, or the state of being joined together; union.
parole.testo: Latin coagmentatio.

parole.significato: That causes coagulation or that coagulates.
parole.testo: From Latin coagulans, present participle of coāgulō (“to thicken”).

parole.significato: To become congealed; to convert from a liquid to a semisolid mass.
parole.testo: From Middle English coagulaten (“(of blood) to clot or, make blood coagulate; (of tissue) to consolidate”), from coagulat(e) (“coagulated; (blood) clotted; (milk) curdled; (humor) thickened, viscous; (material) solidified, cohesive; (wine) boiled down, reduced”, also used as the past participle of c

parole.significato: A mass of coagulated material; a clot or curd
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin coagulum.

parole.significato: To join into a single mass or whole.
parole.testo: From Latin coalēscō, from co- + alēscō (“grow up”).

parole.significato: Causing or undergoing coalescence.
parole.testo: From Latin coalēscēns, present participle of coalescō. By surface analysis, coalesce + -ent.

parole.significato: To cause to unite or coalesce.
parole.testo: Back-formation from coalition, from Latin coalitus, past participle of coalēscō (see coalesce).

parole.significato: Pressed close together, constricted, narrowed, compressed.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin coarctātus, perfect participle of coarctō (“to press together, compress, contract, confine”), from co- (“being or bringing together, co-”) + arctō (“to draw or press close together”).

parole.significato: A congenital stricture or narrowing of a short section of the aorta.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin coarctātiō (“drawing or crowding together”, noun), from coarctō (“to press together, compress, contract, confine”) + -ātiō (“-ation”, action noun suffix); equivalent to coarctate + -ion.

parole.significato: Bearing or producing berries.
parole.testo: From Latin coccum (“a berry”) + -ferous. See coccus.

parole.significato: Scarlet.
parole.testo: From Latin coccineus, suffixed with -ous.

parole.significato: The fishberry (fruit of Anamirta cocculus).
parole.testo: From Latin cocculus, diminutive of coccum (“kermes berry”) + Indicus (“of India”).

parole.significato: A muscle of the pelvic wall, that in combination with the levator ani forms the pelvic diaphragm.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: The final (bottom-most) fused vertebrae at the base of the spine, the tailbone.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin coccyx, borrowed from Ancient Greek κόκκῡξ (kókkūx), referring to the curved shape of a cuckoo's beak when viewed from the side.

parole.significato: The complex, spirally coiled, tapered cavity of the inner ear of higher vertebrates, which contains the organ of Corti…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cochlea (“a snail”), from Ancient Greek κόχλιας (kókhlias, “a snail with a spiral shell”).

parole.significato: In Ancient Rome, a small spoon with a long tapering handle.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: Having the form of a snail's shell; spiral; turbinated
parole.testo: From Latin cochleatus (“spiral or screw-formed”). See cochlea.

parole.significato: Having the form of a snail shell
parole.testo: From Latin cochlea (“shell”) + -iform.

parole.significato: A document issued by the bond office stating that duty has been paid and goods may be sold.
parole.testo: From Middle English coket, possibly from Latin quo quietus.

parole.significato: Any of several field weeds, such as the common corncockle (Agrostemma githago) and darnel ryegrass (Lolium temulentum).
parole.testo: From Middle English cockil, cokil, cokylle, from Old English coccel (“darnel”), of unknown origin, perhaps from a diminutive of Latin coccus (“berry”).

parole.significato: Made by baking, or exposure to heat.
parole.testo: Borrowed from the Latin coctilis (“burned, built of burned bricks”), from coquō (“to cook, to roast or dry”).

parole.significato: An act of boiling.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin coctiō.

parole.significato: Any of various types of sea fish or the meat from said fish.
parole.testo: From Middle English cod, codde, of uncertain origin: * Oldest English form cotfich as a surname in the 13th century; for more see cot (“chamber, cottage”). * A bag or pouch, related to its bloated shape; see Etymology 2 below. * From Latin gadus, from Ancient Greek γάδος (gádos, “cod”) with a possib

parole.significato: An early manuscript book, especially one bound in the modern manner, by joining pages, as opposed to a rolled scroll.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cōdex, variant form of caudex (“tree trunk, book, notebook”); compare caudex (in botany). Doublet of code.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a code or codex
parole.testo: From Latin cōdic- + -al.

parole.significato: A handbell used for summoning monks.
parole.testo: From Latin codon, from Ancient Greek κώδων (kṓdōn).

parole.significato: Someone who has coeliac disease.
parole.testo: From Latin coeliacus, from Ancient Greek κοιλιακός (koiliakós), from κοιλία (koilía, “belly”). By surface analysis, coel- + -i- + -ac. Cognate with coelom.

parole.significato: A device that rotates a telescope so as to keep its orientation constant with relation to the stars.
parole.testo: Related to Latin coelestis (“sky”), corrupted form of caelestis, + -stat.

parole.significato: The outermost part of the cosmos in the Ptolemaic system; Heaven.
parole.testo: From Latin coelum empireum.

parole.significato: Equal to each other in size, rank or position.
parole.testo: From Middle English coequalle, from Latin coaequālis; equivalent to co- + equal.

parole.significato: To restrain by force, especially by law or authority; to repress; to curb.
parole.testo: From Latin coërceō (“to surround, encompass, restrain, control, curb”), from co- (“together”) + arceō (“to inclose, confine, keep off”).

parole.significato: A bluish-violet crystalline substance obtained in the purification of crude wood vinegar, regarded as a complex quinone…
parole.testo: From Latin coeruleus (“cerulean”) + lignum (“wood”) + English quinone.

parole.significato: Thinkable, conceivable, able to be imagined.
parole.testo: From Latin cogitabilis, from cogito.

parole.significato: Deep in thought; meditative, thoughtful.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin cōgitābundus (“thinking, thoughtful”), from cōgitō (“to think; to consider, ponder; to intend, plan”) + -bundus (suffix forming adjectives with an active or transitive meaning). Cōgitō is derived from con- (prefix indicating a bringing together of several things) + agitō

parole.significato: thinking, that thinks
parole.testo: From Latin cōgitans, present active participle of cōgitō (“think”).

parole.significato: To meditate, to ponder, to think deeply.
parole.testo: First attested in 1570; borrowed from Latin cōgitātus, perfect passive participle of cōgitō (“to think”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Allied by blood; kindred by birth; specifically (law) related on the mother's side.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cognātus (“related by blood”), from co- + gnātus (“born”). Compare Portuguese cognato and Spanish cognado. Doublet of connate and cognatus.

parole.significato: An object of kindred sense or derivation; specifically, that which may adverbially follow an intransitive verb (for exa…
parole.testo: Calque of Latin accūsātīvus cognātus (“a cognate accusative”).

parole.significato: relatives by the mother's side
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin.

parole.significato: A cognate relationship.
parole.testo: From Middle English cognacion, cognacioun, from Latin cognātiō; equivalent to cognate + -ion.

parole.significato: A blood relative
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin cognatus (“kinsman”). Doublet of cognate and connate.

parole.significato: aware, cognizant
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cognōscentem, nominative cognōscēns, participle of cognōsco (“learn, get to know”) (See cognizant). The unetymological spelling will have been influenced by similar Latin borrowings, such as proficient, efficient, sufficient, etc. (See Rhymes: -ɪʃənt).

parole.significato: The process of knowing, of acquiring knowledge and understanding through thought and through the senses.
parole.testo: From Middle English cognicion, cognicioun from Latin cognitiō (“knowledge, perception, a judicial examination, trial”), from cognitus, past participle of cognoscere (“to know”), from co- (“together”) + *gnoscere, older form of noscere (“to know”); see know, and compare cognize, cognizance, cognizor,

parole.significato: A personal epithet or clan name added to the given name and family name of Ancient Romans.
parole.testo: From Latin cognōmen, from con- (“with”) + nōmen (“name; family name”).

parole.significato: To give a cognomen; to name.
parole.testo: From Latin cognominatus, the perfect passive participle of cognominare.

parole.significato: A cognomen, surname
parole.testo: Latin cognominatio.

parole.significato: To determine a person to be insane or mentally incompetent.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin cognosco.

parole.significato: Cognizance (awareness).
parole.testo: From Latin cognoscentia, from cognōscere (“to know”). See also cognizance. By surface analysis, co- + Latin gnōsc(ere) + -ence.

parole.significato: Knowledgeable; discerning.
parole.testo: From Latin cognōscēns, from cognōscere (“to know”). By surface analysis, co- + Latin gnōsc(ere) + -ent.

parole.significato: having the power of knowing
parole.testo: From Latin cognōscō (“to know”) + -itive.

parole.significato: An instrument in writing whereby a defendant in an action acknowledges a plaintiff's demand to be just.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cognovit.

parole.significato: To live together with someone else, especially in a romantic and sexual relationship but without being married.
parole.testo: From Latin cohabitō; co- + habitō (“to dwell, to live in”).

parole.significato: To stick together physically, by adhesion.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cohaereō (“cohere, cling (closely) together, harmonise, be consistent (with), be in agreement with”).

parole.significato: The state of being coherent; a coherent relationship.
parole.testo: From Latin cohaerēntia.

parole.significato: Having cohesion.
parole.testo: From Latin cohaesus, past participle of cohaereō, + -ive.

parole.significato: To restrain; to inhibit.
parole.testo: From Latin cohibitus, past participle of cohibere (“to confine”), from co- + habere (“to hold”). Compare inhibit.

parole.significato: hindrance; restraint or obstacle
parole.testo: From Latin cohibitio.

parole.significato: A group of people supporting the same thing or person.
parole.testo: From Latin cohors (stem cohort-); borrowed into Old English as coorta, but reintroduced into Middle English as cōhort and chōors via Old French cohorte. Doublet of court.

parole.significato: The requirement of a grant bestowing right of assembly and allowing the formation of a collegium under the Roman Empire.
parole.testo: Latin: coīre (“to assemble”, “to come together”, present active indicative form of coeō, “I assemble”, “I come together”) + licet (“it is permitted”) = “it is permitted [for a group] to assemble”.

parole.significato: Sexual intercourse.
parole.testo: From the oblique stem of Latin coitiō.

parole.significato: Sexual intercourse, especially that involving penile–vaginal penetration.
parole.testo: From Latin coitus.

parole.significato: Sexual intercourse in which the penetrative partner does not attempt to ejaculate but rather remain at the plateau phas…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin coitus reservātus.

parole.significato: A bowl-shaped kitchen utensil with holes in it used for draining food that has been cooking in water, such as pasta.
parole.testo: From Middle English colyndore, coloundour, colonur, variants of Middle English culdor, culdore, culatre, ultimately from Latin cōlātōrium, from Latin cōlum. Cognates include Italian colino and Spanish colador.

parole.significato: The matter that is strained with a strainer
parole.testo: From Latin colatura. Compare French colature. See colander.

parole.significato: Cabbage.
parole.testo: From Middle English cole, col, from Old English cawel, an early Germanic borrowing from Latin caulis (“cabbage”). Cognate with Dutch kool, German Kohl, Danish kål, Norwegian Bokmål kål, Norwegian Nynorsk kål, Swedish kål. Doublet of caulis, gobi, and kale.

parole.significato: Escherichia coli, a Gram-negative bacterium commonly found in the lower intestine of warm-blooded organisms.
parole.testo: Ellipsis of Bacterium coli or Bacillus coli, obsolete taxonomic names of the species (now called Escherichia coli). The word itself derives from Latin colī, genitive of colon (“colon, large intestine”).

parole.significato: Female collaborator.
parole.testo: From Latin collaboratrix.

parole.significato: To break apart and fall down suddenly; to cave in.
parole.testo: From Latin collāpsus (past participle of collābor).

parole.significato: collapse
parole.testo: Latin collapsio.

parole.significato: To examine diverse documents and so on, to discover similarities and differences.
parole.testo: From Latin collātus, perfect passive participle of conferō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of confer. See also infer, delate and defer (Etymology 2), relate and refer, as well as prelate and prefer among others. Not related to collateral.

parole.significato: Characterised by the contributions of many people.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin collātītius, later form of collātīcius (“brought together, raised by contribution”). See collation.

parole.significato: Having the power of conferring.
parole.testo: From the Latin collātīvus (“brought together, collected, joint”). Compare the French collatif.

parole.significato: To join in praising or worshiping.
parole.testo: From Latin collaudāre, from col- + laudāre (“to praise”).

parole.significato: A committee or council.
parole.testo: From Latin collēgium. Doublet of college.

parole.significato: A small elevation.
parole.testo: From Latin colliculus, diminutive of collis (“hill”).

parole.significato: To make a direct impact, especially if violent.
parole.testo: From Latin collīdō (“to clash, strike, dash, beat, or press together”), from con- (“together”) + laedō (“to strike, collide, hurt”) (whence col- (“assimilated form of com-”)).

parole.significato: To tie or bind together.
parole.testo: First attested in 1471, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English colligat(e) (“bound together”)(adjective), Latin colligātus, perfect passive participle of colligō (“to bind, fasten; to unite, combine”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix). By surface analysis,

parole.significato: A binding together.
parole.testo: From Latin colligātiō. By surface analysis, colligate + -ion.

parole.significato: To focus into a narrow beam or column; to adjust a focusing device so that it produces a narrow beam.
parole.testo: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin collimātus, perfect passive participle of collīmō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), itself originating from a misreading of collīniō, collīneō.

parole.significato: The act of collineating; collimation.
parole.testo: From Latin collineare to direct in a straight line. See collimation.

parole.significato: A melting together; the reduction of different bodies into one mass by fusion.
parole.testo: From Latin colliquefactus (“melted”), from col- + liquefacere.

parole.significato: (said of certain words) To be often used together, form a collocation; for example strong collocates with tea.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin collocatum, supine of collocō. Doublet of couch.

parole.significato: The grouping or juxtaposition of things, especially words or sounds.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin collocātiō (“a putting together”). By surface analysis, col- (“together”) + location. The technical sense in linguistics was established in 1951, although it may actually be earlier. First attested in 1605.

parole.significato: To hold colloquy; to converse.
parole.testo: Apparently from Latin colloquī.

parole.significato: Characteristic of familiar conversation, of common parlance; informal.
parole.testo: 1751, from earlier term colloquy (“a conversation”), from Latin colloquium (“conference, conversation”), from con- (“together”) + loquor (“to speak”), + -al.

parole.significato: A colloquy; a meeting for discussion.
parole.testo: From Latin colloquium. Doublet of colloquy. Equivalent to colloquy + -ium.

parole.significato: A conversation or dialogue.
parole.testo: From Middle English colloquies pl, from Latin colloquium (“conversation”), from com- (“together, with”) (English com-) + form of loquor (“speak”) (from which English locution and other words). Doublet of colloquium.

parole.significato: struggling, conflict, strife
parole.testo: From Latin colluctor (“to struggle or contend with”).

parole.significato: to act in concert with; to conspire.
parole.testo: * From Latin collūdere, from con- and lūdere (“to play”).

parole.significato: A neck, cervix, or neckline part or process.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin collum (“the neck”). Doublet of col.

parole.significato: Secretly acting together for a fraudulent or illegal purpose.
parole.testo: From Latin collūs- + -ive, from Latin collūdere, from con- + lūdere.

parole.significato: collusive
parole.testo: From Latin collusorius.

parole.significato: A mouthwash.
parole.testo: From Latin colluere, collutum (“to wash”).

parole.significato: effluvium
parole.testo: From Latin colluvies, from colluō (“to wash thoroughly, wash out, rinse”).

parole.significato: A loose accumulation of rock and soil debris at the foot of a slope.
parole.testo: From Latin colluvio (“jumble”)

parole.significato: A lotion or liquid wash used as a cleanser for the eyes; an eye-salve.
parole.testo: From Latin collȳrium, from Ancient Greek κολλύριον (kollúrion, “poultice”). Doublet of koulouri.

parole.significato: Taro; eddo.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin colocasia.

parole.significato: A viny plant, of species Citrullus colocynthis, native to the Mediterranean Basin and Asia. It produces a lemon-sized,…
parole.testo: From Latin colocynthis, from Ancient Greek κολοκυνθίς (kolokunthís), ultimately Pre-Greek.

parole.significato: Pigeon fancying.
parole.testo: From Latin columbus + -philia.

parole.significato: The punctuation mark ⟨:⟩.
parole.testo: From Latin cōlon (“a member of a verse of poem”), from Ancient Greek κῶλον (kôlon, “a member, limb, clause, part of a verse”).

parole.significato: Part of the large intestine; the final segment of the digestive system, after (distal to) the ileum and before (proxima…
parole.testo: From Latin cŏlon (“large intestine”), from Ancient Greek κόλον (kólon, “the large intestine, also food, meat, fodder”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to farmers or farming; agricultural.
parole.testo: Latin colonus (“husbandman”).

parole.significato: A sharecropping tenant farmer of the late Roman Empire and Early Middle Ages.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin colōnus.

parole.significato: A geographical area under the remote control of a country; especially to extract resources or exploit labor from that a…
parole.testo: From Middle English colane, colonye, from Latin colōnia (“colony”), from colōnus (“farmer; colonist”), from colō (“till, cultivate, worship”), from earlier *quelō, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷel- (“to move; to turn (around)”). Doublet of Cologne, Colonia, and Köln.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Lydian city of Colophon.
parole.testo: From Latin Colophōnius (from Colophōn (“Colophon”)) + English -an

parole.significato: Rosin; the residue left after the distillation of oil of turpentine from liquid resin, used in pharmaceutical preparati…
parole.testo: From Latin colophonia (“of Colophon”) resina (“resin”); named after the Ionic city of Colophon, which was known for producing hardened resin.

parole.significato: Colored.
parole.testo: From Latin colōrātus, past participle of colōrō (“to color”). Equivalent to color + -ate (adjective-froming suffix)

parole.significato: A statue of gigantic size. The name was especially applied to certain famous statues in antiquity, as the Colossus of N…
parole.testo: From Latin colossus, from Ancient Greek κολοσσός (kolossós, “large statue, especially the colossus of Rhodes”), from an unknown Pre-Greek etymon (and erroneously associated with κολοφών).

parole.significato: A form of milk produced by the mammary glands in late pregnancy and the few days after giving birth.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin colostrum, of uncertain origin.

parole.significato: Having the form of a snake
parole.testo: From Latin coluber and translingual Coluber + -iform.

parole.significato: Snakelike.
parole.testo: From Latin colubrinus, from colubra (“snake”) + -inus (“-ine”).

parole.significato: A columbary, especially a large and architecturally impressive one for housing a large colony of pigeons or doves, such…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin columbārium, from columba (“pigeon”) + -ārium (“place for”).

parole.significato: A pigeon house, pigeon loft, or dovecot.
parole.testo: From Latin columbarium, columba (“a dove”).

parole.significato: A person who makes a great discovery.
parole.testo: From Latin columbus (“a dove”). Doublet of Colombo. The common noun and verb are references to the Italian explorer.

parole.significato: Any of various small structures in plants or animals that are columnar in shape.
parole.testo: From Latin columella (“small column”).

parole.significato: Synonym of nasal septum.
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: Having the shape of a column.
parole.testo: From Latin columnāris. By surface analysis, column + -ar.

parole.significato: Either of two great circles (meridians) that intersect at the poles and either the equinoxes or solstices.
parole.testo: From Latin colurus, ultimately from Ancient Greek κόλουρος (kólouros, “truncated, dock-tailed”).

parole.significato: The form of con- used before b, m, and p
parole.testo: From Latin com (“with”), an archaic form of cum (“with”).

parole.significato: A cloud of dust surrounding the nucleus of a comet.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin coma (“hair of the head”), borrowed from Ancient Greek κόμη (kómē, “hair of the head”).

parole.significato: comose (having a coma, or bushy, hairy appearance).
parole.testo: First attested in 1600; borrowed from Latin cōmātus, from cōma (“hair”) + -ātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The result of a combining of two or more components.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin combīnātus.

parole.significato: To burn up, to burn away, to consume with fire.
parole.testo: From Latin combūrere.

parole.significato: Promoting combustion (for example, by reacting with fuel and promoting a redox reaction). (Contrast combustible.)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin combūrēns, present active participle of combūrere. By surface analysis, combure + -ent.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, caused by, or partaking in combustion.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin combustīvus, from combūrō + -īvus. By surface analysis, combust + -ive.

parole.significato: A chamber acting as the furnace in a jet engine or turbine engine, where intense combustion is induced.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin combustor, from combūrō + -tor.

parole.significato: A clogged hair follicle in the skin, formed when keratin combines with oil to block the follicle.
parole.testo: From Latin comedō (“glutton”). Applied to blackheads on account of the popular belief that they were parasitic worms that consumed the host’s nutrients, especially in children, thereby causing weight loss and illness. Compare Danish hudorm (“comedo”, literally “skin-worm”). More information In Johan

parole.significato: The answer to the theme, or dux, in a fugue.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin comes (“a companion”). Doublet of comte, conte, and count.

parole.significato: An instrument intended to represent the revolution of a comet around the Sun.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: Any of several species of perennial herbs of the genus Symphytum, often specifically common comfrey (Symphytum officina…
parole.testo: From Middle English cumfiria, from Latin (herba) cōnfirma in Pseudo-Apuleius, also called cōnsolida, cōnserva, cōnferva, from conferveo (“to boil together”); from the use of the plant in tea to aid in healing bones.

parole.significato: Pertaining to comedy, as a literary genre.
parole.testo: From Latin comicus, from Ancient Greek κωμικός (kōmikós, “relating to comedy”), from κῶμος (kômos, “carousal”).

parole.significato: Originally, relating to comedy.
parole.testo: From Middle English comicalle, from Latin cōmicus + Middle English -alle (modern -al). By surface analysis, comic + -al.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a count or earl.
parole.testo: From oblique stem of Latin comes, comitis (“count, earl, companion, comrade”) + -al. Doublet of comtal.

parole.significato: Of, or relating to the grammatical case that is used in some languages to indicate accompaniment.
parole.testo: From Latin comitātum (“that which is accompanied”).

parole.significato: A group of warriors or nobles accompanying a king or other leader.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin comitatus, from comes (“companion”). Doublet of county, from Anglo-Norman/Old French.

parole.significato: A popular legislative assembly in ancient Rome.
parole.testo: From Latin comitium (“assembly”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a comitia.
parole.testo: From Latin comitialis.

parole.significato: Courtesy and considerate behaviour towards others; social harmony.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English comite (“association”), from Latin cōmitās.

parole.significato: The punctuation mark ⟨,⟩ used to indicate a set of parts of a sentence or between elements of a list.
parole.testo: From Latin comma, from Ancient Greek κόμμα (kómma), from κόπτω (kóptō, “to cut”).

parole.significato: Items that are created especially to honour or memorialize something, particularly an event, person, or institution.
parole.testo: Morphologically, borrowed from Latin commemorābilia, the nominative neuter plural of Latin commemorābilis; semantically, a blend of commemorate + memorabilia.

parole.significato: Worthy of being, or able to be, commemorated.
parole.testo: Latin commemorabilis.

parole.significato: To honour the memory of someone or something with a ceremony or object.
parole.testo: First attested in 1599; borrowed from Latin commemorātus, perfect passive participle of commemorō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Sporadic usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English.

parole.significato: A person who commemorates something
parole.testo: First attested in 1854; borrowed from Latin commemorātor, by surface analysis, commemorate + -or.

parole.significato: A vacant benefice commended to a cleric until an incumbent was provided.
parole.testo: From Latin in commendam (“in trust”).

parole.significato: A cleric who held a commendam.
parole.testo: From Latin commendātor.

parole.significato: Able to be measured using a common standard.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin Latin commensurabilis (“having a common measure”) in 1550s, from Latin com- (“with”) + mensurabilis (“measurable”). Equivalent to com- + mensurable.

parole.significato: To remark.
parole.testo: From Middle English commenten, comenten, from Latin commentārī (“to consider thoroughly, think over, discuss, write upon”).

parole.significato: A person who makes a commentary, particularly
parole.testo: In form, from Middle English commentator, from Latin commentātor (“author, inventor, interpreter, jailer”), from commentātus + -or (“-er: forming agent nouns”), from commentāri (“to ponder, to study, to write upon”), from comminīscor (“to think over, to invent”) + -tārī (“to frequently be ~ed”). In

parole.significato: fictitious, imaginary.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin commentīcius.

parole.significato: To migrate together.
parole.testo: First attested in 1755; borrowed from Latin commigrātus, perfect passive participle of commigrō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). By surface analysis, con- + migrate.

parole.significato: Migration together.
parole.testo: Latin commigratio.

parole.significato: A formal denunciation; especially one threatening divine punishment.
parole.testo: From Latin comminātiō, from comminor (“to threaten”).

parole.significato: That can be comminuted or pulverized.
parole.testo: From Latin comminuere + -ible.

parole.significato: To break into smaller portions.
parole.testo: From Latin comminūtus (“crumbled, lessened”).

parole.significato: The breaking or grinding up of a material to form smaller particles.
parole.testo: From Latin comminūtiō (“breaking into pieces, crumbling, shattering; crushing, pulverizing”), from Latin comminuō (“to break or crumble into small pieces; to crush, pulverize”) (from com- (prefix indicating completeness) + minuō (“to make smaller; to diminish, lessen”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-Eu

parole.significato: pitiable
parole.testo: Formed as commiser-, the present active indicative stem of the Latin commiseror (whence commiserate) + English -able. Compare miserable.

parole.significato: A commission appointed to take evidence by deposition where the deponent is unwilling or unable to come to court and th…
parole.testo: From Latin de bene esse (“for the good cause”).

parole.significato: The joint between two bones.
parole.testo: From Latin commissura (“a joining or connecting together”), from commissus (passive perfect participle of committo (“to join, to connect”)) + -ura.

parole.significato: Commixture.
parole.testo: From Middle English commistion, from Latin commistiō.

parole.significato: To give in trust; to put into charge or keeping; to entrust; to consign; used with to or formerly unto.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English committen, itself borrowed from Latin committō (“to bring together, join, compare, commit (a wrong), incur, give in charge, etc.”), from com- (“together”) + mittō (“to send”). See mission.

parole.significato: To mix separate things together.
parole.testo: From Middle English commixt, commixte, commyxt (past participle), from Latin commixtus, past participle of commisceō, with the -t later re-analyzed as the past participial ending; equivalent to com- + mix, modelled on Latin commisceō.

parole.significato: A gratuitous loan.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin commodātum (“something lent, a loan”), see -ate (noun-forming suffix).

parole.significato: To put in order, adjust, arrange.
parole.testo: First attested in 1595; borrowed from Latin commodātus, perfect passive participle of commodō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A gratuitous loan for the temporary use of a thing to be returned after a fixed or determinable time.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Latin commodātum (“loan”), neuter substantive of commodātus (“borrowed, lent”).

parole.significato: The act of grinding together.
parole.testo: From Latin commolitus, from Latin commolō (“to shake or grind thoroughly”).

parole.significato: Aquilegia vulgaris, native to most of Europe, excepting Scandinavia.
parole.testo: From the Latin adjective columbīna "of [a] pigeon[s], dove[s]" (which was used as a modifier, qualifier (i.e. pigeon-like, pigeonish, dove-like, dovish) before the noun herba "plant"), which comes from the noun columba "pigeon, dove". The adjective columbina was later nominalized, with the noun herb

parole.significato: advice, warning, or instruction.
parole.testo: From Latin commonitio. See monition.

parole.significato: calling to mind; giving admonition
parole.testo: Latin commonitorius.

parole.significato: Ordinary; not having any remarkable characteristics.
parole.testo: A calque of Latin locus commūnis, referring to a generally applicable literary passage, itself a calque of Ancient Greek κοινὸς τόπος (koinòs tópos).

parole.significato: A house for a place of residence, usually a temporary one.
parole.testo: From stem of Latin commorāns, present participle of commorārī (“to remain, delay”), from mora (“a delay”), + -cy.

parole.significato: Ordinarily residing; inhabiting.
parole.testo: From Latin commorans.

parole.significato: The use of several synonyms to emphasize something.
parole.testo: From Latin commorātiō. Doublet of commoration.

parole.significato: residence (the act of staying or residing somewhere).
parole.testo: From Latin commoratio. Doublet of commoratio.

parole.significato: Dying together or at the same time.
parole.testo: From Latin commoriens, present participle of commori.

parole.significato: An often lethal disruption of heart rhythm as a result of a blow to the area directly over the heart at a critical time…
parole.testo: From Latin commōtiō cordis (literally “agitation/disruption of the heart”), from commōtiō (“agitation”) + cordis (“of the heart”, genitive of cor (“heart”)).

parole.significato: Communicated, (made) commune, joined.
parole.testo: From Middle English communicate, an adapted borrowing of Latin commūnicātus (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), perfect passive participle of commūnicō (“to make commune”).

parole.significato: Someone who, or something that communicates.
parole.testo: From communicate + -or, after Latin commūnicātor (“partner, sharer, participant”); compare Middle French communicateur (“sharer, participant”).

parole.significato: A female communicator.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin commūnicātrīx. By surface analysis, communicate + -trix.

parole.significato: The prevailing doctrine or generally accepted view; consensus.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin commūnis opīniō (“common opinion”).

parole.significato: An unstructured community of common experience.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin commūnitās. Doublet of community.

parole.significato: To exchange substantially; to abate but not abolish completely, a penalty, obligation, or payment in return for a great…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin commūtō.

parole.significato: member of a noble family who ruled the Byzantine Empire from 1081 to 1185
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Comnenus, from Byzantine Greek Κομνηνός (Komnēnós).

parole.significato: Bearing a tuft of soft hairs or down.
parole.testo: From Latin comōsus (“hairy”).

parole.significato: An agreement or contract.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin compactum (“agreement”).

parole.significato: The fact of being closely put together; compact nature or structure.
parole.testo: From Latin compactūra.

parole.significato: The union of parts; the putting together.
parole.testo: Latin compaginatio.

parole.significato: A thing to which something is compared.
parole.testo: From Latin comparandum; By surface analysis, compare + -and.

parole.significato: Something that is compared; the subject of a comparison.
parole.testo: From Latin comparandum, gerundive (neuter singular) of comparō.

parole.significato: One of two things being compared.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin comparātus, perfect passive participle of comparō, see -ate (noun-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A comparison.
parole.testo: Latin comparatio. See compare (“to get”) (obsolete sense). Doublet of comparison.

parole.significato: The act of dividing into parts or compartments.
parole.testo: Latin compartitio.

parole.significato: Having, feeling or showing compassion (to or toward someone).
parole.testo: Pseudo-Latinism, derived from a pseudo-Latin form of French compassionné, past participle of compassionner (“to feel sorry for”). By surface analysis, compassion + -ate.

parole.significato: The relationship of a godparent to their godchild.
parole.testo: From Latin compaternitas, from compater (“godfather”), from com- + pater (“father”).

parole.significato: Suffering or enduring together.
parole.testo: From Latin compatients, present participle of compati. See compassion.

parole.significato: An act of addressing a person by a certain name or title.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin compellātiōnem (“act of addressing”) + English -ion (suffix indicating the result of an action or process).
