parole.significato: Pertaining to, derived from, or containing iron.
parole.testo: From Latin ferricus, from ferrum (“iron”).

parole.significato: Any of a family of iron-carrying globular protein complexes consisting of 24 protein subunits; the key protein of intra…
parole.testo: From Latin ferrātus (“iron-bearing”) and -in; compare also ferri- and ferro-.

parole.significato: ferrous
parole.testo: Latin ferrum (“iron”).

parole.significato: An orthorhombic-dipyramidal mineral containing aluminum, hydrogen, iron, magnesium, manganese, oxygen, silicon, and tit…
parole.testo: From ferro- + carpholite, from Latin ferrum (“iron”), for being the ferrous analog of carpholite.

parole.significato: A student of ferroequinology; a person who studies trains as a hobby.
parole.testo: From Latin ferrum (“iron”) + Latin equus (“horse”) + English -logist (“one who studies”).

parole.significato: The study of railways in general, but especially locomotives.
parole.testo: Latin ferrum (“iron”) + Latin equus (“horse”) + English -logy; from iron horse

parole.significato: Of or containing iron.
parole.testo: From ferro- + -ous, from Latin ferreus directly or via French ferreux, from ferrum (“iron”) + -eus (“-ous: forming adjectives”).

parole.significato: Synonym of ferrous, of or related to iron.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ferrūgineus, from ferrūgo (“rust”).

parole.significato: rust (plant disease).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ferrūgō (“iron rust”), from ferrum (“iron”).

parole.significato: A band or cap (usually metal) placed around a shaft to reinforce it or to prevent splitting.
parole.testo: From Middle English verel, virel, virole (“ferrule; metal pivot on the end of an axle”), altered under the influence of Latin ferrum (“iron”), from Old French virole (“ferrule”), from Latin viriola (“little bracelet”), diminutive of viria (“bracelet worn by men”), from Gaulish, from Proto-Celtic *we

parole.significato: Any of various remedies made from iron-containing compounds.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ferrum.

parole.significato: To solder, fuse together, merge or unite, as if metals.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ferrūminātus, perfect passive participle of ferrūminō (“to cement, solder”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ferrūmen (“cement”).

parole.significato: The soldering or uniting of metals.
parole.testo: Latin ferruminatio: compare French ferrumination.

parole.significato: A ferule.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ferula (“giant fennel”), whose stalks were once used in punishing schoolboys. Doublet of ferule.

parole.significato: Pertaining to reeds and canes.
parole.testo: From Latin ferulaceus, from ferula (“rod”). Compare French férulacé.

parole.significato: Growing hotter.
parole.testo: From Latin fervescens, present participle of fervescere (“to become boiling hot, inchoate”), from fervere. See fervent. By surface analysis, Latin ferv- + -escent.

parole.significato: Intensely hot; radiating with energy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fervidus, from ferveō. By surface analysis, Latin ferv- + id.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the ancient Etruscan town of Fescennia
parole.testo: From the Latin Fescennīnus.

parole.significato: Obscene or scurrilous.
parole.testo: From Latin Fescennīnus, from the name of the ancient Etruscan town of Fescennia, noted for the "Fescennine Verses", a tradition of scurrilous songs performed on special occasions.

parole.significato: To become involuntarily quicker, such as when walking or speaking, due to certain disorders.
parole.testo: First attested in 1556; Borrowed from Latin festīnātus, perfect passive participle of festīnō (“to hurry”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Of a straw colour; greenish-yellow.
parole.testo: From Latin festula (“stalk, straw”). Compare fescue. The chemical is called "festucine" because it is found in Festuca.

parole.significato: Formed of, consisting of, or similar to, straw.
parole.testo: From Latin festūcōsus, from festūca.

parole.significato: A member of the Roman college of priests who acted as representatives in disputes with foreign nations.
parole.testo: From Latin fētiālis (“priest who sanctioned treaties and demanded satisfaction from enemies before formal declarations of war”). The root of the Latin word is thought to be Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to do, place, put”), also the source of the verb Latin faciō (“to do; to build, construct; to app

parole.significato: A fetial.
parole.testo: From Latin fētiālis.

parole.significato: Foul-smelling, stinking.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fētidus (“having offensive odour”), originally fēteō (“to stink”).

parole.significato: Producing young; fruitful, productive.
parole.testo: From Latin fētifer (“causing fruitfulness”) + -ous, from fētus (“pregnant, fruitful”) + -fer (“bearing, carrying, bringing”).

parole.significato: An unpleasant smell.
parole.testo: From Latin fētor.

parole.significato: An unborn or unhatched vertebrate showing signs of the mature animal.
parole.testo: A learned borrowing from Latin fētus (“offspring”). Doublet of fawn.

parole.significato: Used to call for or reference the act of getting an abortion (hence destroying the fetus).
parole.testo: From fetus + rhyming alteration of delete with Latin -us after fetus. Compare Latin dēlētus (“deleted”).

parole.significato: A fetus growing inside the body of another fetus, either from an unsuccessful twin pregnancy, or as a tumorlike growth.
parole.testo: From Latin fētus in fētū.

parole.significato: Relating to feudalism, feudal.
parole.testo: From the Latin feudātōrius, from the Mediaeval Latin feudāre (“to enfeoff”), from feudum, feodum.

parole.significato: and the following (pages, paragraphs etc.)
parole.testo: Abbreviation of Latin foliō (“on the (next) page”), ablative of folium (“leaf, page”).

parole.significato: An arbitrary or authoritative command or order to do something; an effectual decree.
parole.testo: From Latin fīat (“let it be done”).

parole.significato: Let there be light, especially in the context of light being a metaphor for wisdom.
parole.testo: From Latin fīat lūx (“let there be light”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Fibonacci sequence.
parole.testo: From Latin filius (“son”) + Italian Bonacci, a diminutive of Bono, from Latin bonum, ultimately meaning literally, "son of the (little) good man."

parole.significato: A fine fibre or filament.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fibrilla, diminutive of Latin fibra. Doublet of fibrilla. Compare fibre.

parole.significato: Synonym of fibril (“a fine fibre or filament”).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fibrilla, diminutive of Latin fibra + -illa. Doublet of fibril. Compare fibre. By surface analysis, fibre + Latin -illa.

parole.significato: An ancient kind of brooch used to hold clothing together, similar in function to the modern safety pin.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fībula (“buckle, clasp, pin”). The bone is so named because the shape it makes with the tibia resembles a clasp, the fibula being the pin.

parole.significato: Any of a family of calcium-binding glycoproteins found in the extracellular matrix and in plasma.
parole.testo: From Latin fibula (“clasp, buckle”) + -in.

parole.significato: Fig-shaped.
parole.testo: From Latin ficus (“fig”) + -iform.

parole.significato: Capable of being molded into the shape of an artifact or art work
parole.testo: Latin fictilus, from fictus (from fingere (“to shape, form, devise”)) + -ilis

parole.significato: Fictitious.
parole.testo: From ficti(on) + -ous, as if Latin *fictiōsus, from fictiō.

parole.significato: Invented; contrived.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fictīcius.

parole.significato: An artist who models or forms statues and reliefs in any malleable material.
parole.testo: From Latin fictor, from fingo (“to shape, to sculpt”).

parole.significato: Worthless.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fīculneus (“of the fig or fig tree”).

parole.significato: Any plant belonging to the genus Ficus, including the rubber plant, of species Ficus elastica.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fīcus (“fig”).

parole.significato: A benefit bequeathed to a beneficiary who inherits the benefit, subject to the obligation of bequeathing it to another.
parole.testo: Latin fidei (“trust”) (genitive) + commissum, from committō (“give, entrust”), from con- + mittō (“to send”).

parole.significato: suretyship.
parole.testo: From Latin fideiussiōnem (with -ion), from fidēiussus, from fideiubeō, from fidēs (“faith”) + iubēre (“order”). Compare French fidéjussion.

parole.significato: A surety or guarantor.
parole.testo: From Latin fīdēiussor (with -or (“agent suffix”)), from fidēiussus, from fideiubeō, from fidēs (“faith”) + iubēre (“order”). Compare French fidéjusseur.

parole.significato: One who pledges himself as security for another; bail, surety
parole.testo: From Latin fidēprōmissor (“guarantor, surety”), from fidēprōmittō (“make a promise on behalf of another person, stand as guarantor or surety”) + -tor, from fidē (“in faith”) + prōmittō (“promise”) + -or (“agent suffix”).

parole.significato: A piece of paper used for lighting a pipe, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fidibus.

parole.significato: stringed (of or pertaining to a stringed instrument).
parole.testo: From Latin fidicen, fidicinis (“lute player”) + -al.

parole.significato: Relating to an entity that owes to another good faith, accountability and trust, often in the context of trusts and tru…
parole.testo: From Latin fīdūciārius (“held in trust”), from fīdūcia (“trust”).

parole.significato: designating a durative and dynamic action performed by the subject
parole.testo: From Latin fīēns (“becoming; happening”, present active participle of fīō (“to become; to happen”)), on the pattern of words such as stative, durative, iterative, causative etc.

parole.significato: Made of potter's clay.
parole.testo: From Latin figulātus, perfect passive participle of figulō, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Any of the non-signifying constituents of signifiers.
parole.testo: From Latin figūra. Coined by Louis Hjelmslev.

parole.significato: Composed of threads, stringy.
parole.testo: Latin fīlum (“thread”) + -aceous.

parole.significato: Having a thread across the field of view.
parole.testo: From Latin filum (“a thread”).

parole.significato: A machine for forming threads.
parole.testo: From Latin filatorium (“place for spinning”), from filare (“to spin”), from filum (“a thread”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to or befitting a son or daughter.
parole.testo: From Middle English filial, from Latin fīliālis, from fīlius (“son”) / fīlia (“daughter”) + -al.

parole.significato: Derived from ferns
parole.testo: From Latin filix (“a fern”) + -icis.

parole.significato: The killing of one's own child.
parole.testo: From Latin fīlius (“son”), fīlia (“daughter”) + -cide.

parole.significato: Shaped like a fern or like the parts of a fern leaf.
parole.testo: From Latin filix (“fern”) + Latin -icis + English -form. Compare French filiciforme.

parole.significato: Any fern-like plant.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin filix (“fern”) + English -oid.

parole.significato: The botanical study of ferns.
parole.testo: From Latin filic- (stem of filix (“fern”)) + English -ology (a variant of -logy (suffix denoting the study of a particular subject)). Filix is probably derived from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“henbane”) + Latin -ix (a variant of -ex (suffix found in plant names such as cārex (“sedge”) and rumex (“s

parole.significato: Producing or constituting threads.
parole.testo: From Latin filum (“a thread”) + -ferous.

parole.significato: Shaped like or resembling a thread or filament; filamentous.
parole.testo: Latin filum (“filament”), + -iform.

parole.significato: The use of the Latin word filioque (“and from the son”) in the Western form of the Nicene Creed, to indicate that the H…
parole.testo: From Latin filioque, from filiō (“from the son”, ablative) + -que (“and”).

parole.significato: The philosopher's stone.
parole.testo: Latin filius philosophorum (literally “philosophers' child”)

parole.significato: A hair-like feather; a feather with a slender scape and without a web in most or all of its length.
parole.testo: From Latin filum (“a thread”) + pluma (“a soft feather”).

parole.significato: Terminating in a thread-like process, or threadlike
parole.testo: From Latin filum (“a thread”).

parole.significato: a filamentous anatomical structure
parole.testo: From Latin fīlum (“thread”). Doublet of file.

parole.significato: To fringe; to hem.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fimbriātus (“fibrous, fringed”), participial adjective formed on fimbriae (“fibers, threads, fringe”) + -ātus (participial adjective-forming suffix). See -ate (verb-forming suffix), -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Growing on dung.
parole.testo: From Latin fimēta + -ous.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to dung
parole.testo: From Latin fimētum (“dunghill”) + -ic.

parole.significato: Inhabiting dung.
parole.testo: An adaptation of the Latin fimicolus (“dung-dwelling”).

parole.significato: Given to fashioning or molding.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fingēns (“shaping, fashioning”).

parole.significato: The final pilot-in-command, pilot-flying flight of a pilot during a stage of life, such as on a particular aircraft, ai…
parole.testo: fini + flight. Ultimately from Latin finis (“ending”). See also Middle English finis (“the end”) and Romance latin derivations of Latin finis (French finis (“fini”), French fin; Spanish fine (“fini”), Spanish fin)

parole.significato: Of a book or other work: the end.
parole.testo: From Middle English finis, from Latin fīnis (“end; limit”). Doublet of fin, fine, and finish.

parole.significato: Having an end or limit; (of a quantity) constrained by bounds; (of a set) whose number of elements is a natural number.
parole.testo: The adjective is derived from Middle English fynyte, finit, from Latin fīnītus, perfect passive participle of fīniō (“to finish; to terminate”), from fīnis (“boundary”). The word displaced Old English ġeendodlīċ. The noun is derived from the adjective.

parole.significato: Synonym of alchemist.
parole.testo: A calque of Latin philosophus per ignem (“philosopher by fire”).

parole.significato: strength; stability
parole.testo: From Latin firmitudo. See firm.

parole.significato: strength; firmness; stability
parole.testo: Latin firmitas.

parole.significato: A person or position that is formally of equal rank to others in a group, but nonetheless takes a leading role within t…
parole.testo: Calque of Latin primus inter pares.

parole.significato: Forms of pronouns or verbs used for the speaker or writer of the sentence in which they occur.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin prīma persōna, itself a calque of Ancient Greek πρῶτον πρόσωπον (prôton prósōpon). Displaced native Old English forma had, literally, "form hade".

parole.significato: All matters concerning taxation
parole.testo: Recorded since 1854, cognate with Dutch fiscaliteit and (derived from?) older French fiscalité, all from Latin fiscalis (“fiscal”), itself from fiscus (“imperial treasury”) + -alis (“-al”). By surface analysis, fiscal + -ity.

parole.significato: A government treasury.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fiscus (“treasury”).

parole.significato: cleft, split, cloven
parole.testo: Combining form of Latin fissus (“cleft”), past participle of Latin findere (“to cleave, split”).

parole.significato: Able to be split.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fissilis.

parole.significato: Having a forked tongue.
parole.testo: From Latin fissus (p.p. of findere (“to split”)) + lingual.

parole.significato: The process whereby one item splits to become two.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin fissiōnem, accusative singular of fissiō (“the act of breaking up”), from findō (“split, divide”).

parole.significato: Having the toes separated from each other.
parole.testo: From Latin fissiped-, fissipēs.

parole.significato: Being or relating to a fissiped.
parole.testo: From Latin fissus (“split”) + pedis (“foot”).

parole.significato: A small, connective tissue-filled cleft in the temporal bone, located just anterior to the oval window in the inner ear…
parole.testo: From Latin fissula (“small cleft, slit”), from Latin fissum + -ula + Latin ante (“in front of, before”) + Latin fenestram (“window”), accusative of fenestra.

parole.significato: A kind of pile driver.
parole.testo: From Latin fistūca.

parole.significato: An abnormal connection or passageway between organs or vessels that normally do not connect.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin fistula (“pipe, ulcer, catheter”). Doublet of fester.

parole.significato: Resembling the genus Fistularia (cornetfishes); having a long, tubular body.
parole.testo: From Fistulari(a) (“genus of cornetfishes”) + -oid (“resembling”), from Latin fistula (“pipe, tube”) and Ancient Greek εἶδος (eîdos, “form, likeness”). By surface analysis, fistule + -arioid.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a fistula.
parole.testo: From Latin fistula (“pipe, tube”) + -ary.

parole.significato: Fistula.
parole.testo: From Latin fistula (“pipe, tube”) + -o-.

parole.significato: An operation to create a surgical connection between a fistula and the intestine.
parole.testo: From fistulo- (“fistula”) + entero- (“intestine”) + -stomy (“mouth, surgical connection”), from Latin fistula (“pipe, tube”), Ancient Greek ἔντερον (énteron, “intestine”), and Ancient Greek στόμα (stóma, “mouth”).

parole.significato: Formed like a fistula; hollow; reed-like.
parole.testo: Latin fistulosus.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a fistula.
parole.testo: Possibly from Latin fistulōsus (“pipe-shaped, hole-filled, fistulous”), or an English medical pseudo-Latinism via fistula + -ous.

parole.significato: A seizure or convulsion.
parole.testo: Unknown. From Middle English fit (“hardship, danger”), possibly from Old English fitt (“conflict”)—a word only attested once. Compare Cornish fit (“game match, bout”); or else, maybe cognate with Italian fitta (“sudden and stabbing pain”) (see further at Latin fīgere).

parole.significato: Cinquefoil.
parole.testo: From Middle English fivelefe, fyflef; from Old English fīflēaf, a calque of Latin quīnquefolium. By surface analysis, five + leaf.

parole.significato: Fixed position; stable condition; firmness.
parole.testo: From Latin fixura (“a fastening”), from figere (“to fix”). See fix, and compare fixture.

parole.significato: A fan or flabellum.
parole.testo: From Latin flabellum (“a fan”), diminutive of flabrum (“a breeze”), from flare (“to blow”).

parole.significato: The act of keeping cool by use of a fan or fan-like instrument.
parole.testo: From Latin flabella (“fan”) + -ation.

parole.significato: Having many nerves diverging radiately from the base.
parole.testo: Latin flabellum a fan + English nerve.

parole.significato: A large fan used for religious ceremonies.
parole.testo: From Latin flabellum (“fan”).

parole.significato: Liable to be blown about; pertaining to wind or breath.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin flabilis.

parole.significato: Flabby; lacking firmness or muscle tone.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin flaccid(us).

parole.significato: a person who whips themselves or others either as part of a religious penance or for sexual gratification.
parole.testo: From Latin flagellāns, present participle of flagellāre (“to whip”).

parole.significato: To whip or scourge.
parole.testo: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin flagellātus perfect passive participle of flagellō (“to whip, flog”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The formation by plants of flagella, or their arrangement
parole.testo: From flagellum (“elongated filiform appendage”), itself a diminutive of Latin flagrum (“whip”), closely related to etymology 1.

parole.significato: shaped like a whip
parole.testo: Latin flagellum (“whip”) + -form

parole.significato: One who administers punishment by whipping.
parole.testo: From Latin flagellum (“whip”) + -ist.

parole.significato: A penchant for whipping, or being whipped.
parole.testo: From Latin flagellō (“to whip, flog”) + -mania.

parole.significato: In protists, a long, whiplike membrane-enclosed organelle used for locomotion or feeding.
parole.testo: From Latin flagellum (“whip”), diminutive of flagrum.

parole.significato: To importune; to demand fiercely or with passion.
parole.testo: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin flāgitātus, perfect passive participle of flāgitō (“to demand, ask urgingly”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: begging; passionate asking
parole.testo: Latin flagitatio.

parole.significato: To burn.
parole.testo: First attested in 1756; borrowed from Latin flagrātus, perfect passive participle of flagrō (“to burn”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A priest devoted to the service of a particular god, from whom he received a distinguishing epithet. The most honored w…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin flāmen (“ancient Roman priest devoted exclusively to one deity”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to a flamen.
parole.testo: From oblique stem of Latin flāmen, flāminis (“priest”) + -ic + -al.

parole.significato: A dense cumuliform cloud associated with fire or volcanic eruptions.
parole.testo: From Latin flamma (“flame”) + genitus (“begotten”), past participle of gignō.

parole.significato: Pertaining to, consisting of, or resembling fire; fiery.
parole.testo: From Latin flammeus (“fiery”), derivative of flamma (“a flame”).

parole.significato: Producing flame; blazing.

parole.significato: A motion like that of waves; a moving in this and that direction; an irregular rising and falling.

parole.significato: A physician.
parole.testo: From Middle English Galen, from Latin Galēnus, from Ancient Greek Γαληνός (Galēnós), from γαλήνη (galḗnē, “calm, tranquillity”).

parole.significato: A mineral, lead sulphide (PbS), mined as an ore for lead.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin galēna (“dross from smelting lead”).

parole.significato: A guinea fowl.
parole.testo: From Latin gallīna (“hen”).

parole.significato: A cretaceous fossil sea urchin of the genus †Galerites.
parole.testo: Latin galerum a hat, cap: compare French galérite. See -ite.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Geoffrey of Monmouth (c.1100–c.1155), cleric and one of the major figures in the development of Briti…
parole.testo: From his Latin name, Galfridus Monemutensis, + -ian.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Galilee, or a native or inhabitant thereof.
parole.testo: Originated 1605–15 from Latin Galilaeus [from Ancient Greek Γαλιλαῖος (Galilaîos)] + -an.

parole.significato: An alloy of gallium, indium and tin which is liquid at room temperature.
parole.testo: Trade name, from gallium, indium, and Latin stannum (“tin”).

parole.significato: A verse consisting of four Ionics a minore, with variations and substitutions.
parole.testo: From Latin Galli + iambus. Used by the Galli, priests of the Phrygian goddess Cybele. The first element, Ancient Greek γάλλος (gállos), was said by Ovid to be named after a Phrygian river.

parole.significato: Of or related to Gaul or the Gauls.
parole.testo: From Latin Gallicus (“of or related to Gaul”), from Gallia (“Gaul”) + -icus (“-ic: forming adj.”), used archaically in New Latin and English in reference to modern France.

parole.significato: Relating to Gaul or France; Gallic; French.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Gallicānus (“pertaining to Gaul or France; Gallican”), from Gallicus (“Gaulish, French”) (from Gallia (“Gaul”)) + -ānus (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’).

parole.significato: Synonym of frenchify, to make French or more French-like.
parole.testo: From Gallic + -ize, from Latin Gallicus (“of or relating to Gaul”) and used archaically in English in reference to modern France.

parole.significato: Affecting chickens; applied to certain alphaherpesviruses.
parole.testo: From Latin gallus (“cock, rooster”) + -id.

parole.significato: Synonym of Gallophilia.
parole.testo: From Latin gallicus + -mania.

parole.significato: Related to the genus Gallus, poultry; notably said of the order Galliformes.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin gallīnāceus, from gallīna (“hen”), itself from gallus (“cock”).

parole.significato: A chemical element (symbol Ga) with an atomic number of 31; a soft bluish metal.
parole.testo: Named by its discoverer Lecoq, after Latin Gallia (“Gaul”). It was claimed that Lecoq had named the element after himself, since gallus is the Latin translation of the French le coq, but Lecoq denied this in an article of 1877.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Galloway, Scotland.
parole.testo: From Latin Gallovidia (“Galloway”), from Cumbric/Welsh Gallgwyddel.

parole.significato: The metacarpus or metatarsus of ruminants, etc.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin gamba (“leg”); compare gambol. Doublet of gam, gamb, jamb, and jambe.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the river Ganges.
parole.testo: From Latin Gangēticus, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek Γαγγητικός (Gangētikós), from Γάγγης (Gángēs, “(River) Ganges”).

parole.significato: a gargle; a liquid used to gargle with.
parole.testo: From Latin gargarisma, from Ancient Greek γαργάρισμα (gargárisma).

parole.significato: To gargle (rinse or wash mouth and throat).
parole.testo: From Latin gargarizo, from Ancient Greek γαργαρίζω (gargarízō).

parole.significato: A fermented fish sauce popular as a condiment in Ancient Rome.
parole.testo: From Latin garum, from Ancient Greek γάρον (gáron, “the fish whose intestines were originally used in the condiment's production”).

parole.significato: A highly esteemed variety of garum from Cartagena and Gades in Hispania Baetica.
parole.testo: Latin [Term?] (literally “garum of the allies”)

parole.significato: Related to, or from, the region of the river Garonne.
parole.testo: From Latin Garumna.

parole.significato: omnium-gatherum
parole.testo: Pseudo-Latinism, derived from gather + Latin -um.

parole.significato: A students' merrymaking.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin gaudeamus (“may we rejoice”)

parole.significato: A reunion held by one of the colleges of the University of Oxford for alumni, normally during the long vacation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin gaudium (“joy”). Doublet of joy and jo.

parole.significato: A native or inhabitant of the historical region of Gaul, or poetically the modern nation of France.
parole.testo: From Middle English Gall, from Latin Gallus. The change in spelling is due to the influence of the place-name Gaul, which is thought to be etymologically unrelated (see above).

parole.significato: Capable of being congealed, or converted into jelly.
parole.testo: From Latin gelare (“to congeal”). Compare French gelable. See geal.

parole.significato: The formation of a solid by cooling; freezing.
parole.testo: From Latin gelātiō (“freezing”), from gelātus (“frozen”), past participle of gelō (“to freeze”).

parole.significato: Young and weakly developed soils that form in very cold climates where permafrost is present near the surface and that…
parole.testo: From Latin gelāre (“freeze”) + (inc)ept(isol).

parole.significato: Very cold; icy or frosty; frigid.
parole.testo: First attested in 1630. From Latin gelidus (“cold”), from gelu (“frost”).

parole.significato: A kind of soil found in cold climates, containing permafrost near the surface.
parole.testo: Latin gelāre (“freeze”) + + -sol

parole.significato: A tribe of Scythia settled near the river Borysthenes
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Gelōnī, from Ancient Greek Γελωνοί (Gelōnoí).

parole.significato: A person who studies humour and laughter
parole.testo: From Latin zelus (“laughter”).

parole.significato: Producing twins
parole.testo: From Latin gemellipara f, from gemellus (“twin”) + parere (“to bear, produce”).

parole.significato: Describing identical atoms or groups attached to the same atom in a molecule
parole.testo: From Latin geminālis, from geminī (“twins”).

parole.significato: Forming a pair.
parole.testo: First attested in 1589; borrowed from Latin geminātus, perfect passive participle of geminō (“to double”), see -ate (etymology 1,2 and 3).

parole.significato: The process of indicating that a vowel is pronounced long by writing it twice, especially as was sometimes done in Lati…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin geminatio vocalium (“doubling of vowels”).

parole.significato: A doubling.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin geminātiō, geminātiōnis (“a doubling”).

parole.significato: Someone who has the Gemini star sign.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin geminī, plural of geminus (“twin”), calque of Ancient Greek Δίδυμοι (Dídumoi), calque of Akkadian 𒀯𒈠𒀸 (māšu), calque of Sumerian 𒀯𒈦𒋰𒁀 (ᵐᵘˡMAŠ.TAB.BA, “the Divine Twins, in Mesopotamia identified as Lugal-irra and Meslamta-ea; name of constellation”). See Lugal-irra and Meslamta-e

parole.significato: Having the flowers arranged in pairs.
parole.testo: From Latin geminus (“twin”) + flos, floris (“flower”).

parole.significato: Having a structure consisting of two identical parts.
parole.testo: From Latin geminī (“twins”) + -form.

parole.significato: The study of twins; gemellology.
parole.testo: From Latin gemini (“twins”) + -logy.

parole.significato: double; appearing or growing in pairs
parole.testo: Latin geminus.

parole.significato: An asexual reproductive structure, as found in animals such as hydra (genus Hydra) and plants such as liverworts (divis…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin gemma (“bud on a plant”). Doublet of gem and Gemma.

parole.significato: Relating to, or containing, gemmae.
parole.testo: From Latin gemma + -aceous.

parole.significato: Having buds; reproducing by buds.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin gemmātus, perfect passive participle of gemmō (“to put forth buds”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from gemma (“a bud”).

parole.significato: Resembling or relating to gems.
parole.testo: From Latin gemmeus. See gem.

parole.significato: Producing gemmae or buds.
parole.testo: From Latin gemma (“bud”) + -ferous. Compare French gemmifère.

parole.significato: The production of a bud or gem.
parole.testo: From Latin gemma (“bud”) + -ficare (“in comparative) to make”). See -fy.

parole.significato: The branch of mineralogy that studies mineral gems and petrified gemstones.
parole.testo: From Latin gemma (“gem”) + -logy (“science”).

parole.significato: The use of remedies made from the embryonic tissue of various trees and shrubs, or other meristematic parts
parole.testo: From Latin gemma (“bud”) + therapy.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Gemonian Stairs, a flight of steps used as a place of execution in Ancient Rome.
parole.testo: From Latin gemoniae (“of laments”) (from gemō) + -an, referring to the scalae gemoniae ("stairway of laments") where the bodies of executed people were exposed.

parole.significato: new genus and species
parole.testo: From Latin genus et species novus.

parole.significato: The cheek; the feathered side of the under mandible of a bird.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin gena (“cheek”). Doublet of chin.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the cheeks
parole.testo: From Latin gena (“cheek”) + -al.

parole.significato: generalities; general terms
parole.testo: Neuter plural, from Latin generalis.

parole.significato: The quality of being general.
parole.testo: From Middle English generalite, from Anglo-Norman and Middle French generalité (modern French généralité), from general + -ité; also influenced by Latin generālitās. By surface analysis, general + -ity.

parole.significato: generative; producing
parole.testo: From Latin generans.

parole.significato: Generated, not self-existent.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin generātus, perfect passive participle of generō (“beget, procreate, produce”). See Etymology 1 and -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more.

parole.significato: One who, or that which, generates, begets, causes, or produces.
parole.testo: From Latin, from past participle of genero (“beget, father”), equivalent to generate + -or.

parole.significato: A curve that, when rotated about an axis, produces a solid figure.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin generātrīx. By surface analysis, generator + -trix.

parole.significato: The process of making generic; the conversion to use generics.
parole.testo: From Latin genus (“kind, class”). See -fy.

parole.significato: The trait of being willing to donate money, resources, or time.
parole.testo: From Middle English generosite, from Latin generōsitās, equivalent to generous + -ity.

parole.significato: The origin, start, or point at which something comes into being.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin genesis (“generation, nativity”), from Ancient Greek γένεσις (génesis, “origin, source, beginning”). Related to Ancient Greek γίγνομαι (gígnomai, “to be produced, become, be”). Doublet of kind, gens, and jati.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the casting of horoscopes at a person's birth
parole.testo: From Latin genethliacus, from Ancient Greek γενεθλιακός (genethliakós, “belonging to a birthday”).

parole.significato: A birthday ode.
parole.testo: Via Latin genethliacon from Ancient Greek γενεθλιακόν (genethliakón, “of or related to a birthday”, neuter sg.).

parole.significato: The quality of being genial; friendly cheerfulness; warmth of disposition and manners.
parole.testo: From Latin geniālitās, and perhaps also partly formed within English as genial + -ity.

parole.significato: Bent abruptly, with the structure of a knee.
parole.testo: PIE word  *ǵónu Learned borrowing from Latin geniculātus (“with bended knee”), from geniculum (“little knee”) + -ātus (participial adjective-forming suffix), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: To form joints or knots on.
parole.testo: From Latin geniculātus (more at etymology 1), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The act of kneeling.
parole.testo: Latin geniculatio a kneeling.

parole.significato: Of the structure of a knee.
parole.testo: From Latin geniculātus (“with bended knee”) + -o-, from geniculum (“little knee”) + -ātus (participial adjective-forming suffix), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A small genu, or angular knee-like structure, especially (anatomy) a sharp knee-like bend in a small structure or organ.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin geniculum.

parole.significato: Of or relating to biological reproduction.
parole.testo: From Middle English genital, from Latin genitalis (“of or belonging to generation”), from genitus, past participle of gignō (“to beget, generate”); see genus.

parole.significato: External sex organs.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin (membra) genitālia, substantive use of neuter plural of genitālis (“pertaining to generation or birth”). First attested in 1651.

parole.significato: an independent phrase in a sentence conveying additional circumstances in the genitive case; present in many Indo-Europ…
parole.testo: Calque of Latin genitīvus absolūtus.

parole.significato: The biological mother of a child.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin genitrīx. By surface analysis, genitor + -trix.

parole.significato: Someone possessing extraordinary intelligence or skill; especially somebody who has demonstrated this by a creative or…
parole.testo: From Latin genius (“inborn nature; a tutelary deity of a person or place; wit, brilliance”), from gignō (“to beget, produce”), Old Latin genō, from the Proto-Indo-European root *ǵenh₁-. Doublet of genio. See also genus and genie.

parole.significato: A spirit presiding over or guarding a family or household.
parole.testo: From Latin genius (“lar”) + familiae (“of (a) person”), genitive singular form of familia (“family”, “household”) = “(guardian) spirit of a family”.

parole.significato: The tutelary deity or spirit watching over a particular person.
parole.testo: A borrowing of Latin genius hominis (“tutelary deity of a person”), from the nominative possessive form of homo (“person”).

parole.significato: The minor deity or spirit watching over a particular place.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin genius loci (“tutelary deity of a/the place”), from the singular genitive form of locus (“place”).

parole.significato: A single spirit or minor deity (genius) which watches over several places, rather than only one.
parole.testo: A borrowing of Latin genius locorum (“tutelary spirit of the places”), employing the genitive plural of locus (“place”).

parole.significato: A legally defined unit of Roman society, being a collection of people related through a common ancestor by birth, marri…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin gēns (“gens; people, tribe”), from Proto-Italic *gentis, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵénh₁tis (“birth; production”), from *ǵenh₁- (“to beget; to give birth; to produce”) + *-tis (suffix forming abstract or action nouns from verb roots). Doublet of kind, genesis, and jati. See also

parole.significato: Any of various herbs of the family Gentianaceae found in temperate and mountainous regions with violet or blue flowers.
parole.testo: Via Middle English from Latin gentiāna, which, according to Pliny the Elder, was named after Gentius (Ancient Greek Γένθιος (Génthios)), the last king of Illyria, who supposedly discovered the plant's medicinal benefits. This has been dismissed as folk etymology but the word may still ultimately be

parole.significato: The killing of a race or nation of people; the slaughter of an ethnic group; a genocide.
parole.testo: From the Latin gēns (“a race, nation, people; a clan, family”, oblique stem: gent-) + -cide (“a killing of”). The combination represents a hypothetical Latin etymon of the form *genticīdium, regularly formed from gēns + -cīdium. Compare genericide and genocide.

parole.significato: Tribal or national.
parole.testo: From Latin gentilis (“of a clan or gens”) + English suffix -ic.

parole.significato: Synonym of gentilicial.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin gentīlicius.

parole.significato: The knee.
parole.testo: PIE word  *ǵónu Borrowed from Latin genu (“knee”).

parole.significato: The condition in which the knees are abnormally close together and the ankles far apart.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin genū valgum (“knockkneed”).

parole.significato: The act of genuflecting.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin genuflexio, though with standardized spelling. By surface analysis, genuflect (“to bend the knee”) + -ion (Latinate abstract-noun suffix).

parole.significato: Belonging to, or proceeding from the original stock; native.
parole.testo: From Latin genuīnus (“innate, native, natural”).

parole.significato: A category in the classification of organisms, ranking below family (Lat. familia) and above species.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin genus (“birth, origin, a race, sort, kind”) from the root gen- in Latin gignō (“to beget, produce”). Doublet of gender and genre, further related to kin.

parole.significato: Pertaining to geography (or to geographics).
parole.testo: From Latin geōgraphicus; see French géographique. By surface analysis, geography + -ic.

parole.significato: Of or relating to geomancy.
parole.testo: From Latin geōmanticus. By surface analysis, geo- + -mantic.

parole.significato: Of or relating to geometry.
parole.testo: From Latin geōmetricus, from Ancient Greek γεωμετρικός (geōmetrikós), from γεωμέτρης (geōmétrēs). By surface analysis, geometer + -ic or geo- + -metric.

parole.significato: A unit of measure used in the 16th century, defined as "five feet" or "five geometrical feet".
parole.testo: Calque of Latin passus geometricus or French pas géometrique.

parole.significato: radiotelephony clear-code word for the letter G.
parole.testo: Name of an early saint, from Middle English George, from Latin Geōrgius, from Ancient Greek Γεώργῐος (Geṓrgĭos), from γεωργός (geōrgós, “farmer, earth worker”), from γῆ (gê, “earth”) (combining form γεω- (geō-)) + ἔργον (érgon, “work”) Doublet of Jorge and Geevarghese. The aircraft autopilot sense i

parole.significato: A British citizen during the reign of a king named George.
parole.testo: From George + -ian, possibly with influence from its Latin equivalent (as other regnal adjectives and nouns so derived), Geōrgius.

parole.significato: A rural poem; a poetical composition on husbandry, containing rules for cultivating land, etc.
parole.testo: From Latin georgicum, georgicus, from Ancient Greek γεωργός (geōrgós, “farmer, earth worker”), from γῆ (gê, “earth”) (combining form γεω- (geō-)) + ἔργον (érgon, “work”).

parole.significato: A member of an East Germanic people related to the Goths.
parole.testo: From Latin Gepidae.

parole.significato: The Gepids, an East Germanic people.
parole.testo: From Latin Gepidae, from Gothic *𐌲𐌹𐌱𐌹𐌳𐍉𐍃 (*gibidōs), from Proto-Germanic *gibidōz (which see for more).

parole.significato: Any flowering plant of the genus Geranium, of family Geraniaceae.
parole.testo: From Latin geranium, from Ancient Greek γερᾰ́νῐον (gerắnĭon), from γέρᾰνος (gérănos, “crane”) + -ῐον (-ĭon, diminutive suffix).

parole.significato: A manager.
parole.testo: From Latin gerēns, present participle of gerō.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the nation of Germany.
parole.testo: From Latin Germānus, Germānī (“the peoples of Germānia”), as distinct from Gauls (in the writings of Caesar and Tacitus), and of uncertain ultimate origin (possibly Celtic/Gaulish). Not related to german (“closely related”) or germane (from the Latin adjective germānus, through Old French). Attested

parole.significato: Relating to the Germanic peoples (such as Germans, Scandinavians or Anglo-Saxons).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin germānicus, equivalent to German + -ic.

parole.significato: The basic form of an organism; the seed or germ.
parole.testo: From Latin germen (“germ, seed”). Doublet of germ.

parole.significato: Relating to spring
parole.testo: From oblique stem of Latin germen, germinis (“seed”) + -al.

parole.significato: Of a seed, to begin to grow, to sprout roots and leaves.
parole.testo: From oblique stem of Latin germen, germinis (“shoot, sprout, bud”) + -ate, from germinātus (“sprouted, budded, grown”), past participle of germinō (“to sprout, bud, grow”), from germen, germinis (“shoot, sprout, bud”).

parole.significato: The process of germinating; the beginning of vegetation or growth from a seed or spore; the first development of germs,…
parole.testo: From oblique stem of Latin germen, germinis (“shoot, sprout, bud”) + -ation, from Latin germinātiō, germinātiōnem (“sprouting, budding, growing”), from germinātus (“sprouted, budded, grown”), past participle of germinō (“to sprout, bud, grow”), from germen, germinis (“shoot, sprout, bud”). By surfac

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to germination
parole.testo: From germinate + -ive. From oblique stem of Latin germen, germinis (“shoot, sprout, bud”) + -ate, from germinātus (“sprouted, budded, grown”), past participle of germinō (“to sprout, bud, grow”), from germen, germinis (“shoot, sprout, bud”).

parole.significato: A verbal form that functions as a verbal noun.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin gerundium, from gerendus (“which is to be carried out”), future passive participle (gerundive) of gerō (“carry, bear”).

parole.significato: A verbal adjective that describes obligation or necessity, equivalent in form to the future passive participle.
parole.testo: From Middle English gerundif, gerundyf, gerundyfe, gerundyffe, gerundyve, from Latin gerundīvum (“gerundive”), from gerundium (“gerund”), from gerundus (“which is to be carried out”), future passive participle (gerundive) of gerō (“carry, bear”). By surface analysis, gerund + -ive.

parole.significato: Pertaining to or behaving like a gerund.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin gerundīvus. By surface analysis, gerund + -ive.

parole.significato: Having within; laden; burdened; or pregnant, gestating.
parole.testo: From Latin gestāns, present participle of gestō.

parole.significato: The period of time during which an animal or human offspring physically develops inside the mother's body until it is b…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin gestātiō.

parole.significato: A sedan chair used as a portable throne by popes.
parole.testo: A calque of Latin and Italian sedia gestatoria (“carrying chair”).

parole.significato: gestational (pertaining to gestation or pregnancy)
parole.testo: From Latin gestatorius (“that serves for carrying”). Compare French gestatoire.

parole.significato: To make gestures or motions, as in speaking.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin gesticulātus, perfect active participle of gesticulor (“to gesticulate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from gesticulus (“a mimic gesture”), diminutive of gestus (“gesture”), from gerō (“to bear, carry, perform”).

parole.significato: The act of gesticulating, or making gestures to aid expression of thoughts, sentiments or passion.
parole.testo: From Middle English gesticulation, from Latin gesticulatio.

parole.significato: One who gesticulates
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin gesticulātor.

parole.significato: A manager of another's affairs.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin gestor.

parole.significato: Do not tempt or torment me; I reject you, your statements, or your beliefs.
parole.testo: Originally uttered by Christ in the King James Bible, Matthew 16:23: “get thee behind me, Satan”; Latin vāde retrō, Satanā; Ancient Greek ὕπαγε ὀπίσω μου, Σατανᾶ (húpage opísō mou, Satanâ).

parole.significato: A Dacian tribe inhabiting the regions of the lower Danube.
parole.testo: From Latin Getae, from Ancient Greek Γέται (Gétai).

parole.significato: humped; protuberant; having one or more large elevations
parole.testo: From Latin gibbosus, from gibbus, gibba (“hunch, hump”). Compare gibbous.

parole.significato: Curved or bulged outward.
parole.testo: From Middle English gibbous, from Latin gibbus (“humped, hunched”), probably cognate with cubō (“bend oneself, lie down”), Italian gobba (“humpback”), Ancient Greek κῡφός (kūphós, “humpback, bent”), κύβος (kúbos, “cube, vertebra”), Spanish giboso (“humped”). Also ultimately compare dialectal Norwegi

parole.significato: giant-like; gigantic, mighty.
parole.testo: From Latin giganteus. See giant.

parole.significato: The killing of a giant.
parole.testo: From Latin gigāns, gigantis + -cide.

parole.significato: The gizzard of some birds.
parole.testo: Latin gigeria (“(plural) the cooked entrails of poultry”).

parole.significato: The internal flesh of a mushroom gill.
parole.testo: A macaronic blend of gill + Latin trāma (“woof”)

parole.significato: The gum, consisting of the tissue surrounding the roots of the teeth and covering the jawbone.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin gingīva (“gums”).

parole.significato: to distribute or circulate something
parole.testo: (to surround): Calque of Latin circumdō (“to surround”), which is formed from circum- (“around, about”) + dō (“give”).

parole.significato: The space between the eyebrows and above the nose.
parole.testo: From Latin glaber (“smooth, hairless, bald”).

parole.significato: smoothness or baldness.
parole.testo: Latin glabritas.

parole.significato: Bald, hairless; smooth.
parole.testo: From Latin glaber (“smooth; bald, hairless”) + English -ous (suffix forming adjectives, denoting possession or presence of a quality in any degree, commonly in abundance). Glaber is ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *gʰleh₂dʰ- (“smooth; bright, shining”), possibly from *ǵʰelh₂- (“to shine”

parole.testo: From Latin guttur (“throat”) + -ize.

parole.significato: Charged or sprinkled with drops.
parole.testo: From goutte + -y, or anglicization of (Old or Middle French) goutté, ultimately from Latin gutta (“drop (of a liquid)”) (also the ultimate source of English goutte and French goutte). Compare guttated.

parole.significato: An officer who had various powers and duties connected with the gymnasia, such as the payment of training, oil, or othe…
parole.testo: From Latin gymnasiarchus, from Ancient Greek γυμνασίαρχος (gumnasíarkhos).

parole.significato: A large room or building for indoor sports.
parole.testo: From Latin gymnasium, from Ancient Greek γυμνάσιον (gumnásion, “exercise, school”), from γυμνός (gumnós, “naked”), because Greek athletes trained naked.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to gymnastics.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin gymnasticus. By surface analysis, gymnast + -ic.

parole.significato: A sport involving the performance of sequences of movements requiring physical strength, flexibility, and kinesthetic a…
parole.testo: From gymnastic: see -ics; from Latin gymnasticus, from Ancient Greek γυμναστικός (gumnastikós), from γυμναστής (gumnastḗs, “athlete, gymnast”), from γῠμνᾰ́ζω (gŭmnắzō, “to train, exercise”), from γυμνός (gumnós, “naked”), because Greek athletes trained naked. By surface analysis, gymnast + -ics.

parole.significato: Gymnastic; athletic.
parole.testo: From Latin gymnicus, from Ancient Greek γυμνικός (gumnikós), from γυμνός (gumnós, “naked”).

parole.significato: The women's quarters in a household; (hence, loosely) any building or area for women.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin gynaecēum, gynaecīum, from Ancient Greek γυναικεῖον (gunaikeîon), from γυνή (gunḗ, “woman”) (stem: γῠναικ- (gŭnaik-)) + -εῖον (-eîon, noun-forming suffix meaning “place or building associated with a specific purpose or person”).

parole.significato: A gynaeceum.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin gynaecōnītis, from Ancient Greek γυναικωνῖτις (gunaikōnîtis).

parole.significato: A mineral consisting of hydrated calcium sulphate. When calcinated, it forms plaster of Paris.
parole.testo: From Latin gypsum, from Ancient Greek γύψος (gúpsos). Doublet of gesso.

parole.significato: A swirling vortex.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin gȳrus (“circle; circular motion”), from Ancient Greek γῦρος (gûros, “circle; ring”), from Proto-Indo-European *gew- (“to bend; to curve”). The English word is a doublet of gyro and gyrus.

parole.significato: a gyrus in the frontal lobe of the brain, adjacent to the longitudinal fissure
parole.testo: From Latin gyrus + rectus.

parole.significato: A writ ordering that a person be brought before a court or a judge, most frequently used to ensure that a person's impr…
parole.testo: From Latin habeas corpus ad subiciendum (“You (shall) have the body to be subjected to (examination)”), referring to the body of the detainee (not the body of a victim, similar to corpus delicti).

parole.significato: A restricting bandage or frenum
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin habena.

parole.significato: The part of a deed that formally defines the extent of ownership or tenancy granted.
parole.testo: From Latin, neuter singular gerundive of habeo (“have", "own", "possess”): "that which must or should be possessed".

parole.significato: A circumscript mass of cells in the caudal and dorsal aspect of the dorsal thalamus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin habenula, diminutive of habena.

parole.significato: Equipment; qualification.
parole.testo: From Latin habilitatio, from Latin habilitāre.

parole.significato: An action performed on a regular basis.
parole.testo: From Middle English habit, from Latin habitus (“condition, bearing, state, appearance, dress, attire”), from habeō (“to have, hold, keep”). Distantly related to gift. Replaced Middle English abit, from Old French abit, itself from the same Latin source. Displaced native Old English þēaw, wuna, ġewun

parole.significato: Conditions suitable for an organism or population of organisms to live.
parole.testo: From Latin habitat (“it dwells, lives”), the 3rd person singular present active indicative form of habitō (“to live or dwell”). In Linnaeus and similar authors, the geographical ranges of species were customarily denoted in Latin by a sentence beginning with "Habitat", e.g. "Habitat in Europa" ("It

parole.significato: A dweller; an inhabitant.
parole.testo: From Latin habitātor.

parole.significato: To make accustomed; to accustom; to familiarize.
parole.testo: From Middle English habituat(e) (“physically established or present”) (borrowed from Late Latin habituātus, perfect passive participle of habituō (“to bring into a condition or habit of body”)). See -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Relating to habitus or habitude.
parole.testo: From Latin habitūdin- + -al, from oblique stem of Latin habitūdō, from habitus + -tūdō, past participle of habeō. By surface analysis, habitude + -al.

parole.significato: Habitude; mode of life; bearing.
parole.testo: From Latin habitus (“habit”), from habeō (“have; maintain”). The plural habiti is a misconstruction, as the Latin plural is in fact habitūs. habiti may have been influenced by Latin habitī, the plural of the participle habitus; however, it is not the etymon of the English term.

parole.significato: The essence of a particular thing; those qualities that define it and make it unique.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin haecceitās.

parole.significato: Young goat, kid.
parole.testo: From Latin haedus.

parole.significato: Resembling in form or exhibiting the behaviour typical of a kid (i.e., a juvenile goat); compare caprine, hircine.
parole.testo: From the Latin haedīnus (“kidlike”), from haedus (“kid, young goat”); compare caprine, hircine. By surface analysis, haed- (“kid, young goat”) + -ine.

parole.significato: A magical plant mentioned by John Milton, said to be good against enchantments.
parole.testo: Coined by John Milton for the play Comus around 1634 (see quotation below). Various scholars suggest that the word comes from a classical source such as Latin Haemonia (“Thessaly”, a place associated with magic), Ancient Greek αἷμα (haîma, “blood”), or Ancient Greek αἵμων (haímōn, “skillful”).

parole.significato: A chemical element (symbol Hf) with an atomic number of 72: a lustrous, silvery-grey tetravalent transition metal.
parole.testo: From Latin Hafnia (“Copenhagen”) + -ium.

parole.significato: A kingfisher whose nesting by the sea was said, in classical mythology, to cause the Gods to restrain the wind and wave…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English Alceoun, from Latin halcyōn, alcyōn (“kingfisher”), from Ancient Greek ἀλκυών (alkuṓn).

parole.significato: A period of calm during the winter, when storms do not occur.
parole.testo: From halcyon, from Latin Alcyone, from Ancient Greek Ἀλκυόνη (Alkuónē), daughter of Aeolus and wife of Ceyx. When her husband died in a shipwreck, Alcyone threw herself into the sea whereupon the gods transformed them both into halcyon birds (kingfishers). When Alcyone made her nest on the beach, wa

parole.significato: A treatise upon fish or the art of fishing, especially in Ancient Rome.
parole.testo: From Latin halieuticus ("halieutic, of or about fishing"), from Ancient Greek ἁλιευτικός (halieutikós) (alieutikós, "of or about fishermen"), from ἁλιεύς (halieús, “fisherman”). The Christianity definition comes from the fish being a symbol of the Christian faith.

parole.significato: The condition of having stale or foul-smelling breath.
parole.testo: Coined by doctor Joseph William Howe in 1874 and described as being derived from the Latin hālitus (literally “whiff, breath”) and the Ancient Greek νόσος (nósos, literally “disease”). It can be also understood as combination of the Latin hālitus and the English suffix -osis.

parole.significato: Produced by, or like, breath; vaporous.
parole.testo: From Latin halitus (“breath, vapor”), from halare (“to breathe”): compare French halitueux.

parole.significato: A vapour.
parole.testo: From Latin halitus.

parole.significato: To seem to perceive things (with one or more of one's senses) which are not really present; to have visions; to experie…
parole.testo: First attested in 1604; borrowed from Latin hallūcinātus, alternative form of alūcinātus, perfect active participle of alucinor (“to dream”); see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A sensory perception of something that does not exist, often arising from disorder of the nervous system, as in deliriu…
parole.testo: From hallucinate + -ion, from Latin hallucinatus. Compare French hallucination. The first known usage in the English language is from Sir Thomas Browne.

parole.significato: A wood-nymph who was physically a part of her tree; she would die if her tree were felled.
parole.testo: From Latin Hamadryas, from Ancient Greek Ἁμαδρυάς (Hamadruás), from ἅμα (háma, “together”) + δρῦς (drûs, “tree”).

parole.significato: One of the eight bones of the wrist (carpals).
parole.testo: From Latin hāmātus (“hooked, crooked”).

parole.significato: The hamate bone.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hamatum.

parole.significato: Curved at the extremity.
parole.testo: First attested in glossaries in 1842 and first used in 1870; either directly from the Latin hāmiformis (1651, 1806) or formed from the suffixation of its etymon, hāmus (“hook”), with the English -form.

parole.significato: A certain stone with spangles of gold color in it, known to Pliny, perhaps golden mica or yellow mica schist.
parole.testo: From Latin hammochrȳsos, (h)ammochrȳsus, from Ancient Greek ἀμμόχρῡσος (ammókhrūsos), from ἄμμος (ámmos, “sand”) + χρῡσός (khrūsós, “gold”).

parole.significato: Having the end hooked or curved.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hāmōsus, from hāmus (“hook”).

parole.significato: Hamose.
parole.testo: Latin hamus (“hook”), + -ous.

parole.significato: A little hook.
parole.testo: Latin hamulus

parole.significato: Bearing a small hook at the end
parole.testo: Latin hamulus, diminutive of hāmus (“hook”)

parole.significato: A hook, or hook-like process.
parole.testo: Latin hamulus (“a little hook”).

parole.significato: A hook- or barb-like structure.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hāmus (“hook, barb”).

parole.significato: Any primate of the evolved clade (half of the order) which comprises all apes (including hominoids), monkeys and even (…
parole.testo: From Neo-Latin Haplorrhini, from Ancient Greek ἁπλόος (haplóos, “simple”) + ῥίς (rhís, “nose”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to harmony.
parole.testo: From Latin harmonicus, from Ancient Greek ἁρμονικός (harmonikós), from ἁρμονία (harmonía, “harmony”). By surface analysis, harmony + -ic. Doublet of armónico.

parole.significato: Synonym of corvus (“grappling hook in Ancient Roman naval warfare”).
parole.testo: From Latin harpagō.

parole.significato: A grappling hook.
parole.testo: Adapted from Latin harpagō, gen. harpagōnis, from Ancient Greek ἁρπάγη (harpágē, “hook”), from ἁρπάζω (harpázō, “to snatch away, to carry off, to seize, to captivate”), of uncertain origin. Doublet of harpoon.

parole.significato: A student of law or medicine at Cambridge who, being of the same standing as the students in arts in his year, is allow…
parole.testo: According to a 17th century chronicler, from Latin sophister Henricianus after King Henry VIII, but remodeled to fit a fanciful Ancient Greek *ἐρίσοφος (*erísophos, “very wise indeed”), from ἐρι- (eri-) + σοφός (sophós).

parole.significato: A soothsayer or priest in Ancient Rome (originally Etruscan) who practiced haruspicy, divination by inspecting entrails.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin haruspex.

parole.significato: Divination by use of animal entrails, usually the victims of sacrifice.
parole.testo: From Latin haruspicium, from haruspex (“diviner of entrails”) + -ium (forming abstract nouns).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the patriotic Jewish family to which the Maccabees belonged; Maccabean.
parole.testo: From Latin Asmonaeus (latinized name of the family's founder) + English -an, from (Hellenic) Ancient Greek Ἀσαμωναῖος (Asamōnaîos), from Hebrew חַשְׁמוֹנַאי (ḥašmōnay).

parole.significato: An artificially-produced transuranic chemical element (symbol Hs) with atomic number 108.
parole.testo: From Latin Hassia (“Hesse”), the location of the institute where the element was first synthesized, + -ium.

parole.significato: A spear carried by early Roman legionaries.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin hasta.

parole.significato: Shaped similarly to a halberd, with pointed lobes pointed outward from the base.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English hastate, borrowed from Latin hastātus (“armed with a spear”), from hasta (“spear”) + -ātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A medieval martial game.
parole.testo: From Latin hastiludum, from hasta (“spear”) and ludus (“sport, game”).

parole.significato: Of a fish, etc.: in a vertical orientation, with its head up (to chief) and tail down (to base).
parole.testo: From Latin hauriēns (“drawing (water, etc.); draining”), the present participle of hauriō (“to draw (water, etc.); to drain”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ews- (“to draw water”).

parole.significato: A root of a parasitic plant modified to take nourishment from its host.
parole.testo: From Latin haustor (“drainer”) + -ium.

parole.significato: Any of the small pouches of the colon caused by sacculation, giving the colon its segmented appearance.
parole.testo: From Latin haustrum.

parole.significato: Lasting seven days.
parole.testo: From Latin hebdomadālis. According to The Poly-Olbion Project, coined by John Selden in 1612.

parole.significato: Blunt, dull.
parole.testo: From Latin hebes (“blunt, dull, dim”).

parole.significato: Ebony.
parole.testo: From Middle English ebenif, hebenyf (influenced by Late Latin hebeninus), from Ecclesiastical Latin ebenius (“of ebony”), from Latin hebenus (“ebon tree”), from Ancient Greek ἔβενος (ébenos), from Egyptian hbnj, U13:n-Z4:M3

parole.significato: Causing lethargy.
parole.testo: From Latin hebetāns, present participle of hebetō (“to dull, deaden”).

parole.significato: Obtuse, dull.
parole.testo: First attested in 1574; borrowed from Latin hebetātus, perfect passive participle of hebetō (“to dull”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The act of making blunt, dull, or stupid.
parole.testo: Latin hebetatio: compare French hébétation.

parole.significato: unintelligent; stupid.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin hebes, hebetis (“dull, stupid”), from hebere (“to be dull”).

parole.significato: Displaying mental lethargy or dullness.
parole.testo: From Latin hebetūdin- + -ous, from oblique stem of Latin hebetūdō, from hebes + -tūdō, from hebeō. By surface analysis, hebetude + -ous.

parole.significato: The traditional Hebrew and Aramaic text of the Jewish Bible, viewed as its original, correct, and authoritative text.
parole.testo: Composed of the Latin hebraica (“Hebrew”, feminine nominative singular of adjective hebraicus) + vēritās (“truth”).

parole.significato: A great public sacrifice to the gods, originally of a hundred oxen; also, a great number of animals reserved for such a…
parole.testo: The noun is a learned borrowing from Latin hecatombē (“great sacrifice of a hundred oxen, hecatomb”), from Ancient Greek ἑκατόμβη (hekatómbē, “great sacrifice of a hundred oxen, hecatomb; any animal sacrifice or large sacrifice”, from ἑκᾰτόν (hekătón, “hundred”) + βοῦς (boûs, “cattle, cow, ox”)). Th

parole.significato: Sometimes in the form Hector: a blustering, noisy, turbulent fellow; a braggart, bully.
parole.testo: From Hector (“in Greek and Roman mythology, a character in Homer’s Iliad who is the greatest warrior of Troy”), from Late Middle English Hector (“warrior with the qualities of Hector”), from Latin Hectōr or Ancient Greek Ἕκτωρ (Héktōr), from ἕκτωρ (héktōr, “holding fast”), from ἔχειν (ékhein), prese

parole.significato: Any Old World ivy of the genus Hedera
parole.testo: From the genus name Hedera, in turn from Latin hedera (“ivy”).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or resembling ivy.
parole.testo: Latin hederaceus, from hedera (“ivy”).

parole.significato: ivy-shaped
parole.testo: From Latin hedera (“ivy”) + -iform.

parole.significato: methyl orange
parole.testo: Probably Latin helianthes (“sunflower”), alluding to its colour.

parole.significato: snail farming
parole.testo: From helici- + culture, from the genus of snails Helix, from helix, from Latin helix, from Ancient Greek ἕλιξ (hélix, “something twisted”).

parole.significato: helix, spiral
parole.testo: From Latin helic- + -o-, from Ancient Greek ἕλιξ (hélix).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Helicon.
parole.testo: Latin Heliconius

parole.significato: A curve on the surface of a cylinder or cone such that its angle to a plane perpendicular to the axis is constant; the…
parole.testo: From Latin helix, from Ancient Greek ἕλιξ (hélix, “something twisted or spiral”).

parole.significato: A glutton, a gormandizer.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin helluo (“glutton, squanderer”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Helvetii, the ancient inhabitants of the Alps, now Switzerland, or to the modern states and inh…
parole.testo: From Latin helveticus, from Helvetii (“the Helvetii”).

parole.significato: Helvite.
parole.testo: From Latin helvus (“of a light bay color”) + -ine.

parole.significato: A yellowish mineral consisting chiefly of silica, beryllium, manganese, iron, and sulfur. Its chemical formula is Mn₄Be…
parole.testo: From Latin helvus (“of a light bay color”) + -ite.

parole.significato: An antibiotic chemical compound found in Aspergillus.
parole.testo: Coined by Chain et al. in 1944, in reference to the mold Aspergillus fumigatus, mut. helvola Yuill. The epithet helvola is a feminine diminutive of Latin helvus (“honey-yellow”). By surface analysis, Latin helvus + -ole + -ic.

parole.significato: A variety of agate, sprinkled with spots of red jasper.
parole.testo: From Latin haemachātēs, from Ancient Greek *αἱμᾰχᾱ́της (*haimăkhā́tēs), from αἷμᾰ (haîmă, “blood”) + ᾰ̓χᾱ́της (ăkhā́tēs, “agate”).

parole.significato: A Roman unit of liquid measure reckoned as the volume of ⁵⁄₆ Roman pound of wine, equivalent to around 0.27 L.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hēmīna (“half-sextarius”), from Ancient Greek ἡμῑ́νᾱ (hēmī́nā).

parole.significato: To divide along the mesial plane or median plane.
parole.testo: From hemi- + Latin secare (“to cut”).

parole.significato: Half of the celestial sphere, as divided by either the ecliptic or the celestial equator .
parole.testo: From Latin hemisphaerium, from Ancient Greek ἡμισφαίριον (hēmisphaírion), from ἡμι- (hēmi-, “half”) + σφαῖρα (sphaîra, “sphere”). Equivalent to hemi- + sphere. Displaced native Old English healftrendel (literally “half-sphere”).

parole.significato: A semitone.
parole.testo: Latin hemitonium, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: A heavy release of blood within or from the body.
parole.testo: From Latin haemorrhagia, from Ancient Greek αἱμορραγία (haimorrhagía, “a violent bleeding”), from αἱμορραγής (haimorrhagḗs, “bleeding violently”), from αἷμα (haîma, “blood”) + -ραγία (-ragía), from ῥηγνύναι (rhēgnúnai, “to break, burst”); see ῥήγνῡμῐ (rhḗgnūmĭ) for more.

parole.significato: Having eleven syllables.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hendecasyllabus, from Ancient Greek ἑνδεκασύλλαβος (hendekasúllabos), from ἕνδεκα (héndeka, “eleven”) + συλλαβή (sullabḗ, “syllable”).

parole.significato: A line, verse, or word that comprises eleven syllables.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hendecasyllabus, from Ancient Greek ἑνδεκασύλλαβος (hendekasúllabos); equivalent to hendeca- + syllable.

parole.significato: Relating to someone named Henry, especially a king or his reign; supporting or on the side of Henry.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Hēnrīciānus, from Hēnrīcus (“Henry”) + -iānus (“relating to”).

parole.significato: liver of sulphur; a substance of a liver-brown colour, sometimes used in medicine, formed by fusing sulphur with carbon…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hepar (“liver”). Cf. liver of antimony.

parole.significato: A variety of barite that emits a foetid odour when rubbed or heated.
parole.testo: From Latin hepatitis, an unknown precious stone, from Ancient Greek ἧπαρ (hêpar, “liver”); compare French hépatite.

parole.significato: Inflammation of the liver, sometimes caused by a viral infection.
parole.testo: From Latin hēpatītis, from hēpar (“liver”), from Ancient Greek ἧπαρ (hêpar, “liver”). By surface analysis, hepat- + -itis.

parole.significato: A valuable metal alloy in antiquity, thought to have been an alloy of copper with gold and silver, mixed and treated to…
parole.testo: From the Latin hēpatizon, from the Ancient Greek ἡπᾰτῐ́ζον (hēpătĭ́zon), from ἡπᾰτῐ́ζων (hēpătĭ́zōn, “liver-coloured”).

parole.significato: Any of a people who comprised a nomadic confederation in Central Asia during the 5th–6th centuries CE.
parole.testo: Hypercorrect respelling of Ephthalite, with unetymological initial h-, from Latin Ephthalītēs, from Ancient Greek Ἐφθαλίτης (Ephthalítēs), from Bactrian Ηβοδαλο (Ēbodalo) + Ancient Greek -ίτης (-ítēs).

parole.significato: A government of seven people.
parole.testo: From New Latin heptarchia, from Ancient Greek ἑπτά (heptá, “hepta-: seven”) + -αρχία (-arkhía, “-archy: rule”). Equivalent to hepta- + -archy.

parole.significato: A messenger, especially one bringing important news.
parole.testo: From Latin heraldus, from Middle English herald, herauld, heraud, from Anglo-Norman heraud, from Old French heraut, hiraut (modern French héraut), from Frankish *heriwald, from Proto-Germanic *harjawaldaz, a compound consisting of Proto-Indo-European *ker- (“army”) + *h₂welh₁- (“to be strong”). Doub

parole.significato: The plant Logfia filaginoides.
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: Not woody, lacking lignified tissues.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin herbāceus (“grassy”). By surface analysis, herb + -aceous.

parole.significato: A collection of dried plants or parts of plants.
parole.testo: From Latin herbārium. Doublet of arbor.

parole.significato: Growing into herbs.
parole.testo: From Latin herbescens, present participle of herbescere.

parole.significato: Covered with herbs.
parole.testo: Latin herbidus.

parole.significato: Feeding chiefly on plants.
parole.testo: Adapted borrowing of New Latin herbivorus + -ous, from Latin herba (“grass”) and -vorus, from vorō (“to devour”).

parole.significato: Having an abundance of herbage; full of herbs.
parole.testo: From the Latin herbōsus (“grassy, full of grass or herbs”).

parole.significato: A Hercules beetle.
parole.testo: From Latin Herculēs, from Etruscan 𐌇𐌄𐌓𐌂𐌋𐌄 (hercle), from Ancient Greek Ἡρακλῆς (Hēraklês), apparently cognate of Ἥρα (Hḗra, “Hera”) and, according to Haudry, from Proto-Indo-European *yóh₁r̥ (“year, season”) + κλέος (kléos, “glory”). Doublet of Heracles.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Hercynian Forest, an extensive forest in ancient Germany.
parole.testo: From Latin Hercynia silva, Hercynius saltus (“the Hercynian forest”).

parole.significato: A fanciful notation, commonly attributed to historical maps, held to indicate either the belief that unknown dangers ex…
parole.testo: Evidence of the use of this term as a notation on actual historical maps is lacking. The only known appearance of an equivalent phrase in any language on a historical map is of Latin HC SVNT DRACONES (“here are dragons”), placed on the east coast of Asia, on the Hunt-Lenox Globe, which dates from c.

parole.significato: A phrase written on gravestones followed by the buried person's name.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin hīc jacet (whence also English hic jacet, a direct borrowing).

parole.significato: Passed on as an inheritance, by last will or intestate.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English hereditarie, from Latin hērēditārius, from hērēditās (“inheritance”), from hērēs (“heir”).

parole.significato: In Ancient Rome, inheritance or hereditary succession.
parole.testo: Latin [Term?]

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a master.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin erīlis, herīlis.

parole.significato: A rectangular pillar bearing a bust of Hermes, once used as a boundary marker and later as decoration.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Herma, a Latinization of Hermēs, from Ancient Greek Ἑρμῆς (Hermês).

parole.significato: A cell annexed to an abbey, for the use of a hermit.
parole.testo: Compare Latin hermitorium, eremitorium.

parole.significato: Protruded viscus, rupture.
parole.testo: From Latin hernia (“protruded viscus”).

parole.significato: A disorder in which a part of the body protrudes abnormally through a tear or opening in an adjacent part, especially o…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin hernia (“protruded viscus”). See also yarn and cord.

parole.significato: Heroic.
parole.testo: From Middle English heroicalle, from Latin hērōicus + -al. By surface analysis, hero + -ical.

parole.significato: A female hero.
parole.testo: From Latin hērōīna, from late Ancient Greek ἡρωΐνη (hērōḯnē) (2nd century), a feminine equivalent of ἥρως (hḗrōs, “hero, demigod”), equivalent to hero + -ine (suffix forming feminine nouns). * English from 1587. The sense of "female lead character" is from 1715.

parole.significato: A temple dedicated to a hero, often over his supposed tomb.
parole.testo: From Latin hērōon, from Ancient Greek ἡρῷον (hērōîon), from ἡρῷος (hērōîos, “of a hero”).

parole.significato: Seeking infamy.

parole.significato: Fame (or infamy) won through crime, destruction, or some other misdeed.
parole.testo: Herostratic is derived from Herostratus (learned borrowing from Latin Hērostratus, from Ancient Greek Ἡρόστρατος (Hēróstratos) + -ic (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives from nouns)).
