parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English infaunt, borrowed from Latin īnfantem, accusative masculine singular of īnfāns, nominal use of the adjective meaning 'not able to speak', from īn- (“not”) + fāns, present participle of for (“to speak”). The verb is from Anglo-Norman enfanter, from the same Latin source.

parole.significato: Pertaining to infants.
parole.testo: Mid-15th century, "pertaining to infants," from Latin infantilis (“pertaining to an infant”), equivalent to infant + -ile, from īnfāns. Sense of "infant-like" is from 1772.

parole.significato: To stuff or to swell.
parole.testo: From Latin infarcire, from in- (“in”) + farcire, fartum, farctum (“to stuff, cram”).

parole.significato: An area of dead tissue caused by a loss of blood supply; a localized necrosis.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin īnfarctus, tu-stem derivation of īnfarciō.

parole.significato: The process which causes an infarct.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin infarctiō, equivalent to infarct + -ion.

parole.significato: To inspire with unreasoning love, attachment or enthusiasm.
parole.testo: First attested in 1533; from Middle English infatuate and/or borrowed from Latin infatuātus, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and Etymology 2 for more.

parole.significato: Infatuated, foolishly attracted to someone.
parole.testo: First attested in 1477, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English infatuate (“foolish”, adjective), from Latin infatuātus, perfect passive participle of infatuō, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Unlucky, unfortunate, ill-omened; unpropitious; sinister.
parole.testo: From Latin īnfaustus, from in- (“not”) + faustus (“fortunate, lucky”).

parole.significato: Representing an action not yet completed.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin īnfectus, equivalent to in- (“not”) + factus, perfect passive participle of faciō (“to do, make”).

parole.significato: Lack of fecundity or fruitfulness
parole.testo: From in- + fecundity, from Latin infecunditas.

parole.significato: The condition of being infelicitous.
parole.testo: From in- + felicity, from Latin infelicitas.

parole.significato: To introduce (something) as a reasoned conclusion; to conclude by reasoning or deduction, as from premises or evidence.
parole.testo: From Latin inferō, from Latin in- (“in, at, on; into”) + Latin ferō (“bear, carry; suffer”) (cognate to Old English beran, whence English bear), from Proto-Italic *ferō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰéreti (“to bear, carry”), from the root *bʰer-. Literally “carry forward”, equivalent to “bear in”, as

parole.significato: The act or process of inferring by deduction or induction.
parole.testo: From Latin inferentia. Morphologically infer + -ence.

parole.significato: Sacrifices offered to the souls of deceased heroes or friends.
parole.testo: From Latin inferiae, from inferus (“underneath”).

parole.significato: Lower in rank, status, or quality.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin īnferior (“lower in situation or place”), comparative of īnferus (“below, underneath”).

parole.significato: lapis infernalis, lunar caustic
parole.testo: Calque of Latin lapis infernalis.

parole.significato: inferior
parole.testo: Latin inferus (“lower”).

parole.significato: Mischievous; harmful; dangerous.
parole.testo: From Latin infestus. See infest (adjective). By surface analysis, infest + -u- + -ous.

parole.significato: An act of fastening.
parole.testo: From Latin infībulō (“to close with a clasp or pin”).

parole.significato: The narrowest of species; one that that is not a genus to anything else.
parole.testo: From Latin infima (“lowest”) + species.

parole.significato: (of a subset) the greatest element of the containing set that is smaller than or equal to all elements of the subset. T…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin infimum (“lowest part”), from infimus (“lowest”).

parole.significato: Weak or ill, not in good health.
parole.testo: * The noun is from Middle English infirme, from Latin infirmus (“weak, feeble”). * The verb is from Latin īnfirmāre, from īnfirmus (“sick, weak, infirm”) + -ō.

parole.significato: disconfirmation
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin infirmātiō.

parole.significato: To set; to fasten or fix by piercing or thrusting in.
parole.testo: Back-formation from Middle English infixed (“stuck in”), from Latin infixus, past participle of infigō (“to fasten in”).

parole.significato: Relating to inflammation.
parole.testo: From inflamm(ation) + -o-.

parole.significato: To enlarge an object by pushing air (or a gas) into it; to raise or expand abnormally
parole.testo: From Latin īnflātus, perfect passive participle of īnflō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of inblow.

parole.significato: To cause to curve inwards.
parole.testo: From Latin īnflectō, from in- (“in”) + flectō (“to bend”).

parole.significato: To thrust upon; to impose.
parole.testo: From Latin īnflīctus, from in- + flīctus, past participle of īnflīgō (“to knock or strike against”), from in- + flīgō (“strike”) (whence in-).

parole.significato: The act of inflicting or something inflicted; an imposition.
parole.testo: From Latin īnflīctiōnem (“imposition”), from Latin īnflīctus, from in- + flīctus, past participle of īnflīgō (“to knock or strike against”), from in- + flīgō (“strike”) (whence in-). By surface analysis, inflict + -ion.

parole.significato: A group or cluster of flowers arranged on a stem that is composed of a main branch or a system of branches.
parole.testo: From Latin inflōrēscentia, from inflōrēscō (“to begin to flower”), inchoative verb of flōreō (“to flower”).

parole.significato: A stream which flows into another stream or a lake.
parole.testo: From Latin influent-, the present participle stem of īnfluere.

parole.significato: A flow inward or into something; a coming in.
parole.testo: From Latin īnflūxus (“inflow; influence”), from īnfluō (“flow or run into”).

parole.significato: An influx or infusion.
parole.testo: Latin influxio

parole.significato: Without regular form; shapeless; ugly; deformed.
parole.testo: From Latin īnfōrmis.

parole.significato: Not formidable; not to be feared or dreaded.
parole.testo: From Latin informidabilis. See in- (“not”) + formidable.

parole.significato: Absence of regular form; shapelessness.
parole.testo: From Latin informitas. See inform (adjective).

parole.significato: Misshapen; having no real form.
parole.testo: From Latin informis + -ous.

parole.significato: Unfortunate, unlucky.
parole.testo: The adjective is first attested circa 1390, in Middle English, the verb in 1570; inherited from Middle English infortunat(e), borrowed from Latin infortūnātus, see -ate (etymology 1, 2 and 3). Doublet of unfortunate.

parole.significato: misfortune
parole.testo: From Latin infortunium. See in- (“not”), and fortune.

parole.significato: To pour in; to infuse.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin infundere (“to pour in”). See infuse.

parole.significato: Discussed later.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin infra (“below”).

parole.significato: Beneath one's dignity.
parole.testo: Shortened form of Latin infrā dignitātem (literally “beneath [one's] dignity”).

parole.significato: below, beneath, inferior
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin īnfrā (“below”).

parole.significato: A person who loves or admires underdogs.
parole.testo: Pseudo-Latinism, derived from infra- + canine + -phile. An early twentieth-century coinage by American writer Christopher Morley.

parole.significato: To infringe, violate or disobey (a rule).
parole.testo: From Latin īnfringō, past participle īnfractus. See infringe.

parole.significato: Not broken or fractured; unharmed; whole.
parole.testo: From Latin īnfractus, from in- (“not”) + fractus (“broken”), past participle of fringō (“break”).

parole.significato: Cyclical with a periodicity significantly longer than 24 hours, that is, less frequent than circadian.
parole.testo: Uncertain. Possibly from the Latin infra (“below”) and diēs (“a day”) with the English suffix -an. Compare circadian, ultradian, and infra etc.

parole.significato: The characteristic of being infrequent.
parole.testo: From Latin infrequentia (“scantiness”), equivalent to in- + frequency or infrequent + -cy.

parole.significato: To make (something) cold; to chill.
parole.testo: From Latin infrigidatus, past participle of infrigidare (“to chill”). See in- and frigid.

parole.significato: The act of chilling or making cold; freezing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin infrigidatio + English -ion.

parole.significato: To break or violate a treaty, a law, a right, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin īnfringō, īnfringere (“to break off, break, bruise, weaken, destroy”), from in (“in”) + frangere (“to break”).

parole.significato: Not yielding fruit.
parole.testo: Latin infructuosus.

parole.significato: A fillet of white wool, worn on the head by ancient Roman priests.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin īnfula.

parole.significato: To dry by exposing to smoke; to expose to smoke.
parole.testo: First attested in 1847; borrowed from Latin infumātus, perfect passive participle of infumō (“to infumate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from in- (“in”) + fumō (“to smoke”), from fumus (“smoke”).

parole.significato: funnel-shaped
parole.testo: From infundibulum (“a funnel-shaped cavity or organ”), from Latin infundibulum (“funnel”), from īnfundō (“pour in or upon”).

parole.significato: having the shape of a funnel or cone.
parole.testo: From Latin īnfundibulum (“funnel”) + -form.

parole.significato: infundibulum
parole.testo: From Latin infundibulum. By surface analysis, infundibul- + -o-.

parole.significato: A funnel-shaped cavity or organ.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin infundibulum (“funnel”).

parole.significato: To darken; to make black or obscure.
parole.testo: The verb is first attested in 1650, the adjective in 1826; borrowed from Latin īnfuscātus, perfect passive participle of īnfuscō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from in- (“in”) + fuscō (“to make dark”), from fuscus (“dark”).

parole.significato: To cause to become an element of something; to insert or fill.
parole.testo: From Middle English infusen, from Latin infusus, from infundo.

parole.significato: Capable of being infused.
parole.testo: From Latin īnfūsibilis. By surface analysis, infuse + -ible.

parole.significato: To say (a statement, word etc.) two or more times; to reiterate, to emphasize through repetition.
parole.testo: Borrowed from the participle stem of Latin ingeminō (“repeat, reiterate”).

parole.significato: Innate, inborn.
parole.testo: First attested in 1528; borrowed from Latin ingenerātus, perfect passive participle of ingenerō, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The quality of being ingenious.
parole.testo: From Latin ingeniositas.

parole.significato: Innate, inborn.
parole.testo: From Latin ingenitus.

parole.significato: The ability to solve difficult problems in original, clever, and inventive ways; ingeniousness.
parole.testo: From Latin ingenuitās. Compare genius.

parole.significato: Naive and trusting.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ingenuus (“of noble character, frank”). Doublet of ingenu.

parole.significato: natural gift or talent; ability; wit; ingenuity
parole.testo: From Latin ingenium. See ingenious.

parole.significato: To take (a substance, e.g., food) into the body of an organism, especially through the mouth and into the gastrointesti…
parole.testo: From Latin ingerō (“to carry in”).

parole.significato: The process of ingesting, or consuming something orally, whether it be food, drink, medicine, or other substance. It is…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ingestionem, accusative of ingestio (“a pouring in”), action noun of the perfect passive participle of ingerere (“pour in”), from in- (“in, into”) + gero (“to carry, to bear”).

parole.significato: Ignominious; disgraceful.
parole.testo: From Latin inglōriōsus. By surface analysis, in- + glorious.

parole.significato: The crop, or craw, of birds.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ingluviēs.

parole.significato: Ungrateful.
parole.testo: First attested in 1393, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English ingrat, from Latin ingrātus (“disagreeable”), from in- (“not”) + grātus (“pleasing”). Cognate with French ingrat.

parole.significato: ungrateful; not grateful
parole.testo: From ingrate (“unfriendly”) + -ful, from Latin ingrātus (“disagreeable”), from in- (“not”) + grātus (“pleasing”).

parole.significato: Increasing in severity.
parole.testo: From Latin ingravēscent.

parole.significato: To impregnate (literal or figurative).
parole.testo: From Latin ingravidatus, past participle of ingravidare (“to impregnate”).

parole.significato: The act of entering.
parole.testo: From Latin ingressus, from the verb ingredior.

parole.significato: The groin or genitalia.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin inguen.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the groin.
parole.testo: From Latin inguinālis, from inguen.

parole.significato: inguen; groin
parole.testo: From inguinālis, from inguen + -ālis, from Latin inguen.

parole.significato: To swallow greedily or in large amounts.
parole.testo: From the participle stem of Latin ingurgitāre, from in- + gurges (“whirlpool”).

parole.significato: The act of swallowing greedily or immoderately; gulp.
parole.testo: Latin ingurgitatio: compare French ingurgitation.

parole.significato: tasteless; insipid
parole.testo: From Latin ingustabilis. See gustable.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the North Sea Germanic languages.
parole.testo: From Latin Ingaevōnēs + -ic. The first element is of Germanic origin and could mean "descendant of Yngvi."

parole.significato: Not apt or fit; inappropriate; unsuitable.
parole.testo: From Latin inhabilis: compare French inhabile. See in- and habile, and compare unable.

parole.significato: To draw air into the lungs, through the nose or mouth by action of the diaphragm.
parole.testo: From Latin inhalare (“to breathe on (breathe in)”), from in (“in, into, on”) + halare (“to breathe”).

parole.significato: To be inherent; to be an essential or intrinsic part of; to be fixed or permanently incorporated with something.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin inhaerēre (“stick in, stick to, inhere to”), from in (“in”) + haereō (“stick”); see hesitate. Compare adhere, cohere.

parole.significato: Naturally as part or consequence of something.
parole.testo: From Latin inhaerentem, accusative singular of inhaerēns, present active participle of inhaereō (“to be closely connected with; to adhere to”).

parole.significato: To open the jaws; to gape.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin inhiō, inhiāre, inhiāvī, inhiātum. First attested in 1542. By surface analysis, in- + hiate.

parole.significato: A gaping after; eager desire; craving.
parole.testo: From Latin inhiātiō, from inhiō, from in- + hiō (“gape”).

parole.significato: To hold in or hold back; to keep in check; restrain.
parole.testo: From Latin inhibitus, perfect passive participle of inhibeō (“to hold in, check, restrain”), from in (“in, at, on”), + habeō (“to have, hold, keep”).

parole.significato: Lack of hospitality.
parole.testo: From in- + hospitality, from Latin inhospitalitas.

parole.significato: To inhume; to bury.
parole.testo: First attested in 1612; borrowed from Latin inhumātus, perfect passive participle of inhumō (“to put in the earth, plant; (Ecclesiastical Latin) to inhume”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from in- (“in”) + humō (“to cover with earth”). Doublet of inhume.

parole.significato: To bury in a grave.
parole.testo: Latin in and humō (“to bury”).

parole.significato: Inimical.
parole.testo: From Latin inimīcus. Doublet of enemy.

parole.significato: Synonym of inimical (“harmful, hostile”).
parole.testo: From in- + amicable, after Latin inimīcus (“enemy”) from in- + amīcus, inimical. Piecewise doublet of inamiable, inamicable, unamiable, and unamicable.

parole.significato: Harmful in effect.
parole.testo: From Late Latin inimīcālis (“hostile”), from inimīcus (“enemy”) (from in- (“not”) + amīcus (“friend”)) + -ālis.

parole.significato: Inimical; unfriendly, hostile.
parole.testo: From Latin inimicitia (“enmity”), from inimicus (“enemy”).

parole.significato: Synonym of iniquitous.
parole.testo: From Latin inīquus, from in- (“not”) + aequus. See equal.

parole.significato: To begin; to start.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin initiātus, perfect passive participle of initiō (“to begin, originate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from initium (“a beginning”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix), from initus (“an entrance, coming in, approach”) + -ium, from ineō + -tus, from in- + eō (“to go”). Cognate with Fren

parole.significato: Unpracticed, untried, new.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin initiātus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more.

parole.significato: One who initiates.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin initiātor. By surface analysis, initiate + or.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to initiation.
parole.testo: From Latin initiāt-, past participial stem of initiō, + -ory. By surface analysis, initiate + -ory.

parole.significato: A female initiator.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin initiātrīx. By surface analysis, initiator + -trix.

parole.significato: Synonym of prozeugma
parole.testo: From Latin iniunctum, neuter singular of iniunctus, perfect passive participle of iniungō (“to join together, enjoin”).

parole.significato: To push or pump (something, especially fluids) into a cavity or passage.
parole.testo: From Latin iniectus, injectus, participle of iniciō, injiciō (“to throw in”), from in- + iaciō (“I throw”).

parole.significato: The quality of being unpleasant; disagreeableness.
parole.testo: From Latin injucunditas. See in-[Term?] + not, and jocund.

parole.significato: injury; invasion of another's rights
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin iniuria. Doublet of injury.

parole.significato: A legal wrong that causes no actual damage or injury to anyone.
parole.testo: From Latin injūria (“injury”) + sine (“without”) + damnō, ablative singular of damnum (“financial or property loss”). Literally meaning "injury without financial loss".

parole.significato: To convert into a stony substance; to petrify.
parole.testo: From in- (“in”) + Latin lapis, lapidis (“stone”).

parole.significato: The fact of God's being invested in a book (the Qur'an), as opposed to in flesh as held by Christianity.
parole.testo: Coined by Harry A Wolfson (1887–1974) on the model of incarnation, from in- + inflected stem of Latin liber (“book”) + -ation.

parole.significato: Inborn; existing or having existed since birth.
parole.testo: The adjective is first attested in the 1420s, the verb in 1602; from Middle English innat(e) (“innate, inborn”), borrowed from Latin innātus (“inborn, innate”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), perfect active participle of innāscor (“to be born in, grow up in”), from in- (“in, at on”) + nāscor

parole.significato: Incapable of being navigated; impassable by ships etc.
parole.testo: From Latin innāvigābilis. By surface analysis, in- + navigable.

parole.significato: A burden; a dead weight.
parole.testo: From Latin innītor (“to lean upon”) + -ency.

parole.significato: A leaning or resting upon something; an instance of a thing being supported by another; innitency.
parole.testo: Formed as innix-, the perfect active participial stem of the Latin innītor (“to lean or rest upon”, “to be supported by”) + the English -ion, forming nouns of action.

parole.significato: Synonym of innocence:
parole.testo: From Middle English innocencie, from Latin innocentia. Doublet of innocence.

parole.significato: Harmless; producing no ill effect.
parole.testo: From Latin innocuus (“harmless”) (therefore, no gemination in + nocuous).

parole.significato: (with anathema or interdict) To bind up, as in a knot, with the punishment of anathema or interdict; to anathemize or i…
parole.testo: First attested in 1630; adapted from Medieval Latin vinculis anathematis innodare (“to bind (someone) with/in the bounds of anathema”), borrowed from Latin innōdātus, perfect passive participle of innōdō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from in- (“in”) + nodus (“knot”).

parole.significato: Not to be named.
parole.testo: From Middle English innominable, from Latin innominabilis, from in- (“not”) + nominare (“to name”). Compare French innominable.

parole.significato: Having no name, nameless, unnamed; anonymous.
parole.testo: From Latin innōminātus, from in- (“not”) + nōminātus (“named”).

parole.significato: To alter, to change into something new; to revolutionize.
parole.testo: First attested in 1548; borrowed from Latin innovātus, perfect passive participle of innovō (“to renew”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A woman who innovates; a female innovator.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin innovātrīx. By surface analysis, innovate + -trix.

parole.significato: Having no harmful effect; harmless, innocuous.
parole.testo: From Latin innoxius.

parole.significato: Cloudless.
parole.testo: From Latin innubilus. By surface analysis, in- + nubilous.

parole.significato: A derogatory hint or reference to, or (often sexual) insinuation about, a person or thing.
parole.testo: From the Latin innuendō (“by nodding”), ablative singular form of innuendum (“a nodding”), gerund of innuō (“to give a nod”).

parole.significato: Conveying a hint or innuendo.
parole.testo: From Latin innuens, present participle.

parole.significato: The state of being innumerable.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin innumerābilitās.

parole.significato: Not capable of being counted, enumerated, or numbered.
parole.testo: From in- + numerable; from Middle English innumerable, from Latin innumerābilis, from in- + numerābilis.

parole.significato: Not capable of being counted or numerated; indefinitely numerous.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin innumerus.

parole.significato: unobservable
parole.testo: From Latin inobservabilis. Compare French inobservable. See in- (“not”) + observable.

parole.significato: Not observant
parole.testo: Latin inobservans.

parole.significato: To introduce an antigenic substance or vaccine into something (e.g. the body) or someone, such as to produce immunity t…
parole.testo: First attested in c. 1440; inherited from Middle English inoculaten (“to graft”), from Latin inoculātus, perfect passive participle of inoculō (“to ingraft an eye or bud of one plant into (another), implant”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from in- (“in”) + oculus (“an eye”) + -ō (verb-forming su

parole.significato: The introduction of an antigenic substance or vaccine into the body to produce immunity to a specific disease.
parole.testo: From Latin inoculātio. Equivalent to inoculate + -ion.

parole.significato: One who inoculates.
parole.testo: Latin: compare French inoculateur.

parole.significato: The active material used in an inoculation; an inoculant (i.e., a material or a dose thereof).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin inoculum.

parole.significato: Indifferent to obligation or duty.
parole.testo: From Latin inofficiōsus. Compare French inofficieux. See in- (“not”) + officious.

parole.significato: agency; influence; production of effects
parole.testo: From Latin inoperari (“to effect”), from in- (“in”) + operari (“to operate”).

parole.significato: Not to be expected; inconceivable.
parole.testo: From Latin inopinabilis. See inopinate.

parole.significato: Not expected, thought of, or looked for.
parole.testo: From Latin inopīnātus. See in- (“not”), and opine.

parole.significato: Unsuitable for some particular purpose.
parole.testo: From Latin inopportūnus. By surface analysis, in- + opportune.

parole.significato: Lack of opportunity or chances to do something
parole.testo: From in- + opportunity, from Latin inopportunitas.

parole.significato: Excessive; unreasonable or inappropriate in magnitude.
parole.testo: From Middle English inordinat, from Latin inōrdinātus (“not arranged, disordered, irregular”), from in- + ordinatus, past participle of ōrdināre (“to arrange, order”).

parole.significato: Deviation or irregularity from custom, rule, order, or right
parole.testo: Latin inordinatio.

parole.significato: To homogenize; to make continuous.
parole.testo: First attested in 1672; from in- + osculate or its Latin etymon ōsculātus, perfect active participle of Latin osculor (“to kiss”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)) from ōsculum (“a kiss”). The adjective is a back-formation from inosculation, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: To disquiet.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin inquietare: compare French inquiéter. See quiet.

parole.significato: A condition of being restless, uneasy or nervous.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin inquiētūdō.

parole.significato: An animal that lives commensally in the nest, burrow, gall, or dwelling place of an animal of another species.
parole.testo: From Latin inquilīnus (“tenant, lodger”). Doublet of inquilino.

parole.significato: To pollute or make dirty.
parole.testo: From Latin inquināre (“polluting”).

parole.significato: defilement;pollution; stain or impurity
parole.testo: Latin inquinatio.

parole.significato: To ask (about something).
parole.testo: From Latin inquīrō (“to seek for”), composed of in- (“in, at, on; into”) + quaerō (“to seek, look for”), of uncertain origin, but possibly from Proto-Italic *kʷaizeō, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeh₂- (“to acquire”). Displaced Middle English enqueren (from Old French enquerre, of the same source) and

parole.significato: An authority to inquire.
parole.testo: From Latin inquirendo.

parole.significato: Making enquiry; questioning.
parole.testo: From Latin inquirens.

parole.significato: A female inquisitor.
parole.testo: From Latin inquīsītrīx or inquisitor + -trix.

parole.significato: Not salutary or wholesome; bad for the health.
parole.testo: From Latin insaluteris. Compare French insalutaire. See in- (“not”) + salutary.

parole.significato: Not capable of being healed, incurable, irremediable.
parole.testo: From Latin īnsānābilis. Compare Old French insanable. See in- (“not”) + sanable.

parole.significato: Exhibiting unsoundness or disorder of mind; not sane; utterly mad.
parole.testo: From Latin īnsānus (“unsound in mind; mad, insane”), from in- + sānus (“sound, sane”), equivalent to in- + sane.

parole.significato: The state of being insane; madness.
parole.testo: A three-part word (root 'sane', prefix 'in-' meaning 'not', suffix '-ity', meaning 'the state of'). Derived from Latin precursory equivalents. Two possible candidates for construction order: * insane + -ity: īnsānus (“unhealthy; insane”) + -itās *: Latin īnsānus (“unsound in mind; mad, insane”), fro

parole.significato: The condition of being insatiable
parole.testo: From Latin insatiabilitas.

parole.significato: That is not satiated; insatiable.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English insaciate, insaciat, insacyate (“insatiable”), from Latin insatiātus, from in- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + satiātus (“satisfied; having been satisfied”) (perfect passive participle of satiō (“to satisfy”), from satis (“enough; filled; plenty”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-Europe

parole.significato: insatiableness
parole.testo: From Latin insatietas. Compare French insatieté, Portuguese insaciedade. See satiety.

parole.significato: Not capable of being saturated.
parole.testo: From Latin īnsaturābilis. Compare French insaturable, Portuguese insaturável. See in- (“not”) + saturable.

parole.significato: To write or cut (words) onto (something, especially a hard surface, or a book to be given to another person); to engrav…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin īnscrībō, from in- (“upon”) and scrībō (“to write”).

parole.significato: The act of inscribing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin īnscrīptiō.

parole.significato: To engrave; to carve; to sculpt.
parole.testo: From Latin insculpere. Compare French insculper. See in- and sculptor.

parole.significato: indivisible (literal or figurative)
parole.testo: From Latin insecabilis, from in- (“not”) + secabilis (“that may be cut”). Compare French insecable.

parole.significato: pursuit; harassment; persecution
parole.testo: From Latin insectatio. See insectator.

parole.significato: of, or pertaining to insects
parole.testo: From Latin īnsectum (“insect”) + -ile, from the neuter of Latin -ilis (adjective-forming suffix), after reptile.

parole.significato: Feeding on insects.
parole.testo: From Latin insectum (“insect”) and -vorus, from vorō (“to eat”), equivalent to insectivore + -ous or insect + -i- + -vorous.

parole.significato: Able to be inseminated or impregnated.
parole.testo: From Latin insēminābilis.

parole.significato: To sow (to disperse or plant seeds).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin inseminātus, the perfect passive participle of insemināre (“to sow”). By surface analysis, in- + seminate.

parole.significato: Having no sensation or consciousness; unconscious; inanimate.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin īnsēnsātus. By surface analysis, in- + sensate.

parole.significato: To render insensate; to deprive of sensation or consciousness.
parole.testo: From Latin īnsēnsātus, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The condition of being inseparable
parole.testo: From Latin inseparabilitas.

parole.significato: To put in between or into.
parole.testo: From Latin insertus, past participle of inserō, from in- + serō (“join, bind together, connect, entwine, interweave”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“to bind, put together, to line up”). Compare exsert.

parole.significato: To be useful for a purpose, or to somsone
parole.testo: From Latin inservire, from in- (“in”) + servire (“to serve”).

parole.significato: Conducive; instrumental.
parole.testo: From Latin inserviens, present participle of inservire.

parole.significato: The act of sitting, as in a tub or bath.
parole.testo: From Latin insessio, from insidere, insessum (“to sit in”). See insidious.

parole.significato: pertaining to a member of the Order Insessores, or perching birds; perching or designed for perching
parole.testo: From modern Latin Insessores ‘perchers’, from Latin insidere (“sit upon”), from in- + sedere (“sit”).

parole.significato: To lie in ambush for.
parole.testo: From Latin insidiatus, past participle of insidiare (“to lie in ambush”), from insidiae. See insidious.

parole.significato: Someone who lies in ambush, or plots
parole.testo: From Latin īnsidiātor.

parole.significato: An insignia.
parole.testo: From Latin.

parole.significato: A patch or other object that indicates a person's official or military rank, or membership in a group or organization.
parole.testo: From Latin īnsīgnia, nominative plural of īnsīgne (“emblem, token, symbol”). Doublet of ensign.

parole.significato: Not expressing meaning
parole.testo: From Latin insignificativus. See in- (“not”) + significative.

parole.significato: To accuse.
parole.testo: From Latin insimulatus, past participle of insimulare (“to accuse”).

parole.significato: Expressing words or behaviors that one does not genuinely feel or endorse; not genuine; artificial; factitious.
parole.testo: From Latin insincerus.

parole.significato: Insinuating; insinuative.
parole.testo: From Latin insinuans, present participle: compare French insinuant.

parole.significato: To hint; to suggest tacitly (usually something bad) while avoiding a direct statement.
parole.testo: First attested in 1529; Borrowed from Latin īnsinuātus, perfect passive participle of īnsinuō (“to push in, creep in, steal in”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from in- (“in”) + sinus (“a winding, bend, bay, fold, bosom”) -ō (verb-forming suffix). Regular parti

parole.significato: One who insinuates.
parole.testo: From Latin īnsinuātor.

parole.significato: stupidity; folly
parole.testo: From Latin insipientia: compare Old French insipience.Equivalent to in- + sapience.

parole.significato: Standing or resting on something.
parole.testo: From Latin insistens, participle of insisto.

parole.significato: Not sociable or companionable.
parole.testo: From Latin īnsociābilis.

parole.significato: To dry in, or expose to, the sun's rays; to ripen or prepare by such exposure.
parole.testo: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin insōlātus, perfect passive participle of insōlō (“to expose to the sun”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from in- (“in”) + sōl (“the sun”) + -ō.

parole.significato: The quality of being insolent.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin īnsolentia.

parole.significato: The quality of being insoluble
parole.testo: From Latin insolūbilitās or from insoluble + -ity.

parole.significato: A sleeping disorder that is known for its symptoms of unrest and the inability to sleep.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin īnsomnia, from Latin in- (“without”) + somnus (“sleep”, noun) + -ia, equivalent to in- + somn- + -ia.

parole.significato: restless; sleepless
parole.testo: From Latin insomniosus, from insomnia (“insomnia”). See English insomnia and -ous.

parole.significato: To examine critically or carefully; especially, to search out problems or determine condition; to scrutinize.
parole.testo: From Latin inspectum, past participle of inspicere (“to look into”), from in (“in”) + specere (“to look at”), equivalent to in- + -spect.

parole.significato: Engaged in inspection; involving inspection.
parole.testo: Latin inspectivus.

parole.significato: A person employed to inspect something.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin īnspector, from īnspiciō, equivalent to inspect + -or.

parole.significato: To sprinkle; to scatter.
parole.testo: From Latin inspersus, past participle of inspergere (“to sprinkle upon”); prefix in- (“in, on”) + spargere (“to sprinkle”).

parole.significato: The act of sprinkling.
parole.testo: Latin inspersio.

parole.significato: A confirmation and reaffirmation of one or several royal grants made in the past, generally at the request of a putativ…
parole.testo: Latin, "we have inspected". It was the first word of ancient English charters confirming a grant made by a former king.

parole.significato: A female inspirator.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin inspīrātrīx. By surface analysis, inspirator + -trix.

parole.significato: To urge, press (someone); to insist on, demand (something).
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin īnstāre; its precise evolution is uncertain. OED hints at (unattested) Middle French *instanter.

parole.significato: Any one of the several stages of postembryonic development which an arthropod undergoes, between molts, before it reach…
parole.testo: From Latin instar (“form, likeness”), which is of obscure origin.

parole.significato: To renew or renovate.
parole.testo: First attested in 1583; borrowed from Latin īnstaurātus, perfect passive participle of īnstaurō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Cognate with French instaurer.

parole.significato: A restoration after decay or dilapidation; a renewal; a repair.
parole.testo: From Latin instauratio: compare French instauration.

parole.significato: One who renews or restores to a former condition.
parole.testo: Latin: compare French instaurateur.

parole.significato: To bring about by urging or encouraging.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin īnstīgātus, perfect passive participle of īnstīgō (“to instigate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A person who intentionally instigates, incites, or starts something, especially one that creates trouble.
parole.testo: From Latin īnstīgātor (“stimulator”), from īnstīgāre (present infinitive of īnstīgō (“to incite, set on, stimulate, rouse or urge”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *(s)teyg- (“to be sharp, to stab; to puncture; to goad”)) + -or (from -ō (suffix forming masculine agent nouns), from Proto-Indo-Euro

parole.significato: To cause a quality to become part of someone's nature.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin instillō.

parole.significato: To stimulate; to excite.
parole.testo: From Latin instimulatus, past participle instimulare (“to stimulate”). See in- and stimulate.

parole.significato: A natural or inherent impulse or behaviour.
parole.testo: From Latin īnstīnctus, past participle of īnstinguō (“to incite, to instigate”), from in (“in, on”) + stinguō (“to prick”).

parole.significato: Relating to an agent or factor.
parole.testo: From Latin institor (“agent, broker”).

parole.significato: To begin or initiate (something); to found.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Latin īnstitūtus, past participle of īnstituō (“to set up, place upon, purpose, begin, institute”), from in (“in, on”) + statuō (“set up, establish”).

parole.significato: One who institutes something.
parole.testo: From Latin īnstitūtor. Compare French instituteur. By surface analysis, institute + -or.

parole.significato: A female institutor.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin institūtrīx. By surface analysis, institutor + -trix.

parole.significato: To teach by giving instructions.
parole.testo: From Latin īnstrūctus, perfect passive participle of īnstruō (“I instruct; I arrange, furnish, or provide”).

parole.significato: One who instructs; a teacher.
parole.testo: From Latin instructor, equivalent to instruct + -or.

parole.significato: A female instructor.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin īnstrūctrīx. By surface analysis, instruct + -trix.

parole.significato: Lack of suavity; unpleasantness.
parole.testo: From Latin insuavitas. Compare French insuavité. See in- (“not”) + suavity.

parole.significato: The act of soaking or moistening; maceration; solution in the juice of herbs.
parole.testo: From Latin insucare, insucatum (“to soak in”), from in- + succus, sucus (“sap”).

parole.significato: Fluid collection within an arterial wall.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin insūdātum, from the perfect passive participle of insūdō (“to sweat in”), see -ate (noun-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The state or quality of being unaccustomed; lack of habit.
parole.testo: From Latin insuetūdō, from in- (“not”) + suēscō (“to be accustomed”) + -tūdō.

parole.significato: To breathe or blow into or on.
parole.testo: First attested in 1670; borrowed from Latin īnsufflātus, perfect passive participle of īnsufflō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)) from in- + sufflō (“to blow on”). Cognate with French insuffler.

parole.significato: A block of buildings in a Roman town.
parole.testo: From Latin īnsula (“island”). Doublet of isle.

parole.significato: Of or being, pertaining to, situated on, or resembling an island or islands.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin īnsulāris (“of or belonging to an island”), from īnsula (“an island”), of uncertain origin.

parole.significato: A polypeptide hormone that regulates carbohydrate metabolism (in various animals including humans).
parole.testo: From Latin īnsula (“island”) (named for the islets of Langerhans, where insulin is produced) + -in.

parole.significato: inflammation of the islands of Langerhans
parole.testo: From Latin insula (“island”) + -itis.

parole.significato: Abounding in islands.
parole.testo: Latin insula (“island”) + suffix -ous.

parole.significato: insipid, dull, stupid or tasteless
parole.testo: From Latin īnsulsus; prefix in- not + salsus (“salted”), from salīre (“to salt”).

parole.significato: lack of taste, insipidity
parole.testo: Latin insulsitas.

parole.significato: The act of insulting; abusive or insolent treatment; insult.
parole.testo: Latin insultatio, from insulto: compare Old French insultation.

parole.significato: To take in; to absorb.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin insumere; prefix in- (“in”) + sumere (“to take”).

parole.significato: Impossible to achieve or overcome or be negotiated.
parole.testo: From Latin insuperabilis.

parole.significato: Rebellious, opposing authority.
parole.testo: From Latin īnsurgentem, accusative singular of īnsurgēns, present active participle of īnsurgō (“to rise up against, revolt”), from in (“against”) + surgō (“to rise”), itself from sub (“up from below”) + regō (“to guide, direct, rule, govern, administer”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵ- (“to move

parole.significato: The act of whispering into something.
parole.testo: From Latin insūsurrātiō, insūsurrātiōnem (whence -ation), from īnsusurrātus, past participle of īnsusurrō (“to whisper into”), from susurrus (“whisper, murmur”).

parole.significato: uncontaminated
parole.testo: From Latin intaminatus. See contaminate.

parole.significato: A number that is not a fraction; an element of the infinite and numerable set {..., -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, ...}.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin integer (“whole”), from Proto-Italic *n̥tagros (“untouched”). Doublet of entier and entire. Related to English tact, thack, and thwack.

parole.significato: To include as a constituent part or functionality.
parole.testo: First attested in the 1450's as an adjective, first attested in 1638 as a verb; from Middle English integrat(e) (“intact, whole”), borrowed from Latin integrātus, perfect passive participle of integrō (“to make whole, renew, repair, begin again”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-f

parole.significato: A shell or other outer protective layer.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin integumentum (“a covering”).

parole.significato: The mental activity or process of grasping with the intellect; apprehension by the mind; understanding.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin intellectiō, intellectiōnem.

parole.significato: Pure, undefiled, chaste.
parole.testo: First attested in 1492, in Middle English; borrowed from Latin intemerātus, from in- (“not”) + temerātus, perfect passive participle of temerō (“to violate”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from temerē (“by chance, casually, rashly”).

parole.significato: intemperate
parole.testo: From Latin intemperāns, -antis. See in- (“not”) + temperant.

parole.significato: untimely, happening at an inappropriate moment
parole.testo: From Latin intempestīvus, from in- + tempestīvus (“seasonable”).

parole.significato: Unseasonability; untimeliness.
parole.testo: From the Latin intempestīvitās; cognate with the French intempestivité.

parole.significato: Intensity or the act of becoming intense.
parole.testo: From Latin intēnsiō (“straining, effort; intensifying”), from intēnsus (“stretched”), perfect passive participle of intendō (“strain or stretch toward”).

parole.significato: Among other things.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin inter alia.

parole.significato: Among other people.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin inter aliōs.

parole.significato: between ourselves
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin inter nos (“between us”). Cognate with Italian inter nos, French entre nous and Spanish entre nos.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or characteristic of a proceeding where multiple parties to a dispute are present.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin inter partes (“between parties/sides”).

parole.significato: Between alcoholic drinks; during a drinking session.
parole.testo: From Latin inter pōcula (“among drinking cups”).

parole.significato: A position which is in between two (or more) of the kind indicated by the root.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin inter- (“between, amid”), a form of prepositional inter (“between”).

parole.significato: Situated between rivers.
parole.testo: From inter- + Latin amnis (“river”). Compare Latin interamnus.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to an interbellum (period of time between two wars), especially the period between the two World Wars…
parole.testo: From inter- + Latin bellicus (“of or pertaining to war; military”). Equivalent to inter- + bellic.

parole.significato: The time period between wars.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin inter bellum (literally “between war”).

parole.significato: Describing a time period inserted between others; leap, (as in leap day, leap month, or leap year)
parole.testo: From Latin intercalārius, from intercalāris, from intercalō, from inter (“among”) + calō (“call out, proclaim”).

parole.significato: To insert an extra leap day into a calendar in order to maintain synchrony with natural phenomena.
parole.testo: The verb is first attested in 1614, the noun in 1964; borrowed from Latin intercalātus, perfect passive participle of intercalō (“to proclaim that a day, an event, etc. has been intercalated; to insert”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-forming suffix)), from inter- (“between, among”)

parole.significato: A period inserted into a calendar as in a leap year.
parole.testo: From Latin intercalō, from inter (“among”) + calō (“call out, proclaim”).

parole.significato: To stop, deflect or divert (something in progress or motion).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin interceptum, past participle of intercipiō.

parole.significato: An act of intercepting something, the state of being intercepted, or a thing that is intercepted.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin interceptiō; compare French interception.

parole.significato: One who intercedes, particularly
parole.testo: Late 15th century, from Latin intercessor, from Latin intercēdō, from inter (“between”) + cēdō (“to go”) (English cede), literally “go-between”.

parole.significato: Coming or falling between; happening accidentally.
parole.testo: From Latin intercidens, intercedentis, present participle of intercidere (“to fall between”); inter (“between”) + cadere (“to fall”).

parole.significato: Intercepting; stopping.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin intercipiēns, present participle of intercipiō. See intercept.

parole.significato: To cut off or shut off (something) from a course or place, by something intervening; to intercept, to interrupt.
parole.testo: From Latin interclūdō; inter (“between”) + claudō (“to shut”). See close.

parole.significato: A space between columns.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin intercolumnium. By surface analysis, inter- + column.

parole.significato: To intervene; to come or occur in the meantime.
parole.testo: From Latin intercurrere. See intercourse.

parole.significato: Running between or among, in a physical sense; interlayered.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin intercurrens, equivalent to inter- + current.

parole.significato: A prohibition: a legal order issued by a praetor (or, in the provinces, a proconsul) at the request of a claimant and a…
parole.testo: From Latin interdictum.

parole.significato: The act of murder or killing.
parole.testo: From Latin interfectiō.

parole.significato: flowing into one another.
parole.testo: From Latin interfluens, present participle, and interfluus. See inter-, and fluent.

parole.significato: Between leaves or leaf-like structures.
parole.testo: From inter- + Latin folium (“leaf”).

parole.significato: Shining between, through, or among.
parole.testo: From Latin interfulgentem.

parole.significato: A constructed language devised by Lancelot Hogben (1895–1975).
parole.testo: From Latin inter- + Ancient Greek γλῶσσα (glôssa, “language”).

parole.significato: To pass or change from one state to another by steps or stages.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin intergredior.

parole.significato: transitional
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin interim (“meanwhile”).

parole.significato: Within any limits, enclosure, or substance; inside; internal; inner.
parole.testo: From Latin interior (“inner, interior”).

parole.significato: Situated between; lying among.
parole.testo: From Latin inter- (“between”) + jacēre (“to lie down”).

parole.significato: To insert something between other things.
parole.testo: From Latin interiectus, perfect passive participle of intericiō (“place between”).

parole.significato: A place where two or more things join or cross.
parole.testo: From Latin interjunctus, past participle of interjungere (“to join together”). See inter- and join, and compare interjoin.

parole.significato: The thinning of a forest to let in light.
parole.testo: Latin interlucatio.

parole.significato: shining between
parole.testo: From Latin interlucens.

parole.significato: A flowing between; intervening water.
parole.testo: From Latin interluens, present participle of interluere (“to flow between”), from inter + luere.

parole.significato: interlunation
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin interlunium.

parole.significato: The middle pair of tail feathers, or middle rectrices.
parole.testo: Latin intermedius intermedial.

parole.significato: To menace; to threaten.
parole.testo: From Latin intermināt-, passive perfect participial stem of interminor (“to threaten, menace”).

parole.significato: A menace or threat.
parole.testo: Latin interminatio.

parole.significato: A break, especially between two performances or sessions, such as at a concert, play, seminar, or religious assembly.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin intermissiō, from intermittō (“interrupt, omit”) + -tiō.

parole.significato: To interrupt, to stop or cease temporarily or periodically; to suspend.
parole.testo: From Latin intermittere, from inter- + mittere.

parole.significato: A space between worlds.
parole.testo: From Latin intermundium, singular of intermundia.

parole.significato: Between walls; enclosed by walls.
parole.testo: From Latin intermūrālis. By surface analysis, inter- + mural.

parole.significato: Between pregnancies or births.
parole.testo: From inter- + Latin nātālis (“relating to birth”).

parole.significato: Between the buttocks; intergluteal.
parole.testo: From inter- + Latin natis (“rump”) + -al.

parole.significato: Mutually destructive; most often applied to warfare.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin internecīnus (“deadly”), from internecium (“a massacre, bloodbath; an eradication”) + -īnus. In Latin, the sememe 'between' was here not expressed by the prefix, it instead either had a somewhat emphatic meaning or meant "down, under", comparable to its use in other Latin terms r

parole.significato: destruction, massacre
parole.testo: From Latin interneciō.

parole.significato: internecine
parole.testo: From Latin internecīvus.

parole.significato: intimate connection
parole.testo: From Latin internectere (“to bind together”), from inter (“between”) + nectere (“to fasten”).

parole.significato: To interrupt, break in upon, or intercede with.
parole.testo: Latin interpello, from inter (“between”) + pellare, akin to pellere (“to drive”), compare French interpeller.

parole.significato: interrupting.
parole.testo: From Latin interpellans. See interpel.

parole.significato: To interrupt (someone) so as to inform or question (that person about something).
parole.testo: First attested in 1599; borrowed from Latin interpellātus, perfect passive participle of interpellō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Cognate with French interpeller.

parole.significato: To introduce (something) between other things; especially to insert (possibly spurious) words into a text.
parole.testo: From Latin interpolātus, perfect passive participle of interpolō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Compare French interpoler.

parole.significato: To interpose; to insert or place between.
parole.testo: From Latin interponere; inter (“between”) + ponere (“to place”). See position.

parole.significato: An intermediate depot or station between one commercial city or country and another.
parole.testo: From Latin interpositus, past participle of interponere. See interposition.

parole.significato: interpretation
parole.testo: From Latin interpretamentum.

parole.significato: The punctuation mark ⟨·⟩.
parole.testo: From Latin interpunctus, from inter- (“between, mid-”) + punctus (“point”).

parole.significato: punctuation (insertion of points between words or sentences)
parole.testo: From Latin interpunctio, from interpungere, interpunctum (“to interpoint”). See inter- and point.

parole.significato: A period of time between the end of one monarch's reign and the accession of their successor.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin interrēgnum, from inter- (prefix meaning ‘between’) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁entér (“between”)) + rēgnum (“reign; royal power”) (nominalized from the neuter of *rēgnus, from rēx (“king; ruler”, oblique stem rēg-) + -nus (suffix forming adjectives), ultimat

parole.significato: An official in Ancient Rome who acted as single head of state during the interregnum between two consulates.
parole.testo: From Latin inter- (“between”) + rex (“king”).

parole.significato: To question or quiz, especially in a thorough or aggressive manner.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin interrogātus, the perfect passive participle of Latin interrogō (“to inquire, interrogate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: One who interrogates; a person who asks questions, especially one who is adversarial.
parole.testo: From Latin interrogātor. By surface analysis, interrogate + -or.

parole.significato: A female interrogator.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin interrogātrīx. By surface analysis, interrogator + -trix.

parole.significato: To disturb or halt (an ongoing process or action, or the person performing it) by interfering suddenly, especially by s…
parole.testo: From Middle English interrupten, derived from Latin interruptus, past participle of interrumpere (“to break apart/off, interrupt”), from inter (“between”) + rumpere (“to break”).

parole.significato: To write or draw between.
parole.testo: From Latin interscribere; inter (“between”) + scribere (“to write”). By surface analysis, inter + scribe.

parole.significato: Crossing, intersecting; (figuratively) clashing, conflicting.
parole.testo: From Latin intersecans, present participle of intersecare. See intersect.

parole.significato: To cut into or between; to cut or cross mutually; to divide into parts.
parole.testo: From Latin intersecare (“to cut between, cut off”), from inter (“between”) + secare (“to cut”).

parole.significato: To put in between other things; to insert.
parole.testo: From Latin intersertus, past participle of interserere (“to intersert”), from inter (“between”) + serere (“to join, weave”).

parole.significato: sounding between
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin intersonāns.

parole.significato: A space or interval between two things; an interstice
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin interspatium. By surface analysis, inter- + space.

parole.significato: To mix two things irregularly, placing things of one kind among things of other.
parole.testo: From Latin interspergō, interspersus.

parole.significato: spiritual inspiration at separate times, or at intervals
parole.testo: From Latin interspiratio. See inter- and spirit.

parole.significato: a planetary-mass object which has either been ejected from its system or was never gravitationally bound to any star or…
parole.testo: Constructed from Latin: inter- + stellar + planet. The latter derives from Middle English planete, from Old English planēta (“planet, chasuble”), from Latin planeta, planetes, from Ancient Greek πλανήτης (planḗtēs) variant of πλάνης (plánēs, “wanderer, planet”), from πλανάω (planáō, “wander about, s

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or situated in an interstice.
parole.testo: From Latin interstitiālis. By surface analysis, interstitium + -al.

parole.significato: An interstice or interstitium; an interstitial space.
parole.testo: From Latin interstitiō, or by confusion with interstitium.

parole.significato: An interstitial space within a tissue or organ.
parole.testo: From Latin interstitium, from inter (“between”) + sistō (“to stand, place”).

parole.significato: To intertwine; to weave or bind together.
parole.testo: From Latin intertexere, from inter (“between”) + texere (“to weave”).

parole.significato: Chafing or dermatitis occurring between two folds of skin.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin intertrīgō.

parole.significato: An interval.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin intervallum.

parole.significato: To become involved in a situation, so as to alter or prevent an action.
parole.testo: Back-formation from intervention, and/or from Latin interveniō (“come between”, verb).

parole.significato: Being only in between other more important things; secondary, incidental.
parole.testo: From the present participle stem of Latin intervenīre.

parole.significato: One who intervenes; a mediator, especially one designated by a church to reconcile parties and unite them in the choice…
parole.testo: From Latin interventor. Compare French interventeur.

parole.significato: To turn to another course or use.
parole.testo: From Latin interverto.

parole.significato: The state of being intervolved or coiled up; a convolution
parole.testo: From Latin inter (“between”), from volvere (“to roll”).

parole.significato: To involve one with another.
parole.testo: From Latin inter (“between”), from volvere (“to roll”).

parole.significato: Without a valid will indicating whom to leave one's estate to after death.
parole.testo: From Latin intestātus, from in- (“not”) + testātus (“testate”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Relating to the intestines.
parole.testo: From Latin intestīnālis. By surface analysis, intestine + -al.

parole.significato: The alimentary canal of an animal through which food passes after having passed all stomachs.
parole.testo: From Latin intestīnum, neuter of intestīnus (“internal”), as Etymology 2, below.

parole.significato: Domestic; taking place within a given country or region.
parole.testo: From Latin intestīnus (“internal”), from intus (“within”).

parole.significato: The innermost part of an anatomical structure, particularly a tubular one
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin intima, feminine form of intimus (“innermost”).

parole.significato: Closely acquainted; familiar.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin intimātus, the perfect passive participle of intimō (“to put or bring into, to impress, to make familiar”) (see -ate (adjective forming suffix)), from intimus (“inmost, innermost, most intimate”), superlative of intus (“within”), from in (“in”); see interior.

parole.significato: To suggest or disclose (something) discreetly.
parole.testo: From Latin intimātus, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more. Cognate with French intimer.

parole.significato: inward; internal; intimate
parole.testo: From Latin intimus (“innermost”) perhaps via French intime. Compare intimate (adjective).

parole.significato: The act of steeping or soaking the bread (or 'body' of Christ) in the wine (or 'blood' of Christ) so the communicant ma…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin intinctiō, from intingere (“to dip in”).

parole.significato: The state of being intolerable; intolerableness.
parole.testo: From Latin intolerabilitas.

parole.significato: To thunder or to utter in a sonorous or thunderous voice.
parole.testo: First attested in 1631; borrowed from Latin intonātus, perfect passive participle of intonō (“to thunder forth”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A winding, bending, or twisting.
parole.testo: From Latin intortio (“a curling, crisping”). Compare French intorsion. See intort, and compare intortion.

parole.significato: To twist in and out; to twine; to wreathe, wind, or wring.
parole.testo: Latin intortus, past participle of intoquere (“to twist”) equivalent to in- (“in-”) + torquereto (“twist”).

parole.significato: within the legal power or authority of a person or body
parole.testo: Latin “within the power”

parole.significato: Within a single entity indicated by the root word:
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin intrā (“within”).

parole.significato: Within the ear.
parole.testo: From intra- (“within”) + aural (“ear”), from Latin roots.

parole.significato: Within the walls; within one institution, particularly a school.
parole.testo: From Latin intramuralis, from intra (“within”) + muralis (“of a wall”).

parole.significato: Internal, that is within.
parole.testo: From Latin intrāneus (“from within”).

parole.significato: Incapable of being transgressed; not to be passed over or crossed.
parole.testo: From Latin intragressibilis (“that can not be crossed”). See in- (“not”) + transgress + -ible.

parole.significato: That enters or penetrates.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin intrans, present participle of intrare (“to enter”).

parole.significato: During parturition (childbirth; labor).
parole.testo: From intra- + Latin partum (“giving birth”).

parole.significato: A piece of music which serves as an introduction.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin intrata.

parole.significato: During the life of an organism.
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: Having a great deal of fine detail or complexity.
parole.testo: From Middle English intricat(e) (“entangled, intricate”), from Latin intrīcātus, perfect passive participle of intricō, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: To become enmeshed or entangled.
parole.testo: As for Etymology 1; from Latin intrīcātus, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: An introduction.
parole.testo: Clipping of introduction, from Latin intrōductiō (“lead-in, introduction”) – the abbreviation removes the second part of the compound; the first part ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁énteros (“inner, what is inside”). The demoscene sense comes from the fact that they were originally prepended

parole.significato: inward, inwards.
parole.testo: From Latin intro- (“inwards”), from intro (“inward, inwards”), q.v.

parole.significato: A depression or inward sinking of parts.
parole.testo: From Latin introcedere, introcessum (“to go in”), from intro (“within”) + cedere (“to go”).

parole.significato: Someone who introduces someone or something.
parole.testo: From Latin introductor.

parole.significato: To infiltrate the genes of one species into the gene pool of another through repeated backcrossing of an interspecific…
parole.testo: From Latin introgredior (“to step in, enter”).

parole.significato: The entrance to a hollow organ or canal; often specifically the entrance to the vagina.
parole.testo: From Latin introitus.

parole.significato: The entrance to the vagina.
parole.testo: From Latin introitus vāgīnæ (“entrance of [a/the] vagina”).

parole.significato: To intermeddle with the effects or goods of another.
parole.testo: From Latin intrōmittō.

parole.significato: Facing or turned inwards or towards an axis.
parole.testo: From Latin introrsus, introrsum (“toward the inside”, adverb), variant of introversus, from intrō + versus (“turned”).

parole.significato: To engage in introspection.
parole.testo: From Latin intrōspectus, past participle of intrōspiciō. By surface analysis, intro- + -spect.

parole.significato: Examining one's own perceptions and sensory experiences; contemplative or thoughtful about oneself.
parole.testo: From Latin intro "inward, within" (see intro-) + Latin specere "look at".

parole.significato: Coming in together; entering; commingling.
parole.testo: From Latin introveniens, present participle of introvenire (“to come in”), from intro (“within”) + venire (“to come”).

parole.significato: An organ or other body part that is or can be turned inside out, especially an anterior portion of some annelid worms c…
parole.testo: From New Latin intrōvertere, from intro- (“within”) and vertere (“to turn”). Popularized as a psychological term by the German works of Carl Jung. By surface analysis, intro- + -vert.

parole.significato: To thrust oneself in; to come or enter without invitation, permission, or welcome; to encroach; to trespass.
parole.testo: From Latin intrudere, from in- + trudere (“to thrust”).

parole.significato: To know intuitively or by immediate perception.
parole.testo: A back-formation from intuition and intuitive; compare Latin intuitus (“observed; considered”), perfect participle of intueor (“to look at, upon or towards; to observe, regard; to consider, contemplate”), from in- (“in, inside”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁én (“in”)) + tueor (“to look or

parole.significato: To swell or enlarge (abnormally)
parole.testo: From Latin intumēscō.

parole.significato: That becomes swollen, especially upon exposure to heat.
parole.testo: From Latin intumēscēns, present participle of intumescō (“rise, swell”), from tumescō (“become inflated”).

parole.significato: unburied
parole.testo: From Latin intumulātus. See in- (“not”) + tumulate + -ed.

parole.significato: A swelling (the act of swelling, or state of being swelled).
parole.testo: From Latin inturgescens, present participle of inturgescere (“to swell up”), equivalent to in- + turgescence. See turgescent.

parole.significato: A bruise; a contusion.
parole.testo: From Latin intundere (“to bruise”), from in- (“in”) + tundere, tusum (“to beat, bruise”).

parole.significato: Any of several plants of the genus Inula, such as elecampane.
parole.testo: From Latin inula. Compare elecampane.

parole.significato: To put in shadow; to darken.
parole.testo: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin inumbrātus, perfect passive participle of inumbrō (“to shade”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: To smear with ointment.
parole.testo: From Latin inunctus, perfect passive participle of inunguere (“to anoint”). Doublet of anoint.

parole.significato: The anointing or rubbing in of oil or balm.
parole.testo: From Latin inunctio, from inunctus, past participle of inungo (“anoint”), from in- + ungo (“anoint”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃engʷ- (“anoint”).

parole.significato: overflowing
parole.testo: From Latin inundans, present participle of inundare.

parole.significato: To cover with large amounts of water; to flood.
parole.testo: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin inundātus, the perfect passive participle of inundō (“to flood, overflow”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from in- + undō (“to overflow, wave”), from unda (“wave”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: uncivil; unpolished; rude
parole.testo: From Latin inurbānus. By surface analysis, in- + urbane.

parole.significato: Unusual.
parole.testo: From Latin inūsitātus (“unusual; new; unseen; different”). See use.

parole.significato: burnt in
parole.testo: From Latin inurere, inustus (“to burn in”), from in- (“in”) + urere (“to burn”).

parole.significato: Uselessness.
parole.testo: From in- + utility, from Latin inutilitas.

parole.significato: To move into.
parole.testo: From Latin invādō (“enter, invade”).

parole.significato: strength; health
parole.testo: From Latin invalescens, present participle of invalescere (“to become strong”). See in- and convalesce.

parole.significato: To import or introduce.
parole.testo: From Latin invehō (“bring in, carry in”), from in- + vehō (“carry”).

parole.significato: Having a border consisting of semicircles with the convex part outwards (and the points inwards).
parole.testo: From Latin invectus.

parole.significato: An inveighing against; invective.
parole.testo: From Latin invectio. See inveigh.

parole.significato: To complain loudly, to give voice to one's censure or criticism
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin invehō (“bring in, carry in”), from in- + vehō (“carry”). Compare vehicle, invective.

parole.significato: Not vendible or saleable.
parole.testo: From Latin invendibilis. See in- (“not”) + vendible.

parole.significato: One of the five canons of classical rhetoric: the method used for the discovery of arguments.
parole.testo: From Latin inventiō. Doublet of invention.

parole.significato: One who invents, either as a hobby or as an occupation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin inventor. By surface analysis, invent + -or.

parole.significato: A female that invents.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin inventrīx. By surface analysis, inventor + -trix.

parole.significato: Immodest; shameless.
parole.testo: From Latin inverecundus, from in- + verecundus (“modest”), from vereri (“to revere”).

parole.significato: To curve so as to extend into
parole.testo: From Latin invergo, from in- + vergō (“to incline, turn”).

parole.significato: Opposite in effect, nature or order.
parole.testo: Recorded since 1440, from Latin inversus, the past participle of invertere (“to invert”), itself from in- (“against, in”) + vertere (“to turn”).

parole.significato: The action of inverting.
parole.testo: From Latin inversiōnem.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, characterised by, or causing inversion.
parole.testo: From Latin invers-, the past participial stem of invertō, + -ive.

parole.significato: The inverted part of a composition.
parole.testo: From Latin inversus.

parole.significato: The condition of being invertible.
parole.testo: From invertible + -ity, from Latin invertibilitas.

parole.significato: Serving to cover or clothe.
parole.testo: From Latin investiens, present participle of investire.

parole.significato: Capable of being investigated or studied.
parole.testo: From Latin investigabilis.

parole.significato: To inquire into or study in order to ascertain facts or information.
parole.testo: Recorded since circa 1510, a back-formation from investigation on the basis of -ate (verb-forming suffix), from Latin investīgātiō (“a searching into”), from investīgātus, the perfect passive participle of investīgō, equivalent to in- + vestigate. Displaced native Old English undersēċan (literally “

parole.significato: One who investigates.
parole.testo: Attested in the mid‐16th century; from Latin investigator, from investigare, equivalent to investigate + -or.

parole.significato: Firmly established from having been around for a long time; of long standing.
parole.testo: The adjective is first attested in 1528, the verb in 1574; borrowed from Latin inveterātus (“of long standing, chronic”), perfect passive participle of inveterō and participial adjective (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from in- (“in, into”) + veterō (“to age”),

parole.significato: The act of making inveterate.
parole.testo: From Latin inveteratio.

parole.significato: Unconquered; unsubdued.
parole.testo: From Latin invictus.

parole.significato: Causing ill will, envy, or offense.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin invidiōsus, from invidia (“envy, ill will”), from in- (“upon”) + videō (“to see”); the meaning developed from “look back at” to “look askance at” to “envy.” Doublet of envious, from Old French.

parole.significato: To oversee a test or exam.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin invigilātus, past participle of invigilō (“to stay awake, watch over”).

parole.significato: A person who supervises students during an examination; a proctor
parole.testo: From invigilate + -or, from Latin invigilatus, past participle of invigilo.

parole.significato: Not violated; free from violation or hurt of any kind; secure against violation or impairment.
parole.testo: From Middle English inviolat, inviolate, from Latin inviolātus. By surface analysis, in- (“not”) + violate (adjective).

parole.significato: untrodden
parole.testo: From Latin invius, from in- (“not”) + via (“way”).

parole.significato: To daub, catch, or entangle with glue or birdlime or other viscous matter.
parole.testo: From Latin inviscatus, past participle of inviscare (“to birdlime”), from in- (“in”) + viscum, viscus (“mistletoe, birdlime”).

parole.significato: Deep-seated; internal.
parole.testo: Latin invisceratus, past participle.

parole.significato: The act of inviting; solicitation; the requesting of a person's company.
parole.testo: From Middle English invitacioun, ynvytacioun, from Latin invītātio, reinforced by Middle French invitation. By surface analysis, invite + -ation. Displaced native Middle English lathinge from Old English laþung (see dialectal English lathing).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to an invitation
parole.testo: From Latin invitatorius.

parole.significato: To implore or invoke.
parole.testo: First attested in 1530; borrowed from Latin invocātus, perfect passive participle of invocō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of invoke.

parole.significato: Containing or characterized by invocation; invoking.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin invocō (“I invoke”) + -ory. Compare French invocatoire.

parole.significato: An involucel.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: A protein component of human skin.
parole.testo: From Latin involūcrum (“wrapper, covering”) + -in.

parole.significato: A sheath that covers or envelopes, especially one that forms around the sequestrum of new bone.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin involūcrum. Doublet of involucre.

parole.significato: Difficult to understand; complicated.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin involutus.

parole.significato: Entanglement; a spiralling inwards; intricacy.
parole.testo: From Latin involūtiō, from involvō.

parole.significato: Invulnerable or unscathed.
parole.testo: First attested in 1680; borrowed from Latin invulnerātus (“unwounded”), from in- (“not”) + vulnerātus see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A form of witchcraft: piercing a wax or clay image of a person in order to harm them.
parole.testo: From Latin invultare (“to stab the face of”), from vultus (“face”).

parole.significato: An exclamation of joy or triumph.
parole.testo: From Latin iō; compare Ancient Greek ἰώ (iṓ, “oh!”).

parole.significato: Solitary masturbation.
parole.testo: From Latin ipse (“self”).

parole.significato: Denoting a measure that forces a person to choose among multiple desirable options.
parole.testo: From Latin ipse (“of the self”).

parole.significato: A dogmatic and unproved proposition or dictum that is accepted solely on the authority of someone who is known to have…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ipse dīxit (“he himself said it”), calque of Ancient Greek αὐτὸς ἔφα (autòs épha).
