parole.significato: An unfounded, false and dogmatic assertion; an ipse dixit.
parole.testo: From Latin ipse dīxit (“he himself said it”, used in the Middle Ages in reference to Aristotle) + -ism. Coined in the late 18th century by Jeremy Bentham.

parole.significato: selfhood; individual identity
parole.testo: From Latin ipse + -ity.

parole.significato: self
parole.testo: By alteration of Latin ipse (“self”).

parole.significato: The actual words (spoken or transcribed).
parole.testo: From Latin ipsissima verba (“the very words”).

parole.significato: By that very fact itself; actually.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ipsō factō (“by the fact itself”).

parole.significato: Of an intersex person: identifying with the sex they were medically assigned; having a gender which matches their assig…
parole.testo: Coined by C. G. Costello in 2014. Latin ipso means "at the very same" (gender as they were assigned), compare ipso facto or ipso substitution.

parole.significato: Used for expressing negation; not
parole.testo: From Latin ir-, assimilated form of in- used before r-.

parole.significato: Angry; irritable
parole.testo: From Latin iracundus.

parole.significato: The quality of being irascible; irritability of temper.
parole.testo: From Latin īrāscor (“to be angry, to be enraged”) + -ibility. See also irascible.

parole.significato: Extremely angry; wrathful; enraged.
parole.testo: From Latin īrātus (“angered, angry”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from īrāscor (“to be angry”), from īra (“anger, wrath”).

parole.significato: An officer in Ancient Greece having functions corresponding to those of a Justice of the Peace.
parole.testo: From Latin īrēnarcha, īrēnarchēs, from Ancient Greek εἰρηνάρχης (eirēnárkhēs), from εἰρήνη (eirḗnē, “peace”) + ἀρχή (arkhḗ, “rule”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to a rainbow.
parole.testo: Formed from (the stem of) Latin īris, Ancient Greek ἶρις (îris) + -al.

parole.significato: A plant of the genus Iris, common in the northern hemisphere, and generally having attractive blooms (See Iris (plant)…
parole.testo: From Middle English iris, from Latin īris, from Ancient Greek ἶρις (îris, “rainbow”). Presuming an earlier form *ϝῖρις (*wîris), possibly from a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *w(e)ih₁-ro- (“a twist, thread, cord, wire”), from *weh₁y- (“to turn, twist, weave, plait”). If so, it would be cognate t

parole.significato: Archaic form of irrational.
parole.testo: From Latin irratiōnābilis, from ir- + ratiōnābilis.

parole.significato: Not rational; unfounded, nonsensical or wrong-headed.
parole.testo: From Latin irratiōnālis, from ir- + ratiōnālis.

parole.significato: Synonym of intangible, immaterial, not composed of things, having no concrete existence.
parole.testo: From Latin irrealis, from in- (“un-: not”) + reālis (“real, material, tangible, composed of physical things”), from res (“thing”) + -ālis (“-al: forming adjectives”). Doublet of irrealis.

parole.significato: Not regible; ungovernable, unmanageable, intractable.
parole.testo: From the post-Classical Latin irregibilis (“ungovernable”), from ir- (“un-”) + regibilis (“governable”, “tractable”); equivalent to the English ir- (“un-”) + regible (“governable”, “tractable”).

parole.significato: The quality of being irreligious.
parole.testo: From Latin irreligiōsitās.

parole.significato: Having no relation to religion.
parole.testo: From Latin irreligiōsus. By surface analysis, ir- + religious.

parole.significato: Admitting no return; from or by which one cannot return.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin irremeābilis, from in- (“not”) + remeābilis (“returning”), from remeō. Compare French irréméable. See remeant.

parole.significato: Unable to be remedied, cured, corrected or repaired; irreparable, incurable.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin irremediābilis. By surface analysis, ir- + remediable.

parole.significato: Not remunerable.
parole.testo: From Latin irremūnerābilis. Compare French irrémunérable. See remunerate.

parole.significato: not reprehensible, blameless, without blame; innocent
parole.testo: From Latin irreprehēnsibilis. Compare French irrépréhensible. See reprehensible.

parole.significato: surreptitious; spurious
parole.testo: From Latin irrēpō (“I creep into”); ir- (“in”) + rēpō (“I creep”).

parole.significato: The quality of being irresistible.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin irresistibilitās. By surface analysis, irresistible + -ity.

parole.significato: Impossible to resist.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin irresistibilis, equivalent to ir- + resistible.

parole.significato: Regardless of; without regard for; without considering.
parole.testo: Opposite of Medieval Latin respectivus, "having regard for", from Latin respectus.

parole.significato: The state or quality of being irreverent; want of proper reverence; disregard of the authority and character of a super…
parole.testo: From Middle English irreverence, from Latin irreverentia, from irreverēns (“irreverent”) + -ia (suffix forming abstract nouns). By surface analysis, ir- + reverence.

parole.significato: Lacking respect; not having or not showing respect for or seriousness towards something that is usually treated with re…
parole.testo: From Latin irreverēns. By surface analysis, ir- + reverent.

parole.significato: To supply (farmland) with water, by building ditches, pipes, etc.
parole.testo: First attested in 1615; borrowed from Latin irrigātus, perfect passive participle of irrigō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). See also Middle English irrigat(e) (“watered, irrigated”).

parole.significato: Irrigated, well-watered.
parole.testo: From Latin irriguus, from in- + riguus (“watered”), from rigāre (“to wet”).

parole.significato: The act of laughing at another; derision.
parole.testo: From Latin irrīsiō, from irrīdēre (“to laugh at”); ir- (“in”) + rīdeō (“to laugh”): compare French irrision.

parole.significato: The state or quality of being irritable; quick excitability.
parole.testo: From Latin irritabilitās, equivalent to irritable + -ity.

parole.significato: To provoke impatience, anger, or displeasure in.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin irrītātus, perfect passive participle of irrītō (“excite, irritate, incite, stimulate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: To render null and void.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin irritātus, perfect passive participle of irritō (“to invalidate, render void, annul”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from irritus (“invalid”), the equivalent of in- + ratus (“valid, established, fixed”).

parole.significato: To sprinkle or moisten with dew; to bedew.
parole.testo: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin irrōrātus, perfect passive participle of irrōrō (“to bedew”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: rushing, moving quickly, especially inwards
parole.testo: From the present participle stem of Latin irruere.

parole.significato: To wrinkle.
parole.testo: First attested in 1566; borrowed from Latin irrūgātus, perfect passive participle of irrūgō (“to wrinkle”), from rūga (“a wrinkle”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: To thrust the penis into the mouth; to practice irrumation.
parole.testo: First attested in 1887; borrowed from Latin irrumātus, perfect passive participle of irrumō (“to irrumate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The act of, or an instance of, thrusting the penis into the mouth; active penetration of a mouth.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin irrumātiō, from irrumō + -tiō.

parole.significato: To break into.
parole.testo: From Latin irruptus, past participle of irrumpō.

parole.significato: An introduction, especially (particularly capitalized) Porphyry's introduction to the works of Aristotle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin īsagōgē, from Ancient Greek εἰσαγωγή (eisagōgḗ, “lead-in”), from εἰς (eis, “into”) + ἀγωγή (agōgḗ, “to lead”).

parole.significato: A muscle just below the surface of the perineum, used to flex the anus, stabilize the erect penis (in males), and tense…
parole.testo: From ischio- + Latin cavernōsus.

parole.significato: The lowest of the three bones that make up each side of the pelvis.
parole.testo: 17th century, from Latin ischium, from Ancient Greek ἰσχίον (iskhíon, “hip joint”).

parole.significato: The inability to empty the bladder
parole.testo: Latin ischuria, Ancient Greek ἰσχουρία (iskhouría, “retention of urine”), from ἴσχω (ískhō, “to keep back, restrain”) + οὖρον (oûron, “urine”).

parole.significato: A temple dedicated to the worship of the Egyptian goddess Isis.

parole.significato: The act of shaking or weakening or the resulting state; overthrow, ruination.

parole.significato: The folds of tissue of the vulva, at either side of the vulval vestibule.

parole.significato: A liplike structure; especially one of the vulva's two pairs of folds of skin on either side.

parole.significato: A chemist.

parole.significato: To produce or develop (something).

parole.significato: Having thick lips (any sense).
parole.testo: From Latin labrosus, from labrum (“lip”).

parole.significato: The uppermost of the mouthparts (trophi) of a typical insect, such as a cockroach. Typically resembles an upper lip and…
parole.testo: From Latin labrum (“lip”).

parole.significato: The fox grape (Vitis labrusca).
parole.testo: From the species epithet in Vitis labrusca, from Latin labrusca.

parole.significato: Any tree of the genus Laburnum.

parole.significato: A maze-like structure built by Daedalus in Knossos, containing the Minotaur.

parole.significato: labyrinthine; like or relating to a labyrinth
parole.testo: From Latin labyrinthicus. Compare French labyrinthique.

parole.significato: To tear, rip or wound.

parole.significato: An irregular open wound to soft tissue.
parole.testo: From Latin lacerātiō, first attested in 1598. By surface analysis, lacerate + -tion. Compare lacerate.

parole.significato: Pertaining to or resembling a lizard; lizard-like.

parole.significato: lamentable

parole.significato: To cry or weep.
parole.testo: From Latin lachrymātus, lacrimātus, perfect passive participle of lachrymō, lacrimō; see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Pertaining to or causing tears.
parole.testo: From Latin lachrymātōrius. By surface analysis, lachrymate + -ory.

parole.significato: A vase supposedly intended to hold tears; formerly used by archaeologists to designate certain urns found in Roman buri…
parole.testo: From Latin lachrymātōrium. By surface analysis, lachrymate + -ory.

parole.significato: Shaped like a teardrop
parole.testo: From Latin lacrima (“tear”) + -form. Compare French lacrymiforme.

parole.significato: Tearful, sorrowful, sad, pertaining to tears, weeping, causing tears or crying.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin lachrymōsus, lacrimōsus, from lachryma, lacrima (“tear”) + -osus (“-ful”), from Old Latin dacrima, from Proto-Indo-European *dakru-, cognate with English tear.

parole.significato: One of the narrow, jagged, irregular pieces or divisions which form a sort of fringe on the borders of the petals of so…

parole.significato: Of speech or writing, communicative through the use of as few words as possible.

parole.significato: A hot dry sweating room, next to the caldarium in the Roman baths.

parole.significato: Extreme brevity in expression.

parole.significato: Shaped like a teardrop.

parole.significato: The “tears of things”; the inherent tragedy of existence.
parole.testo: An allusion to Virgil’s Aeneid (29–19 BC), book I, line 462; Latin: lacrimae (“tears”, the nominative plural form of lacrima, “tear”) + rērum (“of things”, the genitive plural form of rēs, “thing”) = “tears of things”.

parole.significato: The shedding or flow of tears; crying.
parole.testo: From Latin lacrimātiō. By surface analysis, lacrimate + -ion.

parole.significato: causing the production of tears
parole.testo: From Latin lacrima (“tear”) + -genous.

parole.significato: lactating; producing milk.
parole.testo: From Latin lactans, present participle of lactare (“to suck”), from lac, lactis (“milk”).

parole.significato: A dairyhouse.
parole.testo: From Latin lactārius.

parole.significato: To secrete or produce milk.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin lactātus, perfect passive participle of lactō (“to suckle, give suck, contain milk”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from lac (“milk”), cognate to Ancient Greek γάλα (gála, “milk”).

parole.significato: The secretion of milk from the mammary gland of a female mammal.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin lactātiō, lactātiōnis. Equivalent to lactate + -ion.

parole.significato: milky
parole.testo: From Latin lactescens, present participle of lactescere.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or derived from milk.

parole.significato: Producing or yielding milk.

parole.significato: A medicine to check the secretion of milk, or to dispel a supposed accumulation of milk in any part of the body

parole.significato: Synonym of Mothering Sunday: the fourth Sunday of Lent.

parole.significato: To make, or become, happy.

parole.significato: Becoming fatigued or languid.

parole.significato: A slip, lapse, or error.

parole.significato: An inadvertent remark; a slip of the tongue.
parole.testo: From Latin lāpsus linguae (literally “slip or fault of the tongue”), from lāpsus (“fault”) and linguae (the genitive form of lingua (“tongue”)).

parole.significato: A slip of memory; an instance of forgetting.

parole.significato: Synonym of slip of the pen.

parole.significato: lascivious

parole.significato: Wanton; lewd, driven by lust, lustful.
parole.testo: From Latin lascīviōsus, from lascīvia (“sportiveness, lustfulness”).

parole.significato: lasciviousness
parole.testo: From Latin lascīvitās. By surface analysis, Latin lascīv(us) + -i- + -ty.

parole.significato: A gum resin obtained from certain umbelliferous plants.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin laser.

parole.significato: silphium resin
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin laserpicium.

parole.significato: Characterized by lassitude.
parole.testo: From Latin lassitūdin- + -ous, from oblique stem of Latin lassitūdō, from lassus + -tūdō. By surface analysis, lassitude + -ous.

parole.significato: A duty exacted, in some fairs or markets, for the right to carry things where one will.
parole.testo: From lestage (“ballasting”), from lest (“ballast”), or Latin lastagium, lestagium. See last (“a load”).

parole.significato: Of a penalty, coming into force as soon as a law is broken, by force of the law itself (such as excommunication for var…
parole.testo: From Latin latae sententiae (“of a sentence [already] passed”).

parole.significato: The cavity in the foodyolk of a meroblastic ovum.
parole.testo: From Latin latebra (“hidden recess”). Doublet of latibulum.

parole.significato: Of an animal, especially a spider: living concealed in a hole.
parole.testo: From Latin latebricola, from latebra + -cola.

parole.significato: To the side; of or pertaining to the side.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin laterālis (“belonging to the side”), from latus (“the side or flank”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix).

parole.significato: A red hard or gravel-like soil or subsoil formed in the tropics that has been leached of soluble minerals leaving insol…
parole.testo: From Latin later (“brick”) + -ite.

parole.significato: Of the reddish color of bricks.
parole.testo: From Latin latericius, from later (“brick”).

parole.significato: To retreat and lie hidden; to hide in a corner.
parole.testo: From Latin latibulārī + -ate, from latibulum (“a hiding-place, lair”) + -ārī. See also latibulize.

parole.significato: To retire into a den, or hole, and lie dormant in winter.
parole.testo: From Latin latibulum (“hiding place”), from latere (“to lie hid”) + -ize.

parole.significato: A concealed hiding place, especially of an animal; a burrow, hole, or lair.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin latibulum (“den of animals; hiding place, refuge”), from lat(eō) (“to conceal, hide, lie hidden; to be hidden and in safety”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *leh₂- (“to be concealed”)) + -bulum (suffix denoting a place or vessel). Doublet of latebra. The plural for

parole.significato: Containing latex; applied to the tissue or tubular vessels in which the latex of the plant is found.
parole.testo: From Latin latex, laticis (“a liquid”) + -ferous.

parole.significato: Having broad leaves.
parole.testo: Latin latifolius.

parole.significato: A great landed estate with absentee ownership and labor often in a state of partial servitude.
parole.testo: From Latin lātifundium, from lātus (“wide, extensive”) + fundus (“ground, base, estate, farm”). Doublet of latifundio.

parole.significato: Of or derived from Latin.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin latināt(us) (“Latin-speaking”), from Latin latīnō (“to speak Latin”). By surface analysis, Latin + -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The quality of a particular person's Latin speech or writing; the Latin language, as an area of study or interest.
parole.testo: From Latin Latīnitās, from Latin Latīnus (“Latin”).

parole.significato: To translate something into the Latin language; or make a word similar in appearance or form to a Latin word.
parole.testo: From Latin latīnizō. By surface analysis, Latin + -ize.

parole.significato: Motion of a celestial object from one place to another; local motion.
parole.testo: From Latin lātiō.

parole.significato: A large, flat, dorsolateral muscle on the trunk, posterior to the arm, and partly covered by the trapezius on its media…
parole.testo: From Latin lātissimus (“widest, broadest”) (superlative of lātus (“wide, broad”)) + dorsī (genitive of dorsum (“the back”)).

parole.significato: Having a broad breastbone, or sternum (said of Pithecina, a former taxonomic classification that is now probably Pithec…
parole.testo: Latin latus (“broad”) + English sternal.

parole.significato: A writ based upon the presumption that the person summoned was hiding.
parole.testo: Latin, meaning "he lies hidden", from latito.

parole.significato: The act of concealment or hiding.
parole.testo: From Latin latitatio.

parole.significato: Relating to latitude.
parole.testo: From Latin lātitūdin- + -al, from oblique stem of Latin lātitūdō, from lātus + -tūdō. By surface analysis, latitude + -al.

parole.significato: Not restrained; not confined by precise limits.
parole.testo: From Latin lātitūdin- + -arian, from oblique stem of Latin lātitūdō, from lātus + -tūdō. By surface analysis, latitude + -arian.

parole.significato: Having latitude, or broad range; wide-ranging or of broad scope
parole.testo: From Latin lātitūdin- + -ous, from oblique stem of Latin lātitūdō, from lātus + -tūdō. By surface analysis, latitude + -ous.

parole.significato: In the broad sense; broadly.
parole.testo: From Latin lātō sēnsū and sēnsū lātō, both meaning the same. Various misspellings exist, such as lato senso, latu sensu, senso lato and sensu latu, which can be attributed to ignorance of the underlying Latin grammar causing analogical leveling of the endings. parole.significato: A lateritic soil of forested temperate or tropical regions.
parole.testo: From Latin later (“brick”) + -o- + -sol.

parole.significato: The ability or tendency to bark.
parole.testo: From Latin lātrābilis (“barking, able to bark, characterized by barking”) + English -ity (“forming abstract nouns”). Equivalent to latrate + -ability.

parole.significato: Synonym of barking, particularly (figurative) snarling, bitterly or angrily complaining.
parole.testo: From Latin lātrans (“barking, ranting”), present participle of lātrāre (“to bark, to rant”). Equivalent to latrate + -ant.

parole.significato: To bark; to make doglike noises.
parole.testo: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin lātrātus, perfect passive participle of lātrō (“to bark”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Compare Spanish ladrar (“to bark”). Originally seemingly attested as a ghost word.

parole.significato: Barking, an instance of barking.
parole.testo: From Latin lātrātio, from lātrāre (“to bark”) + -tiō (“-tion: forming abstract nouns”). Equivalent to latrate + -ion.

parole.significato: Theft or robbery.
parole.testo: From Latin latrōcinium (“highway robbery”), from latrōcinor, from latrō (“brigand, robber, mercenary”) + -cinor (“verbal suffix”). Doublet of larceny.

parole.significato: A robber or brigand; one who plunders.
parole.testo: From Latin latrō (“mercenary, brigand”). Doublet of ladrone.

parole.significato: Synonym of flank.
parole.testo: From Latin latus (“side”) of uncertain etymology.

parole.significato: The chord passing through a focus of a conic section, parallel to the directrix and terminated both ways by the curve.…
parole.testo: Latin latus (“side”) + rectum (“right”)

parole.significato: laudableness
parole.testo: From Latin laudabilitas.

parole.significato: To laud.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin laudātus, perfect passive participle of laudō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of laud.

parole.significato: The act of lauding; high praise or commendation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin laudatio; compare Old English taudation. See laud.

parole.significato: laudatory
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin laudativus (“laudatory”): compare French laudatif.

parole.significato: One who lauds.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin laudator.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to praise, or the expression of praise.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin laudatōrius: compare Old French laudatoire.

parole.significato: praise
parole.testo: From Latin laudite, second-person plural imperative of laudere (“to praise”).

parole.significato: Belonging to, or resembling, a natural order (Lauraceae) of trees and shrubs having aromatic bark and foliage, and incl…
parole.testo: From Lauraceae, from Latin laurus (“laurel”) + -aceous.

parole.significato: Crowned, or decked, with laurel.
parole.testo: First attested during the end of the 15th century, in Middle English; borrowed from Latin laureātus, from laurea (“laurel crown, wreath”, a high reward given to poets and later to the triumphant) + -ātus (forming adjectives indicating possession) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-f

parole.significato: Relating to a Precambrian geological region in eastern Canada, or the period of its formation.
parole.testo: From Latin Laurentius (“Laurence”) + -ian, after the Saint Lawrence River. Piecewise doublet of Laurencian and Lawrentian; compare also lawrencium.

parole.significato: Relating to Lorenzo de' Medici, or to the Laurentian Library in Florence named after him.
parole.testo: From Latin Laurentius (“Laurence”) + -ian, after the Latinized name of Lorenzo de' Medici.

parole.significato: Producing, or bringing, laurel
parole.testo: From Latin laurifer, from laurus (“laurel”) + ferō (“to bear”). See also laurel.

parole.significato: Having leaves like those of the bay laurel.
parole.testo: An etymological hybrid of the Latin laurus (“bay laurel”) and the English -phyllous (from the Ancient Greek φύλλον, phúllon, “leaf”).

parole.significato: Synonym of laurestine.
parole.testo: From Latin laurus (“laurel”) + tīnus (“Viburnum tinus”). See also laurestine.

parole.significato: A ritual involving the washing of one's hands at a church's offertory before handling the Eucharist.
parole.testo: From the Christian ritual, which was traditionally accompanied in Catholicism by a recitation of Psalm 25:6 (Psalm 26:6, in the Hebrew and in most modern translations) which in Latin begins with the word lavābō (“I will wash”). The sense of "room with a toilet" developed under the influence of lavat

parole.significato: washing or cleansing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin lavatio, lavationem; compare Old French lavation. Doublet of lotion.

parole.significato: Washing, or cleansing by washing.
parole.testo: From Latin lavātōrius.

parole.significato: A red alga/seaweed, Porphyra umbilicalis (syn. Porphyra laciniata), eaten as a vegetable.
parole.testo: From Middle English laver, lavre, lever, levre, laber (“a kind of water plant”), from Old English læfer, leber (“a rush (plant)”), a borrowing from Latin laver (“water plant”).

parole.significato: A body of commercial law.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin lex mercatoria

parole.significato: Synonym of international law.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin iūs gentium, originally meaning legal principles that are general to humanity. parole.significato: Lenient and allowing for deviation; not strict.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin laxus (“wide, roomy, loose”).

parole.significato: The act of loosening or slackening, or the state of being loosened or slackened.
parole.testo: From Latin laxātiō, from laxō (“to loosen”), from laxus (“loose, slack”).

parole.significato: A muscle whose contraction loosens some part. Modern anatomy general defines this as a group of tendons.
parole.testo: From Latin laxare, laxatum (“to loosen”).

parole.significato: Pale blue
parole.testo: From Latin lazulum (“heaven, sky”).

parole.significato: A kind of Roman litter, typically with bedding, curtains, and four legs.
parole.testo: From Latin lectīca (“litter”), from lectus (“bed, couch”) + -īca (“forming related nouns”), q.v.

parole.significato: The more difficult reading, held to be the more likely when faced with two manuscripts that disagree on a particular re…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin lectiō difficilior (“more difficult reading”).

parole.significato: An ancient "feast of the gods", at which images of the gods were set on couches around a feast table.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin lectisternium.

parole.significato: One that strives after an inheritance.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin hērēdipeta.

parole.significato: Relating to the law or to lawyers.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin lēgālis (“legal”), from lēx (“law”). Doublet of loyal and leal.

parole.significato: A legatee.
parole.testo: From Latin legatarius, from legaturius (“enjoined by a last will”). Compare French légataire. See legacy.

parole.significato: A legacy or bequest.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin lēgātum (“a legacy”), substantivized from the neuter forms of the perfect passive participle of lēgō (“to bequeath, leave as legacy, legate”). Doublet of legacy.

parole.significato: The purpose for which a legate is sent; a legate's mission or commission. Now rare (cf. OED)
parole.testo: From Latin lēgātiō.

parole.significato: A testator.
parole.testo: From Latin lēgātor (“testator”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to lawmaking.
parole.testo: From Latin lex, legis (“law”) + -ficare (“to make”, comparative). See -fy.

parole.significato: A soldier belonging to a legion; a professional soldier of the ancient Roman army.
parole.testo: From legion + -ary. From Latin legiōnārius. Doublet of legionnaire.

parole.significato: Bacteria of the genus Legionella.
parole.testo: From legion + translingual -ella, from Latin legio. Constructed from American Legion, after an outbreak of a then-unknown "mystery disease" (Legionnaires' disease) at a convention of the American Legion in Philadelphia in 1976.

parole.significato: Someone who creates or enacts laws.
parole.testo: From Latin lēgislātor.

parole.significato: A female legislator.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin lēgislātrīx. By surface analysis, legislate + -trix.

parole.significato: Legal
parole.testo: From Latin lēguleius (“pettifogger”), from lēx, lēgis (“law”).

parole.significato: One of two oval bodies hanging from the interior walls of the body in the Acanthocephala.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin lēmniscus (“pendent ribbon”), from Ancient Greek λημνῐ́σκος (lēmnĭ́skos), from Λῆμνος (Lêmnos, “a Greek island Lemnos”) + -ίσκος (-ískos, “noun-forming diminutive suffix”).

parole.significato: Any strepsirrhine primate of the superfamily Lemuroidea, native only to Madagascar and some surrounding islands.
parole.testo: From Latin lemurēs (“spirits of the dead”). The name was originally given to the red slender loris (then Lemur tardigradus) in 1754 by Carl Linnaeus. parole.significato: The spirits or ghosts of the dead, considered as malignant.
parole.testo: From Latin lemurēs. See lemur.

parole.significato: The smooth breathing (spiritus lenis).
parole.testo: Anglicisation of Latin lēnis. Doublet of lenis.

parole.significato: Leniency: mercy or forgiveness in the assignment of punishment.
parole.testo: From Latin lēn(iō) (“to soften, soothe”) -i- + -ence, from lēnis (“soft”).

parole.significato: The quality of mercy or forgiveness, especially in the assignment of punishment as in a court case.
parole.testo: From lenience + -y, from Latin lēn(iō) (“to soften, soothe”), from lēnis (“soft”).

parole.significato: To assuage or mitigate; to soften (fever/pain/effects etc.).
parole.testo: From Latin lēnis (“soft, mild”) + -ify. Compare French lénifier. See lenition.

parole.significato: Something that soothes; a sedative or comforter.
parole.testo: From Latin lenimentum. Compare Old French leniment. See lenient.

parole.significato: Relatively weakly articulated, hence unaspirated and possibly voiced; especially as compared to the others of a group o…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin lēnis (“soft, smooth”).

parole.significato: Analgesic, able to reduce pain or suffering.
parole.testo: From Latin lēnīt(us) (“softened”) + -ive, from lēniō (“to soften, soothe”), from lēnis (“soft”).

parole.significato: The quality or habit of being lenient; lenity.
parole.testo: Latin lenitudo.

parole.significato: Lewd; lascivious; lustful.
parole.testo: From Latin lenocinans, present participle of lenocinari (“to pander, cajole”), akin to leno (“pimp”).

parole.significato: A husband's connivance at his wife's adultery.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin lenocinium (“pimping, prostitution”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to, or living in still waters (such as lakes, ponds, or wetlands).
parole.testo: From Latin lentus (“slow”) + -ic.

parole.significato: A kind of eruption upon the skin; lentigo; freckle.
parole.testo: From Latin lenticula. See lenticel. Doublet of lentil.

parole.significato: Shaped like a biconvex lens.
parole.testo: From lent-, stem of Latin lens + -iform.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, resembling or having lentigines.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin lentīginōsus (“freckled”).

parole.significato: A brown pigmented spot on the skin.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin lentīgo. Earliest attestation as Late Middle English lentigines (plural).

parole.significato: The mastic-tree (Pistacia lentiscus).
parole.testo: From Latin lentiscus. Doublet of lentisk.

parole.significato: A tree, the lentiscus, Pistacia lentiscus.
parole.testo: From Latin lentiscus. Doublet of lentiscus.

parole.significato: Slowness; sluggishness.
parole.testo: From Latin lentitūdo, from lentus (“slow”). Compare Old French lentitude.

parole.significato: slow; sluggish
parole.testo: From Latin lentitūdin- + -al, from oblique stem of Latin lentitūdō, from lentus + -tūdō. By surface analysis, lentitude + -al.

parole.significato: viscid; viscous; tenacious
parole.testo: From Latin lentus. See lentor.

parole.significato: Someone with a Leo star sign
parole.testo: From Latin leō (“lion”), calque of Ancient Greek λέων (léōn), calque of Akkadian 𒉈𒍑 (nēšu)/Akkadian 𒌨𒄞𒆷 (urgulû), from Sumerian 𒌨𒄞𒆷 (UR.GU.LA, “lion; name of constellation”). Doublet of Leon, leu, lev, lion, and Lyon.

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to Leontini
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Leontīnus, from Ancient Greek Λεοντῖνος (Leontînos).

parole.significato: In the form of a lion.
parole.testo: From Latin leō (“lion”) + -morphic.

parole.significato: pleasant; amusing
parole.testo: Latin lepidus.

parole.significato: Synonym of rabbitlike.
parole.testo: From Latin lepor- (“hare”) + -iform.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or characteristic of a hare or a rabbit.
parole.testo: The adjective is a learned borrowing from Latin leporīnus + English -ine (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’). Leporīnus is derived from leporis (the genitive singular form of lepus (“hare”)) + -īnus (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’). The noun is derived from the adjective.

parole.significato: Fear of rabbits.
parole.testo: From Latin lepor- (“hare”) -i- + phobia.

parole.significato: To (cause to) take part in lesbian sex, or other lesbian activity.
parole.testo: From Latin Lesbiana, from Ancient Greek Λέσβος (Lésbos) + Latin adjective suffix -iana; by reference to Sappho of Lesbos (whence also sapphist, sapphic), known for her sentimental poems about women. This sense of the word may have been borrowed from, or influenced by, the German cognate lesbisch, wh

parole.significato: It is the buyer’s responsibility to ensure the soundness of goods or services prior to their purchase.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin caveat ēmptor.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or causing death; deadly; mortal; fatal.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin lētālis (“deadly, mortal, fatal”), improperly written lēthālis, from lētum (“death”), improperly written as lēthum, from a supposed connection with Ancient Greek λήθη (lḗthē, “oblivion, forgetfulness”).

parole.significato: A quiescent sleeplike state in some arthropods and nematodes.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin lethargus (“lethargy”).

parole.significato: Forgetfulness of the past; oblivion.
parole.testo: From Latin Lēthē, from Ancient Greek Λήθη (Lḗthē, “forgetfulness”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the river Lethe, one of the four rivers of Hades. Those who drank from it experienced complete forget…
parole.testo: From Latin Lēthē, from Ancient Greek Λήθη (Lḗthē).

parole.significato: Of or relating to death or forgetfulness.
parole.testo: From Latin Lēthē, from Ancient Greek Λήθη (Lḗthē).

parole.significato: Deadly, lethal.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin lethifer, letifer, from lethum, letum (“death”) + ferre (“to bear, to bring”). Compare French léthifère.

parole.significato: quinoline.
parole.testo: From leuco- + Latin oleum (“oil”).

parole.significato: A writ of execution at common law.
parole.testo: Latin levārī faciās (“cause to be levied”).

parole.significato: The act of raising; elevation or upward motion.
parole.testo: From Latin levatio.

parole.significato: a broad, thin muscle, situated on the side of the pelvis, that forms part of the pelvic floor. In humans it supports th…
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: A skeletal muscle located at the back and side of the neck.
parole.testo: From Latin levator scapulae (“lifter of the shoulder blade”)

parole.significato: Smooth.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin lēvigātus, perfect passive participle of Latin lēvigō (“to smoothen”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from lēvis (“smooth”).

parole.significato: The act or operation of levigating (making into fine powder)
parole.testo: Latin levigatio (“a smoothing”): compare French lévigation.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or in accordance with levirate marriage.
parole.testo: From levirate + -ical. From Latin levir (“a husband's brother, brother-in-law”), akin to Ancient Greek δᾱήρ (dāḗr). Compare French lévirat (“leviration”).

parole.significato: The raising of something, such as a body, without apparent physical cause, allegedly using the power of the mind.
parole.testo: From levitate + -ion, from Latin levitas (“lightness”), patterned in English on gravitate.

parole.significato: A lightness of manner or speech, frivolity; flippancy; a lack of appropriate seriousness; an inclination to make a joke…
parole.testo: Coined in 1564, from Latin levitās (“lightness, frivolity”), from levis (“lightness (in weight)”). Cognate to lever, and more distantly, light.

parole.significato: Left; on the left; toward the left.
parole.testo: From Latin laevus (“left”).

parole.significato: A Roman or Latin law (particularly in ancient Rome or in medieval Europe).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin lēx, lēges (“law(s)”).

parole.significato: A doubtful law is not binding.
parole.testo: A Latin sentence; from lēx (“law”) + dubia (“doubtful”) + nōn (“not”) + obligat (“is binding”).

parole.significato: The law as it is.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin lēx lāta (“the law borne”) (see below).

parole.significato: law of equivalent retaliation.
parole.testo: From Latin lex (“proposition or motion for a law, a bill”) + talionis, genitive singular of tālio (“retaliation”), from tālis (“of such kind”).

parole.significato: A lexical item corresponding to the set of all words (or of all multi-word expressions) that are semantically related t…
parole.testo: From Latin lexis, from Ancient Greek λέξις (léxis, “word”) + -eme, a suffix indicating a fundamental unit in some aspect of linguistic structure, on the model of phoneme.

parole.significato: word; lexeme.
parole.testo: Derived from lexis, a borrowing from Latin lexis, itself from Ancient Greek λέξις (léxis).

parole.significato: Concerning the vocabulary, words, sentences or morphemes of a language.
parole.testo: From Latin lexis, from Ancient Greek λέξις (léxis, “word”) + -al.

parole.significato: A member of an ethnic group living predominantly in southern Dagestan and northeastern Azerbaijan.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Lesgi.

parole.significato: A libation.
parole.testo: Latin libamentum.

parole.significato: Sipping; touching lightly.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin lībāns, present participle of lībō (“to taste, touch”).

parole.significato: To pour a liquid, most often wine, in sacrifice on the ground, on a ritual object, or on a victim, in honor of some dei…
parole.testo: First attested in 1866; borrowed from Latin lībātus, perfect passive participle of lībō (“to pour out, taste”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The act of pouring a liquid, most often wine, in sacrifice on the ground, on a ritual object, or on a victim, in honor…
parole.testo: From Latin lībātiō, from lībāre (“to take a little from anything, to taste, to pour out as an offering”).

parole.significato: A small balance.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin lībella, diminutive of libra (“balance”). Doublet of level and niveau.

parole.significato: Pertaining to the Roman form of law in which the plaintiff files a formal petition.
parole.testo: From Latin libellus (“petition”) + Latin adjective suffixes -aris and -arius.

parole.significato: Synonym of phloem.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin liber (“the inner bark of a tree; book”). See libel.

parole.significato: An early form of autograph book that originated in Germany.

parole.significato: To render mammonic, to cause to pursue great wealth.
parole.testo: From Latin: Mammon + -ize.

parole.parola: man is a wolf to man

parole.significato: The act of emanation or flowing out.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Mandaeans.

parole.significato: Synonym of Mandaean.

parole.significato: An idiom or other feature borrowed from Mandaic.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Mandaismus, equivalent to Manda + -ism.

parole.testo: From Latin mandāmus (“we command”).

parole.significato: To (officially) require someone to do something or act in a certain way, to give them the authority to do so; to comman…
parole.testo: First attested in 1623; partly directly borrowed from Latin mandātus (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and Etymology 1 for more), partly from the above noun by metanalysis.

parole.significato: To chew (something); to masticate.
parole.testo: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin mandūcātus, perfect passive participle of to chew, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Cognate with French manger.

parole.significato: The souls or spirits of dead ancestors, conceived as deities or the subjects of reverence, or of other deceased relativ…
parole.testo: From Latin manes (“spirits of the dead”).

parole.significato: Used in stage directions; literally, he, she or it remains. Compare exit, exeunt.
parole.testo: From Latin manet (“he remains”), manent (“they remain”), inflections of maneō.

parole.significato: To make (something) appear more attractive or appealing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mangōnizō (“to adorn wares for sale”), from mangō (“dealer who adorns his wares to make them look more valuable”) (the source of English monger) + -izō (“-ize”).

parole.significato: Violent derangement of mind; madness; insanity.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mania, from Ancient Greek μανία (manía, “madness”).

parole.significato: Madness caused by alcohol intoxication.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin mania ā pōtū (literally “madness from the drink”).

parole.significato: Covered with hairs or pubescence so interwoven as to form a mass easily removed.
parole.testo: From Latin mānicātus (“sleeved”), from mānicae (“sleeves”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Synonym of Manichaean
parole.testo: From Latin Manichaicus, from Ancient Greek Μανιχαϊκός (Manikhaïkós).

parole.significato: A clavichord.
parole.testo: From Latin monochordon, from Ancient Greek μονόχορδον (monókhordon), influenced by Latin manus (“hand”). So called because it originally had only one string. See monochord.

parole.significato: A symbol resembling a hand with the index finger extended, used to draw attention to or indicate something.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin manicula (“little hand”). Doublet of manacle and manicle.

parole.significato: Evident to the senses, especially to the sight; apparent; distinctly perceived.
parole.testo: From Middle English manifest, manifeste, from Latin manifestus, manufestus (“palpable, manifest”), from Latin manus (“hand”) + an uncertain second element. Doublet of manifesto.

parole.significato: Having the form of a hand.
parole.testo: Latin mani, stem of manus (“hand”)) + -form.

parole.significato: of or relating to a maniple (Roman army division)
parole.testo: From Latin manipulāris: compare French manipulaire.

parole.significato: To mutilate.
parole.testo: From Middle English manken, from Old English *mancian, bemancian (“to maim, mutilate”), of obscure origin. parole.significato: tame; gentle
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mānsuētus.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or characterized by mansuetude; mild; meek; gentle.
parole.testo: From Latin mansuētūdin- + -ous, from oblique stem of mansuētūdō, from mansuēscō + -tūdō, from man(us) + suēscō. By surface analysis, mansuetude + -ous.

parole.significato: A beast with the body of a lion (usually red), the tail of a scorpion, and the head/face of a man with a mouth filled w…
parole.testo: From Latin mantichōras, from Ancient Greek μαρτιχόρας (martikhóras, “man-eater; tiger”), from Old Persian *martyahvārah (“man-eater”), from 𐎶𐎼𐎫𐎡𐎹 (m-r-t-i-y /⁠martyaʰ⁠/, “man”).

parole.significato: Any of various large insects of the order Mantodea that catch insects or other small animals with their powerful forele…
parole.testo: From New Latin mantis, from Ancient Greek μάντις (mántis, “soothsayer”). Distant doublet of mind via Proto-Indo-European *méntis. Noncognate with mantissa.

parole.significato: A minor addition to a text.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mantissa, mantīsa, of unknown origin (said by Festus to be a loanword from Etruscan, but it may actually be from Celtic, possibly through Etruscan mediation). parole.significato: The mantle worn by the pope, which is very similar to a cope, but longer and fastened in the front by an elaborate mors…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin mantum. Doublet of manto.

parole.significato: With military aid.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin manū mīlitārī.

parole.significato: Easily handled or carried.
parole.testo: From Latin manus (“hand”). By surface analysis, man(us) + -u- + -able.

parole.significato: Of organ music requiring the use of the manuals only.
parole.testo: From Latin manuāliter (“manually”), from manuālis (“manual, hand”).

parole.significato: Manual; involving (skills using) the hands.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin manuārius.

parole.significato: Taken as or relating to the spoils of war; funded from the spoils of war (especially in the Roman Empire).
parole.testo: From Latin manubialis from manubiae (“money obtained from the sale of booty, plunder”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to the spoils of war.
parole.testo: From Latin manubiārius.

parole.significato: The broad, upper part of the sternum.
parole.testo: From Latin manubrium (“handle”).

parole.significato: The chief novice in an order.
parole.testo: From Latin manus (“hand”) + ductor (“leader”).

parole.significato: A manufactured (manmade) object.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin manufactus.

parole.significato: To release (someone) from slavery; to free.
parole.testo: From Middle English manumitten, from Latin manūmittere, from pre-Classical Latin manū ēmittere (literally “send out from one’s hand”).

parole.significato: A small wheeled vehicle, similar to a velocipede but powered by the seated occupant's arms.
parole.testo: From Latin manus (“hand”) + mōtō (“to move, set in motion”).

parole.significato: A natural (not man-made) object of an excavation site, which was originally brought into the site by humans.
parole.testo: From Latin manū (“with a hand”) portāre (“to carry”).

parole.significato: A hand, as the part of the fore limb below the forearm in a human, or the corresponding part in other vertebrates.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin manus (“hand”). Doublet of mano.

parole.significato: Synonym of masturbation.
parole.testo: From Latin manus (“hand”) + stuprō (“debauch”). The verb is often wrongly quoted as stupō, stupare.

parole.significato: maintenance
parole.testo: From Latin manus (“hand”) + tenere (“to hold”).

parole.significato: manuterge
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin manutergium.

parole.significato: A medieval European map of the world.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mappa mundī (“map of the world”).

parole.significato: A medieval map of the known or imagined world.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin mappa mundī (“map of the world”).

parole.significato: progressive atrophy of the aged
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: Withered, but still attached.
parole.testo: From Latin marcescens, present participle of marcescere.

parole.significato: lean, withered.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin marcidus.

parole.significato: Shouted by a player of the game Marco Polo. Compare Polo.
parole.testo: From Marco Polo, from Latin Marcus Paulus, from Marcus.

parole.significato: an ancient Germanic tribe.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Marcomanni, from Proto-Germanic *markō (“border”) + *mann- (“man”).

parole.significato: The state of withering or wasting; leanness; loss of flesh.
parole.testo: From Latin marcor.

parole.significato: A large, dark plain, which may have the appearance of a sea, such as those on the Moon.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mare (“sea”). Doublet of maar and mere (“a body of standing water”).

parole.significato: A body of water within the jurisdiction of a particular nation, and not part of the open sea.
parole.testo: From Latin mare clausum (“closed sea”).

parole.significato: A body of water within the open sea to which all countries have access.
parole.testo: Latin, "free sea".

parole.significato: Producing pearls.
parole.testo: from Latin margarītifer, from margarīta (“pearl”) + ferre (“to bear”). Compare French margaritifère.

parole.significato: Divination by pearls.
parole.testo: Latin margarita (“pearl”).

parole.significato: The edge of the paper, typically left blank when printing but sometimes used for annotations etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English margyn, from Latin marginem (possibly via Old French margin), accusative of margō (“edge, brink, border, margin”). Doublet of marge and margo.

parole.significato: With a well marked edge or margin.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin marginātus, perfect passive participle of marginō (“to margin”), see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: border, margin
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin margō. Doublet of marge and margin.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Mariavite Church.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin qui Mariae vitam imitantur (“Let them imitate the Life of Mary”).

parole.significato: aquaculture using seawater
parole.testo: From Latin mare, maris (“sea”) + culture.

parole.significato: Produced in or by the sea.
parole.testo: From Latin mare (“sea”) -i- + -genous.

parole.significato: A device used to measure tidal levels.
parole.testo: From Latin mare (“sea”) + -graph.

parole.significato: A harbour for small boats.
parole.testo: From Latin marinus (“of the sea, marine”), by way of Italian marina and Spanish marina.

parole.significato: Adoration or veneration of the Virgin Mary to an extent regarded as inappropriate or even idolatrous.
parole.testo: From Latin Marīa or English Mary (“the Virgin Mary, the mother of Jesus Christ”) + -olatry, modelled after idolatry. The English word is cognate with French mariolâtrie, Italian mariolatria, Late Latin mariolatria.

parole.significato: A hemorrhoid.
parole.testo: From Latin marisca (“large kind of fig; haemorrhoid”).

parole.significato: The act of killing one's spouse, especially the murder of a husband by his wife.
parole.testo: From Latin maritus (“married, husband”) + -cide, from caedere (“to kill”).

parole.significato: Containing, or similar to, marble.
parole.testo: From Latin marmor (marble) + -aceous.

parole.significato: variegated like marble; marbly
parole.testo: From Latin marmoratus, past participle of marmorate (“to overlay with marble”).

parole.significato: A covering, casing or encrusting of marble
parole.testo: From Latin marmoratio.

parole.significato: Resembling marble or a marble statue; cold, smooth, white, etc.; marblelike.
parole.testo: From Latin marmoreus (“of, pertaining to, consisting of or made of marble; resembling marble; adorned with statues”) + English -al (suffix forming adjectives). parole.significato: marmoreal.
parole.testo: From Latin marmoreus (“of marble”), from marmor (“marble”) + -e- + -an.

parole.significato: Of, or pertaining to, marble.
parole.testo: From Latin marmor (“marble”) + -ic.

parole.significato: The metamorphosis of limestone into marble.
parole.testo: From Latin marmor (“marble”) + -osis.

parole.significato: An instrument for measuring the tides.
parole.testo: From Latin mare (“sea”) + -graph.

parole.significato: An ancient tribe who inhabited a region in central Italy, around the basin of the lake Fucinus.

parole.significato: A small Germanic tribe settled between the Rhine, Ruhr and Lippe rivers in northwest Germany.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Marsī.

parole.significato: A fossil crinoid of the genus Marsupites, resembling a purse.

parole.significato: The external pouch in which female marsupials rear and feed the young.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin marsūpium, from Ancient Greek μαρσίππιον (marsíppion), diminutive of μάρσιππος (mársippos, “pouch”), perhaps of Oriental origin.

parole.significato: A battle; a contest.
parole.testo: From Latin Mārs. See Mart.

parole.significato: A miniature greenhouse with a humidifier, used for growing mushrooms.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the planet Mars, or (science fiction) its imagined inhabitants.
parole.testo: From Latin Mārtius (“of or relating to the planet Mars”) + -an (adjective-forming suffix). parole.significato: The study of martyrs and martyrdom; the names and stories of martyrs, particularly
parole.testo: From martyr + -ology or from Latin martyrologium.

parole.significato: A shrine in honor of a (usually religious, notably Christian) martyr, possibly at his grave.

parole.significato: Synonym of masculinity.

parole.significato: Masturbation.
parole.testo: An alternate form of masturbation, apparently to resemble or provide overtones of Latin manus (“hand”) + stupro (“defile”). Compare manustupration.

parole.testo: A back-formation from masturbation, or else from Latin masturbātus (see -ate), past participle of masturbor. Further derivation of the Latin verb is uncertain; see masturbor for more.

parole.significato: Mother.
parole.testo: From Latin māter (“mother”), partly via Late Middle English matere. Doublet of mata and mother. Ancestor of matrix.

parole.significato: The Virgin Mary represented as the sorrowing mother.
parole.testo: From Latin mater dolorosa (“sorrowful mother”).

parole.significato: The female head of a household.
parole.testo: From Latin māter familiās (“mother of the household”).

parole.significato: The physical substances which create the natural world: matter, materials, substance, etc.

parole.significato: Synonym of pharmacology, particularly its development in early modern Europe.
parole.testo: From Latin māteria (“material”) + medica (“curative, medical”).

parole.significato: A materialist; one who believes only in physical matter, or the material world.

parole.significato: Consisting of matter; material.

parole.significato: The act of creating matter; materialization

parole.significato: Synonym of materteral (“of or relating to, or in the manner of, an aunt”)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin mātertera (“maternal aunt”), + from -ine (suffix meaning ‘of or relating to’ forming adjectives). Mātertera is derived from māter (“mother”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr (“mother”)) + ‑tera (feminine form of ‑ter (suffix forming nouns).

parole.significato: of or relating to matins

parole.significato: The process of becoming (and coming to inhabit the role of) a mother.

parole.significato: Exhibiting matrescence; becoming a mother.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin mātrēscēns, mātrēscō (“to become a mother”).

parole.significato: mother
parole.testo: From Latin māter.

parole.significato: A register of students who are enrolled.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin matricula (“register”).

parole.significato: To enroll as a member of a body, especially of a college or university.

parole.significato: A line of descent from a female ancestor to a descendant (of either sex) in which the individuals in all intervening ge…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mater (“mother”) + linea (“line”). By surface analysis, matri- + line.

parole.significato: Having mostly maternally inherited characteristics.
parole.testo: From Latin mātr- + -o- + Ancient Greek κλίνειν (klínein) + -ous.

parole.significato: In Ancient Rome, a wife of an honorable man.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mātrōna (“matron”), from māter (“mother; matron”). Doublet of matron.

parole.significato: A final exam that young adults (aged 18 or 19) take at the end of their secondary education in certain European countri…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mātūra.

parole.significato: A medicine or application which promotes suppuration.
parole.testo: From Latin maturans. See maturate.

parole.significato: To bring to ripeness or maturity; to ripen.
parole.testo: From Latin māturātus, perfect passive participle of māturō (“to ripen”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Compare French maturer.

parole.significato: Approaching maturity or ripeness.
parole.testo: From Latin maturescens, present participle of maturescere (“to become ripe”), verb inchoate from maturus. See mature (adjective). By surface analysis, mature + -escent.

parole.significato: Of or relating to early morning; occurring in the early morning; matutinal.
parole.testo: From Latin matutinus (“pertaining to morning”), from Matuta (“Roman goddess of the morning”); related to Latin maturus (“early”) (compare mature). By surface analysis, Matuta + -ine.

parole.significato: A large stately tomb or a building housing such a tomb or several tombs.
parole.testo: From Middle English mausoleum, from Latin Mausōlēum, from Ancient Greek Μαυσωλεῖον (Mausōleîon, “Mausoleum, the grand tomb built around 353–351 BCE at Halicarnassus for Mausolus, a ruler of Caria and satrap of the Achaemenid Empire; one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World”), from Μαύσωλος (Maú

parole.significato: Of or relating to Maxentius (c. 278 – 312), Roman emperor.
parole.testo: From Latin Maxentiānus. By surface analysis, Maxentius + -an.

parole.significato: Denotes a larger than usual version of an item.
parole.testo: Back-formation from maximum on the analogy of minimum and mini-, ultimately from Latin maximus (“large”).

parole.significato: Synonym of jaw.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Latin māxilla (“the jawbone, jaw”), diminutive of māla (“the cheekbone, jaw”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the jaw or jawbone.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin māxillāris (“of or belonging to the jaw”), from māxilla (“the jawbone, jaw”) + -āris (“-ar, -ary”, adjectival suffix); equivalent to maxilla + -ary.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the maxilla (jaw).
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin māxilla.

parole.significato: A music note typically equal to two longae (eight semibreves).
parole.testo: From Latin maxima (“greatest”). Doublet of maxim.

parole.significato: A Bachelor of Medicine and Surgery.
parole.testo: From Latin, initialism of medicinae baccalaureus et baccalaureus chirurgiae.

parole.significato: in my judgement
parole.testo: From Latin.

parole.significato: My fault, due to my error; I am to blame.
parole.testo: From the Latin phrase meā culpā (“through my fault”), ablative case of mea culpa (“my fault, guilt”), taken from the Confiteor, a traditional penitential prayer in Western Christianity.

parole.significato: One of the turns of a winding, crooked, or involved course.
parole.testo: From Latin Maeander, from Ancient Greek Μαίανδρος (Maíandros) – a river in Asia Minor (present day Turkey) known for its winding course (modern Turkish Menderes).

parole.significato: The branch of physics that deals with the action of forces on material objects with mass.
parole.testo: From Latin mēchanicus, from Ancient Greek μηχανικός (mēkhanikós), from μηχανή (mēkhanḗ, “machine, tool”).

parole.significato: A dark green mass, the contents of the fetal intestines during the later stages of mammalian gestation, that forms the…
parole.testo: From Latin mēcōnium (“opium; excrement of a newborn child”), from Ancient Greek μηκώνιον (mēkṓnion, “poppy-juice, opium”), from μήκων (mḗkōn, “poppy”).

parole.significato: Any of a Western Iranian people who inhabited the ancient region of Media.
parole.testo: From Latin Medus, from Ancient Greek Μῆδος (Mêdos).

parole.significato: The middle layer of the wall of a blood vessel or lymph vessel which is composed of connective and muscular tissue.

parole.significato: The means and institutions for publishing and broadcasting information.
parole.testo: Latinate plural of medium, particularly as a clipping of communications media and often reinterpreted as singular or mass noun, from Latin media, neuter plural form of medius (“middle”, adjective), from Proto-Italic *meðjos, from Proto-Indo-European *médʰyos (“between”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a mean or average.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mediālis (“middle”), from medius (“that is in the middle or midst”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix).

parole.significato: Relating to or befitting a mediator (one who mediates).
parole.testo: Latin mediatorius (equivalent to English mediator + -ial)

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to medicines; medical.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin medicus m (“of or belonging to healing, curative, medical; as a noun, medicus, masculine, a physician, doctor, surgeon”), Late Latin medica f (“a female physician, midwife”), from mederi (“to heal”).

parole.significato: Capable of being medicated
parole.testo: Latin medicabilis, from medicare, medicari, to heal, from medicus physician. See medical.

parole.significato: Designating the four largest moons of Jupiter (Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto), as named by Galileo in honour of his…
parole.testo: From post-classical Latin Mediceus (16th century; from the family name Medici) + -an.

parole.significato: Having the properties of medicine, or pertaining to medicine; medical.
parole.testo: From Latin medicīnālis. By surface analysis, medicine + -al.

parole.significato: Any of various European and North African herbs, of the genus Medicago, several of which are grown for fodder etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English medike, from Latin mēdica, from Ancient Greek μηδίκη (mēdíkē), short for Μηδικὴ πόα (Mēdikḕ póa, “Median grass”); so called because medick was imported from Media to Greece during the Greco-Persian Wars.

parole.significato: The interthalamic adhesion
parole.testo: Latin medius (“middle”) + English commissure.

parole.significato: The middle or inferior horn of each lateral ventricle of the brain.
parole.testo: From Latin medius (“middle”) + cornu (“horn”).

parole.significato: A jury or inquest consisting half of aliens and half of natives.
parole.testo: Latin, literally "half tongue".

parole.significato: The middle part; half; moiety.
parole.testo: From the late Middle English medietee (“a half”), borrowed from the Classical Latin medietās. Doublet of moiety.

parole.significato: The adoption of Persian interests by a Greek, regarded as treachery.
parole.testo: From Latin mēdismus, from Ancient Greek μηδισμός (mēdismós). By surface analysis, Mede + -ism.

parole.significato: To contemplate; to keep the mind fixed upon something; to study.
parole.testo: First attested in 1560; borrowed from Latin meditātus, perfect active participle of meditor (“to think or reflect upon, consider, design, purpose, intend”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), morphologically as if frequentative of medeor (“to heal, to cure, to remed

parole.significato: Mediterranean.
parole.testo: From Latin mediterraneus.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Mediterranean Sea and its surrounding region.
parole.testo: From Latin mediterrāneus (“inland”, from medius (“middle”) + terra (“earth, land”) + -āneus (adjectival suffix)) + -an.

parole.significato: A mostly enclosed sea that has limited exchange of deep water with outer oceans, and where the water circulation is dom…
parole.testo: PIE word  *médʰyos The word mediterranean is from Latin mediterrāneus (“inland, remote from the coast”) + English -an (suffix forming adjectives with the sense ‘of or pertaining to’). Mediterrāneus is derived from medius (“middle”) + terra (“dry land, ground”), modelled after Ancient Greek μεσόγαιος

parole.significato: The material of the surrounding environment, e.g. solid, liquid, gas, vacuum, or a specific substance such as a solvent.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin medium, neuter of medius (“middle”), from Proto-Italic *meðjos, from Proto-Indo-European *médʰyos (“between”). Compare middle. Doublet of mid, medio, media, and meson.

parole.significato: The soft inner part of something, especially the pith of a fruit.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin medulla (“pith, marrow”), perhaps from medius (“middle”).

parole.significato: Spinal cord.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin medulla spīnālis.

parole.significato: Irish elk
parole.testo: New Latin, from Ancient Greek, meaning "great horn".

parole.significato: Pertaining to, or in honour of, Cybele.
parole.testo: Latin Megalesius, from Ancient Greek word for "the Great", a surname of Cybele, the Magna Mater.

parole.significato: Of, from, or pertaining to, Megara
parole.testo: Derived from Latin megaricus, from Ancient Greek Μεγαρικός (Megarikós). Also Megara + -ic.

parole.significato: A sporangium which produces only megaspores
parole.testo: From neo-Latin, from mega- (“major”) + sporangium. The prefix is from Ancient Greek μέγας (mégas, “great”), and the base from spora + Ancient Greek ἀγγεῖον (angeîon, “vessel”).

parole.significato: Honey, when used as an ingredient in cosmetic products.
parole.testo: From Latin mel (“honey”). Doublet of mell.

parole.significato: A Scythian tribe which dwelt in Pontus
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Melanchlaenī, from Ancient Greek Μελάγχλαινοι (Melánkhlainoi).

parole.significato: Filled with or affected by melancholy—great sadness or depression, especially of a thoughtful or introspective nature.
parole.testo: From Latin melancholicus, from Ancient Greek μελαγχολικός (melankholikós, “atrabilious, impulsive, of atrabilious or melancholic temperament”), from μελαγχολία (melankholía, “melancholy”). By surface analysis, melancholy + -ic.

parole.significato: A tan or dark skin discoloration, particularly common in pregnant women, thought to be caused by the stimulation of mel…
parole.testo: From Latin melasma, from Ancient Greek μέλασμα (mélasma), from μελαίνειν (melaínein, “to blacken”) + -σμα (-sma), from μέλας (mélas, “black”).

parole.significato: A very large wine bottle (named after the King) with the capacity of about 18 liters, equivalent to 24 standard bottles.
parole.testo: From Latin Melchior, from Hebrew מלכיאור (“king of light”), from מלך (“king”) + אור (“light”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the genus Meleagris, including turkeys.
parole.testo: From Latin meleagris (“turkey”) + -ine.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Greek lyric verse.
parole.testo: From Latin melicus, from Koine Greek μελικός (melikós), from Ancient Greek μέλος (mélos, “song, lyric”).

parole.significato: Consisting of or containing honeylike matter; said of certain encysted tumours.
parole.testo: From Latin meliceris (“a kind of tumor”), from Ancient Greek μελικηρίς (melikērís, “honeycomb”), from μέλι (méli, “honey”) + κηρός (kērós, “wax”).

parole.significato: A fragrant plant of the genus Melilotus, often having small yellow or white flowers.
parole.testo: From Latin melilōtos, from Ancient Greek μελίλωτος (melílōtos), from μέλι (méli, “honey”) + λωτός (lōtós, “lotus”); later reinforced by Old French mellilote.

parole.significato: Having the qualities of or relating to a badger.
parole.testo: From Latin mēlīnus.

parole.significato: The view or doctrine that the world can be improved through human effort (often understood as an intermediate outlook b…
parole.testo: From Latin melior (“better”) + -ism. Reportedly coined by British author George Eliot in her letters, published in 1877.

parole.significato: A proponent of meliorism
parole.testo: From Latin melior (“better”) and English -ist. Reportedly coined by British author George Eliot in her letters, published in 1877.

parole.significato: The state or quality of being better; melioration.
parole.testo: From Latin melioritas, from melior. See meliorate.

parole.significato: A writ commanding a further enquiry into something.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: In 5th-century Syria and Egypt, a sobriquet applied to Chalcedonians by their opponents, denoting the Chalcedonians' fi…
parole.testo: From Latin Melchita, from Byzantine Greek Μελχίτης (Melkhítēs), from Classical Syriac ܡܠܟܝܐ (malkāyāʾ, “royal; royalist”) + Byzantine Greek -ῑ́της (-ī́tēs). See these for more.

parole.significato: Honey.
parole.testo: From Middle English mel, mell, melle, from Latin mell-, mel. Doublet of mel.

parole.significato: Pertaining to honey.
parole.testo: From Latin melleus (“of, pertaining to or resembling honey”), from mel (“honey”).

parole.significato: Of a plant or its parts: bearing any substance (such as nectar or pollen) which is collected by bees to produce honey.
parole.testo: PIE word  *mélit Learned borrowing from Latin mellifer (“honey-bearing, honey-producing, melliferous”) + English -ous (suffix forming adjectives denoting the presence of a quality, typically in abundance). Mellifer is derived from mel (“honey”) (plural form mella; ultimately from Proto-Indo-European

parole.significato: Producing honey.
parole.testo: From Latin mel, mellis (“honey”) + -ficare (“to make”) (in comp.). See -fy.

parole.significato: The production of honey by honey bees.
parole.testo: From Latin mellificare (“to make honey”). Compare French mellification. See mellific.

parole.significato: Mellifluous.
parole.testo: From Latin mellifluēns.

parole.significato: Flowing like honey.
parole.testo: From Middle English mellifluous, mellyfluous, from Latin mellifluus (“flowing like honey”) + -ous, from mel (“honey”) + fluō (“flow”). Compare superfluous and fluid, from same root, and with dulcet (“sweet speech”), alternative Latinate term with a similar meaning.

parole.significato: To embalm in honey.
parole.testo: From Latin mellificāre (“to make honey”), or mel (“honey”) + -ify.

parole.significato: Having the qualities of honey.
parole.testo: From Latin mel, mellis + -genous.

parole.significato: honeydew (sweet sticky substance found on plants)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin melligo.

parole.significato: Speaking sweetly or harmoniously.
parole.testo: From Latin mel, mellis (“honey”) + loquens (“speaking”), present participle of loqui (“to speak”).

parole.significato: A mineral that is the aluminium salt of mellitic acid; honeystone.
parole.testo: From Latin mell-, stem of mel (“honey”) + -ite.

parole.significato: Synonym of hyenanchin.
parole.testo: Latin mel (“honey”), and English toxin.

parole.significato: Relating to a member, in various senses; especially, (anatomy, zoology) pertaining to a limb.
parole.testo: From Latin membrum + -al.

parole.significato: A membrane.
parole.testo: From Latin membrāna (“membrane, parchment”). Doublet of membrane.

parole.significato: Resembling or having properties of a membrane.
parole.testo: From Latin membrānāceus.

parole.significato: A flexible enclosing or separating tissue forming a plane or film and separating two environments.
parole.testo: Late Middle English, borrowed from Latin membrāna (“skin or membrane that covers parts of the body”), from membrum (“a limb or member of the body”) + -āna. Doublet of membrana.

parole.significato: A small membrane
parole.testo: Anglicized form of Latin membrānula.

parole.significato: The penis.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin membrum virile.

parole.significato: A keepsake; an object kept as a reminder of a place or event.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mementō (“remember”), imperative form of meminī (“to remember”).

parole.significato: An emblematic object or personal ornament, such as a skull, used as a reminder of one's mortality.
parole.testo: From Latin mementō morī (literally “be mindful of dying”).

parole.significato: Objects that are connected to or remind their owner of past events.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin memorābilia (“things to be remembered”); its use as noun is after Ancient Greek ἀπομνημονεύματα (apomnēmoneúmata) of the neuter plural of memorābilis (“memorable”). Its English use is perhaps after the Latin title Memorabilia of Xenophon’s collection of Socratic dialogues.

parole.significato: Worthy to be remembered; very important or remarkable.
parole.testo: From Middle English memorable, memorrable, from Latin memorābilis, from memorō (“to bring to remembrance”), from memor (“mindful, remembering”). By surface analysis, memory + -able, see memory. Doublet of memorabile (singular of memorabilia).

parole.significato: A short note serving as a reminder.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin memorandum, neuter of memorandus (“to be remembered”).

parole.significato: an oral narrative from memory relating a personal experience, especially the precursor of a legend.
parole.testo: From Latin memorātus, past participle of memorāre (“to bring to remembrance, mention, recount”), from memor (“remembering”); see memory.

parole.significato: One of the five canons of classical rhetoric: the discipline of memory and recall.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin memoria, from memor (“mindful, remembering”). Doublet of memoir and memory.

parole.significato: Synonym of mnemotechny.
parole.testo: Latin [Term?]

parole.significato: By, or from, memory; by heart.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin memoriter.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Memphis or the Memphites.
parole.testo: From Middle English memphetik, from Latin Memphīticus. By surface analysis, Memphite + -ic.

parole.significato: The action of telling lies in an artful way
parole.testo: From Latin mendācitās (“falsehood”), and -loquence from Latin loquor (“to speak”).

parole.significato: Depending on alms for a living.
parole.testo: From Middle English mendicant, from Latin mendīcāns, present participle of mendīcō (“beg”). Compare French mendiant.

parole.significato: To beg.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mendīcātus, perfect passive participle of mendīcō (“to beg”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Of or relating to a Cambrian lithostratigraphic group in west Wales.
parole.testo: From Latin Menevia (“St Davids, a city in Wales”).

parole.significato: The three membranes that envelop the brain and spinal cord.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mēningēs, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek μῆνιγξ (mêninx, “membrane”).

parole.significato: A reactive mind, a conscious knowing by the individual that an act was committed, either by themselves or by another.
parole.testo: From Latin mēns + reus (literally “guilty mind”), from the English common law precept Actus non facit reum nisi mens rea sit ("The act does not make a person guilty unless the mind is also guilty").

parole.significato: In planetary geology, a large mesa-like area of raised land.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin mēnsa (“table, altar”). Doublet of mesa.

parole.significato: Occurring once in a month; monthly.
parole.testo: From Latin mensis (“month”).

parole.significato: Belonging to the table; transacted at table.
parole.testo: Latin mensalis, from mensa (“table”).

parole.significato: The discharge of blood and cellular tissue that flows from the inner lining of the uterus out through the vagina, occur…
parole.testo: From Latin mēnsis (“month”), the plural being mēnsēs (“months”), corresponding to the approximately month-long span of the menstrual cycle. Compare month.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the menses.
parole.testo: From Middle English menstruall, from Latin mēnstruālis, from mēnstrua (“menses”), from neuter plural of mēnstruus (“of a month, monthly, of menstruation”), from mēnsis (“month”) + -ālis (“-al”); see moon.

parole.significato: The menses; menstrual discharge.
parole.testo: From Latin mēnstruum (“menstrual discharge”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a month.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mēnsuālis (“monthly”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to measure or measurement.
parole.testo: From Latin mēnsūrālis, from mēnsūra (“measure”) + -ālis.

parole.significato: To measure absolutely the height, latitude and longitude of a point on the earth.
parole.testo: First attested in 1653; borrowed from Latin mēnsūrātus, perfect passive participle of mēnsūrō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of measure.

parole.significato: sycosis
parole.testo: From Latin mentāgra, from mentum (“chin”) + Ancient Greek ἄγρα (ágra, “a catching”).

parole.significato: Any of the mint genus Mentha, mints and similar species.
parole.testo: From the genus name, Mentha, from Latin mentha (“mint”). Doublet of mint.

parole.significato: A cyclic monoterpene alcohol; the major component of the essential oil of peppermint; used in pharmaceutical preparatio…
parole.testo: From Latin mentha (“mint”) + -ol.

parole.significato: Brain-washing, conditioning people to abandon their beliefs.
parole.testo: From Latin mēns (“mind”) or mentālis (“mental”) + -cide (“killing”), from Latin -cīdium, by analogy to homicide, genocide, etc. Coined during the 1950s.

parole.significato: A female mentor.
parole.testo: From Latin mentrix or mentor + -trix.

parole.significato: A penis.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mentula.

parole.significato: The chin.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin mentum (“the chin”). Doublet of menton.

parole.significato: As is my wont (custom, habit).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin meō mōre (“as is my custom”).

parole.significato: Foul-smelling or noxious, particularly of a gas or atmosphere.
parole.testo: From Latin mephīticus, from mephītis; compare French méphitique.

parole.significato: A poisonous or foul-smelling gas, especially as emitted from the earth; an unpleasant smell.
parole.testo: From Latin mefītis, mephītis, from the name of a Samnite goddess who personified the poisonous gases emitted from swamps and volcanoes.

parole.significato: Without mixture or adulteration; strong; racy.
parole.testo: From Latin meracus, from merus (“pure, inmixed”).

parole.significato: Capable of being bought or sold.
parole.testo: From Latin mercabilis, from mercari (“to trade, traffic, buy”). See merchant.

parole.significato: The univalent radical -SH
parole.testo: From mercaptan, from Latin mercurius captans (“mercury capturing”).

parole.significato: an organosulfur compound that contains a carbon-bonded sulfhydryl or sulphydryl
parole.testo: The term mercaptan was introduced in 1832 by the Danish chemist William Christopher Zeise and is derived from the Latin mercurium captāns (capturing mercury) because the thiolate group bonds very strongly with mercury compounds.

parole.significato: Market; trade.
parole.testo: From Latin mercātus. See market.

parole.significato: Synonym of Mercator projection.
parole.testo: From Gerardus Mercator, Latinized name of Gerard de Cremer (1512–1594), Flemish cartographer and mathematician, from Latin mercātor (“merchant”).

parole.significato: An orthomorphic map projection, in which meridians appear at right-angles to the equator, and lines of latitude are hor…
parole.testo: From Gerardus Mercator, Latinized name of Gerard de Cremer (1512–1594), Flemish cartographer and mathematician, from Latin mercātor (“merchant”).

parole.significato: The tendency of transnational commerce to operate outside any system of national laws, making use, instead, of a system…
parole.testo: From Latin mercator (“merchant, trader”) + -ism.

parole.significato: commerce; trade
parole.testo: From Latin mercatura (“commerce”).

parole.significato: One motivated by gain, especially monetary.
parole.testo: From Middle English mercenarye (“someone paid to work, hireling”), from Latin mercēnārius (“hired for money”), from mercēs (“reward, wages, price”).

parole.significato: A male given name from Latin.
parole.testo: From Latin Mercurius, of uncertain origin.

parole.significato: Quicksilver, mercury. (No longer capitalized, as the name of the metal is no longer recognized as that of the planet.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English Mercurie, from Latin Mercurius.

parole.significato: Senses relating to the metal.
parole.testo: The noun is derived from Middle English mercurie (“metallic chemical element, quicksilver; a plant, probably goosefoot (genus Chenopodium); (possibly) dog’s mercury (Mercurialis perennis); etc.”), borrowed from Late Latin mercurius (“metallic chemical element, quicksilver”), Latin Mercurius (“Mercur

parole.significato: Dung-eating, coprophagous.
parole.testo: From Latin merda (“excrement”) + -vorous.

parole.significato: Tastelessly gaudy; superficially attractive but having in reality no value or substance; falsely alluring.
parole.testo: From Latin meretrīcius, from meretrīx (“harlot, prostitute”), from mereō (“earn, deserve, merit”) (English merit) + -trīx (“(female agent)”) (English -trix).

parole.significato: A prostitute in Ancient Rome.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin meretrīx.

parole.significato: To combine into a whole.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin mergō (“to dip; dip in; plunge; sink down into; immerse; overwhelm”).
