parole.testo: From Latin nūlliparus. By surface analysis, null + parous.

parole.significato: Any of various algae which secrete calcium carbonate, such as those of the order Corallinales.
parole.testo: From Latin nullus (“none”) + porus (“pore”).

parole.significato: Describing an action which has no side effect. Queries are typically nullipotent: they return useful data, but do not c…
parole.testo: Latin roots, Latin nullus (“not any”) + potent (“having power”) – literally, “having no power”.

parole.significato: No one's property.
parole.testo: From Latin nūllīus (“of no one”) (genitive of nūllus) + in + bonīs (“goods, property”) (ablative of bōna).

parole.significato: A foundational principle dictating that a person cannot be prosecuted or punished for an act unless that specific condu…
parole.testo: Latin.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the ancient Celtiberian city of Numantia.
parole.testo: From Latin Numantīnus.

parole.significato: A divinity, especially a local or presiding god.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nūmen.

parole.significato: Able to be counted; countable.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin numerābilis.

parole.significato: Numerical skill.
parole.testo: From numerate + -cy, from Latin numerus; coined with numerate in 1959 by the UK Committee on Education, presided over by Sir Geoffrey Crowther.

parole.significato: A symbol that is not a word and represents a number, such as the Arabic numerals 1, 2, 3 or the Roman numerals I, V, X,…
parole.testo: As an adjective, from Middle English numeral, numerall, from Latin numerālis (“pertaining to a number”), from numerus (“a number”). As a noun, via Middle French numeral.

parole.significato: Relating to numbers or numbering.
parole.testo: From Latin numerarius, from numerus (“number”). Doublet of numéraire.

parole.significato: To count.
parole.testo: From Latin numerātus, perfect past participle of numerō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix, of participial origin)). By surface analysis, Latin numerus + -ate.

parole.significato: Numbered; counted.
parole.testo: From Middle English numerat, numerate, from Latin numerātus, perfect past participle of numerō (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix, of participial origin)).

parole.significato: The act of counting or numbering; enumeration.
parole.testo: From Middle English numeracioun, from Latin numerātiō. By surface analysis, numerate + -ion.

parole.significato: The sign ⟨ № ⟩.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin numerō, the ablative singular form of numerus (“number”).

parole.significato: The combining form of number.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin numerus (“number”) + -o-.

parole.significato: The condition of being numerous.
parole.testo: From numerous + -ity, from Latin numerositas.

parole.significato: An indefinite large number of.
parole.testo: From Middle English numerous from Latin numerōsus (“numerous, abundant; harmonious”), from numerus (“number”). Doublet of numerose. Analyzeable as numero- + -ous.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to coins or money.
parole.testo: From Latin nummarius (“pertaining to money”), from nummus (“a coin, a piece of money”), akin to Ancient Greek νόμος (nómos, “a custom, law”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to coins or money.
parole.testo: From Latin nummulus (“(small amount of) money”) + English -ar (suffix forming adjectives with the sense ‘of, pertaining to, or near’). Nummulus is the diminutive of nummus (“a coin; piece of money”) + -ulus (diminutive suffix); while nummus is from Doric Greek νοῦμμος (noûmmos), from Ancient Greek ν

parole.significato: The arrangement or aggregation of red blood cells into rouleaux, resembling piles of coins.
parole.testo: From Latin nummulus (“money”) + -ation. By surface analysis, numm(us) + -ule + -ate + -ion.

parole.significato: Any of a range of low-value copper coins issued by the Roman and Byzantine empires during Late Antiquity.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nummus. Doublet of luma.

parole.significato: Performed so as to have the same legal force and effect as if it had been performed at an earlier time.
parole.testo: Latin "now for then"

parole.significato: Eternal existence as an attribute of God.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nunc (“now”) + stāns (“staying, remaining”).

parole.significato: The status or rank of a nuncio (diplomatic representative of the Roman Catholic Church).
parole.testo: From Latin nūnciāre, nūntiāre (“to announce, report”), from nūncius, nūntius (“messenger”). Compare French nonciature, Italian nunziatura.

parole.significato: A nuntius.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nūncius, medieval form of nūntius (“messenger”).

parole.significato: To dedicate.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nuncupātus, past participle of nuncupō (“pronounce, name as heir”), contraction of nōmen (“name”) and capiō (“take, seize”).

parole.significato: Nuncupative; oral rather than written.
parole.testo: From Latin nuncupāt-, past participial stem of nuncupō, + -ory. Compare Late Latin nuncupātōrius.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a nundine
parole.testo: From Latin nundinalis.

parole.significato: nundinal
parole.testo: From Latin nundinarius.

parole.significato: Traffic at fairs; buying and selling.
parole.testo: From Latin nundinatio.

parole.significato: A market or fair held every eight days, particularly (historical) in Roman contexts.
parole.testo: From Latin nundinae (“ninth-days”), a clipped form of nundinae feriae (“ninth-day festivals”), from its observance every eighth day (9 counting inclusively) and from the Latin practice of treating most recurring calendrical days as plurals.

parole.significato: A messenger.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nūntius (“messenger”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to wedding and marriage.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nūptiālis (“pertaining to marriage”), from nūptiae (“wedding”), from nūbō (“to marry, to take as husband”).

parole.significato: A wedding ceremony.
parole.testo: From nuptial, borrowed from Latin nūptiālis (“pertaining to marriage”), from nūptiae (“wedding”) (also plural only), from nūpta, from nūbō (“to marry, to take as husband”), from Proto-Indo-European *sneubho-, *snewbʰ- (“to marry, wed”). Cognate with French noces and Italian nozze.

parole.significato: To rock or sway involuntarily.
parole.testo: First attested in 1880; back-formation from nutation (1610s) on the basis of -ate (verb-forming suffix), from Latin nūtātiō (“a nodding”), from nūtō (“to nod”), from Proto-Indo-European *neu-. Compare mutate.

parole.significato: A bobbing motion that accompanies the precession of a spinning rigid body.
parole.testo: 1610s, from Latin nūtātiō (“nodding”), from nūtō (“to nod”). Compare mutation.

parole.significato: feeding or nourishment
parole.testo: From Latin nutricatio, from nutricare, nutricari (“to suckle, nourish”), from nutrix (“a nurse”).

parole.significato: Relating to a nurse.
parole.testo: From Latin nūtrīx + -al.

parole.significato: A source of nourishment, such as food, that can be metabolized by an organism to give energy and build tissue.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin nūtriēns, present participle of nūtriō (“to suckle, nourish, foster”).

parole.significato: A source of nourishment; food.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English nutriment, from Latin nūtrīmentum.

parole.significato: Providing nutrients; healthy to eat or drink.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin nūtrītius, from nūtrītus, from nūtrīre.

parole.significato: nutrition; nourishment
parole.testo: Latin nutritura.

parole.significato: A nurse, primarily a wet nurse or similar hired child carer.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin nūtrīx.

parole.significato: A strychnine tree (Strychnos nux-vomica), an evergreen tree found in southeastern Asia.
parole.testo: From Latin nux (“nut”) and vomica (“vomiting”).

parole.significato: A nymph.
parole.testo: From Latin nympha, from Ancient Greek νύμφη (númphē, “bride, nymph”). Doublet of nymph.

parole.significato: the European white water lily.
parole.testo: From Latin nymphaea, from Ancient Greek νυμφαῖα (numphaîa), feminine singular form of νυμφαῖος (numphaîos, “sacred to the nymphs”), from νύμφη (númphē, “nymph”). Sense 2 is a semantic loan from translingual Nymphaea, from the same Latin and Greek.

parole.significato: A shrine consecrated to water nymphs, often with a fountain.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin nymphaeum, from Ancient Greek νυμφαῖον (numphaîon), a substantivisation of νυμφαῖος (numphaîos, “sacred to the nymphs”), from νύμφη (númphē, “nymph”).

parole.significato: a halfpenny
parole.testo: From Latin ob, abbreviation of obolus.

parole.significato: Against; facing; a combining prefix found in verbs of Latin origin.
parole.testo: From Latin ob-.

parole.significato: Synonym of died, particularly used with historical dating.
parole.testo: From Latin ob., abbreviating obiit (“he or she passed on”) or obiter (“incidentally”).

parole.significato: To walk about; to wander aimlessly.
parole.testo: First attested in 1614; borrowed from Latin obambulātus, perfect passive participle of obambulō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Wandering about; a casual outing.
parole.testo: From obambulate + -ion. From Latin obambulatio.

parole.significato: To cover.
parole.testo: From Latin obducere, obductum; ob (see ob-) + ducere (“to lead”).

parole.significato: The act of drawing or laying over, as a covering.
parole.testo: Latin obductio; see Latin ob, ductio.

parole.significato: Stubbornly persistent, generally in wrongdoing; refusing to reform or repent.
parole.testo: First attested in the 1450s, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English obdurat(e), borrowed from Latin obdūrātus (“hardened”), perfect passive participle of obdūrō (“to harden”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from ob- (“against”) + dūrō (“to harden, render hard”), from dūrus (“hard”).

parole.significato: To harden; to obdure.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin obdūrātus, see Etymology 1 and -ate (verb-forming suffix) for more

parole.significato: A hardening of the heart; hardness of heart.
parole.testo: From Latin obduratio.

parole.significato: Of or related to obedience; or obedient.
parole.testo: From Latin *obedientialis, from obēdientia + -ālis. Compare French obédientiel.

parole.significato: A wandering about.
parole.testo: Latin oberrate to wander about.

parole.significato: Extremely overweight, especially: weighing more than 20% (for men) or 25% (for women) over their conventionally ideal w…
parole.testo: From Latin obēsus, derived from obedō (“to devour, eat away”), from ob (“away”) + edō (“to eat”).

parole.significato: A small, crescentic fold of white matter that covers the inferior angle of the floor of the fourth ventricle.
parole.testo: From Latin obex (“barrier, wall”).

parole.significato: To make firm or stubborn.
parole.testo: From Latin obfirmare (“to make steadfast”).

parole.significato: stubbornness; obduracy.
parole.testo: Latin obfirmatio.

parole.significato: The act or process of obfuscating, or obscuring the perception of something; the concept of concealing the meaning of a…
parole.testo: From Middle English obfuscacioun, from Latin obfuscātiō, obfuscātiōnem, from obfuscāre (“to darken”), from ob (“over”) + fuscāre (“to make dark”), from fuscus (“dark”).

parole.significato: Incidentally; in passing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin obiter.

parole.significato: An incidental remark; especially (law) a statement or remark in a court's judgment that is not essential to the disposi…
parole.testo: From Latin obiter dictum (“something said by the way”).

parole.significato: A smaller piece, written during the process of writing a larger piece, which is supplementary or incidental to that lar…
parole.testo: From Latin: obiter scrīptum (“[a thing] written on the way”), from obiter (“on the way, incidentally”) + scrīptum (“text, anything written, writing”). Formed on the pattern of the earlier obiter dictum, with which it is often paired (especially in the plural).

parole.significato: A person who objects to something.
parole.testo: Partly from Latin obiector and partly from object + -or.

parole.significato: A woman who objects; a female objector; compare objectress.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin obiectrīx. By surface analysis, object + -trix.

parole.significato: Attracted to inanimate objects, especially sexually or romantically, but can be other types such as platonic or familia…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin obiectum. Coined by Eija-Ritta Eklof Berliner-Mauer in the early 1970s as part of the terms objectum-sexual and objectum-sexuality. Doublet of object and objet.

parole.significato: One who makes objection; an objector.
parole.testo: From Latin obiiciēns, present participle of obiiciō (“to object”).

parole.significato: To rebuke or scold strongly.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin obiūrgātus, perfect passive participle of obiūrgō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ob- (“to, against”) + iūrgō (“to dispute, chide”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éǵeti.

parole.significato: A strong rebuke or scolding.
parole.testo: From Latin obiūrgō.

parole.significato: Strongly rebuking or scolding.
parole.testo: From Latin obiūrgātōrius, from obiūrgō (“to rebuke”).

parole.significato: To offer as either a gift or an oblation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin oblātus, perfect passive participle of offerō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of offer.

parole.significato: The act of barking at someone or something; (figuratively) the act of ranting at someone or something; an instance of t…
parole.testo: From Latin oblātrātio, from oblātrāre (“to bark at, to rail against”) + -tiō (“-tion: forming abstract nouns”), from ob- (“ob-: against, at”) + lātrāre (“to bark, to rant”). Equivalent to ob- + latration.

parole.significato: Submitted for publication; especially, of academic articles, submitted for peer review before publication.
parole.testo: From Latin oblātum, past participle of offerō (“bring to, offer”), from ob (“in front of”) + ferō (“bring”). Compare oblate.

parole.significato: To delight; to please greatly.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin oblectātus, perfect passive participle of oblectō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and ob-.

parole.significato: The act of pleasing highly, or state of being greatly pleased; delight.
parole.testo: From Latin oblectātiō (“delight, amusement”). Equivalent to oblectate + -ion.

parole.significato: To bind, compel, constrain, or oblige by a social, legal, or moral tie.
parole.testo: First attested in 1533; borrowed from Latin obligātus, perfect passive participle of obligō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of oblige, taken through French.

parole.significato: Requiring a (specified) way of life, habitat, etc.
parole.testo: Partly inherited from Middle English obligat(e) (“bound (by any obligation), obliged”), partly directly borrowed from Latin obligātus, see Etymology 1, -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-forming suffix) for more.

parole.significato: Imposing obligation, legally, morally, or otherwise; binding; mandatory.
parole.testo: From Middle English obligatorie, from Latin obligatōrius.

parole.significato: That which is, or must be, granted.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin obligātum.

parole.significato: The act of becoming oblique; a turning to one side
parole.testo: From Latin obliquātiō, from obliquō (“to turn obliquely”). See oblique.

parole.significato: An obliquus muscle; a muscle running obliquely.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin oblīquus.

parole.significato: Producing obstruction due to inflammation and fibrosis.
parole.testo: From Latin oblitterare (“to hide writing”), from ob (“out”) + littera (“letter”).

parole.significato: Completely destroyed or erased; effaced, obliterated.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin obliterātus (see more at Etymology 1 and -ate (adjective-forming suffix, of participial origin)).

parole.significato: Lacking awareness; unmindful; unaware, unconscious of.
parole.testo: From Middle English oblivious, from Latin oblīviōsus (“forgetful, oblivious”), formed from oblīvium (“forgetfulness, oblivion”) + -ōsus (“full of, overly, prone to”), from oblīvīscor (“to forget”).

parole.significato: Oblivion.
parole.testo: From Latin oblīvium.

parole.significato: A gainsayer; a critic.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin oblocūtor. First attested in 1563.

parole.significato: Having a length and width that are different; not square or circular.
parole.testo: From Middle English oblong, oblonge, borrowed from Latin oblongus.

parole.significato: opposition; resistance
parole.testo: From Latin ob + luctor (“to struggle”) + -ation.

parole.significato: Silence; inability or refusal to speak.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin obmūtēscō.

parole.significato: Silent; unable or refusing to speak.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin obmutescens, obmutescentis.

parole.significato: Extremely offensive or unpleasant; very annoying, contemptible, or odious.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin obnoxiōsus.

parole.significato: Covered or darkened as with a cloud; overclouded; obscured.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin obnūbilātus, perfect passive participle of obnūbilō (“to cover with clouds or fog”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ob- + nūbilō (“be cloudy”), from nūbēs (“cloud”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)newdʰ- (“to cover”). By surface

parole.significato: A silver coin minted in Ancient Greece, valued at a sixth of a drachma.
parole.testo: From Latin obolus, from Ancient Greek ὀβολός (obolós), from ὀβελός (obelós). Doublet of obole and pul.

parole.significato: The act of creeping upon with secrecy or by surprise.
parole.testo: From Latin obreptio, from obrepo, obreptum (“to creep up to”), from ob (see prefix ob-) + repo (“to creep”).

parole.significato: Done or obtained by surprise, with secrecy, or by concealment of the truth.
parole.testo: From Latin obreptitus. See obreption.

parole.significato: To annul a law by enacting a new law, as opposed to repealing the former law.
parole.testo: From Latin obrogō.

parole.significato: Nearly but not completely round; roundish.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin obrotundus (“somewhat round”), from ob- (“towards; against”) + rotundus. Analyzeable as ob- + rotund.

parole.significato: Something that is obscene.
parole.testo: From obscene + -ity, from Latin obscenitas.

parole.significato: A state of opposition to human progress or enlightenment.
parole.testo: From Latin obscūrans, from obscūrō (“to cover, darken, obscure”) + -ism.

parole.significato: The state of being obscured.
parole.testo: From Latin obscūrātiō. By surface analysis, obscure + -ation.

parole.significato: Synonym of ignotum per ignotius (“explaining an obscure subject by resort to one even more obscure”).
parole.testo: From Latin obscūrum per obscūrius, “[to explain] the obscure by the more obscure”.

parole.significato: Compliance, obsequiousness, deference, willingness to serve.
parole.testo: Probably from Latin obsequentia, equivalent to obsequy + -ence.

parole.significato: Obedient; submissive; obsequious.
parole.testo: From Latin obsequens, present participle of obsequi, from ob (see ob-) + sequi. See sequence.

parole.significato: Funeral rites.
parole.testo: Plural of obsequy; from Middle English obsequias, obsequies, obsequyes, from Latin obsequiae.

parole.significato: Excessively eager and attentive to please or to obey instructions; fawning, subservient, servile.
parole.testo: From Middle English obsequyous, from Latin obsequiōsus (“complaisant, obsequious”), from obsequium (“compliance”), from obsequor (“comply with, yield to”), from ob (“in the direction of, towards”) + sequor (“follow”) (cf. sequel).

parole.significato: A thing to be observed.
parole.testo: From Latin observandum, gerundive of observo.

parole.significato: An observatory.
parole.testo: From Latin observātōrium.

parole.significato: To be preoccupied with a single topic or emotion.
parole.testo: From Latin obsessus, perfect passive participle of obsideō (“sit on or in, remain, besiege”), from ob- (“before”) + sedeō (“to sit”); see sit, session, etc.; compare assess, possess.

parole.significato: The quality of being obsessed; an unshakeable feeling that one topic or activity must be pursued above other interests.
parole.testo: From Latin obsessio (“a besieging”), from obsidere (“to besiege”); see obsess. Equivalent to obsess + -ion.

parole.significato: A type of naturally occurring black glass produced by volcanoes.
parole.testo: From Latin obsidianus; named after Obsidius, who was, according to Pliny, the Roman who discovered the stone in Aethiopia.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a siege.
parole.testo: From Middle English obsidional, from Latin obsidiōnālis, from obsidiō (“siege, blockade”), from obsidēre (“beset, besiege, hem in”).

parole.significato: To seal; to confirm, as by a seal or stamp.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin obsignō. Doublet of obsignate.

parole.significato: To seal or ratify.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin obsignātus, perfect passive participle of obsignō (“to seal”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of obsign.

parole.significato: The act of sealing or ratifying.
parole.testo: Latin obsignatio.

parole.significato: To become or be rendered obsolete; to undergo obsolescence.
parole.testo: From Latin obsolescere (“to wear out, fall into disuse, grow old, decay”), from obs- + olesco (“to grow”). Compare adolescent.

parole.significato: The state of being obsolete—no longer in use; gone into disuse; disused or neglected.
parole.testo: From Latin obsolēscēns (present participle of obsolēscere).

parole.significato: In the process of becoming obsolete, but not obsolete yet.
parole.testo: From Latin obsolēscēns.

parole.significato: No longer in use or no longer useful; now disused or neglected (often in favour of something newer, better, or more fas…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin obsolētus (“worn out, gone out of use”), past participle of obsolēscere (“to wear out, fall into disuse, grow old, decay”); see obsolesce.

parole.significato: A caterer, a manciple.
parole.testo: From Latin.

parole.significato: Opposition, impediment, or obstruction.
parole.testo: From Latin obstantia, from obstans, present participle of obstare. See obstacle.

parole.significato: Of or relating to obstetrics (the care of women during and after pregnancy).
parole.testo: From Medical Latin obstetricus (“belonging to a midwife”), from Latin obstētrīx (“midwife”).

parole.significato: Serving to assist childbirth; obstetric.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin obstetrīcius.

parole.significato: A midwife.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin obstetrīx.

parole.significato: Stubbornly adhering to an opinion, purpose, or course, usually with implied unreasonableness; persistent.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English obstinat(e) (“obstinate, stubborn”), from Latin obstinātus, perfect passive participle of obstinō (“set one's mind firmly upon, resolve”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from ob (“before”) + *stinare, from stare (“to stand”). Doublet of ostinato.

parole.significato: stubbornness
parole.testo: From Latin obstinatio, obstinatione ,from obstinātus, past participle of obstinō (“set one's mind firmly upon, resolve”).

parole.significato: Attended by, or making, a loud and tumultuous noise; boisterous.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin obstreperus, first attested circa 17th c. Compare obstropulous.

parole.significato: The state of being constrained, bound, obliged, or obligated.
parole.testo: From Latin obstringere, obstrictum (“to bind to or about”).

parole.significato: To block or fill (a passage) with obstacles or an obstacle.
parole.testo: From Latin past participle stem obstruct- (“blocked up”), from verb obstruere, from ob (“against”) + struere (“pile up, build”).

parole.significato: The act of obstructing, or state of being obstructed.
parole.testo: From Latin obstructio (“hindrance”), from obstruo (“build against, block, stop”).

parole.significato: Causing obstruction; blocking up.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin obstruēns, obstruentis.

parole.significato: stupefaction
parole.testo: Latin obstupefacere (“to stupefy”).

parole.significato: covered; protected
parole.testo: From Latin obtectus, past participle of obtegere (“to cover over”).

parole.significato: To obey, comply or submit to.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin obtemperātus, perfect passive participle of obtemperō (“to obey”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Doublet of obtemper.

parole.significato: To oppose; to hold out in opposition.
parole.testo: From Latin obtendere, obtentum (“to stretch or place before or against”), from ob (see ob-) + tendere (“to stretch”).

parole.significato: The act of darkening, or darkness.
parole.testo: From Latin obtenebrate (“to make dark”).

parole.significato: The act of obtending.
parole.testo: From Latin obtentio. See obtend.

parole.significato: The act of obtaining.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin obtentiōnem, accusative of obtentiō.

parole.significato: To implore, beseech, plead, beg.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin obtestor.

parole.significato: The act of obtesting; supplication; protestation.
parole.testo: From Latin obtestatio.

parole.significato: To proffer (something) by force; to impose (something) on someone or into some area.
parole.testo: From Latin obtrūdō (“thrust off or against”), from ob- (“ob-”) + trūdō (“thrust”).

parole.significato: To truncate or lop the head off, to decapitate (also figurative).

parole.testo: From Latin oryza (“rice”) + -ol.

parole.significato: A particular strobilurin fungicide.
parole.testo: From Latin oryza (“rice”) and strobilurin.

parole.significato: Having a diet rich in rice.
parole.testo: From Latin orȳza (“rice”) + -vorous.

parole.significato: Synonym of bone.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin os (“bone”).

parole.significato: An opening or entrance to a passage, particularly one at either end of the cervix, internal (to the uterus) or external…
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin ōs (“mouth”).

parole.significato: The baubellum.
parole.testo: From Latin os (“bone”) + clitoridis (“of the clitoris”).

parole.significato: Ossified cardiac cartilagenous tissue, typically parts of the cardiac skeleton.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin os cordis (literally “heart bone”).

parole.significato: Synonym of hip bone.
parole.testo: From Latin os (“bone”) and coxa (“hip”).

parole.significato: The baculum.
parole.testo: From Latin ōs (“bone”) + pēnis (genitive of pēnis (“penis”)). Literally, “bone of the penis”.

parole.significato: Against; facing; a combining prefix found in verbs of Latin origin.
parole.testo: From Latin ob.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Oscan language or Oscan people, or their writing system.
parole.testo: From Latin Osci, Opsci ("worshippers of Ops"), an Italic harvest goddess, related to Latin ops, opis (“riches, wealth, plenty”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ep-os- (“work”), from the verbal root *h₃ep- (“to work”).

parole.significato: An ancient Italic people from Campania in Italy.
parole.testo: From Latin Osci, worshippers of Ops (“earth goddess, fertility deity”), from ops (“plenty”). Known by the Greeks as Ὀπικοί (Opikoí), Ὀσκοί (Oskoí).

parole.significato: To swing back and forth, especially if with a regular rhythm.
parole.testo: First attested in 1726; borrowed from Latin ōscillātus, perfect passive participle of Latin ōscillō (“to swing”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ōscillum (“a swing”), usually identified with ōscillum (“a little face or mask hung on a tree that sways with the wind”), diminutive of ōs (“mouth,

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to songbirds (suborder Passeri).
parole.testo: From Latin oscen (“songbird”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Oscines, or songbirds (birds of the clade Passeri).
parole.testo: Latin oscen (“songbird”)

parole.significato: yawning or gaping
parole.testo: From Latin ōscitāns, present participle of ōscitō. Compare French oscitant.

parole.significato: To gape or yawn.
parole.testo: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin ōscitātus, perfect passive participle of ōscitō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ōs (“the mouth”) + citō (“to cause to move”).

parole.significato: The act of yawning or gaping.
parole.testo: Latin ōscitātiō, from ōscitō (“to gape”).

parole.significato: Adhering closely; applied to certain creeping animals, such as caterpillars.
parole.testo: From Latin osculans, osculantis, present participle of osculari (“to kiss”). See osculate.

parole.significato: To kiss.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ōsculātus, perfect active participle of ōsculor (“to kiss”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ōsculum (“a kiss”) + -or (verbal suffix), from ōs (“mouth”) + -culum (diminutive suffix). See also oscillate.

parole.significato: Relating to kissing.
parole.testo: From Latin ōsculātus.

parole.significato: The action of kissing.
parole.testo: From Latin ōsculātiō (“a kissing”), from ōsculor (“to kiss”). By surface analysis, osculate + -ion.

parole.significato: A religious tablet, usually carrying a representation of Christ or the Virgin Mary, which is kissed by the priest durin…
parole.testo: From Latin ōsculātōrium.

parole.significato: A small opening or orifice.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ōsculum (“little mouth”).

parole.significato: A witch's supposed ritual greeting of kissing the anus of the Devil.
parole.testo: Latin, "shameful kiss".

parole.significato: Of or relating to Andreas Osiander (1498–1552), German Lutheran theologian.
parole.testo: From the Latin Osiandriānus, from Osiander.

parole.significato: One of a pair of scent organs in the larvae of certain swallowtail butterflies.
parole.testo: New Latin, from Ancient Greek ὀσμή (osmḗ, “smell”), ὀσμητός (osmētós, “smelled”) + -τήριον (-tḗrion).

parole.significato: An ossuary.
parole.testo: From Latin ossārium.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or made of bone; bony.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin osseus (“bony, (attributive) bone”), from os (“bone”) + -eus.

parole.significato: A small bone (or bony structure), especially one of the three of the middle ear.
parole.testo: Late 16th century, from Latin ossiculum (“little bone, ossicle”) from os (“bone”).

parole.significato: An ossicle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ossiculum (“little bone”), from os (“bone”) + -culum, neuter of -culus (diminutive suffix).

parole.significato: Containing or yielding bone.
parole.testo: From Latin os, ossis (“bone”) + -ferous. Compare French ossifère.

parole.significato: Capable of producing bone; having the power to change cartilage or other tissue into bone.
parole.testo: From Latin os, ossis (“bone”) + facere (“to make”). Compare French ossifique.

parole.significato: The collection of the bones of a dead person, after decomposition of the soft tissue, for placement in an ossuary
parole.testo: From Latin os (“bone”) + legō (“to pick, select, gather”).

parole.significato: A charnel house; an ossuary.
parole.testo: From Latin ossuarium.

parole.significato: To exhibit or show
parole.testo: Latin ostendere (“to show”).

parole.significato: A display, an exhibition; an appearance, a manifestation.
parole.testo: From Latin ostentus (“a display, exhibition, show”), from ostendere (“to exhibit, show”); see further at etymology 1.

parole.significato: One sixtieth of an hour: a minute (60 seconds).
parole.testo: Perhaps from Latin ostentum.

parole.significato: To make an ambitious display of; to exhibit or show boastingly.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ostentātus, perfect passive participle of ostentō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), intensive from ostendō. Doublet of ostent.

parole.significato: a boaster, ostentatious person
parole.testo: Latin ostentātor.

parole.significato: An ostentatious woman
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ostentātrīx. By surface analysis, ostentator + -trix.

parole.significato: A disorder of the joints in which cracks form in the articular cartilage and the underlying subchondral bone.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: An ostiary; a doorman; a porter.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ōstiārius.

parole.significato: The mouth of a river; an estuary.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ostiārius, from ostium (“door, entrance”). See usher, which may be a doublet.

parole.significato: A small hole or opening through which certain fungi release their mature spores.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ostiolum.

parole.significato: A small opening or orifice, as in a body organ or passage.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ōstium.

parole.significato: Any bivalve of the family Ostreidae; an oyster.
parole.testo: From Latin ostrea (“an oyster”). See oyster.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to an oyster, or to a shell.
parole.testo: From Latin ostrea (“an oyster”). See oyster.

parole.significato: An lover or aficionado of oysters as food.
parole.testo: From Latin ostrea (“oyster”), + -phile.

parole.significato: earache
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ōtalgia, from Ancient Greek ὠταλγία (ōtalgía).

parole.significato: At ease, at leisure; idling, indolent.
parole.testo: From Latin ōtior (“be at ease, enjoy leisure”).

parole.significato: Having no effect.
parole.testo: From Latin ōtiōsus (“idle”), from ōtium (“ease”).

parole.significato: A person who is unable to feel a connection to social groups or collectives, as distinct from both an introvert and an…
parole.testo: From Spanish otro (“other”) + -vert, from Latin vertere (“to turn”). Coined by American psychiatrist w: in 2025.

parole.significato: A skeleton.
parole.testo: Variant of otamy, corruption and clipping of anatomy, from Latin anatomia, from ἀνατομή (anatomḗ, “cutting up”), from ἀνά (aná, “up”) + τέμνω (témnō, “to cut, incise”). Doublet of anatomy.

parole.significato: exultant
parole.testo: From Latin ovans (“triumphant”), present participle of ovare (“to exult”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to or made up of eggs.
parole.testo: From Latin ōvum + -arious.

parole.significato: appendix testis
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: Shaped like an egg.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ōvātus, from ōvum (“an egg”) + -ātus; see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-forming suffix).

parole.significato: To give someone an ovation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ovātus, perfect passive participle of ovō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A victory ceremony of less importance than a triumph.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ovātiōnem.

parole.significato: Of a work submitted for publication, unsolicited.
parole.testo: A transom is a lintel or crosspiece over a door; likely an alteration of Latin trānstrum (“crossbeam”). parole.significato: Sheep.
parole.testo: From Latin ovis (“sheep”).

parole.significato: Of, resembling, or pertaining to an egg.
parole.testo: Latin ovum (“an egg”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Latin poet Ovid; resembling the style of Ovid.
parole.testo: From Latin Ovidianus, equivalent to Ovid + -ian.

parole.significato: A leg, of some pycnogonids, that is modified to carry eggs
parole.testo: From Latin ovum (“egg”) and gero (“to carry”), or related forms. By surface analysis, ovi- + Latin -ger.

parole.significato: Any of several bipedal dinosaurs, of the genus Oviraptor, from the late Cretaceous period.
parole.testo: From scientific Latin Oviraptor (genus name), from Latin ōvi- (“ovi-”) + raptor (because it is believed to have fed on the eggs of other dinosaurs).

parole.significato: The basal part of the ovipositor of some species of insects, typically the non-retractile sheath that remains exposed w…
parole.testo: From Latin ovum (“egg”) plus scāpus (“stem or shaft”), from Ancient Greek (Doric) σκᾶπος (skâpos).

parole.significato: The oviscape or ovipositor.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ovum (“egg”) + captare (“to conduct”)

parole.significato: The belief that the ovum holds all material needed for the development of the embryo.
parole.testo: From Latin ovum (“egg”) + -ism.

parole.significato: Someone who believes that the complete embryo is contained preformed within the ovum; a proponent of ovism.
parole.testo: From Latin ōvum + -ist.

parole.significato: egg; ovum
parole.testo: From ovum or its etymon Latin ōvum (“egg”) + -o-.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to such kind of animals such as some reptiles whose eggs hatch inside their body.
parole.testo: From ovo- +, from Latin ōvum (“egg”) + -o-, + viviparous, from Latin vīviparus, from vīvus (“alive, life, living”) + pariō (“give birth, produce, bring forth”).

parole.significato: The female gamete in animals; the egg cell.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ōvum (“egg”). Doublet of egg, ey, huevo, and oeuf.

parole.significato: Eggcorn of onus; the condition of being obligated or responsible for something.
parole.testo: An eggcorn of onus, as owe (“to be under obligation”, verb) + -ness (abstract-noun suffix), interpretable as "the state of being under obligation." parole.significato: Sour milk.
parole.testo: From Latin oxygala, from Ancient Greek ὀξύγαλα (oxúgala).

parole.significato: A figure of speech in which two words or phrases with opposing meanings are used together intentionally for effect.
parole.testo: First attested in the 17th century, noun use of 5th century Latin oxymōrum (adjective), neut. nom. form of oxymōrus (adjective), from Ancient Greek ὀξύμωρος (oxúmōros), compound of ὀξύς (oxús, “sharp, keen, pointed”) (English oxy-, as in oxygen) + μωρός (mōrós, “dull, stupid, foolish”) (English moro

parole.significato: The act of eating or feeding.
parole.testo: From pābulātiōn-, the stem of the Classical Latin pābulātiō (“action of collecting fodder or food; foraging”), from pābulor (“eat fodder, graze; collect fodder, forage”), from pābulum (“food, fodder”); compare the Middle French pabulation (“action of providing oneself with forage”).

parole.significato: nourishing
parole.testo: Latin pabulosus (“abounding in fodder”), from pabulum (“food or nourishment”).

parole.significato: Food or fodder, particularly that taken in by plants or animals.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pābulum (“food, nourishment; fodder or pasture for animals; nourishment for the mind, food for thought”), from pā(scō) (“to nourish”) + -bulum (suffix denoting an instrument), or directly from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂-dʰlom (*peh₂- (“to protect, shepherd”) + *-dʰlom, variant of

parole.significato: Able to be easily pacified.
parole.testo: From Latin pacare + -able.

parole.significato: peaceful, tranquil
parole.testo: From Latin pācātus, perfect passive participle of pācō (“to make peaceful, pacify”), from pāx (“peace”).

parole.significato: pacified, placated
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pācātus + -ed, By surface analysis, pacate + -d.

parole.significato: pacifying, placation
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pacatio.

parole.significato: With all due respect to.
parole.testo: From Latin pāce (“in peace”), ablative form of pāx (“peace”).

parole.significato: A steam locomotive of the 4-6-2 wheel arrangement.
parole.testo: From Latin pācificus (“peace-making”), so called by Magellan because he sailed peacefully over it after weathering Cape Horn.

parole.significato: Synonym of pacify.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin pācificāt-, the past participial stem of pācificō. Also sometimes an independent back-formation from pacification. For its use by non-native speakers, compare Portuguese and Spanish pacificar and Italian pacificare.

parole.significato: A peacemaker, a pacifier.
parole.testo: From Latin pācificātor.

parole.significato: Promoting peace; conciliatory.
parole.testo: From Latin pācificātōrius.

parole.significato: Something which is packed, a parcel, a box, an envelope.
parole.testo: Equivalent to pack + -age. Possibly influenced by Anglo-Latin paccagium or Old French pacquage.

parole.significato: A taxane antineoplastic drug C₄₇H₅₁NO₁₄ originally isolated from the bark of the Pacific yew, Taxus brevifolia, but now…
parole.testo: From Pac(ific yew) + Latin (brevifo)li(a) + -taxel (“alteration of taxol”).

parole.significato: Agreements must be kept.
parole.testo: Latin plural of pactum (“pact”) + sunt servanda (“must be kept”), after pacta et promissa semperne servanda sint (“whether agreements and promises should always be kept”) in Cicero, De Oficiis 3.92.

parole.significato: Settled by a pact or treaty; relating to pacts or treaties.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pactītius, pactīcius.

parole.significato: An agreement in which a creditor promises not to enforce a debt.
parole.testo: Latin: pactum (“agreement”) + dē (“concerning”, “about”) + nōn (“not”) + petendō (“which is to be sued for”, the ablative singular of the neuter substantive of the future passive participle of petō, “I demand or claim at law”, “I bring an action to recover”, “I sue for”) ≅ “agreement not to sue”.

parole.significato: An unlawful agreement.
parole.testo: From Latin pactum illicitum.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the river Po in Italy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Padānus, from Padus + -ānus. By surface analysis, Padus + -an.

parole.significato: A kind of woollen cloak or mantle used by Romans, worn on journeys and in rainy weather.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin paenula.

parole.significato: The rule of Classical Latin pronunciation which states that a word receives antepenultimate stress if its penult is a s…
parole.testo: First attested in 1892; Latin paenultima (“penult”) + English law.

parole.significato: Relating to, characteristic of religions that differ from main world religions.
parole.testo: From Middle English pagan (adjective and noun), from Latin pāgānus (“rural, rustic; civilian”), replaced Middle English payen from the same root. The meaning “not Christian” arose in Vulgar Latin, probably from the 4th century, owing to the Roman countryside being largely non-Christian, or potential

parole.significato: Any indigenous polytheistic religion.
parole.testo: From Latin pāgānismus (“heathenism”), from pāgānus (“peasant, rural, rustic”). The term was used pejoratively by local Orthodox Christian Demonyms to belittle what remained of alternative native ideas and ideals. By surface analysis, pagan + -ism.

parole.significato: The surface of a leaf or of a flattened thallus.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin pāgina. Doublet of page.

parole.significato: A country district with scattered hamlets.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pāgus.

parole.significato: A part of an insect's leg that is spade-shaped and can be used as a scoop for feeding.
parole.testo: From Latin pāla. Doublet of peel.

parole.significato: A public area in ancient Greece and Rome dedicated to the teaching and practice of wrestling and other sports; a wrestl…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin palaestra, from Ancient Greek παλαίστρα (palaístra, “wrestling school”).

parole.significato: The office or rank of a palatine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin palātīnātus.

parole.significato: Pertaining to the Elector Palatine or the German Palatinate or its people.
parole.testo: From Latin Palātīnus, from Palātium.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the palate.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin palātum (“the palate”).

parole.significato: The interior chaff or husk of grasses.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin palea (“chaff”).

parole.significato: chaffy; resembling or consisting of paleae, or chaff
parole.testo: From Latin palea (“chaff”) + -aceous.

parole.significato: A diminutive or secondary palea
parole.testo: Diminutive of Latin palea.

parole.significato: Part of the lung of birds formed by the parabronchi from the mediolateral and medioventral bronchi
parole.testo: From paleo- + Latin pulmō (“lung”).

parole.significato: chaffy; like chaff
parole.testo: From Latin palea (“chaff”) + -ous.

parole.significato: A Philistine.
parole.testo: From Latin Palaestinus, from Ancient Greek Παλαιστινὸς (Palaistinòs). Cognate with Middle French palestin, Palestin.

parole.significato: The act or practice of driving piles or posts into the ground to make it firm.
parole.testo: From Latin palus (“a stake”) + -ficare (“to make”, in comparative). Compare French palification. See -fy.

parole.significato: A manuscript or document that has been erased or scraped clean, for reuse of the paper, parchment, vellum, or other med…
parole.testo: From Latin palimpsēstus, from Ancient Greek παλίμψηστος (palímpsēstos, “scraped again”).

parole.significato: A rectangular piece of cloth worn by ladies in Ancient Rome and fastened with brooches.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin palla. Doublet of pall.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Pallas, an epithet of Athena, the goddess of wisdom, and potentially to other female Greek figures su…
parole.testo: From Latin Palladius (“of or relating to Pallas”) + -an (suffix forming adjectives from nouns). Palladius is derived from Pallas (from Ancient Greek Παλλάς (Pallás), genitive Παλλάδος (Palládos), an epithet of Athena, the Greek goddess of wisdom) + -ius (suffix forming adjectives from nouns).

parole.significato: A safeguard.
parole.testo: The sense of "safeguard" comes from Latin Palladium (the image of Pallas that protected Troy), from Ancient Greek Παλλάδιον (Palládion), from Παλλάς (Pallás), an epithet used before Athena.

parole.significato: Growing or becoming pale.
parole.testo: From (the present participle stem of) Latin pallēscere (“to become pale”).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or produced by a mantle, especially the mantle of mollusks.
parole.testo: Latin pallium (“a mantle”).

parole.significato: A dress; a robe.
parole.testo: Latin palliare (“to clothe”), from Latin pallium (“a mantle”). See pall, the garment.

parole.significato: Appearing weak, pale, or wan.
parole.testo: From Latin pallidus. Doublet of pale.

parole.significato: Pallidum (pale globe) in the basal ganglia of the brain.
parole.testo: From Latin pallidus (“pale yellow-green”).

parole.significato: Relating to the globus pallidus.
parole.testo: From Latin pallidus (“pale yellow-green”). By surface analysis, pallid- + -o-.

parole.significato: The globus pallidus.
parole.testo: From Latin pallidus (“pale yellow-green”).

parole.significato: A large cloak worn by Greek philosophers and teachers.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pallium (“a cloak”). Doublet of pall.

parole.significato: Any of various evergreen trees from the family Palmae or Arecaceae, which are mainly found in the tropics.
parole.testo: From Middle English palme, from Old English palm, palma (“palm-tree, palm-branch”), from Latin palma (“palm-tree, palm-branch, palm of the hand”), from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₂meh₂, *pl̥h₂emeh₂ (“palm of the hand”), from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂- (“flat”). Cognate with Dutch palm, German Palme,

parole.significato: Any castor oil plant of species Ricinus communis.
parole.testo: From Latin palma Christi, “palm of Christ.”

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the palm of the hand or comparable appendage.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin palmāris. By surface analysis, palm + ar.

parole.significato: Worthy of the palm; preeminent; superior.
parole.testo: From Latin palmarius, palmaris (“belonging to palms, deserving the palm or prize”). Cognate to Spanish palmario.

parole.significato: Having three or more lobes or veins arising from a common point.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin palmātus (“hand-shaped, palm-leaf shaped”), from palma (“palm, palm-tree”). Equivalent to palm + -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Compare French palmé.

parole.significato: Having digits connected by a thin membrane; webbed.
parole.testo: From Latin palmātus (“embroidered with palms”).

parole.significato: Synonym of palmatilobate; palmate lobed, with the divisions separated less than halfway to the common centre.
parole.testo: Latin palmatus (“palmate”) + English lobed.

parole.significato: Bearing palm trees.
parole.testo: From Latin palmifer, from palma (“a palm”) + ferre (“to bear”). Compare French palmifère.

parole.significato: A web-footed bird.
parole.testo: From Latin palmipes, palmipedis (“broad-footed”); palma (“the palm of the hand”) + pes (“a foot”). Compare French palmipède.

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to ancient Palmyra or Palmyrena.
parole.testo: From Latin Palmȳrēnus, from Ancient Greek Παλμυρηνός (Palmurēnós). By surface analysis, Palmyra + -ene.

parole.significato: To examine or otherwise explore through touch, particularly (medicine) in reference to an area or organ of the human bo…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin palpātus, perfect passive participle of palpō (“touch softly”).

parole.significato: Someone who palpates.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin palpātor.

parole.significato: An eyelid.
parole.testo: Borrowing from Latin palpebra (“an eyelid”). Compare Middle English palpebre.

parole.significato: To beat strongly or rapidly; said especially of the heart.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin palpitō, palpitātus (“throb, pulsate, palpitate”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to marshes, marshy, palustral, (especially designating a plant's habitat).
parole.testo: From Latin palus (“marsh”).

parole.significato: Synonym of paludamentum.
parole.testo: From Latin palūdāmentum.

parole.significato: A military cloak worn by a general and his principal officers, fastened at one shoulder.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin palūdāmentum.

parole.significato: A tank or vivarium containing both aquatic and terrestrial elements.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin palūs, palūdis (“marsh, swamp”) + -arium.

parole.significato: Pertaining to marshes and swamps.
parole.testo: From Latin palūdem (palūs).

parole.significato: A member of any of various schools in Slough, Berkshire, England.
parole.testo: From Latin paludis (“of a slough or mire”).

parole.significato: Paludicolous; inhabiting marshes.
parole.testo: From Latin palūs (“marsh”) + -cole. Compare French paludicole.

parole.significato: That lives in swamps or marshes.
parole.testo: From Latin palūs (“marsh”) + -colous.

parole.significato: The productive use of wet peatland.

parole.significato: The innermost, secret or hidden parts; mysteries.

parole.significato: To enter into; to make way into the interior of; to pierce.
parole.testo: From Latin penētrātus, perfect passive participle of penētrō (“to put, set, or place within, enter, pierce, penetrate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from penes (“within, with”) by analogy to intrō (“to go in, enter”). Compare French pénétrer.

parole.testo: Uncertain. First attested in the 16th century in reference to the auk of the Northern hemisphere; the word was later applied to the superficially similar birds of the Southern hemisphere (as was woggin). Possibly from Welsh pen (“head”) and gwyn (“white”), or from Latin pinguis (“fat”). See citation

parole.significato: A tent or pledget for wounds or ulcers.
parole.testo: From Latin penicillum, penicillus (“a painter's brush, a roll of lint, a tent for wounds”).

parole.significato: Falling in the position after initial position; second.
parole.testo: Blend of penultimate + initial, treating pen- (from Latin paene (“almost”)) as a prefix.

parole.significato: A piece of land projecting into water from a larger land mass.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin paenīnsula, from paene (“almost”), and īnsula (“island”).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, resembling, or connected with a peninsula or peninsulas.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin paenīnsulāris. By surface analysis, peninsula + -ar. In the historical sense borrowed from Spanish peninsular.

parole.significato: The male erectile reproductive organ used for sexual intercourse that in the human male and other placental mammals is…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin pēnis, from Proto-Italic *peznis, from Proto-Indo-European *pes-ni-s, from *pes- (“penis”). First attested in the late 17th century. Doublet of pencil. Displaced native English pintle, tarse, pillicock.

parole.significato: a contour feather
parole.testo: From Latin penna (“feather”). Doublet of panne, pen, and pinna.

parole.significato: having the structure of a normal feather
parole.testo: From Latin penna (“feather”) + -aceous.

parole.significato: feathery covering; plumage
parole.testo: From penna + -age, from Latin penna, pinna (“wing, feather”). Perhaps analogous to French pennage, the same Latinate root and suffix elements having both entered at an earlier stage (cf. Middle English penne, -age).

parole.significato: Having a feather-like shape
parole.testo: From Latin pennātus.

parole.significato: Any of numerous species of Pennatula, Pteroides, and allied genera of Alcyonaria, having a feather-like form; a sea pen.
parole.testo: From Latin pennatulus, from pennātus + -ulus, from penna + -ātus.

parole.significato: A forelimb, found on various species of extinct and extant coelurosaur, that is not used in flight or gliding but still…
parole.testo: From Latin penna (“feather”) + brachium (“arm”). Coined by Sullivan et al. in 2010.

parole.significato: Bearing feathers or quills.
parole.testo: From Latin penniger, from penna (“feather”) + gerere (“to bear”), + -ous.

parole.significato: Strong of wing; strong on the wing.
parole.testo: From Latin pennipotens, from penna (“wing”) + potens (“strong”).

parole.significato: Study of the processes devised and adopted for the punishment and prevention of crime.
parole.testo: From Latin poena (“penalty, punishment”) + -ology.

parole.significato: Hanging down, suspended.
parole.testo: From classical Latin pēnsilis, from the past participle stem of pendere (“to hang”).

parole.significato: A task or imposition set as a school punishment.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pensum. Doublet of peso.

parole.significato: A noun having five cases.
parole.testo: From Latin pentaptōtum, from Ancient Greek πεντάπτωτος (pentáptōtos).

parole.significato: The commander of a platoon of fifty men.
parole.testo: From Latin pentēcontarchus, from Ancient Greek πεντηκόνταρχος (pentēkóntarkhos, literally “commander of fifty”).

parole.significato: A military unit commanded by a pentecontarch.
parole.testo: From Latin pentēcontarchia, from Ancient Greek πεντηκονταρχία (pentēkontarkhía). By surface analysis, pentecontarch + -y.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Mount Pentelicus (Penteliko Mountain), near Athens, famous for its fine white marble quarries.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Pentelicus, from Ancient Greek Πεντελικός (Pentelikós).

parole.significato: A white marble with a uniform, faint yellow tint, quarried on Mount Pentelicus near Athens.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin marmor Pentelicum.

parole.significato: A prosal group of two and a half feet.
parole.testo: From Latin penthēmimeris, from Ancient Greek πενθημιμερής (penthēmimerḗs, “having five half-feet”): πέντε (pénte, “five”) + ἡμι- (hēmi-) + μέρος (méros, “part, metrical foot”).

parole.significato: the next to last syllable in a word
parole.testo: From Latin, from pēnultimus, paenultimus (“the last but one”).

parole.significato: Extreme need or want; destitution, poverty; (countable) an instance of this.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English penuri, penurie (“destitution, need, poverty; dearth, lack, scarcity”), borrowed from Latin pēnūria (“need, scarcity, want”) + Middle English -i, -ie (suffix forming abstract and collective nouns); further etymology uncertain, possibly related to paene (“almost, nearly; bare

parole.significato: A flowering plant of the genus Paeonia with large fragrant flowers.
parole.testo: From Old English peonie, peonia et al., from Latin paeōnia; later reinforced by Anglo-Norman peonie, Old French peone, pyoine (French pivoine), from Latin paeōnia, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek παιωνία (paiōnía), from Ancient Greek Παιών (Paiṓn, “Paeon, the physician of the gods”)/παιών (paiṓn, “a

parole.significato: A peplos, an Ancient Greek garment formed of a tubular piece of cloth folded back upon itself halfway down so that the…
parole.testo: From Latin peplum, from Ancient Greek πέπλον (péplon), accusative singular of πέπλος (péplos).

parole.significato: An upper garment worn by women in Ancient Greece and Ancient Rome.
parole.testo: From Latin, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: A fruit of plants of the gourd family Cucurbitaceae, possessing a hard rind and producing many seeds in a single, centr…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pepō, from Ancient Greek πέπων (pépōn, “large melon”), from πέπων (pépōn, “ripe”), from πέπτω (péptō, “ripen”). Doublet of pumpion; compare pumpkin.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, capable of, or aiding digestion.
parole.testo: From Latin pepticus, from Ancient Greek πέψις (pépsis, “digestion”), a form of πέσσω (péssō).

parole.significato: For each.
parole.testo: From Latin per (“through, during”), from Proto-Indo-European *per. Doublet of par.

parole.significato: By others; through others. Said of a proposition held to be true because it follows from other true propositions.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin per alia, from per (“by; through”) + alia (“others”).

parole.significato: via the anus
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin per anum.

parole.significato: Per person.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin per capita (“per head”).

parole.significato: Percent.
parole.testo: Latin per + centum

parole.significato: in contrast, on the contrary
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin per contra.

parole.significato: An opinion delivered by an entire court rather than a single judge.
parole.testo: Latin per (“by means of”) curiam (“the court”)

parole.significato: Per day; daily.
parole.testo: From Latin per + diem (“day”).

parole.significato: As is impossible.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin per impossibile.

parole.significato: By letter; in a message to the author.
parole.testo: Abbreviation of Latin per litterās (“by letter”).

parole.significato: monthly; by the month
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: via the nose
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin per nasum.

parole.significato: At night.
parole.testo: From Latin.

parole.significato: by the agency of, especially when signing a letter in place of someone else
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin per procurationem (“by the agency of/on the instruction of/by proxy”).

parole.significato: By or through the rectum, as (usually, more specifically) the rectal route of administration for drugs.
parole.testo: From Latin.

parole.significato: At a single leap; all at once.
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: Without determination by or involvement of extraneous factors; by its very nature.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin per sē (“by itself”), from per (“by, through”) and sē (“itself, himself, herself, themselves”).

parole.significato: A method of distributing an estate to the descendants or heirs of a deceased legatee in which the estate is divided equ…
parole.testo: From Latin per (“by, through”) and stirpēs (“rootstock”).

parole.significato: Through the vagina, as (usually, more specifically) by the vaginal route of administration.
parole.testo: Naturalized into medical English from neoclassical use of Latin in the professions. parole.significato: To go through with, perform, or carry out
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin peractus, past participle of peragere.

parole.significato: Very sharp; very violent.
parole.testo: From Latin peracūtus.

parole.significato: To travel around or through.
parole.testo: From Latin peragratus (“wandered through”), past participle of peragro (“to wander”). See peregrine, peregrinate.

parole.significato: The act or state of travelling, or passing through any space.
parole.testo: From Latin peragratio: compare French peragration.

parole.significato: To walk around, roam, or stroll.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin perambulō, perambulātus. Equivalent to per- + ambulate.

parole.significato: The amount, number or rate of something, regarded as part of a total of 100; a part of a whole.
parole.testo: From percent, from Latin per centum (“for every hundred”), + -age (suffix indicating a rate).

parole.significato: Having or showing keenness or sharpness of perception, insight, understanding, or intuition.
parole.testo: From Latin perceptīvus.

parole.significato: That which perceives.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin perceptor.

parole.significato: Resembling a perch (the fish).
parole.testo: From Latin perca (“perch”) + -ine.

parole.significato: perception
parole.testo: From percipient, itself from the Latin percipiens, the past participle of percipere (“to perceive”).

parole.significato: The faculty, act or power of perceiving; perception.
parole.testo: From percipient + -cy, from Latin percipiō (“perceive”)

parole.significato: That which is to be perceived.
parole.testo: From Latin percipiendum.

parole.significato: Having the ability to perceive, especially to perceive quickly.
parole.testo: From Latin percipiēns, present participle of percipiō (“to perceive”).

parole.significato: Of or belonging to Percoidea, a taxonomic superfamily in the order Perciformes.
parole.testo: From Latin perca (“perch”).

parole.significato: To pass a liquid through a porous substance; to filter.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin percōlātus, perfect passive participle of percōlō (“to filter”), itself, from per (“through”) + cōlō (“to strain”) (from cōlum (“a strainer”), of unknown origin); see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The seepage or filtration of a liquid through a porous substance.
parole.testo: From Latin percōlātiō.

parole.significato: an enquiry
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin percontatiō (“inquiry, questioning”), from percontor (“to interrogate, investigate”) + -tiō.

parole.significato: That is, expressed in, or having the character of the grammatical mood (mode) of rhetorical questioning; percontatorial.
parole.testo: From the Latin percontativus.

parole.significato: Given to or characterised by the asking of questions, especially open-ended ones (percontations).
parole.testo: First attested in 1853; formed from Latin percontātōrius (from percontōr (“to inquire”)) + -al.

parole.significato: Indissolubly associated.
parole.testo: A humorous neologism and nonce word coined by Canadian sketch comedy troupe The Kids in the Hall for a 1991 episode of their eponymous Canadian sketch comedy. In principle, Latin per- (“throughout”) + *cumbō (“to lie down”).

parole.significato: Running through the entire length; running through from top to bottom, as the midrib of a dicotyledonous leaf, the nerv…
parole.testo: From Latin percurrens, present participle of percurrere (“to run or pass through”), from per (“through”) + currere (“to run”).

parole.significato: rushed, hasty or cursory.
parole.testo: From Latin percursor (“one who runs through”), from percurrere. See percurrent.

parole.significato: To strike; to hit; to knock; to give a blow to.
parole.testo: From Latin percussus, past participle of percutiō (“to strike, to beat”), from per (“through”) + quatiō (“to shake, to strike”).

parole.significato: Striking; having the power of striking or hitting.
parole.testo: From Latin percutiens. See percuss.

parole.significato: Any deciduous plant.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin perdere (“to lose”) + folium (“leaf”).

parole.significato: A woman who has fallen into prostitution.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin perdita (“lost woman”).

parole.significato: treason
parole.testo: Latin perduellio.

parole.significato: To travel from place to place, or from one country to another, especially on foot; hence, to sojourn in foreign countri…
parole.testo: From Latin peregrinari (“to live or travel abroad”). See also peregrine and pilgrim.

parole.significato: Peregrine; having travelled; exotic, foreign.
parole.testo: From Latin peregrinatus (“having travelled abroad”), past participle of peregrinari.

parole.significato: One who peregrinates; one who travels about.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin peregrīnātor.

parole.significato: The quality of being foreign or strange.
parole.testo: From peregrine + -ity, from Latin peregrīnitās. Compare French pérégrinité.

parole.significato: To destroy or defeat.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin peremptum, past participle of perimere.

parole.significato: A quashing (of law, lawsuit, appeal etc.)
parole.testo: Latin peremptio: compare French péremption.

parole.significato: To procrastinate for a long time, especially two days.
parole.testo: From Latin perendinare (“to defer until the day after tomorrow”), from Latin perendie (“on the day after tomorrow”), from dies (“day”).

parole.significato: To survive from one growing season to the next
parole.testo: From Latin perennō.

parole.significato: Lasting or remaining active throughout the year, for multiple years, or all the time.
parole.testo: The adjective is borrowed from Latin perennis (“lasting through the whole year or for several years, perennial; continual, everlasting, perpetual”) + English -al (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives). Perennis is derived from per- (“completive or intensifying prefix with the sens

parole.significato: The quality of being perennial.
parole.testo: From perenn + -ity, from Latin perennitas.

parole.significato: A rambling or wandering through various places.
parole.testo: From Latin pererrare, pererratum (“to wander through”).

parole.significato: A number that is the sum of all of its divisors except itself.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin numerus perfectus, with this use of perfectus itself a semantic loan from Ancient Greek τέλειος (téleios).

parole.significato: the office of a perfectissimus
parole.testo: From Latin perfectissimatus.

parole.significato: Synonym of perfect (“leader of the Cathar movement”).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin perfectus. Doublet of parfait, perfect, and perfecto.

parole.significato: A very ardent disposition.
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?]; see perfervid.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or representing perfidy; disloyal to what should command one's fidelity or allegiance.
parole.testo: From Latin perfidiōsus (“treacherous”), from perfidia. By surface analysis, perfidy + -ous.

parole.significato: Capable of being blown through; permeable to air currents.
parole.testo: From Latin perflābilis. Compare perflate.

parole.significato: The act of perflating, or blowing through.
parole.testo: Latin perflatio.

parole.significato: The long flexor muscle of the toes, or the deep flexor muscle of the fingers.
parole.testo: From Latin perforans.

parole.significato: IPA⁽ᵏᵉʸ⁾: /ˈpɜː.fə.ɹeɪt/
parole.testo: The adjective is first attested in 1425, in Middle English, the verb in 1538; from Middle English perforat(e) (“perforated, pierced”), borrowed from Latin perforātus, the perfect passive participle of perforō (“to bore or pierce through, to perforate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjec

parole.significato: The short flexor of the toes, or the superficial flexor of the fingers.
parole.testo: From Latin perforātus.

parole.significato: To rub over.
parole.testo: From Latin perfricatus, past participle of perfricare.

parole.significato: A severe chill
parole.testo: From Latin perfrictio (“a chilling through”).

parole.significato: To permeate or suffuse something, especially with a liquid or with light.
parole.testo: From 1520s, from Latin perfusus, past participle of perfundo (“to pour over, besprinkle”) from per- + fundo (“to pour”) (from nasalised form of PIE root *gheu- ("to pour")); compare diffuse, suffuse.

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to Pergamum.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Pergamēnus or its etymon Ancient Greek Περγαμηνός (Pergamēnós). By surface analysis, Pergam(um) + ene.

parole.significato: Reminiscent of parchment.
parole.testo: From the suffixation of post‑Classical Latin pergament(um) (“parchment”) with the suffix -aceous (“of the nature of”) (itself from the Latin compound adjectival suffix ‑āceus).

parole.significato: To shudder (at).
parole.testo: From Latin perhorrēscere.

parole.significato: To endanger.
parole.testo: From the past participle stem of Latin periclitari, from periculum (“experiment, risk”). Compare peril.

parole.significato: The state of being in peril.
parole.testo: From Latin periclitatio. Compare French périclitation.

parole.significato: Surrounding the locus coeruleus
parole.testo: From peri- + Latin coeruleus.

parole.significato: The membrane (or periosteum) which covers the outer surface of the skull.
parole.testo: From late Latin pericranium, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek περικράνιον (perikránion), noun use of the neuter form of περικράνιος (perikránios, “around the skull”), from περί (perí, “around”) + κρανίον (kraníon, “skull”).

parole.significato: dangerous, hazardous, perilous
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin periculosus (“dangerous, hazardous, perilous”). Doublet of perilous.

parole.significato: accident or casus, as distinguished from dolus and culpa, and hence relieving one from the duty of performing an obliga…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin periculum. Doublet of peril.

parole.significato: The point of an elliptical lunar orbit where the distance between the satellite and the Moon is at its minimum.
parole.testo: From peri- + Latin lūna (“moon”).

parole.significato: The sum of the distance of all the lengths of the sides of an object.
parole.testo: From Latin perimetros, Ancient Greek περίμετρος (perímetros). Equivalent to peri- + meter.

parole.significato: That occurs around the time of labor and childbirth (parturition) (typically, within a few weeks before, intrapartum, o…
parole.testo: From peri- + Latin partum (“giving birth”), thus "around [the time of] birth".

parole.significato: The use of more words than are necessary to express the idea; a roundabout, or indirect, way of speaking; circumlocutio…
parole.testo: From Latin periphrasis from Ancient Greek περίφρασις (períphrasis), from περιφράζομαι (periphrázomai, “to consider all sides of an issue”), from περί (perí, “around”) + φράζω (phrázō, “to show, point out”). See phrase.

parole.significato: An account of a voyage, particularly those of Hanno and Arrian, recording ports and coastal landmarks.
parole.testo: From Latin periplūs (“account of a voyage”) and Ancient Greek περίπλους (períplous, “voyage, naval manouver, account of a voyage”), from περί (perí, “peri-: around”) + πλοῦς (ploûs, “voyage”), from πλεῖν (pleîn, “to sail”). Cf. French périple, Spanish periplo, & Italian periplo.

parole.significato: pneumonic (of or pertaining to pneumonia (an inflammation of the lungs))
parole.testo: Latin peripneumonicus, Ancient Greek: compare French péripneumonique. peripneumonia + -ic

parole.significato: Superfluity of words; verbosity; long-windedness.
parole.testo: From Latin perissologia, from Ancient Greek περισσός (perissós, “odd, uneven”) + Ancient Greek -λογία (-logía). By surface analysis, perisso- + logy or periss- + -ology.

parole.significato: A peristyle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin peristylium.

parole.significato: A peristyle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin peristylum.

parole.significato: skilled

parole.significato: In mammals, the serous membrane lining the cavity of the abdomen and that is folded over the viscera.
parole.testo: From Latin peritonaeum, from Ancient Greek περιτόναιον (peritónaion), from περιτόναιος (peritónaios, “stretched or strained over”).

parole.significato: A Roman Catholic theologian attending an ecumenical council to give advice.
parole.testo: From Latin perītus (“skillful”).

parole.significato: Any of several evergreen plants of the genus Vinca with blue or white flowers.
parole.testo: Diminutive of Middle English perwinke, from Old English perfince, perwince (compare Middle High German berwinke), from Latin pervinca (compare French pervenche, Italian pervinca).

parole.significato: A mollusk of family Littorinidae.

parole.significato: A loincloth worn by men and women in ancient Greece.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin perizoma. from Ancient Greek περίζωμα (perízōma).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to perjury.
parole.testo: From Latin perjuriosus.

parole.significato: Describes a case, in very few inflected languages, that expresses movement through or along a referent noun, as "along"…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin perlātus + -ive. By surface analysis, per- + lative.

parole.significato: the reading through of something.
parole.testo: From Latin perlēctiō (“the act of reading through”), from perlegō (“read through”), from per (“through”) + legō (“read”).

parole.significato: To travel through an area in examination or survey.
parole.testo: Latin perlustratus, the perfect participle of perlustro, from per- + lustro (“wander through”), from lustrum.

parole.significato: The state or quality of permanence.
parole.testo: From Latin permanentia. Compare permanence.

parole.significato: Permanence.
parole.testo: From Latin permansio, from the participle stem of permanere.

parole.significato: permanent, stative, maintaining the same state
parole.testo: From Latin permaneo.

parole.significato: Able to be permeated; absorbing or allowing the passage of fluids.
parole.testo: From Middle English permeable, permiable, from Latin permeābilis.

parole.significato: A measure of the degree to which a material allows a fluid to permeate it.
parole.testo: From stem of Latin permeare (“to penetrate”) + -ance.

parole.significato: To pass through the pores or interstices of; to penetrate and pass through without causing rupture or displacement; app…
parole.testo: First attested in 1656; borrowed from Latin permeātus, perfect passive participle of permeō (“to pass through”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Capable of being mixed.
parole.testo: From Latin permiscere (“to mingle”), from per + miscere (“to mix”).

parole.significato: To warn, to admonish

parole.significato: swiftness; celerity
parole.testo: From pernic(ious) + -ity, from Latin pernicitas. See pernicious.

parole.significato: Synonym of chilblain.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pernio.

parole.significato: To stay up all night; to pass the night (especially in prayer).
parole.testo: From the Latin pernoctō (“to spend the night”).

parole.significato: sheathed with a covering
parole.testo: From Latin peronātus (“wearing low boots”)

parole.significato: A small sesamoid bone in the foot found in some humans.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin peroneum.

parole.significato: To speak or declaim at great length, especially in a pompous or grandiloquent manner; to harangue.
parole.testo: First attested in 1603; borrowed from Latin perōrātus, perfect passive participle of perōrō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix). By surface analysis, per- + orate.

parole.significato: The concluding section of a discourse, either written or oral, in which the orator or writer sums up and commends his t…
parole.testo: From Latin perōrō (“to speak at length, to conclude a speech”) (from per- (“very”) + ōrō (“to speak, to orate”) (English orate)) + -ation (“action (nominalizer)”) (from Latin -ātiō).

parole.significato: To ponder, consider.

parole.significato: Madness, especially as caused by inflammation of the brain; encephalitis, encephalomeningitis, or meningitis.
parole.testo: From Latin phrenītis, from Ancient Greek φρενῖτις (phrenîtis), from φρήν (phrḗn, “mind”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to Phrygia, its people, or their culture.
parole.testo: From Latin Phrygiānus + English -an (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives). Phrygianus is derived from Phrygia + -ānus (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’); and Phrygia is from Ancient Greek Φρῠγῐ́ᾱ (Phrŭgĭ́ā, “region in Anatolia”), from Φρῠ́ξ (Phrŭ́x, “person from Phrygia”) (fu

parole.significato: An infestation by pubic lice (Pthirus pubis).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin phthīriāsis, from Ancient Greek φθειρίασις (phtheiríasis).

parole.significato: phthisic
parole.testo: From Latin phthisicus, from Ancient Greek: compare French phthisique. See phthisis.

parole.significato: An atrophy of the body or part of the body, especially pulmonary tuberculosis.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin phthisis, from Ancient Greek φθίσις (phthísis, “consumption, decline, wasting away”), from φθίω (phthíō, “to waste away”).

parole.significato: A gelatin in which the algae spores have been supposed to vegetate.
parole.testo: From phyco- + Latin mater (“mother”).

parole.significato: The ruler of a phyle in Ancient Greece.
parole.testo: From Latin phylarchus, from Ancient Greek φύλαρχος (phúlarkhos), from φῡλή (phūlḗ, “large clan or tribe of ancient Greece”).

parole.significato: A flattened petiole or leaf rachis that resembles and functions as a leaf, and may or may not be combined with an actua…
parole.testo: From Latin phyllodium, from Ancient Greek φυλλώδης (phullṓdēs, “resembling a leaf”).

parole.significato: A leaf, or something (flat) resembling a leaf.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin phyllon, from Ancient Greek φύλλον (phúllon, “leaf”). Doublet of phyllo, distantly also with foil, folio, and folium.

parole.significato: A rank in the classification of organisms, below kingdom and above class; also called a divisio or a division, especial…
parole.testo: From Latin phylum, from Ancient Greek φῦλον (phûlon, “tribe, race”).

parole.significato: A member of the genus Physeter; a sperm whale.
parole.testo: From Latin physeter.

parole.significato: Relating to or concerning existent materials; physical.
parole.testo: From Middle English phisik, from Latin physicus, from Ancient Greek φῠσῐκός (phŭsĭkós, “natural; physical”), from φύσις (phúsis, “origin, birth; nature, quality; form, shape; type, kind”), from φῠ́ω (phŭ́ō, “grow”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH- (“to appear, become, rise up”).

parole.significato: The ring finger.
parole.testo: Calque of the Latin digitus medicus.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to physiology.
parole.testo: Either from physio- + -logic or Latin physiologicus.

parole.significato: Feeding on plants; herbivorous.
parole.testo: From phyto- + Latin vorare (“to eat greedily”).

parole.significato: A heinous offense that requires expiation.
parole.testo: From Latin piāculum.

parole.significato: The quality of being piacular, of requiring atonement.
parole.testo: From Latin piaculariter (“by way of atonement; sinfully”), piacularius (“atoning, expiatory”) from piaculo (“to appease or propitiate with an offering”). See pius (“dutiful”).

parole.significato: Piacular; atoning for sin or crime.
parole.testo: Coined a. 1920 by T.S. Eliot, from Latin piaculum (“propitiatory sacrifice”) + -ative.

parole.significato: An expiatory sacrifice.
parole.testo: From Latin piāculum. Doublet of piacle.

parole.significato: A member of the Order of Poor Clerics Regular of the Mother of God of the Pious Schools, a Catholic educational order f…
parole.testo: From Latin pius (“pious”), + -ist.

parole.significato: atonement or expiation.
parole.testo: From Latin piatio. See piacle.

parole.significato: A disorder characterized by appetite and craving for non-edible substances, such as chalk, clay, dirt, ice, or sand.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pīca (“jay; magpie”). Doublet of pie (“magpie”). * (pathology): From the idea that magpies will eat almost anything.
