parole.significato: An oily liquid hydrocarbon extracted from the creosote of beechwood tar, and consisting essentially of certain derivati…
parole.testo: From Latin pix, picis (“pitch”) + amarus (“bitter”).

parole.significato: Money paid at fairs for permission to set up booths.
parole.testo: Latin piccadium, from French piquer (“to prick”).

parole.significato: A resident of ancient Picenum in Italy.
parole.testo: From Latin Picenum.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to pitch (“a sticky, dark brown substance obtained from distilling turpentine or wood tar, or crude oi…
parole.testo: From Latin piceus (“like pitch; pitch-black”) + -ous (suffix forming adjectives denoting possession or presence of a quality). Piceus is derived from pix (“pitch, tar”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peyH- (“fat; milk”)) + -eus (suffix forming adjectives indicating the sources of attributes).

parole.significato: A member of an ancient people of northern and central Scotland.
parole.testo: From Latin Pictus, probably rendering a Pictish autonym; see the Latin entry for details. Compare Old English Peohtas, which appears to show the effects of Grimm's law.

parole.significato: The picture or image component of something, such as an emblem or poem, that contains a combination of imagery and text…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin pictūra (“a painting”). Doublet of picture.

parole.significato: A representation of anything (as a person, a landscape, a building) upon canvas, paper, or other surface, by drawing, p…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English picture, from Latin pictūra (“the art of painting, a painting”), from pingō (“to paint”). Doublet of pictura.

parole.significato: A raised platform built from the shore out over water, supported on piles; used to secure, or provide access to shippin…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English pere (“bridge pillar, breakwater”), from either Anglo-Norman pere (“stone”, from Latin petra) or Old French *piere (Old Northern French pire, from either Late Latin *petricus or pēra "satchel"); compare Medieval Latin pira.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Pierides or Muses.
parole.testo: Latin Pierius, from Mount Pierus in Thessaly, sacred to the Muses.

parole.significato: Any color in plant or animal cells.
parole.testo: From Middle English pigment, from Latin pigmentum (“pigment”), itself from pingō (“to paint”) + -mentum; variants of this word may have been known in Old English (e.g. 12th century pyhmentum). Doublet of pimiento, pimento, and piment.

parole.significato: Being or relating to a probability that a rational person will assign to an option when required to make a decision.
parole.testo: Coined by Philippe Smets from Latin pignus (“a bet”) + -istic.

parole.significato: The act of pledging or pawning.
parole.testo: From Latin pignorātio, pignerātio, derivation of pignerāre (“to pledge”), derivation of pignus, genitive pignoris, pigneris (“a pledge, a pawn”). Compare French pignoration.

parole.significato: A gift or keepsake that is symbolic of a love relationship; a love token.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pignus amōris.

parole.significato: Slothfulness, laziness.
parole.testo: From Latin pigritūdō.

parole.significato: A mortar.
parole.testo: From Latin pīla (“mortar”).

parole.significato: Relating to hair.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin pilāris, from Latin pilus (“a hair”) + -ar.

parole.significato: A ceremonial chariot or carriage, used by Roman noblewomen.
parole.testo: From Latin pilentum.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or consisting of hair.
parole.testo: From Latin pilus + -eous, perhaps by alteration of pilous or pilose.

parole.significato: Haemorrhoids.
parole.testo: From Latin pila (“ball”).

parole.significato: The top of a bird's head, from the base of the bill to the nape.
parole.testo: From Latin pileum.

parole.significato: The cap of a mushroom.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pīleus, a form of pilleus (“a felt cap”).

parole.significato: A condition of the skin appendage, characterized by short and brittle hairs that appear flattened and twisted when view…
parole.testo: Plural form of Latin pilus (“hair”) + tortus (“twisted”).

parole.significato: Containing or producing hair.
parole.testo: From Latin pilus + -iferous.

parole.significato: Resembling hair.
parole.testo: Latin pilus (“hair”) + -form

parole.significato: piliferous (covered in hair)
parole.testo: From Latin pilus (“hair”) + -gerous. Compare French piligère.

parole.significato: To peel; to remove the outer layer of hair, skin, or bark.
parole.testo: From Middle English pillen, pilen, from Old English pilian (“to peel”), from Latin pilō (“depilate”), from pilus (“hair”). Doublet of peel.

parole.significato: hair
parole.testo: From Latin pilus (“hair”).

parole.significato: Any cell with prominent external hair-like structures.
parole.testo: From Latin pilus + -cyte.

parole.significato: Having body hairs which have grown in a concentrated area on the skin and formed a cyst or abscess.
parole.testo: From Latin pilus (“hair”) and nidus (“nest”).

parole.significato: Covered with fine hair.
parole.testo: From Latin pilōsus, from pilus (“hair”).

parole.significato: A little pill.
parole.testo: From Latin pilula.

parole.significato: Resembling a pill or pilule.
parole.testo: From Latin pilula (“a pill”) + -ous.

parole.significato: A Roman military javelin.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pilum. Doublet of pile.

parole.significato: A hair.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin pilus (“hair”). Doublet of pile.

parole.significato: A colourless oily liquid related to the ketones, and obtained by the decomposition of pinacone.
parole.testo: From pinacone + Latin oleum (“oil”) + -in.

parole.significato: An art gallery, especially one exhibiting pictures.
parole.testo: From Latin pinacotheca, from Ancient Greek πινακοθήκη (pinakothḗkē).

parole.significato: The saturated bicyclic hydrocarbon 2,6,6-trimethyl-, (1a,2b,5a)-bicyclo[3.1.1]heptane made by the hydrogenation of pine…
parole.testo: From pine + -ane, from Latin pinus (“pine tree”).

parole.significato: The maritime pine (species Pinus pinaster), that grows in southern Europe.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pīnaster (“a wild pine”).

parole.significato: A tablet or register.
parole.testo: From Latin pinax, from Ancient Greek πίναξ (pínax, “tablet”).

parole.significato: Either of two isomeric bicyclic monoterpene hydrocarbons that are the principal components of pine resin.
parole.testo: From pine + -ene, from Latin pinus (“pine tree”).

parole.significato: An arboretum, or part of an arboretum or garden, devoted to growing conifers.
parole.testo: From Latin pīnētum (“pine grove”).

parole.significato: the process of growing obese
parole.testo: From Latin pingu(is) (“fat”) + -escence, ultimately from Latin pinguēscō.

parole.significato: growing obese, fattening
parole.testo: From Latin pingu(is) (“fat”) + -escent.

parole.significato: Relating to fat.
parole.testo: From Latin pinguis (“fat”) + -id.

parole.significato: Containing fat; fatty.
parole.testo: From Latin pinguedo (“fatness”), from pinguis (“fat”).

parole.significato: fatness; obesity
parole.testo: From Latin pinguitudo, from pinguis (“fat”).

parole.significato: A dicarboxylic acid and recognized as an oxidation product of α-pinene, a common terpene found in pine resin.
parole.testo: From Latin pinus (“pine”).

parole.significato: The visible part of the ear in most therians that resides outside of the head, the auricle; outer ear excluding the ear…
parole.testo: From Latin pinna (“dorsal fin; wing, feather”). Doublet of pen, penna, and panne.

parole.significato: Resembling a feather.
parole.testo: From Latin pinnātus (“feathered”), from pinna (“feather”).

parole.significato: Shaped like a fin or feather.
parole.testo: From Latin pinna (“feather, fin”) + -form.

parole.significato: A marine mammal belonging to the parvorder Pinnipedia, comprising walruses, eared seals and earless seals, characterize…
parole.testo: From Latin pinna (“fin”) + pes (“foot”).

parole.significato: A small crab of the genus Pinnotheres, which live symbiotically in the shells of certain molluscs.
parole.testo: From Latin pīnotērēs, from Ancient Greek πινοτήρης (pinotḗrēs), from Ancient Greek πίνη (pínē, “pen shell”) + Ancient Greek τηρέω (tēréō, “to guard”).

parole.significato: A pinnule or subleaflet.
parole.testo: From Latin pinnula.

parole.significato: Any of the ultimate leaflets of a bipinnate or tripinnate leaf; a subleaflet.
parole.testo: From Latin pinnula.

parole.significato: Any gymnosperm (of the division Pinophyta)
parole.testo: Latin pinus (“pine”) + -phyte (“plant”)

parole.significato: An inscription indicating the identity of the one who created a painting.
parole.testo: From the appearance of the Latin word pinxit (“he/she painted (this)”), perfect indicative third-person singular of pingo (“to paint”), after a painter's name on a painting.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to piety, exhibiting piety, devout, god-fearing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pīus (“pious, dutiful, blessed, kind, devout”), from Proto-Indo-European *pewH- (“pure”). Cognate with Old English fǣle (“faithful, trusty, good; dear, beloved”). More at feal.

parole.significato: An act of innocent deceit, technically using the methods of a fraudster but for an honest, honorable purpose.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin pia fraus.

parole.significato: Babesia, a genus of hematozoa that invades the red blood cells of humans and domesticated animals such as dogs and sheep
parole.testo: From Latin pirum (“pear”) + Ancient Greek πλάσμα (plásma, “image, formation”).

parole.significato: Synonym of calefactory: the room holding an abbey, convent, or monastery's communal fire.
parole.testo: From Latin pisalis.

parole.significato: fishery
parole.testo: From Latin piscarius (“relating to fishes or to fishing”), from piscis (“a fish”). By surface analysis, Latin pisc- + -ary.

parole.significato: fishing; fishery
parole.testo: From Latin piscatio, from piscari (“to fish”).

parole.significato: The study of fishing.
parole.testo: Irregular formation from the stem of Latin piscārī (“to fish”), + -ology.

parole.significato: A fisherman; an angler.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin piscātor.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to fishermen or fishing.
parole.testo: From Latin piscātor (“fisherman”), from piscis (“fish”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to fishermen or fishing.
parole.testo: From Latin piscātor (“fisherman”), from piscis (“fish”).

parole.significato: A female fishmonger in ancient times.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin piscātrīx. By surface analysis, piscator + -trix.

parole.significato: Someone with a Pisces astrological sign.
parole.testo: From Latin piscēs, the nominative plural of piscis (“fish”), calque of Ancient Greek ἰχθύες (ikhthúes, “fish (pl); name of constellation”). Compare Akkadian 𒁺𒉺𒉺 (DU.NU.NU, “fish-cord”); the constellation is often depicted as two fish tied by a ribbon.

parole.significato: Related to fish.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin piscis (“fish”). By surface analysis, Latin pisc- + -i-.

parole.significato: Having the shape of a fish.
parole.testo: Latin piscis (“fish”) + -form

parole.significato: A drained basin near a church's altar for the disposal of water from liturgical ablutions.
parole.testo: From Latin piscīna (“fishpond; swimming pool”), from piscis (“fish”). Compare Middle English piscyne (“pool, pond”), from the same Latin word. By surface analysis, Latin pisc- + -ina.

parole.significato: That feeds on fish; fish-eating.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin piscivorus. By surface analysis, piscivore + -ous or pisci- + -vorous.

parole.significato: fishy.
parole.testo: From Latin piscōsus (“full of fish”).

parole.significato: Abundant with fish.
parole.testo: From Latin pisculentus (“fishy, full of fish”), from pisces (“fish”) + -ulentus (“full of, abounding in”) (whence -ule and -ent).

parole.significato: Resembling a pea or peas in size and shape
parole.testo: Latin pisum (“pea”) + -iform

parole.significato: A concretionary grain, typically of calcium carbonate, between a microid and a macroid in size.
parole.testo: From Latin pisum + -oid.

parole.significato: A sedimentary rock formed from pisoids
parole.testo: From Latin pisum + -lite.

parole.significato: A pisoid.
parole.testo: From Latin pisum + -lith.

parole.significato: A soft, black, tarry bitumen, intermediate between petroleum and asphalt.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pissasphaltus, from Ancient Greek πισσάσφαλτος (pissásphaltos), from πίσσα (píssa, “pitch”) + ἄσφαλτος (ásphaltos, “asphalt”).

parole.significato: Having faith; trusting
parole.testo: From Latin pisticus (“pure; genuine”), from Ancient Greek πιστικός (pistikós).

parole.significato: A pistil.
parole.testo: From Latin pistillum. Doublet of pestle and pistil.

parole.significato: Synonym of epistle.
parole.testo: The noun is derived from Middle English pistel, pistle (“letter; epistle”) [and other forms], from Old English pistol (“letter, epistle”), an aphetic form of epistol, epistola, from Latin epistola (“letter, epistle; literary work in letter form”): see further at epistle. The verb is derived from the

parole.significato: Phlegm; mucus.
parole.testo: From Latin pītuīta (“mucus, phlegm”). Doublet of pip.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the pituitary gland.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin pītuītārius (“mucous”), from pītuīta (“mucus, phlegm”). First attested in the 1610s. First attested as a noun by 1899. The term was adopted as the name for the gland, because it was believed that it channeled mucus to the nose.

parole.significato: Consisting of, or resembling, pituite or mucus.
parole.testo: From Latin pituitosus: compare French pituiteux.

parole.significato: The quality of being placable or appeasable.
parole.testo: From Latin plācābilitās. Compare French placabilité.

parole.significato: Able to be easily pacified; quick to forgive.
parole.testo: From Latin plācābilis.

parole.significato: To calm; to bring peace to; to influence someone who was furious to the point that they become content or at least no l…
parole.testo: First attested in the late 17ᵗʰ century; borrowed from Latin plācātus, perfect passive participle of plācō (“appease, placate”, literally “smooth, smoothen”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more), ultimately thought to be from Proto-Indo-European *plāk- (“smoo

parole.significato: A process or act of placating; appeasement or an expression of appeasement.
parole.testo: From Latin placatio.

parole.significato: A dummy medicine containing no active ingredients; an inert treatment.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English placebo, borrowed from Latin placēbō (“I will please”), the first-person singular future active indicative of placeō (“to please”).

parole.significato: A dessert cake originating in ancient Greece, consisting essentially of layered dough interwoven with cheese and honey.
parole.testo: From Latin placenta (“flat cake”); the dessert is the original sense of the word placenta.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the placenta.
parole.testo: From post-classical Latin placentalis, corresponding to placenta + -al.

parole.significato: pleasing or pleasant
parole.testo: From Latin placentius, from placeō (“to please”).

parole.significato: A vote of assent, as of the governing body of a university, an ecclesiastical council, etc.
parole.testo: Latin placet (“it is pleasing”), inflection of placeō (“to be pleasing”).

parole.significato: The state of being placid; peacefulness.
parole.testo: From placid + -ity, from Latin placiditās (“mildness, placidity”).

parole.significato: A decree or dictum.
parole.testo: From Latin placitum, from placitus, from placeō (“be pleasing”). Doublet of plea.

parole.significato: To use, and pass off as one's own, someone else's writing, speech, ideas, or other intellectual or creative work, espec…
parole.testo: From plagiary + -ize, ultimately from Latin plagiare (“to kidnap, to abduct”).

parole.significato: The crime of literary theft; plagiarism.
parole.testo: From Latin plagiārius (“kidnapper, plagiarist”), from plagium (“kidnapping”), probably from plaga (“a net, snare, trap”).

parole.significato: abduction, especially of a child
parole.testo: From Latin plagium (“kidnapping”), compare plagiarism, probably from plaga (“a net, snare, trap”).

parole.significato: Fond of flogging.
parole.testo: From Latin plagosus. See plague.

parole.significato: A form of monophonic chant in unison using the Gregorian scale, sung in various Christian churches.
parole.testo: From plain + song, calque of Latin cantus planus.

parole.significato: A lament or dirge, a popular literary form in the Middle Ages.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: Of a surface: flat or level.
parole.testo: From Latin plānum (“flat surface”), a noun use of the neuter of plānus (“plain”). The word was introduced in the 17th century to distinguish the geometrical senses from the other senses of plain. Doublet of llano, piano, plain, and plan.

parole.significato: Membership of a particular planet or moon, by origin, birth, naturalization, ownership, allegiance or otherwise.
parole.testo: From planet + -ality from Latin planeta, planetes, from Ancient Greek πλανήτης (planḗtēs, “wanderer”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to planets; planetary.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin planeticus, from Ancient Greek πλανητικός (planētikós), from πλανητός (planētós, “wandering; planetary”), from πλανήτης (planḗtēs, “wanderer, planet”), from πλανάω (planáō, “to wander”) + -της (-tēs, masculine agent noun suffix).

parole.significato: A little planet.
parole.testo: From planet + -ule, ultimately from Latin planetula.

parole.significato: Having a loud, mournful sound.
parole.testo: From Latin plangēns, present participle of plangō (“to beat; to lament”).

parole.significato: flat, level, plane
parole.testo: From Latin plānus + -i-. See plane (adjective).

parole.significato: To repeatedly hammer (a sheet of metal) so as to shape and smooth it or create a decorative indented finish.
parole.testo: From Latin planus (“flat”).

parole.significato: The sole of the foot.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin planta (“sole of the foot”). Doublet of clan and plant.

parole.significato: Relating to the sole of the foot.
parole.testo: From Latin plantāris, from planta (“sole of the foot”) + -āris. By surface analysis, planta + -ar.

parole.significato: A muscle running at the posterior compartment of the calf from the knee to over the hump of the heel.
parole.testo: From Latin plantāris.

parole.significato: Plantar; related to the foot.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin planta (“sole of the foot”) with the interfix -o-

parole.significato: In embryonic development, a vesicle filled with fluid, formed from the morula by the divergence of its cells in such a…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin plānula, diminutive of plāna (“plane”).

parole.significato: any flat surface
parole.testo: From Latin plānum (“level ground, plain”).

parole.significato: An Irish or Welsh melody for the harp, sometimes of a mournful character.
parole.testo: Compare Latin planxī (“to have mourned ...”), planctus (“a lament or dirge”), and plangere (“to mourn aloud”).

parole.significato: The act of forming or moulding.
parole.testo: Latin plasmatio.

parole.significato: One who forms or creates; creator.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin plasmātor.

parole.significato: A paste applied to the skin for healing or cosmetic purposes.
parole.testo: From Middle English plaster, plastre, from Old English plaster, from late Latin plastrum, shortened from Classical Latin emplastrum (“a plaster, bandage”); later reinforced by Anglo-Norman plastre. Displaced native Old English clīþa. The verb is from Middle English plastren, from the noun.

parole.significato: A synthetic, solid, hydrocarbon-based polymer, whether thermoplastic or thermosetting.
parole.testo: From Latin plasticus (“of molding”), from Ancient Greek πλαστικός (plastikós), from πλάσσω (plássō, “to mold, form”). Doublet of plastique.

parole.significato: A planetree.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin platanus; later reborrowed from Middle French platane.

parole.significato: Characterized by banality or triteness.
parole.testo: From platitude + -al on analogy of other adjectives ending in -tudinal, from Latin -tūdin- + -al, the oblique stem of -tūdō.

parole.significato: One who uses many platitudes in speaking or writing.
parole.testo: From platitude + -arian on analogy of other adjectives ending in -tudinarian, from Latin -tūdin- + -arian, the oblique stem of -tūdō.

parole.significato: To utter one or more platitudes; to make obvious, trivial, or clichéd remarks concerning a topic.
parole.testo: From platitude + -ize on analogy of other adjectives ending in -tudinize, from Latin -tūdin- + -ize, the oblique stem of -tūdō. Compare platitudinous.

parole.significato: Characterised by clichés or platitudes.
parole.testo: From platitude + -ous on analogy of other adjectives ending in -tudinous, from Latin -tūdin- + -ous, the oblique stem of -tūdō. Compare platitudinize.

parole.significato: A Platonist; a follower of Plato's ideas.
parole.testo: From Latin Platōnicus. By surface analysis, Platon (“Plato”) + -ic (“relating to”).

parole.significato: Intimate but non-sexual and non-romantic affection.
parole.testo: Attested 1636 in Platonic Lovers by William Davenant. Earlier coined in Latin in the 15th century as amor platōnicus by Florentine scholar Marsilio Ficino (originally in 1476 letter to Alamanno Donati, later expounded in De amore (1484)), based on his interpretation of the Symposium by Plato, specif

parole.significato: Pertaining to Plato or his philosophy; Platonic.
parole.testo: From Latin Platōnicus + -al. By surface analysis, Platonic + -al or Platon + -ical.

parole.significato: A member of the philosophical school of thought established by Plato; a believer in Platonism.
parole.testo: From Latin Platonista, from Plato + -ista, equivalent to Plato + -ist.

parole.significato: A mark or expression of applause; praise bestowed.
parole.testo: For earlier plaudite, borrowed from Latin plaudite, second-person plural imperative of plaudere (“to applaud”).

parole.significato: Seemingly or apparently valid, likely, or acceptable; conceivably true or likely.
parole.testo: From Latin plausibilis (“deserving applause, praiseworthy, acceptable, pleasing”), from the participle stem of plaudere (“to applaud”).

parole.significato: Laudable, praisable.
parole.testo: From Latin plaus-, from Latin plaudere (“to applaud”) + -ive.

parole.significato: Of or relating to a wagon.
parole.testo: From Latin plaustrum (“wagon”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to, or in the style of, Plautus (a Roman comic playwright), his works, or his authorship.
parole.testo: From Latin Plautīnus.

parole.significato: Synonym of Plautine (“of or pertaining to, or in the style of, Plautus”).
parole.testo: From Latin Plautīnus + -ian, from Latin Plautus.

parole.significato: A plebeian, a member of the lower class of Roman citizens.
parole.testo: From Latin plēbs (“the plebeian class”), probably via Middle French plebe (“plebeians, commoners, the rabble”) and possibly later understood as a clipping of plebeian. Cognate with Italian plebe, Spanish plebe, Portuguese plebe.

parole.significato: A member of the plebs, the common citizens of ancient Rome.
parole.testo: From Latin plēbēius (“a commoner; common”) + -an (adjective-forming suffix), from Latin plēbēs + -ius (adjective-forming suffix), possibly under the influence of Middle French plebeyen, plebein, plebien (“a commoner”) and plebeien (“concerning the common people”). Cf. Medieval Latin plēbēiānus (“a c

parole.significato: Someone who flatters, or curries favor with the general public; a demagogue.
parole.testo: From Latin plebs (“the common people”) + colere (“to cultivate”) + -ist.

parole.significato: Making plebeian; vulgarizing.
parole.testo: From Latin plebs (“the common people”) + -ficare (“to make”, in comparative). See -fy.

parole.significato: A law enacted by the plebs, under the superintendence of a tribune or some subordinate plebeian magistrate, without the…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin plēbiscītum, plēbis scītum, plēbī scītum (“law of the common people or plebs”), from plēbis (the genitive singular of plēbs (“common people, plebeians”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₁- (“to fill”)) + scītum (“decree, ordinance, statute”) (from scīscō (“to as

parole.significato: The plebeian class of Ancient Rome or its equivalent in other ancient societies.
parole.testo: From Latin plēbs (“the plebeian class”), variant of earlier plēbēs. Later also understood as the plural of pleb.

parole.significato: A small piece of plastic, metal, ivory, etc., for plucking the strings of a guitar, lyre, mandolin, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin plēctrum, from Ancient Greek πλῆκτρον (plêktron, “anything to strike with, an instrument for striking the lyre, a spear point”), from πλήσσειν (plḗssein, “to strike, to smite, to sting”). Displaced native Old English sleġel.

parole.significato: full; complete
parole.testo: From Latin plenus (“full”). Compare plenary.

parole.significato: With matres lectionis (letters indicating vowels) written out.
parole.testo: From Latin plēnus (“full”) (adjective) or plēnē (“fully”) (adverb).

parole.significato: Excessive or overly full speech.
parole.testo: From Latin plenus and Latin loquentia.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or resembling the full moon.
parole.testo: From Latin plēnilūnium (“full moon”).

parole.significato: The full moon.
parole.testo: From Latin plēnilūnium, from plēnus (“full”) + lūna (“moon”).

parole.significato: Having full power.
parole.testo: From Latin plenus (“full”) + potens, potentis (“potent”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to a plenipotentiary; having full authority.
parole.testo: From (the stem of) Latin plenipotens + -ial.

parole.significato: The belief that all space is full of matter; horror vacui
parole.testo: Latin plenus (“full”) + -ism.

parole.significato: A believer in plenism; someone who believes that all space is full of matter.
parole.testo: Latin plenus (“full”); compare French pléniste.

parole.significato: Having plenitude; full; complete; thorough.
parole.testo: From Latin plēnitūdin- + -ary, from oblique stem of Latin plēnitūdō, from plēnus + -tūdō. By surface analysis, plenitude + -ary or plenitudine + -ary.

parole.significato: abundance
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin plenitudine.

parole.significato: Characterised by plenitude; abundant
parole.testo: From Latin plēnitūdin- + -ous, from oblique stem of Latin plēnitūdō, from plēnus + -tūdō. By surface analysis, plenitude + -ous or plenitudine + -ous.

parole.significato: Of or relating to all the light, travelling in every direction, in a given space.
parole.testo: Coined circa 1991, Latin plenus (“full”) + optic.

parole.significato: A space that is completely filled with matter.
parole.testo: From Latin plēnum n (“space filled with matter”), from plēnus (“full”). The sense of "legislative meeting" is a semantic loan from Russian пле́нум (plénum, “plenary session”), from the same Latin source.

parole.significato: A plethora.
parole.testo: Alteration of Latin plethora after + -y.

parole.significato: Pleurisy (inflammation of the pleura).
parole.testo: From pleur + itis or borrowed from Latin pleuritis.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the pleura; pleural.
parole.testo: From Latin pleura. By surface analysis, pleur- + -o-.

parole.significato: A network of anastomosing or interwoven nerves, blood vessels, or lymphatic vessels.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin plexus (“a twining, plaiting, braid”).

parole.significato: A condition characterised by matted and unhygienic hair.
parole.testo: From Latin plica (“plica”) + feminine singular form of Polonicus (“Polish”).

parole.significato: Folded multiple times lengthwise like a fan, usually lending stiffness to a flat structure such as a leaf; corrugated;…
parole.testo: From Latin plicātus, perfect passive participle of plicō (“to fold”), see -ate.

parole.significato: A doubling; a fold; a plication.
parole.testo: From Latin plicatura, from plicare (“to fold”).

parole.significato: A form of dentin which shows sinuous lines of structure in a transverse section of the tooth.
parole.testo: Latin plica (“fold”) + English dentine.

parole.significato: A figure of speech in which a word is repeated so as not only to signify the individual thing denoted by it, but also i…
parole.testo: From Latin plŏcē, from Ancient Greek πλοκή (plokḗ, “complication”).

parole.significato: A feather.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin plūma. Doublet of plume.

parole.significato: A plant of the genus Plumbago; leadwort.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin plumbāgō (“type of lead ore”), from plumbum (“lead”).

parole.significato: A lead-weighted dart, used by soldiers in Antiquity and the Middle Ages.
parole.testo: From Latin plumbāta.

parole.significato: Consisting of, or resembling, lead.
parole.testo: From Latin plumbeus, from plumbum (“lead”).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, resembling, or containing lead.
parole.testo: From Latin plumbum (“lead”) + -ic, originally in calques of French plombique, from plomb (“lead”) + -ique (“-ic”). See also molybdic.

parole.significato: Synonym of lead poisoning.
parole.testo: From Latin plumbum (“lead”) + -ism.

parole.significato: lead
parole.testo: From Latin plumbum (“lead”).

parole.significato: An orthorhombic-disphenoidal colorless mineral containing hydrogen, lead, oxygen, and silicon.
parole.testo: From Latin plumbum (“lead”), in the mineral's composition, and the locality, Tsumeb, Namibia, + -ite.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, resembling, or containing lead.
parole.testo: From plumb- + -ous, from Latin plumbōsus (“of or related to lead”), from plumbum (“lead”) + -ōsus (“-ous: forming adjectives”).

parole.significato: Synonym of lead, chiefly in scientific contexts.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin plumbum.

parole.significato: Synonym of argentarium.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin plumbum argentārium.

parole.significato: An ear tuft of feathers, as in the horned owls.
parole.testo: From Latin pluma (“feather”) + cornu (“horn”).

parole.significato: Feathered; having feathers.
parole.testo: From Latin plumiger, from pluma (“feather”) + gerere (“to bear”).

parole.significato: Having the shape of a plume or feather.
parole.testo: From Latin plumula (“little feather”, dim. of pluma (“feather”)) + -form.

parole.significato: Having feet covered with feathers.
parole.testo: From Latin plumipes, plumipedis, from pluma (“feather”) + pes.

parole.significato: Having feathers or plumes.
parole.testo: From Latin plūmōsus (“feathered”), from plūma (“feather”): compare French plumeux. By surface analysis, plume + -ose.

parole.significato: A plumule.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin plūmula (“a small feather”).

parole.significato: The first bud, or growing point, of a plant embryo, situated above the cotyledons.
parole.testo: From Latin plūmula, diminutive of plūma (“feather”); compare French plumule. By surface analysis, plume + -ule.

parole.significato: More than perfect, utterly perfect, ideal.
parole.testo: Shortening of plusquamperfect, from Latin plusquamperfectum (“more than perfect”), from plus (“more”) + quam (“than”) + perfectum, neuter singular of perfectus (“achieved; finished; perfected”).

parole.significato: Tense of a verb used when referring to something that happened before a past setting or the imperfect; formed in Englis…
parole.testo: From Latin plus (“more”) + perfectus (“perfect”).

parole.significato: A noun (either in certain of its senses or in all its senses) that does not generally have a singular form.
parole.testo: From Latin plūrāle tantum (“plural as such; plural only”), from plūrāle + tantum.

parole.significato: several
parole.testo: From Latin pluri-, combining form of plūris, from plūs, from Old Latin *plous, from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₁- (“many”). Related to plenty, plural (via Latin) and fele, full (via PIE).

parole.significato: A writ issued in the third place, after two former writs have been disregarded.
parole.testo: From Latin plūriēs (“many times, often”), which occurs in the first clause.

parole.significato: Of many kinds or types; multifarious.
parole.testo: From Latin plurifarius, from plus, pluris (“many”). Compare English bifarious.

parole.significato: Producing several young at a single birth
parole.testo: From pluri- + Latin parere (“to bring forth”). See parous.

parole.significato: And; sum of the previous one and the following one.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin plūs (“more”).

parole.significato: An intensifying prefix, roughly equivalent to more or very.
parole.testo: From plus, from Latin plūs (“more”). Coined by George Orwell in 1949 as part of the Newspeak in his novel Nineteen Eighty-Four.

parole.significato: more than; beyond (in degree)
parole.testo: From Classical Latin plūs (“more”) + quam (“than”); compare plusquamperfect and plusquamperfection.

parole.significato: pluperfect
parole.testo: From Latin plusquamperfectum (“more than perfect”), from plus (“more”) + quam (“than”) + perfectum, neuter singular of perfectus (“achieved; finished; perfected”).

parole.significato: Any specific edition of a work by Plutarch, often specifically Plutarch's Lives
parole.testo: Via Latin Plūtarchus from Ancient Greek Πλούτᾰρχος (Ploútărkhos).

parole.significato: A low screen between columns, especially one that surrounds the choir of a church
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pluteus.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Pluto, the Greek and Roman god of the underworld; demonic, infernal.
parole.testo: The adjective is derived from Latin Plūtōnius (“of or relating to Pluto, Greek and Roman god of the underworld”) + -an (suffix forming adjectives). Plūtōnius is from Ancient Greek Πλουτώνιος (Ploutṓnios, “of or relating to Pluto”), from Πλούτων (Ploútōn, “Pluto”) (from πλοῦτος (ploûtos, “riches, wea

parole.significato: rain; rainfall
parole.testo: From Latin pluvius (“rain”).

parole.significato: A scientific instrument for measuring the amount of rainfall.
parole.testo: From Latin pluvius (“rain”) + -meter.

parole.significato: The scientific measurement of rainfall.
parole.testo: From Latin pluvius (“rain”) + -metry.

parole.significato: Involving or relating to rain; rainy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pluviōsus (“rainy”).

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or resembling air or other gases
parole.testo: From Latin pneumaticus, from Ancient Greek πνευματικός (pneumatikós, “relating to wind or air”), from πνεῦμα (pneûma, “wind, air, breath, spirit”), from πνέω (pnéō, “to blow, breath”).

parole.significato: Of, or relating to the lungs; pulmonary.
parole.testo: From the post-Classical Latin pneumonicus and its etymon, the Ancient Greek πνευμονικός (pneumonikós).

parole.significato: Inflammation of the tissue of the lungs.
parole.testo: From the post-Classical Latin pneumonitis.

parole.significato: Any grass of the genus Poa, especially Poa annua.
parole.testo: From scientific Latin Poa (genus name), from Ancient Greek πόα (póa, “fodder”).

parole.significato: In the shape of a small cup.
parole.testo: From Latin pōcillum (“small cup”) + -iform.

parole.significato: Drinking of wine or other intoxicating liquor.
parole.testo: From Latin poculum (“cup”) + -ation.

parole.significato: Fit for drink.
parole.testo: From Latin poculentus, from poculum (“cup”).

parole.significato: Having the shape of a goblet or drinking cup.
parole.testo: Latin pōculum (“cup”) + -iform; compare French poculiforme.

parole.significato: A drinking-cup used in Ancient Rome.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin poculum. Doublet of bucchero.

parole.significato: Of or relating to gout.
parole.testo: From Latin podagricus, from Ancient Greek ποδαγρικός (podagrikós, “gouty”).

parole.significato: The anus, rectum, or buttocks of a human.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pōdex.

parole.significato: anal (applied to certain body parts)
parole.testo: From Latin pōdicis (“anus, butt”), genitive form of pōdex.

parole.significato: A platform on which to stand, as when conducting an orchestra or preaching at a pulpit; any low platform or dais.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin podium, from Ancient Greek πόδιον (pódion, “base”), a diminutive of πούς (poús, “foot”). Doublet of pew.

parole.significato: A form of execution in Ancient Rome consisting of being sewn up in a sack, sometimes with live animals, and then being…
parole.testo: From Latin poena culleī (literally “punishment of the sack”).

parole.significato: The study of poesy or poetry.
parole.testo: From Latin poēsis [itself from Ancient Greek ποίησις (poíēsis)] + -logy.

parole.significato: The star visible to the naked eye which was in the past, is now, or will be in the future nearest a celestial pole of a…
parole.testo: From pole (“either of the two points on the Earth’s surface around which it rotates; similar points on any other rotating object”) + star, possibly a calque of Latin stēllam polārem (“the Pole Star”).

parole.significato: The military commander-in-chief in Athens, one of the nine archonts.
parole.testo: From Latin polemarchus, from Ancient Greek πολέμαρχος (polémarkhos). By surface analysis, polem- + -arch.

parole.significato: A medical condition resulting from deficient hair care in which the uncombed hair becomes irreversibly entangled, formi…
parole.testo: From Latin Plica polonica, Plica neuropathica.

parole.significato: Well-mannered, civilized.
parole.testo: From Latin polītus (“polished”), past participle of poliō (“to polish, smooth”); see polish.

parole.significato: Government that is in some manner chosen by the governed citizens.
parole.testo: From Latin politicus, from Ancient Greek πολιτικός (politikós), from πολίτης (polítēs, “citizen”) + -cracy.

parole.significato: Pertaining to the role of citizens in the organization and choice of government.
parole.testo: From Latin politicus, from Ancient Greek πολιτικός (politikós), from πολίτης (polítēs, “citizen”) + -cratic.

parole.significato: polish; gloss
parole.testo: Latin politura, from polire (“to polish”).

parole.significato: A fine, granular substance produced in flowers.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin pollen (“fine flour”), used by Carl Linnaeus in the 18th century to describe the spores produced in the anthers of flowers.

parole.significato: Power.
parole.testo: From Latin polleō (“I am strong/powerful”).

parole.significato: Powerful, strong.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pollēns, pollentem (“able, being strong; mighty, powerful”), present active participle of polleō (“to be strong”).

parole.significato: The thumb; the first, or preaxial, digit of the forelimb, corresponding to the hallux in the hind limb. In birds, the p…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pollex.

parole.significato: of the thumb
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pollicis, genitive form of pollex (“thumb”), with the suffix -al.

parole.significato: To gesture with the thumb.
parole.testo: From Latin pollex (“thumb, big toe”).

parole.significato: A voluntary engagement, or a paper containing it; a promise.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pollicitātiō.

parole.significato: To apply pollen to (a stigma).
parole.testo: From pollin- (compound form of "pollen") + -ate (verb-forming suffix). From oblique stem of Latin pollen, pollinis.

parole.significato: undertaker
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pollinctor.

parole.significato: Of or relating to pollen.
parole.testo: From oblique stem of Latin pollen, pollinis + -ic.

parole.significato: Bearing or producing pollen.
parole.testo: From oblique stem of Latin pollen, pollinis + -i- + -gerous.

parole.significato: Any animal that feeds on pollen; a palynivore.
parole.testo: From oblique stem of Latin pollen, pollinis + -i- + -vore.

parole.significato: Having the surface covered with a fine yellow dust, like pollen.
parole.testo: From oblique stem of Latin pollen, pollinis + -ose.

parole.significato: An allergy to grass and other pollen which causes cold symptoms in sufferers; hay fever.
parole.testo: From oblique stem of Latin pollen, pollinis + -osis.

parole.significato: To make something harmful, especially by the addition of some unwanted product.
parole.testo: From Middle English polluten, borrowed from Latin pollūtum, from pollūtus (“no longer virgin", "unchaste”), perfect passive participle of polluō (“soil", "defile", "dishonor”).

parole.significato: Shouted by a player of the game Marco Polo. Compare Marco.
parole.testo: From Marco Polo, from Latin Marcus Paulus, from Paulus.

parole.significato: To give the cry of "polo!" in the marco polo game.
parole.testo: From the game marco polo, from the explorer Marco Polo, from Latin Paulus.

parole.significato: A whitish, woolly plant (Teucrium polium) of the family Lamiaceae, found throughout the western Mediterranean.
parole.testo: From Latin polium, the name of a plant, perhaps Teucrium polium.

parole.significato: A state of many rulers, many leaders.
parole.testo: From Latin, from Ancient Greek πολύς (polús, “many”) + ἀρχή (arkhḗ, “beginning”).

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Polygonum, especially knotgrass.
parole.testo: From Latin polygonium, from Ancient Greek πολύγονον (polúgonon). More at polygonum.

parole.significato: Someone gifted or learned to a great extent or in multiple disciplines; a great scholar.
parole.testo: From Latin polyhistor (“very learned”), from Hellenistic Ancient Greek πολυΐστωρ (poluḯstōr, “greatly learned”).

parole.significato: A cylindrical coelenterate, such as the hydra, having a mouth surrounded with tentacles.
parole.testo: From Latin polypus (“a polyp, a polypus in the nose”), from Ancient Greek πολύπους (polúpous, from πολύς (polús, “many”) + πούς (poús, “foot”)). Doublet of polypus.

parole.significato: Producing or bearing a great number; bringing forth many.
parole.testo: From poly- + Latin parere (“to produce”).

parole.significato: A stylistic scheme in which words from the same root are used together, or a word is repeated in a different inflection…
parole.testo: Via Latin, from Ancient Greek πολύπτωτον (polúptōton), neuter of πολύπτωτος (polúptōtos, “having many cases”), from πολύς (polús, “many”) + πίπτω (píptō, “to fall”).

parole.significato: A medical phenomenon.
parole.testo: From Latin polypus, from Ancient Greek πολύπους (polúpous). Doublet of polyp.

parole.significato: A very large galley with more than five rows of oars on each side.
parole.testo: poly- + Latin rēmus (“oar”). See trireme.

parole.significato: A machine consisting of many pulleys
parole.testo: From Latin polyspaston (“hoisting-tackle with many pulleys”), from Ancient Greek πολύσπαστον (polúspaston, “compound pulley”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the afternoon.
parole.testo: From Latin pomeridianus (“of the afternoon”), contraction of postmeridianus.

parole.significato: the cultivation of fruit; fruit-growing
parole.testo: From Latin pomum + culture.

parole.significato: Producing or bearing fruit, especially apples
parole.testo: From Latin pōmifer (“fruit-bearing”) + -ous.

parole.significato: The study of pome fruit and of the cultivation of such fruit.
parole.testo: From Latin pōmum (“fruit”) and -ology.

parole.significato: pompous
parole.testo: Latin pompaticus.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Pompey
parole.testo: From Latin Pompeiānus, from Pompeius + -ānus. By surface analysis, Pompey + -ian.

parole.significato: dyshidrosis eczema
parole.testo: From Latin pompholyx, from Ancient Greek πομφόλυξ (pomphólux, “a bubble; the slag on the surface of smelted ore”).

parole.significato: The quality of being pompous; self-importance.
parole.testo: From Middle English pomposite (“solemnity”), from Latin pompōsitās. By surface analysis, pomp + -osity.

parole.significato: Pertaining to weight.
parole.testo: From post-Classical Latin ponderālis, from pondus (“weight”).

parole.significato: Weight; gravity.
parole.testo: From Latin ponderans, present participle of ponderare (“to weigh”). Compare Old French ponderant (“of weight”).

parole.significato: To have weight or influence.
parole.testo: From Latin ponderatus.

parole.significato: Heavy, massive, weighty.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin ponderōsus (“weighty”).

parole.significato: An old English measure of weight, usually of wool, perhaps equal to 3 cloves.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pondus (“a weight”).

parole.significato: A weight attached to the penis in order to restore the foreskin to someone who has been circumcised, chiefly with refer…
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: The last player to bet or play in turn.
parole.testo: Perhaps borrowed from Latin ponere.

parole.significato: The capability of being placed or located.
parole.testo: From Latin ponere (“to place”).

parole.significato: A bridge-like tissue connecting two parts of an organ.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pōns (“bridge”). Doublet of Pontus.

parole.significato: A duty or tax paid for repairing bridges.
parole.testo: From Latin pons, pontis (“a bridge”): compare French pontage.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the pons or bridges.
parole.testo: From Latin pont- (“bridge”) + -al (“of, pertaining to”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to kingdom of Pontus.
parole.testo: From Latin ponticus, from Ancient Greek Ποντῐκός (Pontĭkós), from Πόντος (Póntos, “Black Sea, Pontus”) + -ικός (-ikós, “-ic: forming adjectives”). Equivalent to Pontus + -ic. Doublet of bonduc and bundook.

parole.significato: A false tooth that forms part of a dental bridge.
parole.testo: From Latin pont- (“bridge”) + -ic (“of, pertaining to”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the ponticulus
parole.testo: From Latin ponticulus + -ar (“of, pertaining to”).

parole.significato: a ridge of cartilage on the eminentia conchae of the ear
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ponticulus.

parole.significato: A pontiff, state minister, or high priest, in Ancient Rome.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin pontifex. Doublet of pontiff.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a pontiff.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin pontificālis.

parole.significato: The status or term of office of a pontiff or pontifex.
parole.testo: From Latin pontificatus, from pontifex (“high priest”), from pons (“bridge”) + facere (“make”).

parole.significato: Bridgework; structure or edifice of a bridge.
parole.testo: From Latin pontificem, accusative singular of pontifex, from the noun pons, pontis (“a bridge”) + facere (“to make”). Compare pontiff.

parole.significato: papal; pontifical
parole.testo: From Latin pontificius.

parole.significato: pontifical
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pontificius.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the pons.
parole.testo: From Latin pont- (“bridge”) + -ile (“tending to, capable of”).

parole.significato: Describing a bone of the skull of certain fishes
parole.testo: From Latin pont- (“bridge”) + -ine (“of, pertaining”) + -al (“of, relating to”). By surface analysis, pontine + -al.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Pontine Marshes, a formerly extensive swampy area between Rome and Naples. The area has since bee…
parole.testo: Latin Pontinus or Pomptinus, an appellation given to a district in Latium, near Pometia.

parole.significato: Pertaining to Ponza, an island in the Tyrrhenian Sea
parole.testo: From Latin Pontia + -ine.

parole.significato: Pons; pontine; bridge, connecting tissue.
parole.testo: From Latin pont- (“bridge”) + -o-.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; or from; either; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: A social club and debating society at Eton College.
parole.testo: Uncertain. The OED suggests either from (lolli)pop ("because the meetings were held in the rooms of Mrs Hatton, who kept the lollipop shop"), or from Latin popīna (“cookshop”). The second sense derives from the first.

parole.significato: An Ancient Roman bar or bistro, selling wine and simple foods.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin popīna. Doublet of cuisine and kitchen; more at cook.

parole.significato: The shallow depression (fossa) located at the back of the knee joint.
parole.testo: An adaptation of poplit-, the oblique stem of the Latin poples (“the ham of the knee; the knee itself”).

parole.significato: poplar
parole.testo: From Middle English popul, popil, from Old English popul, from Latin populus.

parole.significato: The quality or state of being popular; especially, the state of being widely liked or in favor with the people at large.
parole.testo: From popular + -ity, from Latin popularitas (“an effort to please the people”).

parole.significato: A wood or plantation of poplar trees.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin populetum.

parole.significato: A glycoside, related to salicin, found in the bark of certain species of the poplar (Populus).
parole.testo: From Latin populus (“poplar”) + -in. Compare French populine.

parole.significato: Having a large population.
parole.testo: First used in English in the mid 15th century; from Latin populosus (“full of people, populous”).

parole.significato: Having grooves or furrows broader than the intervening ridges; furrowed.
parole.testo: Latin porca (“a ridge between two furrows”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Porcellian Club, a final club at Harvard University.
parole.testo: From Latin porcellus (“piglet”) + -ian after the dinners of roasted pig that the club originally held.

parole.significato: The killing of a pig or pigs.
parole.testo: Latin porcus (“pig”) + -cide

parole.significato: Love or admiration for pigs.
parole.testo: From Latin porcus (“pig”) + -philia.

parole.significato: A fear or dislike of pigs.
parole.testo: From Latin porcus (“pig”) + -phobia.

parole.significato: Resembling a pore
parole.testo: From Latin porus (“pore”) + -form. Compare French poriforme.

parole.significato: Resembling the leek in colour; greenish.
parole.testo: From Latin porrāceus, from porrum, porrus (“a leek”).

parole.significato: stretched out or forward
parole.testo: From Latin porrectus, past participle of porrigō (“stretch out”).

parole.significato: The act of stretching forth, or holding forward, as if offering.
parole.testo: From Latin porrēctiō, from porrēctus, past participle of porrigō. Compare French porrection. By surface analysis, porrect + -tion.

parole.significato: A neume denoting a set of three tones which first fall from the original tone, then rise.
parole.testo: From Latin porrectus, from porrigō (“to stretch”).

parole.significato: Any of various skin diseases.
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: A place on the coast at which ships can shelter, or dock to load and unload cargo or passengers.
parole.testo: From Old English port, borrowed from Latin portus (“port, harbour”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pértus (“crossing”) (and thus a distant doublet of ford). The directional sense, attested since at least the 1500s, derives from ancient vessels with the steering oar on the right (see etymology

parole.significato: An entryway or gate.
parole.testo: Inherited from the Old English port, from the Latin porta (“passage, gate”), reinforced by the Old French porte. Doublet of porta.

parole.significato: The part of the liver or other organ where its vessels and nerves enter; the hilum.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin porta (“a gate”). See port.

parole.significato: Borne diagonally athwart an escutcheon with the central column going from dexter chief to sinister base (a cross tilted…
parole.testo: From Latin portatus, past participle of portare (“to carry”).

parole.significato: The act of carrying or transporting something; transportation.
parole.testo: From Latin portatio.

parole.significato: To serve as a warning or omen of.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin portendere (“to foretell”), from por- (“forward”) + tendere (“to stretch”).

parole.significato: Something that portends an event about to occur, especially an unfortunate or evil event; an omen.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin portentum, participle of portendere, from portendō (“to predict, to foretell”).

parole.significato: portent; omen
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin portentiō.

parole.significato: Of momentous or ominous significance.
parole.testo: Of multiple origins: * Borrowed from Latin portentōsus, from portentus (“predicted”) + -ōsus. Compare earlier portentuous (via Middle English from Latin portentuōsus). By surface analysis, portent + -ous. * Borrowed from French portentueux

parole.significato: Synonym of portreeve.
parole.testo: From Latin portgrevius, from Old English portgerēfa, from port + gerēfa (“reeve”).

parole.significato: A small room in a church, commonly forming extensions to the north and south sides of it, giving the building a crucifo…
parole.testo: From Latin porticus. Doublet of porch, portego, and portico.

parole.significato: A drink in Ancient Rome and Greece, made by mixing sour wine or vinegar with water and herbs.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin posca.

parole.significato: To assume the existence of; to postulate.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin positus, perfect participle of pōnō (“put, place”). Noun sense 3 (type of number format) was coined by American computer scientist and businessman John Gustafson in 2017.

parole.significato: A control or occupancy of something for which one does not necessarily have private property rights.
parole.testo: From Latin possessiō, possessiōnis. Equivalent to possess + -ion.

parole.significato: Something which is possessed.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: Something that is possible
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: Synonym of after, particularly used with historical dating.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin post.

parole.significato: After the fact; after the focus of an activity has already occurred.
parole.testo: From Latin: "after the fact".

parole.significato: After the fact; too late.
parole.testo: Latin post (“after”) + festum (“feast”).

parole.significato: After the fact.
parole.testo: From Latin post hoc.

parole.significato: An instance of the post hoc ergō propter hoc fallacy, in which temporal order is confused with causation.
parole.testo: From Latin post hoc ergō propter hoc.

parole.significato: After death.
parole.testo: From Latin post (“afterwards”) + mortem, from mors (“death”).

parole.significato: After the death date of the author of a work.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin post mortem auctoris.

parole.significato: After death.
parole.testo: From Latin post obitum.

parole.significato: after; later.
parole.testo: From Latin post (“after, behind”). Cognate with Spanish pues (“well, so, then”)

parole.significato: pedestal, particularly of a pillar or pilaster
parole.testo: German Postament, from Italian postare and French poster. Ultimately from Latin postamentum.

parole.significato: Of the period following a war.
parole.testo: From Latin post bellum (literally “after the war”).

parole.significato: The return of the judge before whom a cause was tried, after a verdict, of what was done in the cause, which is endorse…
parole.testo: From Latin posteā (“after those things”).

parole.significato: Nearer the rear or hind end; nearer the caudal end of the body in quadrupeds or the dorsal end in bipeds.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin posterior (“that comes or follows after; later, latter”).

parole.significato: After the death of someone.
parole.testo: From Latin posthumus, a variant spelling of postumus, superlative form of posterus (“coming after”), the ⟨h⟩ added by association with humus (“ground, earth”) referring to burial.

parole.significato: backward; rear
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin posticus, from post after, behind.

parole.significato: Oriented towards the base.
parole.testo: From Latin postīcus (“posterior, hinder”).

parole.significato: To do something later, when the time has come.
parole.testo: From the Latin verb posticipare, composed of post (“later, after”) + cipare (“as in cipere, to take part”).

parole.significato: posterior
parole.testo: From Latin posticus.

parole.significato: The act of postillating; writing of postils in a text, or (Christianity) preaching by exposition of Scripture.
parole.testo: From Latin postillatio.

parole.significato: Somene who postillates; one who expounds the Scriptures verse by verse.
parole.testo: * postillate + -or * Latin

parole.significato: The return to his own country, and his former privileges, of a person who had gone to sojourn in a foreign country, or…
parole.testo: From Latin postlīminium.

parole.significato: subsequent
parole.testo: From Latin postnatus (“second or subsequently born”), from post (“after”) + natus (“born”).

parole.significato: posterior to the occiput
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin postoccipitālis. By surface analysis, post- + occipital.

parole.significato: After giving birth (often defined as within 30 days after childbirth).
parole.testo: 1844, from Latin post (“after”) + partum (“giving birth”), form of partus, from pariō (“to give birth”), from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“to bring forth”).

parole.significato: To delay or put off an event, appointment, etc.
parole.testo: From Latin postpōnō (“to put after; to postpone”) from post (“after”) + pōnō (“to put; to place”), compare forestall.

parole.significato: To postpone; to defer.
parole.testo: From Latin postpositus, past participle. See postpone.

parole.significato: The part of a theater behind the stage; the backstage area.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin postscaenium.

parole.significato: To make or add a postscript.
parole.testo: From Latin postscribere.

parole.significato: A thing that has been written afterwards; something appended in writing.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin postscriptum, from From post (“after, behind”) + scrīptum (“text, something written”).

parole.significato: Something assumed without proof as being self-evident or generally accepted, especially when used as a basis for an arg…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin postulātum, a neuter nominalization of postulātus, perfect passive participle of postulō, possibly from poscō. See -ate (noun-forming suffix) for more. Cognate with French postulat.

parole.significato: To assume as a truthful or accurate premise or axiom, especially as a basis of an argument.
parole.testo: From Latin postulātus, perfect passive participle of postulō (“to request”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix) for more. Cognate with French postuler.

parole.significato: Of the nature of a postulate.
parole.testo: Latin postulātōrius.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to drinking.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin pōtō (“to drink”) + -atory.

parole.significato: Power, authority.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin potentia. Doublet of Potenza.

parole.significato: Powerful; possessing power; effective.
parole.testo: From Middle English potent, borrowed from Latin potens, potentis (“powerful, strong, potent”), present participle of posse (“to be able”), from potis (“able, powerful, originally a lord, master”).

parole.significato: authoritative
parole.testo: From Latin potestativus, from potestas (“power”). Compare French potestatif. See potent.

parole.significato: An excessive and persistent desire to drink alcoholic beverages.
parole.testo: From Latin pōtō (“to drink (liquor)”) + -mania.

parole.significato: Fit to drink; potable.
parole.testo: From Latin potulentus, from potus (“a drinking, drink”), from potare (“to drink”).

parole.significato: A soft, moist mass, usually wrapped in cloth and warmed, that is applied topically to a sore, aching or lesioned part o…
parole.testo: From Middle English pultes, from Latin pultes, plural of puls. The phonological development from Middle English is regular; compare poultry.

parole.significato: Capable of being accomplished; feasible.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin prācticābilis, partly modelled on Middle French praticable. By surface analysis, practice (verb) + -able.

parole.significato: A practitioner.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin prācticāns. By surface analysis, practice + -ant.

parole.significato: A writ demanding action, or requiring a reason for neglecting it.
parole.testo: From Middle English presepe, from Latin praecipe, imperative of praecipere (“to give rules or precepts”). See precept.

parole.significato: Things previously known, or which should be known in order to understand something else.
parole.testo: From Latin praecognitus, past participle of praecognoscere (“to foreknow”). See pre- and cognition.

parole.significato: Synonym of precordium.
parole.testo: From Latin, from prae (“before”) + cor, cordis (“the heart”).

parole.significato: An imperial official in Ancient Rome who was charged with the supervision of the grain supply to the city of Rome.
parole.testo: Latin, literally "prefect of the provisions".

parole.significato: A tall vase with a handle, used in Ancient Roman sacrifices
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin praefericulum.

parole.significato: A construction commonly found in Greek and Hebrew in which either a verb of motion is paired with a locative prepositio…
parole.testo: From Latin cōnstructiō (“a grammatical construction”) and Latin praegnāns (“pregnant”).

parole.significato: The offence in English law of bringing suit in or obeying a foreign (especially papal) court or authority, thus challen…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin praemūnīre, shortened form of praemunire facias (“that you cause to be forewarned”) from the opening words of the writ: praemūnīre (“to fortify (defend in advance)”) (an error for praemonēre (“to forewarn”)) + faciās (“you make”).

parole.significato: More fully writ of praemunire facias: a writ directing a sheriff to forewarn a person that they must appear before a co…
parole.testo: From Middle English premunire facias, premunire fac', from Latin praemunire facias (“that you cause to be forewarned”) from the opening words of the writ: praemūnīre (“you fortify (defend in advance)”) (an error for praemonēre (“you forewarn”)) + faciās (“you make”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to Praeneste
parole.testo: From Latin Praenestīnus. By surface analysis, Praeneste + -ine.

parole.significato: A first name or given name; particularly the first of the tria nomina (three nouns) borne by free male Roman citizens.
parole.testo: From Latin praenōmen, from prae- (“pre-: before”) + nōmen (“name, family name”).

parole.significato: Relating to a praenomen.
parole.testo: From Latin praenōmin-, praenōmen (“praenomen”) + -al.

parole.significato: Of the prepuce.
parole.testo: From Latin praeputium.

parole.significato: The clitoral hood
parole.testo: Directly from Latin praeputium clitoridis (“prepuce of the clitoris”), clitoridis being a genitive.

parole.significato: The penile foreskin
parole.testo: Directly from Latin praeputium penis (“prepuce of the penis”), penis being a genitive.

parole.significato: A governor in Ancient Rome.
parole.testo: Latin [Term?]

parole.significato: A white robe with a purple border, worn by a Roman boy before he was entitled to wear the toga virilis, or until about…
parole.testo: From Latin praetexta (toga), from praetextus, perfect passive participle of praetexō (“to weave before, to fringe, border”); prae- (“before”) + texō (“to weave”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a praetor.
parole.testo: From Middle English pretorian, from Latin praetōriānus.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a type of Ancient Greek wine.
parole.testo: Latin Pramnium, from Ancient Greek Πράμνιος (Prámnios).

parole.significato: A variety of cryptocrystalline of a green colour.
parole.testo: From Latin prasius, from Ancient Greek πράσιος (prásios, “of a green colour”), from πράσον (práson, “leek”).

parole.significato: Of a clear, light green color.
parole.testo: From Latin prasinus, from Ancient Greek πρᾰ́σῐνος (prắsĭnos, “leek-green, light green”).

parole.significato: Any of several species of birds in the genera Glareola and Stiltia.
parole.testo: From Latin pratincola (“meadow-dweller”).

parole.significato: The practical application of any branch of learning.
parole.testo: Partly from Latin prāxis and partly from its etymon Ancient Greek πρᾶξις (prâxis, “action, activity, practice”).

parole.significato: Before (something significant).
parole.testo: From Latin prae (“in front of”); see pre-.

parole.significato: Before; physically in front of.
parole.testo: From Middle English pre-, borrowed from Latin prae-, from the preposition prae (“before”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a prebend; prebendary.
parole.testo: From Latin praebenda (“the support or allowance afforded by the state to a private person”).

parole.significato: Dangerously insecure or unstable; perilous.
parole.testo: From Latin precārius (“begged for, obtained by entreaty”), from prex, precis (“prayer”). Compare French précaire, Portuguese precário, and Spanish and Italian precario.

parole.significato: Resembling or pertaining to an entreaty.
parole.testo: From Latin precativus (“of prayer”), derived from precatio (“prayer”).

parole.significato: A female precentor.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin praecentrīx. By surface analysis, precentor + -trix.

parole.significato: A preconception or presupposition.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin praeceptiō.

parole.significato: A teacher or tutor.
parole.testo: From Middle English preceptor, preceptur, from Latin praeceptor (“commander; instructor”), from the verb praecipiō + -or (“-er: forming agent nouns”), from prae- (“pre-, fore-: before”) + capiō (“to take; to get, to take in, to understand”).

parole.significato: The alternate responsive petitions, as the versicles and suffrages, between the clergyman and the congregation in litur…
parole.testo: From Latin precēs (“prayers”).

parole.significato: A predecessor; one who came before.
parole.testo: Latin praecessor.

parole.significato: Before a meal.
parole.testo: From Latin cibus (“food”).

parole.significato: Commanding; directing; willing.
parole.testo: From Latin praecipiens. See precept.

parole.significato: To make something happen suddenly and quickly.
parole.testo: From Latin praecipitātus, perfect passive participle of praecipitō (“throw down, hurl down, throw headlong”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) for more), from praeceps (“head foremost, headlong”) (praecipit- in its oblique stem), from prae (“before”) + -ceps (“headed”).

parole.significato: headlong; falling steeply or vertically.
parole.testo: From Latin praecipitātus (see Etymology 1 and -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more).

parole.significato: One who or that which precipitates (causes something to happen or urges it on with vehemence or rashness).
parole.testo: Latin praecipitator (“an overthrower”); equivalent to precipitate + -or.

parole.significato: illustrious, distinguished
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin praeclarus.

parole.significato: To remove the possibility of; to rule out; to prevent or exclude; to render impossible.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin praeclūdere.

parole.significato: The act of precluding.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin praeclusio, praeclusionis, from Latin praecludo.

parole.significato: Hatched from the egg already covered in down and with eyes open; capable of leaving the nest within a few days.
parole.testo: From Latin praecŏcĭa (“places where fruits ripen early”).

parole.significato: Characterized by exceptionally early development or maturity.
parole.testo: From Latin praecox (“premature, precocious, ripe before time, early ripe”), from praecoquō (“to ripen beforehand, ripen fully, also boil beforehand”), from prae (“before”) + coquō (“to cook, boil, ripen”). Doublet of apricot.

parole.significato: To cogitate beforehand.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin praecōgitātus, perfect passive participle of praecōgitō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) for more. By surface analysis, pre- + cogitate.

parole.significato: Previous cogitation.
parole.testo: Latin praecogitatio.

parole.significato: To examine (e.g. witnesses or evidence) beforehand.
parole.testo: Latin praecognoscere (“to foreknow”).

parole.significato: To proclaim in public; especially (of the Pope) to announce the appointment of a bishop.
parole.testo: From Latin praecō (“herald”) + -ize or Latin praecōnizō.

parole.significato: The region of the body over the heart and thorax.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin praecordium.

parole.significato: To forerun or precede.
parole.testo: English pre- + curse, from Latin praecursum (supine of praecurrō [“run before”]).

parole.significato: Being or relating to a precursor; relating to events that will follow.
parole.testo: From Latin praecursor.

parole.significato: Any carnivorous animal.
parole.testo: Latin praeda (“prey”).

parole.significato: Surviving by preying on other animals.
parole.testo: From Latin praedor + -aceous.

parole.significato: The quality of being predaceous.
parole.testo: From Latin praedor + -acity.

parole.significato: Of or relating to prey; plundering; predatory.
parole.testo: From Latin praeda (“prey”).

parole.significato: The preying of one animal on others.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin praedātiō, praedātiōnis, from praedor (“pillage, plunder”), from praeda (“plunder, spoils”).

parole.significato: Any animal or other organism that hunts and kills other nonplant organisms (their prey), primarily for food.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin praedātor, from praedor (“loot, pillage”), from praeda (“booty, spoils, prey”).

parole.significato: Predatory.
parole.testo: From Latin praedatori(us) + -al, equivalent to predator + -ial.

parole.significato: predatory
parole.testo: From Latin praedatorius, equivalent to predatory + -ous.

parole.significato: Of, or relating to a predator.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin praedātōrius, equivalent to predator + -y.

parole.significato: To prey; to plunder.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin praedārī. Doublet of prey.

parole.significato: prey; plunder; booty
parole.testo: From Middle English prede, from Latin praeda. Doublet of prey.

parole.significato: To predestine.
parole.testo: From Middle English predestinate, from Latin praedestinātus, past participle of praedestināre. By surface analysis, pre- + destinate.

parole.significato: To determine or decide in advance.
parole.testo: From Latin praedēterminō; equivalent to pre- + determine.

parole.significato: Predicating; affirming; declaring; proclaiming.
parole.testo: From Latin praedicāns.

parole.significato: To announce, assert, or proclaim publicly.
parole.testo: From Latin praedicātus, perfect passive participle of praedicō (“to publish, declare, proclaim”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), further from prae- (“before”) + dicō (“to proclaim, dedicate”), related to dīcō (“to say, tell”). Doublet of preach.

parole.significato: affirmative; making a clear assertion or statement of praise, especially one with religious or moral implications.
parole.testo: Compare Latin praedicatorius (“praising”).

parole.significato: To make a prediction: to forecast, foretell, or estimate a future event on the basis of knowledge and reasoning; to pro…
parole.testo: Early 17th century, from Latin praedicō (“to mention beforehand”) (perfect passive participle praedictus), from prae- (“before”) + dīcō (“to say”). Equivalent to Germanic forespeak, foretell, and foresay.

parole.significato: A statement of what will happen in the future.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin praedictiō, praedictiōnis; equivalent to predict + -ion. Compare the Germanic equivalents forespeaking, foretale, foretelling.

parole.significato: Useful in predicting.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin praedictivus, from praedico. Equivalent to predict + -ive.

parole.significato: To dominate, have control, or succeed by superior numbers or size.
parole.testo: From Latin praedominātus, past participle of praedominor. By surface analysis, pre- + dominate.

parole.significato: The status of being preeminent, dominant or ascendant.
parole.testo: From Latin praeēminēntia.

parole.significato: Someone who preempts; especially one who appropriates public land.
parole.testo: Compare Latin praeemptor.

parole.significato: Preference.
parole.testo: From Latin praeferentia.

parole.significato: That which is preferred.
parole.testo: From Latin praeferendum, modelled on German.

parole.significato: Trusting beforehand; overconfident.
parole.testo: Compare Latin praefidens (“overconfident”). See pre- and confident.

parole.significato: Synonym of prefixation.
parole.testo: From the present stem of Latin praefīgō (“to attach in front”) + -ation. The formation on the Latin present stem is unusual; perhaps originally an innovation in German.

parole.significato: To prefigure.
parole.testo: From Latin praefiguratus. Equivalent to pre- + figurate.

parole.significato: To show or suggest ahead of time; to represent beforehand.
parole.testo: From Middle English prefiguren, from Latin praefigurare, from figurare (“to shape, picture”).

parole.significato: To limit beforehand.
parole.testo: From Latin praefinire.

parole.significato: a previous limitation or definition
parole.testo: From Latin praefīnītiō.

parole.significato: The act of prefixing: synonym of prefixation.
parole.testo: From Latin praefīxiō. Compare Old French prefixion. By surface analysis, prefix + -ion.

parole.significato: Superior brightness or effulgency.
parole.testo: From Latin praefulgens, present participle of praefulgere (“to shine forth”). See pre- and fulgent.

parole.significato: The parent hydrocarbon for a range of steroids including the progesterones
parole.testo: From Latin praegnans + -ane, from praegnās, from prae- (“before”) + gnā- (the root of *gnāscor, an archaic form of nāscor (“be born”)).

parole.significato: To bear down; to depress.
parole.testo: From Latin praegravatus, past participle of praegravare (“to be heavy upon”), from praegravis (“very heavy”).

parole.significato: To perceive in the manner of Alfred North Whitehead's concept of prehension.
parole.testo: From Latin prehendere. See prehensile.

parole.significato: The act of grasping or gripping, especially with the hands.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin prehensio, prehensionis. Doublet of prison.

parole.significato: Influenced by prejudice; biased.
parole.testo: From Latin praeiūdicāns, present participle of praeiūdicō (“to prejudge”).

parole.significato: Prejudiced, biased.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin praeiūdicātus, past participle of praeiūdicō (“pre-judge”). Doublet of prejudge.

parole.significato: Of or relating to printing; typographical.
parole.testo: Latin prelum (“a press”) + -al.

parole.significato: Of, or relating to the period of innocence before the Fall of man; innocent, unspoiled.
parole.testo: From pre- + Latin lapsus (“fall”) + -arian.

parole.significato: The setting of one item above another; preference.
parole.testo: From Latin praelatio. Compare French prélation. See prelate, and compare prefer.

parole.significato: To speak publicly; to lecture.
parole.testo: From Latin praelectus, past participle of praelegō.

parole.significato: A public lecture or reading, especially delivered at a college or university.
parole.testo: From the stem of Latin praelēctiō (“the act of reading aloud to others”), from the perfect participle stem of praelegō (“read something to others”).

parole.significato: Someone who reads lectures or discourses; a lecturer.
parole.testo: From Latin praelēctor.

parole.significato: A tasting beforehand, or by anticipation; a foretaste.
parole.testo: From Latin praelibatio, from praelibare (“to taste beforehand”).

parole.significato: prelude, portent
parole.testo: From Latin praeludium.

parole.significato: A prelude; something that comes first.
parole.testo: From Latin praelūsiō, praelūsiōn-, from praelūsus, past participle of praelūdere (“to play beforehand”); see prelude.

parole.significato: Acting as a prelude; preliminary.
parole.testo: From the past participle stem of Latin praelūdere + -ive.

parole.significato: Occurring before a state of readiness or maturity has arrived.
parole.testo: From Latin praemātūrus, equivalent to pre- + mature. First use appears c. 1440 in a translation of Palladius's De Re Rustica.

parole.significato: To meditate, consider, or plan beforehand; to think about and revolve in the mind beforehand.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin praemeditātus, past participle of praemeditor (“to premeditate”). By surface analysis, pre- + meditate.

parole.significato: The act of planning or plotting something in advance, especially a crime.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin praemeditātiō.

parole.significato: Serving to reward; rewarding.
parole.testo: From Latin praemialis. See premium.

parole.significato: To give a prize to.
parole.testo: From premium or Latin praemium (“prize”).

parole.significato: The act of giving a reward; compensation;
parole.testo: From Latin *praemiatio, *premiatio, ultimately from praemium.

parole.significato: To premise.
parole.testo: From Latin praemitto.

parole.significato: Superior in quality; higher in price or value.
parole.testo: From Latin praemium (“prize”).

parole.significato: A tooth located in front of the molars, especially the bicuspid tooth between the cuspids and molars in humans.
parole.testo: Clipping of premolar tooth, calque of Latin dens praemolaris. Equivalent to pre- + molar.

parole.significato: One who, or that which, gives premonition; a harbinger
parole.testo: From Latin praemonitor.

parole.significato: Serving as a warning or premonition.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin praemonitōrius.

parole.significato: To show beforehand; to foreshow.
parole.testo: From Latin praemonstratus, past participle of praemonstrare, from prae (“before”) + monstrate (“to show”).

parole.significato: A showing beforehand; foreshowing.
parole.testo: Latin praemonstratio.

parole.significato: Someone or something that premonstrates.
parole.testo: Latin praemonstrator.

parole.significato: Terminated abruptly, or as if bitten off.
parole.testo: From Latin praemorsus, past participle of praemordere (“to bite off”), from prae (“before”) + mordere (“to bite”).

parole.significato: aforementioned
parole.testo: From Latin praenominatus, past participle of praenominare (“to give the prenomen to, to prenominate”).

parole.significato: To note or designate beforehand.
parole.testo: From Latin praenotare, equivalent to pre- + note.

parole.significato: The act of seizing with violence; seizure
parole.testo: From Latin prensatio, from prensare, prehensare, verb frequentative from prehendere (“to seize”).

parole.significato: The act of announcing or proclaiming beforehand.
parole.testo: From Latin praenunciatio, from praenunciare (“to announce beforehand”). See pre- and announce.

parole.significato: announcing beforehand
parole.testo: From prenunciate (“announce before”, whence prenunciation) + -ive, with influence from Latin praenuntiātīvus, a misreading in Pliny of praenuntiōs, praenuntius (“foreboding”) and by analogy with praenuntiō (“announce beforehand; foretell”) + -īvus.

parole.significato: To influence, to occupy (the mind) in advance; to be preoccupied with.
