parole.significato: cave-dwelling
parole.testo: From Latin spelaeum (“cave”).

parole.significato: hopeful or hoped for
parole.testo: From Latin sperabilis. Compare esperance and see -ible.

parole.significato: hoped for
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin speratus, past participle of sperare (“to hope”).

parole.significato: The reproductive cell or gamete of the male; a spermatozoon.
parole.testo: From Middle English sperme, from Latin sperma, from Ancient Greek σπέρμα (spérma, “seed, semen”). Compare also Old French esperme, sparme.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or resembling sperm.
parole.testo: From Middle English spermatik, from Latin spermaticus, from Ancient Greek σπερματικός (spermatikós). By surface analysis, spermat- + -ic.

parole.significato: To produce or emit sperm.
parole.testo: From Latin spermatizare (“to spermatize”), possibly via French spermatiser, from Ancient Greek σπερματίζειν (spermatízein, “to sow, spread seed upon”), from σπέρμα (spérma, “seed, sperm”). By surface analysis, spermat- + -ize.

parole.significato: To disperse.
parole.testo: Apheretic form of asperse, from Latin aspersus, past participle of aspergere.

parole.significato: An idealised conception of the celestial sphere in which the celestial equator is perpendicular to the local horizon an…
parole.testo: First attested in 1932; Latin: sphaera (“sphere”, “globe of the heavens”) + rēcta (feminine nominative singular of rēctus, “right”, “upright”) = “upright sphere”.

parole.significato: A spherical aggregation of raphides in a plant cell
parole.testo: Derived from Latin sphaera + Ancient Greek ῥαφίς (rhaphís).

parole.significato: A reddish-violet pigment found in the cell walls of several mosses of the genus Sphagnum.
parole.testo: From sphagno- + possibly rub(y) or Latin rub(er) + -in.

parole.significato: A compound bone at the base of the skull behind the eyes in humans and various other animals.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin os sphēnoīdeum.

parole.significato: Shaped as a sphere; being a sphere.
parole.testo: English spheric [from Latin sphaericus, from Ancient Greek σφαιρικός (sphairikós)] + -al.

parole.significato: A small sphere.
parole.testo: From Latin sphērula, sphaerula, from sphēra, sphaera (“sphere”) + -ula (diminutive suffix).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Sphinx.
parole.testo: From the stem of Latin Sphinx + -ian.

parole.significato: Sphinx-like.
parole.testo: From (the stem of) Latin sphinx + -ine.

parole.significato: An aluminous earth of a grayish yellow color; a medicinal clay.
parole.testo: From Latin sphragis, sphragidis (“Lemnian earth”), from Ancient Greek σφραγίς (sphragís, “a seal”), so called because sold in sealed packets.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the circulatory pulse.
parole.testo: From Latin sphygmicus, from Ancient Greek σφυγμικός (sphugmikós), from σφυγμός (sphugmós, “pulse”), whence sphygm-.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Sphyraenidae, a family of marine fishes, the barracudas.
parole.testo: Latin sphyraena a kind of sea fish, + -oid.

parole.significato: A spike (kind of inflorescence in which sessile flowers are arranged on an unbranched elongated axis).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin spica.

parole.significato: Having the form of a spike, or ear; arranged in a spike or spikes.
parole.testo: From Latin spicatus, past participle of spicare (“to furnish with spikes, or ears”).

parole.significato: Bearing ears or spikes; spicate.
parole.testo: From Latin spicifer (“bearing spikes or ears”), from spica (“ear”) + ferre (“to bear”).

parole.significato: spike-shaped
parole.testo: From Latin spica (“a spike, ear”) + -form.

parole.significato: A little spike; a spikelet or spiculum.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin spīcula.

parole.significato: Covered with, or having, spicules.
parole.testo: From Latin spiculatus.

parole.significato: A sharp, needle-like piece.
parole.testo: From Latin spīculum.

parole.significato: A thrusting javelin used by Romans that replaced the pilum in the late 3rd century.
parole.testo: From Latin spīculum (“a little sharp point”), from spīcum, alternative form of spīca (“point, spike”).

parole.significato: Synonym of love dart (“calcareous spicule involved in gastropod molluscs' copulation”).
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: Of a plant: producing spikes (“ears (as of corn); inflorescences in which sessile flowers are arranged on unbranched el…
parole.testo: From spike (“kind of inflorescence in which sessile flowers are arranged on an unbranched elongated axis”) + -y (suffix forming adjectives with the sense “having the quality of”). Spike is derived from Middle English spik, spike (“ear of grain; clove of garlic; plant having spikes; plant of the genu

parole.significato: A spine; the backbone.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin spīna (“a thorn; a prickle, spine”). Doublet of spine.

parole.significato: A spinney.
parole.testo: From Latin spīnētum. Doublet of spinney

parole.significato: Bearing a spine or spines; thorn-bearing.
parole.testo: From Latin spiniger, from spina (“spine”) + gerere (“to bear”).

parole.significato: Having a spine, or spines
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin spinōsus.

parole.significato: Having many spines.
parole.testo: From spine + -ous, or borrowed from Latin spinōsus.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to sex or fornication (especially homosexual) between three or more people.
parole.testo: From Latin spintria (“male prostitute”), from Ancient Greek σφιγκτήρ (sphinktḗr, “something which binds”), referring to the anal sphincter.

parole.significato: Capable of being breathed; respirable.
parole.testo: Latin spirabilis.

parole.significato: A pore or opening used (especially by arthropods and some fish) for respiration.
parole.testo: From Latin spiraculum, from spirare (“to breathe”).

parole.significato: A spiracle.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin spīrāculum.

parole.significato: a natural acid, found in the plant genus Spiraea (spirea)
parole.testo: From spiraeic (from the Latin plant name Spiraea (“spirea”) + -ic) + acid.

parole.significato: A non-sibilant fricative.
parole.testo: From Latin spirans, present participle of spīrō (“to blow”). Compare inspire, expire, respiration, etc.

parole.significato: One of certain minute coiled threads in the coating of some seeds.
parole.testo: Diminutive, from Latin spira (“a coil”).

parole.significato: Any of numerous species of fossil brachiopods of the genera †Spirifer and †Delthyris and allied genera in order †Spirif…
parole.testo: From Latin spira (“a coil”) + fero (“to bear”).

parole.significato: Any of various aerobic bacteria of the genus Spirillum, having an elongated spiral form and bearing a tuft of flagella.
parole.testo: From the genus name, from Latin spira (“coil”).

parole.significato: Aqua vitae prepared by distilling wine.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English spirit of wyn, calque of Latin spiritus vini.

parole.significato: A breathing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin spīritus. Doublet of spirit, spirytus, sprite, spright, and esprit.

parole.significato: Synonym of rough breathing.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin spīritus asper, from Ancient Greek δασὺ πνεῦμα (dasù pneûma).

parole.significato: stannic chloride.

parole.significato: Synonym of smooth breathing.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin spīritus lēnis, from Ancient Greek ψιλὸν πνεῦμα (psilòn pneûma).

parole.significato: The spirit, outlook, point of view, or social and cultural values characteristic of an era of human history.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin spīritus mundī (literally “spirit of the world”).

parole.significato: A ruling or guiding spirit.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin spīritus rector (literally “guiding spirit”), an alchemical term. First attested in 1729 in the writings of E. Strother.

parole.significato: A polycyclic compound or system that contains a single atom as the only common member of two rings.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin spīra (“coil, twist”).

parole.significato: Resembling or having the form of a spiral or helix.
parole.testo: From Latin spiroïdes, from Ancient Greek Ancient Greek σπειροειδής (speiroeidḗs). By surface analysis, spire + -oid.

parole.significato: A wet meter used to determine the breathing capacity of the lungs.
parole.testo: From Latin spirare (“to breathe”) + -scope.

parole.significato: Any mollusk of the cephalopod genus Spirula, of which Spirula spirula is the only extant species.
parole.testo: Diminutive of Latin spira (“a coil”)

parole.significato: thick, compact, dense, or crowded
parole.testo: From Latin spissus.

parole.significato: A cloud species which consists of dense, high level strands, which can haze, or block the sun. Associated only with cir…
parole.testo: From Latin spissatus.

parole.significato: pertaining to the spleen
parole.testo: From Latin splēn (“spleen”) + -ative.

parole.significato: A lienculus.
parole.testo: Diminutive of Latin splēn.

parole.significato: Possessing or displaying splendor; shining; very bright.
parole.testo: From Latin splendidus, from splendere (“to shine”) + -idus (“adjective forming suffix”).

parole.significato: Of, related to, or located near the spleen.
parole.testo: From Latin splēnicus, from Ancient Greek σπληνικός (splēnikós, “of the spleen”). By surface analysis, splen- + -ic.

parole.significato: The thick posterior part of the corpus callosum of the brain.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin splēnium (“plaster, patch”), from Ancient Greek σπληνῐ́ον (splēnĭ́on, “pad or compress of linen”).

parole.significato: Either of two flat oblique muscles which are attached to the vertebrae on each side of the neck and upper thoracic regi…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin splēnius, from splēnium (“a plaster, patch”) + -ius (adjectival suffix).

parole.significato: Bone charcoal, used as bleaching material or in the purification of sugar.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin spodium.

parole.significato: Old objects, artifacts, and/or sculptural elements reused in a later work of architecture.
parole.testo: Latin spolia (“spoils”).

parole.significato: The spoils taken by a Roman general from an opponent commander, originally after single combat.
parole.testo: From Latin spolia opīma.

parole.significato: To plunder
parole.testo: From Latin spoliātus, perfect passive participle of spoliō (“plunder, pillage, rob”).

parole.significato: The property of a beneficed ecclesiastic not transmissible by will.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin spolium.

parole.significato: Having or relating to spondees.
parole.testo: From Latin spondaicus, spondiacus, from Ancient Greek σπονδειακός (spondeiakós, “(music) used at a libation”).

parole.significato: A word or metrical foot of two syllables, either both long or both stressed.
parole.testo: From Latin spondēus (“spondee”), from Ancient Greek σπονδεῖος (spondeîos, “associated with a libation”) from σπονδή (spondḗ, “libation”): spondees were often used in melodies sung at libations.

parole.significato: A joint of the backbone; a vertebra.
parole.testo: From Middle English spondile, spondyle, from Latin spondylus, from Ancient Greek σφόνδῠλος (sphóndŭlos, “vertebra”).

parole.significato: Inflammation of the spine.
parole.testo: Latin spondylus (“vertebra”) + -itis

parole.significato: A forward displacement of a vertebra over a lower vertebra, due to a congenital defect or injury.
parole.testo: From Latin spondylolisthesis, equivalent to spondylo- (“spine”) + Ancient Greek ὀλισθάνω (olisthánō, “to slip, slide”) + -esis.

parole.significato: Any of various marine invertebrates of the phylum Porifera, that have a porous skeleton often of silica.
parole.testo: From Middle English sponge, from Old English spunge, taken from Latin spongia, from Ancient Greek σπογγιά (spongiá), from σπόγγος (spóngos). Displaced native Old English swamm (“fungus, sponge”).

parole.significato: A supposed sponge-like expansion of the tip of a rootlet for absorbing water.
parole.testo: Latin spongiola (“a rose gall, small roots”), diminutive of spongia: compare French spongiole.

parole.significato: Somewhat spongy; spongelike; full of small cavities.
parole.testo: From Latin spongiosus, spongeosus. Compare French spongieux. See sponge.

parole.significato: Characteristic of a sponge; spongy
parole.testo: From Middle English spongious, from Latin spongiōsus. By surface analysis, sponge + -ious.

parole.significato: Relating to marriage, or to a spouse; spousal.
parole.testo: From Latin sponsalis, from sponsus (“a betrothal”), from spondere, sponsum (“to betroth”). See spouse, and compare espousal, spousal.

parole.significato: The act of becoming surety for another.
parole.testo: From Latin spōnsiō, from spondēre (“to promise solemnly”).

parole.significato: A person or organization with some sort of responsibility for another person or organization, especially where the resp…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin spōnsor (“a surety", in Late Latin "a sponsor in baptism”).

parole.significato: The quality of being spontaneous.
parole.testo: From Latin spontaneus (“voluntary”). By surface analysis, spont(aneous) + -aneity. Compare French spontanéité.

parole.significato: A natural object which by pure chance resembles some other thing.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin lusus naturae

parole.significato: A gift or prize, especially ones given by rich Romans.
parole.testo: Latin sportula (“small basket, by extension a prize”)

parole.significato: A charitable gift or contribution; alms; a sportula.
parole.testo: From Latin sportula (“a little basket, a gift”), diminutive of sporta (“a basket”).

parole.significato: A deadly mushroom, Amanita verna.
parole.testo: From spring + destroying angel, translating Latin vē̆rna (“spring”), occurring in Europe in spring.

parole.significato: Resembling froth or foam; foaming.
parole.testo: From Latin spumescens, p.pr. of spumescere (“to grow foamy”).

parole.significato: spumous; frothy
parole.testo: Latin spumidis.

parole.significato: Producing foam.
parole.testo: From Latin spūmifer. By surface analysis, spume + -i- + -ferous.

parole.significato: frothy or foamy; spumy
parole.testo: From Middle English spumous, from Latin spūmōsus.

parole.significato: Filth, impurity.
parole.testo: From Latin spurcitia.

parole.significato: Spurious things; especially, a counterfeit or forged written work or one of doubtful attribution.
parole.testo: From the Latin spuria, the nominative neuter plural form of spurius, whence spurious; compare trivia.

parole.significato: The act of spitting; expectoration.
parole.testo: From Latin sputare (“to spit”), intensitive from spuere (“to spit”). Compare French sputation.

parole.significato: A linear triterpene hydrocarbon found in shark liver oil and in human sebum; it plays a role in the biosynthesis of ste…
parole.testo: From Latin squālus (“shark”) + -ene, because it is found in shark liver.

parole.significato: Extremely dirty and unpleasant.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin squālidus, from squālēre (“to be rough or dirty”).

parole.significato: The quality or state of being squalid; foulness; filthiness.
parole.testo: From squalid + -ity or a learned borrowing from Latin squāliditās.

parole.significato: Filthiness and degradation, as from neglect or poverty
parole.testo: From the Latin squālor.

parole.significato: A scale cast off from the skin; a thin dry shred of epithelium.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin squāma (“scale”). Doublet of squame.

parole.significato: Covered in scales.
parole.testo: From Latin squāmātus (“scaly”).

parole.significato: The scale, or exopodite, of an antenna of a crustacean.
parole.testo: From Latin squāma. Doublet of squama.

parole.significato: A diminutive scale or bractlet, such as those found on the receptacle in many composite plants; a palea.
parole.testo: Diminutive from Latin squama (“a scale”).

parole.significato: Having the shape or structure of a scale.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin squāmifōrmis.

parole.significato: Bearing scales.
parole.testo: From Latin squamiger; squama (“a scale”) + gerere (“to bear”).

parole.significato: Resembling a scale.
parole.testo: From Latin squama (“scale”) + -oid.

parole.significato: Covered with, made of, or resembling scales; scaly.
parole.testo: From Middle English squamous, from Latin squāmōsus, from squāma (“scale(of a fish or reptile)”).

parole.significato: One of the little hypogynous scales found in the flowers of grasses; a lodicule.
parole.testo: From Latin squamula, diminutive of squama (“a scale”).

parole.significato: Rough or scaly.
parole.testo: From Latin squarrosus (“(perhaps) scurfy, scabby”).

parole.significato: The angel shark (genus Squatina).
parole.testo: From Latin squatina.

parole.significato: A dinner bell, (historical) a shrill little bell used to signal dinner for medieval monks.
parole.testo: From Latin squilla, from Ancient Greek σκίλλα (skílla).

parole.significato: A hymn, sung in Latin, telling of the sorrow of the Virgin Mary at the crucifixion of Jesus Christ; the music for this…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin stabat mater (“the mother was standing”) (the first words of the hymn).

parole.significato: abstract sculpture or structure of wire, sheet metal, etc.
parole.testo: Coined by German-French artist Jean Arp in 1932 from Latin stabilis (“firmly fixed or established”) to describe the stationary works of Alexander Calder as opposed to his better known mobiles.

parole.significato: The act of making firm
parole.testo: From Latin stābilimentum. Equivalent to stable + -ment.

parole.significato: A particular web structure made by some spiders.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin stabilīmentum.

parole.significato: The act of stabling or housing animals.
parole.testo: Latin stabulatio, from stabulari to stable cattle, from stabulum. See stable.

parole.significato: One of the sweet spices used by the Jews in Biblical times for preparing incense; it is thought to have been an oil or…
parole.testo: From Latin stactē, from Ancient Greek στακτή (staktḗ, “oil of myrrh”) from στακτός (staktós, “oozing out in drops”).

parole.significato: Synonym of stadion (“former Greek unit of distance”).
parole.testo: From Latin stadium, from Ancient Greek στάδιον (stádion), a 600-foot racetrack, a distance of 600 Greek feet. Cognate with French stade. Doublet of stadium, stadion, and estadio.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a glacial stade.
parole.testo: From Latin stadiālis, from stadium.

parole.significato: A venue where sporting events are held.
parole.testo: From Latin stadium (“a measure of length, a race course”) (commonly one-eighth of a Roman mile; translated in early English Bibles by furlong), from Ancient Greek στάδιον (stádion, “a measure of length, a running track”), especially the track at Olympia, which was one stadium in length. The Greek wo

parole.significato: Someone from Stagira.
parole.testo: From the Latin Stagirites, from the Ancient Greek Σταγιριτης (Stagiritēs, “natives of Stagira”), from Σταγειρος (Stageiros, “Stagira”).

parole.significato: To cease motion, activity, or progress:
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin stāgnātus, past participle of stāgnō (“cover the land as a lake, stagnate”), from stāgnum (“pond, swamp”).

parole.significato: The state of being stagnant; (countable) an instance of this.
parole.testo: From stagnate + -ation (suffix denoting an action or process, or its result), Stagnate is derived from stagnāt-, the participial stem of Latin stagnāre, the present active infinitive of stāgnō (“of waters: to cover the land as a lake, to become a pool, to stagnate”), from stāgnum (“body of standing

parole.significato: A millpond.
parole.testo: From Latin stāgnum.

parole.significato: The energy and strength for continuing to do something over a long period of time; power of sustained exertion, or resi…
parole.testo: From Latin stāmina, plural of stāmen.

parole.significato: Having functional stamens, but (typically) no carpels.
parole.testo: Latin staminatus (“consisting of threads”), from stamen (“thread”).

parole.significato: Consisting of stamens or threads.
parole.testo: Latin stamineus.

parole.significato: a two-dimensional layer of tin one-atom thick, which is a topological insulator (conducting electricity only along its…
parole.testo: Blend of stannum + graphene (stannum + -ene) from Latin stannum (“tin”) and graphene, due to the analogous situation of tin in the material to carbon in graphene, being a two-dimensional layer one-atom thick.

parole.significato: tin
parole.testo: From Latin stannum (“tin”). By surface analysis, stann- + -o-.

parole.significato: An isometric-hexoctahedral yellow brown mineral containing hydrogen, iron, manganese, niobium, oxygen, tantalum, tin, a…
parole.testo: For its composition, a tin-dominant member of the microlite group, from Latin stannum (“tin”). Discredited as the name of one specific species of mineral; as a mineral, most likely refers to oxystannomicrolite.

parole.significato: Containing bivalent tin.
parole.testo: From stann- + -ous, from Latin stannum.

parole.significato: tin
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin stannum.

parole.significato: Stirrup-shaped.
parole.testo: From Latin stapēs, stapedem (“stirrup”) + -iform.

parole.significato: The uvula of the soft palate.
parole.testo: From Latin staphylē, from Ancient Greek σταφυλή (staphulḗ).

parole.significato: An abnormal protrusion of the uveal tissue through the eyeball.
parole.testo: Latin, from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: The principle of following judicial precedent.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin stāre dēcīsīs, from stāre (“to stand; to stay, to remain”) + dēcīsīs, ablative plural of dēcīsus, from dēcidere (“to sever, to decide”). Literally, “to stand by decided matters”.

parole.significato: Immediately; now.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin statim (“immediately”).

parole.significato: Standing on all four feet or paws.
parole.testo: From Latin stare (“to stand”).

parole.significato: Fixed; settled.
parole.testo: Latin statarius (“standing fast”), from stare (“to stand”).

parole.significato: A gold, silver or electrum coin of ancient Greece.
parole.testo: From Latin statēr, from Ancient Greek στατήρ (statḗr).

parole.significato: Unchanging; that cannot or does not change.
parole.testo: Modern Latin staticus, from Ancient Greek στατικός (statikós), from ἵστημι (hístēmi, “to make stand”). By surface analysis, stasis + -tic.

parole.significato: Plants of the genus Limonium having spikes of white or mauve flowers.
parole.testo: From Latin staticē, from Ancient Greek στατικός (statikós, “standing still”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to a station.
parole.testo: Latin stationalis: compare French stationnale.

parole.significato: Not moving.
parole.testo: From Latin stationarius, from statio, ultimately from stō (“to stand”). Doublet of stationer.

parole.significato: Of a verb: asserting, generally intransitively, that a subject has a particular property, quality or status.
parole.testo: From Latin stativus.

parole.significato: The stationary part of a motor or other machine.
parole.testo: From stationary or static by analogy with rotor; alternatively from a hypothetical Latin stātor (literally “stander”); all ultimately from stāre (“to stand”).

parole.significato: A supporter of the status quo; one who believes that society is in an acceptable state and should not be changed.
parole.testo: From Latin statū quō + -ite.

parole.significato: A statue.
parole.testo: From Latin statua. Doublet of statue.

parole.significato: The craft of making statues.
parole.testo: From Latin statuāria (ars) (“(art) of sculpture”), feminine of the adjective statuārius (“of statues”).

parole.significato: A person who makes or deals in statues.
parole.testo: From Latin statuārius (“maker of statues”).

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or characteristic of statues.
parole.testo: From the noun or the Latin adjective statuārius (“of statues”).

parole.significato: To prop or support.
parole.testo: From Latin statuminatus, past participle of statuminare (“to prop”), from statumen (“a prop”), from statuere (“to place”).

parole.significato: Synonym of absolute state (Latin designation)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin status absolūtus.

parole.significato: An acute exacerbation of asthma which does not respond to standard treatments of bronchodilators and steroids.
parole.testo: From Latin.

parole.significato: Synonym of construct state.
parole.testo: From Latin status cōnstructus.

parole.significato: A serious and potentially life-threatening condition in which an epileptic seizure becomes prolonged or multiple seizur…
parole.testo: From Latin.

parole.significato: The state of things; the way things are, as opposed to the way they could be; the existing state of affairs.
parole.testo: From Latin status (“state”) (sometimes used in the ablative statū) + quō (“in which”), the ablative of quī (“which”).

parole.significato: The state of things as they were before; a preexisting state of affairs.
parole.testo: From the Latin stātus quō ante (“the way things were before”), possibly from stātus quō ante bellum (“the way things were before the war”).

parole.significato: A situation as it existed prior to the war (often implying the withdrawal of enemy troops and the restoration of pre-wa…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin status quō ante bellum (literally “situation as it existed before the war”).

parole.significato: Synonym of governed state (Latin designation)
parole.testo: From Latin status rectus.

parole.significato: Self-hypnosis.
parole.testo: From Latin status + (stem form of) velle (“to will”).

parole.significato: A highly toxic, perennial plant with purple flowers (Staphisagria macrosperma, syn. Delphinium staphisagria).
parole.testo: Late Middle English, from Latin staphisagria, from Ancient Greek σταφίς (staphís, “grape”) (from σταφυλή (staphulḗ, “bunch of grapes”)) + ἀγρία (agría, “wild”) (literally "living in the fields," from ἀγρός (agrós, “field”)).

parole.significato: Soapstone. (often synonymous; more information at soapstone § Terminology).
parole.testo: From Latin steatītis, from Ancient Greek στέαρ (stéar, “tallow”). By surface analysis, steat(o)- (“fat”) + -ite (“stone”).

parole.significato: An obelisk or upright stone pillar, usually as a primitive commemoration or gravestone.
parole.testo: From Latin stēla, from Ancient Greek στήλη (stḗlē). Doublet of stele.

parole.significato: A serving of Stella Artois, a brand of beer.
parole.testo: From Latin stēlla (“star”). Noun sense 2 is after the protagonist of How Stella Got Her Groove Back (1998).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or characteristic of stars.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin stēllāris.

parole.significato: A type of torbanite, which sparks when set on fire.
parole.testo: From stellar (“starry”) + -ite (“mineral”). From being a form of oil coal (“a type of coal”) which emits sparks like stars (“Latin stella”) when burned.

parole.significato: Shaped like a star, having points, or rays radiating from a center.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin stēllātus (“starry”), from stēlla (“star”) + -ātus (“-ate”, adjectival suffix); equivalent to stell(a) + -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: star-shaped; stellate
parole.testo: Latin stellatus (“starry”).

parole.significato: A starfish.
parole.testo: Latin stella a star.

parole.significato: Shaped like a star.
parole.testo: Latin stelliformis, from stella (“star”), + -iform.

parole.significato: A lizard (Laudakia stellio or Stellagama stellio). It is olive-green with small stellate spots, commonly found in the r…
parole.testo: From Latin stellio (“a newt with starlike spots on its back”), from stella (“star”).

parole.significato: Any fraud not distinguished by a more special name; chiefly applied to sales of the same property to two different pers…
parole.testo: From Latin stellionatus (“cozenage, trickery”), from stellio (“a newt, a crafty, knavish person”).

parole.significato: Synonym of astro-.
parole.testo: From Latin stella.

parole.significato: Having the shape or appearance of little stars; stellate; stellated; radiated.
parole.testo: From Latin stellula, diminutive of stella (“a star”).

parole.significato: A family tree or recorded genealogy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin stemma, from Ancient Greek στέμμα (stémma).

parole.significato: A schema, resulting from the stemmatological process of recension, in which all surviving manuscripts of a given text a…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin stemma cōdicum, from stemma (“family tree”) + cōdicum (“book”, genitive plural).

parole.significato: A person with a powerful or stentorian voice.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Stentōr, from Ancient Greek Στέντωρ (Sténtōr), the name of a herald in the Iliad who had a loud voice.

parole.significato: A tetrapyrrolic bile pigment, one of the end products of heme catabolism, responsible for the brown colour of human fae…
parole.testo: From Latin stercus (“dung, excrement”) + Latin bīlis (“bile”).

parole.significato: fecolith
parole.testo: From Latin stercus (“dung”) + -lith.

parole.significato: Consisting of, resembling or pertaining to feces.
parole.testo: From Latin stercorāceus, from stercus (“dung”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to dung.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin stercorārius (“stercorous, fecal”).

parole.significato: A sheltered place for storing dung.
parole.testo: From Latin stercorarium, from stercorarius (“relating to dung”), from stercus.

parole.significato: Manuring with dung.
parole.testo: From Latin stercoratio, from stercorare (“to dung”).

parole.significato: coprostanol
parole.testo: Latin stercus (“dung”), + -in.

parole.significato: A triclinic-pinacoidal mineral containing hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, and sodium.
parole.testo: From Latin stercus (“dung”) + -ite.

parole.significato: Synonym of fecaloma.
parole.testo: From Latin stercus (“dung”) + -oma, from Ancient Greek -ωμα (-ōma, “tumor, mass”). See fecaloma.

parole.significato: fecal; manurelike
parole.testo: From Latin stercus (“feces”).

parole.significato: dung-eating
parole.testo: From Latin stercus (“dung”) + -vorous.

parole.significato: The state or quality of being sterile.
parole.testo: From Middle English sterylite, sterylyte, from Latin sterilitās. By surface analysis, sterile + -ity.

parole.significato: To expel air as a reflex induced by an irritation in the nose.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sternūtāre.

parole.significato: A sneeze; sneezing, especially as a symptom.
parole.testo: Latin sternutatio.

parole.significato: That causes or induces sneezing; sternutative.
parole.testo: From Latin sternūtātōrius, from sternuō (“sneeze”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to a dunghill
parole.testo: From Latin sterquilinium (“a dung pit”), from stercus (“dung”), + -ous. See also Sterquilinus.

parole.significato: The act of snoring, especially heavy snoring.
parole.testo: From Latin stertō (“to snore”).

parole.significato: Sounding like snoring or snorting.
parole.testo: From Latin stertō (“to snore”).

parole.significato: A symbol used by proofreaders and typesetters to indicate that a word or phrase that was crossed out or changed should…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin stet (“let it stand”), an inflection of stō (“to stand”).

parole.significato: antimony

parole.significato: Combined or impregnated with antimony.
parole.testo: From Latin stibium (“antimony”), -ate, + -ed.

parole.significato: of, or relating to antimony
parole.testo: From Latin stibium (“antimony”) + -ic.

parole.significato: antimony
parole.testo: From Latin stibium (“antimony”), which was imported from Ancient Greek στίβι (stíbi), a variant of στίμμι (stímmi), itself originating from Egyptian s-d-m-N33C:Z2ss (sdm).

parole.significato: A grey mineral, Sb₂S₃, that is the main ore of antimony; in powdered form, used as the cosmetic called kohl.
parole.testo: From Latin stibium, from Ancient Greek στίβι (stíbi), a variant of στίμμι (stímmi).

parole.significato: of, or relating to antimony
parole.testo: From Latin stibium (“antimony”) + -ous.

parole.significato: The measurement of books in terms of how many lines of text they contain.
parole.testo: From Latin stichometria, from Byzantine Greek στιχομετρία (stikhometría), from στίχος (stíkhos, “verse”) + μέτρον (métron, “measurement”) + -ία (-ía, abstract noun suffix). By surface analysis, sticho- + -metry.

parole.significato: A technique in drama or poetry, in which alternating lines, or half-lines, are given to alternating characters, voices,…
parole.testo: From Latin, from Ancient Greek στιχομυθία (stikhomuthía), from στίχος (stíkhos, “line of verse”) (see sticho-) + μῦθος (mûthos, “speech”).

parole.significato: An indication of infamy or disgrace.
parole.testo: From Latin stigma, from Ancient Greek στίγμα (stígma, “mark of slavery or disgrace”), from στίζω (stízō, “to mark”). Closely related to stigme, and distantly related to stick.

parole.significato: A device for distilling liquids.
parole.testo: Via Middle English stillen, clip of distillen; Old French distiller; Latin distillare, from dis- + stillare, from Latin stilla.

parole.significato: To trickle, drip.
parole.testo: Aphetic form of distil, or from Latin stillare.

parole.significato: Falling in drops; drippy.
parole.testo: From Latin stillaticius, from stillare (“to drop”), stilla (“a drop”).

parole.significato: Water falling in drops, especially in a row from the eaves of a roof, or from icicles or stalactites.
parole.testo: Anglicisation of Latin stillicidium.

parole.significato: A morbid trickling.
parole.testo: From Latin stillicidium.

parole.significato: Having the shape or structure of a drop.
parole.testo: Latin stilla (“drop”) + -form

parole.significato: To encourage into action.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin stimulātus, perfect passive participle of stimulō (“to urge, goad on”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from Latin stimulus (“a sting or prick; a stimulus, goad”).

parole.significato: A pushing or goading toward action.
parole.testo: From Latin stimulātiō. Morphologically stimulate + -ion.

parole.significato: A person, device or substance that stimulates.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin stimulātor.

parole.significato: A female who stimulates.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin stimulātrīx. By surface analysis, stimulator + -trix.

parole.significato: An external phenomenon that has an influence on a system, by triggering or modifying an internal phenomenon; for exampl…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin stimulus (“goad, prick”).

parole.significato: Pressed together; crowded.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin stīpātus.

parole.significato: Receiving a stipend.
parole.testo: From Latin stipendiarius.

parole.significato: To provide (someone) with a stipend, or salary; to pay, support or fund.
parole.testo: From Latin stipendiatus, past participle of stipendiari (“to receive pay”).

parole.significato: scholarship, stipend
parole.testo: From the Latin stipendium.

parole.significato: The vertical beam of a cross used for crucifixion.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin stīpes.

parole.significato: Having the shape of a stalk.
parole.testo: From stipe + -iform, ultimately from the oblique stem of Latin stīpes, stīpitis.

parole.significato: A stipule.
parole.testo: From Latin stipula (“stalk, stem”). Doublet of stubble.

parole.significato: To require (something) as a condition of a contract or agreement.
parole.testo: From Latin stipulātus, perfect active participle of stipulor (“to demand a formal promise, stipulate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: The act of stipulating; a contracting or bargaining; an agreement.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin stipulātiō.

parole.significato: An icicle-shaped concretion.
parole.testo: From Latin stīria (“icicle”).

parole.significato: Adorned with icicles, or resembling icicles.
parole.testo: Latin stiria (“an icicle”).

parole.significato: Resembling icicles.
parole.testo: Latin stiria (“an icicle”).

parole.significato: branches, lines of descent, used in the legal expression per stirpes.
parole.testo: From Latin stirpēs, a plural and a collateral form of stirps (“rootstock”).

parole.significato: The breeding of special stocks or races; eugenics.
parole.testo: Latin stirps, stirpis (“stem, stock, race”) + cultura (“culture”).

parole.significato: A branch of a family.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin stirps (“rootstock, stem”).

parole.significato: Proponent of stoicism, a school of thought, from in 300 B.C.E. up to about the time of Marcus Aurelius, who holds that…
parole.testo: From Latin stōicus (noun via Middle English Stoycis pl), from Ancient Greek Στωϊκός (Stōïkós), from Ποικίλη Στοά (Poikílē Stoá, “the Stoa Poikile”, literally “painted portico”), the portico in Athens where Zeno of Citium was teaching.

parole.significato: A school of philosophy popularized during the Roman Empire that emphasized reason as a means of understanding the natur…
parole.testo: From Latin stōicismus. By surface analysis, stoic + -ism. First attested in the 1620s.

parole.significato: The quality or state of being stoic; impassiveness, endurance, or indifference to pleasure or pain.
parole.testo: From Latin stōicismus. By surface analysis, stoic + -ness. First attested in the 1700s.

parole.significato: The traditional garment of women in Ancient Rome, corresponding to the toga worn by men.

parole.significato: A kind of underwear worn in Ancient Rome.

parole.significato: An intricately folded cloth used as underwear by both men and women in Ancient Rome.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin subligaria.

parole.significato: The act of binding underneath.

parole.significato: The act of making sublime
parole.testo: From Latin sublimis (“sublime”) + -ification.

parole.testo: From sub- (“beneath, under”) + liminal (“of or pertaining to an entrance or threshold”) (from Latin līminālis, from līmen (“doorstep, threshold; doorway, entrance; beginning, commencement”); possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *Heh₃l- (“to bend, bow; elbow”)) + *-mn̥ (suffix forming action

parole.significato: A muscular secondary tongue found below the primary tongue in prosimian primates.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: Partly lobate, having a somewhat lobey shape.

parole.significato: Almost or imperfectly membranaceous.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin submembrānāceus. By surface analysis, sub- + membranaceous.

parole.significato: To sink out of sight.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin submergere, from sub (“under”) + mergere (“to plunge”). By surface analysis, sub- + merge.

parole.significato: To submerge.
parole.testo: From Latin submersus, past participle of submergo.

parole.significato: The act of submerging, or the state of being submerged; immersion
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin summersio, summersionem.

parole.significato: to supply; to administer
parole.testo: From the Latin subministrō, sumministrō (equivalent to English sub- + minister).

parole.significato: subordinate or subservient
parole.testo: From Latin subministrans.

parole.significato: The act of subministering.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin subministratio.

parole.significato: Submissive.
parole.testo: From Latin submissus.

parole.significato: To yield or give way to another.
parole.testo: From Middle English submitten, borrowed from Latin submittere, infinitive of submittō (“place under, yield”), from sub (“under, from below, up”) + mitto (“to send”). Compare upsend.

parole.significato: To suggest; to prompt.
parole.testo: From Latin submonere, equivalent to summon + -ish.

parole.significato: suggestion; prompting
parole.testo: Latin submonitio.

parole.significato: Growing underneath.
parole.testo: Latin subnascens, present participle of subnasci (“to grow under”), from sub (“under”) + nasci (“to be born”).

parole.significato: To (literally) tie or fasten beneath, or to (figuratively) join beneath, i.e. as an addendum.
parole.testo: From Latin subnecto, from sub (“under”) + necto (“to tie”).

parole.significato: The seasonal microenvironment beneath the snow.
parole.testo: From sub- (“under”) + Latin nix (“snow”) + -ium.

parole.significato: A rescript
parole.testo: From Latin subnotatio (“a signing underneath”).

parole.significato: Synonym of suborder.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin subōrdō.

parole.significato: Only somewhat characteristic of a prism; not quite prismatic.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin subprismaticus. By surface analysis, sub- + prismatic.

parole.significato: Under Roman law, the act of giving false testimony.
parole.testo: From Latin subreptio, from subripere, subreptum (“to snatch or take away secretly”). Compare French subreption. See surreptitious, surreptition.

parole.significato: Surreptitious.
parole.testo: Latin subreptivus.

parole.significato: To replace one person or thing with another.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin subrogātus, perfect passive participle of subrogō, from sub (“under”) + rogō (“to ask, request”). A variant of surrogate.

parole.significato: derision; mockery
parole.testo: Latin subsannatio, from subsannare (“to deride by mimicking gestures”).

parole.significato: A certain large, triangular muscle near the shoulder that plays a key role in rotating the arm
parole.testo: From Latin subscapularis.

parole.significato: To write (one’s name) at the bottom of a document; to sign (one's name).
parole.testo: From Middle English subscriben, subskryben, from Latin subscrībere (“write beneath”). By surface analysis, sub- + scribe. Compare its native English equivalent underwrite.

parole.significato: Access to a resource for a period of time, generally for payment.
parole.testo: From Latin subscriptiō; by surface analysis, sub- + script + -ion. All senses reflect (either literally or figuratively) the notion of signing one's own name beneath some promise or description to indicate that one agrees with it or agrees to it.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a subscription, or signature.
parole.testo: From Latin subscrīptus (perfect passive participle of subscrībō) + -ive. By surface analysis, subscript (literally “underwrite”) + -ive.

parole.significato: Remaining; extra; spare.
parole.testo: From Latin subsecivus, from sub (“under”) and secare (“to cut”).

parole.significato: To follow closely, or so as to overtake; to pursue.
parole.testo: From Latin subsecūtus, past participle of subsequor (“follow close after”). See subsequent.

parole.significato: To be subservient to.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin subservire; by surface analysis, sub- + serve.

parole.significato: Useful in an inferior capacity.
parole.testo: From Latin subserviens, present active of subservio (“to serve under”).

parole.significato: A low-growing woody shrub or perennial with a woody base.
parole.testo: Formed by the combination of sub- + shrub after the scientific Latin suffrutex. Compare the earlier undershrub.

parole.significato: To sink or fall to the bottom; to settle, as lees.
parole.testo: From Latin subsīdō (“to settle, subside”).

parole.significato: The process of becoming less active or severe.
parole.testo: Latin subsidens, subsidentis, present participle of subsidere. Equivalent to subside + -ence.

parole.significato: The principle that initiative (whether in government, business or religion) ought to reside at the lowest feasible leve…
parole.testo: From Latin subsidiarius. By surface analysis, subsidiary + -ity.

parole.significato: To survive on a minimum of resources.
parole.testo: From Latin subsistō (“halt, stop”), from sub (“below”) + sistō (“stand, place”). Compare consist, desist, exist, insist, persist.

parole.significato: Something that subsists.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin substantis. First attested in 1597.

parole.significato: A brain structure located in the mesencephalon (midbrain) that plays an important role in reward, addiction, and moveme…
parole.testo: Scientific Latin, from substantia (“substance”) + nigra (“black”).

parole.significato: The state of being substantial; substantialness.
parole.testo: From substantial + -ity, from Latin substantialitas.

parole.significato: The act of substantiating.
parole.testo: From Latin substantiātiō. By surface analysis, substantiate + -ion.

parole.significato: A substitute; something that substitutes for another.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin substituendus; compare substituendum.

parole.significato: Something to be substituted or replaced.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin substituendum; compare substituend.

parole.significato: To use in place of something else, with the same function.
parole.testo: From Middle English substituten, from Latin substitutus, past participle of substituō, from sub- (“under; beneath”) + statuō (“to put up; establish”). Displaced native Old English spala (“a substitute”) and spelian (“to substitute”).

parole.significato: underbuilding; substructure
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin substructio, from substruere, substructum (“to build beneath”), from sub (“under”) + struere (“to build”).

parole.significato: The act of subsuming.
parole.testo: From sub- + Latin sūmptus + -ion, from past participle of sūmō (“to take”).

parole.significato: Relating to, or containing, a subsumption.
parole.testo: From sub- + Latin sūmptus + -ive, from past participle of sūmō (“to take”).

parole.significato: To use an angle to delimit (mark off, enclose) part of a straight or curved line, for example an arc or the opposite si…
parole.testo: From Latin subtendere, from sub (“under”) + tendere (“to stretch, extend”), itself a semantic loan from Ancient Greek ὑποτείνω (hupoteínō, “to subtend”), from which hypotenuse also derives. See tend.

parole.significato: under; secret
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin subter-.

parole.significato: Running under or beneath.
parole.testo: From Latin subterfluens.

parole.significato: Synonym of subterranean.
parole.testo: From Latin subterrāneus. Doublet of subterraneous.

parole.significato: subterranean
parole.testo: From Latin subterrāneus. Compare subterrane and subterraneous.

parole.significato: underground, subterranean
parole.testo: From Latin subterrēnus. By surface analysis, sub- + terrene.

parole.significato: To make thin or rare; to rarefy.
parole.testo: Latin subtiliare.

parole.significato: To remove or reduce; especially to reduce a quantity or number.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin subtractus, perfect passive participle of subtrahō (“to draw from beneath; withdraw, remove”); from sub (“under”) + trahō (“to draw, pull, drag”).

parole.significato: A number or quantity to be subtracted from another.
parole.testo: 1670s, from Latin subtrahendus numerus (“number to be subtracted”), form of subtrahō (“to pull out from under, to subtract”) (English subtract). By surface analysis, subtract + -end (“patient (recipient) of action”).

parole.significato: To place under; to insert below.
parole.testo: From sub- + Latin trudere (“to thrust”).

parole.significato: A man's undergarment or shirt.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin subucula.

parole.significato: Awl-shaped; tapering into a sharp point from a broader base.
parole.testo: From Latin sūbulātus.

parole.significato: Relating to or characteristic of or situated on the outskirts of a city; of or relating to suburbia or the suburbs.
parole.testo: From Latin suburbanus, from prefix sub- (“under”) + urbs (“city”) + -anus (“adjective suffix”), equivalent to sub- + urban.

parole.significato: The quality of being suburban.
parole.testo: From suburban + -ity, from Latin suburbanitas.

parole.significato: The suburbs as a whole and all that characterizes or pertains to them; (sometimes derogatory) the suburbs as encapsulat…
parole.testo: PIE word  *upó From suburb + -ia (suffix forming abstract nouns, the names of collections of things, etc.), perhaps modelled after Latin suburbia (“suburbs”), the plural of suburbium.

parole.significato: To arrive or happen so as to help or support.
parole.testo: From Latin subveniō (“come to the aid of”), from sub (“under, up towards”) + veniō (“come”).

parole.significato: unfertilized (thought to be produced by the wind).
parole.testo: From sub- + Latin ventus (“wind”).

parole.significato: To subvert.
parole.testo: From Latin subversus, past participle of subvertere. See subvert.

parole.significato: A subordinate warden, a lower-ranking warden.
parole.testo: From sub- + warden, in some cases as a calque of Latin subcustōs.

parole.significato: A substitute, replacement for something else, particularly of a medicine used in place of another.
parole.testo: Modern Latin, neuter singular of Latin succēdāneus (“acting as substitute”).

parole.significato: Describing a small lobe that is sometimes attached to a placenta
parole.testo: From Latin succenturiātus, perfect passive participle of succenturiō (“to add soldiers to fill up a century; to substitute”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix)), from sub- (“under”) + centuriō.

parole.significato: The achievement of one's aim or goal.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin successus, from succēdō (“succeed”), from sub- (“next to”) + cēdō (“go, move”).

parole.significato: Coming one after the other in a series.
parole.testo: From Latin succedere (“to succeed in”).

parole.significato: Relating to or derived from succinic acid.
parole.testo: From Latin succinum (“amber”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to succinic acid
parole.testo: From Latin succin(um) (“amber”) + -ic.

parole.significato: succinic
parole.testo: From Latin succinum (“amber”).

parole.significato: An outward growth from underneath.
parole.testo: From Latin succrescentia, from succresco.

parole.significato: Growing out from underneath.
parole.testo: From Latin succrescens, present participle of succresco.

parole.significato: A female demon or fiend; a succubus.
parole.testo: From Latin succuba, from succubō (“to lie under”).

parole.testo: Pseudo-Latinism, derived from alteration of Late Latin succuba (“strumpet, especially a mythological fiend in female form who has intercourse with men in their sleep”) based on incubus in Middle English, from Latin succubo (“to lie under”), from sub- (“under”) + cubare (“to lie down”).

parole.significato: A bare axis or cylinder with staves or levers in it to turn it round, but without any drum.
parole.testo: From Latin sucula (“a winch, windlass, capstan”).

parole.significato: submissive; yielding
parole.testo: From Latin succumbens, present participle.

parole.significato: The expressed juice or sap of a plant, often for medicinal use

parole.significato: Intestinal juice: the clear to pale yellow watery secretions from the glands lining the small intestine walls.

parole.significato: To shake with vigor.
parole.testo: From Latin succutere (“to shake up”), from sub- + quatere (“to shake”).

parole.significato: The act of succussing or shaking; a shake.
parole.testo: From Latin succussio, from succutere.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to suckitude.
parole.testo: From suckitude + -al by analogy with other adjectives ending in -tudinal, from Latin -tūdin- + -al, the oblique stem of -tūdō.

parole.significato: A force which pushes matter from one space into another because the pressure inside the second space is lower than the…
parole.testo: From Latin sūctiō, sūctiōnem (whence -ion), attested since Late Latin and derived from sūctus, past participle of sūgō (“to suck”). Attested in English since the early 17th century.

parole.significato: Adapted for sucking; living by sucking.
parole.testo: From Latin sūctus + -ory + -al, from past participle of sūgō (“to suck”).

parole.significato: A small blister beneath the skin due to retention of fluid in a sweat follicle, or in the epidermis

parole.significato: A napkin or handkerchief.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin sudarium. Doublet of sudarium.

parole.significato: To perspire, to sweat.
parole.testo: From Latin sūdāre, from Proto-Indo-European *sweyd-.

parole.significato: Perspiration; sweat (fluid).

parole.significato: A sudatorium; a hot room used to induce sweating.
parole.testo: From Latin sūdatorius, from sūdāre (“to sweat”).

parole.significato: Of, from, constituting, inhabiting, or pertaining to the Sudetes or the Sudetenland.

parole.significato: Relating to stimulation of the sweat glands.
parole.testo: From Latin sudor (“sweat”), and motor.

parole.significato: Sweat; the salty fluid excreted by the sweat glands.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin sūdor.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to sweat; caused by sweat; characterised by the production of sweat.
parole.testo: From sudor + -al, from Latin sudor.

parole.significato: Bearing sweat; sweating, sweaty.
parole.testo: From the Latin sūdōrifer (“bearing sweat”). The term originally came from the Latin sūdor (“sweat”) from the Latin verb sūdō (“to sweat”) + -i- + -fer (“-fer, that which carries”) from the Latin verb ferō (“to bring”) + -ous (forming -ferous).

parole.significato: sudoriferous
parole.testo: Latin sudor (“sweat”) + parere (“to produce”).

parole.significato: Consisting of, or relating to, sweat.

parole.significato: A group of Germanic tribes living mostly near Elbe in what is now central Germany around the first century BCE.

parole.significato: pertaining to Sweden or Swedish

parole.significato: An additional Roman consul elected during the official year, especially in order to replace a retiring one

parole.significato: One of the chief magistrates who ruled ancient Carthage.
parole.testo: From Latin suffes, from Late Punic 𐤔𐤐𐤈 (špṭ, “judge”). Doublet of shophet.

parole.significato: Synonym of suffixal.
