parole.significato: Having the testicles naturally concealed within the abdomen, such as in the case of the cetaceans.
parole.testo: From Latin testis (“testis”) + condere (“to hide”).

parole.significato: A certificate of good character that was required to allow travel between parishes in the 18th and early 19th centuries.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin testificātus.

parole.significato: The act of testifying, or giving testimony or evidence.
parole.testo: From Latin testificātiō. Compare Old French testification. See testify.

parole.significato: A testicle of a vertebrate.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin testis.

parole.significato: Of, or relating to, tortoises.
parole.testo: From Latin testūdin- + -al, from oblique stem of Latin testūdō, from testa.

parole.significato: Resembling or pertaining to the shell of a tortoise.
parole.testo: From Latin testūdin- + -ary + -ous, from oblique stem of Latin testūdō, from testa.

parole.significato: Of, like or relating to a tortoise.
parole.testo: From Latin testūdin- + -ate, from oblique stem of Latin testūdō, from testa.

parole.significato: A turtle.
parole.testo: From a substantivation of the above adjective. Equivalent toLatin testūdin- + -ate, from oblique stem of Latin testūdō, from testa.

parole.significato: Characteristic of a tortoise, or the shell of a tortoise.
parole.testo: From Latin testūdin- + -eous, from oblique stem of Latin testūdō, from testa.

parole.significato: Any member of the Testudinidae, the tortoises.
parole.testo: From Latin testūdin- + -id, from oblique stem of Latin testūdō, from testa.

parole.significato: Any turtle of the superfamily Testudinoidea.
parole.testo: Clipping of taxonomic name Testudinoidea. From Latin testūdin- + -oid, from oblique stem of Latin testūdō, from testa.

parole.significato: A shelter formed by a body of troops holding their shields or targets close together over their heads.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin testūdō (“tortoise, turtle, lyre, type of military shelter”).

parole.significato: A serious and often fatal disease caused by the infection of an open wound with the anaerobic bacterium Clostridium tet…
parole.testo: From Latin tetanus, from Ancient Greek τέτανος (tétanos), from τείνω (teínō, “to stretch”).

parole.significato: Extremely foul or ugly; horrible; terrible.
parole.testo: From Latin teterrima (“most foul, most ugly”).

parole.significato: A bird belonging to the tribe Tetraonini, of which the genus Tetrao is the type.
parole.testo: Latin tetrao (“a heath cock, grouse”), from Ancient Greek. Compare French tétraonide.

parole.significato: A combination of wax, resin, lard, and pitch, composing an ointment.
parole.testo: See tetra- (“four”) and Latin pharmacum (“drug”).

parole.significato: In or of four identical experiments.
parole.testo: From Latin plicō (“to fold”) + Ancient Greek τετράς (tetrás, “four”).

parole.significato: A noun that has four cases.
parole.testo: From Latin tetraptōtum, from Ancient Greek τετράπτωτος (tetráptōtos).

parole.significato: A governor or ruler of a quarter of a country, especially of a fourth part of a province in or client state of Ancient…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tetrarchēs, from Ancient Greek τετράρχης (tetrárkhēs), from τετρα- (tetra-, “four”) + -άρχης (-árkhēs, “ruler, leader”).

parole.significato: A government where power is shared by four people, especially (historical) the Herodian tetrarchy established in Judea…
parole.testo: From Latin tetrarchia, from Ancient Greek τετραρχία (tetrarkhía), from τετρα- (tetra-, “four”) + -αρχία (-arkhía, “-archy: rule”), equivalent to tetra- + -archy.

parole.significato: A four-line stanza.
parole.testo: From Latin tetrastichon, from neuter of Ancient Greek τετράστιχον (tetrástikhon, “having four rows”), from τετρα- (tetra-, “four”) + στίχος (stíkhos, “row”).

parole.significato: A collection of the four Gospels
parole.testo: From tetra- + ecclesiastical Latin evangelium (“evangel”).

parole.significato: Morose, bitter.
parole.testo: From Latin tetricus (“stern, severe, gloomy”).

parole.significato: The quality of being tetric: crabbedness, harshness, bitterness.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tetricitas, taetricitas. By surface analysis, tetric + -ity.

parole.significato: One of the ancient Trojans.
parole.testo: From Latin Teucrus, from plural Teucri (“the Trojans”), from Teucer, the name of the first king of Troy.

parole.significato: A member of an early Germanic tribe living in Jutland noted in historical writings by Greek and Roman authors.
parole.testo: PIE word  *tewtéh₂ Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *tewtéh₂der. Latin Teutonēsbor. English Teuton Borrowed from Latin Teutonēs, Teutonī (“the Teutons”) (compare Ancient Greek Τεύτονες (Teútones)), possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *tewtéh₂ (“people”). First attested in the early 1700s.

parole.significato: Relating to the ancient Germanic people, the Teutons.
parole.testo: PIE word  *tewtéh₂ 1580, from Latin Teutonicus, from Teutonēs, Teutonī (“the Teutons”, name of a Germanic tribe that inhabited coastal Germany and devastated Gaul between 113–101 B.C.), equivalent to Teuton + -ic.

parole.significato: Any material made of interlacing or matted fibres, including carpeting and geotextiles, woven or nonwoven.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin textile, substantive use of textilis (“woven”), from texō (“weave”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to weaving.
parole.testo: From Latin textorius, from textor (“a weaver”), from texere, textum (“to weave”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to weaving
parole.testo: Latin textrīnus, for textōrīnus, from textor (“a weaver”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to text.
parole.testo: From Middle English textewell, textueel, textuel, textuele, tixtuel (“learned in texts, bookish”), possibly from Latin textuālis; also compare Middle French textuele; or perhaps a coinage by Chaucer from Latin textus and Middle English -el. English spelling conformed to Latin from late 15c. By surfa

parole.significato: The succession of printed Greek texts of the New Testament which constituted the translation base for various early ver…
parole.testo: From Latin textus receptus (“received text”).

parole.significato: Either of two large, ovoid structures of grey matter within the forebrain that relay sensory impulses to the cerebral c…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin thalamus, from Ancient Greek θάλαμος (thálamos, “an inner chamber, a bedroom, a bed”).

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Thalictrum; meadowrue.
parole.testo: From Latin thalictrum.

parole.significato: The presentation of something as a marvel rather than in a neutrally descriptive way.
parole.testo: From Latin, from Ancient Greek θαυμασμός (thaumasmós, “a wondering”).

parole.parola: the cure is worse than the disease
parole.significato: The medical treatment for an illness produces a worse net result than the illness does (or threatens a non-negligible r…
parole.testo: From Latin aegrescit medendo (literally “it worsens with healing”) attributed to Virgil in book XII of the Aeneid.

parole.significato: A conclusive action has been taken, so events will proceed in an irreversible manner; the point of no return has been p…
parole.testo: Calque of Latin iacta ālea est, which is grammatically, and thereby semantically, an incorrect translation by the Roman historian Suetonius (c. 69 – p. 122 C.E.) in his work Vīta Dīvī Iūlī (On the Life of the Caesars, 121 C.E.) of the Ancient Greek ἀνερρίφθω κύβος (anerrhíphthō kúbos), which was sai

parole.parola: the voice of the people, the voice of God
parole.significato: The voice of the people should be heard.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin vōx populī, vōx Deī (“the voice of the people [is] the voice of God”).

parole.significato: god or deity
parole.testo: From Latin theo- (“god”), combining form of theos (“god”); from Ancient Greek θεο- (theo-, “god”), combining form of θεός (theós, “god”).

parole.significato: theatrical
parole.testo: From Latin theātrālis.

parole.significato: Theban; of or pertaining to Thebes, especially in the context of the Coptic scriptures.
parole.testo: From Latin Thēbaicus, from Ancient Greek Θηϐαϊκός (Thēbaïkós).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Thebes
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Thēbānus, from Thēb(ae) + -ānus. By surface analysis, Theb(es) + -an.

parole.significato: Any of several external cases or sheaths.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Latin thēca, from Ancient Greek θήκη (thḗkē, “a case, box, receptacle”), from τίθημι (títhēmi, “put, set, place”). Doublet of tay.

parole.significato: A toll or custom required from travelling merchants as a tax on doing business.
parole.testo: From Latin telōnium, from Ancient Greek τελώνῐον (telṓnĭon, “custom house”), from τέλος (télos, “due, tax, toll”).

parole.significato: god; deity
parole.testo: From Latin theo- (“god”), combining form of theos (“god”); from Ancient Greek θεο- (theo-, “god”), combining form of θεός (theós, “god”).

parole.significato: A fiador.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Theodōrus, borrowed from Ancient Greek Θεόδωρος (Theódōros), from θεός (theós, “god”) + δῶρον (dôron, “gift”). The name was popularized in reference to the prominent St Theodore of Amasea. Unrelated to Theodoric.

parole.significato: A poor theologian; someone who merely pretends to be a theologian.
parole.testo: From Latin theologus + -aster.

parole.significato: A theologian.
parole.testo: From the stem of Latin theologus or English theology + -er; see -loger.

parole.significato: To discuss or speculate about theological subjects.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin theologizāre, with the transitive sense possibly being formed by theology + -ize.

parole.significato: A student of theology
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin theologus, from Ancient Greek θεολόγος (theológos). Equivalent to theo- + -logue.

parole.significato: Synonym of theologian (“Roman Catholic lecturer”).
parole.testo: From Latin theologus.

parole.significato: Concerned with theories or hypotheses rather than with practical matters.
parole.testo: English theory + -etic, from Latin theōrēticus, from Ancient Greek θεωρητικός (theōrētikós).

parole.significato: Of or relating to theory; abstract; not empirical.
parole.testo: From Middle English theorothycall, probably from Latin theōrēticus + -al, from Ancient Greek θεωρητικός (theōrētikós).

parole.significato: Relating to, or skilled in, theory; theoretical.
parole.testo: From Middle English theoryk, from Latin theōricus and Middle French theorique. By surface analysis, theory + -ic.

parole.significato: theoretical
parole.testo: From Middle English theorycall, from Latin theōricus + -al. By surface analysis, theory + -ical.

parole.significato: A Jewish sect which flourished in Alexandria and other parts of the Diaspora of Hellenistic Judaism in the final years…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin [Term?], from Ancient Greek θερᾰπευταί (therăpeutaí), plural of θερᾰπευτής (therăpeutḗs, “one who serves the gods, worshipper”).

parole.parola: there is nothing new under the sun
parole.significato: There is nothing truly novel in existence; every new idea has some sort of precedent or echo from the past.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin nihil sub sōle novum, itself a calque from the Hebrew אֵין כָּל חָדָשׁ תַּחַת הַשָּׁמֶשׁ (en kol chadásh táchat hashámesh, “there is nothing new under the sun”) found in Ecclesiastes 1:9.

parole.significato: In subjective matters of taste, people have wildly different opinions; disagreements about matters of taste cannot be o…
parole.testo: Adaptation of Latin de gustibus non est disputandum.

parole.significato: Roman-style spring or baths with warm or hot water.
parole.testo: From Latin thermae, plural of therma. See thermal.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the city of Therma.
parole.testo: From Therma + -ean, modelled after Latin Thermaeus, from Ancient Greek Θερμαῖος (Thermaîos).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the city of Therma.
parole.testo: From Latin Thermaicus, from Ancient Greek Θερμαϊκός (Thermaïkós).

parole.significato: A place where food and hot drinks were sold.
parole.testo: From Latin thermopōlium.

parole.significato: A publication that provides synonyms (and sometimes antonyms and other semantic relations) for the words of a given lan…
parole.testo: 16th century, borrowed from Latin thēsaurus, from Ancient Greek θησαυρός (thēsaurós, “storehouse, treasure”); its current English usage/meaning was established soon after the publication of Peter Roget's Thesaurus of English Words and Phrases in 1852. Doublet of treasure.

parole.significato: This document (formerly used in official documents and decrees; now mainly confined to university diplomas).
parole.testo: Calque of Latin hae presentes [litterae], literally "these present [letters]" but idiomatically "this present [document]."

parole.significato: Senses relating to logic, rhetoric, etc.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English thesis (“lowering of the voice”) and also borrowed directly from its etymon Latin thesis (“proposition, thesis; lowering of the voice”), from Ancient Greek θέσῐς (thésĭs, “arrangement, placement, setting; conclusion, position, thesis; lowering of the voice”), from τῐ́θημῐ (t

parole.significato: Of, or relating to drama and acting; dramatic, theatrical.
parole.testo: From Latin Thespis, from the name of the Ancient Greek actor Thespis (fl. 6th century BCE), from Θέσπις (Théspis) + -ian.

parole.significato: Of, or pertaining to, theurgy.
parole.testo: From Latin theurgicus. By surface analysis, theurgy + -ic.

parole.significato: A group of singers and dancers assembled to celebrate the festival of one of the gods.
parole.testo: From Latin, from Ancient Greek θίασος (thíasos).

parole.significato: A cupola, a dome, a rotunda; a tholus.
parole.testo: Anglicization of Latin tholus (“cupola, dome, rotunda”), from Ancient Greek θόλος (thólos, “dome, vault”), further etymology uncertain but possibly cognate with θᾰ́λᾰμος (thắlămos, “bedroom; inner chamber”) and/or English dale. Doublet of tholus and tholos.

parole.significato: A small domical mountain or hill.
parole.testo: From Latin tholus (“dome, rotunda”). Doublet of tholos.

parole.significato: An infidel or doubter.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English Thomas, from Latin Thōmās m (as in the Vulgate), from Ancient Greek Θωμᾶς m (Thōmâs), the Biblical Greek transcription of Aramaic תאומא or תאמא (“twin”), the nickname of one of the Twelve Apostles. In the gospel of John (11:16, 20:24), the Aramaic nickname is also trans

parole.significato: A follower or advocate of Thomism.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin Thōmista.

parole.significato: nuptial
parole.testo: From Latin t(h)orus (“marriage”, literally “(marriage) bed”).

parole.significato: The region of the mammalian body between the neck and abdomen as well as the cavity containing the heart and lungs.
parole.testo: From Latin thorax, from Ancient Greek θώραξ (thṓrax, “a breastplate, cuirass, corslet”).

parole.significato: Boastful, bragging, vainglorious.
parole.testo: From Latin Thrasō, Thrason-, the name of a boastful soldier in the play Eunuchus by Terence. The name is derived from Ancient Greek θρασύς (thrasús, “bold, audacious”).

parole.significato: a dirge or lamentation
parole.testo: From Latin threnus, from Ancient Greek θρῆνος (thrênos, “funeral lament”).

parole.significato: Resembling a tuna.
parole.testo: From Latin thunnus (“tuna”) + -iform.

parole.significato: related to incense
parole.testo: From Latin thūrālis (adjective), from thūs (“incense”).

parole.significato: A censer, especially one hanging on a chain.
parole.testo: Originated 1400–50 from late Middle English turrible, from thoryble, from Latin thūribulum (“censer”), equivalent to thūs (“incense”) (root: thūr-) (from Ancient Greek θύος (thúos, “burnt offering”)) + -bulum (“instrumental suffix”).

parole.significato: A thurifer.
parole.testo: From unattested Latin *thūribulārius, *thūribulāriorum, ultimately from thūribulum.

parole.significato: The fragrant wood of a North African tree (Tetraclinis articulata) in the family Cupressaceae.
parole.testo: From Latin thȳinus.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to thynnic acid or its derivatives
parole.testo: From Latin thynnus (“tuna”) + -ic.

parole.significato: A spot in the wing veins of Neuroptera, Hymenoptera and Trichoptera.
parole.testo: From Latin thyridium, from Ancient Greek θυρίδιον (thurídion), diminutive of θύρᾱ (thúrā, “door”).

parole.significato: A form of thyrotoxicosis caused by the ingestion of exogenous thyroid hormone
parole.testo: From Latin.

parole.significato: A staff topped with a conical ornament, carried by Bacchus or his followers.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin thyrsus, from Ancient Greek θύρσος (thúrsos). Doublet of thyrse, torse, and torso.

parole.significato: The three-tiered papal crown.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tiāra, from Ancient Greek τιάρα (tiára), of unknown ultimate origin.

parole.significato: The inner and usually the larger of the two bones of the leg or hind limb below the knee, the shinbone.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tībia (“shin bone, leg”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a tibia or a structure associated with a tibia.
parole.testo: From Latin tībiālis, equivalent to tibia + -al.

parole.significato: A flute-player; a piper, flautist.
parole.testo: From the Latin tībīcen (“piper, flautist”).

parole.significato: thrice per day, consumed three times per day
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ter in diē.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or characteristic of the tiger.
parole.testo: From Latin tigrīnus.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or resembling the family Tiliaceae (now principally subfamily Tilioideae in family Malvaceae) of flo…
parole.testo: From translingual Tiliaceae + -ous, from Latin tilia (“linden tree”).

parole.significato: Time passes quickly.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin tempus fugit.

parole.significato: The dyeing poison dart frog (Dendrobates tinctorius).
parole.testo: Probably from the Latin specific epithet tinctorius.

parole.significato: A tint or colour.
parole.testo: From Middle English tynct (noun) and tincten, tyncten, tynkten (verb), borrowed from Latin tīnctus, past participle of tingō (“to tinge”). Doublet of tint.

parole.significato: A stain; a preparation for staining.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tinctiō (“a soaking, dipping”).

parole.significato: tincture
parole.testo: From Latin tīnctūra. Doublet of tainture, teinture, and tincture.

parole.significato: A preparation made by macerating or digesting myrrh with alcohol and filtering.
parole.testo: From Latin tīnctūra myrrhae.

parole.significato: Senses relating to colour, and to dipping something into a liquid.
parole.testo: The noun is derived from Late Middle English tincture (“a dye, pigment; a colour, hue, tint; process of colouring or dyeing; medicinal ointment or salve (perhaps one discolouring the skin); use of a medicinal tincture; (alchemy) transmutation of base metals into gold; ability to cause such transmuta

parole.significato: A fungal infection of the skin, known generally as ringworm.
parole.testo: From Latin tinea (“moth; bookworm”).

parole.significato: Jock itch.
parole.testo: From Latin tinea crūris (literally “leg (ring)worm”).

parole.significato: athlete’s foot
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: Ringworm (any of certain fungal infections) of a fingernail or toenail.
parole.testo: From Latin tinea (“worm, moth”) unguis (“fingernail, toenail, claw, hoof”).

parole.significato: A small added amount of colour; (by extension) a small added amount of some other thing.
parole.testo: The verb is derived from Latin tingere, present active infinitive of tingō (“to dip; to moisten; to colour, dye, tinge”). The noun is derived from the verb.

parole.significato: Having the power to tinge (dye).
parole.testo: From Latin tingens, present participle of tingere (“to tinge”). See tinge.

parole.significato: Capable of being stained.
parole.testo: Latin tingere (“to dye”).

parole.significato: Having a ringing or clinking sound.
parole.testo: From Latin tinnīo + -ent.

parole.significato: Synonym of tintinnabulum.
parole.testo: From Latin tinniolum.

parole.significato: The experience of auditory sensations, such as a ringing or pulsating sound, occurring in the absence of any external s…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin tinnītus (“a jingling, ringing”).

parole.significato: Of or related to bells; of the nature of a bell.
parole.testo: From Latin tintinnabulum (“little bell”) + -ar (“forming adjectives”).

parole.significato: A bell-ringer.
parole.testo: From tintinnabular + -ary. Noun sense possibly also under the influence of Latin tintinnabularius (“bell-ringer”).

parole.significato: To ring, tinkle, toll, or otherwise sound like bells.
parole.testo: From Latin tintinnabulatus (“furnished with a bell or bells”), from tintinnabulum ("a bell"). Akin to tinnitus.

parole.significato: A tinkling sound, as of a bell or of breaking glass.
parole.testo: Noun of action from tintinnabulate, from Latin tintinnabulum (“a bell”), from tintinō, a reduplicated form of tinniō (“ring, jingle”).

parole.significato: A compositional style characterized by two types of voice, the first of which (the "tintinnabular voice") arpeggiates t…
parole.testo: From Latin tintinnābulum (“a small monastic bell”).

parole.significato: A small clinking bell, particularly (historical) a small bell used to call monks to certain tasks.
parole.testo: From Latin tintinnābulum (“a small monastic bell”).

parole.significato: A shoulder covering, typically the fur of a fox, with long ends that dangle in front.
parole.testo: From Middle English tippet, Old English tæppet, from Latin tapete (“cloth”).

parole.significato: Any of many species of long-legged dipterous insects belonging to Tipula and allied genera; a common crane fly.
parole.testo: Related to Latin tippula (“water spider”).

parole.significato: Schooling, apprenticeship; novitiate.
parole.testo: From Latin tirocinium (“first military campaign; raw recruit; inexperience; first attempt”), from tīro (“beginner, recruit, novice”) + -cinor (“forming verbs: to be a ...”) + -ium (“forming nouns: the state of ...”), used in the title of William Cowper's 1784 poem on schools Tirocinium, or A Review

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Marcus Tullius Tiro (died circa 4 BCE), scribe of Cicero and inventor of an early shorthand.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Tīrōniānus.

parole.significato: Any one of thousands of signs in a system of shorthand developed in the 60s BC by Cicero’s scribe Marcus Tullius Tiro.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin nota Tīrōniāna

parole.significato: Any one of Uranus and Gaia's daughters; a female Titan.
parole.testo: From Latin Titanis, from Ancient Greek Τιτανίς (Titanís). By surface analysis, Titan + -id.

parole.significato: A chemical element (symbol Ti), atomic number 22; it is a strong, corrosion-resistant transition metal, used to make li…
parole.testo: From Latin titanium.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or denoting those rays of light which produce chemical effects; actinic.
parole.testo: Latin Tithonius (“belonging to Tithonus, the consort of Aurora”), from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: Any kind of spurge, especially Euphorbia cyparissias.
parole.testo: From Latin tithymalus.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Titus Tatius, a king of the Sabines according to the Roman foundation myth.
parole.testo: From Latin Titiānus (“of or relating to Titus; a male given name”), from Titus + -iānus. By surface analysis, Titus + -ian.

parole.significato: To stimulate or excite sensually.
parole.testo: From Latin tītillātus, from tītillāre (“to tickle”).

parole.significato: A pleasurable or sexually exciting sensation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tītillātiō, tītillātiōnem.

parole.significato: The name of a film, musical piece, painting, or other work of art.
parole.testo: From Middle English title, titel, from Old English titul (“title, heading, superscription”), from Latin titulus (“title, inscription”). Doublet of tilde, titer/titre, titlo, tittle, and titulus.

parole.significato: To stagger
parole.testo: From Latin titubatus, past participle of titubare (“to stagger, totter”).

parole.significato: A caption, title or other inscription, especially an Ancient Roman type.
parole.testo: From Latin titulus. Doublet of tilde, titer/titre, title, titlo, and tittle.

parole.significato: Every person is entitled to their personal preferences and tastes.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin suum cuique, short for suum cuique pulchrum est (“to each his own is beautiful”).

parole.significato: Everyone makes mistakes.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin errāre hūmānum est.

parole.significato: An ancient people of Bactria.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Tocharī pl, from Ancient Greek Τόχαροι pl (Tókharoi).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Tochari (people of Bactria).
parole.testo: From Latin Tocharī + -ian, the first element deriving from Ancient Greek Τόχαροι (Tókharoi, “Tochari/Tukharas (an ancient people of Bactria)”), plural of Τόχαρος (Tókharos), probably from an Indo-Iranian source (Old Persian [script needed] (tuxāri-), Khotanese [script needed] (ttahvāra)); compare Sa

parole.significato: A loose outer garment worn by the citizens of Ancient Rome.
parole.testo: Borrowed directly from Latin toga, from tegō (“to clothe”). Doublet of toge. The Philippine (and Indonesian) senses are due to the resemblance of the white ceremonial gowns worn by graduates of institutions to the loose outer garment worn by the citizens of Ancient Rome.

parole.significato: Clad in a toga; represented in art as wearing a toga.
parole.testo: From the Latin togātus (“wearing a toga”).

parole.significato: Dressed in a toga or gown; wearing a gown; gowned.

parole.significato: Easily construed or seen through.

parole.significato: Located beyond the river Tiber.

parole.significato: located beyond the river Tigris

parole.significato: To change, convert

parole.significato: A copy or exemplification of a record.

parole.significato: The act of taking or transporting from one place to another, e.g. of blood.
parole.testo: Latin transumptio, from tran- + sumption.

parole.significato: Metaphorical.

parole.significato: The act or process of pouring out of one vessel into another.

parole.significato: To beat or strike through

parole.significato: A form of religious ecstasy characterized by a piercing sensation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin trānsverberātiō (“empiercement”). By surface analysis, transverberate + -ion.

parole.significato: Situated or lying across; side to side, relative to some defined "forward" direction; perpendicular or slanted relative…

parole.significato: To cause to turn across; to transverse.
parole.testo: From Latin transvertere. See transverse (adjective).

parole.significato: A flight beyond or across.

parole.significato: Shaped like a trapezium.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Trabzon, Trebizond, etc.

parole.significato: Of, caused by, or causing trauma.

parole.significato: A medicine for wounds; a vulnerary.

parole.significato: Used for forming names of large numbers as the third in the sequence in the Conway–Guy system.

parole.significato: A period of thirteen years.

parole.significato: Any fungus of the genus Tremella.

parole.significato: Resembling or characteristic of jelly.
parole.testo: From Latin tremulus (“shaking; trembling; quivering”) + -ose. See also English tremulous.

parole.significato: Synonym of tremendous.
parole.testo: From Latin tremendus. Doublet of tremendous.

parole.significato: Trembling, quivering, or shaking.

parole.significato: Timid, timorous, fearful.
parole.testo: From Latin trepidus (“anxious”).

parole.significato: Trembling with fear or emotion.
parole.testo: From Latin trepidantem.

parole.significato: Anxiety over the uncertain future or possible ill-occurrence.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin trepidātiō, from trepidō (“be agitated”).

parole.significato: Three.
parole.testo: PIE word  *tréyes From Latin tri- (“three”) and Ancient Greek τρι- (tri-, “three”).

parole.significato: The three names borne by free male Roman citizens, consisting of the praenomen, nomen, and cognomen.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin tria nōmina, from tria (neuter of trēs (“three”)) + nōmina (plural of nōmen (“name”)), literally “three names”.

parole.significato: A grouping of three.
parole.testo: PIE word  *tréyes From Latin triad-, stem of trias (“three, triad”), from Ancient Greek τριάς (triás). By surface analysis, tri- + -ad. parole.significato: Characterized by having three (usually equivalent) components.

parole.significato: Synonym of triangular.
parole.testo: From Latin triangulātus. By surface analysis, tri- + angulate.

parole.significato: Occupying the third post or rank.
parole.testo: Latin triarii (plural), a class of Roman soldiers who formed the third rank from the front, from tres, tria (“three”).

parole.significato: Relating to tribadism.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tribadicus. By surface analysis, tribade + -ic.

parole.significato: Of or relating to tribes.
parole.testo: From Latin tribālis. By surface analysis, tribe + -al, first attested in the 1630s. parole.significato: A metrical foot consisting of three short syllables.

parole.significato: The state or office of a tribune.
parole.testo: From Latin tribūnātus, from tribūnus (“tribune, tribal leader”) + -ātus (“-ate”, forming adjectives), from tribus (“tribe”). Compare French tribunat.

parole.significato: The first office of the Roman state that was open to the plebeians, with the power to convene and preside over the Conc…
parole.testo: Calque of Latin tribūnus plēbis.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a Roman tribune.
parole.testo: From Latin tribunicius + -an.

parole.significato: Synonym of tribe.
parole.testo: From Latin tribus. Doublet of tribe.

parole.significato: A natural water stream that flows into a larger river or other body of water.
parole.testo: PIE word  *tréyes From Middle English tributarie (“paying tribute”), from Latin tribūtārius, from tribūtum (“tribute”).

parole.significato: Having three tails.

parole.significato: The highest rank and pay grade for prefectures in Ancient Rome.

parole.significato: Of or related to the number thirty.
parole.testo: From Latin trīcēnārius, from trīcēnus (“thirty each”) + -ārius (“-ary: forming adjectives and related nouns”).

parole.significato: The festival and religious rituals celebrating a Roman emperor's 30th year of rule.
parole.testo: From Latin trīcennālia, from trīcennium (“30-year period”) + -ālia (“-alia: forming the names of festivals”), from trīcennis (“30-year”) + -ium (“forming abstract nouns”), from trīciēs (“thirty each”) + annus (“year”) + -is (“forming compound adjectives”). Equivalent to tricennium + -alia.

parole.significato: Of, related to, lasting, or occurring once every thirty years.
parole.testo: From Latin trīcennium (“30-year period”) + -al, from trīcennis (“30-year”) + -ium, from trīciēs (“30 times”) + annus (“year”) + -is. Compare Latin tricennalis. Equivalent to tri- + decennial. Doublet of tricennal.

parole.significato: A period of thirty years.
parole.testo: From Latin trīcennium, from trīcennis (“30-year”) + -ium, from trīciēs (“30 times”) + annus (“year”) + -is (“forming compound adjectives”). Equivalent to tricennial + -ium.

parole.significato: Any muscle having three heads.
parole.testo: From Latin triceps (“triple-headed”), from trēs (“three”) + caput (“head”). See there for more details.

parole.significato: The belief that three nails were used in the crucifixion of Jesus Christ.
parole.testo: From tri- + Latin clavus (“nail”) + -ian + -ism, coined by George Stanley Faber in 1838.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or using a triclinium, or to the ancient mode of reclining while eating.
parole.testo: From Latin tricliniaris. See triclinium.

parole.significato: A couch for reclining at mealtimes, extending round three sides of a table, and usually in three parts.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin trīclīnium, from Ancient Greek τρικλίνιον (triklínion).

parole.significato: A "rising" tricolon, its parts increasing in magnitude or intensity towards a climax on the third part
parole.testo: From tricolon (“a rhetorical device”) and Latin crēscēns (“increasing, growing, rising”).

parole.significato: A "diminishing" tricolon, its parts decreasing in magnitude or intensity
parole.testo: From tricolon (“a rhetorical device”) and Latin dīminuēns (“decreasing, diminishing”).

parole.significato: A three-cornered hat, with the brim turned up.

parole.significato: A three-pronged spear somewhat resembling a pitchfork.

parole.significato: Relating to Trent, Italy.

parole.significato: Lasting three days.

parole.significato: A period of three days (especially in Roman Catholic liturgy).

parole.significato: Happening every three years.

parole.significato: A period of three years.

parole.significato: A bronze coin minted during the Roman Republic valued at 4 unciae.

parole.significato: The captain of a trireme.

parole.significato: Triennial: occurring once in three years.

parole.significato: Facing three ways; arranged in three vertical ranks, like the leaves of veratrum.

parole.significato: Divided into three lobes.

parole.significato: Bifid, divided into two main parts.
parole.testo: From Latin trifidus, see -ate (adjective-forming suffix). By surface analysis, trifid + -ate.

parole.significato: Having or comprising three leaves, or (loosely) trifoliolate (with three leaflets) or having leaves with three parts, a…

parole.significato: Melilot; sweet clover

parole.significato: Having three different forms

parole.significato: The state of being triform, or having three different shapes.

parole.significato: Forked, with three tines or points.

parole.significato: A three-horse chariot used by the Ancient Romans.

parole.significato: born three together; being one of three born at the same birth
parole.testo: From Latin trigeminus (“born three together”), from tri- + geminus (“twin”). Compare tergeminous.

parole.significato: Thirtieth.

parole.significato: A paper size, (3.75"–5" × 2.5"–3.125"), one thirty-second of a standard uncut flat sheet.

parole.significato: A trental (various senses)

parole.significato: Synonym of tricennial, once every thirty years.

parole.significato: 10⁹³.

parole.significato: Having three angles and three sides, triangular.

parole.significato: trijugate.

parole.significato: A nouveau riche.

parole.significato: A silver coin worth three cents, minted in the US from 1851 to 1873.

parole.significato: The 3,000th anniversary of an event or happening.

parole.significato: Having three ribs or nerves extending unbranched from the base to the apex.

parole.significato: Relating to a trinity or set of three, especially the Holy Trinity.

parole.significato: A trinket.

parole.significato: Lasting for three nights.

parole.significato: Of or relating to dancing.

parole.significato: A galley with three banks of oars, one above the other, used mainly as a warship.

parole.significato: To sadden.

parole.significato: Something having three forks or prongs, especially a trident.
parole.testo: Latin trisulcus; tri- (“three”) + sulcus (“a furrow”).

parole.significato: used so many times that it is commonplace, or no longer interesting or effective; worn out, hackneyed.

parole.significato: A plant of the genus Triticum (wheat and related cereals).

parole.significato: A vessel for separating liquids of different densities.

parole.significato: An embryonic insect which has twice cast its skin before hatching from the egg, such as some mites of Myobia

parole.significato: To grind to a fine powder, to pulverize.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin trītūrāre (“thresh”).

parole.significato: A rubbing or grinding; trituration.

parole.significato: To celebrate victory with pomp; to rejoice over success; to exult in an advantage gained; to exhibit exultation.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or being a triumph.

parole.significato: One granted a triumph.
parole.testo: From Latin triumphātor. Compare Middle English tryumphatour.

parole.significato: One member of a triumvirate.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin triumvir. Compare Middle English triumvir (“committee of three magistrates”).

parole.significato: Of or belonging to the triumviri or the triumvirate.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin triumvirālis. By surface analysis, triumvir + -al.

parole.significato: The crocodile bird, Pluvianus aegyptius.

parole.significato: Any member of the hummingbird genus Trochilus.
parole.testo: From Latin trochilus (“a kind of small bird”), from Ancient Greek τροχίλος (trokhílos), from τρέχω (trékhō, “to run”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to Troy; Trojan.

parole.significato: An officer responsible for weighing wool.

parole.significato: Something recurring across a genre or type of art or literature; a motif.

The verb is derived from the noun.

parole.significato: Mouthpart of certain types of organism such as an insect or a member of the Rotifera.
parole.testo: From Latin trophus, from Ancient Greek τροφός (trophós, “feeder”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to a trophy or to trophies.

parole.testo: From -tropism (suffix meaning ‘growth towards; movement, turning’) (possibly based on geotropism and heliotropism), from Latin tropus + English -ism (suffix forming nouns of action, process, or result). parole.significato: A monument erected (originally on the field of battle) by the prevailing army (without Senatical grant — contrast trium…

parole.significato: Synonym of interpreter.

parole.significato: To slaughter, massacre, kill.

parole.significato: The act of killing; slaughter or massacre.

parole.significato: To drive a truck.

parole.significato: To shorten (something) by, or as if by, cutting part of it off.
parole.testo: From Latin truncātus, perfect passive participle of truncō (“maim, reduce to a trunk”); see trunk as a verb.

parole.significato: The thorax of an insect.
parole.testo: From Latin truncus. Doublet of tronk and trunk.

parole.significato: The act of pushing or thrusting.

parole.significato: The act of weighing.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or resembling, a trout.

parole.significato: An argument whereby an accusation or insult is turned back on the accuser; same to you

parole.significato: Your (singular) fault, due to your error; you are to blame.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from the Latin phrase tuā culpā (“through your (singular) fault”), ablative case of tua culpa (“your fault, guilt”), used in English by analogy with mea culpa; also compare nostra culpa.

parole.significato: A tube or tubular organ.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin tuba.

parole.significato: A fleshy, thickened underground stem of a plant, usually containing stored starch, for example a potato or arrowroot.
parole.testo: From Latin tūber (“bump, hump, swelling”).

parole.significato: The part of the hypothalamus to which the pituitary gland is attached
parole.testo: From Latin.

parole.testo: Derived from Latin tūberculum. Compare tuber.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or having tuberculosis.
parole.testo: Latin tuberculum (“diminutive of tuber (“lump”)”) + -ar

parole.significato: Having tubercles.

parole.significato: Tubercular: having or relating to tuberculosis.
parole.testo: From Latin tuberculum (“little lump”) + -ous.

parole.significato: tubercle
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tūberculum.

parole.significato: tuberous
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tūberōsus (“tuberous”).

parole.significato: The act or process of sounding a trumpet
parole.testo: From Latin tubicinātus (“sounded a trumpet”), past participle of tubicinō (“sound a trumpet”).

parole.significato: tubular
parole.testo: From Latin tubulatus. See tubular.

parole.significato: A small pipe or fistular body; a little tube.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin tubulus, diminutive of tubus.

parole.significato: A tube.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin tubus. Doublet of tube.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or in the style of, Marcus Tullius Cicero (106 BC–43 BC; sometimes anglicized as Tully), Roman philo…
parole.testo: From Latin Tullianus, from Tullius (“the name of a Roman gens”).

parole.significato: The process or result of tumefying, swelling, or rising into a tumour.
parole.testo: From Latin tumefaciō. Compare French tuméfaction.

parole.significato: Swollen or distended with fluid, as of erectile tissue.
parole.testo: From Latin tumēscēns (“swelling, bloating”).

parole.significato: Swollen, enlarged, bulging.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tumidus (“swollen”).

parole.significato: The condition of being tumid; swollenness, distension.
parole.testo: From tumid + -ity, after Latin tumiditās.

parole.significato: Pertaining to or having the appearance of a tumor.
parole.testo: From Latin tumōrōsus (“inflated, bloated”), from tumor (“swelling, tumor”), from tumeō (“to swell”).

parole.significato: of, pertaining to, or shaped like a tumulus (heap or hillock).
parole.testo: From Latin tumulus (“a mound”): compare French tumulaire.

parole.significato: To swell.
parole.testo: From Latin tumulātus (whence -ate), from tumulāre (“cover with a mound, bury, entomb”).

parole.significato: Full of small hills or mounds; hilly; tumulose.
parole.testo: From Latin tumulōsus (“full of hills or hillocks, hilly”) (whence -ous), tumulus (“mound, hill, hillock”) + -ōsus, from tumeō (“to swell”).

parole.significato: Attended by, or producing, a tumult; disorderly; confused; tumultuous.
parole.testo: Latin tumultuārius: compare French tumultuaire.

parole.significato: To make a tumult.
parole.testo: From Latin tumultuātus, past participle of tumultuor (“make a tumult”).

parole.significato: tumult; commotion.
parole.testo: From Latin tumultuatio.

parole.significato: A commotion.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin tumultus; doublet of tumult.

parole.significato: A mound of earth, especially one placed over a prehistoric tomb; a barrow.
parole.testo: From Latin tumulus (“mound, hill”), from tumeō (“to swell”). Doublet of tombolo.

parole.significato: A caning.
parole.testo: Latin tundo (“to beat, strike”), + -ing.

parole.significato: Synonym of tunic (“garment”).

parole.significato: The innermost layer of an artery or vein, made up of one layer of endothelial cells and supported by an internal elasti…

parole.significato: The middle layer of a blood vessel, located between the tunica intima and tunica externa.

parole.significato: tunicate (One of the Urochordata (syn. Tunicata)).
parole.testo: From Latin tunica (“a tunic”).

parole.significato: Any of very many chordate marine animals, of the subphyla Tunicata or Urochordata, including the sea squirts.

parole.significato: Enclosed in a tunic or mantle; covered or coated with layers.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tunicātus, see Etymology 1 and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

parole.significato: A small tunic.
parole.testo: Latin tunicula, diminutive of tunica (“tunic”).

parole.significato: The mixing of soil or sediment, especially pedoturbation.

parole.significato: Having the lees or sediment disturbed; not clear. (of a liquid)
parole.testo: From Middle English turbide, borrowed from Latin turbidus (“disturbed”), from turba (“mass, throng, crowd, tumult, disturbance”).

parole.significato: The state of being turbid; turbidness.
parole.testo: From Latin turbiditās. By surface analysis, turbid + -ity.

parole.significato: Having the shape of a cone resting on its apex.
parole.testo: Latin turbinis (“a top, whirl”).

parole.significato: Shaped or spinning like a top (spinning top).

parole.significato: The act of spinning or whirling.

parole.significato: Turbine-related.

parole.significato: Turkism.

parole.significato: swelling, turgid, or tumourous.

parole.significato: To become turgid; to swell up or bloat.

parole.significato: Distended beyond the natural state by some internal agent, especially fluid, or expansive force.

parole.significato: Turgidity.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin turgor, from turgēre (“to be swollen”) + -or (forms a third-declension masculine abstract noun from a verb root).

parole.significato: A shoot or sprout from the ground.

parole.significato: Producing shoots.

parole.significato: Someone who can change their skin at will, especially into that of a wolf; a werewolf.

parole.significato: Foul; base; wicked; morally depraved.

parole.significato: Characterized by turpitude.

parole.significato: The condition of having a high, prominent forehead.

parole.significato: Furnished with, or formed like, a small turret or turrets; somewhat turreted.

parole.significato: Any fossil ammonite of the genus †Turrilites, the shell forming an open spiral with the later whorls separate.

parole.significato: Someone with turriphilia.
parole.testo: Coined by Theodore Ziolkowski in 1998. Equivalent to Latin turris (“tower”) + -philia, from Ancient Greek φιλία (philía).

parole.testo: Coined by Theodore Ziolkowski in 1998. From Latin turris (“tower”), from Ancient Greek τύρρις (túrrhis) + -philia, from Ancient Greek φιλία (philía, “love, affection”).

parole.significato: A turtle dove.
parole.testo: From Middle English turtle, tortle, turtel, turtul, from Old English turtle, turtla (“turtledove”), ultimately from Latin turtur (“turtledove”), of imitative origin.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Tusculum.

parole.significato: Relating to coughing.

parole.significato: A slight cough, less powerful than a tussis.

parole.significato: A cough.

parole.significato: Related to, caused by, or accompanied by a cough

parole.significato: Serving as a guardian; protective; tutelary.

parole.significato: Relating to guardianship or protection.
parole.testo: From Latin tūtēlārius (“guardian”), from tūtēla (“tutelage, guardianship; dependent, client”) + -ārius (suffix denoting an agent of use); analysable as tutelar + -ary.

parole.significato: tutelage

parole.significato: rigorism

parole.significato: A rigorist.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a tutor; belonging to, or exercised by, a tutor.
parole.testo: The adjective is from tutor (noun) + -ial, ultimately from Latin tūtor (“watcher, protector, defender”). The noun is transferred from the adjective.

parole.significato: A female tutor (teacher).

parole.significato: A conical Etruscan headdress for women.

parole.significato: Relating to callused and swollen things.

parole.significato: Relating to callused and swollen things.
parole.testo: From Latin tylo-, from Ancient Greek τύλη (túlē, “swelling”) and τύλος (túlos, “lump, knot”). By surface analysis, tyl- + -o-.

parole.significato: A bone of the skull which encloses part of the tympanum and supports the tympanic membrane. In humans it is part of the…

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or suffering from, tympany.

parole.significato: A drum.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin tympanum (“a drum, timbrel, tambourine; the eardrum”). Doublet of timbre, timpani, timbal, and tymbal.

parole.significato: A grouping based on shared characteristics; a class.
parole.testo: From Middle English type (“symbol, figure, emblem”), from Latin typus, from Ancient Greek τύπος (túpos, “mark, impression, type”), from τύπτω (túptō, “to strike, beat”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to Typhon (also called Typhoeus), a hundred-headed giant in Ancient Greek mythology.
parole.testo: From Latin Typhoius, from Typhoeus.

parole.significato: Forming terms relating to typing or typography.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin typo-, from Ancient Greek τύπος (túpos).

parole.significato: Of, or relating to tyranny or a tyrant.
parole.testo: From Latin tyrannicus + -al; ultimately from Ancient Greek τύραννος (túrannos) (absolute ruler, despot).

parole.significato: A female Tyrannosaurus rex.
parole.testo: By replacing rex (Latin rēx (“king”)) of Tyrannosaurus rex with Latin rēgīna (“queen”).

parole.significato: The condition of being a tyro or beginner; apprenticeship.

parole.significato: Synonym of Tyrrhenian.

parole.significato: Fruitful.

parole.significato: whereabouts, location

parole.significato: The state of existing in a specific point in space, thereness.
parole.testo: From Latin ubi (“where”) + -iety.

parole.significato: A microorganism that can be found in most types of environment.
parole.testo: From Latin ubique (“everywhere”) + -er.

parole.significato: The belief that the human nature of Christ is omnipresent.
parole.testo: From Latin ubique (“everywhere”) + -ism.

parole.significato: Widespread; ubiquitous.
parole.testo: From Latin ubique (“everywhere”) + -ist.

parole.significato: A neighbor whose house is on fire or has burned down.

He is one of Priam's friends in the Iliad (3.148) and the destruction of his house is referred to in the Aeneid (2.312).

parole.significato: A rain gauge.
parole.testo: Formed from Latin ūdus (“wet”) + -meter.

parole.significato: Relating to udometry.
parole.testo: From Latin ūdus (“wet”) + -metric.

parole.significato: rainfall measurement
parole.testo: From Latin ūdus (“wet”) + -metry.

parole.significato: Having an ulcus, a rounded pore-like aperture, at one or both poles.

parole.significato: To cause an ulcer to develop.

parole.significato: A rounded, pore-like aperture at either pole of a pollen grain.
parole.testo: From Latin ulcus (“sore”). Doublet of ulcer.

parole.significato: A small ulcer.
parole.testo: From Latin ulcusculum; compare corpuscle.

parole.significato: A little ulcer.
parole.testo: From Latin ulcusculum, diminutive of ulcus.

parole.significato: Slimy.
parole.testo: From Latin ūlīginōsus (“swampy”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to ulmin; designating an acid obtained from ulmin.
parole.testo: Formed from the root of Latin ulmus (“an elm”), with the suffix -ic: compare French ulmique.

parole.significato: A brown amorphous substance found in decaying vegetation.
parole.testo: Latin ulmus (“elm”), + -in: compare French ulmine.

parole.significato: The bone of the forearm that extends from the elbow to the wrist on the side opposite to the thumb, corresponding to th…
parole.testo: From Latin ulna (“elbow”). Doublet of ell.

parole.significato: ulna
parole.testo: From English ulna, from Latin ulna.

parole.significato: Situated beyond, or on the farther side.

parole.significato: The final syllable of a word.
parole.testo: From the Latin feminine of ultimus (“last”).

parole.significato: legal philosophy under which penal redress to crime should only be used as a measure of last resort
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: A place beyond the borders of the known world.
parole.testo: From Latin ultima Thūlē, nominative feminine singular of ultimus (“furthest”) + Thule, from mediaeval geography; originally from the Ancient Greek Θούλη (Thoúlē), a (possibly mythical) island to the north of Britain.

parole.significato: A final statement of terms or conditions made by one party to another, especially one that expresses a threat of repris…
parole.testo: From Latin ultimatus (“late, last final”), from Latin ultimus (“extreme, last, furthest, farthest, final”).

parole.significato: The final stage or consequence; finality.
parole.testo: Latin ultimatus extremity, from Latin ultimus the last.

parole.significato: On the last day (of a specified month).
parole.testo: First attested in 1582; from Latin ultimō (elliptically for ultimō diē or ultimō mēnse), masculine ablative singular form of ultimus (“last”); cognate with Dutch ultimo, the German ultimo, the Swedish ultimo, etc.

parole.significato: A last resort.
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: The process whereby the estate of a deceased person with no will or traceable blood relatives goes to the Crown.
parole.testo: From Latin ultimus haeres (“ultimate heir”).

parole.significato: A soil that has a weathered clay horizon as a result of argilluviation.
parole.testo: From Latin ultimus (“final”) and solum (“soil”).

parole.significato: Extreme; far beyond the norm; fanatical; uncompromising.
parole.testo: From Latin ultra.

parole.significato: beyond the legal power or authority of a person or body
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin ultra vires (“beyond the power”).

parole.significato: Greater than normal quantity or importance, as in ultrasecret.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ultrā (“beyond”).

parole.significato: extraordinary; abnormal
parole.testo: From Latin ultrāmundānus.

parole.significato: The quality of being ultroneous.
parole.testo: From ultrone(ous) + -ity, from Latin ultroneitas.

parole.significato: spontaneous; voluntary
parole.testo: From Latin ultroneus, from ultro (“to the further side, on his part, of one's own accord”). See ultra-.

parole.significato: Howling; wailing.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin ululāns, present participle of ululō (“to howl”).

parole.significato: To howl loudly or prolongedly in lamentation or joy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ululō, ululātus, of imitative origin. Cognate with Spanish aullar (“to howl”) and ulular (“to hoot”), and French ululer (“to howl”).

parole.significato: The act of ululating; a long, loud, wavering cry or howl.
parole.testo: ] Borrowed from Latin ululātiō, from ululō (“to howl, shriek, yell”) (from a reduplicated Proto-Indo-European imitative root) + -ātiō (suffix forming nouns relating to some action or the result of an action) (from Proto-Indo-European *-tis (suffix forming abstract or action nouns from verb roots)).

parole.significato: Being or relating to a ululation.
parole.testo: From ululation + -ory, from Latin ululō (“to howl, shriek, yell”).

parole.significato: A flat-topped or rounded flower-cluster (= inflorescence) in which the individual flower stalks arise from the same poi…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin umbella (“umbrella”). Compare umbrella, composed of the same etymological elements but formed independently.

parole.significato: umbellar
parole.testo: From Latin umbella (“a sunshade, parasol, umbrella”) + -ic.

parole.significato: A small, navel-shaped depression, or dimple, at the centre of a rounded body.
parole.testo: From Latin umbilicatus. By surface analysis, umbilic- + -ation.

parole.significato: A navel.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin umbilīcus (“navel”).

parole.significato: The boss of a shield, at or near the middle and usually projecting, sometimes in a sharp spike.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin umbō (“a shield boss”). Doublet of umbone.

parole.significato: The fully shaded inner region of a shadow cast by an opaque object.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin umbra (“shadow”). Doublet of umber.

parole.significato: On a shadow in the shape of a right triangle, the length of the shadow's edge adjacent to a measured angle.
parole.testo: First attested in Modern English in 1688, although the phrase was also used in Middle English by Geoffrey Chaucer (c. 1343–1400) in his Treatise on the Astrolabe; Latin: umbra (“shadow”) + rēcta (feminine nominative singular of rēctus, “straight”) = “straight shadow”; compare umbra versa.

parole.significato: On a shadow in the shape of a right triangle, the length of the shadow's edge opposite to a measured angle.
parole.testo: First attested in Modern English in 1688, although the phrase was also used in Middle English by Geoffrey Chaucer (c. 1343–1400) in his Treatise on the Astrolabe; Latin: umbra (“shadow”) + versa (feminine nominative singular of versus, “turned”) = “turned shadow”; compare umbra recta.

parole.significato: Bearing something like an open umbrella.
parole.testo: From Latin umbraculum (“umbrella”), diminutive of umbra (“shade”) + -ferous.

parole.significato: Having the form of something that offers shade, such as a treetop or especially an umbrella.
parole.testo: From Latin umbraculum (“anything that furnishes shade, a bower, umbrella”), diminutive of umbra (“a shade”) + -form.

parole.significato: Any umbrella-shaped appendage, such as the cap borne on the seta of Marchantia.
parole.testo: From Latin umbrāculum.

parole.significato: Magical control over shadows.
parole.testo: From Latin umbra (“shadow”) + -mancy (“divination of”), from Latin -mantia, ultimately from Ancient Greek μᾰντείᾱ (mănteíā, “divination”).

parole.significato: To shade; to shadow.
parole.testo: Latin umbratus, past participle of umbrare (“to shade”), from umbra (“a shade”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the shade or darkness; shadowy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin umbraticus, from umbra (“shade”). See umbrage.

parole.significato: Shady, shadowy.
parole.testo: From Latin umbratilis, from umbra.

parole.significato: Shadowy; faint; secluded; indistinct; vague; latent; indeterminate.
parole.testo: From Latin umbra (“shade, shadow”).

parole.significato: An Italic tribe of ancient Italy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin umbrī. Also called Ombrii in some Roman sources. Many Roman writers thought the Umbri to be Celtic; Cornelius Bocchus wrote that they descended from an ancient Gaulish tribe. Plutarch wrote that the name might be a different way of writing the name of the Celtic tribe Ambrones, w

parole.significato: providing or making shade; umbrageous.
parole.testo: From Latin umbrifer, from umbra (“a shade”) + ferre (“to bear”).

parole.significato: A kind of soil with a dark topsoil and having organic matter accumulated within the mineral surface soil.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin umbra (“shadow”) + -sol

parole.significato: Shady; umbrageous.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin umbrōsus, from umbra (“a shade”).

parole.significato: Shade, shadiness.
parole.testo: From umbrose + -ity, or borrowed from Latin umbrōsitās.

parole.significato: Used for the digit one to form systematic element names of elements whose existence has been predicted, and which have…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ūnus.

parole.significato: A churchman who holds only one benefice.
parole.testo: Latin unus one.

parole.significato: Based on unanimity, assent or agreement.
parole.testo: From Latin ūnanimus (“of one mind”), from ūnus (“one”) + animus (“mind”). Displaced native Old English ānmōd (literally “one-minded”).

parole.significato: Consisting of or involving a single element or component.
parole.testo: From Latin ūnus (“one”) + -ary, on the pattern of binary, ternary, etc.

parole.significato: The Roman ounce, 1/12 of a Roman pound.
parole.testo: From Latin ū̆ncia (“various Roman units”). Doublet of ounce, inch, onça, onza, oka, ouguiya, and awqiyyah.

parole.significato: Of or relating to an ounce, or an inch, especially to letters printed an inch high.
parole.testo: Attested 1650, from Latin ū̆ncia (“a twelfth part, ounce, inch”) + -al.

parole.significato: Of the shape of a hook; hook-shaped.
parole.testo: From Latin uncus (“hook”) + -form.

parole.significato: Hooked at the end.
parole.testo: From Latin uncīnātus, from uncīnus (“hook, barb”).

parole.significato: A cloud species which consists of fine hair-like strands, with hooked terminations. Associated only with cirrus formati…
parole.testo: From Latin uncīnus (“hook”).

parole.significato: Curved or hook-shaped.
parole.testo: From Latin uncus.

parole.significato: To anoint, especially a monarch or other patriarchal leader.
parole.testo: First appears in Middle English circa 1425, derived from Latin unctus (“anointed”) and related terms. Ayurvedic sense is one of several competing translations of Sanskrit snehana.

parole.significato: An ointment or salve.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin unctiō.

parole.significato: Not cultivated; rude; illiterate.
parole.testo: From un- (“not”) + Latin cultus, past participle of colere (“to cultivate”). Compare incult.

parole.significato: A hook or claw.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin uncus (“hook”).

parole.significato: An organ stop similar to the voix céleste, but typically using a dulciana or a softer-scale string (or even flutes).
parole.testo: From Latin unda maris (literally “sea wave”).

parole.significato: undated; rising and falling in waves
parole.testo: From Latin undātus.

parole.significato: Rising and falling in waves toward the margin, as a leaf; waved.
parole.testo: From Latin undatus, past participle of undare (“to rise in waves, to wave, to undulate”).

parole.significato: eleven
parole.testo: From Latin ūndecim.

parole.significato: A group of eleven musicians; a piece of music written for such a group
parole.testo: From decet on the model of Latin undecim (“eleven”).

parole.significato: Having eleven joints.
parole.testo: From Latin undecim + articulate.

parole.significato: Any member of a group of eleven officials.
parole.testo: From Latin ūndecimvir.

parole.significato: A group of eleven people, especially (politics) a council of eleven men sharing office or power and particularly (histo…
parole.testo: From Latin ūndecimvirātus, from ūndecimvirī (“undecimvirs”) + -ātus (“-ate”).

parole.significato: In base (radix) eleven.
parole.testo: From Latin ūndēnī (“eleven each, eleventh”) + -ary, from ūndēnus.

parole.significato: In secret; secretly, privately.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin sub rosā.

parole.significato: Based upon the number nineteen.
parole.testo: From Latin ūndēvīcēsimus (“nineteenth”) + -al.

parole.significato: That doesn't have a known or readily available explanation.
parole.testo: From un- + explainable. from explain + -able. from Latin explanō (“to flatten, spread out, make plain or clear, explain”).

parole.significato: The surgical removal of a fingernail or toenail.
parole.testo: From Latin unguis (“nail, claw, hoof”) + -ectomy.

parole.significato: Pertaining to or resembling a creature's nail, claw or hoof; unguinal.
parole.testo: From Latin unguis (“nail, claw, hoof”) + -al .

parole.significato: Any cream containing medicinal ingredients applied to the skin for therapeutic purposes.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin unguentum (“ointment”), from unguō (“to smear with ointment”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃engʷ- (“to salve, anoint”). Cognates include Old Prussian anctan, Old High German ancho (German Anke (“butter”)), Welsh ymenyn (“butter”).

parole.significato: A small bottle used to store balms or scented oils
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin unguentarium.

parole.significato: Like, or containing, an unguent.
parole.testo: Latin unguentarius.

parole.significato: ungual
parole.testo: Latin unguis (“a nail or claw”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a claw or nail; ungual.
parole.testo: Latin unguiculus, diminutive of unguis (“a nail”).

parole.significato: A diminutive claw or similar appendage at the end of an insect's foot.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin unguiculus.

parole.significato: Producing, having, or supporting nails or claws.
parole.testo: Latin unguis (“nail, claw”) + -ferous.

parole.significato: Consisting of, or resembling, fat or oil; unctuous; oleaginous.
parole.testo: From Latin unguinosus, from unguinis, from unguen (“fat, ointment”).

parole.significato: The nail, claw, talon, or hoof of a finger, toe, or other appendage.
parole.testo: From Latin unguis (“nail, claw, hoof”). Doublet of onyx.

parole.significato: A hoof, claw, or talon.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ungula (“claw, hoof”), from unguis (“nail, claw, hoof”).

parole.significato: Having hoofs of a tincture different from the body.
parole.testo: Latin ungula (“a claw”), + -ed.

parole.significato: That walks on hooves.
parole.testo: From Latin ungula (“claw, hoof”) + -grade (“means of walking”) (from Latin gradus). Compare French ongulograde.

parole.significato: one, single
parole.testo: From Latin uni-, combining form of unus (“one”).

parole.significato: A unique example or specimen of something
parole.testo: From the Latin ūnicum, the neuter nominative singular form of ūnicus (“unique”). Compare Dutch unicum, German Unicum. See unique.

parole.significato: The state of being the sole begotten.
parole.testo: From Latin unigenitus (“only-begotten”), from unus (“one”) + genitum (“to beget”).

parole.significato: Of a single type, or genus.
parole.testo: From Latin unigena, from unus (“one”) + genere, gignere (“to beget”), + -ous.

parole.significato: Any of the genus Unio of freshwater mussels
parole.testo: From the genus name, Unio, from Latin ūniō (“large pearl”). Doublet of union.

parole.significato: Having a single line or series
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ūniseriātus. By surface analysis, uni- + seriate.

parole.significato: To bring together as one.
parole.testo: From Middle English uniten, from Latin ūnītus, perfect passive participle of ūniō.

parole.significato: One over all.
parole.testo: Latin, or rather dog Latin, from uno (“one”) + ab (“from”) + alto (“height”), thus literally from one height.

parole.significato: At once, at one blast, at the same moment, contemporaneously, simultaneously.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ūnō flātū (“in one breath”, “at one blast”), ablative of time-within-which of ūnus flātus (“a single blast of wind or expulsion of breath”).

parole.significato: improbably
parole.testo: From un- + Latin probabilis (“approvable”), from probare (“to approve”). Compare probable.

parole.significato: Without the ability to reason; unreasoning.
parole.testo: From Middle English unresonable, equivalent to un- + reasonable, originally partly after Latin irratiōnābilis.

parole.significato: Incessant; never slackening.
parole.testo: un- + remitting, from remit (in now rare sense of “diminish, abate”), from Middle English remitten, from Latin remittere (“to send, send back”). Compare Old French remettre, remetre, remitter. Not from nonexistent unremit. First attested in 1728.

parole.significato: To remove a veil from; to uncover; to reveal something hidden.
parole.testo: From Middle English *unveilen (suggested by past participle unveiled, vnueylyd (“unveiled”)). Equivalent to un- + veil. Ultimately from Latin velum (whence also English voile, English reveal, Russian вуа́ль (vuálʹ), Russian завуали́ровать (zavualírovatʹ) (compare typologically)). Also compare typolo

parole.significato: Synonym of inviolate.
parole.testo: From un- + violate (adjective), after Latin inviolātus.

parole.significato: A representation of the sacred asp, symbolising supreme power in ancient Egypt.
parole.testo: From Latin uraeus, from Ancient Greek οὐραῖος (ouraîos). parole.significato: Celestial, heavenly; uranic.
parole.testo: From Latin Ūrania (“muse of astronomy in Greek mythology”) + -an (suffix forming agent nouns). parole.significato: Of or relating to The Urantia Book, a spiritual and philosophical book of unknown authorship in the early 20th century.
parole.testo: From Urantia + -an, from Latin Ūranus, from Ancient Greek Οὐρανός (Ouranós), from οὐρανός (ouranós, “sky, heaven”).

parole.significato: A walled city in Ancient Rome.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin urbs.

parole.significato: Shaped like an urn.
parole.testo: From the Latin urceolatus, from urceolus, diminutive of urceus.

parole.significato: A vessel for water or washing the hands in Roman Catholicism.
parole.testo: From Latin urceolus.

parole.significato: Any urn-shaped organ of a plant.
parole.testo: From Latin urceolus (“a little pitcher”).

parole.significato: A ewer for holding water for washing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin urceus.

parole.significato: Relating to the uredo.
parole.testo: From oblique stem of Latin ūrēdō, ūrēdinis (“blight, burning itch”) + -eous.

parole.significato: Relating to the uredo.
parole.testo: From oblique stem of Latin ūrēdō, ūrēdinis (“blight, burning itch”) + -ous.

parole.significato: urediniospore
parole.testo: From Latin ūrēdō (“blast, blight, burning itch”), from ūrere (“to burn or scorch”).

parole.significato: A strong desire to do something.
parole.testo: From Latin urgeō (“urge”).

parole.significato: The quality or condition of being urgent.
parole.testo: From urgent + -ency or Latin urgentia.

parole.significato: Of a fish: oriented vertically, with the head to base and tail to chief, as if diving.
parole.testo: From Latin ūrīnāns, present active participle of ūrīnor (“to dive”).

parole.significato: A pit used for storing urine, which may be later used to make manure.
parole.testo: Latin ūrīnārium.

parole.significato: A diver, especially someone who searches for things underwater.
parole.testo: From Latin ūrīnātor (“diver”), from ūrīnārī + -tor (suffix forming a (masculine) agent noun). Ūrīnārī is the present active infinitive of ūrīnor (“to plunge under water, dive”), possibly from ūrīna (“urine; water (?)”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wer- (“to moisten; to flow”).

parole.testo: From Middle English uryne, from Latin ūrīna (“urine”), from Proto-Indo-European *uh₁r-, zero grade of *woh₁-r̥ (“water, liquid, milk”). Related to *h₁ówHdʰr̥ (“udder”) (see udder). Cognate with Old English ūriġ (“wet, moist”). Displaced native English land (“urine”) (from Middle English land, from O

parole.significato: Pertaining to urine.
parole.testo: From Latin ūrīnōsus. By surface analysis, urine + -ous.

parole.significato: A Roman unit of liquid measure reckoned as the volume of 40 Roman pounds of wine and equivalent to about 13 L although…
parole.testo: From Latin urna. Doublet of urn.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to urocanic acid or its derivatives
parole.testo: From Latin urina (“urine”) + canis (“dog”), the acid being first isolated from canine urine. By surface analysis, uro- + Latin can(is) + -ic.

parole.significato: An intermediate in the catabolism of L-histidine, transformed in the liver by urocanate hydratase (or urocanase) into 4…
parole.testo: Latin urina (“urine”) and canis (“dog”), because first isolated in 1874 from dog urine.

parole.significato: Any caudate amphibian.
parole.testo: From Latin Urodela.

parole.significato: A substance, apparently the same as indigo, occasionally found in the urine in degeneration of the kidneys. It is readi…
parole.testo: From uro-, Latin glaucus (“bright”), + -in.

parole.significato: Any meteor from a radiant in the constellation Ursa Minor.
parole.testo: From Latin ursa (“she-bear”) + -id.

parole.significato: Shaped like a bear.
parole.testo: From Latin ursus (“bear”) + -form.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or characteristic of bears.
parole.testo: Mid 16th century, from Latin ursīnus, adjectival form of ursus (“bear”) + -ine.

parole.significato: To have or produce a stinging sensation, as of nettles or urticating hair.
parole.testo: From or formed like (post-Classical?) Latin urticatus, from Latin urtīca (“nettle”).

parole.significato: The development of urticaria (hives).
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin urtīca (“nettle”).

parole.significato: The aurochs.
parole.testo: From Latin ūrus. Doublet of ure (“aurochs”).

parole.significato: Denoting usual or customary action.
parole.testo: From Latin usitari (“to use often”).

parole.significato: Intermediate between aridic and udic.
parole.testo: From Latin ustus (“burnt”).

parole.significato: The act of burning, or the state of being burned.
parole.testo: From Latin ustio, from urere, ustum (“to burn”). Compare French ustion.

parole.significato: The site of a funeral pyre.
parole.testo: From Latin ustrinum.

parole.significato: Blackened as if burned.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ustulatus, past participle of ustulare (“to scorch”), urere (“to burn”).

parole.significato: An act of burning, especially roasting.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ustulare (“burn, scorch, sear”) (with the suffix -ation added), from ust-, past participle stem of uro (“burn”). By surface analysis, ustulate + -ion.

parole.significato: The acquisition of right or title to an object by means of the passage of time. The common law analogue is adverse poss…
parole.testo: From Latin usucapio, usucapionis (“to acquire by prescription”).

parole.significato: The acquisition of right or title to an object or property by means of the simple passage of time.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ūsūcapiō.

parole.significato: Usury.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ūsūra.

parole.significato: Usurious.
parole.testo: Latin usurarius (“that serves for use, that pays interest”). See English usurer, French usuraire.

parole.significato: Usurping; encroaching.
parole.testo: Latin usurpans, present participle.

parole.significato: A female usurper.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin ūsūrpātrīx. By surface analysis, usurpator + -trix.

parole.significato: An exorbitant rate of interest, in excess of any legal rates or at least immorally.
parole.testo: From Middle English usurie, from Latin ūsūria, from ūsūra (“lending at interest, usury”) from ūsus (“use”), from stem of ūtī (“to use”). Compare usurp and use.

parole.significato: The use of something.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ūsus (“use”), from Proto-Italic *oissos.

parole.significato: Uterus; uterine.
parole.testo: From uterus, from Latin uterus (“womb, belly”). By surface analysis, uter- + -o-.

parole.significato: A reproductive organ of therian mammals in which the young are conceived and develop until birth.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin uterus.

parole.significato: A fervent wish.
parole.testo: From Latin utinam.

parole.significato: The moderate Hussite ideology that the faithful, specifically including laity, should receive Communion under both kind…
parole.testo: From Latin utraque (“both”) (from their demanding the cup as well as the bread for the laity), + -ism.

parole.significato: Resembling a bladder .
parole.testo: From Latin utriculus (“a little womb, a calycle”) + -oid.

parole.significato: Shaped like a bag or leather bottle.
parole.testo: From Latin uter (“bag, bottle”) + -iform.

parole.significato: In Ancient Roman law, a kind of interdict relating to disputes of possession over movable property.
parole.testo: Borrowed directly from Latin utrubi.

parole.significato: Grape, raisin, grape-like fruit.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin ūva (“grape”).

parole.significato: The bearberry.
parole.testo: Latin uva (“grape”) + ursus (“bear”).

parole.significato: Racemic acid, a particular stereoisomer of tartaric acid.
parole.testo: From Latin ūva (“grape”) + -ic + acid.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the uvula.
parole.testo: From Latin ūvulāris. By surface analysis, uvula + -ar.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a wife, or her genes or relatives.
parole.testo: From Latin uxōrius (“of or pertaining to a wife; overly fond of one’s wife”) + English -al (suffix forming adjectives). Uxōrius is derived from uxor (“wife”) + -ius (suffix forming adjectives).

parole.significato: Very devoted and possibly submissive to one's wife; showing excessive uxorial devotion.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin uxōrius (“of or pertaining to a wife”), from uxor (“wife”) + -ious.

parole.significato: An inordinate fear of one's own wife, or of wives.
parole.testo: From Latin uxor (“wife”) + -phobia.

parole.significato: verse
parole.testo: From Latin versus (“verse”).

parole.significato: Used to introduce an example or list of examples to illustrate what is being discussed.
parole.testo: Abbreviation of Latin verbī grātiā (“for instance”). Grātiā here is in the ablative case.

parole.significato: Indicates a willingly empty portion of an inscription.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin vacat (“it is empty”).

parole.significato: To move out of a dwelling or other property, either by choice or by eviction.
parole.testo: Originally used in the legal sense "to annul", a denominal from Early Modern English vacat (“legal annulment”), a development from Middle English vacat (“absence or cancellation noted in a register”), from Latin vacat, third-person singular present active indicative of vacō (“to be idle; to be unocc

parole.significato: An announcement in court that something is cancelled or set aside; an annulment.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vacātūrus (“about to be void”).

parole.significato: cow
parole.testo: Representing the Latin vacca (“cow”).

parole.significato: Inoculation with a vaccine, in order to protect from a particular disease or strain of disease.
parole.testo: From vaccinia, a cowpox infection. Ultimately from Latin vacca (“cow”). Coined by Edward Jenner (1749-1823) in 1798. parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, caused by, or characteristic of cowpox.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin vaccīnus (“of or derived from a cow”), from vacca (“cow (female cattle)”) + -īnus (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’ forming adjectives). parole.significato: Pertaining to the cowpox virus.
parole.testo: From Latin vacca (“cow”) + -i- + -ole + -ous.

parole.significato: That vacillates; wavering; fluctuating; not constant
parole.testo: From Latin vacillans, present participle of vacillare. Compare French vacillant. See vacillate. By surface analysis, Latin vacill- + -ant.

parole.significato: To sway unsteadily from one side to the other; oscillate.
parole.testo: From Latin vacillātum, supine form of vacillō (“sway, waver”). By surface analysis, Latin vacill- + -ate.

parole.significato: Indecision in speech or action.
parole.testo: From Middle English vacillacion, a learned borrowing from Latin vacillātiō (“swaying”). By surface analysis, vacillate + -ion.

parole.significato: Emptiness; vacancy.
parole.testo: From Latin vacivitas.

parole.significato: Lacking substance; trivial; meaningless.
parole.testo: From Latin vacuus (“empty, vacant”).

parole.significato: Emptiness.
parole.testo: From Latin vacuitās (“empty space, vacancy, vacuity”); equivalent to vacu(ous) + -ity.

parole.significato: Empty; void; lacking meaningful content.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin vacuus (“empty, vacant”) + -ous.

parole.significato: A referential book such as a handbook or manual, especially one that is pocketable.
parole.testo: From the Latin vāde (“come”) mēcum (“with me”).

parole.significato: In Ancient Rome, a court settlement; a promise secured by bail.
parole.testo: From Latin vadimōnium.

parole.significato: A bond or pledge for appearance before a judge on a certain day.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vadimōnium

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to water beneath the surface of the earth which is located above the level of the permanent groundwate…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vadosus.

parole.significato: Crafty; cunning; sly.
parole.testo: Latin vafer + -ous.

parole.significato: A wandering; vagrancy.
parole.testo: From Latin vagans, present participle of vagor. See vagantes.

parole.significato: One whose thought wanders in many directions.
parole.testo: From Latin vagus (“wandering”) + -ist. By surface analysis, Latin vag(us) + -arist.

parole.significato: Crying like a child.
parole.testo: From Latin vagiens, present participle of vagire (“to cry like a young child”).

parole.significato: A sex organ for copulation and birth, found in female therian mammals, consisting of a passage between the vulval vesti…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin vāgīna (“sheath”).

parole.significato: The mythical toothed vagina; often related to castration anxiety.
parole.testo: First attested 1908, from Latin vagina + dentata (“toothed”); popularized chiefly by Sigmund Freud.

parole.significato: Vagina.
parole.testo: Latin vāgīna + -o-.

parole.significato: A little sheath, such as that about the base of the pedicel of most mosses.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin vāgīnula, diminutive of vagina (“sheath”).

parole.significato: To wander or move at random.
