parole.significato: To wail, mewl (as an infant).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vāgiō, vāgīre (“to wail, to squall (as an infant), to cry out”) via a frequentative form vāgītō, vāgītāre, attested in medieval Latin as a verb meaning "to wail, to cry out in distress (of an infant); to cry out (of a hare)". Compare French vagir, English vagitus (“the crying of

parole.significato: The crying of a newborn baby.
parole.testo: From Latin vāgītus (“crying, wailing”), from vāgiō (“cry, wail”).

parole.significato: Wandering; unsettled.
parole.testo: Latin vagus. See vague.

parole.significato: Farewell.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin valē, singular imperative of valeō (“be well”).

parole.significato: The world, a place where difficulties and the sorrows of life are felt, especially (Christianity) as a place to be left…
parole.testo: Calque of Latin lacrimārum vallis from the “Salve Regina” (a hymn to the Virgin Mary), based on Hebrew עמק הבכא (ʿēmeq habbāḵāʾ) from Psalm 84:6 of the Bible. parole.significato: To farewell; to make a valediction or parting gesture.
parole.testo: From Latin valedictus, past participle of valedīcō, from Latin valē (“farewell”) + Latin dīcō (“to speak”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a valediction (“an act of parting company; a speech made when parting company”); designed for or su…
parole.testo: From Latin valedictum + English -ory (suffix forming nouns meaning ‘that which pertains to’, or adjectives meaning ‘of or pertaining to’). parole.significato: A follower of Valentinus, a 2nd-century Egyptian gnostic.
parole.testo: From Latin Valentīniānus, from Valentīnus (“Valentine”) + -iānus (“-ian: forming adjectives”), from valentia (“strength, health”) + -īnus (“-ine: forming adjectives”). Equivalent to Valentine + -ian.

parole.significato: The science of healthy living.
parole.testo: From Latin valeō (“to be strong, well or healthy”) + -logy.

parole.significato: A state of health; especially that of good health.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin valētūdō, valitūdō (“state of health”).

parole.significato: Sickly, infirm, of ailing health; related to ill health.
parole.testo: From Latin valētūdin- + -arian, from oblique stem of Latin valētūdō, from valeō + -tūdō. By surface analysis, valetude + -arian.

parole.significato: Sickly, infirm, valetudinarian.
parole.testo: From Latin valētūdin- + -ary + -ous, from oblique stem of Latin valētūdō, from valeō + -tūdō. By surface analysis, valetude + -ary + -ous. Adapted borrowing of Latin valētūdinārius + -ous. Doublet of valetudinary.

parole.significato: Sickly, infirm, valetudinarian.
parole.testo: From Latin valētūdin- + -ary, from oblique stem of Latin valētūdō, from valeō + -tūdō. By surface analysis, valetude + -arian. Doublet of valetudinarious.

parole.significato: valetudinarian; ill, sick
parole.testo: From Latin valētūdin- + -ous, from oblique stem of Latin valētūdō, from valeō + -tūdō. By surface analysis, valetude + -ous.

parole.significato: knock-kneed (having the distal part of a limb displaced or twisted away from the midline of the body)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin valgus.

parole.significato: Of or relating to a rampart.
parole.testo: From Latin vallaris.

parole.significato: A rampart or entrenchment.
parole.testo: From Latin vallatio, from vallare (“to surround with a rampart”), from vallum (“rampart”). See wall.

parole.significato: Grooved; pertaining to a vallecula.
parole.testo: From vallecula + -ar, derived from diminutive of Latin valles (“valley”).

parole.significato: A rampart; a wall, as in a fortification.
parole.testo: From Latin vallum. Doublet of wall comes from this word via a Proto-Germanic borrowing from Latin.

parole.significato: A paired copulatory organ of males in some species of insects that helps the male clasp the female.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin valva (“double door, valve”). Doublet of valve.

parole.significato: A device that controls the flow of a gas or fluid through a space, such as a pipe, manifold, or plenum.
parole.testo: From Middle English valve, from Latin valva (“double door, valve”). Doublet of valva.

parole.significato: A small valve.
parole.testo: From Latin valvula, from valva (“double door, valve”) + -ula (“-ule, -ling: forming diminutives”). Doublet of valvule.

parole.significato: A fan or other contrivance, such as a sieve, for winnowing grain.
parole.testo: From Latin vannus (“a van, or fan for winnowing grain”): compare French van and English fan, winnow. Doublet of fan.

parole.significato: A member of an ancient east Germanic tribe famous for sacking Rome.
parole.testo: From Latin Vandalus, named after the Germanic tribe, from Proto-Germanic *wandilaz, from Proto-Indo-European *wendʰ-eh₂-, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wendʰ- (“to turn, wind, braid”). Also related to Old English Wendlas.

parole.significato: Idle or vain talk.
parole.testo: From Latin vanus (“vain”) + loquentia (“talk”).

parole.significato: Talking in a vain or foolish way
parole.testo: From Latin vaniloquens.

parole.significato: Idle or vain talk.
parole.testo: From Latin vāniloquium. See -loquy.

parole.significato: A type of still life painting, symbolic of mortality, characteristic of Dutch painting of the 16th and 17th centuries.
parole.testo: From Latin vānitās. Doublet of vanity.

parole.significato: Offering nothing that is stimulating or challenging.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vapidus (“flat, vapid”).

parole.significato: A steam bath.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vaporarium.

parole.significato: To emit vapour
parole.testo: Latin vaporare, vaporatum. See vapour.

parole.significato: To flog or whip; to beat or strike.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vāpulō.

parole.significato: The act of beating or whipping.
parole.testo: Latin vāpulāre (“to be flogged”).

parole.significato: various; variety.
parole.testo: From New Latin, from Latin varius (“various, diverse”).

parole.significato: Any one of the interpretations or readings of a given passage in a text which differ from copy to copy, from edition to…
parole.testo: Latin: varia (feminine singular form of varius, “different”; whence various) + lectiō (“a reading”; whence lection) = “a different reading”

parole.significato: Random variable.
parole.testo: From Latin variatus, past participle of variare. See vary.

parole.significato: Abnormally swollen, dilated or knotty.
parole.testo: From varix, via Middle English [Term?] from Latin varix, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wers-. By surface analysis, varic- + -ose. See also Old Church Slavonic врьхъ (vrĭxŭ, “top, peak”), Ancient Greek ἕρμα (hérma, “reef, rock, hill”), Lithuanian viršus (“top”).

parole.significato: An enlarged vessel or nerve, particularly a blood vessel.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin varicōsitās, from varicōsus, from varix (“varicose vein”).

parole.significato: sheeppox
parole.testo: From Latin [Term?].

parole.significato: A rock containing centimeter-scale spherical or globular structures (varioles) in a fine-grained matrix.
parole.testo: Latin varius (“various”) + -lite: compare French variolite.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to smallpox.
parole.testo: Latin variolosus, from variola (“smallpox”): compare French varioleux.

parole.significato: An instrument used to measure variations in a magnetic field.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin varius (“various”) + -meter.

parole.significato: An edition of a written work (especially the complete works of a classical writer) showing the notes and readings of a…
parole.testo: From Latin variōrum, genitive plural masculine of varius (“various”), in the phrase editio cum notis variorum (“edition with various notes”).

parole.significato: A varicose, i.e. swollen and knotted, vein.
parole.testo: Via Middle English varix from Latin varix, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wers-. See also Old Church Slavonic врьхъ (vrĭxŭ, “top, peak”), Ancient Greek ἕρμα (hérma, “reef, rock, hill”), Lithuanian viršus (“top”).

parole.significato: A pestilent or predatory ground-borne animal, especially one that kills or harasses a farmer's animals or crops.
parole.testo: Dialectal form of vermin, derived from Latin vermis (“worm”), c. 1530–1540s. parole.significato: Cut in the form of vair; battlemented with solid projections and crenelles, both pointed, but in the latter case revers…
parole.testo: Later (1828) variant of variated, from Latin variatus, past participle of variare.

parole.significato: Of or relating to Marcus Terentius Varro (116 BCE–27 BCE), Ancient Roman scholar and writer.
parole.testo: From Latin Varrōniānus, from Varrō + -iānus.

parole.significato: A deformity in which the foot is turned inward.
parole.testo: From Latin varus.

parole.significato: One of a number of straight vasa (tubes), specifically:
parole.testo: First attested in 1750. From Latin vās (“vessel”) + rēctum (neuter nominative singular of rēctus, “straight”), literally “straight vessel”.

parole.significato: The capillaries that supply blood to vessels larger than 1 mm. They supply blood to the adventitia and middle tunicae.
parole.testo: From the Latin vāsa, plural of vās (“vessel”) + vāsōrum, the genitive plural of vās (“vessel”). Meaning "vessels of the vessels."

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Vascons, a people of ancient Iberia, thought to be the ancestors of the Basque.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin Vascones; the name may have originally been borrowed through Spanish vascón, vasco. Doublet of Gascon.

parole.significato: The blood vessels or their arrangement in the body, or within an organ.
parole.testo: From Latin vāsculum (“vessel”) + a suffix -ature. Compare ossature, musculature.

parole.significato: A container used by botanists to store newly-collected samples.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vāsculum (“small vessel”).

parole.significato: vastness; immensity
parole.testo: From Latin vāstitūdō. By surface analysis, vast + -itude.

parole.significato: One of the great muscles upon the front of the thigh.
parole.testo: From Latin vastus (“vast, immense, enormous, huge, monstrous”). Doublet of vast.

parole.significato: The largest and most powerful part of the quadriceps femoris, a group of thigh muscles. Situated on the outside of the…
parole.testo: From Latin.

parole.significato: A poet or bard who is divinely inspired.
parole.testo: From Latin vātēs, from Proto-Indo-European *weh₂t- (“excited, possessed”); cognate with Proto-Celtic *wātis (“seer”) (Gaulish ουατεις, Old Irish fáith, Welsh gwawd) and Proto-Germanic *wōdaz (“mad”) (Old English wōd (“mad, frenzied”), Gothic 𐍅𐍉𐌳𐍃 (wōds, “possessed, mad”), Old High German wuot (“mad,

parole.significato: Pertaining to a prophet; prophetic, oracular.
parole.testo: From Latin vates (“seer, poet”) + -ic.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a prophet; prophetic.
parole.testo: Latin vates a prophet, and + -ical.

parole.significato: Relating to the Vatican City state.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Vātī̆cānus (“Vatican Hill”), further etymology unknown. The connection to vāticinārī (“to prophesy, oracle”) is folk-etymological.

parole.significato: The murder of a prophet.
parole.testo: From Latin; the first element is vātēs. Equivalent to + -cide.

parole.significato: To predict or foretell future events; to prophesy or presage.
parole.testo: From Latin vāticinātus, perfect passive participle of vāticinor (“foretell, prophesy”).

parole.significato: Someone who vaticinates; a prophet.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: A female vaticinator or prophet.
parole.testo: From Latin vāticinātrīx (“vaticinator (female)”). By surface analysis, vaticinator + -trix.

parole.significato: A prediction; a vaticination.
parole.testo: From Latin vāticinium (“prediction, prophecy”).

parole.significato: A fictional prophecy that has been written after the supposedly predicted event but is presented as a genuine predictio…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vāticinium ex ēventū.

parole.significato: Of hatred: extremely strong, bitter, intense.
parole.testo: From Latin Vatinianus (in odium Vatinium, in Catullus), from personal name Vatīnius, reportedly the name of a Roman who was universally hated.

parole.significato: A tax.
parole.testo: From Latin vectīgal, from Latin vect(is) (“lever, leverage”) + Latin ig(ō) (“act, make, do, go”) + -al.

parole.significato: Transport (act of transporting).
parole.testo: From Latin vectio, from vehere, vectum (“to carry”).

parole.significato: Any of various surgical instruments with prying functions.
parole.testo: Naturalized into medical English and ISV from Latin vectis.

parole.significato: Transport.
parole.testo: From Latin vectitatus (“borne about”), from intensive form of vehere, vectum (“to carry”).

parole.significato: A directed quantity, one with both magnitude and direction; the signed difference between two points.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin vector (“carrier, transporter”), from vehō (“to carry, transport, bear”), also ultimately the root of English vehicle. parole.significato: The act of carrying; conveyance; carriage.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin vectūra. Doublet of vettura and voiture.

parole.significato: To grow or sprout.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vegetātus, perfect passive participle of vegetō (“to enliven, to arouse”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: lively; active; sprightly; vigorous.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vegetus.

parole.significato: vigorous; lively; active; energetic.
parole.testo: Latin vegetus. See vegete.

parole.significato: Vehemence.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vehementia.

parole.significato: The ∨ symbol used to represent the inclusive or, which is a logical connective.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vel (“or”).

parole.significato: or not; used when discussing the existence or nonexistence of a condition, circumstance, etc
parole.testo: From Latin vel non.

parole.significato: Or the like; or similar.
parole.testo: Abbreviation of Latin vel similia (“or similar (things), or the like”). First attested in the 19th century; the appearance of the abbreviation in New Latin is roughly contemporary.

parole.significato: A covering membrane or velum
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vēlāmen.

parole.significato: Veil-like.
parole.testo: From Latin velamentum (“covering, screen”), + -ous.

parole.significato: A velamen or membrane.
parole.testo: From Latin vēlāmentum.

parole.significato: Articulated at the velum or soft palate.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vēlāris, from vēlum (“sail; veil, awning”). By surface analysis, vel(um) + -ar.

parole.significato: The marginal membrane of certain medusae belonging to the Discophora.
parole.testo: From Latin vēlārium, from vēlum + -ārium. Doublet of veghar.

parole.significato: Having a veil; veiled.
parole.testo: From Latin vēlātus, past participle of vēlāre (“to veil”). See veil. By surface analysis, vel(um) + -ate.

parole.significato: A veiling; concealment; mystery.
parole.testo: From Latin vēlātiōn-, vēlātiō, from vēlātus (past participle of vēlāre (“to veil”)) + -iōn-, -iō.

parole.significato: Any of two species of fish that make up the family Veliferidae: a spinyfin velifer (Metavelifer multiradiatus) and a sa…
parole.testo: From Latin vēl(um) (“sail, curtain”) + -i- + -fer.

parole.significato: Having or bearing a sail.
parole.testo: Latin velifer, from Latin velum (“sail”) + fero (“to bear”), + -ous. By surface analysis, vel(um) + -i- + -fer + -ous.

parole.significato: The planktonic larva of many kinds of marine and freshwater gastropod molluscs, as well as most bivalve molluscs.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vēliger (“sail-bearing”).

parole.significato: A type of Roman infantryman who worked as a skirmisher.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vēlitēs, plural of vēles.

parole.significato: To touch (a body part) lightly so as to excite the surface nerves and cause uneasiness, laughter, or spasmodic movement…
parole.testo: From Latin vellicatus, past participle of vellicare (“to twitch”). Cognate with Spanish pellizcar (“to pinch”).

parole.significato: The stipe of certain fungi.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin vellus (“fleece”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to a velum, usually the velum palatinum (soft palate, palatum molle)
parole.testo: Derived from Latin vēlum (“cloth, sail, velum”) + -o-.

parole.significato: A device that regulates the rotational speed of a shaft
parole.testo: From Latin velox (“fast”) or velo- + -dyne.

parole.significato: A thin membrane resembling a veil or curtain.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vēlum (“a cloth, covering, awning, curtain, veil”). Doublet of veil.

parole.significato: Synonym of vein.
parole.testo: From Latin vēna. Doublet of vein.

parole.significato: Venous; pertaining to veins.
parole.testo: From Latin vēna (“vein”) + -al.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to hunting.
parole.testo: From Latin venarius, from Latin venari, past participle venatus (“to hunt”).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to or involved in hunting.
parole.testo: From Latin vēnāticus (“of or pertaining to hunting”), from vēnātus (“hunting, the chase”), from vēnor (“hunt, chase”).

parole.significato: The hunting and slaying of wild animals as a form of entertainment in Ancient Roman amphitheaters.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin venatio. Doublet of venison and venation.

parole.significato: The arrangement of veins in a leaf, wing, or similar structure.
parole.testo: From Latin vēna (“vein”) + -ation.

parole.significato: The hunting of wild animals.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vēnātio. Doublet of venison and venatio.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to or involved in hunting or the chase.
parole.testo: From Latin vēnātōrius (“of or pertaining to a hunter or the chase”), from vēnātor (“hunter”), from vēnor (“hunt, chase”).

parole.significato: Salable; able to be bought, sold, or traded.
parole.testo: From Latin vendibilis, from vendere (“to sell”).

parole.significato: To claim, assert, or maintain a right for oneself.
parole.testo: From Latin vendicāre, an alternative form of vindicare ("to claim, assert, avenge"). See also vindicate.

parole.significato: To exhibit, as though for sale; to show off.
parole.testo: From the participle stem of Latin venditare, frequentative of vendere (“to sell”).

parole.significato: boastfulness; showing off.
parole.testo: From Latin venditatio, from venditare, venditatum (“to offer again and again for sale”), v. freq. of vendere. See vend.

parole.significato: The act of vending or selling; sale.
parole.testo: Latin venditio: compare French vendition.

parole.significato: Of, from, or pertaining to Venedotia or Gwynedd.
parole.testo: From Latin Vēnedōtiānus.

parole.significato: poisonous; pertaining to poison or poisoning
parole.testo: From Latin venēficus, from venēnum (“poison”).

parole.significato: The act or practice of poisoning.
parole.testo: From Latin venēficium.

parole.significato: To poison; to infect with poison.
parole.testo: From Latin venenatus, past participle of venenare (“to poison”), from venenum (“poison, venom”).

parole.significato: Synonym of venom.
parole.testo: From Latin venēnum (“juice; venom”). Doublet of venin and venom.

parole.significato: Venomous; poisonous.
parole.testo: From Middle English venenous, from Latin venēnōsus. By surface analysis, venene + -ous. Piecewise doublet of venomous.

parole.significato: The qualities of being venerable; great age, respectability, infirmity, etc.
parole.testo: From venerable + -ity, from Latin venerabilitas.

parole.significato: To treat with great respect and deference.
parole.testo: First attested in 1623; borrowed from Latin venerātus, perfect active participle of veneror (“to worship, venerate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Of or relating to the genitals or sexual intercourse.
parole.testo: From Middle English venereal, venerealle (“of or relating to sexual intercourse”), from Latin venereus, venerius (“of or relating to sexual love”), from Venus (“Roman goddess of love”) (from Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁- (“to love”)) + -eus, -ius (suffix forming adjectives from nouns).

parole.significato: venereal (of diseases)
parole.testo: Latin venereus, venerius.

parole.significato: Venereal.
parole.testo: From Latin venerius.

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to the city of Venice or surrounding province, Veneto region, northeastern Italy.
parole.testo: From Latin Venetianus (“Venetic; Venetian”), from Venetia (“lands of the Veneti; Venice, Veneto; Armorica”) + -anus (“-ian”), from Veneti + -ia. parole.significato: Of or related to the Veneti, an ancient people of northeastern Italy.
parole.testo: From Latin veneticus, from Venetia (“land of the Veneti; Venice, Veneto”) + -icus (“-ic: forming adjectives”), from Venetī + -ia, of uncertain origin. Equivalent to Veneti + -ic.

parole.significato: Describes a belligerent attitude.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vēnī vīdī vīcī (“I came, I saw, I conquered”).

parole.significato: venial; pardonable
parole.testo: From Latin veniabilis, from venia (“forgiveness, pardon”).

parole.significato: A writ of venire facias.
parole.testo: Shortening of Latin venīre faciās, the opening words of a writ.

parole.significato: A judicial writ directing that a new jury be impanelled and that a new trial be held, due to some irregularity (especia…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin venire facias de novo (“that you make/cause to come anew”), from the opening words of the writ.

parole.significato: Indicating motion to or toward a thing.
parole.testo: From Latin veniō (“to come, to approach”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to veins.
parole.testo: Morphologically vein + -ous, which is a borrowing from Latin vēnōsus (“full of veins, veiny”), from vēna (“a blood vessel, vein”) + -ōsus (“-ous, -ose”, adjectival suffix). Doublet of venose.

parole.significato: A woman with offspring.
parole.testo: Borrowing from Latin venter (“the belly; the womb; a swelling”).

parole.significato: To replace stale or noxious air with fresh.
parole.testo: From Middle English, borrowed from Latin ventilātus, past participle of ventilō.

parole.significato: The quality or state of being windy or flatulent; windiness or flatulence.
parole.testo: From ventose + -ity, from Latin ventositas.

parole.significato: ventral; abdominal; abdomen.
parole.testo: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting a New Latin combining form, from Latin venter (“stomach”).

parole.significato: Any small cavity within a body; a hollow part or organ, especially:
parole.testo: From late Middle English, from Latin ventriculus (“the belly”), diminutive of venter (“the belly”). Doublet of ventriculus.

parole.significato: Somewhat distended in the middle.
parole.testo: Latin ventriculosus (“of the belly”).

parole.significato: A digestive cavity such as a gizzard or stomach.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin ventriculus (“the belly”), diminutive of venter (“the belly”). Doublet of ventricle.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a ventriloquist or ventriloquism.
parole.testo: Latin ventriloquus (“a ventriloquist”); venter (“the belly”) + loqui, past participle locutus (“to speak”). See ventral and loquacious.

parole.significato: Ventriloquism.
parole.testo: From Latin ventriloquium, from venter (“stomach”) + loquī (“to speak”). By surface analysis, ventri- + -loquy.

parole.significato: abdomen, belly (especially of an animal)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin venter (“belly”), with the ending possibly changed by backformation from ventral and/or by analogy to dorsum (“back”).

parole.significato: A venule.
parole.testo: From Latin venula.

parole.significato: Sexual activity or intercourse; sex; lust, love.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English Venus, borrowed from Latin Venus.

parole.significato: Synonym of mons veneris.
parole.testo: Calque of Latin mons veneris.

parole.significato: beautiful; having an attractive appearance
parole.testo: From Latin venustus, from Venus (“the goddess of love”).

parole.significato: Elegance; physical beauty.
parole.testo: From Latin venustas. Compare also Middle French vénusté.

parole.significato: The true or real cause of something.
parole.testo: From Latin vera (“true”) + causa (“cause”).

parole.significato: True.
parole.testo: From Latin vērāx (“truthful”) + -acious, from vērus (“true”).

parole.significato: veratrine
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: Any of various poisonous herbs of the genus Veratrum
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vērātrum (“hellebore”).

parole.significato: A word that indicates an action, event, or state of being.
parole.testo: From Middle English verbe, directly from Latin verbum (“word, verb”), reinforced by Old French verbe, from Proto-Indo-European *werdʰo-. Doublet of verve and word.

parole.significato: A word game in which the players are given a set of letters and must form as many words as possible from subsets of tho…
parole.testo: From Latin verbum (“word”) + -arium.

parole.significato: Word-for-word and to the letter.
parole.testo: Latin verbātim (“word-for-word”) + et (“and”) + līterātim (“letter-for-letter”).

parole.significato: Verbena, a genus of herbaceous plants of which several species are extensively cultivated for the great beauty of their…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin verbēna (“leaves or twigs of olive, myrtle, laurel, or other sacred plants employed in religious ceremonies”), from Proto-Indo-European *werbʰ-. Doublet of vervain, via French.

parole.significato: To hit; to beat; to strike
parole.testo: From Latin verberatus, past participle of verberare (“to beat”), from verber (“a lash, a whip”).

parole.significato: The act of verberating; a beating or striking.
parole.testo: Latin verberatio: compare French verbération.

parole.significato: A person whose mental imagery consists of words.
parole.testo: Irregular formation from Latin verbum + -ile.

parole.significato: A fear of words.
parole.testo: From Latin verbō (“word”) + -phobia.

parole.significato: Containing or using more words than necessary; long-winded, wordy.
parole.testo: From Latin verbōsus (“prolix, wordy, verbose”). Verbōsus is derived from verbum (“word”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *werh₁- (“to say, speak”)) + -ōsus (suffix meaning ‘full of, overly, prone to’ forming adjectives from nouns). Equivalent to verb + -ose.

parole.significato: Used to bring something to a conclusion, implying that further comment is unadvisable or unneeded.
parole.testo: A shortening of Latin verbum sapienti sat est (“a word is enough to a wise man”). Compare verbum sat.

parole.significato: Used to bring something to a conclusion, implying that further comment is unadvisable or unneeded.
parole.testo: A shortening of Latin verbum (sapienti) sat est (“a word is enough (to a wise man)”). Compare verbum sapienti.

parole.significato: Freshly green; verdant; covered with verdure, or consisting of it.
parole.testo: Originated c. 1595–1605, verdure + -ous, ultimately from verd (“green”), from Latin viridis.

parole.significato: modest
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin verēcundus (“shy, modest”).

parole.significato: A written document in Old English law detailing the facts presented as true at a trial.
parole.testo: From Latin veredictum. Doublet of verdict.

parole.significato: To be or come very close; to border; to approach.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vergō (“to bend, turn, tend toward, incline”), from Proto-Indo-European *werg- (“to turn”), from a root *wer- (“to turn, bend”) (compare versus); strongly influenced by the above noun.

parole.significato: The metal bar with two pallets that drive the crown wheel in a verge escapement.
parole.testo: Originally just verge (from Latin virga (“staff, rod”)); it acquired the extra staff for clarity.

parole.significato: A magistrate in ancient Gaul who held the highest office in many Gallic cities, especially among the Aedui.
parole.testo: From Latin vergobretus (“chief magistrate amongst the Aedui”), from Gaulish uercobretos.

parole.significato: veridical
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin veridicus.

parole.significato: True.
parole.testo: From Latin veridicus (“truly said”), from verus (“true”) and dīcō (“to say”).

parole.significato: Synonym of verify.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin vērificāt-, past participial stem of vērificō. Also an independent back-formation from verification. For its use by non-native speakers, compare Catalan, Galician, Occitan, Portuguese, and Spanish verificar and Italian verificare.

parole.significato: Serving to verify or authenticate.
parole.testo: From the past participial stem vērificāt- of Latin vērificō (in English verification) + -ory. By surface analysis, verificate + -ive.

parole.significato: Serving to verify something.
parole.testo: From the past participial stem vērificāt- of Latin vērificō (in English verification) + -ory. By surface analysis, verificate + -ory.

parole.significato: Appearing to be true or real; probable; likely.
parole.testo: From Latin vērisimilis, prop. vērī similis (“having the appearance of truth”), from vērī (genitive of vērus (“true”)) + similis (“like, similar”); see very and similar.

parole.significato: Appearing to be verisimilar; exhibiting verisimilitude, in either a neutral or a dubious sense.
parole.testo: From Latin vērisimilitūdin- + -ous, from oblique stem of Latin vērisimilitūdō, from vērī (genitive of vērus) + similitūdō, from similis + -tūdō. By surface analysis, verisimilitude + -ous.

parole.significato: Truth, particularly of a transcendent character.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vēritās. Doublet of verity.

parole.significato: Relating to the vermis
parole.testo: Pseudo-Latinism, from a supposed *vermalis, whereas Latin vermiculātus. From vermis + -al.

parole.significato: Related to worms.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vermis (“worm”).

parole.significato: Any substance used to kill worms, especially parasitic intestinal worms
parole.testo: From Latin vermis (“worm”) + -cide.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or characteristic of worms.
parole.testo: From Latin vermis (“worm”).

parole.significato: To decorate with lines resembling the tracks of worms.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vermiculatus (“inlaid in wavy lines”), past participle of vermiculor (“to be full of worms or worm-eaten”), from vermiculus (“little worm”).

parole.significato: The process of being turned into a worm.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vermiculātiōnem, from vermiculor (“to be worm-eaten, to be wormy”) + -tiō (suffix forming nouns relating to actions or the results of actions) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *-tis (suffix forming abstract or action nouns from verb roots)). The Latin verb is from vermis (“wo

parole.significato: A small worm or worm-like organism.
parole.testo: From Latin vermiculus, diminutive of vermis (“a worm”). See vermicular. Doublet of vermeil.

parole.significato: A hydrated silicate mineral which expands on heating; it is used in insulation and as a medium for planting.
parole.testo: From Latin vermiculus (“wormlet”), for its fibrous nature and tendency to expand into worm-like shapes when heated.

parole.significato: Containing, or full of, worms; resembling worms; wormy.
parole.testo: From Latin vermiculosus. See vermicule.

parole.significato: In the shape of a worm.
parole.testo: From Latin vermis (“worm”) + -form.

parole.significato: Tending to prevent, destroy, or expel worms or vermin; anthelmintic.
parole.testo: From Latin vermis (“a worm”) + fugare (“to drive away”), from fugere (“to flee”). See worm, and fugitive.

parole.significato: Acting as a drug to cause the expulsion or death of intestinal worms.
parole.testo: Attested since about 1720, from Latin vermis (“worm”) + fugāre (“to cause to flee”). Compare -fuge.

parole.significato: To breed vermin.
parole.testo: From the Latin verminare (“to have worms”), from vermis (“worm”).

parole.significato: The generation or breeding of vermin.
parole.testo: Latin verminatio the worms, a disease of animals, a crawling, itching pain.

parole.significato: Giving birth to worms or grubs, such as various insects.
parole.testo: From Latin vermis (“a worm”) + parere (“to bring forth”), + -ous.

parole.significato: An abnormal or irrational fear of worms or being infected by worms.
parole.testo: From Latin vermis (“worm”) + -phobia: Ancient Greek φόβος (phóbos, “fear”).

parole.significato: A narrow, worm-like structure found in animal brains between the hemispheres of the cerebellum; it is the site of termi…
parole.testo: From Latin vermis (“worm”), from Proto-Italic *wormis, from Proto-Indo-European *wr̥mis. Doublet of worm.

parole.significato: A kind of soil subject to worm activity.
parole.testo: From Latin vermis (“worm”) + -sol.

parole.significato: The language of a people or a national language.
parole.testo: From Latin vernāculus (“domestic, indigenous, of or pertaining to home-born slaves”), from verna (“a native, a home-born slave (one born in his master's house)”).

parole.significato: vernacular (of everyday language)
parole.testo: Latin vernaculus. See vernacular.

parole.significato: Pertaining to or occurring in spring.
parole.testo: PIE word  *wósr̥ From Latin vernālis (“(rare) of or pertaining to spring; vernal”), from vērnus (“of or pertaining to spring; vernal”) + -ālis (suffix forming adjectives of relationship). parole.significato: The quality of being vernal or spring-like.
parole.testo: From vernal + -ity, from Latin vernalis (“pertainig to spring”).

parole.significato: Flourishing, as in spring; vernal.
parole.testo: From Latin vernans, present participle vernare (“to flourish”), from ver (“spring”).

parole.significato: Suiting a slave; servile; obsequious.
parole.testo: From Latin vernilis (“servile”). See vernacular.

parole.significato: Fawning or obsequious behaviour; servility.
parole.testo: From vernile + -ity, from Latin vernilitas.

parole.significato: The waxy or "cheesy" white substance found coating the skin of newborn humans.
parole.testo: From Latin vernix (“varnish”) + caseosa (“cheesy”).

parole.significato: Having verricules (thick tufts of parallel hairs, bristles, or branches).
parole.testo: Latin verriculum a net, seine.

parole.significato: A tuft of upright hairs.
parole.testo: From Latin verriculum (“a net”).

parole.significato: A wart, especially one that grows on the foot, caused by a human papilloma virus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin verrūca. Doublet of wart.

parole.significato: Capable of being turned; flexible, changeable, or inconsistent.
parole.testo: From Latin versabilis. Compare French versable. See versatile.

parole.significato: Capable of doing many things competently.
parole.testo: From Latin versātilis (“turning easily”), from versātus, past participle of versō (“to turn, change”), frequentative of vertō (“to turn”).

parole.significato: Having changing or varied colours.
parole.testo: From Latin versicolor.

parole.significato: Synonym of versicle.
parole.testo: From Latin versiculus.

parole.significato: Someone who writes verse; a poet.
parole.testo: From Latin versificator.

parole.significato: A female poet.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin versificātrīx. By surface analysis, versificator + -trix.

parole.significato: The back side of a flat object which is to be examined visually, as for reading, such as a sheet, leaf, coin or medal;
parole.testo: From Latin in versō foliō (“on the turned leaf, on the turned page”), the ablative case of the Latin versus (“turned, changed”) from the perfect passive participle of vertō (“turn”). Compare rēctus (“right”).

parole.significato: A quaternion of norm one.
parole.testo: From Latin vertere, versus (“to turn”). See version.

parole.significato: A true species, neither subspecies nor superspecies.
parole.testo: From Latin vērus (“true”) and species

parole.significato: Against; in opposition to.

parole.significato: To face in competition
parole.testo: From Middle English versus, borrowed from Latin versus (“facing”), past participle of vertere (“to turn, change, overthrow, destroy”).

parole.significato: crafty; wily; artful
parole.testo: From Latin versūtus, from vertö, versum (“to turn”).

parole.significato: To turn.
parole.testo: From Latin vertere (“to turn, overturn”).

parole.significato: Any of the bony or cartilaginous segments which make up the backbone, consisting in some lower vertebrates of several d…
parole.testo: Borrowing from Latin vertebra (“a joint”), from vertō (“to turn”) + -bra (instrumental nominal suffix). Having multiple vertebrae (plural of vertebra) in one's backbone instead of having a single bone or solid spine, allows for the movement of the body with bends and turns. Hence meaning 1.

parole.significato: Having a backbone.
parole.testo: Adapted borrowing of French vertébré, from Latin vertebrātus (“jointed”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more).

parole.significato: The highest point, top or apex of something.
parole.testo: Late Middle English, borrowed from Latin vertex (“whirl, eddy; top, crown, peak, summit”). Doublet of vortex.

parole.significato: A whorl, a group of similar parts such as leaves radiating from a shared axis
parole.testo: From Latin verticillum.

parole.significato: A whorl of flowers apparently of one cluster, but composed of two opposite axillary cymes, as in mint.
parole.testo: Latin verticillus (“a whirl”) + aster (“a star”).

parole.significato: Forming or having whorls
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin verticillātus.

parole.significato: A whorl; a verticil.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin verticillus.

parole.significato: A sensation of whirling and loss of balance, caused by looking down from a great height or by disease affecting the inn…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vertīgō.

parole.significato: A clay soil, containing a high content of montmorillonite, that forms deep cracks in drier conditions.
parole.testo: From Latin vertere (“turn”) + -i- + sol (“soil”).

parole.significato: A monoclinic-prismatic colorless mineral containing aluminum, calcium, hydrogen, oxygen, silicon, and strontium.
parole.testo: From Latin Vertumn(us) + -ite.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the English city of St Albans.
parole.testo: From Latin Verulamium (“an ancient British city near the site of St Albans”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to Verulae.
parole.testo: From Latin Verulānus, from Verulae + -ānus. By surface analysis, Verulae + -an.

parole.significato: Madness, insanity, mental derangement.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin vēsānia, derived from vēsānus (“mad, insane”).

parole.significato: A supposed rare metallic element extracted from Vesuvian lava. Later tests showed it to be a composite.
parole.testo: From Latin Vesuvius, contracted to Vesbius, -ium.

parole.significato: A bladder, especially the urinary bladder or the gall bladder.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin vēsīca (“bladder”).

parole.significato: Synonym of gall bladder.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin vesica biliaris.

parole.significato: Synonym of gall bladder.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin vesica fellea.

parole.significato: Pertaining to the urinary bladder.
parole.testo: From Latin vesica (“bladder”). By surface analysis, vesic- + -al.

parole.significato: bladder, as
parole.testo: From Latin vēsīca (“bladder, sac”) + -o-.

parole.significato: Synonym of vesicle (small blister).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vēsīcula. By surface analysis, vesic- + -ula. Doublet of vesicle.

parole.significato: vesicula (vesicle) (cutaneous or mucosal); blister.
parole.testo: From Latin vēsīcula. By surface analysis, vesic- + -ule + -o-.

parole.significato: bladdery; vesicular; vesiculate; composed of, or covered with, vesicles
parole.testo: From Latin vesiculosus.

parole.significato: To darken as at the beginning of night
parole.testo: From Latin vesper.

parole.significato: westward; moving toward the setting sun.
parole.testo: From Latin vesper.

parole.significato: of, pertaining to, or characteristic of bats.
parole.testo: From Latin vespertīliō (“bat”) + -ian.

parole.significato: Of or related to the evening; that occurs in the evening.
parole.testo: From Middle English vespertyne, from Latin vespertīnus (“evening”).

parole.significato: A nest built by a social wasp species.
parole.testo: From Latin vespa (“wasp”), formed in imitation of apiary (a similar structure for bees).

parole.significato: One who carried out the dead bodies of the poor at night for burial.
parole.testo: From Latin vespillo.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to Vesta, the virgin goddess of the hearth.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin Vestālis.

parole.significato: A virgin dedicated to the service of the goddess Vesta.
parole.testo: From Latin; virgines Vestales referred to the priestesses in charge of the sacred fire in the temple of Vesta in Rome.

parole.significato: Pertaining to clothes or clothing.
parole.testo: From Latin vestiarius, from vestis as Etymology 1, above.

parole.significato: A cavity into which, in certain bryozoans, the esophagus and anus open.
parole.testo: Unadapted borrowing from Latin vestibulum (“a forecourt, entrance court; an entrance”). Doublet of vestibule.

parole.significato: To investigate.
parole.testo: From Latin vestigatus, past participle of vestigare. See vestige.

parole.significato: A vestige.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin vestīgium. Doublet of vestige.

parole.significato: Clothing, clothes, especially ecclesiastical.
parole.testo: A variant of vestment influenced by its etymon Latin vestīmentum (from vestiō (“to clothe”)).

parole.significato: Your fault, due to your error; you are to blame.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from the Latin phrase vestrā culpā (“through your (plural) fault”), ablative case of vestra culpa (“your fault, guilt”), used in English by analogy with mea culpa and nostra culpa.

parole.significato: A kind of firework supposed to resemble a volcano eruption.
parole.testo: From Latin Vesuvius, of uncertain origin.

parole.significato: Growing old.
parole.testo: From Latin veterāscēns.

parole.significato: Of long standing, experienced, seasoned.
parole.testo: From Latin veterātus.

parole.significato: aging
parole.testo: From Latin vetero (“to age”).

parole.significato: A medical doctor who treats non-human animals.
parole.testo: From Latin veterīnārius (“cattle doctor”) + -an, from veterīnae (“beasts of burden, draught-”), probably from vehō (“to convey, draw”), or from vetus (“old”). By surface analysis, veterinary + -an.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the medical or surgical treatment of non-human animals, especially domestic and farm animals.
parole.testo: From Latin veterīnārius, from veterīnus and veterīnae (“cattle;"beasts of burden/of draught"”); compare with veterinarian.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Old Testament of the Bible.
parole.testo: PIE word  *tréyes From Latin vetus, veteris (“ancient, old”) + English testamentary (“pertaining to a testament or will”).

parole.significato: A political right to disapprove of (and thereby stop) the process of a decision, a law etc.
parole.testo: From Latin vetō (“to forbid”).

parole.significato: antique; ancient; old, in a positive way
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vetustus (“old, ancient”).

parole.significato: The state of being old; old age.
parole.testo: From Latin vetustās (“old age”) + -ity, from vetus (“old”).

parole.significato: antiquity; great age
parole.testo: From Latin vetustās.

parole.significato: A vexed, unresolved, or intractable question.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin vexāta quaestiō.

parole.significato: Creating a partition.
parole.testo: From Latin vexillarius: compare French vexillaire.

parole.significato: A company of soldiers (especially in ancient Rome) grouped under the same flag.
parole.testo: From Latin vexillatio, from vexillum.

parole.significato: A flag, banner, or standard.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vēxillum (“flag, banner”).

parole.significato: By force, violently; specifically, causing damage to a person or property.
parole.testo: From Latin vi et armis (“with force and arms”).

parole.significato: A main road or highway, especially in ancient Rome. (Mainly used in set phrases, below.)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin via (“road”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *weǵʰ-. Possible doublet of way. The sense in electronics is also explained as vertical interconnect access.

parole.significato: By way of; passing through.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin viā (“by the way (of)”), ablative singular of via (“way, road”), from Proto-Indo-European *weǵʰ-. Compare typologically Polish drogą, Russian путём (putjóm).

parole.significato: A kind of Ancient Roman road, made from earth with gravel on top.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: A third way; a middle course, a compromise.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin via media (“a middle way”).

parole.significato: A kind of Ancient Roman road, paved with stone blocks.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: A kind of Ancient Roman road, made from levelled earth.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: A bridge with several spans that carries rail or road traffic over a valley or other obstacles.
parole.testo: Coined in 1816, from Latin via (“highway; road”) + English -duct, on the basis of aqueduct.

parole.significato: An early type of odometer.
parole.testo: Latin via (“a way”) + -meter.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to roads, or occurring on roads.
parole.testo: From Latin viarius, from via (“a way, road”).

parole.significato: The art of making roads or other patha travelling, including the construction of bridges, canals, viaducts, etc.
parole.testo: From Latin via (“way”) + -tecture, as in architecture.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to traveling or a journey.
parole.testo: Latin viaticus (“relating to a journey”), from via (“road”).

parole.significato: Life insurance policies which are sold at a discount to the face amount, or death benefit, of people who have been medi…
parole.testo: From Latin viaticum (“provisions for a long journey”).

parole.significato: The Eucharist, when given to a person who is dying or one in danger of death.
parole.testo: From Latin viāticum (“travelling-money, provisions for a journey”), from viāticus (“of a road or journey”), from via (“road”). Doublet of voyage.

parole.significato: A wayfarer, traveler.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin viātor (“traveler”).

parole.significato: A narrow streak of subcutaneous extravasation of blood, often one of many in a patch of such streaks, which may be exte…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vībex (“the mark of a blow”).

parole.significato: Characteristic of a vibraculum
parole.testo: From Latin vibrō + -acule + -oid.

parole.significato: A long, whiplike, modified zooid on the surface of certain colonies of bryozoa
parole.testo: From Latin vibrō + -aculum.

parole.significato: The quality of being vibrant.
parole.testo: From Latin vibrans, present participle of vibrare, equivalent to vibrant + -cy.

parole.significato: To shake with small, rapid movements to and fro.

parole.significato: A minuscule or slight vibration; specifically, a vibration in brain tissue caused by the comparatively greater vibratio…
parole.testo: From modern Latin vibratiuncula, diminutive form of Latin vibrātio (“vibration”).

parole.significato: Any of the tactile whiskers on the nose of an animal such as a cat.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vibrissae.

parole.significato: Vibrant.
parole.testo: From Latin vibrissāns, present participle of vibrissō, from vibrō (“to vibrate”) + -issō.

parole.significato: The way an organism responds to mechanical (physical) vibrations.
parole.testo: From vibro-, from Latin vibrāre (“vibrate”) + Ancient Greek τάξις (táxis, “arrangement”)

parole.significato: Any of many shrubs and trees, of the genus Viburnum, native to the Northern Hemisphere that have showy clusters of flow…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vīburnum.

parole.significato: Someone who walks or wanders streets.
parole.testo: From Latin vīcus (“street”) + -ambulist (“walker”). Later popularized by its inclusion in the Oxford English Dictionary and thence various "rare word" lists.

parole.significato: A priest entrusted by the bishop with a certain degree of leadership in a territorial division of a diocese or a pastor…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vicārius forāneus. See forane.

parole.significato: in place of; subordinate to; designating a person below another in rank
parole.testo: From Latin vice (“in place of”), ablative form of vicis. Compare French fois (“time”) and Spanish vez (“time, turn”).

parole.significato: The same but with the two items mentioned reversed.

parole.significato: Taking the place or rank of (another person); deputy.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin vice (“in place of”), ablative form of vicis (“alternation, turn”). Compare viscount.

parole.significato: A viscount.
parole.testo: From Latin vicecomes. Doublet of vicomte and viscount.

parole.significato: The official administrative deputy of a ruler, head of state, or church official.
parole.testo: From Latin vicegerens.

parole.significato: A person whose age is between twenty and twenty-nine years, inclusive; someone in their twenties.
parole.testo: From vicenary + -ian, from Latin vīcēnārius (“vicenary”), from vīcēnus (“twenty each”) + -ārius (“-ary: forming adjectives and related nouns”).

parole.significato: Synonym of vicenary: of, pertaining to, or based on the number twenty.
parole.testo: From Latin vīcēnārius, from vīcēnus (“twenty each”) + -ārius (“-ary: forming adjectives and related nouns”). Doublet of vicenary. Ultimately cognate with English vigenary.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or based on the number twenty.
parole.testo: From Latin vīcēnārius, from vīcēnus (“twenty each”) + -ārius (“-ary: forming adjectives and related nouns”). Doublet of vicenarious. Ultimately cognate with English vigenary.

parole.significato: The festival and religious rituals celebrating a Roman emperor's 20th year of rule.
parole.testo: From Latin vīcennālia, from vīcennium (“20-year period”) + -ālia (“-alia: forming the names of festivals”), from vicennis (“20-year”) + -ium (“forming abstract nouns”), from vīciēs (“twenty each”) + annus (“year”) + -is (“forming compound adjectives”). Equivalent to vicennium + -alia.

parole.significato: Synonym of vicennalia: the festival and religious ritual held on the 20th anniversary of a Roman emperor's reign.
parole.testo: From Latin vīcennālia, from vīcennis (“20-year”) + -ālia (“-alia: forming festival names”), from vīciēs (“twenty times”) + annus (“year”) + -is (“forming compound adjectives”).

parole.significato: Occurring once every twenty years.
parole.testo: From vicennium + -al or directly from Latin vīcenniālis, from vīcennium (“20-year span”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjective-forming suffix), from vīcennis (“20-year”) + -ium (“-ium”, suffix forming abstract nouns), from vīciēs (“20 times”) + annus (“year”) + -is (suffix forming compound adjectives). Equivale

parole.significato: A period of twenty years.
parole.testo: From Latin vicennium, from vīcennis (“20-year”) + -ium, from vīciēs (“20 times”) + annus (“year”) + -is (suffix forming compound adjectives). Equivalent to vicennial + -ium.

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to the city or province of Vicenza in the Veneto region in northeastern Italy.
parole.testo: From Latin Vīcentīnus, by-form of Vīcētīnus.

parole.significato: The destruction of one-twentieth of something; especially, the killing or putting to death of every twentieth person, e…

parole.significato: A paper size, (2.5"–3.3" x 5"–6.25"), one twenty-fourth of a standard uncut flat sheet.
parole.testo: From Latin ablatives of vīcēsimus (“twentieth”) and quartus (“fourth”).

parole.significato: By turns; in succession; alternatim.
parole.testo: From the Latin vicibus, the ablative plural form of vicis (“change”, “alternation”, “turn”; “succession”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a neighborhood; neighboring.
parole.testo: From Latin vīcīnālis, from vīcus (“village”).

parole.significato: Nearby; neighbouring; vicinal.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vīcīnus.

parole.significato: An organic compound from Lathyrus sativus.

parole.significato: Proximity; the state of being near.

parole.significato: Viciousness.
parole.testo: From vitiosity under influence of vicious, both of which derive ultimately from Latin vitiōsus.

parole.significato: pertaining to change, alteration, or mutation.
parole.testo: From Latin vicissitūdin- + -ary, from oblique stem of Latin vicissitūdō, from vicis + -tūdō. By surface analysis, vicissitude + -ary.

parole.significato: Characterized by or filled with vicissitudes.
parole.testo: From Latin vicissitūdin- + -ous, from oblique stem of Latin vicissitūdō, from vicis + -tūdō. By surface analysis, vicissitude + -ous.

parole.significato: A change, as of fortune.
parole.testo: From viciss(itous) + -ity, from Latin vicissitas. Mentioned since at least 1717, in Elisha Coles's An English Dictionary.

parole.significato: A kind of police commandant in Ancient Rome, responsible for a vicus.

parole.significato: To make a victim of; to sacrifice; to immolate.

parole.significato: The overall champion in a sports contest, typically at a public school

parole.significato: One of an American breed of medium-sized white pigs with a slightly dished face and very erect ears.
parole.testo: From Latin Victōria, from victōria (“victory”). Doublet of Vitória. The given name can also be analyzed as the male name Victor + -ia. The places were named in honour of Queen Victoria of Great Britain.

parole.significato: A silver coin, stamped with an image of Victory, minted during the Roman Republic, and valued at half a denarius.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin victōriātus.

parole.significato: Being the winner in a contest, struggle, war, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin victōriōsus, from victōria (“victory”), from victor (“conqueror”). Displaced native Old English siġefæst.

parole.significato: A female victor; a victress.
parole.testo: From Middle English victrice, from Latin victrīx.

parole.significato: victor (female); victress.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin victrīx. By surface analysis, victor + -trix.

parole.significato: A small civilian settlement outside a Roman fort.

parole.significato: A remark directing the reader to look to the specified place for epexegesis; see; consult; refer to.

parole.significato: Namely, to wit, that is to say (used when clarifying or naming the preceding item or topic)

parole.significato: That which is to be seen.

parole.significato: Transient visual content or media, processed with technology, especially electronic.

parole.significato: See; consult; refer to—a remark directing the readers to look to the specified place for epexegesis.

parole.significato: A group of observers.

parole.significato: A preliminary drawing of something to be designed and constructed.

parole.significato: Relating to widowhood, or widowed.

parole.significato: the state of being a widow; widowhood

parole.significato: A vigil.

parole.significato: Synonym of vicennial, occurring every twenty years.

parole.significato: twenty.

parole.significato: Any member of a group of twenty-six officials.

parole.significato: The quality of being vile or base.

parole.significato: A country house, with farm buildings around a courtyard.

parole.significato: Having villi; having the shape of villi or small hairs.

parole.significato: Hairy, covered with soft long hair.

parole.significato: A small projection from a membrane, particularly those found in the mucous membranes of the intestines.

parole.significato: life force

parole.significato: A long flexible shoot or branch of a plant.

parole.significato: Capable of being defeated or overcome; assailable or vulnerable.

parole.significato: A binding.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the harvesting of grapes.

parole.significato: An official who supervised tax collection in the ancient Roman Empire.

parole.significato: A person who vindicates.

parole.significato: A vindicatress.

parole.significato: Having a tendency to seek revenge when wronged, vengeful.
parole.testo: From Latin vindicta (“vengeance”) + -ive. Contrast Latin vindicātīvus.

parole.significato: A cane originally made of twisted grapevine trimmings and used by Roman centurions to beat the soldiers under their com…

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, bearing, or containing, vines.

parole.significato: Synonym of viticulture, the cultivation of grape vines for producing wine.

parole.significato: Yielding wine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin vīnifer.

parole.significato: To convert fruit juice—particularly grape juice—into wine by fermentation.
parole.testo: From Latin vinis (“wine”) + -ify (“to make into”).

parole.significato: Drunkenness.
parole.testo: From Latin vinolentina. See vinolent.

parole.significato: fond of drinking wine, especially to excess

parole.significato: Soaked with wine.

parole.significato: The quality or state of being vinous, or of having some essential characteristic of wine.

parole.significato: Pertaining to or having the characteristics of wine.

parole.significato: To make wine from fruit.

parole.significato: The univalent radical CH₂=CH−, derived from ethylene.

parole.significato: Any of several flowering plants, of the genus Viola, including the violets and pansies.
parole.testo: From Latin viola (“violet”).

parole.significato: Capable of being violated, broken, or injured.
parole.testo: From Latin violābilis. Compare Middle English violable (“destructive”), a hapax legomenon.

parole.significato: Violet-colored.
parole.testo: From Latin violāceus (“violet-coloured”).

parole.significato: To break or disregard (a rule or convention).

parole.significato: One who violates (a rule, a boundary, another person's body, etc.); offender
parole.testo: From Middle English violator, from Latin violātor. By surface analysis, violate + -or.

parole.significato: Violence.

parole.significato: Somewhat violet in colour.

parole.significato: Of, relating to or resembling a viper

parole.significato: The condition or disease of having a virus in the bloodstream.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a virago; having the qualities of a virago.

parole.significato: Resembling an overbearing woman; shrew-like.

parole.significato: A woman given to undue belligerence or ill manner at the slightest provocation.

parole.significato: green in color, or unwithered

parole.significato: The quality or state of being virescent.

parole.significato: Green or greenish.

parole.significato: A type of note used in plainsong notation, having a tail and representing a single tone.

parole.significato: Made of twigs or rods.

parole.significato: Rod-shaped: straight, long, and thin, (particularly botany) the habitus of plants with straight, erect branches.

parole.significato: Striped; streaked with rod-shaped (long and narrow) streaks.

parole.significato: A girl or woman whose hymen remains unbroken.

parole.significato: A small, thin, straight growth

parole.significato: A slash used to mark a pause or disjunction, similar to a comma.

The Middle English derives from Latin zēlōtēs, from Ancient Greek ζηλωτής (zēlōtḗs, “emulator, zealous admirer, follower”), from ζηλόω (zēlóō, “to emulate, to b

parole.significato: Full of zeal; ardent, fervent; exhibiting enthusiasm or strong passion, particularly in matters of religion.
parole.testo: From Middle English zelose, from Latin zēlōsus, from zēlus + -ōsus, from Ancient Greek ζῆλος (zêlos, “zeal, jealousy”), from ζηλόω (zēlóō, “to emulate, to be jealous”). By surface analysis, zeal + -ous. Doublet of jealous.

parole.significato: A zealot; the male counterpart of a zelatrix.
parole.testo: From Latin zēlātor.

parole.significato: A nun who oversees the behavior of young nuns.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin zēlātrīx (“female zealot; zealous female”). By surface analysis, zelator + -trix.

parole.significato: Characteristic of zealots, especially those that were part of rebellious movements in biblical times.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin zēlōticus, from Ancient Greek ζηλωτικός (zēlōtikós). Equivalent to zealot + -ic.

parole.significato: jealousy
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: Requiring or involving an infinite number of intervals within a finite time.
parole.testo: Via Latin Zēnō, from Ancient Greek Ζήνων (Zḗnōn), an ancient derivative of Ζεύς (Zeús), from Proto-Hellenic *dzéus, from Proto-Indo-European *dyḗws. Modern scientific and philosophical use derives from Zeno of Elea, poser of Zeno's paradoxes.

parole.significato: Pertaining to any of various people named Zeno or Zenon, or to their philosophies.
parole.testo: From Latin Zēnōn (also Zēnō) or its etymon Ancient Greek Ζήνων (Zḗnōn) + -ian. By surface analysis, Zenon + -ian.

parole.significato: A light wind from the west.
parole.testo: From Latin zephyrus (“west wind”), from Ancient Greek Ζέφυρος (Zéphuros). Doublet of zefir, zéphire, Zephyr, and Zephyrus. The confectionery sense is a semantic loan from Russian зефи́р (zefír).

parole.significato: An on-board hostess on the California Zephyr train, which originally operated between 1949 and 1970.
parole.testo: From zephyr (“light wind from the west”) + -ette (suffix forming nouns meaning the female equivalent of something). Zephyr is derived from Latin zephyrus, Zephyrus (“personification of the west wind”), from Ancient Greek Ζέφῠρος (Zéphŭros, “personification of the west wind”), possibly ultimately fro

parole.significato: Zinc.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin zincum. Doublet of zinc.

parole.significato: Any of several aquatic North American grasses, of the genus Zizania, grown for their edible grain; wild rice.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin zizania (“cockle, tares”).

parole.significato: The belief that one has transformed into an animal.
parole.testo: From Latin zōanthrōpia. By surface analysis, zoanthrope + -y.

parole.significato: A colony of zooids.
parole.testo: From Latin; equivalent to zo- + -arium.

parole.significato: A zone or band; a layer.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin zōna. Doublet of zone.

parole.significato: The most superficial layer of the adrenal cortex, lying directly beneath the adrenal gland's capsule, and responsible f…
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: A horizontally elongated region of grey matter in the subthalamus, of unknown function.
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: A glycoprotein membrane surrounding the plasma membrane of an oocyte.
parole.testo: Latin zōna (“zone”) + pellūcida (“transparent”).

parole.significato: A radiately striated membrane situated next to the yolk of an ovum, or separated from it by a very delicate membrane on…
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: The innermost layer of the adrenal cortex, responsible for the production of precursor androgens including dehydroepian…
parole.testo: Latin

parole.significato: Each of the five regions of the earth's surface into which it was divided by climatic differences, namely the torrid zo…
parole.testo: From Latin zōna, from Ancient Greek ζώνη (zṓnē, “girdle, belt”). Doublet of zona.

parole.significato: Any of several small belt-like regions.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin zōnula (“small belt or girdle”). Doublet of zonule.

parole.significato: A little zone, or girdle; a zonula.
parole.testo: From Latin zōnula (“small belt or girdle”). By surface analysis, zone + -ule. Doublet of zonula.

parole.significato: A yellow carotenoid pigment present in the feathers of some birds
parole.testo: From zoo-, Latin tawny, + -in.

parole.significato: The frieze of a column, especially one decorated with animals.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin zōophorus, from Ancient Greek ζωοφόρος (zōophóros).

parole.significato: a follower of Zoroastrianism
parole.testo: From Latin Zōroastrēs + -ian.

parole.significato: An ancient Greek waist-belt for men.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin zōstēr (“shingles”), from Ancient Greek ζωστήρ (zōstḗr, “girdle”).

parole.significato: A craniometric point at the base of the suture between the zygomatic and maxillary bones.
parole.testo: From zygo- + Latin maxillāris, from maxilla (“jawbone, jaw”).

parole.significato: An unfermented kind of Egyptian malt beer.
parole.testo: From Latin zȳthum, from Ancient Greek ζῦθος (zûthos).

parole.significato: The pre-decimal pounds, shillings, pence.
parole.testo: An abbreviation of the Latin lībra solidus dēnārius, see also £.

parole.significato: Of the age; aged.
parole.testo: Abbreviation of Latin aetātis (“of age”).

parole.significato: A prescription.
parole.testo: An R with a cross-stroke indicating an abbreviation (of recipe, response, retrograde etc). In the case of a prescription, abbreviating Latin recipe (“take this”, second-person singular imperative of recipiō); it is sometimes typeset as, or even interpreted as, a digraph Rx. Compare also Dx (“diagnos

parole.significato: Forms abstract nouns.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman -ice and Old French -ice, from either (1) Latin -īcius (“adjective suffix”), from -īcus + -ius or (2) Latin -itia (“noun suffix denoting condition”).

parole.significato: Used to form feminine nouns.
parole.testo: From French -ine, feminine of -in; Latin -īna, feminine of -īnus. Doublet of -ina.

parole.significato: a system of rules, laws, or knowledge about a body of a particular field; distribution, arrangement, management
parole.testo: Borrowed from French -nomie, and a learned borrowing from Latin -nomia, from Ancient Greek νόμος (nómos, “law, custom”).

parole.significato: Creates an agent noun, often from a verb, indicating a person or object (often machines or parts of them) that do the v…
parole.testo: From Middle English -our, from Old French -eor, from Latin -ātor; reinforced by Old French -or and its source, Latin -tor, -tōrem.

parole.significato: Diminutive suffix.
parole.testo: Derived from Latin -ula and French -ule.

parole.significato: To shorten by omitting parts or details.
parole.testo: From Middle English abbreviaten, from abbreviat(e) (“abbreviated”, used as the participle of abbreviaten) + -en (verb-forming suffix), borrowed from Latin abbreviātus, perfect passive participle of abbreviō (“to shorten”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), formed from ab- + breviō (“to shorten”), fro

parole.significato: A low or downcast condition; meanness of spirit; abasement; degradation.
parole.testo: From Middle English abjeccioun, from either Middle French abjection or Late Latin abiectiōn-, from Latin abiectus (“cast down”). * See abject.

parole.significato: Not conforming to rule or system; deviating from the usual or normal type.
parole.testo: From ab- + normal. First attested in 1835, replacing the earlier anormal and even earlier abnormous, from Latin abnormis (“departing from normal”), from either ab- (“away from”) + norma (“rule, norm”), or Ancient Greek ἀνώμαλος (anṓmalos).

parole.significato: To flee, often secretly; to steal away.
parole.testo: Either borrowed from Middle French abscondre or directly from Latin abscondō (“hide”); formed from abs, ab (“away”) + condō (“put together, store”), from con- (“together”) + *dʰeh₁- (“to put, place, set”). * Cognate with sconce (“a type of light fixture”).

parole.significato: To make clean by wiping; to wipe away.
parole.testo: From French and Middle French absterger or from Medieval Latin abstergēre (“wipe off or away”); formed from Latin abs- + tergeō (“to wipe off”).

parole.significato: Act of wiping clean; a cleansing; a purging.
parole.testo: From Middle English abstersioun, from either Old French or Medieval Latin abstertion, from Latin abstersus, past participle of abstergēo (“to wipe off or away”).

parole.significato: The act of abstracting, separating, withdrawing, or taking away; withdrawal; the state of being taken away.
parole.testo: From Middle English abstraccyone; either from Middle French abstraction or from Medieval Latin abstrāctiō (“separation”), from Latin abstrahō (“draw away”). Equivalent to abstract + -ion.

parole.significato: That which is absurd; an absurd action; a logical contradiction.
parole.testo: First attested around 1472. From Middle English absurdite, then from either Middle French absurdité, or from Late Latin absurditas (“dissonance, incongruity”), from Latin absurdus + -itas (“quality, state, degree”). Equivalent to absurd + -ity.

parole.significato: Improper treatment or usage; application to a wrong or bad purpose; an unjust, corrupt or wrongful practice or custom.
parole.testo: From Middle English abusen, then from either Old French abus (“improper use”), or from Latin abūsus (“misused, using up”), perfect active participle of abūtor (“make improper use of, consume, abuse”), from ab (“away”) + ūtor (“to use”). Equivalent to ab- + use.

parole.significato: A way or means of approaching or entering; an entrance; a passage.
parole.testo: From Middle English accesse, acces, borrowed from Middle French acces (“attack, onslaught”) or from its source Latin accessus, perfect passive participle of accēdō (“approach; accede”), from ad (“to, toward, at”) + cēdō (“move, yield”). Doublet of accessus. First attested in the early 14th century.

parole.significato: A provisional name for a plant which has not had its flowers botanically examined, and therefore has not been referred…
parole.testo: Either from Ancient Greek ἄδηλος (ádēlos, “not manifest”) + ἀστήρ (astḗr, “star”) or from Ancient Greek ἄδηλος (ádēlos, “not manifest”) + Latin -aster.

parole.significato: An assistant.
parole.testo: Probably in part from Spanish ayudante and in part from Portuguese ajudante (“assistant, helper, aide”), nominal uses of present participial adjectives from respectively ayudar and ajudar, from Latin adiūtō (“to help, assist”), with remodeling after its present participle adiūtāns (acc. adiūtantem).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the Adriatic Sea.
parole.testo: From Latin Adriāticum, variant of Hadriātricum, from Hadria, ultimately from either: * an Etruscan settlement at the northern shore of the Adriatic Sea. * Illyrian *adur, from Proto-Indo-European *wódr̥ (“water”), related to Proto-Albanian *udrijā, or from Venetic [script needed] (adur, “water”), in

parole.significato: Used to form the names of musical instruments that use a vibrating reed.
parole.testo: From Latin Aeolian “related to Aeolus” or “of or from the Aeolian Islands”, ultimately from Ancient Greek Αἴολος (Aíolos), a god of the winds.

parole.significato: An attempt to assume or exhibit what is not natural or real; false display; artificial show.
parole.testo: From Middle French affectation and its etymon Latin affectātiōnem, from affectō (“to feign”). By surface analysis, affect + -ation.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Probably; perhaps; or from; either; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: Any of various large seabirds of the family Diomedeidae ranging widely in the Southern Ocean and the North Pacific and…
parole.testo: Uncertain. parole.significato: To state under oath, to plead.
parole.testo: From Middle English aleggen, perhaps from Old French alleguer, or from Anglo-Norman aleger, the form perhaps from Old French esligier (“to acquit”), from Medieval Latin *exlītigāre (“to clear at law”), from Latin ex (“out”) + lītigō (“sue at law”), but the meaning from Old French alleguer, from Lati

parole.significato: A woman employed to look after children; (formerly) a wet nurse.
parole.testo: From Portuguese ama (“female nurse”), from Medieval Latin amma (“wet nurse, amma”), perhaps an alteration of Latin mamma, of imitative origin, or from Ancient Greek.

parole.significato: An imaginary flower that does not wither.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French amarante, or directly from its etymon Latin amarantus (the word ending influenced by plant names derived from Ancient Greek ἄνθος (ánthos, “a bloom, blossom, flower”)), from Ancient Greek ἀμάραντος (amárantos, “eternal, undying, unfading, unwilting; amaranth; everlasting flower”

parole.significato: A battle with Amazons (“mythical female warriors thought to inhabit the Black Sea region”); also (art), an artistic rep…
parole.testo: Borrowed from French Amazonomachie or German Amazonomachie, or a direct learned borrowing from their etymon Ancient Greek Ἀμαζονομᾰχῐ́ᾱ (Amazonomăkhĭ́ā), from Ἀμαζών (Amazṓn, “mythical female warrior from the Black Sea region”) (for further etymology see that entry) + μᾰ́χη (mắkhē, “battle, combat”)

parole.significato: Softening; mollification; appeasing; mitigation.
parole.testo: From French amollissement, from amolliss- [extended stem of amollir (“to soften”, verb), from a- {from Latin ad (“to”)} + mollir, from French mou, or from Latin mollīre (“to make soft, soften”)] + -ment (suffix forming nouns from verbs) [from Late Latin -mentum, from Latin -menta]; equivalent to Eng

parole.significato: A word or phrase that is created by rearranging the letters of another word or phrase.
parole.testo: Late 16th century, either from Middle French anagramme or Latin anagramma, formed on Ancient Greek ἀνά (aná, “up, back”) + γράμμα (grámma, “letter”). Analyzable as ana- (“up, back”) + -gram (“letter”).

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to anatomy and dissection, or to individual structures of the anatomy.
parole.testo: From French anatomique or its etymon Latin anatomicus, from Ancient Greek ἀνατομικός (anatomikós, “skilled in anatomy”). By surface analysis, anatomy + -ic.

parole.significato: To connect an object, especially a ship or a boat, to a fixed point.
parole.testo: From Middle English anchoren, ankeren, either from the noun or perhaps (via Old French ancrer) from a Medieval Latin verb ancorare, from the same Latin word ancora.

parole.significato: An anchorite or anchoress.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English ankre, ancre, from Old English ancer, ancra, from Latin anachōrēta, anachōrīta, either with significant shortening of the word within Old English or via an unattested Old Irish form.

parole.significato: The meaning of this term is uncertain. Possibilities include
parole.testo: Uncertain. Possibly from ane (a variant of one) + -able, or an alteration of onlepy. Alternatively, from the Latin inhabilis, used to refer to an unmarried man, or Old French anable. Whether the word was used as an adjective or a noun is uncertain.

parole.significato: Any plant of the genus Anemone, of the Ranunculaceae (or buttercup) family, such as the windflower.
parole.testo: From Latin anemōnē, from Ancient Greek ἀνεμώνη (anemṓnē), from ἄνεμος (ánemos, “wind”) + matronymic suffix -ώνη (-ṓnē, “daughter of”). Or from Phoenician *𐤍𐤏𐤌𐤍 (*nʿmn), akin to Arabic شَقَائِق اَلنُّعْمَان (šaqāʔiq an-nuʕmān, “anemones”) and Hebrew (Isaiah Scroll) נִטְעֵי נַעֲמָנִים (nit'ei na'amani

parole.significato: A member of a Germanic tribe first mentioned by Tacitus, one of several which invaded Britain and merged to become the…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin Anglus, in turn borrowed from a Germanic source (compare Old English Ængle/Engle (“Angle”)). parole.significato: The third-to-last syllable of a word.
parole.testo: Either formed from ante- + penult and modelled on Latin or a shortening of Latin antepaenultima/antepēnultima (syllaba).

parole.significato: The external orifice of the rectum in most mammals, teleost fish, and many invertebrates, through which feces and flatu…
parole.testo: Either from Middle French anus or Latin ānus (“ring, anus”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eh₂no- (“ring”). First attested in 1658. See also anal, annular, annelid.

parole.significato: Connected with the apogee; apogeic.
parole.testo: From Latin apogēus, from Ancient Greek ἀπόγειος (apógeios), ἀπόγαιος (apógaios), or from apogee + -al.

parole.significato: Synonym of appraise (“to determine the value or worth of (something)”).
parole.testo: From Middle English aprisen, apprisen (“to determine or estimate the value of (something), to appraise, evaluate; to regard (something) as important, valuable, or worthy, to esteem, prize; to praise or worship (God)”), and then either: * from Old French apriser, aprisier (“to appraise, evaluate”), f

parole.significato: Suitable; appropriate; fit or fitted; suited.
parole.testo: From Old French apte, from Latin aptus (“suitable, fitting”). Either from obsolete apere (“to fasten, to join, to fit”), akin to apisci (“to reach, attain”) (compare with Greek ἅπτειν (áptein, “to fasten”) and Sanskrit आप्त (āpta, “fit”), from आप् (āp, “to reach, attain”)) or from *h₂ep- (“to join,

parole.significato: Someone with an Aquarius star sign
