parole.significato: Of or relating to water.
parole.testo: Formed from Latin aqua + -ous (or from Medieval Latin aqueus), partly the analogy of Middle French aqueux (itself actually from Latin aquosus). Or based on the analogy of Latin terreus from terra.

parole.significato: Very dry.
parole.testo: From French aride or directly from Latin āridus (“dry, arid, parched”), compare its synonymous contracted form ardus. Originally from the verb āreo (“to be dry, to be parched”), akin to ārdeō (“to be on fire, to burn”).

parole.significato: Relating to Armorica; Armorican.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English Armorik, from Latin Armoricus directly or from Middle French Armorique.

parole.significato: To officially charge someone in a court of law.
parole.testo: From Middle English areynen (“to interrogate, arraign, reprimand”), from Anglo-Norman areiner, arener, from Old French araisnier, areisnier, aresnier (“to speak to, address; accuse (in a law court)”) (whence modern French arraisonner (“to verify cargo, to arraign”)), from Vulgar Latin *arratiōnāre,

parole.significato: artery
parole.testo: Either from the Latin artēria or directly from its etymon, the Ancient Greek ἀρτηρία (artēría, “trachea”, “artery”).

parole.significato: A particular model or individual specimen of the Atlas missile and launch vehicle line.
parole.testo: From Latin Ā̆tlās, from Ancient Greek Ἄτλας (Átlas), either from ἁ- (ha-, copulative prefix) + Proto-Indo-European *telh₂- (“bear, undergo, endure”) or of Pre-Greek origin.

parole.significato: A divination based on the appearance and behaviour of animals.
parole.testo: From augur + -y, or from Middle English augurie, from Old French augurie, from Latin augurium.

parole.significato: The sister or sister-in-law of one’s parent.
parole.testo: From Middle English aunte, from Anglo-Norman aunte, from Old French ante, from Latin amita (“father's sister”). Displaced native Middle English modrie (“aunt”) (from Old English mōdriġe (“maternal aunt”); compare Old English faþu, faþe (“paternal aunt”)). Notes on pronunciation and spelling The digr

parole.significato: A beast of burden; chiefly a workhorse, but also a working ox or other animal.
parole.testo: From Middle English aver, avere (“workhorse; any beast of burden (?); things which are owned, possessions, property, wealth; state of being rich, wealth; ownership, possession”) [and other forms], and then either: * from Old French aver, aveir, avoir (“possession, property; (collectively) beasts of

parole.significato: Of, from or relating to the Balearic Islands, Spain.
parole.testo: From Latin Balearis, from Ancient Greek Βαλλιαρεῖς (Balliareîs), from either βάλλω (bállō) or Phoenician (see Baal).

parole.significato: From or characteristic of the Baroque period.
parole.testo: Via French (which originally meant a pearl of irregular shape) from Portuguese barroco (“irregular pearl”); related to Spanish barrueco and Italian barocco and Sicilian baroccu, of uncertain ultimate origin, but possibly from Latin verruca (“wart”), or possibly from the technical construction of sch

parole.significato: To join in battle; to contend in fight
parole.testo: From Middle English batel, batell, batelle, batayle, bataylle, borrowed from Old French bataille, from Late Latin battālia, variant of battuālia (“fighting and fencing exercises”) from Latin battuō (“to strike, hit, beat, fight”), of uncertain origin. Possibly from a Gaulish or Proto-Germanic root f

parole.significato: An aromatic gum-like balsam extracted from one of several species of tree in the genus Commiphora.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin bdellium, from Ancient Greek βδέλλιον (bdéllion), itself perhaps from Hebrew בְּדֹלַח (bdólakh), cognate with Akkadian 𒁉𒁺𒌨𒄷 (bidurḫu) or from Sanskrit भिदुर (bhidura, “something brittle, fragile, easily split or broken”).

parole.significato: A flat-bottomed, straight-sided, glass vessel, with a lip and often a small spout, used as a laboratory container.
parole.testo: From Middle English bekyr, biker, from Old Norse bikarr (“cup”), from Old Saxon bikeri (“cup”), from Proto-West Germanic *bikārī, from Late Latin bīcārium (“wine vat, jug”), of disputed origin. Possibly from Ancient Greek βῖκος (bîkos, “earthenware jug, wine jar”), or from Latin bacarium (“wine vat,

parole.significato: To dress (somebody) in a bib.
parole.testo: Originally verb sense “drink heartily”, from Middle English bibben, either from Latin bibō (“to drink”) or of imitative origin. Noun sense (clothing) presumably either because worn while drinking, or because the clothing itself “drinks up” spills.

parole.significato: A library.
parole.testo: An Anglicisation either of bibliotheca (from the Old English biblioþece) or of its etymon, the Latin bibliothēca (“library”, “collection of books”); compare French bibliothèque.

parole.significato: A cold, often dry, northeasterly wind which blows, sometimes in violent gusts, down from mountains on the eastern shore…
parole.testo: Either from Serbo-Croatian bura (“downslope wind, northeast or ENE wind”), or from a dialectal form of Italian borea (“north wind”) from Latin Boreās.

parole.significato: Borago officinalis, a Mediterranean plant with rough, cucumber-flavored leaves and stems, used in salads and cooked.
parole.testo: From Middle English borage, borrowed from Old French borage (compare French bourrache), from Medieval Latin borrago, either from Latin borra (“short wool, rough hair”) or Arabic أَبُو العَرَق (ʔabū l-ʕaraq, literally “father of sweat”).

parole.significato: A bush.
parole.testo: From Middle English bosk, busk, variants of bush (“grove, wood; thicket, underbrush; bush; branch of a shrub or tree”), from Old English *busc (attested only in place names), likely from Anglo-Latin bosca (“firewood”), from Late Latin busca, buscus, boscus (“wood; woodland”), from Frankish and Proto

parole.significato: The quality of being brief in duration.
parole.testo: First attested in English in 1509; either: * Borrowed directly from Latin brevitās; or * from Anglo-Norman brevité, from Old French brieveté, from Latin brevitātem, accusative of brevitās, from brevis (“short”). By surface analysis, brief + -ity.

parole.significato: A stopper, alternative to a cork, often made of rubber, used to prevent fluid passing through the neck of a bottle, vat…
parole.testo: From Medieval Dutch bonge, bonne or bonghe (“stopper”), or perhaps from French bonde, which may itself be either of Germanic origin or from Proto-Celtic *bunda—either way probably from puncta (“hole”), the feminine singular form of Latin punctus, perfect passive participle of pungō (“pierce into, pr

parole.significato: A float moored in water to mark a location, warn of danger, indicate a navigational channel or for other purposes
parole.testo: From Middle English boy, boye, from Middle Dutch boeye (“float, buoy”), from Old French boue (“piece of wood or cork that floats above an anchor to indicate where it is anchored”) (modern French bouée), ultimately from Frankish *baukn (“beacon”), from Proto-Germanic *baukną. Doublet of beacon. Alter

parole.significato: An inhabitant of a borough with full rights; a citizen.
parole.testo: From Middle English burgeis, from Anglo-Norman burgeis (“town-dweller”), of Proto-Germanic origin; either from Late Latin burgensis (from Latin burgus), or from Frankish *burg, both from Proto-Germanic *burgz (“stronghold, city”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerǵʰ-. See also borough, bourgeois, burgi

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or characteristic of butter

parole.significato: A type of spicy, spreadable salami from Calabria.

parole.significato: Synonym of necromancer.
parole.testo: Either an alteration of nigromant, or from French nécromant, Latin necromantis, or Ancient Greek νεκρόμᾰντῐς (nekrómăntĭs).

parole.significato: Synonym of ninetysomething: a person between 90 and 99 years old.

parole.significato: Of or related to the number ninety.

parole.significato: A novice.

parole.significato: Of or relating to a numen (divinity); indicating the presence of a divinity.

parole.significato: A framework on a post, with holes for the hands and head, used as a means of punishment and humiliation.

parole.significato: A tactic, strategy, or scheme.
parole.testo: Possibly from a shortened form of employ or deploy. Or from earlier ploye, from Middle English, borrowed from Middle French ployer (compare modern plier), from Latin plicāre.

parole.significato: Someone who prepares or deals in ornamental plumes or feathers.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French plumassier, from Middle French plumas, from plume, or from Latin plūmācium.

parole.significato: The ritually established and sacred formal boundary of the territory of a Roman city; the territory thus bound.

parole.significato: Populousness.

parole.testo: Either a back-formation from prolongation, or from Old French prolonguer or porloignier, from Latin prōlongō, from prō + longō. Doublet of purloin.

parole.significato: A dry-cured ham from Italy, thinly sliced.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Italian prosciutto (meaning 'ham', in general), from asciutto, with a change of prefix, or from a Vulgar Latin *perexsūctus, from per + Latin exsūctus.

parole.significato: Of a purple colour.

parole.significato: Synonym of fortysomething: a person between 40 and 49 years old.

parole.significato: Synonym of quadragenarian: Of or related to fortysomethings.

parole.significato: Of or related to the number 40, particularly

parole.significato: Synonym of pentecoster: an officer who commands 50 men.

parole.significato: Synonym of pentecoster: an officer who commands 50 men.

parole.significato: In the International System of Units and other metric systems of units, multiplying the unit to which it is attached by…
